Distributed Systems

Caching, messaging, distributed systems and transactions, reliability, concurrency, storage, search, real-time, jobs, LLM backends, RAG and data engineering.

Part 26 — Caching and Redis

26.1 Why caching exists

Most developers meet caching as "put Redis in front of the database and things get faster". That sentence is true and dangerous in equal measure. It is true because a Redis read costs about 0.3 ms and a PostgreSQL query costs 2 to 20 ms. It is dangerous because the moment you keep a second copy of any data, you own a consistency problem, and nobody warned you that the consistency problem is the whole job.

This part teaches caching the way a principal engineer meets it: as a set of copies of data, each with a rule for when it is allowed to be wrong, and a plan for what happens when the copy disappears. Redis is the tool we use for most of it, so the second half of this part goes deep on Redis itself: how it executes commands, how it loses data, how it clusters, and what every data structure is actually for in a backend.

26.1.1 The latency and load argument

Concept

A cache is a copy of data kept somewhere cheaper to read than the original. "Cheaper" means lower latency, lower CPU cost, or both. The original is called the source of truth. The cache is never the source of truth; it is a convenience that is allowed to be stale or absent.

Caching exists because two things are expensive: computing an answer, and moving an answer across a network. A product page in an e-commerce app might need six queries, two joins and a price calculation. Doing that once and reusing the result 10,000 times is the entire idea.

Why does it exist?

Look at the numbers for one GET /products/:id request on a typical NestJS plus PostgreSQL stack:

Step Cost Notes
Node.js parses request, runs guards and pipes 0.1 to 0.3 ms CPU only
PostgreSQL point query by primary key, warm buffers 1 to 3 ms Network round trip plus planner plus executor
PostgreSQL query with two joins and aggregation 5 to 20 ms Planner cost, possibly a sort, more pages read
PostgreSQL query with cold buffers 20 to 200 ms Disk reads
Redis GET of a serialized product, same region 0.2 to 0.5 ms Mostly network round trip
Node.js in-process Map.get 0.001 ms No network at all

Latency is only half the story. The other half is load. PostgreSQL executes a query with one backend process per connection, and each query burns CPU for parsing, planning and executing. A 4-vCPU PostgreSQL instance can serve perhaps 5,000 to 15,000 simple indexed reads per second before CPU saturates. A single Redis instance serves 100,000 or more GETs per second on one core because it does almost no work per command: hash the key, find the value, write bytes to the socket.

Without a cache, a product catalog with 3,000 reads per second at 4 ms each keeps the database busy for 12 CPU-seconds every second. That is three cores dedicated to answering the same 200 popular products over and over. With a 95 percent hit ratio in Redis, the database sees 150 reads per second and the other 2,850 get an answer in under a millisecond.

Mental model

Imagine a busy restaurant kitchen. The pantry (PostgreSQL) holds every ingredient, organized and safe, but walking there takes a minute. The chef's station (Redis) has small bowls of the ingredients used most, prepared and within arm's reach. The chef's own hands (in-process memory) hold the knife and the salt. Nobody stores the restaurant's inventory at the chef's station; the pantry is where truth lives. But the station is why the restaurant can serve 200 covers an hour. When a bowl runs empty (a cache miss), someone walks to the pantry, refills it, and service continues.

How it works

At the highest level every cache does four things:

  1. Lookup. On a read, compute a key from the request (for example products:v3:8812) and ask the cache.
  2. Hit or miss. If the value is there and not expired, return it. Otherwise go to the source of truth.
  3. Fill. After a miss, store the fresh value under the key, usually with a time-to-live (TTL).
  4. Invalidate. When the source changes, remove or overwrite the cached copy, or let the TTL expire it.

Step 4 is where the engineering lives. Steps 1 to 3 take ten lines of code; step 4 is a career.

Practical example

A food-delivery app shows a restaurant menu. The menu changes a few times per day (items go out of stock, prices change at lunch). It is read 50,000 times per day per popular restaurant. The menu query joins restaurants, menu_sections, menu_items, item_options and inventory, and costs 12 ms. Caching the rendered menu JSON for 60 seconds cuts database load by roughly 99 percent and improves p50 latency from 18 ms to 3 ms. The business accepts that an item might show as available for up to 60 seconds after it sells out, because the order placement step re-checks stock in PostgreSQL anyway.

That last sentence is the pattern to remember: cache the read, verify at the write.

Production scenario

A marketplace with 2 million products and 400 requests per second on product detail pages. Without a cache, PostgreSQL runs at 70 percent CPU and p99 latency is 180 ms during flash sales. After adding cache-aside with a 5 minute TTL and event-driven invalidation on price change, PostgreSQL drops to 12 percent CPU, Redis serves 380 of the 400 requests per second, and p99 falls to 25 ms. Redis memory: 2 million products at roughly 3 KB each is 6 GB if everything were cached, but only 300,000 products are ever requested in a 5 minute window, so actual memory sits at about 1 GB.

26.1.2 Cache is already everywhere: the layers

Concept

Before you add Redis, understand that a request already passes through half a dozen caches. Adding one more layer is a choice about where staleness is acceptable, not a switch from "no cache" to "cache".

Browser cache (Cache-Control, ETag)          minutes to days, per user
        |
        v
CDN edge cache (CloudFront, Cloudflare)      seconds to hours, shared, geographic
        |
        v
API gateway / reverse proxy cache (nginx)    seconds, shared per region
        |
        v
NestJS in-process memory (Map, LRU)          milliseconds to seconds, per pod
        |
        v
Redis (shared, network)                      seconds to hours, shared across pods
        |
        v
PostgreSQL shared_buffers                    hot pages in RAM, managed by PG
        |
        v
OS page cache                                file blocks in RAM, managed by Linux
        |
        v
Disk (NVMe / EBS)                            the only thing that is truly durable

How it works

Each layer catches a share of traffic so the layer below sees less:

  • Browser cache removes repeat requests entirely. Cache-Control: max-age=300 on a public product image means the browser does not even ask.
  • CDN serves static assets and, if you let it, whole API responses (Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60). It is the cheapest cache per request you will ever have and the one most teams forget.
  • Gateway cache is rare for authenticated APIs but valuable for public read endpoints.
  • In-process memory is the fastest layer and the least consistent, because each pod has its own copy. We return to it in section 26.6 on multi-level caching.
  • Redis is the shared application cache. Every pod sees the same value, which is why it is the default for anything invalidated on write.
  • PostgreSQL shared_buffers is a cache you already run. A table that fits in shared_buffers (say 8 GB) serves point reads from RAM without disk I/O. This is why "the database is slow" often means "the working set no longer fits in memory", and why a Redis layer sometimes helps less than adding RAM to the database.
  • OS page cache sits under PostgreSQL. Data files read once stay in Linux memory until evicted.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before adding Redis, a senior asks: is the expensive thing the query, or the request? If PostgreSQL answers in 1 ms from shared_buffers and the request costs 30 ms because of serialization and three downstream HTTP calls, Redis in front of the query saves nothing. If the endpoint is public and identical for every user, the CDN saves more than Redis and costs less to operate. Redis is the right answer when the data is shared across users, changes on a timescale of seconds to hours, and the read is expensive relative to the request.

26.2 Cache strategies

A cache strategy answers two questions: who fills the cache, and who writes to the database. The five classic patterns differ only in those answers, but the operational consequences are very different.

26.2.1 Cache-aside (lazy loading)

Concept

In cache-aside, the application code owns both the cache and the database. On a read it checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and writes the result into the cache. On a write it updates the database and then deletes (or updates) the cache entry. The cache never talks to the database on its own.

This is the pattern behind 90 percent of Redis usage in NestJS applications, and it is the one you should default to.

Why does it exist?

Cache-aside exists because it is simple, it requires nothing from Redis except GET, SET and DEL, and it only caches data that is actually requested. A product nobody views never enters the cache. A Redis restart is survivable: the cache refills lazily as requests arrive.

Mental model

Imagine a librarian with a small desk shelf. When you ask for a book, she checks the shelf first. If it is not there, she walks to the stacks, brings it back, hands it to you, and leaves a copy on the shelf for the next person. If a book is corrected in the stacks, she throws the shelf copy away so the next reader triggers a fresh fetch.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as ProductsService
    participant R as Redis
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    C->>S: GET /products/8812
    S->>R: GET products:v3:8812
    alt cache hit
        R-->>S: serialized product
        S-->>C: 200 product (0.5 ms)
    else cache miss
        R-->>S: nil
        S->>P: SELECT ... WHERE id = 8812
        P-->>S: row (3 ms)
        S->>R: SET products:v3:8812 value PX 300000
        S-->>C: 200 product (5 ms)
    end
  1. Build the key from the identity of the thing (products:v3:8812). The v3 is a schema version; we cover it in 26.4.
  2. GET the key. Redis returns the value or nil.
  3. On hit, deserialize and return.
  4. On miss, query PostgreSQL, serialize, SET with a TTL, return.
  5. On write, update PostgreSQL inside a transaction, then DEL the key after commit.

NestJS example

A minimal but production-shaped implementation using ioredis directly. The important lines are the TTL with jitter, the fail-open behaviour when Redis is down, and the delete after commit.

// products/products.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { Product } from './product.entity';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';
import { Inject } from '@nestjs/common';

const KEY_VERSION = 'v3';
const BASE_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000;

@Injectable()
export class ProductsService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ProductsService.name);

  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Product) private readonly repo: Repository<Product>,
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
  ) {}

  private key(id: string): string {
    return `products:${KEY_VERSION}:${id}`;
  }

  async findOne(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    const key = this.key(id);
    const cached = await this.safeGet(key);
    if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached) as Product;

    const product = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id } });
    if (!product) throw new NotFoundException(`Product ${id} not found`);

    // Jitter spreads expiry so 10,000 keys do not expire in the same second.
    const ttl = BASE_TTL_MS + Math.floor(Math.random() * 30_000);
    await this.safeSet(key, JSON.stringify(product), ttl);
    return product;
  }

  async updatePrice(id: string, priceCents: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo.manager.transaction(async (manager) => {
      await manager.update(Product, { id }, { priceCents });
    });
    // Delete AFTER commit. Deleting before commit lets a concurrent reader
    // re-fill the cache with the old row.
    await this.safeDel(this.key(id));
  }

  // Fail open: a cache outage must degrade to "slower", never to "down".
  private async safeGet(key: string): Promise<string | null> {
    try {
      return await this.redis.get(key);
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn(`redis GET failed for ${key}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
      return null;
    }
  }

  private async safeSet(key: string, value: string, ttlMs: number): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.redis.set(key, value, 'PX', ttlMs);
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn(`redis SET failed for ${key}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    }
  }

  private async safeDel(key: string): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.redis.del(key);
    } catch (err) {
      // This is the dangerous one: a failed delete leaves stale data until TTL.
      this.logger.error(`redis DEL failed for ${key}; stale until TTL`, (err as Error).stack);
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The database side of cache-aside is ordinary, but one detail matters: the cache delete must happen after COMMIT, and the query you cache should be the expensive one. Here is the product read with its plan so you can see what you are saving.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price_cents, p.currency,
       c.name AS category_name,
       COALESCE(i.quantity_on_hand - i.quantity_reserved, 0) AS available,
       (SELECT avg(rating) FROM reviews r WHERE r.product_id = p.id) AS avg_rating
  FROM products p
  JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
  LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.product_id = p.id
 WHERE p.id = '8812';
Nested Loop Left Join  (cost=0.99..48.71 rows=1 width=120) (actual time=0.310..2.842 rows=1 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=41
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.57..16.62 rows=1 width=88) (actual time=0.052..0.061 rows=1 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using products_pkey on products p  (actual time=0.031..0.033 rows=1 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using categories_pkey on categories c  (actual time=0.014..0.015 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using inventory_product_id_key on inventory i  (actual time=0.019..0.020 rows=1 loops=1)
  SubPlan 1
    ->  Aggregate  (actual time=2.690..2.691 rows=1 loops=1)
          ->  Index Scan using reviews_product_id_idx on reviews r  (actual rows=1843 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.412 ms
Execution Time: 2.901 ms

Nearly all of the 2.9 ms is the review average over 1,843 rows. Caching this response for 5 minutes removes that work from 99 percent of reads. A senior would also ask whether avg_rating should be a denormalized column updated by a trigger or job, which would remove the cost without a cache. Caching and denormalization are competitors; pick the one with the simpler invalidation story.

TypeORM example

TypeORM has a built-in query result cache that can use Redis. It is a form of cache-aside keyed by the query text and parameters. It is convenient and also easy to misuse, because invalidation is by TTL or by explicit cache id only.

// data-source.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const dataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  cache: {
    type: 'ioredis',
    options: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST, port: 6379 },
    duration: 30_000, // default TTL in ms
  },
});

// somewhere in a service
const popular = await this.repo
  .createQueryBuilder('p')
  .where('p.category_id = :categoryId', { categoryId })
  .orderBy('p.sales_rank', 'ASC')
  .limit(20)
  .cache(`popular:${categoryId}`, 60_000) // cache id + TTL
  .getMany();

// on category change
await this.dataSource.queryResultCache?.remove([`popular:${categoryId}`]);

Use this for read-only listings. Do not use it for anything with per-user data, because a forgotten .cache() on a query that includes userId in a where still keys correctly, but one that filters in application code after the query does not.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no built-in query cache. The honest approach is the same service-level cache-aside shown above, wrapping Model.findByPk. Third-party plugins exist, but a ten-line wrapper you understand is better than a plugin that silently keys on the wrong thing.

// products/products.repository.ts (Sequelize flavour)
async findByIdCached(id: string): Promise<ProductAttributes | null> {
  const key = `products:v3:${id}`;
  const hit = await this.redis.get(key);
  if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit);
  const row = await this.productModel.findByPk(id, { raw: true });
  if (row) await this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(row), 'PX', 300_000);
  return row;
}

Production scenario

Cache-aside on a product catalog with 400 RPS: hit ratio 94 to 97 percent after warm-up, Redis p99 0.8 ms, PostgreSQL load reduced by 20x. After a deploy that changes the Product entity shape, the key version bumps from v3 to v4, the new pods miss on every read for about two minutes while the cache refills, and PostgreSQL briefly climbs to 40 percent CPU. That is the cold-cache cost of cache-aside, and it is why warm-up scripts exist for the top 1,000 keys.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 on a Tuesday, the marketing team changes the price of 2,000 products via a bulk import. The import updates PostgreSQL in one transaction and then loops over the products issuing DEL for each key. Halfway through, Redis hits a network blip and 800 deletes fail. The code logs a warning and continues. For the next five minutes (the TTL), 800 products show the old price on the site while checkout charges the new price. Support gets 40 tickets. The fix was to write failed deletes to a retry table and to add a price_version to the cache key so a bulk update invalidates by changing the version instead of deleting each key.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A read that arrives between the database commit and the cache delete gets the old value and re-caches it. The window is tiny but real; see 26.5.1 on invalidation races.
  • Redis down: reads go to the database. Make sure the database can survive 100 percent of the traffic for the outage duration, or add a circuit breaker so the app stops waiting on Redis timeouts.
  • A null result from the database is not cached by the code above, so a missing product hammers the database. Negative caching fixes that; see 26.5.4.
  • Serialization changes (a renamed field) with the same key version means old pods and new pods read each other's format during a rolling deploy.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Cache-aside is the default because it fails safe: the worst case is a slow system, not a wrong one, provided invalidation happens after commit and the TTL bounds the staleness. A senior sets the TTL from the business question "how stale is acceptable" and never from "what number feels right". They also refuse to cache anything whose staleness would produce a wrong financial answer.

Common mistakes

  • Deleting the cache key before the database commit. A concurrent read re-fills with stale data.
  • No TTL at all, so a failed delete means stale forever.
  • Catching Redis errors on GET but letting a Redis error on SET fail the request.
  • Caching entire ORM entities with circular references or Date objects, then being surprised that JSON.parse returns strings instead of dates.

26.2.2 Read-through

Concept

In read-through, the application talks only to the cache. The cache itself knows how to load a value from the database on a miss. The loader is configured once, and callers never write "if miss then query".

How it works

The cache library wraps your loader function. cache.wrap(key, loader, ttl) checks the key, calls loader() on miss, stores the result, and returns it. Structurally the same as cache-aside; organizationally different, because the loading logic lives next to the cache rather than in every service.

NestJS example

@nestjs/cache-manager exposes cache-manager's wrap, which is a read-through helper.

// menus/menus.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CACHE_MANAGER } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';
import { Cache } from 'cache-manager';
import { MenusRepository } from './menus.repository';

@Injectable()
export class MenusService {
  constructor(
    @Inject(CACHE_MANAGER) private readonly cache: Cache,
    private readonly menus: MenusRepository,
  ) {}

  getMenu(restaurantId: string) {
    // wrap(): read-through with the loader colocated with the key.
    // TTL is milliseconds in cache-manager v5+.
    return this.cache.wrap(
      `menus:v1:${restaurantId}`,
      () => this.menus.loadRenderedMenu(restaurantId),
      60_000,
    );
  }
}

The advantage is that every read path goes through one place, so adding single-flight or metrics later is one change. The disadvantage is that wrap hides what happens when Redis is down; check your cache-manager version's behaviour and test it with Redis stopped.

26.2.3 Write-through

Concept

In write-through, every write goes to the cache and the database together, synchronously, before the write returns. The cache is always populated for anything recently written, and reads never see a miss for hot data that was just changed.

Why does it exist?

Write-through exists for data that is read immediately after being written and where a miss right after a write is expensive or visible. A user updates their profile and the next screen renders it; a write-through cache guarantees the next read is a hit with the new value.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as ProfilesService
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    participant R as Redis
    C->>S: PATCH /me displayName
    S->>P: BEGIN, UPDATE users, COMMIT
    P-->>S: ok
    S->>R: SET users:v2:41 newValue PX 3600000
    R-->>S: ok
    S-->>C: 200
    Note over S,R: If SET fails, delete the key so readers fall back to PostgreSQL
    C->>S: GET /me
    S->>R: GET users:v2:41
    R-->>S: newValue (hit)
  1. Write to PostgreSQL inside a transaction.
  2. After commit, SET the cache with the new value and a TTL.
  3. If the SET fails, DEL the key (best effort) so the stale value cannot survive.
  4. Reads use cache-aside as usual.

NestJS example

// users/profile.service.ts
async updateDisplayName(userId: string, displayName: string): Promise<UserProfile> {
  const updated = await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
    await manager.update(User, { id: userId }, { displayName });
    return manager.findOneOrFail(User, { where: { id: userId } });
  });

  const key = `users:v2:${userId}`;
  try {
    await this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(updated), 'PX', 3_600_000);
  } catch (err) {
    this.logger.warn(`write-through SET failed, deleting ${key}`);
    await this.redis.del(key).catch(() => undefined);
  }
  return updated;
}

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two writes to the same key in quick succession can arrive at Redis out of order (request A commits first but its SET lands second). The cache now holds A's value while the database holds B's. Fix: include a version or updated_at in the value and use a Lua script that only sets if the new version is higher, or fall back to delete-on-write instead of set-on-write.
  • Write-through doubles write latency by one Redis round trip. Fine at 0.5 ms; not fine if Redis is cross-region.
  • Everything written is cached, including data nobody reads. Memory grows with write volume, not read volume.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Write-through is a good fit for user-owned data with read-after-write expectations: profile, cart, settings. It is a poor fit for high-volume writes with low read ratio (event logs, audit rows). When in doubt, use delete-on-write (cache-aside) rather than set-on-write, because deleting cannot leave a wrong value behind; it can only cause a miss.

26.2.4 Write-behind (write-back)

Concept

In write-behind, writes go to the cache only, and the cache (or a worker) flushes them to the database later, in batches. The application returns as soon as Redis acknowledges. The database is eventually updated.

Why does it exist?

Write-behind exists for write volumes the database cannot absorb one row at a time: view counters, "last seen" timestamps, like counts, telemetry. A social feed that increments a post's view counter 5,000 times per second cannot issue 5,000 UPDATE posts SET views = views + 1 per second without turning that row into a hot row and the WAL into a firehose. Incrementing in Redis and flushing every 10 seconds turns 50,000 updates into one.

How it works

  1. The write path does HINCRBY post:views 8812 1 (or INCR) in Redis. Sub-millisecond, no database involvement.
  2. A scheduled worker runs every N seconds, reads the accumulated counters, and applies them to PostgreSQL in one batched UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...).
  3. The worker resets or decrements the Redis counters by the amount it flushed, so counts that arrived during the flush are not lost.

NestJS example

// posts/view-counter.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

const HASH = 'post:views:pending';

@Injectable()
export class ViewCounterService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ViewCounterService.name);
  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
    @InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource,
  ) {}

  // Hot path: one Redis op, no PostgreSQL.
  recordView(postId: string): Promise<number> {
    return this.redis.hincrby(HASH, postId, 1);
  }

  // Flush every 10 seconds. Only one instance should run this; use a lock (16.9).
  @Cron('*/10 * * * * *')
  async flush(): Promise<void> {
    const pending = await this.redis.hgetall(HASH);
    const entries = Object.entries(pending).filter(([, n]) => Number(n) > 0);
    if (entries.length === 0) return;

    await this.db.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const values = entries.map(([id, n]) => `('${id}'::uuid, ${Number(n)})`).join(',');
      await manager.query(
        `UPDATE posts p SET view_count = p.view_count + v.n
           FROM (VALUES ${values}) AS v(id, n)
          WHERE p.id = v.id`,
      );
    });

    // Decrement by what we flushed, not reset to 0: views arriving during the
    // UPDATE would otherwise be lost.
    const pipeline = this.redis.pipeline();
    for (const [id, n] of entries) pipeline.hincrby(HASH, id, -Number(n));
    await pipeline.exec();
    this.logger.log(`flushed ${entries.length} view counters`);
  }
}

In real code, build the VALUES list with parameters rather than string interpolation; the inline version above is for readability only.

Failure scenario

Redis restarts without AOF persistence at 03:12. Every pending counter since the last flush (up to 10 seconds of views) is gone. For view counts that is acceptable and the team documents it. For "points earned" in a loyalty program it is not, and the team that used write-behind for loyalty points spent a week reconciling from application logs. Write-behind trades durability for throughput. Say so out loud before using it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The question is always "what is the cost of losing the last N seconds of writes?" If the answer is "nobody notices", write-behind is a great tool. If the answer involves money, refunds or legal records, the write goes to PostgreSQL first and the cache is derived from it.

26.2.5 Refresh-ahead

Concept

Refresh-ahead recomputes a cached value shortly before it expires, in the background, so that readers never experience a miss on hot keys. The key never actually goes cold as long as it is popular.

How it works

  1. Store the value with a TTL and, inside the value or a side key, the time it was computed.
  2. On each read, if the remaining TTL is below a threshold (say the last 20 percent), trigger a background refresh and still return the current value.
  3. The refresh writes a fresh value and resets the TTL.
  4. Keys nobody reads simply expire; only hot keys stay warm.

This is the mechanism behind "stale-while-revalidate" and probabilistic early expiration, both of which we cover with code in 26.5.2 on stampedes, because refresh-ahead is really a stampede prevention technique.

Production scenario

A home page feed computed from 12 queries and taking 300 ms. TTL 60 seconds. With plain cache-aside, once per minute one unlucky user waits 300 ms and, worse, if 50 requests miss in the same 300 ms window, the database runs the 12 queries 50 times. With refresh-ahead triggered at 48 seconds, a single background refresh runs while every user continues to get the cached value. No user ever sees the 300 ms.

26.2.6 Choosing a strategy

Use case Strategy Why
Product catalog, restaurant menus, CMS content Cache-aside with event-driven invalidation and a 5 to 15 minute safety TTL Read heavy, changes are known events, staleness of seconds is acceptable
User sessions Redis as the store, not a cache (no PostgreSQL copy); TTL equals session lifetime Read on every request, written at login, naturally expiring
Inventory counts shown on a product page Cache-aside with a short TTL (5 to 30 seconds); source of truth stays in PostgreSQL and is re-checked at checkout Display can lag; the reservation cannot
Inventory counts used for reservation Do not cache. PostgreSQL row lock or a Redis Lua script that is the source of truth for that flow A stale count means overselling
Personalized feed Refresh-ahead or write-behind fan-out into a per-user ZSET Expensive to compute, tolerant of minutes of staleness, hot for active users
View counters, likes, "last seen" Write-behind with periodic flush Extreme write volume, loss of seconds of data acceptable
User profile, cart, settings Write-through (set after commit) or delete-on-write Read-after-write expectations

26.3 What to cache and what not to cache

Concept

Cache what is expensive to produce, read far more often than written, and tolerant of being slightly wrong. Do not cache anything where a stale read produces a wrong action.

How it works

Good candidates:

  • Immutable data: a completed order's line items, a published article, a rendered invoice PDF URL. Infinite TTL is fine; version the key if the format changes.
  • Slow-changing data: product catalog, category tree, country and currency lists, feature flag definitions, configuration.
  • Expensive derived data: search facets, recommendation lists, aggregated dashboards, "top 10" rankings.
  • Read-heavy per-user data with clear ownership: profile, preferences, cart. Cache per user, key includes the user id.
  • External API responses: exchange rates, geocoding results, third-party product data, with a TTL matching the provider's update frequency.

Bad candidates:

  • Money balances: a wallet balance, available credit, an account ledger total. A stale read here leads to a double spend or a wrongly declined payment. Read from PostgreSQL with the right isolation level; see Part 20 — Database Transactions.
  • Stock counts used for decisions: the display can be cached; the reservation must hit the source of truth.
  • Anything that is the result of an authorization decision for longer than a few seconds: a revoked permission that stays cached for an hour is a security bug.
  • Large blobs that change often: a 2 MB report regenerated every minute burns bandwidth and Redis memory for little gain.
  • Data with unbounded key cardinality: caching search results keyed by the raw query string creates millions of one-hit keys.

Per-user versus shared is the other axis. A shared key (products:v3:8812) is hit by every user, so it has a high hit ratio and a small memory footprint. A per-user key (cart:v1:{userId}) is hit by one user; its value is not the hit ratio but the removal of a query from a request that happens on every page. Never let a per-user value leak into a shared key. The classic bug is an interceptor-level cache keyed only by URL on an endpoint whose response depends on the Authorization header; see 26.13 on CacheInterceptor.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior question is "what is the blast radius of this being wrong for T seconds?" If the answer is "a user sees an old product description", cache it. If the answer is "we ship an item we do not have" or "we double-charge", do not. A product manager understands this framing immediately: "we can make the page faster, and the price of that is up to 60 seconds where an out-of-stock item still shows as available; checkout will still refuse it. Is that acceptable?" Usually yes. Ask.

26.4 Key design and TTL

Concept

A cache key is a contract. It must be unique for the thing it identifies, stable across pods and deploys, cheap to build, and safe to change when the value format changes.

How it works

Namespacing. Use a colon-separated hierarchy: entity:version:identifier, for example orders:v2:7c9e6679. Redis has no folders, but tools like RedisInsight and SCAN with MATCH orders:v2:* treat colons as separators, and the namespace tells you what a key is when you are staring at a memory report at 2 a.m.

Versioned keys. Put a version in the key that changes whenever the serialized shape changes. Deploying a new Product DTO with v3 in the key means new pods read and write v3 keys, old pods keep using v2 keys during the rollout, and nothing ever deserializes the wrong shape. Old keys expire by TTL. This is far safer than a "flush the cache on deploy" step, which causes a stampede.

Hashing long keys. A key like search:v1:{"q":"running shoes","filters":{"size":[42,43],"brand":["nike"]},"page":2} is 90 bytes of JSON that may vary in property order. Canonicalize (sort keys, trim, lowercase where appropriate) and hash: search:v1:${sha1(canonical)}. Redis keys are stored in memory; a million 200-byte keys is 200 MB of pure key overhead.

Cardinality. Before adding a dimension to a key, multiply out how many distinct values exist. products:v3:{id} has 2 million possible keys. products:v3:{id}:{currency} has 2 million times 30. products:v3:{id}:{currency}:{userId} has effectively infinite. Each dimension you add divides your hit ratio and multiplies your memory.

TTL choice. Start from the business tolerance for staleness, then halve it for safety. Common anchors: sessions match the session lifetime; catalog 5 to 15 minutes with event invalidation; external rate data matches provider refresh; computed rankings 1 to 5 minutes; negative results 30 to 60 seconds.

TTL jitter. Never set the same TTL on thousands of keys filled at the same time. Add a random 5 to 20 percent so they expire spread out. This single line prevents the avalanche problem in 26.5.3.

NestJS example

A small key builder that enforces the conventions so nobody builds keys by hand.

// redis/cache-key.ts
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

export class CacheKey {
  static entity(ns: string, version: number, id: string): string {
    return `${ns}:v${version}:${id}`;
  }

  // Deterministic key for structured queries: sort keys, then hash.
  static query(ns: string, version: number, params: Record<string, unknown>): string {
    const canonical = JSON.stringify(params, Object.keys(params).sort());
    const digest = createHash('sha1').update(canonical).digest('hex').slice(0, 20);
    return `${ns}:v${version}:q:${digest}`;
  }

  // TTL with jitter: base plus up to `spread` percent.
  static ttlMs(baseMs: number, spreadPct = 15): number {
    return baseMs + Math.floor(Math.random() * baseMs * (spreadPct / 100));
  }
}

Common mistakes

  • Keys with no namespace (8812), which collide across entities and cannot be scanned by type.
  • Building keys with user input unsanitized, so a productId of * or one containing spaces creates keys that break tooling and SCAN patterns.
  • Changing the value shape without changing the version, then debugging undefined fields for a day.
  • TTL of zero (never expires) on data that is supposed to be a cache. If it never expires it is a store, and it needs backup, capacity planning and a memory budget.

Interview questions

  1. Why delete the cache entry after the database commit rather than before? Expected: a read between the pre-commit delete and the commit re-fills the cache with the old row; deleting after commit closes that path except for a much smaller window. Follow-up: what remains, and how do you close it? (Double delete or versioned keys; see 26.5.1.)
  2. When would you choose write-behind, and what do you give up? Expected: extreme write rates on counters; you give up durability of the unflushed window and accept that the database lags.
  3. Why put a version in the cache key rather than flushing Redis on deploy? Expected: flush causes a cold-cache stampede and breaks old pods during a rolling deploy; versioned keys let both versions coexist and expire naturally.
  4. A product page endpoint is 80 percent serialization and downstream HTTP calls and 20 percent database. Does a Redis query cache help? Expected: barely; cache the rendered response or fix the downstream calls. Shows the candidate measures before caching.
  5. How do you pick a TTL? Expected: from the business staleness tolerance, with jitter; not from a feeling.

Practical exercise

Implement cache-aside for GET /restaurants/:id/menu in a NestJS service using ioredis. Acceptance criteria: (a) the key is namespaced and versioned; (b) TTL is 60 seconds with 15 percent jitter; (c) PATCH /menu-items/:id deletes the menu key after the transaction commits; (d) with Redis stopped, the endpoint still returns 200 within 50 ms of the database latency and logs one warning per failed operation; (e) a Jest test proves that a read between commit and delete does not leave stale data for longer than the TTL.

26.5 The classic cache problems

Every cache problem in this section has the same shape: a copy of data behaves differently from the original under concurrency, time or load. Each sub-section gives the mechanism, how you detect it in production, and the fix in code.

26.5.1 Cache invalidation

Concept

Invalidation is the act of making the cache forget a value because the source of truth changed. It is famously "one of the two hard problems in computer science" because the cache and the database are two systems with no shared transaction, so every invalidation is a small distributed-systems problem.

There are two families. TTL-based invalidation lets values expire on a timer; simple, bounded staleness, no coordination. Event-driven invalidation removes or updates the value when the write happens; fresher, but you now depend on every write path remembering to invalidate, and on the invalidation actually reaching Redis.

Why does it exist?

Without invalidation, a cache is a snapshot that drifts from reality forever. With TTL only, staleness is bounded but users see old prices for up to the TTL. With event-driven only, a single missed event means stale forever. Production systems use both: events for freshness, TTL as the safety net.

Mental model

Imagine a price board outside a petrol station and the real price in the till system. When head office changes the price, someone must walk out and change the board. If they forget, the board is wrong until someone notices. A TTL is a rule that says "re-check the board every hour whether or not anyone told you to". Event-driven is the phone call from head office. You want both.

How it works

The invalidate-on-write sequence has two orderings, and the order matters.

Delete then write. Delete the cache key, then update the database. Between the delete and the commit, a reader misses, reads the old row, and re-caches it. The stale value now lives until TTL.

Write then delete. Update the database and commit, then delete the key. The remaining race is narrower but real: a reader that missed before the commit and is slow to write its SET can land after your delete.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Writer
    participant R1 as Reader
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    participant R as Redis
    R1->>R: GET products:v3:8812
    R-->>R1: nil (miss)
    R1->>P: SELECT price (old = 999)
    P-->>R1: 999
    W->>P: UPDATE price = 899, COMMIT
    W->>R: DEL products:v3:8812
    R-->>W: ok
    R1->>R: SET products:v3:8812 999
    Note over R: Stale 999 now cached until TTL

The race needs a reader that is slower than an entire write transaction, which is rare but happens under GC pauses, slow networks or a reader waiting on a lock. Three mitigations:

  1. Double delete. Delete after commit, then delete again after a short delay (200 to 500 ms) so a late SET from a slow reader gets wiped. Cheap and ugly. Works.
  2. Versioned values. Store { version, data } and only SET if the stored version is not newer, using a Lua script. The slow reader's SET with updated_at = 10:00:00 loses to a value with updated_at = 10:00:01.
  3. Short TTL as the backstop. With a 60 second TTL, the worst case of any race is 60 seconds. Many teams accept this and skip 1 and 2.

Invalidation via Kafka or CDC. In a system with several services writing to the same tables, or where invalidation must fan out to many pods' local caches, the write path publishes a ProductUpdated event (through the outbox pattern; see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency) or a CDC tool such as Debezium reads the PostgreSQL WAL and emits change events. A consumer deletes the Redis keys. This decouples invalidation from every code path that writes, at the cost of a delay of 50 to 500 ms between commit and invalidation, which you must state as the consistency window.

NestJS example

Double delete plus versioned invalidation in one service. The Lua script sets only if the incoming updatedAt is newer than the stored one.

// products/product-cache.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

// KEYS[1] = cache key, ARGV[1] = new updatedAt (epoch ms), ARGV[2] = json, ARGV[3] = ttl ms
const SET_IF_NEWER = `
  local cur = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
  if cur then
    local curVer = tonumber(cjson.decode(cur).updatedAt)
    if curVer and curVer >= tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
  end
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'PX', ARGV[3])
  return 1
`;

@Injectable()
export class ProductCacheService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ProductCacheService.name);
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('setIfNewer', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: SET_IF_NEWER });
  }

  key(id: string): string {
    return `products:v3:${id}`;
  }

  // Called by readers after a miss. Loses to any newer value already cached.
  async fill(id: string, value: { updatedAt: number } & Record<string, unknown>, ttlMs: number) {
    const client = this.redis as Redis & {
      setIfNewer(key: string, ver: number, json: string, ttl: number): Promise<number>;
    };
    return client.setIfNewer(this.key(id), value.updatedAt, JSON.stringify(value), ttlMs);
  }

  // Called by writers after COMMIT. Second delete catches a late SET from a slow reader.
  async invalidate(id: string): Promise<void> {
    const key = this.key(id);
    await this.redis.del(key);
    setTimeout(() => {
      this.redis.del(key).catch((err) => this.logger.warn(`late DEL failed for ${key}: ${err.message}`));
    }, 300);
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The updated_at column that powers versioned invalidation must be set by the database, not by application clocks, so two pods with skewed clocks cannot produce out-of-order versions.

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now();

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := clock_timestamp();
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER products_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON products
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

clock_timestamp() rather than now() because now() is frozen at transaction start; two updates in one long transaction would share a version.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on-call is paged: "prices on the site do not match checkout". A deploy at 01:50 introduced a new bulk price update endpoint that updated PostgreSQL through a raw query and never called invalidate(). Every product touched by the nightly price job shows its old price for the remaining TTL of 15 minutes, and the job touched 60,000 products. The temporary fix is redis-cli --scan --pattern 'products:v3:*' | xargs redis-cli unlink in batches. The permanent fix is a single ProductsWriteService through which every price change must pass, and an integration test that asserts the cache is invalidated for each write endpoint.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Invalidation event published but consumer is down: stale until TTL. Monitor consumer lag on the invalidation topic.
  • Invalidation for a key that depends on several entities (a rendered menu depends on menu_items, inventory and restaurants): every write to any of them must invalidate the composite key. Track dependencies explicitly or use a short TTL.
  • Many keys per entity (products:v3:8812, products:v3:8812:reviews, search:v1:* that included it): use a "tag" set (tag:product:8812 holding the dependent keys) and delete the members, or accept TTL for the derived keys.
  • A transaction that rolls back after DEL was already issued: harmless, only a miss.

26.5.2 Cache stampede (dogpile)

Concept

A stampede happens when a popular key expires or is missing and many concurrent requests all miss at once, all query the database for the same value, and all write it back. One expensive computation becomes hundreds, at the exact moment the database can least afford it.

Why does it exist?

The naive cache-aside code has no coordination between concurrent misses. At 1,000 RPS on a key whose recompute takes 200 ms, the moment it expires, 200 requests are in flight before the first SET lands. Each runs the full query. This is the mechanism behind "the site went down when the cache expired".

Mental model

Imagine a coffee shop where the display case is empty. Twenty customers each walk into the kitchen and each bakes their own croissant, at the same time, in the same oven. What you want is one baker while the other nineteen wait for the tray, or better, a baker who starts a new tray before the case is empty.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as RequestA
    participant B as RequestB
    participant R as Redis
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    A->>R: GET feed:v1:home
    R-->>A: nil
    B->>R: GET feed:v1:home
    R-->>B: nil
    A->>R: SET lock:feed:v1:home token NX PX 5000
    R-->>A: OK (A owns the lock)
    B->>R: SET lock:feed:v1:home token NX PX 5000
    R-->>B: nil (B waits)
    A->>P: 12 queries (300 ms)
    P-->>A: rows
    A->>R: SET feed:v1:home value PX 60000
    A->>R: release lock via Lua compare-and-delete
    B->>R: GET feed:v1:home (retry after 50 ms)
    R-->>B: value (hit)

Four fixes, from simplest to most refined:

  1. Distributed lock with SET NX PX. The first miss acquires a short lock; others wait and re-read. One database query per expiry across all pods.
  2. In-process single-flight. A Map<string, Promise<T>> per pod. Concurrent callers for the same key inside one pod share one promise. Zero Redis cost; still one query per pod.
  3. Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch). Each reader recomputes early with a probability that rises as expiry approaches. Statistically one reader refreshes before the key dies, so it never actually expires under load.
  4. Stale-while-revalidate. Store the value with a logical expiry earlier than the physical TTL. After logical expiry, return the stale value immediately and trigger one background refresh.

NestJS example

Single-flight plus lock plus stale-while-revalidate in one reusable helper. Callers pass a loader; the helper handles everything.

// redis/cached-loader.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { REDIS } from './redis.module';

interface Envelope<T> { data: T; staleAt: number; }

const RELEASE = `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0`;

@Injectable()
export class CachedLoader {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(CachedLoader.name);
  private readonly inflight = new Map<string, Promise<unknown>>(); // per-pod single-flight

  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('releaseLock', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: RELEASE });
  }

  async get<T>(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>, opts: { freshMs: number; ttlMs: number }): Promise<T> {
    const raw = await this.redis.get(key);
    if (raw) {
      const env = JSON.parse(raw) as Envelope<T>;
      if (Date.now() < env.staleAt) return env.data;            // fresh
      void this.refresh(key, loader, opts);                      // stale: serve now, refresh once
      return env.data;
    }
    return this.refresh(key, loader, opts);                       // miss: compute with coordination
  }

  private refresh<T>(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>, opts: { freshMs: number; ttlMs: number }): Promise<T> {
    const existing = this.inflight.get(key) as Promise<T> | undefined;
    if (existing) return existing;                                // single-flight inside this pod

    const p = this.withLock(key, loader, opts).finally(() => this.inflight.delete(key));
    this.inflight.set(key, p);
    return p;
  }

  private async withLock<T>(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>, opts: { freshMs: number; ttlMs: number }): Promise<T> {
    const lockKey = `lock:${key}`;
    const token = randomUUID();
    const got = await this.redis.set(lockKey, token, 'PX', 5000, 'NX');
    if (got !== 'OK') {
      // Another pod is computing. Poll briefly for its result, then fall back to loading ourselves.
      for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
        const raw = await this.redis.get(key);
        if (raw) return (JSON.parse(raw) as Envelope<T>).data;
      }
      return loader();                                            // lock holder died; do not hang forever
    }
    try {
      const data = await loader();
      const env: Envelope<T> = { data, staleAt: Date.now() + opts.freshMs };
      await this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(env), 'PX', opts.ttlMs);
      return data;
    } finally {
      const client = this.redis as Redis & { releaseLock(k: string, t: string): Promise<number> };
      await client.releaseLock(lockKey, token).catch(() => undefined);
    }
  }
}

Usage: this.loader.get('feed:v1:home', () => this.feeds.compute(), { freshMs: 50_000, ttlMs: 120_000 }). The value is fresh for 50 seconds, served stale for up to 70 more while one refresh runs, and never physically missing under steady traffic.

Production scenario

A home feed endpoint at 1,200 RPS, recompute cost 280 ms. Before: every 60 seconds a spike of 300 concurrent recomputes, PostgreSQL CPU to 100 percent for two seconds, p99 to 1.8 s. After the helper above: one recompute per minute per pod at most (usually one total, thanks to the lock), PostgreSQL flat, p99 12 ms. Detection was the sawtooth pattern on the database CPU graph that lined up exactly with the TTL.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lock holder crashes: the lock expires after 5 seconds; waiters fall back to loading themselves. Set the lock TTL above the loader's p99 but not so high that a crash stalls everyone.
  • Redis down: SET NX throws; catch it and run the loader without coordination. Degraded but alive.
  • The in-process map grows unbounded if a loader never resolves: always wrap loaders in a timeout.
  • Stale-while-revalidate serves stale data indefinitely if every refresh fails. Log refresh failures and alert on their rate.

26.5.3 Cache avalanche

Concept

An avalanche is a stampede across many keys at once: thousands of keys expire in the same second because they were filled in the same second (after a deploy, a restart, a bulk warm-up, or a FLUSHALL), and the database receives thousands of misses simultaneously.

How it works

The mechanism is simply synchronized TTLs. Detection: a database load spike that recurs at an interval exactly equal to your TTL, or a spike shortly after each deploy. Fixes:

  1. TTL jitter. ttl = base + random(0, base * 0.2). Ten thousand keys filled at 10:00:00 with a 5 minute TTL now expire spread across 10:05:00 to 10:06:00 instead of all at 10:05:00.
  2. Warm-up on deploy. Before a pod receives traffic, load the top N keys (from yesterday's access log or a Redis ZSET of hot keys) so the cold-cache miss storm never happens. Do this in onApplicationBootstrap with a bounded concurrency, and make the readiness probe wait for it.
  3. Versioned keys instead of flush. Never FLUSHALL in production. Bump the key version and let old keys expire naturally.
  4. Circuit breaker to the database. If misses exceed a budget, serve stale from a longer-TTL backup key rather than forwarding everything to PostgreSQL.
// products/catalog-warmup.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ProductsService } from './products.service';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Injectable()
export class CatalogWarmupService implements OnApplicationBootstrap {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(CatalogWarmupService.name);
  constructor(
    private readonly products: ProductsService,
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
  ) {}

  async onApplicationBootstrap(): Promise<void> {
    // hot:products is a ZSET maintained by an interceptor: ZINCRBY on each read.
    const ids = await this.redis.zrange('hot:products', 0, 999, 'REV');
    let loaded = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < ids.length; i += 20) {              // bounded concurrency
      await Promise.all(ids.slice(i, i + 20).map((id) => this.products.findOne(id).catch(() => null)));
      loaded += 20;
    }
    this.logger.log(`warmed ${loaded} product keys`);
  }
}

26.5.4 Cache penetration

Concept

Penetration is traffic for keys that do not exist in the database. The cache never gets filled because there is nothing to fill, so every request goes to PostgreSQL. A scraper iterating product ids, a bot guessing user ids, or a bug in a client requesting undefined as an id all produce it.

How it works

Detection: a high miss ratio combined with a high rate of "not found" from the database, or SELECT queries for ids that return zero rows dominating pg_stat_statements. Fixes:

  1. Negative caching. Cache the fact that the key does not exist, with a short TTL (30 to 60 seconds). Store a sentinel value like "__nil__" rather than an empty string, so the code can distinguish "cached as missing" from "not cached".
  2. Input validation. A UUID pipe rejects undefined, null and ../etc before they reach the cache or the database.
  3. Bloom filter. For very large key spaces, keep a Bloom filter of all existing ids (Redis Stack has BF.ADD / BF.EXISTS; without it, a bitmap of hashed ids works). A Bloom filter says "definitely not present" or "maybe present" with no false negatives. Definitely-not-present requests are rejected without touching Redis strings or PostgreSQL.
// products/products.service.ts (excerpt)
const NEG = '__nil__';

async findOne(id: string): Promise<Product> {
  const key = this.key(id);
  const cached = await this.safeGet(key);
  if (cached === NEG) throw new NotFoundException();          // negative hit
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const product = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id } });
  if (!product) {
    await this.safeSet(key, NEG, 45_000);                        // short negative TTL
    throw new NotFoundException();
  }
  await this.safeSet(key, JSON.stringify(product), CacheKey.ttlMs(300_000));
  return product;
}

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A newly created row is hidden by a negative entry created seconds earlier. On create, delete the key for the new id (it is cheap and usually a no-op). This is one of the failure modes in 26.15.
  • Negative entries with a long TTL turn a scraper into a memory attack: millions of __nil__ keys. Keep the TTL short and consider rate limiting the caller.

26.5.5 Hot keys

Concept

A hot key is a single key receiving a disproportionate share of traffic: a viral post, the home page config, a flash-sale product, a global feature flag read on every request. Redis Cluster spreads keys across shards, but one key lives on exactly one shard, so 100,000 RPS on one key is 100,000 RPS on one core.

How it works

Detection: redis-cli --hotkeys (needs an LFU eviction policy), per-shard CPU imbalance in Cluster, or client-side sampling of key access counts. Fixes:

  1. Local in-process cache for the hottest keys with a very short TTL (1 to 5 seconds). A global config read on every request becomes one Redis read per pod per second.
  2. Key replication. Write the value to N copies (flag:v1:checkout:0 to flag:v1:checkout:7) that land on different shards; readers pick a random copy. Invalidation must delete all copies.
  3. Request coalescing. The single-flight map from 26.5.2 also coalesces hot reads inside a pod.
// config/hot-config.service.ts
import { Injectable, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Injectable()
export class HotConfigService {
  private local = new Map<string, { value: string; expiresAt: number }>();
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async get(name: string): Promise<string | null> {
    const hit = this.local.get(name);
    if (hit && hit.expiresAt > Date.now()) return hit.value;        // L1: no network
    const replica = Math.floor(Math.random() * 8);                  // L2: spread across shards
    const value = await this.redis.get(`cfg:v1:${name}:${replica}`);
    if (value !== null) this.local.set(name, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + 2000 });
    return value;
  }
}

The cost is staleness of up to 2 seconds per pod plus the replica write fan-out. For a feature flag that is exactly right; for a price it is not.

26.5.6 Big keys

Concept

A big key is a value so large that single commands on it stall Redis: a 20 MB serialized catalog, a SET with 5 million members, a LIST used as a queue that nobody consumes. Because Redis executes commands on one thread, a 200 ms DEL of a huge set is 200 ms during which every other client waits.

How it works

Detection: redis-cli --bigkeys, MEMORY USAGE key, slowlog entries for DEL, SMEMBERS, HGETALL on the same key. Fixes:

  1. UNLINK instead of DEL. UNLINK removes the key from the keyspace immediately and frees memory on a background thread. Use it everywhere you would use DEL on anything that might be big. Also set lazyfree-lazy-expire yes and lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes so expiry and eviction of big keys also happen off the main thread.
  2. Split. A 5 million member set becomes 100 sets of 50,000 (members:{groupId}:{bucket}), bucketed by hash of the member. A 20 MB catalog becomes per-category keys.
  3. Never read whole collections. SSCAN, HSCAN, ZSCAN with a cursor instead of SMEMBERS, HGETALL, ZRANGE 0 -1.
  4. Cap value size at write time. Refuse to cache a serialized response above, say, 512 KB; log and skip instead. A cache that stores 5 MB responses is cheaper to not have.

26.5.7 Stale data and how much staleness the business accepts

Concept

Every cached read is potentially stale. The engineering question is not "can it be stale" but "how stale, for what, and what happens when it is". Write this down per data type, get product's agreement, and encode it as the TTL.

Data Acceptable staleness Consequence when stale Encoded as
Product description, images Minutes to hours Cosmetic TTL 15 min plus event invalidation
Product price on listing page Seconds to a minute Confusion; checkout re-prices TTL 60 s plus event invalidation
Inventory on product page 5 to 30 s Shows available when sold out; checkout rejects TTL 10 s
Inventory for reservation Zero Oversell Not cached
User permissions Under 5 s after revoke Security exposure TTL 5 s or event invalidation with sync delete
Feature flags 1 to 10 s A feature rolls out unevenly across pods Local TTL 2 s over Redis
Wallet balance Zero for decisions; seconds for display Double spend Display cached 5 s; decision from PostgreSQL with SELECT FOR UPDATE

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the staleness table as a product decision they facilitate, not an engineering decision they hide. They also design flows so that stale reads are harmless: display from cache, decide from the database. That pattern, "cache the read, verify at the write", makes most staleness questions disappear.

26.6 Multi-level caching

Concept

A multi-level cache stacks an in-process memory cache (L1) in front of Redis (L2) in front of PostgreSQL. L1 removes the network round trip for the hottest keys; L2 gives every pod the same view; PostgreSQL is truth.

Why does it exist?

Two reasons. First, hot keys (26.5.5): the only cache that can absorb 100,000 reads per second of one key on every pod is one with no network. Second, resilience: if Redis is unavailable for 10 seconds, a 5 second L1 keeps most reads answered without a database storm.

Mental model

Imagine your desk (L1), the office filing cabinet (L2), and the archive building across town (PostgreSQL). You keep the three files you are working on right now on your desk, the department's active files in the cabinet, and everything in the archive. When a file is updated, the archive is corrected first, the cabinet copy is replaced, and everyone is told to throw away any desk copies. The desk is fast and slightly untrustworthy; that is the deal.

How it works

flowchart LR
    C["Request"] --> L1{"L1 in-process LRU"}
    L1 -->|hit| OUT["Response"]
    L1 -->|miss| L2{"L2 Redis"}
    L2 -->|hit| FILL1["fill L1"] --> OUT
    L2 -->|miss| PG["PostgreSQL"]
    PG --> FILL2["fill L2 then L1"] --> OUT
    W["Write path"] --> PGW["UPDATE + COMMIT"]
    PGW --> DELL2["DEL L2 key"]
    DELL2 --> PUB["PUBLISH invalidate channel"]
    PUB -.-> L1
  1. Read L1 (a bounded LRU map in the pod, TTL 1 to 5 seconds). Hit: return.
  2. Miss: read L2 (Redis). Hit: fill L1, return.
  3. Miss: read PostgreSQL, fill L2 with the long TTL, fill L1 with the short TTL, return.
  4. Write: update PostgreSQL, delete the L2 key, PUBLISH the key on an invalidation channel. Every pod is subscribed and deletes its L1 entry.
  5. Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget (26.8.7). A pod that is disconnected at that moment misses the message, so L1's short TTL is the safety net: staleness is bounded by the L1 TTL even if the invalidation never arrives.

NestJS example

// redis/two-level-cache.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache';
import { REDIS, REDIS_SUBSCRIBER } from './redis.module';

const CHANNEL = 'cache:invalidate';

@Injectable()
export class TwoLevelCache implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TwoLevelCache.name);
  private readonly l1 = new LRUCache<string, string>({ max: 5000, ttl: 3000 });

  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
    @Inject(REDIS_SUBSCRIBER) private readonly sub: Redis, // a dedicated connection: subscribers cannot run other commands
  ) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.sub.subscribe(CHANNEL);
    this.sub.on('message', (_ch, key) => this.l1.delete(key));
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> {
    await this.sub.unsubscribe(CHANNEL);
  }

  async get<T>(key: string, loader: () => Promise<T>, l2TtlMs: number): Promise<T> {
    const l1 = this.l1.get(key);
    if (l1) return JSON.parse(l1);
    let l2: string | null = null;
    try {
      l2 = await this.redis.get(key);
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn(`L2 unavailable for ${key}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    }
    if (l2) {
      this.l1.set(key, l2);
      return JSON.parse(l2);
    }
    const value = await loader();
    const json = JSON.stringify(value);
    this.l1.set(key, json);
    this.redis.set(key, json, 'PX', l2TtlMs).catch(() => undefined);
    return value;
  }

  async invalidate(key: string): Promise<void> {
    this.l1.delete(key);
    await this.redis.unlink(key);
    await this.redis.publish(CHANNEL, key); // other pods drop their L1 copy
  }
}

Production scenario

An API with 24 pods, each handling 500 RPS, reading a tenant configuration object on every request. Before L1: 12,000 Redis GETs per second for the same 300 keys, one Redis shard at 60 percent CPU. After a 2 second L1: Redis sees roughly 24 pods times 300 keys divided by 2 seconds, about 3,600 reads per second in the worst case and far fewer in practice, and the shard sits at 8 percent. Config changes propagate within 2 seconds to every pod via Pub/Sub, or within 2 seconds by TTL if a pod missed the message.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Consistency: two pods can serve different values for up to the L1 TTL. Never use L1 for data where two users seeing different values in the same second is a bug.
  • Memory: an unbounded L1 is a memory leak. lru-cache with max and ttl is the minimum; also cap the byte size for large values.
  • Pub/Sub delivery is not guaranteed; the L1 TTL is the real bound. Say so in the design doc.
  • A pod's subscriber connection drops and reconnects: ioredis re-subscribes automatically, but messages during the gap are lost. The TTL covers it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

L1 is a scalpel, not a default. It is justified by a measured hot-key problem or a resilience requirement, and it always comes with a short TTL and a memory cap. The senior asks: which specific keys, how many per pod, what TTL, and which bug appears if two pods disagree for that long.

Common mistakes

  • Using an in-process cache without a TTL "because we invalidate via Pub/Sub". Pub/Sub is lossy.
  • Subscribing on the same ioredis connection used for commands. A subscribed connection can only run subscribe-family commands; every other call throws.
  • Storing objects by reference in L1 and mutating them later in request code, so the "cache" changes under other requests. Store serialized strings or deep-frozen objects.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the write-then-delete race and two ways to close it. Expected: slow reader re-caches an old row after the writer's delete; double delete or version-checked SET.
  2. How do you prevent a stampede on one hot key across 20 pods? Expected: SET NX lock so one pod recomputes; single-flight inside each pod; stale-while-revalidate so nobody waits. Follow-up: what if the lock holder dies?
  3. What is the difference between avalanche and stampede? Expected: stampede is many requests on one expired key; avalanche is many keys expiring together. Jitter fixes avalanche; locking fixes stampede.
  4. A scraper is hitting /products/:id with random ids and PostgreSQL CPU is high. What do you do? Expected: validate ids, negative-cache with short TTL, rate-limit the client, Bloom filter if the key space is huge.
  5. Why is DEL on a large set dangerous and what replaces it? Expected: single-threaded Redis blocks all clients during the free; UNLINK frees on a background thread.
  6. When is an in-process L1 cache wrong? Expected: when pods disagreeing for the L1 TTL is a correctness bug, or when memory per pod is tight.

Practical exercise

Build a CachedLoader for a NestJS feed endpoint and prove it under load. Acceptance criteria: (a) with autocannon -c 200 -d 30 against a 300 ms loader, the loader runs at most once per freshMs window across two app instances, verified by a counter in PostgreSQL; (b) killing the lock holder mid-compute does not stall waiters for more than 5 seconds; (c) stopping Redis mid-test keeps the endpoint returning 200; (d) a PATCH that changes the feed source invalidates L2 and every pod's L1 within 3 seconds, verified with a test that polls both instances.

26.7 Redis fundamentals

You cannot operate a cache you do not understand. This section is the Redis internals a senior engineer needs: how commands execute, where memory goes, how data survives (or does not) a restart, how eviction chooses victims, and how Redis scales from one process to a cluster.

26.7.1 Single-threaded command execution

Concept

Redis executes commands on a single thread, one at a time, in the order they arrive. Newer versions use extra threads for network I/O and for freeing memory, but the command itself, the part that reads or mutates a data structure, is always serialized. There are no locks inside Redis because there is no concurrency to lock against.

Why does it exist?

A single thread with no locks is why Redis is fast and predictable: no contention, no context switches, and every command is atomic by construction. INCR cannot race with another INCR. A Lua script sees a frozen world. The price is that one slow command delays every other client.

Mental model

Imagine a single very fast bank teller with one queue. Each customer's transaction takes a millisecond, so the queue never builds. Then one customer asks for a printout of every transaction since 1998. Everyone behind them waits, and the queue out the door is the incident.

How it works

  1. Clients send commands over TCP. I/O threads (Redis 6 and later, if enabled) read and parse them.
  2. The main thread takes commands from the parsed queue and executes them one at a time.
  3. A GET on a string is O(1) and takes microseconds. KEYS * on 10 million keys is O(N) and takes seconds. SMEMBERS on a 5 million member set is O(N) and allocates a 5 million element reply. DEL on a huge hash is O(N) to free.
  4. While the main thread runs a slow command, every other connection's commands sit in the socket buffer. Your NestJS app sees commandTimeout errors on trivial GETs and concludes "Redis is slow", when actually one command was slow.

The rules that follow:

  • Never run KEYS in production. Use SCAN with a cursor and COUNT; it walks the keyspace in small steps and lets other commands interleave.
  • Never read a whole large collection. SSCAN, HSCAN, ZSCAN, LRANGE with bounds.
  • Use UNLINK rather than DEL and enable lazy freeing.
  • Keep Lua scripts short. A script that loops 100,000 times blocks Redis for the duration.
  • Watch the slowlog (SLOWLOG GET 25) and treat any entry over 10 ms as a bug.
// redis/scan.util.ts: the correct way to find keys by pattern in production
export async function scanKeys(redis: Redis, pattern: string, onBatch: (keys: string[]) => Promise<void>) {
  const stream = redis.scanStream({ match: pattern, count: 500 });
  for await (const keys of stream as AsyncIterable<string[]>) {
    if (keys.length) await onBatch(keys);   // e.g. redis.unlink(...keys)
  }
}

26.7.2 Memory

Concept

Everything in Redis lives in RAM. Memory is the capacity dimension you plan for, and maxmemory is the ceiling you must set. Without it Redis grows until the kernel OOM-kills it.

How it works

  • INFO memory reports used_memory (bytes of data plus overhead), used_memory_rss (what the OS sees), and mem_fragmentation_ratio (rss / used). A ratio of 1.0 to 1.5 is healthy. Above 1.5 means fragmentation: memory freed in small pieces that the allocator cannot reuse; activedefrag yes helps. Below 1.0 means Redis is swapping, which is an emergency.
  • Per-key overhead is about 50 to 100 bytes for the key object, the dictionary entry and the expiry entry. A million tiny keys costs 100 MB before any values. Hashes with fewer than 128 small fields are stored as a compact "listpack" that is far cheaper than a million separate string keys, which is why HSET user:41 name ... email ... beats SET user:41:name, SET user:41:email.
  • Reply buffers count too. A client that requests a 100 MB SMEMBERS allocates 100 MB of output buffer. client-output-buffer-limit protects against that.
  • Plan for maxmemory at 60 to 70 percent of the instance RAM when using RDB persistence, because the fork for a snapshot uses copy-on-write pages and a write-heavy workload can double memory during the save.

26.7.3 Persistence: RDB versus AOF

Concept

Redis can write its data to disk two ways. RDB is a point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset, taken periodically. AOF (append-only file) logs every write command as it happens, and is replayed on restart.

How it works

Property RDB AOF
What is written Compact binary snapshot Every write command, in order
When On a schedule (save 300 100: every 5 min if 100 keys changed) or BGSAVE Continuously; fsync policy always, everysec (default) or no
Data loss on crash Everything since the last snapshot: minutes Up to 1 second with everysec; near zero with always at a big throughput cost
Restart time Fast (load one file) Slower (replay commands); Redis 7 uses a base RDB plus incremental AOF to speed this up
Runtime cost A fork() per snapshot; copy-on-write memory spike Constant small write I/O; periodic rewrite to compact
Best for Cache, where losing minutes is fine and restart speed matters Sessions, queues, counters, anything you would be sad to lose

For a pure cache, many teams disable persistence entirely (save "", appendonly no) and accept that a restart means a cold cache. For anything that is a store rather than a cache (sessions, rate limit counters, idempotency keys, Streams used as a queue), turn on AOF with everysec and accept up to one second of loss, and then ask whether the data belongs in PostgreSQL instead.

26.7.4 Eviction policies and maxmemory

Concept

When used_memory reaches maxmemory, Redis must either refuse writes or evict keys. maxmemory-policy decides which.

How it works

Policy Behaviour Use when
noeviction Writes fail with OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'; reads keep working Redis is a store (sessions, queues) and losing keys silently is worse than failing writes
allkeys-lru Evict the approximately least-recently-used key, from all keys Pure cache; the default choice
allkeys-lfu Evict the least-frequently-used Cache with a stable hot set and long-tail noise; also enables --hotkeys
volatile-lru LRU among keys that have a TTL only Mixed store and cache in one instance; keys without TTL are never evicted
volatile-ttl Evict keys with the nearest expiry first Mixed instance where soon-to-expire keys are the cheapest loss
allkeys-random, volatile-random Random victim Rarely

Two things surprise people. First, "LRU" is approximate: Redis samples maxmemory-samples keys (default 5) and evicts the oldest of the sample, which is close enough and far cheaper than a true LRU list. Second, volatile-* policies with no keys carrying a TTL behave exactly like noeviction, and your first OOM error is how you find out.

The senior rule: one Redis instance per role. A cache instance with allkeys-lru and no persistence; a store instance with noeviction and AOF. Mixing them means your session store evicts sessions when the product cache grows, or your cache refuses writes because the session store filled the memory.

26.7.5 Replication, Sentinel and Cluster

Concept

A single Redis process is a single point of failure and a single core's worth of throughput. Replication copies data from a primary to one or more replicas. Sentinel watches a primary and promotes a replica when it dies. Cluster splits the keyspace across many primaries (each with replicas) so that data and throughput scale horizontally.

How it works

Replication is asynchronous. The primary acknowledges a write to the client, then streams it to replicas. If the primary dies before the stream catches up, those writes are lost when a replica is promoted. WAIT numreplicas timeout lets a client block until N replicas have the write, which narrows the window but does not close it. Replicas serve reads (READONLY in Cluster, or by connecting directly) with replication lag of typically under a millisecond in the same availability zone.

Sentinel is a set of three or more processes that ping the primary. When a quorum agrees it is down, they elect a replica, promote it, and reconfigure the other replicas. Clients (ioredis with sentinels: [...], name: 'mymaster') ask Sentinel for the current primary address. Failover takes about 10 to 30 seconds by default, during which writes fail. Sentinel gives high availability, not horizontal scaling: the dataset must still fit on one primary.

Cluster divides the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots. Each key maps to a slot by CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns a range of slots. Clients learn the slot map and send each command to the right node. Add a node, move slots to it, and both memory and throughput scale.

flowchart TB
    K1["orders:v2:7c9e"] -->|"CRC16 mod 16384 = 3421"| S1
    K2["user:41 with hash tag"] -->|"slot of user:41 = 9012"| S2
    K3["cart:v1:88"] -->|"slot 15001"| S3
    subgraph Cluster
        S1["Primary A slots 0 to 5460"] --- R1["Replica A"]
        S2["Primary B slots 5461 to 10922"] --- R2["Replica B"]
        S3["Primary C slots 10923 to 16383"] --- R3["Replica C"]
    end

Cluster constraints that bite application code:

  • Multi-key commands must hit one slot. MGET a b, SUNION s1 s2, a Lua script touching two keys, a MULTI block: all fail with CROSSSLOT unless every key hashes to the same slot. The fix is hash tags: only the part of the key inside {...} is hashed. cart:{user:41}:items and wishlist:{user:41} share a slot, so a script can update both atomically.
  • MOVED and ASK redirections. When a slot migrates, a node replies MOVED 3421 10.0.0.5:6379 and the client must retry there. ioredis in cluster mode (new Redis.Cluster([...])) handles this and refreshes its slot map; a plain Redis client pointed at a cluster node does not, and you see MOVED errors in your logs.
  • No SELECT database numbers (only db 0), no cross-slot transactions, KEYS and SCAN are per node.
  • Failover per shard. If Primary B dies, Replica B is promoted within seconds; slots 5461 to 10922 are unavailable meanwhile; the other two thirds of the keyspace keep serving.

Production scenario

A single Redis primary at 80,000 ops per second and 40 GB of data with a 64 GB machine. RDB snapshots cause 20 second latency spikes because the fork copies page tables for 40 GB. The options: move to AOF only, or split into a 6 shard Cluster where each shard holds 7 GB and forks in under a second. The team picks Cluster, adds hash tags to the two multi-key flows, switches ioredis to cluster mode, and the p99 drops from 21 ms to 1.1 ms. They also lose the ability to run a pipeline across arbitrary keys in one round trip, which cost one endpoint 3 ms and was worth it.

26.7.6 Pipelining and Lua scripts

Concept

Pipelining sends many commands without waiting for each reply, then reads all replies at once. It removes the per-command network round trip, which is most of the cost of a Redis call.
