Lua scripts run several commands atomically on the server, so no other client can interleave between them, and the script's logic (compare, branch, compute) happens next to the data.

How it works

  • Fetching 50 product keys one at a time costs 50 round trips, about 15 ms at 0.3 ms each. A pipeline sends all 50 in one write and reads 50 replies in one read: about 0.6 ms. MGET does the same for strings in one command (single slot in Cluster, or ioredis cluster mode splits it for you).
  • A pipeline is not atomic; other clients' commands can interleave. MULTI ... EXEC is atomic (all commands run together) but cannot branch on intermediate results. A Lua script is atomic and can branch, which makes it the tool for check-and-set logic: "if the lock token matches, delete", "if stock is at least N, decrement and return the new value".
  • EVALSHA sends a SHA of a script already loaded; ioredis defineCommand handles loading and falls back to EVAL if the script is missing after a restart.
  • Scripts must be deterministic and fast. No calls out, no randomness that affects writes, no loops over unbounded data.
// A pipeline for a product listing: 20 keys, one round trip.
const pipeline = this.redis.pipeline();
for (const id of ids) pipeline.get(`products:v3:${id}`);
const results = await pipeline.exec();               // [[err, value], ...]
const hits = new Map<string, string>();
results?.forEach(([err, value], i) => { if (!err && value) hits.set(ids[i], value as string); });
const missingIds = ids.filter((id) => !hits.has(id)); // load these from PostgreSQL in one query

26.7.7 Latency numbers to remember

Operation Typical latency Notes
GET/SET same AZ 0.2 to 0.5 ms Dominated by network
GET via loopback (same host) 0.05 to 0.1 ms Rare in production
Pipeline of 100 GETs 1 to 2 ms Versus 30 to 50 ms unpipelined
ZADD / ZRANGEBYSCORE on a 1M member ZSET 0.3 to 1 ms O(log N)
SMEMBERS on 1M members 100 to 300 ms Blocks everyone; do not
Cross-AZ Redis 1 to 2 ms Plan for it in multi-AZ deployments
Cross-region Redis 50 to 150 ms Never put Redis cross-region on the request path
Sentinel failover 10 to 30 s Writes fail during it
Cluster shard failover 1 to 5 s One shard's slots unavailable

Interview questions

  1. Why is KEYS * dangerous, and what do you use instead? Expected: O(N) on a single thread blocks all clients; SCAN with cursor and COUNT.
  2. Your app's Redis p99 jumped from 1 ms to 40 ms with no traffic change. First three things you check? Expected: slowlog for a blocking command, INFO for a running BGSAVE fork or AOF rewrite, and memory (evictions, fragmentation, swapping).
  3. What happens when Redis reaches maxmemory with noeviction? Expected: writes fail with OOM errors, reads work; the app must handle write failures. Follow-up: which policy for a session store versus a product cache?
  4. Why do multi-key operations fail in Cluster and how do you fix it? Expected: keys hash to different slots; hash tags {...} force co-location.
  5. What data can you lose during a Sentinel failover and why? Expected: writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated; replication is asynchronous.
  6. When is a pipeline the wrong tool and a Lua script the right one? Expected: when the second command depends on the first's result, or when the sequence must be atomic.

26.8 Redis data structures and their backend uses

Redis is not a key-value store; it is a server of data structures. Choosing the right one is the difference between a 0.3 ms answer and a design that does not work. For each structure: what it is, the commands that matter, the backend use, the NestJS code, and the trap.

26.8.1 Strings

Concept

A string is a byte sequence up to 512 MB: a serialized object, a number, a flag. It is the structure behind the plain cache, counters and locks.

How it works

  • SET key value PX ms / GET: the cache. SET ... NX sets only if absent (locks, dedup). SET ... XX sets only if present.
  • INCR, INCRBY, DECR, INCRBYFLOAT: atomic counters; the string is parsed as an integer or float. A new key starts at 0.
  • MGET, MSET: batch reads and writes.
  • GETEX key PX ms: read and refresh the TTL in one command (sliding sessions).
  • SETRANGE/GETRANGE, APPEND: rarely useful in backends.

Practical example

Three backend uses in one service: a serialized cache, a request counter per API key, and a SET NX guard that makes a webhook handler ignore duplicates.

// webhooks/webhook-dedup.service.ts
import { Injectable, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Injectable()
export class WebhookDedupService {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  // Returns true the first time a webhook id is seen within 24 h, false on replays.
  async claim(provider: string, eventId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const result = await this.redis.set(`webhook:seen:${provider}:${eventId}`, '1', 'PX', 86_400_000, 'NX');
    return result === 'OK';
  }

  // Per-API-key daily counter for usage billing; INCR is atomic across all pods.
  async countCall(apiKey: string, day: string): Promise<number> {
    const key = `usage:${day}:${apiKey}`;
    const n = await this.redis.incr(key);
    if (n === 1) await this.redis.pexpire(key, 3 * 86_400_000); // set TTL on first increment only
    return n;
  }
}

The incr then pexpire pair is a classic small race: if the process dies between them, the key never expires. Wrap both in a Lua script or use SET key 0 PX ttl NX before INCR when it matters.

26.8.2 Hashes

Concept

A hash is a map of field to value under one key: user:41 -> { name, email, plan }. It is the right structure for an object whose fields you read or update individually, and it is far more memory-efficient than one key per field.

How it works

  • HSET key f1 v1 f2 v2, HGET key f, HMGET key f1 f2, HGETALL key (careful on large hashes; HSCAN instead).
  • HINCRBY key field n: atomic per-field counter. HINCRBYFLOAT for decimals.
  • HSETNX, HDEL, HEXISTS, HLEN.
  • TTL applies to the whole key, not to individual fields (Redis 7.4 adds per-field expiry with HEXPIRE; check your version before relying on it).

Practical example

A user profile cache where the write path updates one field without rewriting the whole object, and an "inventory-ish" counter map per warehouse. Note the word "ish": HINCRBY on stock is fine for a display estimate or a soft reservation with a PostgreSQL reconciliation; it is not the source of truth for "did we sell it" (26.10).

// users/profile-cache.service.ts
async cacheProfile(u: { id: string; name: string; email: string; plan: string }): Promise<void> {
  const key = `user:v1:${u.id}`;
  await this.redis.multi()
    .hset(key, { name: u.name, email: u.email, plan: u.plan })
    .pexpire(key, 3_600_000)
    .exec();
}

async updatePlan(userId: string, plan: string): Promise<void> {
  // After the PostgreSQL commit: touch one field, keep the rest.
  await this.redis.hset(`user:v1:${userId}`, 'plan', plan);
}

// inventory/soft-counts.service.ts
async decrementDisplayStock(warehouseId: string, sku: string, qty: number): Promise<number> {
  return this.redis.hincrby(`stock:display:${warehouseId}`, sku, -qty); // can go negative; the DB is truth
}

26.8.3 Sets

Concept

A set is an unordered collection of unique strings. It answers "is X a member", "how many members", and set algebra (union, intersection, difference) in one command.

How it works

  • SADD, SREM, SISMEMBER, SMISMEMBER (many members at once), SCARD.
  • SINTER, SUNION, SDIFF and their *STORE variants; O(N) across the sets, so keep them small or run them offline.
  • SRANDMEMBER, SPOP for random selection.
  • SSCAN to iterate.

Practical example

Unique visitors per product per day (exact counting; see HyperLogLog in 26.8.9 for the approximate version), product tags for filtering, and a deduplication set for a batch job.

// analytics/visitors.service.ts
async recordVisit(productId: string, visitorId: string, day: string): Promise<void> {
  const key = `visitors:${day}:${productId}`;
  await this.redis.multi().sadd(key, visitorId).expire(key, 3 * 86_400).exec();
}

async uniqueVisitors(productId: string, day: string): Promise<number> {
  return this.redis.scard(`visitors:${day}:${productId}`);
}

// products/tags.service.ts: products tagged both 'vegan' and 'gluten-free'
async intersectTags(tags: string[]): Promise<string[]> {
  if (tags.length > 3) throw new Error('At most 3 tags per query'); // bound the O(N) work
  return this.redis.sinter(...tags.map((t) => `tag:v1:${t}`));
}

The memory trap: a set of a million visitor UUIDs is about 60 MB. A thousand products times 30 days of that is not a cache, it is a data warehouse in RAM. Use HyperLogLog for counts and keep exact sets only where you need membership.

26.8.4 Sorted sets

Concept

A sorted set (ZSET) is a set where each member has a floating-point score, and members are kept ordered by score. It supports rank queries, range-by-score queries and range-by-rank queries, all in O(log N). It is the most versatile Redis structure for backends.

How it works

  • ZADD key score member, ZINCRBY key delta member.
  • ZRANGE key start stop by rank; ZRANGE key min max BYSCORE by score; add REV for descending, WITHSCORES for scores, LIMIT for paging.
  • ZRANK / ZREVRANK (position), ZSCORE, ZCARD, ZCOUNT min max.
  • ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZREMRANGEBYRANK for trimming.
  • ZPOPMIN / BZPOPMIN to pop the lowest-score member (with blocking).

Practical example

Four uses that cover most backend needs:

  1. Leaderboard: score is points, ZREVRANK gives a player's position, ZRANGE ... REV LIMIT 0 10 gives the top 10.
  2. Sliding-window rate limiter: score is a timestamp; count members in the last 60 seconds (full code in 26.11).
  3. Delayed job scheduling: score is the time the job should run; a worker polls ZRANGE key 0 now BYSCORE LIMIT 0 100 and removes what it claims.
  4. Recently active / ranking: score is last_seen epoch, trim with ZREMRANGEBYRANK key 0 -1001 to keep the top 1,000.
// jobs/delayed-jobs.service.ts: schedule a payment retry for later
import { Injectable, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

const QUEUE = 'delayed:payment-retry';

// Atomically claim due jobs: read them and remove them in one script so two workers never take the same job.
const CLAIM_DUE = `
  local due = redis.call('ZRANGE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[1], 'BYSCORE', 'LIMIT', 0, ARGV[2])
  if #due > 0 then redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], unpack(due)) end
  return due
`;

@Injectable()
export class DelayedJobsService {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('claimDue', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: CLAIM_DUE });
  }

  schedule(paymentId: string, runAtMs: number): Promise<number> {
    return this.redis.zadd(QUEUE, runAtMs, paymentId);
  }

  async claimDue(limit = 100): Promise<string[]> {
    const client = this.redis as Redis & { claimDue(k: string, now: number, limit: number): Promise<string[]> };
    return client.claimDue(QUEUE, Date.now(), limit);
  }
}

For anything beyond a small delayed queue, use BullMQ (@nestjs/bullmq), which implements exactly this on top of ZSETs and Lists with retries, concurrency and a UI. Writing your own is a good way to learn and a poor way to run production.

26.8.5 Lists

Concept

A list is a doubly linked sequence of strings with O(1) push and pop at either end. It is a queue (LPUSH + BRPOP), a stack, or a capped "recent items" log.

How it works

  • LPUSH / RPUSH, LPOP / RPOP, BLPOP / BRPOP (block until an item arrives, with a timeout).
  • LRANGE key 0 9 for the first 10; LTRIM key 0 99 to cap length.
  • LMOVE src dst RIGHT LEFT (formerly RPOPLPUSH): pop from one list and push to another atomically, which is the "reliable queue" pattern: move the item to a processing list, delete it after success, re-queue it from the processing list if the worker dies.

Practical example

Recently viewed products per user, capped at 20, and a simple work queue for thumbnail generation where losing a job on Redis restart is acceptable.

// users/recently-viewed.service.ts
async push(userId: string, productId: string): Promise<void> {
  const key = `recent:v1:${userId}`;
  await this.redis.multi()
    .lrem(key, 0, productId)      // remove any older occurrence
    .lpush(key, productId)        // newest first
    .ltrim(key, 0, 19)            // keep 20
    .expire(key, 30 * 86_400)
    .exec();
}

// media/thumbnail-queue.service.ts
enqueue(job: { uploadId: string }): Promise<number> {
  return this.redis.lpush('q:thumbnails', JSON.stringify(job));
}

async dequeueBlocking(timeoutSec = 5): Promise<{ uploadId: string } | null> {
  // Move to a processing list so a crash between pop and completion is recoverable.
  const raw = await this.redis.blmove('q:thumbnails', 'q:thumbnails:processing', 'RIGHT', 'LEFT', timeoutSec);
  return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;
}

The limits of a List as a queue: no consumer groups, no acknowledgement, no replay, no per-message metadata, and the "processing" list needs a janitor to re-queue stuck items. When you find yourself building those, you want Streams (next section) or a real broker (Part 27 — Messaging).

Common mistakes across structures

  • Storing JSON blobs in a hash field and updating the whole blob, which throws away the reason to use a hash.
  • Using a set for a count you never need membership for; HyperLogLog is 12 KB regardless of cardinality.
  • A ZSET of every event ever with no trimming, which grows until eviction takes it and the "leaderboard" disappears.
  • A List queue read with RPOP in a setInterval loop instead of BRPOP, which either burns CPU or adds latency; BRPOP blocks that one connection, so give it a dedicated ioredis instance.

Practical exercise

Implement a "trending products" feature: increment a product's score on each view, decay all scores every 10 minutes, and expose GET /products/trending returning the top 20. Acceptance criteria: (a) uses a ZSET with ZINCRBY; (b) decay uses ZUNIONSTORE with a weight of 0.5 rather than iterating members; (c) the ZSET is trimmed to 10,000 members; (d) the read endpoint costs one Redis command plus one MGET for product details; (e) the endpoint keeps working, returning an empty list, when Redis is down.

26.8.6 Streams

Concept

A Stream is an append-only log of entries, each with an auto-generated id (1725600000000-0, a millisecond timestamp plus a sequence) and a map of fields. Consumers read from a position; consumer groups let several workers share a stream, each entry delivered to one member of the group, with explicit acknowledgement and a record of pending (delivered but unacknowledged) entries. It is a lightweight Kafka inside Redis.

Why does it exist?

Lists as queues lose messages on consumer crash and cannot fan out to several independent consumers. Pub/Sub loses messages if nobody is listening. Streams give durable (as durable as your Redis persistence), replayable, acknowledged delivery with consumer groups, without running a broker. For moderate volumes (tens of thousands of messages per second) with modest retention, they are enough.

Mental model

Imagine a ticker tape in a newsroom. Every story is printed with a timestamp and stays on the tape. Each desk (consumer group) has a marker showing how far it has read. Inside a desk, several editors (consumers) each tear off the next story; the desk keeps a note of which editor has which story until they say "done". If an editor goes home with a story in their pocket, the desk can reassign it.

How it works

flowchart LR
    P1["Producer XADD"] --> S["Stream orders:events"]
    S --> G1["Consumer group notifications"]
    S --> G2["Consumer group analytics"]
    G1 --> C1["worker-1"]
    G1 --> C2["worker-2"]
    G2 --> C3["analytics-1"]
    C1 -->|XACK| G1
    C2 -->|XACK| G1
    G1 --> PEL["Pending entries list"]
    PEL -->|"XAUTOCLAIM after idle"| C2
  1. XADD orders:events * type OrderPlaced orderId 123 MAXLEN ~ 100000 appends an entry and trims the stream to roughly 100,000 entries (the ~ makes trimming cheap).
  2. XGROUP CREATE orders:events notifications $ MKSTREAM creates a group starting at the end (0 to start from the beginning).
  3. Each worker loops on XREADGROUP GROUP notifications worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders:events >. The > means "entries never delivered to this group". Delivered entries go into the group's pending entries list (PEL) tagged with the consumer name and delivery time.
  4. After processing, XACK orders:events notifications <id> removes the entry from the PEL.
  5. If a worker dies, its entries stay in the PEL. XPENDING shows them; XAUTOCLAIM orders:events notifications worker-2 60000 0-0 transfers entries idle for more than 60 seconds to worker-2, which processes them. A delivery counter in the PEL lets you detect poison messages and move them to a dead-letter stream after N attempts.
  6. Different groups read the same stream independently: notifications and analytics each have their own last-delivered id and PEL.

NestJS example

A consumer as a long-running provider with graceful shutdown. Note the dedicated connection: BLOCK ties up the connection while waiting.

// events/order-events.consumer.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_BLOCKING } from '../redis/redis.module';
import { NotificationsService } from '../notifications/notifications.service';

const STREAM = 'orders:events';
const GROUP = 'notifications';
const MAX_DELIVERIES = 5;

@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsConsumer implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderEventsConsumer.name);
  private running = true;
  private loop?: Promise<void>;
  private readonly consumer = `${process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local'}-${process.pid}`;

  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS_BLOCKING) private readonly redis: Redis,
    private readonly notifications: NotificationsService,
  ) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.redis.xgroup('CREATE', STREAM, GROUP, '$', 'MKSTREAM');
    } catch (err) {
      if (!(err as Error).message.includes('BUSYGROUP')) throw err; // group already exists
    }
    this.loop = this.run();
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = false;          // finish the in-flight batch, then stop
    await this.loop;
  }

  private async run(): Promise<void> {
    while (this.running) {
      // 1. Reclaim entries another worker abandoned (idle > 60 s).
      const [, claimed] = await this.redis.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, this.consumer, 60_000, '0-0', 'COUNT', 10);
      await this.handleBatch(claimed as [string, string[]][]);

      // 2. Read new entries, blocking up to 5 s.
      const res = await this.redis.xreadgroup('GROUP', GROUP, this.consumer, 'COUNT', 10, 'BLOCK', 5000, 'STREAMS', STREAM, '>');
      if (!res) continue;
      for (const [, entries] of res as [string, [string, string[]][]][]) await this.handleBatch(entries);
    }
  }

  private async handleBatch(entries: [string, string[]][]): Promise<void> {
    for (const [id, fields] of entries) {
      const data = Object.fromEntries(fields.reduce<string[][]>((acc, v, i) => (i % 2 ? (acc[acc.length - 1].push(v), acc) : [...acc, [v]]), []));
      try {
        await this.notifications.handleOrderEvent(data);   // must be idempotent: redelivery is normal
        await this.redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, id);
      } catch (err) {
        const [pending] = await this.redis.xpending(STREAM, GROUP, id, id, 1) as [string, string, number, number][];
        if (pending && pending[3] >= MAX_DELIVERIES) {
          await this.redis.multi().xadd(`${STREAM}:dlq`, '*', 'originalId', id, 'error', String(err), ...fields).xack(STREAM, GROUP, id).exec();
          this.logger.error(`moved ${id} to DLQ after ${pending[3]} deliveries`);
        } else {
          this.logger.warn(`entry ${id} failed, will be reclaimed: ${(err as Error).message}`);
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Production scenario

An order service publishes 200 events per second to a Stream trimmed at 1 million entries (about 300 MB at 300 bytes per entry). Three consumer groups: notifications (3 workers), analytics (1 worker), search indexer (2 workers). Consumer lag is measured with XINFO GROUPS (the lag field in Redis 7) and alerted at 10,000 entries. AOF everysec persistence means a crash loses at most one second of events, which the team documents and accepts; anything needing stronger guarantees goes through the outbox and Kafka.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A consumer that processes but crashes before XACK causes redelivery. Handlers must be idempotent.
  • MAXLEN trimming can delete entries a slow group has not read yet. Monitor lag against the trim size.
  • XAUTOCLAIM on an entry that a slow (not dead) worker is still processing causes double processing. Set the idle threshold above the handler's p99.
  • A stream with no MAXLEN grows until eviction or OOM.
  • Entries in the PEL with a delivery count climbing forever and no DLQ logic are a silent poison-message loop.

26.8.7 Pub/Sub

Concept

PUBLISH channel message sends a message to every client currently subscribed to that channel. It is fire-and-forget: no persistence, no acknowledgement, no replay. A subscriber that is disconnected at the moment of publishing never sees the message.

How it works

  • SUBSCRIBE channel, PSUBSCRIBE pattern*, PUBLISH channel payload. A subscribed connection is in a special mode and can only run subscribe-family commands, so it must be a dedicated ioredis instance.
  • In Cluster, PUBLISH is broadcast to every node so any subscriber anywhere sees it; sharded Pub/Sub (SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE, Redis 7) scopes it to a slot's shard for efficiency.
  • Use it for: cache invalidation broadcasts (26.6), fan-out of WebSocket messages across pods (a chat message received by pod A must reach a user connected to pod B), live config reloads.
  • Do not use it for: jobs, events that must be processed, anything where losing a message matters. Use Streams or a broker.
// chat/chat.gateway.ts (excerpt): fan out across pods with Pub/Sub
@WebSocketGateway()
export class ChatGateway implements OnGatewayInit {
  @WebSocketServer() server!: Server;
  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly pub: Redis,
    @Inject(REDIS_SUBSCRIBER) private readonly sub: Redis,
  ) {}

  async afterInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.sub.subscribe('chat:messages');
    this.sub.on('message', (_ch, raw) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(raw) as { roomId: string; text: string; userId: string };
      this.server.to(msg.roomId).emit('message', msg);   // deliver to sockets on THIS pod
    });
  }

  @SubscribeMessage('send')
  async onSend(@MessageBody() msg: { roomId: string; text: string; userId: string }): Promise<void> {
    await this.pub.publish('chat:messages', JSON.stringify(msg)); // every pod, including this one, receives it
  }
}

The @socket.io/redis-adapter package does this generically for Socket.IO rooms. The point stands: Pub/Sub is the right tool because a lost chat message during a pod restart is acceptable and a queued one arriving 30 seconds late is not.

26.8.8 TTL and expiry mechanics

Concept

A key with a TTL is removed by Redis after the TTL elapses. Removal happens in two ways: lazily, when a client accesses an expired key and Redis deletes it before answering "nil"; and actively, by a background task that samples keys with TTLs 10 times a second and deletes expired ones.

How it works

  1. EXPIRE key seconds, PEXPIRE key ms, EXPIREAT, or the EX/PX options on SET. TTL key and PTTL key report remaining time; -1 means no expiry, -2 means the key does not exist. PERSIST removes the TTL.
  2. The active expiry cycle takes 20 random keys from the set of keys with TTLs, deletes the expired ones, and repeats while more than 25 percent of the sample was expired, bounded by a time budget (about 25 ms per 100 ms by default). Under a mass expiry, expired keys can linger for seconds and still count toward memory; INFO shows expired_keys climbing.
  3. SET on an existing key without EX/PX removes the TTL (KEEPTTL preserves it). HSET, SADD, ZADD on an existing key preserve the TTL. This asymmetry is a frequent bug: a "refresh the cached value" SET silently makes the key permanent.
  4. Expiry uses the server clock. On replicas, keys are not expired independently; the primary sends explicit DELs. A replica that has lost contact keeps serving logically expired keys (it returns them as expired for reads, but they occupy memory).
  5. During a snapshot or AOF rewrite, expiry still runs on the main thread; it is not a source of blocking on its own.

The practical rules: always pass a TTL on every SET for cache data; use GETEX or PEXPIRE explicitly when you want to extend; and never rely on the exact millisecond of expiry for correctness.

26.8.9 HyperLogLog

Concept

A HyperLogLog (HLL) estimates the number of unique elements in a set using about 12 KB of memory, regardless of whether you add ten elements or ten billion, with a standard error of 0.81 percent. It cannot tell you whether a specific element was added; it only counts.

How it works

  • PFADD key element... adds elements; returns 1 if the estimate changed.
  • PFCOUNT key... returns the estimated cardinality (of the union if several keys are passed).
  • PFMERGE dest src... merges HLLs, so daily HLLs can be combined into a monthly count.
// analytics/unique-visitors.service.ts
async recordVisitor(day: string, visitorId: string): Promise<void> {
  await this.redis.pfadd(`uv:${day}`, visitorId);          // 12 KB per day, forever
}

async uniqueVisitorsLast7Days(days: string[]): Promise<number> {
  return this.redis.pfcount(...days.map((d) => `uv:${d}`)); // union estimate, one command
}

Use it for dashboards, "seen by N people", unique IPs per endpoint. Do not use it where 1 percent error matters (billing, quotas).

26.8.10 Bitmaps

Concept

A bitmap is a string treated as an array of bits. SETBIT key offset 1 sets one bit; BITCOUNT counts set bits; BITOP combines bitmaps with AND/OR/XOR. With user ids as offsets, a bitmap of 10 million users costs 1.25 MB.

How it works

  • SETBIT dau:2026-09-06 41 1 marks user 41 active today. GETBIT reads it. BITCOUNT dau:2026-09-06 counts active users.
  • BITOP AND result dau:2026-09-05 dau:2026-09-06 finds users active both days; BITCOUNT result counts them. BITOP OR over 30 daily bitmaps gives monthly active users exactly.
  • BITPOS key 1 finds the first set bit. BITFIELD reads and writes integers of arbitrary width at bit offsets, useful for packed counters.
  • Offsets must be integers, so this needs sequential integer user ids or a mapping. UUIDs need HLL or sets instead.
// analytics/dau.service.ts
markActive(userIntId: number, day: string): Promise<number> {
  return this.redis.setbit(`dau:${day}`, userIntId, 1);
}

async retained(dayA: string, dayB: string): Promise<number> {
  await this.redis.bitop('AND', `tmp:retained:${dayA}:${dayB}`, `dau:${dayA}`, `dau:${dayB}`);
  const n = await this.redis.bitcount(`tmp:retained:${dayA}:${dayB}`);
  await this.redis.unlink(`tmp:retained:${dayA}:${dayB}`);
  return n;
}

Also good for: feature flag rollouts by user id bucket, "has this user seen this onboarding step" flags (one bitmap per step), and daily check-in streaks.

26.8.11 Geo

Concept

Geo commands store members with a longitude and latitude (encoded as a geohash score inside a sorted set) and answer "what is within radius R of this point" in O(log N + M).

How it works

  • GEOADD drivers:online lon lat driverId adds or updates a position. Because it is a ZSET underneath, ZREM removes a driver and ZCARD counts them.
  • GEOSEARCH drivers:online FROMLONLAT lon lat BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 20 WITHDIST returns the 20 nearest drivers within 3 km with distances.
  • GEODIST key m1 m2 km, GEOPOS key member.
  • Positions update with the driver's location ping, typically every 3 to 5 seconds, so a ride-booking app with 50,000 online drivers does 10,000 to 16,000 GEOADDs per second, which one Redis instance handles easily.
// dispatch/driver-locations.service.ts
async updateLocation(driverId: string, lon: number, lat: number): Promise<void> {
  await this.redis.geoadd('drivers:online', lon, lat, driverId);
  await this.redis.set(`driver:lastseen:${driverId}`, Date.now(), 'PX', 30_000); // presence with its own TTL
}

async nearestDrivers(lon: number, lat: number, radiusKm = 3, limit = 20) {
  const rows = await this.redis.geosearch('drivers:online', 'FROMLONLAT', lon, lat, 'BYRADIUS', radiusKm, 'km', 'ASC', 'COUNT', limit, 'WITHDIST') as [string, string][];
  return rows.map(([driverId, dist]) => ({ driverId, distanceKm: Number(dist) }));
}

Members in a Geo ZSET have no individual TTL. A driver who goes offline without a clean disconnect stays in the set. The presence key with its own TTL handles that: a sweeper removes members whose presence key is gone, or the dispatcher checks presence for each candidate before offering a ride.

26.9 Distributed locks

Concept

A distributed lock lets one process among many claim exclusive rights to do something: run the nightly report, flush the view counters, process a specific order. Redis implements a simple lock with SET key token NX PX ms: the first caller sets the key and owns the lock; others see it already set; the TTL guarantees release if the owner dies.

Why does it exist?

Without a lock, every pod runs the cron job, three workers process the same order, and two requests both think they are the first to reserve the last item. A process-level mutex does not help across pods; you need shared state, and Redis is the cheapest shared state you have.

Mental model

Imagine a single key hanging on a hook by the storeroom door. Whoever takes the key has the room. The key has a note: "if not returned within 30 seconds, the janitor will cut a new one". That note is the TTL, and it is why the lock is not perfectly safe: if the holder is still inside when the janitor cuts a new key, two people are in the room.

How it works

  1. Acquire: SET lock:report:daily <random-token> NX PX 30000. OK means acquired; nil means someone holds it.
  2. Do the work, ideally in far less time than the TTL.
  3. Release with compare-and-delete in Lua: if GET == token then DEL. A plain DEL could delete another holder's lock if yours had already expired and been re-acquired.
  4. TTL versus job duration: if the job can run longer than the TTL, either extend the lock periodically from a heartbeat (a Lua PEXPIRE if the token matches) or design the job to be safe under duplicate execution. The lock alone does not guarantee mutual exclusion once its TTL passes.
  5. Fencing tokens: a monotonically increasing number handed out with each lock acquisition (an INCR on a counter). The protected resource (say PostgreSQL) rejects writes carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen. This makes a stale lock holder's late write harmless, and it is the only way to make a TTL-based lock genuinely safe. Redis alone cannot fence; the store being protected must check the token.
  6. Redlock is an algorithm that acquires the lock on a majority of N independent Redis nodes to survive a single node failure. Its safety has been criticized (Martin Kleppmann's analysis) because it relies on bounded clock drift and bounded pauses, neither of which a GC pause or a VM freeze respects. The honest position: Redlock is fine for efficiency locks (avoid doing work twice) and not sufficient for correctness locks (never do this twice) without fencing.
  7. When PostgreSQL is the better lock: if the thing you are protecting lives in PostgreSQL, lock it there. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the order row gives you a lock that is released exactly at commit or rollback, with no TTL guessing, no token, and no second system. pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('report:daily')) gives a named lock with the same properties. Redis locks are for coordinating work whose state is not in a database, or where holding a database transaction open for the duration would be too long.

NestJS example

// redis/redis-lock.service.ts
import { Injectable, Inject, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { REDIS } from './redis.module';

const RELEASE = `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0`;
const EXTEND  = `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) end return 0`;

@Injectable()
export class RedisLockService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(RedisLockService.name);
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('lockRelease', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: RELEASE });
    this.redis.defineCommand('lockExtend', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: EXTEND });
  }

  // Runs fn only if the lock is acquired. Heartbeats to extend while fn runs. Fails closed if Redis is down.
  async withLock<T>(name: string, ttlMs: number, fn: (fence: number) => Promise<T>): Promise<T | null> {
    const key = `lock:${name}`;
    const token = randomUUID();
    const got = await this.redis.set(key, token, 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');
    if (got !== 'OK') return null;
    const fence = await this.redis.incr(`fence:${name}`);   // monotonically increasing fencing token

    const client = this.redis as Redis & {
      lockRelease(k: string, t: string): Promise<number>;
      lockExtend(k: string, t: string, ttl: number): Promise<number>;
    };
    const heartbeat = setInterval(async () => {
      const ok = await client.lockExtend(key, token, ttlMs).catch(() => 0);
      if (!ok) this.logger.error(`lost lock ${name} while working; results may be duplicated`);
    }, Math.floor(ttlMs / 3));

    try {
      return await fn(fence);
    } finally {
      clearInterval(heartbeat);
      await client.lockRelease(key, token).catch(() => undefined);
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The same coordination without Redis, for a job whose state is in the database. The advisory lock is released automatically at transaction end, even on crash, because the session dies.

BEGIN;
-- Returns immediately with false if another session holds it; no TTL needed.
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('report:daily')) AS acquired;
-- if acquired: do the work in this transaction
INSERT INTO daily_reports (report_date, total_cents)
SELECT current_date, sum(total_cents) FROM orders WHERE created_at::date = current_date - 1;
COMMIT;  -- lock released here, exactly when the work is durable

And the fencing token consumer side: a table that refuses stale writers.

UPDATE report_runs
   SET status = 'done', finished_at = now(), fence = $1
 WHERE report_date = $2 AND fence < $1;   -- a stale holder with a lower fence updates zero rows

Failure scenario

The nightly settlement job takes a Redis lock with a 60 second TTL and normally runs in 20 seconds. One night PostgreSQL is slow and the job runs for 95 seconds. At second 60 the lock expires; a second pod, retrying on its own schedule, acquires it and starts the same settlement. Both write settlement rows; finance sees doubled payouts. The fix was three things: a heartbeat that extends the lock, a fencing token checked by the settlements insert, and a unique constraint on (merchant_id, settlement_date) so that duplicate runs fail loudly instead of silently doubling. The unique constraint was the one that would have saved them on its own.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first question is "what are we protecting, and where does it live?" If it lives in PostgreSQL, lock it in PostgreSQL. If the lock is for efficiency (do not run the same expensive job twice), a Redis SET NX with a TTL is fine and the occasional duplicate is a cost, not a bug. If the lock is for correctness, a lock is not enough by itself; the operation must be idempotent or fenced, because every lock with a timeout can be held by two parties. A senior never lets a lock be the only line of defense against a double payout.

Common mistakes

  • Releasing with DEL instead of compare-and-delete.
  • TTL shorter than the job's p99 and no heartbeat.
  • Using a lock to protect a database row that SELECT FOR UPDATE would protect better.
  • Failing open when Redis is down ("could not get lock, run anyway"). For locks, fail closed: skip the run and alert.

26.10 Atomic operations and the source-of-truth question

Concept

Because Redis executes one command at a time, every single command is atomic: INCR cannot lose an increment, SETNX cannot be won by two clients, HINCRBY on stock cannot interleave. Lua scripts extend atomicity to a sequence with logic: read, compare, write, all as one unit.

How it works

  • INCR, DECR, INCRBY, INCRBYFLOAT: numeric read-modify-write in one step. Use for counters, quotas, sequence numbers.
  • SETNX (or SET ... NX): claim a key once. Use for dedup and locks.
  • MULTI/EXEC: queue several commands and run them without interleaving. No branching, but WATCH key gives optimistic concurrency: EXEC fails if a watched key changed. Rarely worth it versus a Lua script.
  • Lua scripts: check-and-set. The canonical example is inventory reservation: "if stock >= qty then stock = stock - qty, return remaining, else return -1".
// inventory/redis-reservation.service.ts
// KEYS[1] = stock key, ARGV[1] = qty. Returns remaining stock or -1 if insufficient.
const RESERVE = `
  local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
  local qty = tonumber(ARGV[1])
  if stock < qty then return -1 end
  return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
`;

async tryReserve(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<number> {
  const client = this.redis as Redis & { reserve(k: string, q: number): Promise<number> };
  return client.reserve(`stock:flash:${sku}`, qty);
}

The honest answer about source of truth

Reserving stock in Redis is fast (0.3 ms, 50,000 reservations per second on one core) and atomic. It is also volatile: a failover loses the last few writes, noeviction OOM rejects the decrement, an operator's FLUSHALL sets every stock to zero. If Redis says 0 left and PostgreSQL says 40, which is right? You must decide before you build.

The pattern that works in practice for a flash sale:

  1. PostgreSQL holds inventory.quantity_on_hand as truth.
  2. At sale start, load the sellable quantity into stock:flash:{sku} in Redis.
  3. The hot path reserves in Redis with the Lua script. A -1 returns "sold out" in under a millisecond without touching PostgreSQL; this is what protects the database from 100,000 people clicking at once.
  4. A successful reservation creates an order in PostgreSQL inside a transaction that also decrements quantity_on_hand with a CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0) constraint. If that fails (Redis and PostgreSQL disagree), the request fails and a compensating INCRBY returns the Redis unit.
  5. A reconciliation job compares Redis and PostgreSQL every minute and logs drift.

Redis is the gatekeeper; PostgreSQL is the judge. For normal traffic (tens of orders per second), skip Redis entirely and use UPDATE inventory SET quantity_reserved = quantity_reserved + $1 WHERE product_id = $2 AND quantity_on_hand - quantity_reserved >= $1 with a row lock; it is simpler and cannot disagree with itself. See Part 20 — Database Transactions for the locking detail.

26.11 Rate limiting in Redis

Concept

A rate limiter bounds how many requests a caller may make in a time window. Redis is the natural place for it because the counter must be shared across pods and updated atomically under high concurrency.

How it works

Four algorithms, each with a Redis shape:

Algorithm Redis shape Accuracy Memory Notes
Fixed window INCR rl:{key}:{windowStart} + EXPIRE Allows 2x burst at window edges One int per key per window Simplest; fine for coarse limits
Sliding window log ZADD timestamp per request; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE old; ZCARD Exact One member per request in window Costly at high limits (1,000 per minute means 1,000 members)
Sliding window counter Two fixed windows weighted by overlap Close to exact, no edge burst Two ints Best default for API limits
Token bucket Lua: refill tokens by elapsed time, take one if available Exact, allows configured bursts Two fields in a hash Best for smoothing and per-client burst allowances

Sliding window log in Lua, exact and atomic:

// KEYS[1] = zset key, ARGV[1] = now ms, ARGV[2] = window ms, ARGV[3] = limit, ARGV[4] = unique member
const SLIDING_LOG = `
  redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1] - ARGV[2])
  local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
  if count >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then return 0 end
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[4])
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
  return 1
`;

Token bucket in Lua, the one to use for "100 requests per second with bursts of 200":

// KEYS[1] = hash key, ARGV[1] = now ms, ARGV[2] = capacity, ARGV[3] = refill per second, ARGV[4] = tokens requested
const TOKEN_BUCKET = `
  local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
  local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[2])
  local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
  local elapsed = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[1]) - ts) / 1000
  tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[2]), tokens + elapsed * tonumber(ARGV[3]))
  local allowed = 0
  if tokens >= tonumber(ARGV[4]) then tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[4]); allowed = 1 end
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[1])
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(tonumber(ARGV[2]) / tonumber(ARGV[3]) * 2000))
  return allowed
`;

NestJS example

A guard using the token bucket, and @nestjs/throttler with Redis storage for the common case.

// rate-limit/token-bucket.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, HttpException, HttpStatus, Injectable, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Injectable()
export class TokenBucketGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('tokenBucket', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: TOKEN_BUCKET });
  }

  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const subject = req.user?.id ?? req.ip;                         // per user if authenticated, else per IP
    const client = this.redis as Redis & { tokenBucket(k: string, now: number, cap: number, rate: number, n: number): Promise<number> };
    let allowed: number;
    try {
      allowed = await client.tokenBucket(`rl:tb:${subject}`, Date.now(), 200, 100, 1);
    } catch {
      return true;                                                   // Redis down: fail open for public API, log it
    }
    if (!allowed) throw new HttpException('Too Many Requests', HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS);
    return true;
  }
}
// app.module.ts: @nestjs/throttler with Redis storage
import { ThrottlerModule, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ThrottlerStorageRedisService } from '@nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis';
import { APP_GUARD } from '@nestjs/core';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
      throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: 60_000, limit: 300 }],  // 300 per minute
      storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL!)),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }],
})
export class AppModule {}

@nestjs/throttler keys by IP through getTracker by default; override it in a subclass of ThrottlerGuard to key by user id or API key, otherwise every user behind one corporate NAT shares a limit.

Fail open or fail closed?

When Redis is unavailable, a rate limiter must choose. Fail open means unlimited traffic during the outage; for a public read API that is usually right, because the alternative is a full outage caused by a cache. Fail closed means rejecting everything; for a login endpoint, an OTP sender or a payment initiation, that is right, because unlimited attempts during an outage is an attack window. Make the choice per endpoint, in code, with a log line so the outage is visible.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a SET NX lock not sufficient for correctness, and what makes it sufficient? Expected: TTL expiry lets two holders exist; fencing tokens checked by the protected resource.
  2. Reserve flash-sale stock in Redis or PostgreSQL? Expected: Redis as gatekeeper for the burst, PostgreSQL as truth with a CHECK constraint, reconciliation between them; plain PostgreSQL for normal traffic.
  3. Compare sliding window log and token bucket. Expected: log is exact but memory grows with the limit; bucket is O(1) memory and allows configured bursts.
  4. Redis dies during a rate-limited login flow. What should happen? Expected: fail closed for auth-sensitive endpoints, fail open for public reads, decided per endpoint.
  5. Why does Redlock attract criticism? Expected: it assumes bounded clock drift and process pauses; a GC pause can make a client believe it holds an expired lock. Efficiency yes, correctness only with fencing.
  6. Streams versus Pub/Sub versus Lists for a job queue? Expected: Pub/Sub loses messages; Lists lack acks and groups; Streams have both; a broker when you need more retention, tooling or throughput.

Practical exercise

Implement a per-API-key token bucket rate limiter (capacity 50, refill 10 per second) as a NestJS guard, backed by the Lua script above. Acceptance criteria: (a) a burst of 50 requests in 10 ms all pass, the 51st returns 429 with a Retry-After header computed from the refill rate; (b) with two app instances behind a load balancer the limit is shared; (c) with Redis stopped, /public/* routes pass and /auth/* routes return 503 with a logged reason; (d) a Jest test with a fake clock proves the refill arithmetic.

26.12 Everyday Redis patterns in a NestJS backend

These are the five things almost every production NestJS service ends up putting in Redis. Each one is short because the structures were covered above; the value here is the shape that survives production.

26.12.1 Session store

Concept

A session is server-side state tied to a session id in a cookie. Redis is the standard session store because every pod must see the same session, reads happen on every request, and sessions expire naturally.

How it works

The session id is a random 128-bit value; the Redis key is sess:v1:{id}; the value is a JSON hash of user id, roles, CSRF token and issued-at; the TTL is the idle timeout, refreshed on access (sliding) or fixed (absolute). Logout deletes the key. "Log out everywhere" needs an index: a set user:sessions:{userId} of session ids, deleted together.

// auth/session-store.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class SessionStore {
  private readonly ttlMs = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 min idle timeout
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async create(userId: string, data: SessionData): Promise<string> {
    const sid = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
    await this.redis.multi()
      .set(`sess:v1:${sid}`, JSON.stringify({ userId, ...data, issuedAt: Date.now() }), 'PX', this.ttlMs)
      .sadd(`user:sessions:${userId}`, sid)
      .expire(`user:sessions:${userId}`, 30 * 86_400)
      .exec();
    return sid;
  }

  // GETEX reads and slides the TTL in one round trip.
  async touch(sid: string): Promise<SessionData | null> {
    const raw = await this.redis.getex(`sess:v1:${sid}`, 'PX', this.ttlMs);
    return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;
  }

  async revokeAll(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    const sids = await this.redis.smembers(`user:sessions:${userId}`); // bounded: a user has few sessions
    if (sids.length) await this.redis.unlink(...sids.map((s) => `sess:v1:${s}`), `user:sessions:${userId}`);
  }
}

A session store is a store, not a cache: noeviction and AOF persistence, on its own Redis instance. With allkeys-lru a busy day logs users out at random, and that incident is common enough to deserve its own sentence.

26.12.2 Idempotency-key store

Concept

An idempotency key lets a client safely retry POST /payments without creating two payments. The server remembers the key, the request fingerprint and the response, and replays the response for a repeat.

How it works

  1. On request: SET idem:v1:{key} {status:"processing"} NX PX 86400000. If nil, another request with this key is in flight or done: read the stored value; if processing, return 409; if complete, return the stored response.
  2. Process the request. Store { status: "done", fingerprint, statusCode, body } under the same key.
  3. If processing fails with a non-retryable error, store the error response too. If it fails with a transient error, delete the key so the client can retry.
  4. The window is the TTL (24 hours is common). A retry after that creates a new operation; document it.

For payments and orders, the idempotency record belongs in PostgreSQL in the same transaction as the business write (Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency covers the inbox table). Redis is fine as a fast first check in front of it, and sufficient on its own for non-financial operations.

// idempotency/idempotency.interceptor.ts (excerpt)
async intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Promise<Observable<unknown>> {
  const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
  const key = req.headers['idempotency-key'];
  if (!key) return next.handle();
  const redisKey = `idem:v1:${req.user.id}:${key}`;      // scope to the caller so keys cannot collide across users
  const claimed = await this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify({ status: 'processing' }), 'PX', 86_400_000, 'NX');
  if (claimed !== 'OK') {
    const stored = JSON.parse((await this.redis.get(redisKey)) ?? '{}');
    if (stored.status === 'processing') throw new ConflictException('Request in progress');
    ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().status(stored.statusCode);
    return of(stored.body);                                  // replay
  }
  return next.handle().pipe(
    tap(async (body) => this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify({ status: 'done', statusCode: 201, body }), 'PX', 86_400_000)),
    catchError(async (err) => { await this.redis.del(redisKey); throw err; }),
  );
}

26.12.3 Feature flags and config cache

Concept

Flags and configuration are tiny, read on every request, and changed rarely by humans. They are the textbook hot key, so the pattern is the two-level cache from 26.6: a hash in Redis (flags:v1 with one field per flag), a 2 second in-process cache, and a Pub/Sub broadcast on change.

// flags/flags.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class FlagsService implements OnModuleInit {
  private local: Record<string, string> = {};
  private loadedAt = 0;
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis, @Inject(REDIS_SUBSCRIBER) private readonly sub: Redis) {}

  async onModuleInit() {
    await this.sub.subscribe('flags:changed');
    this.sub.on('message', () => { this.loadedAt = 0; });     // force reload on next read
  }

  async isEnabled(name: string, userId?: string): Promise<boolean> {
    if (Date.now() - this.loadedAt > 2000) {
      try { this.local = await this.redis.hgetall('flags:v1'); this.loadedAt = Date.now(); }
      catch { /* keep the last known flags: fail open to the previous state */ }
    }
    const raw = this.local[name];
    if (!raw) return false;
    const flag = JSON.parse(raw) as { enabled: boolean; percentage?: number };
    if (!flag.enabled) return false;
    if (flag.percentage === undefined || !userId) return flag.enabled;
    const bucket = parseInt(createHash('sha1').update(`${name}:${userId}`).digest('hex').slice(0, 8), 16) % 100;
    return bucket < flag.percentage;                          // stable per user, spreads evenly
  }
}

The source of truth for flags is a feature_flags table in PostgreSQL edited through an admin endpoint that writes the row, updates the hash and publishes. Redis is the distribution mechanism, not the store.

26.12.4 Leaderboards

The ZSET from 26.8.4, with three production details: use ZADD ... GT so a lower score never overwrites a higher one when events arrive out of order; keep one ZSET per period (lb:weekly:2026-W36) with a TTL so old boards expire; and page with ZRANGE ... REV LIMIT offset count plus MGET for display names rather than storing names in the ZSET.

async recordScore(period: string, userId: string, score: number): Promise<void> {
  await this.redis.multi().zadd(`lb:${period}`, 'GT', score, userId).expire(`lb:${period}`, 60 * 86_400).exec();
}

async top(period: string, offset = 0, count = 20) {
  const rows = await this.redis.zrange(`lb:${period}`, offset, offset + count - 1, 'REV', 'WITHSCORES');
  const out: { userId: string; score: number; rank: number }[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i += 2) out.push({ userId: rows[i], score: Number(rows[i + 1]), rank: offset + i / 2 + 1 });
  return out;
}

async rankOf(period: string, userId: string): Promise<number | null> {
  const r = await this.redis.zrevrank(`lb:${period}`, userId);
  return r === null ? null : r + 1;
}

26.13 NestJS integration

26.13.1 CacheModule, CacheInterceptor and their limits

Concept

@nestjs/cache-manager wraps the cache-manager library and gives you an injectable Cache plus an interceptor that caches whole HTTP responses. With a Redis store it is the quickest way to cache read endpoints, and the quickest way to leak one user's data to another if you do not understand its keying.

How it works

The module is configured with a Keyv Redis store (cache-manager v6 and @nestjs/cache-manager v3):

// app.module.ts
import { CacheModule } from '@nestjs/cache-manager';
import { Keyv } from 'keyv';
import KeyvRedis from '@keyv/redis';

@Module({
  imports: [
    CacheModule.registerAsync({
      isGlobal: true,
      useFactory: async () => ({
        stores: [new Keyv({ store: new KeyvRedis(process.env.REDIS_URL), namespace: 'app' })],
        ttl: 60_000, // ms
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

CacheInterceptor applied to a controller or route caches responses for GET requests, keyed by the request URL (path plus query string), for the TTL from @CacheTTL() or the module default, under the key from @CacheKey() if given.

@Controller('products')
@UseInterceptors(CacheInterceptor)
export class ProductsController {
  @Get(':id')
  @CacheTTL(300_000)
  findOne(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) { return this.products.findOne(id); }

  @Get('top')
  @CacheKey('products:top')   // fixed key: every query-string variant shares it, which may or may not be what you want
  @CacheTTL(30_000)
  top() { return this.products.top(); }
}

Its limitations, each of which has caused a real incident:

  • Keyed by URL only. An endpoint whose response depends on the Authorization header, an Accept-Language header or a tenant header serves user A's data to user B. Override trackBy(context) in a subclass to include the user id, or do not use the interceptor on authenticated endpoints.
  • Caches the whole response body, including errors if your handler returns them as values rather than throwing. Only GET is cached by default (isRequestCacheable is overridable), which is correct.
  • No invalidation hook. Writes must call cache.del(key) with the exact key the interceptor built, which for URL-keyed entries is the request path. Teams get this wrong and end up relying on TTL alone.
  • No stampede protection, no negative caching, no jitter. Ten pods and a hot endpoint expire together.
  • Serializes with JSON and stores whatever the handler returned; Date fields come back as strings, BigInt throws.

The senior position: use CacheInterceptor for public, unauthenticated, URL-determined read endpoints (category trees, public product pages, static lists). For everything else, cache in the service with ioredis where the key includes exactly the inputs that determine the output.

26.13.2 A custom RedisModule with ioredis

How it works

Three connections with different roles, configured from environment, with the client options that determine behaviour during an outage.

// redis/redis.module.ts
import { Global, Module, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis, { RedisOptions } from 'ioredis';

export const REDIS = Symbol('REDIS');                     // general commands
export const REDIS_SUBSCRIBER = Symbol('REDIS_SUBSCRIBER'); // Pub/Sub only
export const REDIS_BLOCKING = Symbol('REDIS_BLOCKING');     // BRPOP, XREADGROUP BLOCK

function options(): RedisOptions {
  return {
    host: process.env.REDIS_HOST,
    port: Number(process.env.REDIS_PORT ?? 6379),
    password: process.env.REDIS_PASSWORD,
    tls: process.env.REDIS_TLS === 'true' ? {} : undefined,
    connectTimeout: 2000,
    commandTimeout: 250,          // a cache call slower than this is a miss, not a wait
    maxRetriesPerRequest: 1,      // fail fast; the app decides what to do
    enableOfflineQueue: false,    // do not buffer commands while disconnected; fail immediately
    keepAlive: 10_000,
    lazyConnect: false,
    retryStrategy: (attempt) => Math.min(50 * 2 ** attempt, 5000), // reconnect with capped backoff
    reconnectOnError: (err) => err.message.includes('READONLY'),    // after a failover, reconnect to the new primary
  };
}

function createClient(role: string): Redis {
  const logger = new Logger(`Redis:${role}`);
  const client = new Redis(role === 'blocking' ? { ...options(), commandTimeout: undefined } : options());
  client.on('error', (err) => logger.error(err.message));
  client.on('reconnecting', () => logger.warn('reconnecting'));
  client.on('ready', () => logger.log('ready'));
  return client;
}

@Global()
@Module({
  providers: [
    { provide: REDIS, useFactory: () => createClient('main') },
    { provide: REDIS_SUBSCRIBER, useFactory: () => createClient('subscriber') },
    { provide: REDIS_BLOCKING, useFactory: () => createClient('blocking') },
  ],
  exports: [REDIS, REDIS_SUBSCRIBER, REDIS_BLOCKING],
})
export class RedisModule implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly main: Redis,
    @Inject(REDIS_SUBSCRIBER) private readonly sub: Redis,
    @Inject(REDIS_BLOCKING) private readonly blocking: Redis,
  ) {}

  // Graceful shutdown: QUIT waits for pending replies; disconnect() would drop them.
  async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    await Promise.allSettled([this.main.quit(), this.sub.quit(), this.blocking.quit()]);
  }
}

Why these options matter:

  • commandTimeout: 250: without it, a stalled Redis (blocked by a slow command, or a network black hole) makes every request wait for the TCP timeout, which is minutes. With it, the cache path fails in 250 ms and falls through to PostgreSQL. Blocking commands need it disabled.
  • enableOfflineQueue: false: with the default true, commands issued while disconnected queue in memory and all fire at once on reconnect, which is a thundering herd against a recovering Redis and a memory leak during a long outage.
  • maxRetriesPerRequest: 1: ioredis retries a command on reconnect up to this many times. For a cache, failing fast is better than retrying.
  • Connection pool: ioredis multiplexes all commands on one TCP connection, which is what Redis prefers. You do not need a pool for ordinary commands; you need separate connections only for subscribers and blocking commands, which is why the module has three. In Cluster mode, new Redis.Cluster([...], { redisOptions: options() }) manages one connection per node.
  • Remember to call app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts, or onApplicationShutdown never runs.

26.13.3 Health checks

Terminus has no Redis indicator built in; write one with HealthIndicatorService. Decide whether Redis is part of readiness: for a pure cache it usually is not (the app works without it), for a session store it is.

// health/redis.health.ts
import { Injectable, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicatorService } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Injectable()
export class RedisHealthIndicator {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly his: HealthIndicatorService) {}

  async isHealthy(key = 'redis') {
    const indicator = this.his.check(key);
    const start = Date.now();
    try {
      await this.redis.ping();
      return indicator.up({ latencyMs: Date.now() - start, status: this.redis.status });
    } catch (err) {
      return indicator.down({ error: (err as Error).message, status: this.redis.status });
    }
  }
}

26.13.4 Circuit breaking to Redis

Concept

When Redis is degraded, every cache call pays the 250 ms timeout before falling through. At 1,000 RPS that is 250 concurrent requests waiting on nothing. A circuit breaker counts failures and, past a threshold, skips Redis entirely for a cooling-off period, then probes.

// redis/redis-circuit.ts: a small breaker; the opossum library does this with metrics if you prefer
export class RedisCircuit {
  private failures = 0;
  private openUntil = 0;
  constructor(private readonly threshold = 5, private readonly cooldownMs = 10_000) {}

  async run<T>(op: () => Promise<T>, fallback: () => T): Promise<T> {
    if (Date.now() < this.openUntil) return fallback();       // open: skip Redis
    try {
      const result = await op();
      this.failures = 0;                                        // success closes the circuit
      return result;
    } catch {
      if (++this.failures >= this.threshold) this.openUntil = Date.now() + this.cooldownMs;
      return fallback();
    }
  }
}
// usage: this.circuit.run(() => this.redis.get(key), () => null)

Expose the breaker state as a metric (redis_circuit_open 0 or 1). An open circuit means PostgreSQL is taking 100 percent of reads; you want to know immediately.

26.14 Observability

Concept

A cache you cannot measure is a cache you cannot trust. The four numbers on a Redis dashboard are hit ratio, latency, evictions and memory. Everything else is context.

How it works

From INFO (and exported by redis_exporter to Prometheus):

Metric Source Healthy Alert Meaning
Hit ratio keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses); exporter redis_keyspace_hits_total, redis_keyspace_misses_total 90 to 99 percent for a catalog cache Drops 10 points in 5 min Cold cache, key version change, penetration attack, or TTL too short
Latency (client side) Histogram around every ioredis call in your app p99 under 2 ms same AZ p99 over 10 ms Slow command blocking, network, CPU saturation
Server-side latency LATENCY LATEST, latency-monitor-threshold 10 Empty Any event over 10 ms Blocking command, fork, AOF fsync stall
Evictions evicted_keys; exporter redis_evicted_keys_total 0 for a store; low and steady for a cache Sudden rise At maxmemory; working set larger than memory
Expired keys expired_keys Steady Spike Avalanche in progress
Memory used_memory, maxmemory; exporter redis_memory_used_bytes, redis_memory_max_bytes Under 80 percent of maxmemory Over 90 percent Approaching eviction or OOM
Fragmentation mem_fragmentation_ratio 1.0 to 1.5 Over 1.5 or under 1.0 Fragmentation (enable activedefrag) or swapping
Clients connected_clients, blocked_clients, rejected_connections Stable rejected_connections rising Hit maxclients; connection leak in the app
Replication master_repl_offset minus replica offset; master_link_status Lag under 1 MB Link down Replica behind; failover would lose data
Slowlog SLOWLOG GET 25 (slowlog-log-slower-than 10000 microseconds) Empty Any entry The command name tells you the culprit
Keyspace INFO keyspace: keys and keys with expires per db; exporter redis_db_keys, redis_db_keys_expiring Keys with expires equals keys, for a cache Keys without TTL growing Someone is SETting without PX
Ops per second instantaneous_ops_per_sec; exporter redis_commands_processed_total Depends Sudden drop to zero Redis blocked or app disconnected

Instrumenting the app side is the part people skip. Wrap the client so every call records duration and outcome with the command name as a label; a redis_client_duration_seconds histogram and a redis_client_errors_total counter answer "is it Redis or is it us" in one glance. Also count hits and misses per key namespace (cache_requests_total{namespace="products",result="hit"}), because a global hit ratio hides a single broken namespace.

Production scenario

A dashboard shows hit ratio falling from 96 percent to 71 percent over ten minutes with no deploy. redis_db_keys_expiring is flat, evicted_keys is climbing at 400 per second, memory is pinned at maxmemory. Someone has started caching search results keyed by raw query string: cardinality exploded, evictions pushed out the product keys, and PostgreSQL CPU doubled. The namespace metric points at search:* in one query. The fix is a hashed, canonicalized key with a 60 second TTL, and a per-namespace memory budget checked in review.

26.15 Edge cases and failure modes

Each entry: what happens, how you notice, what to do.

  • Redis unavailable, cache use case. Reads fall through to PostgreSQL. Fail open with a short commandTimeout, a circuit breaker and a load test that proves PostgreSQL survives 100 percent of traffic for the outage duration, or add a longer-TTL L1 to absorb it.
  • Redis unavailable, rate limiter. Decide per endpoint: public reads fail open, auth and payment endpoints fail closed with a 503 and an alert.
  • Redis unavailable, locks. Fail closed. "Could not acquire lock" means skip the run, never "run anyway".
  • Redis unavailable, session store. Every user is effectively logged out. This is why the session store gets Sentinel or Cluster with replicas and AOF, and why readiness depends on it.
  • Stale cache after a failed invalidation. A DEL that failed during a Redis blip leaves an old value until TTL. Log failed deletes at error level, retry them from an outbox-style table, and keep the TTL short enough that the business tolerates the window.
  • Hot key. One shard at 100 percent CPU while others idle; --hotkeys names it. L1 cache with short TTL, key replication across slots, coalescing.
  • Stampede after deploy (cold cache). A version bump or a Redis restart empties the cache and PostgreSQL takes the full miss storm. Warm-up in onApplicationBootstrap, gated readiness, single-flight, and never FLUSHALL.
  • Eviction storm at maxmemory. evicted_keys climbs, hit ratio collapses, PostgreSQL load rises. Find the namespace that grew, fix its cardinality or TTL, raise maxmemory if the working set legitimately grew.
  • noeviction OOM write errors. Writes fail with OOM command not allowed. Reads still work, so the app looks half alive: sessions cannot be created, idempotency keys cannot be claimed. Alert on memory over 85 percent long before this, and handle the error explicitly (for a session store, that is a 503; for a cache, that is a skipped SET).
  • Big key blocking. SLOWLOG shows DEL or SMEMBERS at 300 ms; every client sees timeouts simultaneously. UNLINK, lazy freeing, split the key, cap value sizes at write time.
  • Cluster MOVED / ASK errors. A non-cluster client, or a client with a stale slot map during resharding. Use Redis.Cluster, which follows redirections; if errors persist after a resharding, restart clients so they refresh.
  • Cluster CROSSSLOT errors. A multi-key command or script spans slots. Hash tags, or restructure into single-key operations.
  • Failover losing recent writes. Async replication means the last few milliseconds of acknowledged writes on the old primary are gone. For caches this is a few misses. For counters, idempotency keys and locks, it is a correctness gap: a lock acquired just before failover may not exist on the new primary. Use WAIT 1 100 for the few writes that matter, and design the consumer to survive a lost key.
  • TTL and clock issues. Redis uses its own monotonic-ish clock for expiry; a VM clock jump can expire everything at once or nothing for a while. Application-side timestamps in values (staleAt, ZSET scores) come from pod clocks that can disagree by hundreds of milliseconds without NTP discipline. Never compare a Redis-side time with a pod-side time for correctness.
  • Serialization version mismatch after deploy. Old pods write v3 shape under a v3 key and new pods expect a new field. Symptom: undefined reads and TypeErrors on half the pods during a rolling deploy. Bump the key version with every shape change; treat it as a schema migration.
  • Cache poisoning by caching an error response. A loader that returns a partial object or an error DTO instead of throwing gets cached for the full TTL. Symptom: an outage in a downstream service is "remembered" for 15 minutes after it recovers. Cache only successful, complete results; never cache exceptions; validate the shape before SET.
  • Negative cache hiding a newly created row. GET /products/8812 is negatively cached at 10:00:00; the product is created at 10:00:05; readers see 404 until the negative TTL expires. Delete the key in the create path, keep negative TTLs short, and do not negative-cache ids the client itself just generated (the same client creating then immediately reading is the common case).
  • Subscriber connection reused for commands. ERR only (P)SUBSCRIBE / (P)UNSUBSCRIBE / PING / QUIT / RESET allowed in this context. Dedicated connections per role.
  • Offline queue thundering herd. A long outage with the default enableOfflineQueue: true buffers hundreds of thousands of commands in pod memory and replays them on reconnect. Disable it for cache clients.
  • Pipeline partial failure. pipeline.exec() resolves even when some commands errored; the errors are inside the result array. Check each [err, value] pair.
  • Lua script too slow. A script iterating a large set blocks the server; SCRIPT KILL only works if the script has not written yet, otherwise it is SHUTDOWN NOSAVE. Keep scripts O(1) or O(small N).

26.16 Decision table: use case to Redis design

Use case Redis structure TTL Invalidation Redis-down behaviour
Product detail cache String (JSON) with versioned key 5 to 15 min plus jitter Delete after commit; double delete; CDC or event for cross-service writes Fail open to PostgreSQL; circuit breaker
Rendered menu / page fragment String 60 s plus jitter Event on any dependent write; TTL backstop Fail open
Search results String keyed by hashed canonical query 30 to 60 s TTL only Fail open
Negative "not found" String sentinel 30 to 60 s Delete on create Fail open
User session String (JSON) or Hash; noeviction, AOF Idle timeout, sliding via GETEX Delete on logout; set index for revoke-all Fail closed (503 or re-login); Redis is on the readiness path
Idempotency key (non-financial) String with NX 24 h None; TTL Fail closed for the operation (reject with 503) or fall back to PostgreSQL inbox
Idempotency key (financial) PostgreSQL inbox table; Redis as optional fast pre-check 24 h in Redis None Ignore Redis; PostgreSQL decides
Rate limit Token bucket Hash via Lua, or ZSET sliding log 2x window None; TTL Per endpoint: open for public reads, closed for auth and payments
Distributed lock (efficiency) String SET NX PX with token; heartbeat Job p99 times 2, extended Compare-and-delete on release Fail closed: skip the run
Distributed lock (correctness) Prefer PostgreSQL advisory lock or FOR UPDATE; Redis only with fencing Transaction scope Automatic at commit Not applicable
Counters (views, likes) Hash with HINCRBY, write-behind flush 24 h Flushed to PostgreSQL every 10 s Lose the unflushed window; document it
Inventory display count String 5 to 30 s TTL, or event on stock change Fail open
Inventory reservation (flash sale) String via Lua DECRBY guard Duration of the sale Reconciled with PostgreSQL each minute Fail closed: sale paused
Leaderboard ZSET with GT Period plus 60 days None; new period is a new key Return empty board; read model only
Delayed jobs ZSET score = run time, Lua claim None Removed on claim Use BullMQ; jobs wait
Event log / lightweight queue Stream with consumer groups, MAXLEN Trim by length XACK; DLQ stream AOF everysec; consumers reconnect
Cross-pod broadcast (invalidation, WebSocket fan-out) Pub/Sub None Not applicable Messages lost; L1 TTL covers it
Unique counts (dashboards) HyperLogLog 90 days None Read model only
Daily active users Bitmap 90 days None Read model only
Nearby drivers Geo ZSET plus presence keys Presence 30 s ZREM on offline; sweeper Fail closed for dispatch; retry
Feature flags, config Hash plus L1 plus Pub/Sub L1 2 s; hash none Publish on change; PostgreSQL is truth Keep last known values in L1

Senior Checklist — Part 26

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can state, per cached data type, how stale it may be and what happens when it is
  • I invalidate after commit, with double delete or versioned values, and a TTL as the backstop
  • I can prevent a stampede with a SET NX lock, single-flight and stale-while-revalidate
  • I add TTL jitter everywhere and never FLUSHALL in production
  • I can explain why KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a big set and DEL on a big key hurt every client
  • I run separate Redis instances for cache (allkeys-lru, no persistence) and store (noeviction, AOF)
  • I know what a Sentinel or Cluster failover loses and which of my keys care
  • I can pick the right data structure for a leaderboard, rate limiter, delayed queue, unique count and geo search
  • I release locks with compare-and-delete, extend them with a heartbeat, and fence writes where correctness matters
  • I know when PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE or an advisory lock is the better lock
  • My ioredis client has commandTimeout, enableOfflineQueue: false, a retryStrategy, and a graceful quit()
  • I have decided fail-open versus fail-closed for every Redis use in the service
  • I can read INFO, the slowlog and redis_exporter metrics and find a hot key, a big key or an eviction storm

Part 26 — Key Takeaways

  • A cache is a copy that is allowed to be wrong for a bounded time; write down the bound per data type and turn it into the TTL.
  • Cache the read, verify at the write: display from Redis, decide from PostgreSQL.
  • Cache-aside with delete-after-commit is the default; write-through for read-after-write data; write-behind only when losing seconds of writes is acceptable.
  • Invalidation is the hard part: events for freshness, TTL as the safety net, double delete or versioned values for the race.
  • Stampede, avalanche, penetration, hot keys and big keys each have a cheap fix (lock and single-flight, jitter, negative cache, L1 and replication, UNLINK and splitting); apply them before the incident.
  • Redis is single-threaded per command: one slow command is everyone's outage. SCAN not KEYS, UNLINK not DEL, scan collections, keep Lua short.
  • One Redis per role: cache instances evict, store instances refuse writes and persist.
  • Replication is asynchronous; a failover can lose the last writes. Design locks, counters and idempotency keys to survive that.
  • A lock with a TTL can be held by two parties; only idempotent operations or fencing tokens make it safe, and PostgreSQL is often the better lock.
  • SET NX PX plus Lua compare-and-delete, Lua check-and-set, ZSET sliding windows and token buckets cover locks, atomics and rate limiting; BullMQ and Streams cover queues before you need a broker.
  • The ioredis options commandTimeout, enableOfflineQueue: false and retryStrategy, plus a circuit breaker, decide how your app behaves during a Redis outage; the defaults decide badly.
  • Measure hit ratio per namespace, client-side latency, evictions and memory; the first sign of most cache incidents is one of those four moving.

Part 27 — Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS

27.1 Why asynchronous messaging exists

Every backend starts synchronous. A request comes in, the handler does everything it needs to do, and a response goes out. That model is simple and it works until the "everything" grows: POST /orders must charge the card, reserve stock, send an email, notify the warehouse, update analytics, and refresh the recommendation model. Each of those is a network call that can be slow, can fail, and has nothing to do with whether the customer's order was accepted. Messaging is how we take "the order was placed" and let the rest of the system react to it on its own time, at its own pace, with its own retries.

This part teaches the engineering under queues and topics first, then goes deep on the three brokers you will actually meet (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS), then spends most of its length on the thing that decides whether your system is correct: what happens when a message is delivered twice.

27.1.1 The four reasons to go asynchronous

Concept

Asynchronous messaging means a producer writes a message to a broker and moves on; a consumer reads it later. The producer does not wait for the consumer, does not know whether the consumer exists, and does not fail because the consumer failed.

Why does it exist?

Four distinct engineering problems, each solved by the same mechanism:

  1. Decoupling. The order service should not import the email service's client, know its URL, or break when it deploys. With a topic in between, the order service knows only the shape of OrderPlaced. Consumers can be added (a fraud check next quarter) without touching the producer.
  2. Buffering bursts. A flash sale produces 5,000 orders per minute for ten minutes. The warehouse system handles 500 per minute. Without a queue the warehouse call times out and orders fail. With a queue, orders are accepted instantly, the queue grows to 45,000 messages, and the warehouse drains it over ninety minutes. The queue is a shock absorber.
  3. Retry ownership. If the email provider is down, who retries? In a synchronous design, the order handler, which means the customer waits, or the retry is lost when the handler returns. With a queue, the consumer retries with backoff for as long as it takes, and the order was already accepted.
  4. Fan-out. One event, five interested parties. Synchronous fan-out means five calls in the handler and five ways to fail. A topic delivers the same message to each subscriber independently.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. The waiter (API handler) does not cook. They write the order on a ticket, clip it to the rail (the queue), and go back to the dining room. Cooks (consumers) pull tickets in order. If the grill is backed up, tickets wait on the rail; nobody stops taking orders. If a cook drops a plate, they remake it from the ticket; the waiter is not involved. A copy of the ticket also goes to the cashier and the inventory clerk (fan-out). The rail is the broker; the ticket is the message; the fact that the waiter never waits for the cook is asynchrony.

How it works

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"POST /orders"| API["Orders API"]
    API -->|"INSERT order, COMMIT"| PG["PostgreSQL"]
    API -->|"publish OrderPlaced"| T["Topic orders.events"]
    API -->|"201 Created in 40 ms"| C
    T --> PAY["Payments consumer"]
    T --> INV["Inventory consumer"]
    T --> MAIL["Email consumer"]
    T --> ANA["Analytics consumer"]
    PAY -->|"publish PaymentCaptured"| T2["Topic payments.events"]
