  1. The API validates the request and writes the order to PostgreSQL. This is the only thing the customer is waiting for.
  2. The API publishes OrderPlaced to a topic. (How to do that without losing or duplicating the event is the outbox pattern; see 27.11 and Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency.)
  3. The API responds. Total time: one database transaction plus one publish, about 40 ms.
  4. Each consumer group reads the event independently. Payments captures the card and publishes its own event. Inventory reserves stock. Email sends a confirmation. Analytics records the sale. If email is down for an hour, three of the four still happen, and email catches up later.

Practical example

Before messaging, the same POST /orders handler at a food-delivery company called payment (300 ms), the restaurant's tablet API (200 ms, 2 percent failure rate), a push notification service (150 ms) and an analytics HTTP endpoint (100 ms) in sequence. p50 was 800 ms, p99 was 4 seconds when the tablet API was slow, and 2 percent of orders failed because the tablet API failed after the card had been charged. After messaging, the handler writes the order and the outbox row in one transaction and responds in 35 ms; the tablet notification is a consumer with a retry policy; the failure rate on order placement dropped to under 0.01 percent; and the charged-but-failed case disappeared because the payment consumer is idempotent and the tablet consumer retries independently.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Asynchrony is not free. You trade a simple request-response for eventual consistency (the email arrives a second or a minute later), for a second infrastructure component to run, and for the duplicate-delivery problem that fills the second half of this part. A senior asks: does the caller need the result now? If yes (a price quote, a login), stay synchronous. If the caller needs only to know the request was accepted (an order, an upload, a report), go asynchronous. They also refuse to introduce a broker for one producer and one consumer in the same process; @nestjs/event-emitter or a BullMQ queue on the Redis they already run is enough until there is a second service.

27.2 Core concepts

The vocabulary in this section is shared across every broker. Learn it once and the differences between Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS become configuration details.

27.2.1 Queue versus topic

Concept

A queue delivers each message to exactly one of its consumers. Many workers read the same queue, and each message is processed once (in principle). This is work distribution: "someone, generate this thumbnail".

A topic delivers each message to every subscriber. Each subscriber (or subscriber group) gets its own copy. This is publish/subscribe: "everyone who cares, an order was placed".

Mental model

A queue is the ticket rail in the kitchen: one cook takes each ticket. A topic is the announcement over the PA: everyone hears it, and each department decides what to do.

How it works

flowchart TB
    subgraph Queue
        QP["Producer"] --> Q["thumbnails queue"]
        Q -->|"msg 1"| W1["Worker 1"]
        Q -->|"msg 2"| W2["Worker 2"]
        Q -->|"msg 3"| W1
    end
    subgraph Topic
        TP["Producer"] --> T["orders.events topic"]
        T -->|"every msg"| G1["Payments group"]
        T -->|"every msg"| G2["Email group"]
        T -->|"every msg"| G3["Analytics group"]
    end

In Kafka, a topic with consumer groups gives both: within a group, partitions are split among members (queue behaviour); across groups, every group sees every message (topic behaviour). In RabbitMQ, an exchange fans out to queues (topic behaviour) and each queue is consumed competitively (queue behaviour). In AWS, SNS is the topic and SQS is the queue, and you wire them together. Every broker is these two ideas composed.

27.2.2 Event, command and message

Concept

A message is the envelope: bytes plus metadata that a broker moves from producer to consumer. What the bytes mean is up to you, and the two meanings that matter are:

  • An event states that something happened: OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured, StockDepleted. Past tense. The producer does not know or care who listens. Events go on topics.
  • A command asks a specific party to do something: ReserveStock, SendEmail, GenerateInvoice. Imperative. The producer expects exactly one handler to act. Commands go on queues.

Why does it exist?

The distinction decides ownership. An event's producer owns the fact; consumers own their reactions. A command's sender owns the intent; the handler owns the execution and its failure. Mixing them causes design rot: an "event" called SendWelcomeEmail published by the user service means the user service has decided what email should do, which is coupling wearing an event costume.

Practical example

The order service publishes OrderPlaced (event). The inventory service consumes it and, inside its own logic, decides to enqueue ReserveStock (command) to its own worker queue, then publishes StockReserved or StockReservationFailed (events). The order service consumes those to move the order to confirmed or cancelled. Every arrow has an owner.

Naming rule: events are Noun + past-tense Verb (OrderPlaced); commands are Verb + Noun (ReserveStock). Topic names are dotted, lowercase, owned by the producer: orders.events, payments.events. Queue names say who consumes and why: inventory.reserve-stock.

27.2.3 Producer, consumer, broker, partition, consumer group, offset

Concept

  • Producer: the code that writes messages. It chooses the topic, the key and the payload.
  • Broker: the server that stores messages and hands them to consumers. Kafka brokers, RabbitMQ nodes, the SQS service.
  • Consumer: the code that reads and processes messages.
  • Partition: a topic split into independent, ordered logs. It is the unit of parallelism (one consumer per partition at a time within a group) and the unit of ordering (messages in one partition are read in the order written; across partitions there is no order).
  • Consumer group: a named set of consumers that share a topic's partitions between them. The broker tracks the group's position. Two groups on one topic each get every message.
  • Offset: a consumer's position in a partition, an integer that increases with each message. Committing an offset tells the broker "I have finished everything before this".

Mental model

Imagine a library of logbooks (partitions) for one subject (topic). Each logbook is written front to back and never edited. A reading club (consumer group) assigns one member per logbook; each member keeps a bookmark (offset). Two clubs read the same logbooks independently with their own bookmarks. If a member leaves, their logbooks and bookmarks are handed to someone else in the club.

How it works

topic: orders.events   (3 partitions, key = orderId hashed to partition)

partition 0: [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 ]   <- group "email" committed offset 5
partition 1: [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 ]               <- group "email" committed offset 4 (caught up)
partition 2: [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 ]   <- group "email" committed offset 2 (lag 7)

group "email" has 2 consumers: consumer A owns partitions 0 and 1, consumer B owns partition 2
group "analytics" has 1 consumer owning all three, with its own offsets

The commit semantics decide correctness:

  • Auto-commit (the default in most clients): the client commits the highest offset it has fetched on a timer (every 5 seconds in the Java client, configurable in kafkajs). If the process crashes after the commit but before the handler finished, those messages are lost (at-most-once). If it crashes after the handler finished but before the commit, they are reprocessed (at-least-once). Auto-commit gives you one or the other depending on timing, which is the worst of both.
  • Manual commit after processing: the handler finishes (including the database write), then the offset is committed. A crash in between means reprocessing, never loss. This is at-least-once and it is what you want, paired with an idempotent handler.
  • Manual commit before processing: at-most-once. Acceptable only for data you can afford to lose (metrics samples).

27.2.4 Ordering

Concept

Ordering is the promise that consumers see messages in the sequence they were produced. Brokers give it only within a partition (Kafka), a queue with a single consumer (RabbitMQ), or a message group (SQS FIFO). There is no global ordering across partitions, and there is no ordering once you introduce retries or parallel consumers.

Why does it exist as a problem?

OrderPlaced then OrderCancelled for the same order must be processed in that order, or the consumer cancels nothing and then creates a live order. Global ordering across all orders is neither needed nor possible at scale. Per-order ordering is both, and it is achieved by keying: every message about order 123 uses key 123, hashes to the same partition, and is read by the same consumer in sequence.

How it works

  1. The producer sets the key (orderId, userId, accountId: the entity whose history must be sequential).
  2. The broker hashes the key to a partition. Same key, same partition, always (as long as the partition count does not change).
  3. One consumer in the group owns that partition and reads it in order.
  4. Ordering breaks if: the consumer processes messages from one partition concurrently; a failed message is retried later while newer ones proceed (27.13); the partition count changes (keys re-hash); or the producer retries create an out-of-order duplicate (fixed by the idempotent producer, 27.3).

The design consequence: a consumer must tolerate out-of-order arrival for anything that goes through a retry path. Version numbers on the entity (orderVersion: 7) let the consumer ignore an event older than what it has already applied.

27.2.5 Retry

Concept

A retry re-attempts a failed message. Where the retry happens (in the consumer's memory, back on the same queue, on a separate retry queue with a delay) and how many times decide whether a failing message blocks its neighbours and whether a downstream outage becomes a retry storm.

How it works

  • Immediate in-process retry (2 to 3 attempts, tens of milliseconds apart): for blips such as a connection reset. Cheap; preserves ordering because nothing else moves meanwhile.
  • Delayed retry (seconds to minutes with exponential backoff and jitter): for downstream outages. In RabbitMQ, a retry queue with a TTL and a dead-letter exchange back to the main queue (27.4). In Kafka, retry topics (orders.retry.1m, orders.retry.10m) each consumed with a delay. In SQS, the visibility timeout is the delay.
  • Blocking retry (pause the partition and keep retrying the same message): preserves order at the cost of head-of-line blocking. Right for strictly ordered streams (a ledger), wrong for independent tasks.
  • Attempt counting lives in a header (x-retry-count, x-death in RabbitMQ, ApproximateReceiveCount in SQS). After N attempts the message goes to the dead-letter queue.

27.2.6 Dead-letter queue

Concept

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where messages go when they cannot be processed after the retry budget is exhausted, or when they fail in a way retries cannot fix (malformed payload, unknown type, a business rule violation). It is a parking lot, not a graveyard: someone must look at it.

How it works

  1. The consumer decides the message is dead (retry count exceeded, or a permanent error class).
  2. It publishes the original message plus diagnostic headers (error message, stack summary, consumer name, first and last failure time, original topic and partition and offset) to orders.events.dlq, then acknowledges the original.
  3. An alert fires when the DLQ depth exceeds zero for longer than a few minutes, or exceeds a threshold. A DLQ nobody watches is data loss with extra steps.
  4. Replay tooling reads from the DLQ and republishes to the original topic after a fix is deployed. Replayed messages carry a replayedAt header; consumers must still be idempotent because the original may have partially succeeded.

NestJS example

A minimal envelope for dead-lettering that every consumer in the codebase shares, so the DLQ is uniform and replayable.

// messaging/dead-letter.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Producer } from 'kafkajs';

export interface DeadLetterMeta {
  sourceTopic: string;
  partition: number;
  offset: string;
  consumerGroup: string;
  attempts: number;
  error: string;
}

@Injectable()
export class DeadLetterService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(DeadLetterService.name);
  constructor(private readonly producer: Producer) {}

  async park(key: string | null, value: Buffer | null, headers: Record<string, string>, meta: DeadLetterMeta): Promise<void> {
    await this.producer.send({
      topic: `${meta.sourceTopic}.dlq`,
      messages: [{
        key,
        value,
        headers: {
          ...headers,
          'x-dlq-source-topic': meta.sourceTopic,
          'x-dlq-partition': String(meta.partition),
          'x-dlq-offset': meta.offset,
          'x-dlq-consumer-group': meta.consumerGroup,
          'x-dlq-attempts': String(meta.attempts),
          'x-dlq-error': meta.error.slice(0, 1000),
          'x-dlq-parked-at': new Date().toISOString(),
        },
      }],
    });
    this.logger.error(`parked message ${meta.sourceTopic}/${meta.partition}/${meta.offset}: ${meta.error}`);
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Many teams keep a DLQ mirror in PostgreSQL for searchability and a replay UI. The table is also where an operator marks a message as "resolved manually".

CREATE TABLE dead_letters (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  source_topic  text        NOT NULL,
  partition     int         NOT NULL,
  "offset"      bigint      NOT NULL,
  message_key   text,
  message_id    uuid,
  payload       jsonb       NOT NULL,
  headers       jsonb       NOT NULL,
  error         text        NOT NULL,
  attempts      int         NOT NULL,
  parked_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'parked' CHECK (status IN ('parked', 'replayed', 'discarded')),
  resolved_at   timestamptz,
  resolved_by   text,
  UNIQUE (source_topic, partition, "offset")
);
CREATE INDEX dead_letters_parked_idx ON dead_letters (status, parked_at) WHERE status = 'parked';

Production scenario

An e-commerce platform runs 40 consumer groups across 25 topics. The DLQ alert threshold is "any message parked for more than 10 minutes" in business hours, "more than 100 messages" overnight. A typical week sees 5 to 20 dead letters, almost all from one of three causes: a payload the consumer cannot parse after a producer deployed a breaking change (27.10), a downstream API that returned 4xx for a specific record (bad address for a shipping label), or a bug in a new consumer. The weekly ritual is to review the DLQ table, fix, replay and close.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged for "inventory reservations behind by 40 minutes". The inventory consumer processes messages in order per partition. A single ReserveStock message for a product that was hard-deleted throws a NotFoundException; the consumer's retry policy is "retry forever with a 5 second delay", written by someone who wanted to be safe. Partition 3 has been stuck on that message for 40 minutes; 11,000 reservations behind it wait. The fix at 02:30: classify NotFoundException as permanent, dead-letter it, resume. The permanent fix: a retry policy by error type (27.13) and a maximum attempt count on everything.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A queue consumed by two services that both think it is theirs: each gets half the messages. Queues have one consuming service; use a topic for multiple.
  • A consumer group name reused by a new, unrelated service: it inherits the old group's committed offsets and either skips or reprocesses history. Group names are owned and unique.
  • A partition count increased on a live topic: keys re-hash, and events for the same order now land in two partitions with two consumers. Set the partition count with headroom at creation and treat changing it as a migration.
  • A DLQ with a retention shorter than the time it takes anyone to look at it (Kafka topics default to 7 days): messages vanish silently. Set DLQ retention to 30 days or more.
  • A retry topic consumed with the same group id as the main topic: the same consumer instance handles both and the delay logic breaks. Separate groups per retry tier.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees a topic as a contract with strangers: everything published is a public API of the producing team, versioned and documented. They insist on keys for anything that needs order, on manual commits after processing, on a maximum attempt count for every consumer, and on a DLQ with an owner and an alert. They ask "what happens to this message if the consumer is down for six hours?" before anything is deployed, and they refuse to run a consumer whose handler is not idempotent, because 27.8 will show them why.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing commands to a topic with many subscribers, so three services all "send the email".
  • Relying on auto-commit and discovering during an incident that messages were lost or doubled.
  • No key on the producer, so events for one order arrive out of order across partitions.
  • Retrying forever, blocking a partition on one bad message.
  • Treating the DLQ as a log rather than a work queue for humans.

Interview questions

  1. Queue or topic for OrderPlaced, and why? Expected: topic; several independent consumers each need every event. Follow-up: queue or topic for GenerateInvoice? Queue; exactly one handler.
  2. What is the ordering guarantee of Kafka, precisely? Expected: per partition; achieved by keying; broken by concurrent processing, retries and partition count changes.
  3. What does committing an offset mean, and when should you commit? Expected: "everything before this is done"; after processing, manually; auto-commit gives neither guarantee reliably.
  4. A consumer is stuck retrying one message. What went wrong in the design? Expected: no maximum attempts, no error classification, no DLQ.
  5. Why must a DLQ have an alert? Expected: unmonitored DLQ equals silent data loss; retention will eventually delete the messages.
  6. Explain event versus command to a product manager. Expected: an event is a fact ("the order was placed"); a command is a request ("reserve this stock"). Facts have many listeners; requests have one doer.

Practical exercise

Design the messaging topology for a ride-booking flow: RideRequested, DriverAssigned, RideStarted, RideCompleted, PaymentCaptured, ReceiptSent. Acceptance criteria: (a) a diagram showing which are events on topics and which are commands on queues; (b) the key for each topic and the reason; (c) the consumer groups with their retry policy and DLQ; (d) a written answer to "what happens if the payment service is down for two hours", covering the customer experience and the recovery; (e) which one of these you would build without a broker if the company had one service and ten rides a day.

27.3 Kafka in depth

Kafka is not a queue. It is a distributed, replicated, append-only log that consumers read at their own pace and can re-read. Almost every Kafka surprise ("why did my consumer get kicked out", "why are there duplicates", "why is lag growing on one partition") follows directly from that design, so this section builds the design up from the storage layer.

27.3.1 Log-structured storage and partitions

Concept

A Kafka topic is a set of partitions. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of records stored as files on one broker's disk (the leader) and copied to other brokers (followers). Producers append to the end; consumers read from an offset forward. Nothing is deleted when it is read; records age out by retention.

Why does it exist?

Appending to the end of a file and reading it sequentially is the fastest thing a disk can do, an order of magnitude faster than random reads and writes. By refusing to do anything else (no per-message deletion, no random access, no per-consumer state on the broker beyond an offset), Kafka makes a single broker capable of hundreds of megabytes per second and a cluster of millions of messages per second, and it makes replay free: a new consumer group reads from the beginning of the log.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse of numbered ledger books, one shelf per partition. Clerks (producers) only ever write on the next blank line of the current book. Readers (consumers) stand at a line number and read forward; they never tear out pages. When a book is older than seven days it is shredded. Anyone can start reading from any line they like, including line one, as long as the book still exists.

How it works

  1. A partition on disk is a directory of segment files (00000000000000000000.log, 00000000000012345678.log), each about 1 GB by default, plus sparse index files mapping offset to byte position and timestamp to offset.
  2. A producer's write is appended to the active segment of the leader partition. Kafka relies on the OS page cache: the write goes to memory and is flushed by the kernel; durability comes from replication, not from fsync per message.
  3. A consumer fetch reads a byte range from a segment. Because data is usually in the page cache and Kafka uses sendfile (zero copy), a fetch does not pass through the JVM heap. This is why consumers that are caught up cost almost nothing.
  4. Retention deletes whole segments once every record in them is older than retention.ms (default 7 days) or the partition exceeds retention.bytes. Compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) instead keeps only the latest record per key, forever, which turns a topic into a changelog: the current state of every key is always recoverable by reading it from the start. A record with a null value (a tombstone) deletes the key on the next compaction pass.
  5. Partition count is set at topic creation and can be increased but never decreased. Increasing it changes which partition a key hashes to, breaking per-key ordering during the transition. Choose with headroom: for a topic that needs 6 consumers today, 12 or 24 partitions.
topic orders.events, partition 2, on broker 3 (leader), replicated to brokers 1 and 5

/var/kafka/orders.events-2/
  00000000000000000000.log      offsets 0 .. 4,199,331     (1 GB, sealed)
  00000000000000000000.index
  00000000000000000000.timeindex
  00000000000004199332.log      offsets 4,199,332 .. now   (active, appended)
  00000000000004199332.index

Production scenario

A payments platform runs payments.events with 48 partitions, replication factor 3, 7 day retention, 12,000 messages per second at 600 bytes each: about 7 MB per second in, 21 MB per second across replicas, 4.3 TB of retained data across the cluster. Six brokers with 4 TB disks each hold it comfortably. A new fraud-scoring consumer group is added and reads the last 7 days from offset zero at 150 MB per second without affecting the production consumers, because reads are sequential and the data is on disk anyway.

27.3.2 Replication, ISR and acknowledgements

Concept

Each partition has one leader replica that takes all reads and writes and N-1 follower replicas that copy from it. The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the subset of replicas that are caught up with the leader (within replica.lag.time.max.ms, default 30 seconds). A producer's acks setting says how many of those must have the record before the write is acknowledged.

Why does it exist?

A broker will die. With one copy, its partitions are unavailable and, if the disk is gone, lost. Replication keeps the log alive across broker failures, and the ISR plus acks let each producer choose how much durability it pays for per write.

How it works

Setting Meaning Durability Latency
acks=0 Producer does not wait for any response Lost on any failure, even a dropped packet Lowest
acks=1 Leader has written it to its log Lost if the leader dies before followers copy it Low
acks=all (-1) All replicas in the ISR have it Survives loss of any min.insync.replicas - 1 brokers One extra replication round trip, a few ms

acks=all alone is not enough, because the ISR can shrink to just the leader when followers fall behind; then acks=all means one copy. min.insync.replicas=2 (with replication factor 3) makes the broker refuse the write with NotEnoughReplicas if fewer than 2 replicas are in sync, which is the setting that turns "durable" from a hope into a guarantee. The producer then retries or fails loudly, which is what you want for OrderPlaced.

unclean.leader.election.enable=false (the default since 0.11) means that if every in-sync replica is gone, the partition stays offline rather than electing a stale follower and silently losing the tail of the log. Availability versus consistency in one boolean.

The rule of thumb for business events: replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, and an idempotent producer. For high-volume telemetry where losing a sample is fine: acks=1.

27.3.3 Idempotent producer, keys and partitioning

Concept

A producer that retries after a timeout can write the same record twice, because the first write may have succeeded and only the acknowledgement was lost. The idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) attaches a producer id and a per-partition sequence number to each batch; the broker discards a batch it has already seen. Retries then cannot duplicate or reorder within a partition.

Keys decide partitions. The default partitioner hashes the key (murmur2) modulo the partition count. Records with the same key land on the same partition and are therefore ordered relative to each other. Records with a null key are spread across partitions (round-robin or sticky per batch) with no ordering.

How it works

  1. The producer chooses a key: orderId for order events, userId for user-scoped events, accountId for ledger entries. The key is the entity whose events must be processed in order by one consumer.
  2. The partitioner computes hash(key) mod partitions. If keys are skewed (one enterprise tenant produces 40 percent of traffic), one partition takes 40 percent of the load: partition key skew, covered in 27.16.
  3. The idempotent producer keeps up to 5 in-flight batches per partition in the Java client, with sequence numbers, so it can retry without reordering. In kafkajs, idempotent: true is honoured with maxInFlightRequests: 1.
  4. acks=all is required for idempotence.

NestJS example

A producer provider with the durability settings that business events need, built on plain kafkajs because the @nestjs/microservices ClientKafka does not expose idempotent or acks per send in a discoverable way.

// messaging/kafka-producer.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CompressionTypes, Kafka, Partitioners, Producer } from 'kafkajs';

@Injectable()
export class KafkaProducerService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(KafkaProducerService.name);
  private readonly kafka = new Kafka({
    clientId: process.env.SERVICE_NAME ?? 'orders-api',
    brokers: (process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS ?? 'localhost:9092').split(','),
    retry: { initialRetryTime: 100, retries: 8 },       // client-level retries with backoff
  });
  private readonly producer: Producer = this.kafka.producer({
    idempotent: true,                                    // broker de-duplicates producer retries
    maxInFlightRequests: 1,                              // required for idempotence in kafkajs
    allowAutoTopicCreation: false,                       // topics are created by migration, not by accident
    createPartitioner: Partitioners.DefaultPartitioner,  // Java-compatible murmur2 hashing
  });

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> { await this.producer.connect(); }
  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> { await this.producer.disconnect(); }

  async publish(topic: string, key: string, value: object, headers: Record<string, string> = {}): Promise<void> {
    await this.producer.send({
      topic,
      acks: -1,                                          // all in-sync replicas
      compression: CompressionTypes.GZIP,
      messages: [{ key, value: JSON.stringify(value), headers }],
    });
  }

  get raw(): Producer { return this.producer; }
}

27.3.4 Consumer groups and rebalancing

Concept

A consumer group is a set of consumer instances sharing one groupId. The broker's group coordinator assigns each partition of each subscribed topic to exactly one member. When membership changes (a pod starts, stops, crashes, or is deemed dead), a rebalance reassigns partitions.

Why does it exist?

Rebalancing is what lets you scale consumers by adding pods and survive a pod dying without an operator reassigning partitions by hand. It is also the single largest source of duplicate processing and latency spikes in Kafka systems, so understanding its mechanics is not optional.

Mental model

Imagine a team of readers assigned to shelves. When a new reader arrives, the supervisor (coordinator) shouts "everybody stop, put your books down", re-deals the shelves, and everyone picks up from their bookmark. That is an eager rebalance. A cooperative rebalance is the supervisor saying "you two, hand one shelf each to the new person; everyone else keep reading".

How it works

flowchart LR
    subgraph Topic orders.events
        P0["partition 0"]
        P1["partition 1"]
        P2["partition 2"]
        P3["partition 3"]
    end
    subgraph Group email
        C1["consumer email-1"]
        C2["consumer email-2"]
    end
    subgraph Group analytics
        C3["consumer analytics-1"]
    end
    P0 --> C1
    P1 --> C1
    P2 --> C2
    P3 --> C2
    P0 --> C3
    P1 --> C3
    P2 --> C3
    P3 --> C3

A consumer's life in the group:

  1. Join. The consumer sends JoinGroup to the coordinator with its subscriptions. The coordinator picks one member as leader and gives it the member list.
  2. Assign. The leader runs the assignment strategy (range, round-robin, sticky, cooperative-sticky) and sends the assignment via SyncGroup. Everyone learns their partitions.
  3. Fetch and heartbeat. The consumer polls for records and sends heartbeats every heartbeat.interval.ms (3 seconds). If the coordinator sees no heartbeat for session.timeout.ms (45 seconds in recent Java defaults; 30 seconds in kafkajs), it declares the member dead and triggers a rebalance.
  4. Commit. The consumer commits offsets to the __consumer_offsets internal topic.
  5. Leave. On a clean shutdown the consumer sends LeaveGroup, triggering an immediate rebalance rather than a session-timeout wait.

Eager (stop-the-world) rebalancing. Every member revokes all partitions, the group re-joins, and the new assignment is handed out. During the window (typically 1 to 10 seconds, longer with many partitions or slow members) nothing is consumed. Any message that was being processed when revocation happened and whose offset was not committed will be reprocessed by whoever gets the partition next: a duplicate.

Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing (partition.assignment.strategy=CooperativeStickyAssignor in the Java client; Kafka 2.4 and later). Only the partitions that move are revoked; everyone else keeps consuming. Two rounds of join instead of one, but no pause. kafkajs does not implement the cooperative protocol; its rebalances are eager, which is one of the reasons teams with large groups eventually move to a client with librdkafka underneath (@confluentinc/kafka-javascript).

Static membership (group.instance.id) tells the coordinator "this member will be back with the same id"; a restart within the session timeout does not trigger a rebalance at all. Ideal for Kubernetes StatefulSets with stable pod names.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as email-1
    participant C2 as email-2
    participant CO as Coordinator
    participant C3 as email-3
    C3->>CO: JoinGroup (new pod)
    CO-->>C1: rebalance required
    CO-->>C2: rebalance required
    Note over C1,C2: eager: revoke ALL partitions, stop consuming
    C1->>CO: JoinGroup
    C2->>CO: JoinGroup
    CO-->>C1: SyncGroup assignment p0, p1
    CO-->>C2: SyncGroup assignment p2
    CO-->>C3: SyncGroup assignment p3
    Note over C1,C3: 2 to 10 s with nothing consumed, uncommitted in-flight messages will be re-read

27.3.5 Slow consumers, max.poll.interval.ms and heartbeats

Concept

Heartbeats prove a consumer process is alive. They do not prove it is making progress. The Java client adds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes): if the application does not call poll() within that interval, the consumer is considered stuck and leaves the group. A handler that takes 6 minutes on one batch gets its partitions revoked mid-processing; when it finally commits, the commit is rejected (CommitFailedException or REBALANCE_IN_PROGRESS) and everything it just did is reprocessed elsewhere.

How it works in kafkajs

kafkajs has no max.poll.interval.ms. Instead, heartbeats are sent between fetches from the run loop, and the eachMessage / eachBatch handlers receive a heartbeat() function. If your handler runs longer than sessionTimeout without calling heartbeat(), the coordinator declares the consumer dead, rebalances, and the same partitions are handed to another member while your handler is still running. The result is identical to the Java case: duplicate processing and a failed commit.

The rules:

  • Keep per-message processing well under the session timeout. If a message needs a 3 minute report generated, the consumer should enqueue a job and commit, not do the work inline.
  • Call heartbeat() in long batch loops, at least every few seconds.
  • Set sessionTimeout and rebalanceTimeout deliberately (kafkajs defaults 30 s and 60 s) and make sure the handler's p99 is a fraction of them.
  • Detect the kicked-out case: kafkajs emits consumer.events.CRASH and rebalance events; log and alert on them.
// A batch handler that heartbeats and respects the time budget
await consumer.run({
  autoCommit: false,
  eachBatch: async ({ batch, resolveOffset, heartbeat, commitOffsetsIfNecessary, isRunning, isStale }) => {
    for (const message of batch.messages) {
      if (!isRunning() || isStale()) break;          // partition revoked or shutting down: stop, do not commit further
      await handle(message);                         // idempotent handler
      resolveOffset(message.offset);                 // mark this offset as done
      await heartbeat();                             // keep the session alive during long batches
    }
    await commitOffsetsIfNecessary();                // commit resolved offsets
  },
});

27.3.6 Consumer lag

Concept

Lag is the difference between the last offset written to a partition (the log end offset) and the consumer group's committed offset. It is the number of messages not yet processed, per partition. Lag in messages divided by throughput gives lag in seconds, which is the number the business cares about.

How it works

Lag rises when the producer rate exceeds the consumer rate, when a consumer is stuck or rebalancing, or when a single partition is hot. It is exposed by kafka-consumer-groups --describe, by the kafka-lag-exporter or Burrow projects as kafka_consumergroup_lag, and in every managed offering's console. Per-partition lag is the diagnostic view: uniform lag means too few consumers; one partition lagging means key skew or a poison message on that partition.

27.3.7 Batching, compression and throughput numbers

How it works

  • Producers batch records per partition. linger.ms (how long to wait to fill a batch; 0 by default in Java, 5 to 20 ms is common in production) and batch.size (16 KB default, 64 to 256 KB for throughput) trade latency for efficiency. A batch of 500 records costs one request.
  • Compression (lz4 or zstd for speed, gzip for ratio) is applied per batch and stored compressed; consumers decompress. JSON events compress 5 to 10x.
  • A single partition sustains roughly 5 to 20 MB per second, depending on record size and disk. A broker handles hundreds of partitions. A three-broker cluster comfortably does 100 to 300 MB per second in and several times that out.
  • A consumer processing messages one at a time with a 5 ms database write does 200 messages per second per partition. Sixteen partitions with sixteen consumers do 3,200 per second. Batch the database writes and the same consumers do ten times that. Consumer throughput is almost always bounded by the handler, not by Kafka.

Retention and replay as a feature

Because the log is retained, you can rebuild a read model by resetting a group's offsets (kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z), run a new consumer from the beginning for a new feature, or replay a day of events into a staging environment. This is the capability that RabbitMQ and SQS do not have, and it is the strongest argument for Kafka when it applies.

27.3.8 When Kafka is overkill

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Kafka earns its keep when at least two of these are true: more than a few thousand messages per second; several independent consumers of the same events; replay or long retention needed; event sourcing or CDC; strict per-key ordering at scale. If you have one producer, one or two consumers, a few hundred messages per second and no replay requirement, Kafka is a distributed system you now operate (or pay Confluent, MSK or Redpanda for) in exchange for nothing you use. A RabbitMQ instance, SQS, or BullMQ on the Redis you already run will be simpler, and simpler survives on-call.

The senior also weighs operational cost: partition planning, rebalancing behaviour, consumer lag monitoring, schema governance, a lag exporter, and a team that understands min.insync.replicas. Managed Kafka removes the broker operations and none of the client-side complexity.

PostgreSQL example

Kafka's offset commit and your database write are two systems; this is why consumer idempotency is a database concern. The minimal table that lets a consumer commit its own position in PostgreSQL, atomically with its business write, so that the Kafka offset becomes a hint rather than the source of truth:

CREATE TABLE consumer_positions (
  consumer_group text   NOT NULL,
  topic          text   NOT NULL,
  partition      int    NOT NULL,
  last_offset    bigint NOT NULL,
  updated_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer_group, topic, partition)
);

-- Inside the same transaction as the business write:
INSERT INTO consumer_positions (consumer_group, topic, partition, last_offset)
VALUES ('inventory', 'orders.events', 3, 4199340)
ON CONFLICT (consumer_group, topic, partition)
DO UPDATE SET last_offset = EXCLUDED.last_offset, updated_at = now()
WHERE consumer_positions.last_offset < EXCLUDED.last_offset;  -- never move backwards

On startup the consumer can seek to last_offset + 1 from this table, making a redelivered older message detectable by offset alone. This is a heavier pattern than a dedup table (27.9) and is worth it for exactly-once-into-PostgreSQL semantics on a single partition.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged: inventory lag on orders.events at 180,000 messages and rising. The graph shows lag started at 01:58, the moment a deploy rolled 6 inventory pods. Rebalances: 12 in two minutes (eager, one per pod stop and one per pod start). Each rebalance took 8 seconds because one partition's in-flight batch of 500 messages took 8 seconds to finish and the consumer held up the rejoin. During each pause nothing was consumed; after each, the batch that was in flight was reprocessed. Net effect: two minutes of near-zero throughput at peak, then a backlog that took 25 minutes to drain. Fixes applied that week: static membership so restarts do not rebalance; batch size reduced to 100 so revocation is quick; a maxSurge/maxUnavailable rollout of one pod at a time; and a lag alert with a 5 minute threshold rather than a 30 minute one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Producer with acks=1 and a leader crash: acknowledged records lost. Use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 for business events.
  • NotEnoughReplicas when a broker is down and min.insync.replicas cannot be met: producers fail; this is correct behaviour; alert on under-replicated partitions before it happens.
  • A consumer with autoCommit and a crash: lost or duplicated messages depending on timing.
  • Session timeout during a long handler: partitions revoked mid-work, commit rejected, work duplicated.
  • Partition count increased on a keyed topic: ordering breaks for in-flight keys; do it during a quiet window with consumers drained.
  • Compacted topic misused for events: intermediate events for a key disappear after compaction; compaction is for state, not history.
  • Retention shorter than the longest expected consumer outage: unprocessed messages deleted. Set retention from the recovery time objective, not from disk cost.
  • Group id typo in a new deployment: a fresh group starts at latest by default and silently skips everything before it started, or at earliest and reprocesses a week.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing partition count equal to today's consumer count with no headroom.
  • Null keys on events that need ordering.
  • Treating heartbeats as proof of progress.
  • Committing before processing "to avoid duplicates", and thereby choosing loss.
  • Running Kafka for 50 messages per second between two services.

Interview questions

  1. What does acks=all guarantee without min.insync.replicas, and why is that a trap? Expected: only that the current ISR has it, which can be one replica; min.insync.replicas=2 makes durability real.
  2. How does the idempotent producer prevent duplicates, and what does it not prevent? Expected: producer id plus sequence numbers de-duplicated by the broker; it does not prevent application-level re-sends after a crash, nor consumer-side duplicates.
  3. Describe an eager rebalance and its two costs. Expected: all partitions revoked, consumption pauses, in-flight uncommitted work is duplicated. Follow-up: how do cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce each?
  4. Lag is growing on one partition only. Three causes? Expected: key skew, a poison or slow message on that partition, that partition's consumer is unhealthy.
  5. When would you set cleanup.policy=compact? Expected: for changelog or state topics where only the latest value per key matters; never for event history.
  6. A handler takes 4 minutes per message. What breaks and how do you fix the design? Expected: session or poll timeouts cause revocation and duplicates; move the work to a job queue and commit quickly, or heartbeat and bound the time.

Practical exercise

Stand up a single-node Kafka (KRaft mode) in Docker Compose. Create orders.events with 6 partitions and replication factor 1. Write a kafkajs producer that publishes 10,000 OrderPlaced events with orderId keys across 100 distinct order ids, and a consumer group of 3 instances with manual commits. Acceptance criteria: (a) a PostgreSQL table records every processed (orderId, sequence) and proves per-order sequence was never violated; (b) killing one consumer with SIGKILL mid-run produces duplicates that your dedup logic detects and counts, with zero lost events; (c) restarting a consumer with a fresh groupId and fromBeginning: true replays all 10,000; (d) the per-partition lag is graphed from kafka-consumer-groups --describe output during the run.

27.4 RabbitMQ in depth

RabbitMQ is a message broker in the classic sense: producers publish to exchanges, exchanges route to queues by rules, consumers take messages from queues and acknowledge them, and the broker deletes acknowledged messages. It is optimized for routing flexibility and per-message control rather than for retained logs, and that makes it the better tool for a large class of backend work.

27.4.1 Exchanges, queues, bindings and routing keys

Concept

A producer never publishes to a queue directly. It publishes to an exchange with a routing key. The exchange looks at its bindings (rules linking it to queues) and copies the message into every queue whose binding matches. Consumers subscribe to queues.

Why does it exist?

Separating "where the producer sends" from "where the consumer reads" is what makes fan-out, filtering and topology changes possible without touching code. Add a new queue bound to the same exchange and a new consumer receives the messages; change a binding pattern and a queue starts or stops receiving a category, all at runtime.

Mental model

Imagine a mail room. Senders drop letters in a slot labelled by exchange, with a code written on the envelope (the routing key). The mail room has a rule book (bindings): "envelopes coded order.*.eu go to the EU fulfilment tray and to the analytics tray". Trays are queues; the clerks emptying them are consumers. Senders never know which trays exist.

How it works

flowchart LR
    P["Producer"] -->|"rk = order.placed.eu"| X["Exchange orders type topic"]
    X -->|"binding order.placed.*"| Q1["queue email.order-confirmation"]
    X -->|"binding order.*.eu"| Q2["queue fulfilment.eu"]
    X -->|"binding #"| Q3["queue analytics.all-orders"]
    X -.->|"binding order.cancelled.*"| Q4["queue refunds.cancellations"]
    Q1 --> C1["Email workers"]
    Q2 --> C2["EU fulfilment workers"]
    Q3 --> C3["Analytics worker"]

The four exchange types:

Type Routing rule Use
direct Routing key equals the binding key exactly Work queues: thumbnail.generate to the thumbnail queue
topic Dot-separated key matched against patterns; * matches one word, # matches zero or more Event routing: order.placed.eu to order.placed.* and order.*.eu and #
fanout Ignores the key; every bound queue gets a copy Broadcast: cache invalidation, "everything to the audit log"
headers Match on message header values instead of the key (x-match: all or any) Rare; routing by content type or tenant when keys are not enough

Queues have properties that decide their behaviour: durable (survives broker restart; the messages inside also need persistent delivery mode to survive), exclusive (one connection, deleted when it closes; for RPC reply queues), auto-delete, x-message-ttl, x-max-length, x-dead-letter-exchange, x-max-priority, x-queue-type (classic or quorum).

27.4.2 Acknowledgements, prefetch and fairness

Concept

A consumer receives a message and, when finished, sends ack. Until then the message is "unacked" and belongs to that consumer. nack or reject returns it, with a requeue flag deciding whether it goes back to the queue (to be redelivered, possibly to the same consumer immediately) or is dead-lettered or dropped. If the consumer's connection dies, every unacked message it held is requeued automatically.

Prefetch (basic.qos with prefetch_count) caps how many unacked messages the broker will push to one consumer. Without it, the broker pushes everything in the queue to the first consumer that connects, which then holds 50,000 messages while the other nine consumers idle.

How it works

  1. Consumer sets prefetch(10).
  2. Broker delivers up to 10 messages; then waits for acks before sending more.
  3. Consumer processes one, acks it, receives one more. A slow consumer naturally takes less; a fast one takes more. This is fair dispatch.
  4. nack(msg, allUpTo=false, requeue=false) sends the message to the queue's dead-letter exchange if one is configured, or drops it. requeue=true puts it back at the head of the queue: an immediate retry that, for a permanently failing message, becomes a tight loop at the front of the queue starving everything behind it.

Prefetch guidance: 1 for long tasks where fairness matters most (video transcoding), 10 to 50 for short tasks (sending emails), higher only when the handler is sub-millisecond. A prefetch that is too high also means a crashed consumer requeues a large batch, which is a burst of duplicates for whoever gets them next.

27.4.3 TTL, dead-letter exchanges and delayed retries

Concept

RabbitMQ has no built-in "retry in 30 seconds" operation. The standard construction uses two features: a per-queue message TTL (x-message-ttl) after which a message expires, and a dead-letter exchange (x-dead-letter-exchange) to which expired or rejected messages are republished. A "wait queue" with a TTL and a DLX pointing back at the main exchange is a delay line.

How it works

flowchart LR
    X["exchange orders"] --> Q["queue inventory.reserve"]
    Q --> C["Consumer"]
    C -->|"nack requeue=false on transient error"| DLX1["exchange inventory.retry"]
    DLX1 --> W1["queue inventory.retry.30s TTL 30000 DLX orders"]
    W1 -.->|"expires after 30 s"| X
    C -->|"attempts > 5 or permanent error: publish"| DLQ["queue inventory.reserve.dlq"]
    DLQ --> H["Human plus replay tool"]
  1. The main queue inventory.reserve is declared with x-dead-letter-exchange: inventory.retry.
  2. On a transient failure the consumer nacks with requeue=false. The broker moves the message to the inventory.retry exchange, which routes to inventory.retry.30s.
  3. That queue has x-message-ttl: 30000 and x-dead-letter-exchange: orders with the original routing key preserved. After 30 seconds the message expires and is republished to orders, arriving back in inventory.reserve.
  4. The x-death header (appended by the broker on every dead-lettering) carries a count. The consumer reads it to know the attempt number. After the budget, the consumer publishes the message to a DLQ explicitly and acks the original.
  5. For exponential backoff, use several wait queues (30s, 2m, 10m) and pick by attempt number, or the rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange plugin, which accepts an x-delay header per message.

TTL queues have a subtlety: expiry is checked only at the head of the queue. If a 10 minute message is in front of a 30 second message, the 30 second message waits 10 minutes. One queue per delay value avoids it.

NestJS example

A consumer on the @nestjs/microservices RMQ transport with manual acks, retry counting and dead-lettering. The transport hides the channel behind RmqContext, and you must set noAck: false in the options or every message is auto-acked on receipt.

// main.ts (worker)
const app = await NestFactory.createMicroservice<MicroserviceOptions>(WorkerModule, {
  transport: Transport.RMQ,
  options: {
    urls: [process.env.AMQP_URL!],
    queue: 'inventory.reserve',
    prefetchCount: 10,
    noAck: false,                                            // we ack manually
    queueOptions: {
      durable: true,
      arguments: { 'x-queue-type': 'quorum', 'x-dead-letter-exchange': 'inventory.retry' },
    },
  },
});
app.enableShutdownHooks();
await app.listen();
// inventory/reserve-stock.controller.ts
import { Controller, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Ctx, EventPattern, Payload, RmqContext } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { ChannelWrapper } from 'amqp-connection-manager';
import { InventoryService } from './inventory.service';
import { classifyError } from '../messaging/error-classifier';

const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;

@Controller()
export class ReserveStockController {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReserveStockController.name);
  constructor(private readonly inventory: InventoryService) {}

  @EventPattern('reserve-stock')
  async handle(@Payload() cmd: ReserveStockCommand, @Ctx() ctx: RmqContext): Promise<void> {
    const channel = ctx.getChannelRef();
    const msg = ctx.getMessage();
    const deaths = (msg.properties.headers?.['x-death'] as { count: number }[] | undefined) ?? [];
    const attempt = (deaths[0]?.count ?? 0) + 1;

    try {
      await this.inventory.reserve(cmd);                       // idempotent on cmd.messageId
      channel.ack(msg);
    } catch (err) {
      const kind = classifyError(err);                         // transient | permanent | poison
      if (kind === 'transient' && attempt < MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
        this.logger.warn(`attempt ${attempt} failed for ${cmd.messageId}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
        channel.nack(msg, false, false);                       // to DLX -> retry wait queue -> back here
        return;
      }
      await this.inventory.deadLetter(cmd, msg.properties.headers ?? {}, attempt, err as Error);
      channel.ack(msg);                                        // parked; remove from main queue
    }
  }
}

27.4.4 Quorum queues, publisher confirms and priorities

How it works

  • Classic queues are the original single-node queue type. Their mirrored (HA) mode is deprecated. Use them only for transient, non-replicated work such as RPC reply queues.
  • Quorum queues replicate each queue across a majority of nodes using Raft. A message is confirmed only after a quorum has it. They survive node loss, support x-delivery-limit (after N redeliveries the message is dead-lettered by the broker itself, which kills poison loops), and are the default choice for anything durable.
  • Streams (RabbitMQ 3.9 and later) are an append-only, replayable log type inside RabbitMQ, for the cases where you want Kafka-like retention without Kafka. Consumed with a different protocol and client.
  • Publisher confirms: on a confirm channel, the broker acknowledges each publish once it has been persisted (and, for quorum queues, replicated). Without confirms, publish() returns as soon as the bytes hit the socket and a broker crash loses the message silently. Use the mandatory flag with a return listener to catch messages that matched no binding.
  • Priority queues (x-max-priority: 10): higher-priority messages are delivered first. Useful for "VIP tenant jobs first"; costly if the queue is deep, and never a substitute for capacity.
// messaging/rabbit-publisher.service.ts (amqplib with confirms)
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import amqp, { ChannelModel, ConfirmChannel } from 'amqplib';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

@Injectable()
export class RabbitPublisher implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private conn!: ChannelModel;
  private ch!: ConfirmChannel;

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    this.conn = await amqp.connect(process.env.AMQP_URL!, { heartbeat: 30 });
    this.ch = await this.conn.createConfirmChannel();
    await this.ch.assertExchange('orders', 'topic', { durable: true });
    this.ch.on('return', (msg) => {
      // mandatory publish that matched no queue: this is a topology bug, not a transient error
      console.error(`unroutable message ${msg.properties.messageId} rk=${msg.fields.routingKey}`);
    });
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> { await this.ch.close(); await this.conn.close(); }

  publish(routingKey: string, body: object, headers: Record<string, string> = {}): Promise<void> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      this.ch.publish('orders', routingKey, Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(body)), {
        persistent: true,                  // survive broker restart (with a durable queue)
        contentType: 'application/json',
        messageId: (body as { id?: string }).id ?? randomUUID(),
        timestamp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
        headers,
        mandatory: true,
      }, (err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve()));  // resolves when the broker confirms
    });
  }
}

27.4.5 When RabbitMQ shines

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

RabbitMQ is the right tool for task queues (each message is a unit of work for one worker, acked when done, with fair dispatch and priorities), RPC-style request/reply (a replyTo queue and a correlationId, for services that need a synchronous answer through an async channel), complex routing (route by pattern, header or tenant without consumer-side filtering), and per-message TTL and delayed delivery. It has a first-class management UI, per-queue metrics, and a mental model most engineers pick up in a day. It does not retain messages after ack, so replay is not a feature; it does not scale one queue across nodes the way partitions do (throughput per queue tops out in the low tens of thousands of messages per second); and deep queues (millions of messages) degrade it, because it is designed for messages to flow, not to sit.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on-call sees email.order-confirmation at 2.3 million messages and the RabbitMQ node at 95 percent memory, with the memory alarm blocking all publishers, which means the orders API is now failing to publish and returning 500s. The email provider has been returning 503 for three hours; the consumer nacks with requeue=true, so each message goes straight back to the head of the queue and is redelivered immediately, thousands of times per second, generating log volume that also fills the disk. The fix: nack to a retry wait queue with backoff instead of requeue, x-max-length on the queue with overflow: reject-publish so a backlog cannot take the broker down, and a publisher that treats a blocked connection as "write to the outbox and move on". The email backlog itself was fine to keep; the retry loop and the unbounded queue were the incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • noAck: true (auto-ack) in the NestJS transport: a crash loses every in-flight message.
  • requeue=true on permanent failures: a hot loop at the head of the queue.
  • Missing prefetch: one consumer hoards the queue.
  • Non-durable queue or non-persistent messages: everything vanishes on broker restart.
  • Publishing without confirms: messages lost during a broker failover with no error in the producer.
  • A consumer that acks before processing: at-most-once by accident.
  • Connection-level memory or disk alarm: all publishers on the node are blocked; producers appear to hang rather than error.

27.5 SQS and SNS

27.5.1 SQS standard and FIFO queues

Concept

SQS is a fully managed queue: no brokers, no partitions, no connections to keep alive, just HTTPS calls to send, receive and delete. A standard queue offers nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. A FIFO queue offers strict ordering within a message group and de-duplication within a 5 minute window, at a throughput of roughly 300 messages per second per group (3,000 with batching; higher with high-throughput mode).

How it works

  • Message group id (FIFO only): messages with the same group id are delivered in order, one batch at a time; different groups are processed in parallel. It is the SQS equivalent of a Kafka key. Use orderId or userId.
  • Deduplication id (FIFO only): a message with the same dedup id as one accepted in the last 5 minutes is dropped. Content-based deduplication uses a hash of the body instead. This removes producer-retry duplicates, not consumer-side duplicates.
  • Size is capped at 256 KB; larger payloads go to S3 with a pointer (the extended client library does this).
  • Retention is 4 days by default, 14 days maximum. Unprocessed messages older than that are deleted.

27.5.2 Visibility timeout as the lock

Concept

When a consumer receives a message, SQS does not delete it. It hides it from other consumers for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours). The consumer must delete the message before the timeout expires; if it does not, the message becomes visible again and another consumer receives it. The visibility timeout is a lease, and the delete is the acknowledgement.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as SQS queue
    participant W1 as Worker 1
    participant W2 as Worker 2
    W1->>Q: ReceiveMessage (WaitTimeSeconds 20)
    Q-->>W1: message m1, hidden for 30 s
    W1->>W1: processing takes 45 s (slow database)
    Note over Q: 30 s elapsed: m1 visible again
    W2->>Q: ReceiveMessage
    Q-->>W2: message m1 again (ReceiveCount 2)
    W1->>Q: DeleteMessage m1 (succeeds, receipt still valid)
    W2->>W2: processes m1 a second time
    W2->>Q: DeleteMessage m1 (no error, already gone)

The rules that follow:

  1. Set the visibility timeout above the handler's p99, with margin; for variable work, call ChangeMessageVisibility periodically to extend the lease (a heartbeat).
  2. Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20) makes ReceiveMessage wait for messages instead of returning empty immediately. Always use it; short polling costs money and returns empty responses on a distributed queue even when messages exist.
  3. MaxNumberOfMessages up to 10 per receive; delete in batches with DeleteMessageBatch.
  4. Redrive policy: after maxReceiveCount receives without a delete, SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue. ApproximateReceiveCount is the attempt number. A DLQ redrive back to the source queue is available in the console and API for replay.
  5. A message received but not deleted within the timeout is the SQS duplicate path (27.8).

NestJS example

A polling consumer as a NestJS provider using the AWS SDK v3. There is no official NestJS transport for SQS; the loop below is what the community packages wrap.

// messaging/sqs-consumer.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { SQSClient, ReceiveMessageCommand, DeleteMessageCommand, ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand, Message } from '@aws-sdk/client-sqs';

@Injectable()
export class SqsConsumerService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(SqsConsumerService.name);
  private readonly sqs = new SQSClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });
  private readonly queueUrl = process.env.SQS_QUEUE_URL!;
  private running = true;
  private loop?: Promise<void>;

  constructor(private readonly handler: { handle(body: unknown, attempt: number): Promise<void> }) {}

  onModuleInit(): void { this.loop = this.run(); }
  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> { this.running = false; await this.loop; }

  private async run(): Promise<void> {
    while (this.running) {
      const res = await this.sqs.send(new ReceiveMessageCommand({
        QueueUrl: this.queueUrl,
        MaxNumberOfMessages: 10,
        WaitTimeSeconds: 20,               // long polling
        VisibilityTimeout: 60,
        AttributeNames: ['ApproximateReceiveCount'],
      }));
      for (const msg of res.Messages ?? []) await this.process(msg);
    }
  }

  private async process(msg: Message): Promise<void> {
    const attempt = Number(msg.Attributes?.ApproximateReceiveCount ?? '1');
    const heartbeat = setInterval(() => {
      this.sqs.send(new ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand({ QueueUrl: this.queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: msg.ReceiptHandle!, VisibilityTimeout: 60 }))
        .catch((err) => this.logger.warn(`extend visibility failed: ${err.message}`));
    }, 40_000);                            // extend before the 60 s lease expires
    try {
      await this.handler.handle(JSON.parse(msg.Body ?? '{}'), attempt);  // idempotent
      await this.sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: this.queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: msg.ReceiptHandle! }));
    } catch (err) {
      // Do nothing: the message becomes visible again after the timeout; redrive policy moves it to the DLQ after maxReceiveCount.
      this.logger.warn(`attempt ${attempt} failed for ${msg.MessageId}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    } finally {
      clearInterval(heartbeat);
    }
  }
}

27.5.3 SNS fan-out

Concept

SNS is a topic service: publish once, deliver to every subscription (SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email). The standard AWS pattern is SNS to SQS fan-out: one topic, one queue per consuming service, so each service has its own buffer, retry policy and DLQ while the producer publishes once.

How it works

  1. The producer publishes OrderPlaced to the orders-events SNS topic with message attributes (eventType, region).
  2. Each consuming service owns an SQS queue subscribed to the topic. A filter policy on the subscription ({"eventType": ["OrderPlaced", "OrderCancelled"]}) delivers only matching messages, so consumers do not discard what they do not need.
  3. Raw message delivery on the subscription puts the payload directly in the SQS body rather than wrapping it in an SNS envelope.
  4. SNS delivery to SQS is at-least-once with its own retries; the queue provides the buffering and the consumer's redrive policy provides the DLQ.
  5. FIFO SNS topics fan out to FIFO SQS queues preserving message group ordering.

EventBridge is the other AWS option, with richer routing rules, schema registry and archive/replay; for simple fan-out SNS to SQS is cheaper and simpler.

Production scenario

A marketplace on AWS publishes 800 order events per minute to an SNS topic with five SQS subscribers. Cost: well under 100 dollars a month for the messaging itself. Operational load: zero brokers, IAM policies per queue, CloudWatch alarms on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible (backlog) and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage (lag in seconds) per queue, and one DLQ per queue with an alarm on depth greater than zero. The team never thinks about partitions or rebalancing. What they cannot do is replay last Tuesday's events into a new consumer; when that requirement arrived, they added an S3 archive subscriber to the topic and replayed from S3.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Visibility timeout shorter than processing: guaranteed duplicates under load.
  • Deleting with a stale receipt handle after the timeout expired: the delete succeeds silently in most cases, but the message may already have been received by another consumer.
  • FIFO dedup window of 5 minutes: a producer retry after 6 minutes creates a duplicate; the dedup id does nothing for consumer-side redelivery.
  • FIFO group throughput: one huge message group (tenantId of a giant tenant) serializes that tenant to 300 messages per second.
  • 256 KB limit: a payload with an embedded PDF fails at send time with InvalidParameterValue.
  • Standard queue "best-effort ordering": occasionally out of order even with a single producer; never rely on order from a standard queue.
  • Retention of 4 days: a consumer down over a long weekend loses messages; raise retention to 14 days on business queues.

27.6 Kafka versus RabbitMQ versus SQS

27.6.1 Comparison table

Dimension Kafka RabbitMQ SQS / SNS
Model Partitioned, retained log; consumers pull by offset Exchanges route to queues; broker pushes to consumers; deleted on ack Managed queue (SQS) and topic (SNS); consumers poll over HTTPS
Ordering Per partition, by key Per queue with one consumer; lost with parallel consumers or requeue FIFO: per message group; standard: best effort
Throughput Millions of msgs/s per cluster; 10 to 20 MB/s per partition Tens of thousands msgs/s per node; per-queue ceiling Standard: effectively unlimited; FIFO: 300 to 3,000 msgs/s per group
Retention and replay Days to forever; replay by resetting offsets; compaction for state None after ack; RabbitMQ Streams add a log type 4 to 14 days; no replay except DLQ redrive; archive to S3 yourself
Routing By topic and key only; consumers filter Rich: direct, topic patterns, fanout, headers, bindings changed at runtime SNS filter policies on attributes; otherwise one queue per consumer
Delayed messages Not native; retry topics with delayed consumers, or a scheduler TTL plus DLX wait queues, or the delayed-exchange plugin Per-message DelaySeconds up to 15 min; visibility timeout for retries
Consumer model Consumer groups; one consumer per partition; rebalancing Competing consumers with prefetch; any number per queue Competing consumers polling; visibility timeout as the lease
Duplicates At-least-once; idempotent producer removes producer retries; EOS within Kafka At-least-once; redelivery on nack or connection loss At-least-once; FIFO dedups producer retries for 5 min
Dead letters Build it: DLQ topic plus consumer logic Native DLX; quorum x-delivery-limit Native redrive policy with maxReceiveCount; redrive back
Operational cost High self-hosted (brokers, ZooKeeper or KRaft, partitions, lag tooling); managed via MSK, Confluent, Redpanda Moderate; single node is easy, clusters and quorum queues need care; managed via Amazon MQ, CloudAMQP Near zero; IAM and CloudWatch alarms
Client complexity High: keys, commits, rebalances, heartbeats Low to moderate: channels, acks, prefetch, confirms Low: three API calls
Best fit Event streaming, CDC, event sourcing, high fan-out, replay, analytics pipelines Task queues, RPC, complex routing, delayed work, moderate volumes AWS-native services, simple decoupling, serverless consumers, elastic burst absorption

27.6.2 Decision table: which broker for which job

Job Choose Why
Order events consumed by 6 services, replayable for a new analytics consumer Kafka Fan-out with independent groups, retention, replay
Thumbnail generation, PDF rendering, email sending RabbitMQ (or BullMQ on Redis) Task queue semantics, fair dispatch, priorities, native DLX
Change data capture from PostgreSQL into search and cache Kafka (Debezium) Log semantics, compaction, ordered per key
Fan-out on AWS to Lambda and a few SQS consumers, low ops budget SNS to SQS Managed, cheap, alarms built in
Request/reply between services that must stay decoupled RabbitMQ RPC (replyTo, correlationId) Native pattern; Kafka is awkward for it
Ledger events needing strict per-account order at 50,000 msgs/s Kafka, keyed by accountId Per-partition ordering at scale
Strict order per customer at 200 msgs/s on AWS SQS FIFO with MessageGroupId Ordering without operating anything
Retry in 5 minutes, then 30 minutes, then park RabbitMQ TTL plus DLX, or SQS visibility and redrive Native delay mechanisms
One service, one background job type, Redis already present BullMQ No new infrastructure
Audit log kept for a year and queryable by time Kafka with long retention plus an S3 sink, or just PostgreSQL Retention is a Kafka strength; but a database may be the simplest answer

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior does not ask "Kafka or RabbitMQ"; they ask "what are the messages for". Work to be done once by someone: a queue, and RabbitMQ or SQS or BullMQ depending on what the team already runs. Facts that several parties react to, possibly later, possibly again: a log, and Kafka. Both needs in one system are common; a company often runs Kafka for events and RabbitMQ or SQS for tasks, and that is fine. What they refuse to do is adopt Kafka because it is on the conference circuit, or run three brokers because three teams each chose their own.

Interview questions

  1. Prefetch of 1 versus 50: what changes? Expected: fairness and duplicate burst on crash versus throughput; long tasks want low prefetch.
  2. How do you implement "retry after 2 minutes" in RabbitMQ without a plugin? Expected: wait queue with x-message-ttl and a DLX back to the main exchange; one queue per delay.
  3. Explain the SQS visibility timeout and its failure mode. Expected: a lease; processing longer than the lease causes redelivery and duplicates; extend with ChangeMessageVisibility.
  4. Why does SQS FIFO dedup not solve consumer idempotency? Expected: it removes duplicate sends within 5 minutes; redelivery after a missed delete is a different path.
  5. What can Kafka do that RabbitMQ cannot, and vice versa? Expected: retention and replay, per-partition scale versus routing flexibility, native delays and DLX, RPC.
  6. When is a broker the wrong answer entirely? Expected: single service, low volume, Redis or PostgreSQL job table suffices; a broker adds a failure domain.

Practical exercise

Implement the same "send order confirmation email with retries" consumer twice: once on RabbitMQ with a 30 second and a 5 minute wait queue and a DLQ, once on SQS with a visibility timeout and a redrive policy of 5. Acceptance criteria: (a) a simulated email provider that fails 50 percent of the time results in every email eventually sent exactly once (verified by a unique constraint on (order_id, template) in PostgreSQL); (b) a permanently invalid address lands in the DLQ within one attempt with a readable error header; (c) killing the worker mid-send produces a redelivery that the idempotency check absorbs; (d) a one-page comparison of what you had to build yourself in each case.

27.7 Delivery semantics

Everything in this section and the next two exists because of one sentence: a message broker cannot know whether your consumer finished its work. It can know that it sent the message, and it can know that the consumer said "done". Between those two events the consumer can crash, the network can drop the acknowledgement, or the broker can reassign the work. The semantics you get are decided by what the consumer does in that gap.

27.7.1 At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once

Concept

  • At-most-once: each message is delivered zero or one times. Achieved by acknowledging (committing the offset, deleting from SQS, acking in RabbitMQ) before processing. A crash after the ack loses the message.
  • At-least-once: each message is delivered one or more times. Achieved by acknowledging after processing. A crash after processing but before the ack causes redelivery.
  • Exactly-once: each message's effect happens once. No broker can deliver this across arbitrary systems, because delivery and effect happen in different places. It is achievable in narrow scopes and simulated everywhere else by making duplicates harmless.

Why does it exist as a distinction?

Because the default of most clients, auto-commit on a timer, gives you neither reliably: it commits whatever was fetched, so a crash can lose messages fetched but not processed, or redeliver messages processed but not yet committed. Choosing at-least-once deliberately, and then engineering the consumer to tolerate duplicates, is the only combination that is both correct and achievable.

Mental model

Imagine a postal worker delivering signed-for parcels. At-most-once: they leave the parcel on the step and mark it delivered; if it is stolen, it is gone. At-least-once: they will not mark it delivered until you sign; if you sign but the pen fails, they come back tomorrow with the same parcel. Exactly-once: you would need the parcel and the signature to be one physical act, which is only possible when the parcel and the signature book live in the same place.

27.7.2 What Kafka's exactly-once actually covers

How it works

Kafka's exactly-once semantics (EOS) combine three mechanisms:

  1. The idempotent producer (27.3.3) removes duplicates from producer retries within a partition.
  2. Transactions let a producer write to several partitions and commit the consumer group's offsets in the same atomic unit (sendOffsetsToTransaction in Java; transaction.sendOffsets in kafkajs). Either the output records and the offset commit all become visible, or none do.
  3. isolation.level=read_committed on downstream consumers hides records from uncommitted or aborted transactions.

Together they make a read-process-write loop that stays inside Kafka (consume from topic A, produce to topic B, commit offsets) exactly-once: a crash mid-loop aborts the transaction, the output is invisible, and the offsets are not advanced, so the retry produces the output once. This is what stream processors (Kafka Streams, Flink with Kafka sinks) rely on.

What EOS does not cover is anything outside Kafka. If the "process" step writes to PostgreSQL, calls Stripe, or sends an email, the Kafka transaction knows nothing about those. The database write can commit and the Kafka transaction can abort; the email can be sent and the offset can fail to commit. The phrase "exactly-once with Kafka" in a design that touches a database and an email provider is a myth. The senior phrase is effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer, so that duplicates change nothing.

// kafkajs transactional read-process-write, Kafka to Kafka only
const producer = kafka.producer({ transactionalId: 'enrich-orders-1', idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 1 });
await consumer.run({
  autoCommit: false,
  eachBatch: async ({ batch }) => {
    const tx = await producer.transaction();
    try {
      for (const m of batch.messages) {
        await tx.send({ topic: 'orders.enriched', messages: [{ key: m.key, value: enrich(m.value) }] });
      }
      await tx.sendOffsets({
        consumerGroupId: 'enrich-orders',
        topics: [{ topic: batch.topic, partitions: [{ partition: batch.partition, offset: (Number(batch.lastOffset()) + 1).toString() }] }],
      });
      await tx.commit();       // output and offsets become visible together
    } catch (err) {
      await tx.abort();        // neither is visible; the batch will be re-read
      throw err;
    }
  },
});

27.8 Why duplicate messages are normal

A team that has never seen a duplicate has not looked. Every broker in this part delivers duplicates under ordinary conditions. This section shows the four paths with sequence diagrams so that when you see a double email in production you recognize which one you are looking at.

27.8.1 Producer retry after a timeout

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant B as Broker
    P->>B: produce OrderPlaced id=e1 (attempt 1)
    B->>B: append to log
    B--xP: ack lost (network)
    Note over P: request timeout: retry
    P->>B: produce OrderPlaced id=e1 (attempt 2)
    B->>B: append again (no idempotence) or discard (idempotent producer)
    B-->>P: ack

The producer cannot distinguish "the broker never got it" from "the broker got it and the ack was lost", so it must retry, and retrying may duplicate. Kafka's idempotent producer and SQS FIFO's deduplication id close this path at the broker. RabbitMQ has no producer-side dedup; the consumer's idempotency handles it. An application-level re-send after a process crash (the outbox relay publishes, crashes before marking the row as sent, republishes on restart) is the same path one level up, and no broker feature closes it.

27.8.2 Consumer crash after processing, before commit

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Broker
    participant C1 as Consumer A
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant C2 as Consumer B
    B->>C1: deliver m7 (offset 41)
    C1->>DB: INSERT payment, COMMIT
    Note over C1: crash before committing offset 41
    B->>B: session timeout, rebalance
    B->>C2: deliver m7 again (offset 41)
    C2->>DB: INSERT payment again unless idempotent

This is the canonical at-least-once duplicate, and it is the one you are choosing when you commit after processing. The window is the time between the business write and the offset commit, plus the rebalance. It cannot be closed by ordering the two operations differently; commit-first turns it into message loss. It is closed by making the second INSERT a no-op (27.9).

27.8.3 Rebalance while a message is in flight

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant CO as Coordinator
    participant C1 as Consumer A
    participant C2 as Consumer C (new)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    C1->>C1: processing m9 from partition 2 (slow, 8 s)
    C2->>CO: JoinGroup
    CO-->>C1: revoke partition 2
    CO-->>C2: assign partition 2 from last committed offset
    C2->>DB: process m9
    C1->>DB: finish m9 (duplicate effect)
    C1->>CO: commit offset for partition 2
    CO-->>C1: rejected, not the owner

Nothing crashed. A pod started, the group rebalanced, and the same message was processed by two consumers concurrently. The old owner's commit fails, which is correct, but its side effect already happened. Cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce how often this occurs; only idempotency makes it harmless.
