27.8.4 Redelivery after the SQS visibility timeout

The SQS sequence in 27.5.2 is the same path with different names: the lease expired while the consumer was still working, another consumer received the message, both processed it. RabbitMQ has an equivalent: a consumer's connection drops (a network blip, a heartbeat missed during a GC pause), the broker requeues its unacked messages, and the consumer, unaware, finishes processing them.

27.8.5 The senior conclusion

Every path above has the same shape: the effect happened, the acknowledgement did not, the system redelivered. There is no ordering of operations, no broker feature, and no timeout tuning that removes all four paths. There is exactly one design that makes all four harmless: the consumer must produce the same end state whether it sees a message once or five times. That is the next section.

27.9 Idempotent consumers

27.9.1 Idempotency by dedup table in PostgreSQL

Concept

An idempotent consumer records which message ids it has processed, in the same database transaction as the business write. On redelivery, the record already exists, the transaction does nothing, and the consumer acknowledges. Because the dedup record and the business effect commit atomically, there is no window where one exists without the other.

Why does it exist?

This is the only mechanism that closes every duplicate path from 27.8 with no timing assumptions. It requires that the message carries a stable, unique id assigned by the producer (27.10), and that the consumer's side effect is in the same database as the dedup table. It is also the receiving half of the inbox pattern; see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency for the full treatment, including deferring the actual processing to a worker that reads the inbox.

Mental model

Imagine a bouncer with a guest list who stamps each guest's hand as they enter. A guest who leaves and comes back shows the stamp; the bouncer waves them through without counting them twice. The stamp and the count are one motion. If the stamp were applied at the door but the count kept in another building, the two could disagree.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Broker
    participant C as Consumer
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    B->>C: PaymentCaptured id=m42 (delivery 1)
    C->>DB: BEGIN
    C->>DB: INSERT INTO processed_messages (m42) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    DB-->>C: 1 row inserted
    C->>DB: UPDATE orders SET status = paid ...
    C->>DB: COMMIT
    C->>B: ack / commit offset
    Note over B,C: later: redelivery
    B->>C: PaymentCaptured id=m42 (delivery 2)
    C->>DB: BEGIN
    C->>DB: INSERT INTO processed_messages (m42) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    DB-->>C: 0 rows (already processed)
    C->>DB: ROLLBACK (nothing to do)
    C->>B: ack / commit offset
  1. Begin a transaction.
  2. INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id, consumer) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. If zero rows were inserted, the message has been processed: commit or roll back the empty transaction, acknowledge, return.
  3. Perform the business write.
  4. Commit. The dedup row and the business change are durable together.
  5. Acknowledge to the broker. If the process dies before this step, the redelivery hits step 2 and stops.

The row lock taken by the INSERT also serializes two consumers processing the same message concurrently (the rebalance path): the second blocks on the first's uncommitted row and, after the first commits, sees the conflict.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE processed_messages (
  message_id   uuid        NOT NULL,
  consumer     text        NOT NULL,        -- one consumer group may see the same id as another; scope per consumer
  processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer, message_id)
);

-- Retention: messages older than the broker's retention cannot be redelivered; prune beyond that.
-- Run nightly; partition by month if volume is high.
DELETE FROM processed_messages WHERE processed_at < now() - interval '14 days';
-- The consumer transaction, as executed
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO processed_messages (consumer, message_id)
VALUES ('orders-payment-status', 'b1a7c9e2-3d4f-4a5b-9c6d-7e8f9a0b1c2d')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;              -- returns "INSERT 0 0" on a duplicate
UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', paid_at = '2026-09-06T10:15:02Z', version = version + 1
 WHERE id = '7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7' AND status = 'pending_payment';
COMMIT;

NestJS example

A reusable wrapper so no consumer forgets the pattern.

// messaging/idempotent-handler.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class IdempotentHandler {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(IdempotentHandler.name);
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  // Runs work(manager) exactly once per (consumer, messageId). Returns false if it was a duplicate.
  async once(consumer: string, messageId: string, work: (manager: EntityManager) => Promise<void>): Promise<boolean> {
    return this.db.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const result: { rowCount?: number } | unknown[] = await manager.query(
        `INSERT INTO processed_messages (consumer, message_id) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING message_id`,
        [consumer, messageId],
      );
      const inserted = Array.isArray(result) ? result.length : (result.rowCount ?? 0);
      if (inserted === 0) {
        this.logger.debug(`duplicate ${messageId} for ${consumer}; skipping`);
        return false;
      }
      await work(manager);                 // same transaction, same connection
      return true;
    });
  }
}
// orders/payment-events.consumer.ts (Kafka transport handler using it)
@EventPattern('payments.events')
async onPaymentEvent(@Payload() env: Envelope<PaymentCaptured>, @Ctx() ctx: KafkaContext): Promise<void> {
  if (env.type !== 'PaymentCaptured') { await this.commit(ctx); return; }
  await this.idempotent.once('orders-payment-status', env.id, async (manager) => {
    await manager.createQueryBuilder().update(Order)
      .set({ status: 'paid', paidAt: new Date(env.occurredAt), version: () => 'version + 1' })
      .where('id = :id AND status = :status', { id: env.payload.orderId, status: 'pending_payment' })
      .execute();
  });
  await this.commit(ctx);
}

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const [, inserted] = await this.sequelize.query(
    `INSERT INTO processed_messages (consumer, message_id) VALUES (:consumer, :id) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`,
    { replacements: { consumer: 'orders-payment-status', id: env.id }, transaction: t, type: QueryTypes.INSERT },
  );
  if (!inserted) return;               // duplicate: the transaction commits empty
  await Order.update(
    { status: 'paid', paidAt: new Date(env.occurredAt) },
    { where: { id: env.payload.orderId, status: 'pending_payment' }, transaction: t },
  );
});

27.9.2 Redis SET NX dedup and its window

Concept

SET dedup:{consumer}:{messageId} 1 NX PX ttl claims a message id in Redis. If the claim fails, skip. It is fast, needs no database, and it is not atomic with the business write.

How it works

The gaps:

  1. Claim, then crash before the write. The id is claimed; the redelivery is skipped; the effect never happens. Message lost. Mitigation: delete the claim on failure, but a hard crash cannot delete anything.
  2. Write, then Redis is unavailable for the claim. The effect happens; the claim fails; the redelivery happens again.
  3. TTL shorter than the redelivery window. A DLQ replay a week later is not detected.
  4. Redis failover loses recent claims (asynchronous replication).

Use it where a duplicate is a minor cost and the effect is not in a database you control: sending a push notification, calling a third-party webhook, emitting a metric. Set the TTL to at least the broker's retention. Prefer the PostgreSQL table for anything that changes money, stock or status.

async claim(consumer: string, messageId: string, ttlMs = 7 * 86_400_000): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    return (await this.redis.set(`dedup:${consumer}:${messageId}`, '1', 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX')) === 'OK';
  } catch {
    return true;   // Redis down: process anyway (at-least-once) rather than drop (at-most-once); log it
  }
}

27.9.3 Natural idempotency

Concept

Some operations are idempotent by construction and need no dedup record: setting a value (not incrementing it), an upsert keyed by a natural id, a conditional update guarded by a version or a state.

How it works

  • Upsert: INSERT INTO shipments (order_id, carrier, tracking) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET carrier = EXCLUDED.carrier, tracking = EXCLUDED.tracking. Processing twice writes the same row twice.
  • Conditional state transition: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'paid'. The second attempt updates zero rows.
  • Version guard: the event carries orderVersion: 7; UPDATE orders SET ... WHERE id = $1 AND version < 7. This also handles out-of-order arrival: an older event never overwrites a newer state.
  • Unique constraint as the guard: INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider_charge_id) with a unique index on provider_charge_id; a duplicate raises a unique violation that the consumer catches and treats as success.

Not naturally idempotent, and therefore needing a dedup record: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + 500, INSERT INTO order_items without a unique key, sending an email, calling POST /charges at a payment provider without an idempotency key.

Production scenario

A payments consumer processes 400 PaymentCaptured events per second with the PostgreSQL dedup table. Cost per message: one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (0.3 ms) inside a transaction that was happening anyway. The processed_messages table grows by 35 million rows per day; it is partitioned by day and old partitions are dropped after 14 days (longer than the 7 day topic retention plus DLQ replay window). Measured duplicate rate in normal operation: about 0.02 percent, almost all from deploys. During a broker incident with repeated rebalances it briefly reached 3 percent, and nothing downstream noticed, which is the point.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 a customer emails: "I was charged twice." The consumer that calls the payment provider used Redis SET NX dedup with a 1 hour TTL. A Kafka partition was replayed 90 minutes later during an incident (an operator reset offsets by 2 hours to recover from a different bug). Every charge in the window was re-sent to the provider; the Redis claims had expired. Two fixes: the provider call now carries an idempotency key (Idempotency-Key: charge:{orderId}), which the provider honours for 24 hours, and the dedup moved to PostgreSQL with 30 day retention. The replay was legitimate; the design was not replay-safe.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Message id missing or not unique (a producer reuses ids per batch): dedup silently drops real messages. Validate the envelope and reject messages without an id to the DLQ.
  • Two consumer groups sharing one dedup table without the consumer column: the second group sees "already processed".
  • Dedup table pruned before broker retention plus replay window: late redeliveries slip through.
  • The business write and the dedup insert in different databases (orders in PostgreSQL, dedup in DynamoDB): the atomicity is gone; this is the Redis case with a different name.
  • A dedup insert inside a transaction that later rolls back for an unrelated reason: the row is gone too, which is correct; the redelivery will retry the whole unit.
  • Idempotent consumer, non-idempotent downstream: the consumer skips the duplicate, but the first attempt called the email provider and then crashed before commit; the retry sends the email again. Every external side effect needs its own idempotency key passed to the provider.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior's first question for any consumer is "what happens if this runs twice?" and the second is "what happens if it runs twice concurrently?" They put the dedup row and the business write in one transaction, they pass idempotency keys to every external provider, they set dedup retention from the replay window rather than from table size, and they test the duplicate path explicitly. They explain it to product as: "the system will occasionally receive the same event twice; we have made sure that changes nothing you can see."

Common mistakes

  • Dedup in application memory (a Set of seen ids) that vanishes on restart and is per pod.
  • Committing the offset in a finally block regardless of success, which converts failures into loss.
  • Believing "exactly-once" in the client docs means the email will not be sent twice.
  • Incrementing counters from events (views = views + 1) without dedup, then wondering why analytics drift upward by 0.5 percent a week.

Interview questions

  1. Why can no broker deliver exactly-once to your database? Expected: the effect and the acknowledgement are in different systems; a crash between them is always possible; only an idempotent consumer makes redelivery harmless.
  2. Show the four duplicate paths. Expected: producer retry, consumer crash before commit, rebalance in flight, visibility timeout or connection loss redelivery.
  3. Why must the dedup insert be in the same transaction as the business write? Expected: atomicity; otherwise there is a window where one exists without the other, producing loss or duplication.
  4. When is Redis SET NX acceptable for dedup? Expected: non-critical side effects, long TTL, accepting the crash and failover windows.
  5. An event arrives out of order after a retry. How does the consumer cope? Expected: version guards or conditional state transitions; ignore events older than current state.
  6. What does Kafka EOS cover? Expected: Kafka-to-Kafka read-process-write with transactions and read_committed; not external systems.

Practical exercise

Build a PaymentCaptured consumer with the PostgreSQL dedup table and a chaos test. Acceptance criteria: (a) a Jest test using Testcontainers (Kafka and PostgreSQL) publishes 1,000 events and, using a hook that kills the consumer process after a random 5 percent of business writes but before the offset commit, proves that orders.paid_at is set exactly once per order and processed_messages has exactly 1,000 rows; (b) a second test runs two consumer instances in the same group and forces a rebalance mid-run, with the same assertions; (c) a third test replays the topic from offset zero and asserts zero additional effects; (d) the consumer rejects an envelope without an id to the DLQ with a clear reason header.

27.10 Message design

27.10.1 The envelope

Concept

A message has two parts: the envelope (metadata every message carries, in the same shape, forever) and the payload (the event-specific data). The envelope is what lets generic infrastructure (dedup, tracing, routing, DLQ tooling, replay) work without knowing what the payload means.

Why does it exist?

Without a standard envelope, every consumer parses messages differently, dedup has no id to key on, traces stop at the broker, and nobody can tell from a DLQ entry where the message came from or when. The envelope is a contract with the future: the payload will evolve, the envelope will not.

How it works

Field Type Purpose
id UUID v4 or v7 Unique per message; the dedup key. Assigned by the producer once, reused on every retry
type string, OrderPlaced What happened; routes to the handler
version integer Schema version of the payload; consumers branch on it
occurredAt ISO 8601 UTC When the fact happened in the producer, from the database clock where possible
producer string, orders-api Owning service; for debugging and DLQ triage
correlationId UUID Ties every message in one business flow together (one checkout, one ride)
causationId UUID The id of the message that caused this one; builds the causal chain
traceparent W3C trace header Distributed tracing across the broker (in headers, not the body)
subject or key string The entity id this is about; also used as the partition key
payload object The event-specific data 
// messaging/envelope.ts
import { IsISO8601, IsInt, IsObject, IsString, IsUUID, Min } from 'class-validator';

export class Envelope<T = unknown> {
  @IsUUID() id!: string;
  @IsString() type!: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(1) version!: number;
  @IsISO8601() occurredAt!: string;
  @IsString() producer!: string;
  @IsUUID() correlationId!: string;
  @IsUUID() causationId!: string;
  @IsString() subject!: string;
  @IsObject() payload!: T;
}

export function envelope<T>(type: string, version: number, subject: string, payload: T, ctx: { correlationId: string; causationId?: string }): Envelope<T> {
  const id = randomUUID();
  return {
    id, type, version, subject, payload,
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    producer: process.env.SERVICE_NAME ?? 'unknown',
    correlationId: ctx.correlationId,
    causationId: ctx.causationId ?? id,
  };
}

Consumers validate the envelope with class-validator before touching the payload; an envelope that fails validation goes to the DLQ immediately as a poison message, because retrying cannot fix a missing id.

27.10.2 Schema evolution

Concept

A topic outlives every version of the code that writes to it. Producers and consumers deploy independently, and a topic with 7 days of retention holds messages written by last week's producer. Schema evolution is the discipline that keeps old consumers reading new messages and new consumers reading old ones.

How it works

The rules that keep a JSON payload compatible:

  1. Add fields, never remove or rename them. A consumer that ignores unknown fields (the default with JSON.parse) handles additions. Removal breaks anyone who read the field.
  2. New fields are optional with a default in the consumer, because old messages in the topic do not have them.
  3. Never change a field's type or meaning. amount in cents becoming amount in dollars is a silent financial bug; add amountMinor instead.
  4. Breaking changes get a new version (and often a new type name: OrderPlacedV2), and the consumer handles both for as long as old messages can exist: retention plus DLQ replay window.
  5. A schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) enforces these rules at publish time, rejecting an incompatible schema before it reaches the topic. Part 24 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients covers registries, compatibility modes and the tooling.
  6. Consumer-driven contract tests (Part 40 — Testing) catch a producer change that would break a consumer before deploy.
// A consumer that reads two versions during the transition window
function toOrderPlaced(env: Envelope): OrderPlacedV2 {
  if (env.version === 1) {
    const p = env.payload as OrderPlacedV1;
    return { ...p, currency: 'INR', lines: p.items.map((i) => ({ sku: i.sku, qty: i.quantity, unitMinor: i.priceCents })) };
  }
  if (env.version === 2) return env.payload as OrderPlacedV2;
  throw new PoisonMessageError(`unsupported OrderPlaced version ${env.version}`);
}

27.10.3 Size limits and the claim-check pattern

How it works

  • Kafka's default max.message.bytes is 1 MB; RabbitMQ handles larger but performance degrades above a few hundred kilobytes; SQS is 256 KB.
  • A 5 MB PDF, a base64 image, or a full product catalog does not belong in a message. Put the blob in object storage (S3) and put the URL (with an expiry or a signed URL policy) in the message: the claim-check pattern. The consumer fetches what it needs when it needs it.
  • Keep events small and factual: OrderPlaced carries order id, customer id, totals and line items (ids, quantities, prices at the time), not the customer's full profile and the product descriptions. Consumers that need more query the owning service or a read model. The exception is when consumers must be independent of the producer's availability, in which case a richer "fat event" is a deliberate choice with a documented size cap.
  • Compress at the producer (Kafka batch compression, or gzip the body with a contentEncoding header on RabbitMQ) for JSON above tens of kilobytes.

27.10.4 Personal data in messages

How it works

A retained log is a copy of personal data that lives outside the database you protect. Three consequences:

  1. Retention conflicts with erasure. A "delete my data" request cannot delete an immutable log entry. The pattern is crypto-shredding: encrypt personal fields with a per-user key stored in a key table; to erase, delete the key, and every message with that user's data becomes unreadable.
  2. Minimise. Put the user id in the event, not the email address, unless the consumer genuinely needs it (the email sender does; the analytics consumer does not). Two events for two audiences is often cleaner than one event with everything.
  3. Access control. Topic ACLs so that only the services that need payments.events can read it; TLS in transit; encryption at rest on brokers; no personal data in message keys or headers, which are often logged in plaintext by tooling.

27.11 Producer side

27.11.1 The dual-write problem and the outbox pattern

Concept

A handler that writes to PostgreSQL and then publishes to a broker has two commits that cannot be made atomic. Commit the database and fail to publish: the order exists and nobody knows. Publish and fail to commit: everyone reacts to an order that does not exist. The transactional outbox solves it by writing the event into an outbox table inside the same database transaction as the business change, and having a separate relay process publish rows from that table to the broker.

How it works

  1. BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders ...; INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, key, payload, headers) ...; COMMIT; One transaction, one durability decision.
  2. A relay (a polling worker in the same service, or Debezium reading the WAL) reads unpublished outbox rows in order, publishes them, and marks them published.
  3. The relay can crash after publishing and before marking: the row is published again on restart. This is the producer-side duplicate path; the envelope id is the outbox row's id, so consumers dedup it.
  4. Ordering per key is preserved if the relay publishes rows in insertion order with the row's key as the partition key.

Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency covers the table design, the polling relay versus CDC, batching, and the failure modes in depth. Here the rule is: never publish business events directly from a request handler; write the outbox row and let the relay publish.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id           uuid        PRIMARY KEY,              -- becomes the message id
  topic        text        NOT NULL,
  message_key  text        NOT NULL,
  headers      jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  payload      jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  published_at timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished_idx ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- Relay: claim a batch in order, skipping rows another relay instance holds
SELECT id, topic, message_key, headers, payload
  FROM outbox
 WHERE published_at IS NULL
 ORDER BY created_at
 LIMIT 200
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

27.11.2 Publish after commit, retries, batching and compression

How it works

  • Publish after commit is the minimum discipline even without an outbox (for non-critical notifications, say): never publish inside the transaction, because a rollback after publishing announces something that never happened. With TypeORM, publish in the code after dataSource.transaction() resolves; with Sequelize, use transaction.afterCommit(() => publish()).
  • Retries in the producer client (kafkajs retry.retries, amqplib reconnect via amqp-connection-manager) handle broker blips. Beyond the client's retries, the outbox is the retry: the row stays unpublished and the relay tries again next cycle. A producer without an outbox must choose between failing the request and dropping the event; make the choice explicit.
  • Batching: the relay publishes 100 to 500 outbox rows per send, in key order. kafkajs producer.send with many messages is one batch per partition. linger.ms on the Java producer does the same for direct publishers.
  • Compression per batch (CompressionTypes.GZIP in kafkajs; lz4/zstd need a codec plugin) cuts network and broker disk by 5 to 10x for JSON.

NestJS example

ClientKafka from @nestjs/microservices for the simple case, showing the shape that carries a key and headers. Note that emit returns an Observable and does nothing until subscribed; convert with lastValueFrom and await it, or the publish silently never happens.

// orders/orders-events.publisher.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClientKafka } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { lastValueFrom } from 'rxjs';
import { Envelope } from '../messaging/envelope';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersEventsPublisher implements OnModuleInit {
  constructor(@Inject('KAFKA_CLIENT') private readonly client: ClientKafka) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> { await this.client.connect(); }

  async publish(env: Envelope, traceparent?: string): Promise<void> {
    await lastValueFrom(this.client.emit('orders.events', {
      key: env.subject,                                // partition by order id
      value: JSON.stringify(env),
      headers: { 'x-message-id': env.id, 'x-type': env.type, ...(traceparent ? { traceparent } : {}) },
    }));
  }
}
// app.module.ts registration
ClientsModule.register([{
  name: 'KAFKA_CLIENT',
  transport: Transport.KAFKA,
  options: {
    client: { clientId: 'orders-api', brokers: process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS!.split(',') },
    producer: { allowAutoTopicCreation: false, idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 1 },
    producerOnlyMode: true,                            // do not join a consumer group just to publish
  },
}]),

27.12 Consumer side in NestJS

27.12.1 @EventPattern on the Kafka transport with manual commits

Concept

The @nestjs/microservices Kafka transport runs a kafkajs consumer and dispatches each message to the handler whose @EventPattern (fire-and-forget) or @MessagePattern (request/reply over a reply topic) matches the topic. By default it auto-commits. For at-least-once you configure run: { autoCommit: false } and commit from the handler through KafkaContext.

How it works

// main.ts (consumer service)
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.connectMicroservice<MicroserviceOptions>({
  transport: Transport.KAFKA,
  options: {
    client: { clientId: 'inventory-service', brokers: process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS!.split(',') },
    consumer: {
      groupId: 'inventory',                       // owned, unique, never reused by another service
      sessionTimeout: 30_000,
      heartbeatInterval: 3_000,
      rebalanceTimeout: 60_000,
      allowAutoTopicCreation: false,
    },
    run: {
      autoCommit: false,                          // we commit after processing
      partitionsConsumedConcurrently: 4,          // parallelism across partitions, order kept within each
    },
    subscribe: { fromBeginning: false },
  },
});
app.enableShutdownHooks();                        // SIGTERM -> onModuleDestroy hooks -> consumer.disconnect()
await app.startAllMicroservices();
await app.listen(3000);                           // HTTP for health and metrics
// inventory/order-events.consumer.ts
import { Controller, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Ctx, EventPattern, KafkaContext, Payload } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { validateOrReject } from 'class-validator';
import { plainToInstance } from 'class-transformer';
import { Envelope } from '../messaging/envelope';
import { IdempotentHandler } from '../messaging/idempotent-handler';
import { DeadLetterService } from '../messaging/dead-letter.service';
import { RetryPolicy } from '../messaging/retry-policy';
import { InventoryService } from './inventory.service';

@Controller()
export class OrderEventsConsumer {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderEventsConsumer.name);
  constructor(
    private readonly idempotent: IdempotentHandler,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryService,
    private readonly dlq: DeadLetterService,
    private readonly retry: RetryPolicy,
  ) {}

  @EventPattern('orders.events')
  async onOrderEvent(@Payload() raw: unknown, @Ctx() ctx: KafkaContext): Promise<void> {
    const msg = ctx.getMessage();
    const partition = ctx.getPartition();
    const topic = ctx.getTopic();
    const heartbeat = ctx.getHeartbeat();

    let env: Envelope;
    try {
      env = plainToInstance(Envelope, raw);
      await validateOrReject(env);
    } catch (err) {
      await this.dlq.park(msg.key?.toString() ?? null, msg.value, headersOf(msg), {
        sourceTopic: topic, partition, offset: msg.offset, consumerGroup: 'inventory', attempts: 1, error: `invalid envelope: ${String(err)}`,
      });
      return this.commit(ctx);                    // poison: park and move on
    }

    if (env.type !== 'OrderPlaced') return this.commit(ctx);   // not for us; still commit

    try {
      await this.retry.run(
        () => this.idempotent.once('inventory', env.id, (m) => this.inventory.reserveForOrder(m, env)),
        { maxAttempts: 5, baseDelayMs: 200, onAttempt: heartbeat },   // heartbeat between attempts
      );
    } catch (err) {
      await this.dlq.park(msg.key?.toString() ?? null, msg.value, headersOf(msg), {
        sourceTopic: topic, partition, offset: msg.offset, consumerGroup: 'inventory', attempts: 5, error: String(err),
      });
    }
    await this.commit(ctx);
  }

  private async commit(ctx: KafkaContext): Promise<void> {
    const { offset } = ctx.getMessage();
    await ctx.getConsumer().commitOffsets([
      { topic: ctx.getTopic(), partition: ctx.getPartition(), offset: (Number(offset) + 1).toString() },  // commit the NEXT offset
    ]);
  }
}

function headersOf(msg: { headers?: Record<string, unknown> }): Record<string, string> {
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(msg.headers ?? {}).map(([k, v]) => [k, v == null ? '' : v.toString()]));
}

Important details in that handler:

  • Commit the next offset. Kafka's committed offset means "start here next time", so it is offset + 1. Committing offset reprocesses the last message on every restart.
  • Commit after the DLQ publish, so a message is never both uncommitted and parked.
  • Non-matching types are committed too; otherwise the group never advances past them.
  • Heartbeat during retries. A 5 attempt backoff of several seconds could exceed the session timeout without it.
  • @MessagePattern versus @EventPattern. @MessagePattern expects to send a reply to a <topic>.reply topic and requires the producer to have subscribed to it (client.subscribeToResponseOf). For events, use @EventPattern.

27.12.2 Graceful shutdown

How it works

  1. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. With enableShutdownHooks(), NestJS calls onModuleDestroy, beforeApplicationShutdown and onApplicationShutdown on providers and closes the microservice, which calls consumer.disconnect().
  2. kafkajs disconnect() stops fetching and waits for the in-flight eachMessage or eachBatch handler to return before leaving the group. A handler that takes 40 seconds delays shutdown by 40 seconds; set terminationGracePeriodSeconds above the handler's worst case, or the pod is SIGKILLed mid-handler and the message is reprocessed by the next owner.
  3. Because the consumer sends LeaveGroup on a clean shutdown, the rebalance is immediate rather than waiting for the session timeout.
  4. During shutdown, stop accepting new work from any internal queue (an in-process per-key worker pool, below) and drain it before returning from the hook.

27.12.3 Backpressure, batch consumption and ordering-preserving parallelism

Concept

A consumer that pulls faster than it can process either runs out of memory or exceeds its time budget. Backpressure is the consumer slowing the source. Parallelism is the consumer doing more at once without breaking per-key ordering.

How it works

  • Pause and resume. kafkajs consumer.pause([{ topic, partitions: [p] }]) stops fetching from a partition; resume restarts it. Use it when a downstream dependency is degraded (circuit breaker open) so the consumer stops pulling messages it cannot process, instead of retrying them into the DLQ. In the NestJS transport, ctx.getConsumer() gives you the kafkajs consumer for this.
  • Batch consumption (eachBatch in plain kafkajs) lets you write 100 rows to PostgreSQL in one statement instead of 100 statements: the difference between 200 and 5,000 messages per second per partition. The NestJS transport delivers one message at a time; for batch semantics, run a plain kafkajs consumer inside a NestJS provider.
  • Concurrency per partition is 1 by design. partitionsConsumedConcurrently gives parallelism across partitions. To go further while keeping per-key order, route each message to an in-process worker lane chosen by hash(key) mod lanes: messages with the same key are processed sequentially in one lane, different keys in parallel.
// messaging/keyed-lanes.ts: per-key sequential processing, parallel across keys
export class KeyedLanes {
  private readonly tails: Promise<void>[];
  constructor(private readonly lanes = 8) { this.tails = Array.from({ length: lanes }, () => Promise.resolve()); }

  run(key: string, work: () => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
    const lane = hashToLane(key, this.lanes);
    const next = this.tails[lane].then(work, work);    // chain after whatever this lane is doing
    this.tails[lane] = next.catch(() => undefined);    // a failure must not poison the lane
    return next;
  }

  drain(): Promise<void[]> { return Promise.all(this.tails); }   // call from onModuleDestroy
}

Commit only after every message in the batch has completed across all lanes, or commit per lane at the lowest completed offset; the simple correct approach is batch-level commit after drain().

// A plain kafkajs batch consumer inside a NestJS provider, using lanes and batch commit
await this.consumer.run({
  autoCommit: false,
  eachBatch: async ({ batch, heartbeat, resolveOffset, commitOffsetsIfNecessary, isRunning, isStale }) => {
    const lanes = new KeyedLanes(8);
    for (const message of batch.messages) {
      if (!isRunning() || isStale()) break;
      const key = message.key?.toString() ?? message.offset;
      void lanes.run(key, async () => {
        await this.handle(message);                    // idempotent; own retry and DLQ inside
        resolveOffset(message.offset);
      });
      if (Number(message.offset) % 50 === 0) await heartbeat();
    }
    await lanes.drain();
    await commitOffsetsIfNecessary();
  },
});

Production scenario

An inventory consumer on 24 partitions with 6 pods (4 partitions each), partitionsConsumedConcurrently: 4, and 8 lanes per partition handles 9,000 OrderPlaced events per second with a p99 processing latency of 35 ms and steady-state lag under 500 messages. When PostgreSQL has a failover, the circuit breaker in InventoryService opens, the consumer pauses all partitions for 15 seconds, resumes, and the 135,000 message backlog drains in 20 seconds. No message reached the DLQ during the failover, because pausing is not failing.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on-call sees the notifications consumer restarting every 90 seconds with The group is rebalancing, so a rejoin is needed followed by CrashLoopBackOff. The handler calls a push provider with a 60 second HTTP timeout and no retry budget; during a provider outage every message takes 60 seconds, the session times out at 30, the consumer is kicked, kafkajs crashes the run loop, the pod restarts, the rebalance reassigns the same partition, and the same message is tried again. The fix: a 5 second HTTP timeout, a circuit breaker that pauses the partition when the provider is down, heartbeats during retries, and a session timeout that reflects the real worst case.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Handler throws before commit and there is no DLQ path: the transport logs the error and, with autoCommit: false, the message is redelivered forever after each restart.
  • emit() without subscribing: the event is never published; no error.
  • Committing offset instead of offset + 1: one duplicate per partition per restart.
  • partitionsConsumedConcurrently greater than assigned partitions: harmless; less than: idle capacity.
  • Lanes with a shared downstream connection pool smaller than the lane count: lanes serialize on the pool and throughput collapses; size the pool to lanes times partitions.
  • A @MessagePattern handler on a topic nobody replies to: the consumer tries to produce to <topic>.reply and fails if the topic does not exist and auto-creation is off.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats a consumer as a production service with a time budget per message, a dependency health model (pause when the dependency is down, do not fail messages), an explicit commit strategy, a DLQ, and a shutdown path that is tested by killing pods during load. They keep handlers under a second, move long work to a job queue, and do not let the transport's convenience hide the commit.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving autoCommit on because the handler "never fails".
  • Using the transport's default groupId from an example, shared by two services.
  • Retrying in a loop inside the handler for minutes without heartbeating.
  • Publishing from inside a database transaction.
  • Fat events with the whole customer record, then a support ticket about a customer's address showing up in a log.

Interview questions

  1. Why publish through an outbox instead of directly after commit? Expected: publish-after-commit still loses the event if the process dies between commit and publish; the outbox makes the event part of the transaction and the relay retries. Follow-up: what duplicate does the relay introduce and who handles it?
  2. What offset do you commit after processing offset 41? Expected: 42.
  3. How do you process in parallel without breaking per-order ordering? Expected: partitions plus per-key lanes; commit after the batch drains.
  4. A downstream API is down. Retry, DLQ or pause? Expected: pause the partition (backpressure) with a circuit breaker; DLQ is for messages that cannot succeed, not for a dependency outage.
  5. How does a JSON payload evolve without breaking consumers? Expected: additive changes, optional with defaults, version bump for breaking changes, registry or contract tests.
  6. Where does a 5 MB PDF go? Expected: object storage; the message carries the URL.

Practical exercise

Build an orders.events consumer in NestJS on the Kafka transport with manual commits, envelope validation, the idempotent handler from 27.9, retries with heartbeat, DLQ parking, and graceful shutdown. Acceptance criteria: (a) kill -TERM during a 2 second handler finishes the message and commits before exit, verified by logs and a lag check; (b) a message with version: 99 lands in the DLQ with the reason header and the offset is committed; (c) with the downstream service returning 503, the consumer pauses within 5 seconds, produces zero DLQ entries, and resumes within 30 seconds of recovery; (d) throughput with 8 lanes is at least 5x the single-lane throughput at equal correctness.

27.13 Retry strategy by error type

Concept

Not every failure deserves a retry. A network timeout will probably succeed in a second; a validation error will fail identically a thousand times; a message that crashes the deserializer will never be parsed. A consumer that treats all three the same either loses recoverable work or loops forever on unrecoverable work. Error classification is the difference.

How it works

Error class Examples Retry? Where Then
Transient Connection reset, HTTP 502/503/504, request timeout, PostgreSQL deadlock (40P01) or serialization failure (40001), lock timeout, broker NotEnoughReplicas, rate limited (429) Yes, with exponential backoff and jitter In-process for the first 2 to 3 attempts (tens of ms to seconds); then delayed retry via wait queue or retry topic (30 s, 2 min, 10 min) DLQ after the budget (5 to 8 attempts over roughly 15 minutes); alert if transient DLQ rate rises, because that means an outage, not bad data
Dependency down Circuit breaker open, every call failing for more than N seconds Do not retry individual messages Pause the partition or stop consuming the queue; resume when the breaker half-opens Nothing goes to the DLQ; lag grows and the lag alert tells the story
Permanent (business) Entity not found, state transition not allowed, insufficient stock, HTTP 400/404/409/422 from a downstream, unique violation you did not expect No Nowhere DLQ immediately with the error; commit; often the fix is a data correction and a replay, or a decision that the message is obsolete
Poison Cannot parse, envelope invalid, unknown type or unsupported version, handler throws TypeError, message causes the consumer process to crash No Nowhere DLQ immediately; page if a poison message caused a crash loop; the fix is a code deploy, then replay
Unknown Anything not classified Bounded: 3 attempts In-process DLQ; every unknown error seen in the DLQ gets classified and added to the table

The backoff formula that avoids retry storms: delay = min(cap, base * 2^attempt) * random(0.5, 1.5). With base = 200 ms and cap = 60 s, attempts land at roughly 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, 3.2 seconds and then at wait-queue tiers. Jitter is not optional: 500 consumers retrying at exactly 30 seconds is a synchronized hammer on a recovering dependency.

// messaging/error-classifier.ts
export type ErrorKind = 'transient' | 'permanent' | 'poison' | 'unknown';

export function classifyError(err: unknown): ErrorKind {
  if (err instanceof PoisonMessageError || err instanceof SyntaxError || err instanceof TypeError) return 'poison';
  if (err instanceof NotFoundException || err instanceof ConflictException || err instanceof BadRequestException) return 'permanent';
  const e = err as { code?: string; status?: number; name?: string; message?: string };
  if (e.code === '40001' || e.code === '40P01' || e.code === '55P03') return 'transient';        // PG serialization, deadlock, lock_not_available
  if (e.code === 'ECONNRESET' || e.code === 'ETIMEDOUT' || e.code === 'ECONNREFUSED') return 'transient';
  if (e.status !== undefined && [408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504].includes(e.status)) return 'transient';
  if (e.status !== undefined && e.status >= 400 && e.status < 500) return 'permanent';
  return 'unknown';
}
// messaging/retry-policy.ts
@Injectable()
export class RetryPolicy {
  async run<T>(op: () => Promise<T>, opts: { maxAttempts: number; baseDelayMs: number; capMs?: number; onAttempt?: () => Promise<void> }): Promise<T> {
    const cap = opts.capMs ?? 60_000;
    for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
      try {
        return await op();
      } catch (err) {
        const kind = classifyError(err);
        if (kind === 'permanent' || kind === 'poison') throw err;                      // no retry
        const budget = kind === 'unknown' ? Math.min(3, opts.maxAttempts) : opts.maxAttempts;
        if (attempt >= budget) throw err;
        const delay = Math.min(cap, opts.baseDelayMs * 2 ** attempt) * (0.5 + Math.random());
        await opts.onAttempt?.();                                                      // heartbeat
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
      }
    }
  }
}

27.14 Observability

Concept

A messaging system fails quietly. HTTP failures show up as 500s on a dashboard within seconds; a consumer that stopped processing shows up as a customer complaint three hours later. The observability goal is to turn "silently behind" into a page within minutes.

How it works

Signal Source Alert threshold (starting point) What it tells you
Consumer lag (messages) kafka_consumergroup_lag from kafka-lag-exporter or Burrow; RabbitMQ rabbitmq_queue_messages_ready; SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible Above 2x the normal steady state for 5 minutes, or above a business number (10,000 unshipped orders) Consumers slower than producers, stuck, or crashed
Consumer lag (seconds) kafka_consumergroup_lag_seconds; SQS ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage; or your own now - occurredAt histogram at the consumer Above the business SLO (emails within 60 s; inventory within 5 s) Time-to-effect, the number product cares about
DLQ depth Messages in *.dlq topics or queues; the dead_letters table with status = 'parked' Greater than 0 for 10 minutes in business hours; greater than 100 any time Data that needs a human
DLQ rate Increase per minute Sudden jump A new bug or a producer contract change
Processing latency Histogram per handler (consumer_process_duration_seconds{topic,type,result}) p99 above 50 percent of the session timeout Approaching kick-out; downstream slowness
Rebalance count kafkajs consumer.events.GROUP_JOIN counter; Java rebalance-rate-per-hour More than 3 per 10 minutes outside deploys Flapping consumer, session timeouts, crash loops
Publish failures and latency producer_send_errors_total, producer_send_duration_seconds Any sustained errors Broker unavailable, NotEnoughReplicas, auth
Outbox backlog SELECT count(*) FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL and the age of the oldest Oldest unpublished older than 60 s Relay down or broker unreachable
Under-replicated partitions Broker JMX UnderReplicatedPartitions; MSK CloudWatch Greater than 0 for 5 minutes Broker or disk trouble; durability at risk
Duplicate rate Counter incremented when the dedup table says "already processed" Above 1 percent sustained Rebalance storms or a replay in progress
Consumer liveness Pod ready and a heartbeat gauge updated on every poll Gauge stale for 60 s The process is up but the loop is dead

Two instrumentation habits:

  1. Tag every message metric with topic and type, never with messageId or orderId (unbounded cardinality kills Prometheus).
  2. Propagate the trace. Put the W3C traceparent header on every published message (the OpenTelemetry kafkajs and amqplib instrumentations do this automatically) and start the consumer span as a child of it with a messaging.* semantic convention. One trace then shows the HTTP request, the outbox write, the relay publish, and every consumer's work, with the queue wait time visible as the gap between spans. Part 42 — Observability covers the OpenTelemetry setup; the messaging-specific point is that without header propagation the trace stops at the broker.
// messaging/consumer-metrics.ts (prom-client)
import { Counter, Gauge, Histogram } from 'prom-client';

export const processDuration = new Histogram({
  name: 'consumer_process_duration_seconds',
  help: 'Handler duration per message',
  labelNames: ['topic', 'type', 'result'] as const,               // result: ok | retry | dlq | duplicate
  buckets: [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10],
});
export const endToEndLag = new Histogram({
  name: 'consumer_end_to_end_lag_seconds',
  help: 'now minus occurredAt at processing time',
  labelNames: ['topic', 'type'] as const,
  buckets: [0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 15, 60, 300, 900, 3600],
});
export const dlqParked = new Counter({ name: 'consumer_dlq_parked_total', help: 'Messages parked to DLQ', labelNames: ['topic', 'reason'] as const });
export const rebalances = new Counter({ name: 'consumer_rebalances_total', help: 'Group joins', labelNames: ['group'] as const });
export const lastPollAt = new Gauge({ name: 'consumer_last_poll_timestamp_seconds', help: 'Liveness of the consume loop', labelNames: ['group'] as const });

27.15 Local development and testing

How it works

Docker Compose with a single-node Kafka in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper) and RabbitMQ with the management UI covers development. The KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS line is the one everyone gets wrong: it must be the address your application uses to reach the broker from outside the container.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0
    ports: ["9092:9092"]
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"     # same as production: topics are created explicitly
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3.13-management
    ports: ["5672:5672", "15672:15672"]           # UI at http://localhost:15672, guest/guest
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres }

Create topics with a script that runs in CI and in production migrations alike, with the same partition counts and min.insync.replicas (set to 1 locally, 2 in production through an environment variable), so that the local environment does not hide production constraints.

Testing consumers has three layers (Part 40 — Testing covers the pyramid; here is the messaging shape):

  1. Unit: call the handler method directly with a fake KafkaContext (a small object exposing getMessage, getPartition, getTopic, getConsumer with a spy on commitOffsets, and getHeartbeat). Assert the business effect, the commit, and the DLQ call for each error class. Fast, no broker.
  2. Integration with Testcontainers: @testcontainers/kafka starts a real broker in a container; the test publishes with kafkajs and asserts on PostgreSQL state. This is where you test duplicates, rebalances and ordering, because those behaviours come from the real broker.
  3. Contract: a schema test that fails when a producer changes an envelope or payload incompatibly, run in the producer's pipeline against consumers' expectations.
// test/order-events.consumer.int-spec.ts (excerpt)
import { KafkaContainer, StartedKafkaContainer } from '@testcontainers/kafka';
import { Kafka } from 'kafkajs';

let kafka: StartedKafkaContainer;
beforeAll(async () => {
  kafka = await new KafkaContainer('confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0').withKraft().start();
  process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS = `${kafka.getHost()}:${kafka.getMappedPort(9093)}`;
  const admin = new Kafka({ brokers: [process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS] }).admin();
  await admin.connect();
  await admin.createTopics({ topics: [{ topic: 'orders.events', numPartitions: 3 }] });
  await admin.disconnect();
}, 120_000);

it('processes a duplicated OrderPlaced exactly once', async () => {
  const env = envelope('OrderPlaced', 2, order.id, payload, { correlationId: randomUUID() });
  await producer.send({ topic: 'orders.events', messages: [{ key: order.id, value: JSON.stringify(env) }, { key: order.id, value: JSON.stringify(env) }] });
  await waitFor(async () => (await processedCount(env.id)) === 1, { timeout: 10_000 });
  expect(await reservationsFor(order.id)).toHaveLength(1);
});

Test the duplicate path and the crash path on purpose. A consumer test suite without a duplicate test is testing the happy path of an at-least-once system.

27.16 Edge cases and failure modes

Each entry: what happens, how you notice, what to do.

  • Duplicate message. Normal. Detected by the dedup table's "already processed" count. Idempotent handler; idempotency keys to external providers; a duplicate-rate metric to distinguish "occasional" from "rebalance storm".
  • Consumer crash mid-batch. Messages processed but not committed are redelivered; with batch-level commit, the whole batch. Notice via duplicate-rate spikes after restarts. Keep batches small enough that reprocessing is cheap; idempotency makes it harmless.
  • Consumer lag increasing: slow database. Handler p99 climbs, lag climbs uniformly across partitions. Batch the writes, add an index, or add consumers up to the partition count; beyond that, more partitions.
  • Consumer lag increasing: hot partition. One partition's lag grows while others are flat. Key skew (one tenant, one product on sale) or a slow message on that partition. Change the key to a finer grain (orderId instead of tenantId), or add a random suffix for keys that need no ordering, or process that partition's messages with more internal lanes.
  • Consumer lag increasing: too few partitions. All consumers busy, adding pods does nothing (extra pods sit idle with no partition). Increase partitions during a quiet window with consumers drained, accepting the key re-hash, or start a new topic with more partitions and migrate.
  • Consumer lag increasing: rebalancing storm. Rebalance counter spikes; throughput drops to zero repeatedly. Session timeouts from slow handlers, pods flapping on memory limits, or deploys with too many pods restarting at once. Static membership, cooperative rebalancing where the client supports it, one pod at a time rollouts, handlers well under the session timeout.
  • Rebalancing during deploy. Each pod stop and start triggers a rebalance; in-flight messages duplicate. Expected; mitigated by graceful shutdown (LeaveGroup immediately), maxUnavailable: 1, and idempotency.
  • Out-of-order events after retries. OrderCancelled succeeds while OrderPlaced is in a 2 minute retry queue; the cancel arrives first. Retry topics and wait queues break ordering by design. Consumers must tolerate it: version guards, conditional transitions, or a "pending events" buffer keyed by entity for strictly ordered domains. If order truly matters more than throughput, use blocking retry on the partition instead.
  • Poison message loop. The same message fails, is requeued to the head of the queue, fails again, forever; the partition or queue is blocked. Every consumer has a maximum attempt count and a poison classification; quorum queues get x-delivery-limit; RabbitMQ requeue=true is banned for failures.
  • DLQ never monitored. Messages accumulate, retention deletes them, and the loss is discovered by a customer months later. A DLQ alert with an owner, a weekly review, retention of 30 days or more, and a PostgreSQL mirror for searchability.
  • Broker down, producer side. Direct publishers throw or buffer in memory (kafkajs retries for retry.retries then throws; amqplib connection errors). With an outbox, the request succeeds, rows accumulate, and the outbox age alert fires; publishing resumes automatically. Without an outbox, decide explicitly: fail the request (correct for OrderPlaced) or drop the event (acceptable for a page-view metric). Never buffer unboundedly in process memory.
  • Broker down, consumer side. Consumers reconnect with backoff; nothing is lost because the log is durable. Alert on the consumer's connection state so a broker outage is not first noticed as lag.
  • Partition key skew. One partition takes 40 percent of traffic; its consumer is the bottleneck. Visible as per-partition lag imbalance and one hot consumer pod. Finer key, or composite key with a bounded random suffix for keys that only need per-key order within short windows.
  • Message too large. Kafka rejects with MessageSizeTooLarge (default 1 MB); SQS rejects above 256 KB. The producer sees the error; if it happens in the outbox relay, the row is stuck at the head and blocks the ordered batch. Validate size at outbox insert time, use the claim-check pattern, and let the relay park an oversized row to the DLQ table rather than stall.
  • Retention expiring unprocessed messages. A consumer down for longer than retention (a forgotten staging consumer, a group that was disabled for a migration) comes back and finds its committed offset no longer exists; auto.offset.reset decides whether it jumps to earliest or latest. Set retention from the recovery time objective, alert on lag that approaches retention, and set the reset policy explicitly rather than accepting the default.
  • Schema change breaking consumers. A producer renames priceCents to amount; three consumers start parking every message. DLQ rate alert fires; the trace shows the producer deploy. Roll back the producer, replay the DLQ. Prevent it with a schema registry in backward-compatible mode or contract tests in the producer's CI.
  • Clock skew in occurredAt. Two services with clocks 3 seconds apart produce events whose occurredAt order does not match causal order; a consumer that sorts by occurredAt applies them backwards. Use the database clock (clock_timestamp() at commit) for occurredAt, use causationId and entity version numbers for ordering decisions, and never compare timestamps across producers for correctness.
  • At-least-once plus non-idempotent side effects. The double email, the double charge, the double push notification. Every external call carries an idempotency key derived from the message id or the business key (Idempotency-Key: charge:{orderId} to the payment provider, a dedupKey to the push service). Where the provider offers no idempotency, record the intent in PostgreSQL first (email_sends(message_id) PRIMARY KEY) and treat a conflict as "already sent"; accept that a crash between the send and the record is a duplicate you cannot eliminate, only minimize by making the record write fast and immediately after the send.
  • Consumer group id reused by another service. Two services share offsets; each sees half the messages and both believe they are the only consumer. Group ids are prefixed with the service name and checked in code review.
  • Auto topic creation. A typo in a topic name creates a new topic with default partitions and replication factor 1, and events go nowhere anyone reads. allowAutoTopicCreation: false everywhere; topics come from migrations.
  • Producer acknowledgement lost, no idempotent producer, no consumer dedup. Silent duplicates at the source that no metric distinguishes from real traffic. Turn on idempotence; dedup in consumers; a reconciliation job comparing event counts with source rows for critical flows.
  • Replay into a live system. An operator resets offsets to re-run a day; every non-idempotent consumer re-applies a day of effects. Replay only through consumers proven idempotent, with the dedup table retention longer than the replay reach, and with external side effects gated by idempotency keys.

Senior Checklist — Part 27

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can say for each message whether it is an event or a command, and whether it belongs on a topic or a queue
  • I choose partition keys for ordering and know what breaks when the partition count changes
  • I commit offsets manually after processing and commit offset + 1
  • I can draw the four duplicate paths and explain why no broker setting removes them all
  • Every consumer I ship is idempotent, with the dedup row in the same transaction as the business write
  • Every external side effect from a consumer carries an idempotency key
  • I publish business events through an outbox, never from inside a request handler's transaction
  • I classify errors as transient, permanent or poison and retry only transient ones, with jittered backoff and a maximum attempt count
  • Every consumer has a DLQ with an owner, an alert, retention of 30 days or more, and a replay path
  • I pause consumption when a dependency is down instead of failing messages into the DLQ
  • I configure acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, idempotent producers and no auto topic creation for business events
  • I know what Kafka exactly-once covers and I never promise exactly-once across a database and an email provider
  • I set RabbitMQ prefetch, use quorum queues with delivery limits, publish with confirms, and never requeue=true on failure
  • I set the SQS visibility timeout above p99 processing and extend it for long work
  • I monitor lag in seconds, DLQ depth, rebalance rate and outbox age, and I propagate trace context through message headers
  • I keep personal data out of messages where possible and can erase it where I cannot
  • I can justify not using a broker at all when one service and one job type is the whole requirement

Part 27 — Key Takeaways

  • Messaging buys decoupling, burst absorption, retry ownership and fan-out; it costs eventual consistency, another system to run, and a permanent duplicate-delivery problem.
  • Events are facts on topics with many readers; commands are requests on queues with one handler. Name them that way and the ownership falls out.
  • Ordering exists only per key within a partition, queue or message group; retries and parallelism break it, so consumers must tolerate out-of-order arrival with version guards.
  • Commit after processing, commit offset + 1, and accept at-least-once; auto-commit gives you loss or duplication depending on timing.
  • Duplicates arrive through producer retries, consumer crashes before commit, rebalances mid-flight and lease expiry; the only universal defense is an idempotent consumer with the dedup row in the same transaction as the business write.
  • Exactly-once is a property of a Kafka-to-Kafka loop with transactions; across a database and an email provider it is effectively-once via idempotency and idempotency keys to providers, or it is a myth.
  • Kafka is a retained, partitioned log for streams, replay and high fan-out; RabbitMQ is a router and task queue with native delays and DLX; SQS and SNS are the managed answer when you are on AWS and want no brokers. Pick by what the messages are for.
  • The outbox pattern makes the database commit and the publish one decision; publish-after-commit without an outbox still loses events on a crash between them.
  • Classify errors: retry transient ones with jittered backoff and a cap, park permanent and poison ones immediately, pause when a dependency is down.
  • A DLQ without an alert and an owner is data loss on a delay; retention will delete the evidence.
  • Lag in seconds, DLQ depth, rebalance count, outbox age and end-to-end latency with trace propagation are the metrics; a consumer fails silently unless you make it loud.
  • Keep messages small and factual with a stable envelope (id, type, version, occurredAt, correlationId, causationId); evolve payloads additively; put blobs in object storage and personal data behind erasable keys.

Part 28 — Distributed Systems Fundamentals

28.1 What makes a system "distributed", and why it is hard

Imagine two friends, Asha and Ben, who share one notebook of orders for their small bakery. While the notebook sits on one table, life is easy: whoever holds the pen writes, and the page always shows the truth. Now Asha takes the notebook home and Ben keeps a photocopy at the shop. A customer phones Ben to cancel order 41. Ben crosses it out on his copy. Asha, at home, bakes order 41. Nobody lied and nobody made a mistake; the two copies simply stopped being one notebook. Every hard problem in this Part is a version of that story.

Concept

A system is distributed when its parts run on different machines and can only talk to each other by sending messages over a network. That is the whole definition, and it hides three consequences that change everything:

  1. Parts fail independently. Machine A can be dead while machine B is fine and does not know it.
  2. There is no shared memory. The only way B learns about A's state is by A sending a message, which takes time and may never arrive.
  3. There is no global clock. Each machine has its own clock, and the clocks disagree by milliseconds on a good day and by seconds or minutes on a bad one.

Your NestJS service talking to PostgreSQL is already a distributed system. Add Redis, Kafka, three replicas of the API pod behind a load balancer, a payment gateway and a mobile client with a flaky connection, and you have a system with a dozen independently failing parts and no single place where "the truth" lives.

Why does it exist?

We do not build distributed systems because they are fun. We build them because a single machine has limits: it can only hold so much memory, serve so many requests, and it will eventually crash, lose its disk or need a reboot. We split the work across machines to get more capacity and to survive the failure of any one part. The price is that we now own all the problems of the two-notebook bakery: partial knowledge, delayed messages, and disagreement about what happened and when.

The mistake many teams make is paying that price without needing to. A single PostgreSQL primary with a hot standby, behind three stateless NestJS pods, is a distributed system you can reason about. Fifteen microservices with their own databases is a distributed system that will teach you every lesson in this Part the expensive way. The senior instinct is: the simplest architecture that meets the requirement wins, and every network hop you add must earn its place.

Mental model

Think of every network call as posting a letter. You put it in the box and walk away. Maybe it arrives in a minute; maybe it arrives tomorrow; maybe it is lost; maybe it arrives twice because the post office duplicated it; maybe it arrives after a letter you posted later. If you get no reply, you cannot tell whether your letter was lost, whether the reply was lost, or whether the recipient is simply slow. Everything in distributed systems is a technique for doing useful, correct work while only ever being able to post letters.

How it works: the eight fallacies

In 1994 Peter Deutsch (later extended by James Gosling) listed the assumptions that engineers new to distributed systems make, and that reality punishes. Each one shows up in a backend within its first year of production.

# Fallacy What is actually true How you meet it in a NestJS backend
1 The network is reliable Packets are dropped, connections reset, switches reboot A fetch to the inventory service throws ECONNRESET once per 10,000 calls. Without a retry policy, 0.01% of orders fail for no reason the customer can see.
2 Latency is zero Every hop costs time; cross-AZ ~1 ms, cross-region 80–150 ms A loop that calls the pricing service once per cart item turns a 12-item cart into 12 x 40 ms = 480 ms before any work is done.
3 Bandwidth is infinite Links saturate; big payloads queue behind each other A GET /orders?include=items,customer,history returning 4 MB per call chokes a 1 Gbps link at 30 requests per second.
4 The network is secure Anyone on the path can read or alter traffic Service-to-service HTTP without TLS inside the cluster lets a compromised pod read customer PII off the wire. Use mTLS or at least TLS everywhere.
5 Topology does not change Pods move, IPs change, nodes drain A NestJS service that resolves inventory-svc once at startup and caches the IP keeps calling a dead pod after a rolling deploy. Resolve through the service DNS name or a client-side load balancer every time.
6 There is one administrator Different teams own different parts with different rules The payments team sets a 5 s timeout on their gateway; your team sets 3 s on the call to them. Every slow charge becomes an "unknown outcome" for you.
7 Transport cost is zero Serialization, TLS handshakes and connection setup cost CPU and time Opening a new TLS connection per request to Redis costs ~2 ms and a burst of CPU; the actual GET costs 0.2 ms. Pool connections.
8 The network is homogeneous Different libraries, versions, encodings and MTUs coexist Service A sends Content-Type: application/json with a UTF-16 body from a legacy library; service B assumes UTF-8 and stores garbage names.

Three further truths sit under all eight fallacies:

  • Independent failure. When the inventory pod dies, the order pod does not die with it; it keeps sending requests into the void. Contrast this with a monolith: if the inventory module crashes, the whole process crashes and nobody keeps calling it.
  • No global clock. If order service logs 12:00:00.100 created and inventory logs 12:00:00.090 reserved, the reservation did not happen before the order. The clocks are simply 30 ms apart. Section 28.13 covers this in depth.
  • No shared memory. A JavaScript Map of "orders being processed" in pod 1 is invisible to pod 2. Any in-process state is per-pod state, which is why sections 28.8 and 28.11 exist.

Practical example

An e-commerce checkout in NestJS calls, in order: Redis (cart), PostgreSQL (create order), the payment gateway (charge), Kafka (publish OrderPlaced). Four network dependencies. On one machine, "create order then charge" is one line after another. Distributed, every line has three possible endings (success, failure, unknown), so four lines have 3^4 = 81 combinations of endings, and about 60 of them leave the system in a state that a naive implementation never considered. Most of Part 29 is about handling those 60.

NestJS example

The most common junior mistake is a call with no timeout. Node's fetch will wait for the OS TCP timeout (often 2 minutes) if the far side vanishes without sending a reset. Here is the minimum a senior would accept for a service-to-service call:

// inventory.client.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

export type RemoteOutcome<T> =
  | { kind: 'ok'; value: T }
  | { kind: 'failed'; status: number; body: string }   // the far side answered "no"
  | { kind: 'unknown'; reason: string };                // we do not know what happened

@Injectable()
export class InventoryClient {
  private readonly log = new Logger(InventoryClient.name);
  private readonly baseUrl: string;

  constructor(config: ConfigService) {
    this.baseUrl = config.getOrThrow<string>('INVENTORY_BASE_URL'); // never hard-code hosts
  }

  async reserve(orderId: string, sku: string, qty: number): Promise<RemoteOutcome<{ reservationId: string }>> {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}/reservations`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'idempotency-key': `reserve:${orderId}:${sku}` },
        body: JSON.stringify({ orderId, sku, qty }),
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000), // fallacy 2: latency is not zero, bound it
      });
      if (res.ok) return { kind: 'ok', value: (await res.json()) as { reservationId: string } };
      return { kind: 'failed', status: res.status, body: await res.text() };
    } catch (err) {
      // Timeout or connection error: the request MAY have been applied on the far side.
      this.log.warn(`reserve unknown outcome order=${orderId} reason=${(err as Error).message}`);
      return { kind: 'unknown', reason: (err as Error).message };
    }
  }
}

Notice the return type. It refuses to collapse "the call threw" into "the reservation did not happen". That single design decision is the difference between code that survives a network blip and code that double-books stock.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL is a network dependency too. Every fallacy applies to the app-to-database link:

-- Bound how long a statement may run before the server gives up (fallacy 2).
ALTER ROLE api_user SET statement_timeout = '5s';

-- Bound how long a transaction may sit idle holding locks if the app pod
-- vanished mid-transaction (fallacy 1: the client can disappear).
ALTER ROLE api_user SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

-- See who is connected and from where; topology changes (fallacy 5).
SELECT client_addr, state, wait_event_type, now() - query_start AS running_for
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'shop' AND state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY running_for DESC;

Without idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, a pod that was OOM-killed while inside BEGIN ... UPDATE orders ... leaves a row lock that every other pod waits on until the TCP keepalive finally notices the client is gone, which can be 10 minutes or more with default kernel settings.

Production scenario

A food-delivery platform runs 40 NestJS pods, one PostgreSQL primary (16 vCPU, 64 GB), two async replicas, a 6-node Redis Cluster and a 9-broker Kafka cluster, handling 3,000 requests per second at peak. A typical order request touches Redis twice (0.3 ms each), PostgreSQL three times (2–4 ms each), the payment gateway once (400–900 ms) and Kafka once (5 ms). The p50 latency is 520 ms; almost all of it is the one external dependency. The p99 is 2.8 s, and almost all of that is the same dependency being slow. The internal network is not the problem on an average day. It becomes the problem on the day a top-of-rack switch drops 3% of packets and every service's retry logic decides to help.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call gets paged: checkout error rate 18%. Nothing was deployed. The PostgreSQL dashboard is green, Redis is green, Kafka is green. It takes forty minutes to find that a Kubernetes node was rescheduling pods and, for eight minutes, half of the inventory-svc endpoints listed in the cluster DNS pointed to pods that no longer existed (fallacy 5). Order pods that had cached the resolved address kept sending to dead IPs and waiting for the full 60 s timeout, which exhausted their HTTP agent's socket pool, which made all calls from those pods slow, including calls to healthy services. The fix was three lines: shorter timeouts, resolve through the service name each time, and cap concurrent outbound requests. The lesson was bigger: the failure of a part you did not call took down the part you did.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A DNS change propagates to some pods and not others; two versions of the topology coexist for minutes.
  • A request that is fine at 2 KB is dropped at 70 KB because a proxy in the path has a smaller body limit than your service.
  • A load balancer keeps sending traffic to a pod whose process is alive but whose event loop is blocked (alive is not the same as healthy).
  • TLS certificates expire on one side only; half of the fleet cannot talk to the other half.
  • Clock skew between a token issuer and a verifier rejects every fresh JWT as "issued in the future".
  • A single slow dependency exhausts a shared connection or socket pool and slows unrelated calls.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before adding any network boundary a senior asks: what do I gain (scaling, isolation, team autonomy) and what do I now own (timeouts, retries, idempotency, partial failure, observability)? If the answer to the first is "cleaner code", the boundary is not worth it; a module boundary inside one process gives you clean code for free. They also explain it to product managers plainly: "Every arrow on this architecture diagram is a place where the answer can be I don't know. We have to write code for each of those, and it costs time."

Common mistakes

  • Treating a remote call like a local function call: no timeout, no retry policy, no thought about duplicates.
  • Caching a resolved IP address or a single long-lived connection to a specific pod.
  • Trusting timestamps from two machines to tell you which event happened first.
  • Keeping "in-flight" state in a process-level Map and being surprised when the second replica does not see it.
  • Assuming the internal network is private and skipping TLS and authentication between services.

Interview questions

  1. Name four of the fallacies of distributed computing and give a concrete backend example for each. Expected: any four from the table with a real consequence. Follow-up: which fallacy caused the most incidents in your experience?
  2. Why is "a NestJS app plus PostgreSQL" already a distributed system? Expected: two processes on different machines communicating by messages; they fail independently; a write can commit while the acknowledgement is lost.
  3. What changes when you move a module call into an HTTP call? Expected: latency, the "unknown" outcome, the need for idempotency and timeouts, versioning, independent deployment.
  4. How would you explain to a PM why microservices are slower to build? Expected: every boundary needs failure handling that a monolith gets for free.

Practical exercise

Take one service-to-service call in a project you know. Write down what happens if the call (a) times out, (b) returns HTTP 500, (c) returns 200 but the response is lost, (d) is executed twice. Acceptance criteria: for each case you can name the exact state the database ends in and what the customer sees, and you have added a timeout and an idempotency key if either was missing.

28.2 Partial failure: the three outcomes of every remote call

Concept

Every remote call has exactly three possible outcomes, and only three:

  1. Success: the far side did the work and you received the answer.
  2. Failure: the far side told you it did not do the work (HTTP 4xx/5xx with a clear body, a rejected message, a database constraint error).
  3. Unknown: you got a timeout, a connection reset, or your own process crashed while waiting. The work may or may not have been done.

Most bugs in distributed backends come from code that only knows two outcomes. It treats "unknown" as "failure" and retries, or treats it as "success" and moves on. Both are wrong half the time.

Why does it exist?

On a single machine, a function either returns or throws; there is no third state because the caller and callee share one process that lives or dies together. Across a network the caller and callee live separately, and the message that would have told you the truth can be lost on the way back. The unknown outcome is not a bug in your library. It is a property of the universe, and no amount of clever code removes it. What clever code does is make the unknown outcome safe: it makes repeating the request harmless. That property is called idempotency, and this section is where it is born; Part 29 builds the full machinery.

Mental model

Imagine a bank branch that cannot phone head office. A customer asks to withdraw 500. The teller sends a runner to head office with the request. The runner does not come back. Did head office debit the account? The teller has two bad options: hand over the cash (maybe head office never got the request, and the bank loses 500) or refuse (maybe head office debited the account, and the customer is furious). The only good option is to give the runner a numbered slip, "withdrawal request #7718", and send a second runner with the same slip. Head office, seeing #7718 twice, does the debit once. That numbered slip is an idempotency key.

How it works

flowchart LR
  A["Caller sends request"] --> B{"Did a response arrive?"}
  B -->|"yes, 2xx"| S["Success: work done, caller knows"]
  B -->|"yes, 4xx or 5xx"| F["Failure: work not done, caller knows"]
  B -->|"no: timeout, reset, crash"| U["Unknown: work may or may not be done"]
  U --> R{"Is the operation idempotent?"}
  R -->|"yes"| RT["Retry with the same key: safe"]
  R -->|"no"| Q["Query state, reconcile, or park for a human"]

Where the unknown outcome comes from, step by step, for a POST /charges call to a payment gateway with a 3 s timeout:

  1. Your pod opens a connection and sends the request bytes (5 ms).
  2. The gateway receives it, validates, and starts talking to the card network (300–2,000 ms).
