  3. The gateway commits the charge to its database at t = 2,900 ms.
  4. Your AbortSignal.timeout(3000) fires at t = 3,000 ms and your code throws.
  5. The gateway's response arrives at t = 3,050 ms into a socket you already closed.

The charge exists. Your code saw an exception. If the exception handler says "payment failed, tell the user to try again", the user will try again, and you will charge them twice. That is not a rare edge case; at 1,000 charges per hour with a p99.9 of 3 s, it happens once an hour.

The same three outcomes apply to every dependency:

Dependency "Unknown" looks like What may have happened anyway
PostgreSQL COMMIT Connection dropped after sending COMMIT The transaction committed; your app thinks it failed
Redis SET key NX PX 30000 Timeout The lock was acquired; nobody will release it until the TTL
Kafka producer.send acks=all timeout The record was written to the leader and replicas; you will send it again
HTTP call to another service ETIMEDOUT, ECONNRESET, socket hang up The handler ran to completion
Email/SMS provider 504 from their gateway The message was sent

Practical example

Order service creates an order and then calls the payment service. The payment call times out. Three designs:

  • Naive: catch the error, mark the order PAYMENT_FAILED, tell the user. Risk: user was charged; order says failed. Support ticket, refund, angry customer.
  • Better: catch the error, mark the order PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, and run a reconciliation job that asks the gateway "what is the status of the charge with idempotency key order:8813?" and moves the order to PAID or PAYMENT_FAILED.
  • Best: send the charge with an idempotency key from the start, so the timeout handler can simply retry the same request a few times with backoff, and only fall back to reconciliation if retries also fail. Part 29 builds exactly this.

NestJS example

A payment client that treats the three outcomes as first-class values, and records every attempt so a reconciliation job can find the unknowns:

// payment.client.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { PaymentAttempt } from './payment-attempt.entity';

type ChargeOutcome = { kind: 'ok'; chargeId: string } | { kind: 'declined'; code: string } | { kind: 'unknown' };

@Injectable()
export class PaymentClient {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PaymentClient.name);
  constructor(@InjectRepository(PaymentAttempt) private readonly attempts: Repository<PaymentAttempt>) {}

  async charge(orderId: string, amountCents: number, currency: string): Promise<ChargeOutcome> {
    const idempotencyKey = `charge:${orderId}`;          // same key on every retry for this order
    await this.attempts.upsert({ idempotencyKey, orderId, status: 'SENT' }, ['idempotencyKey']);

    try {
      const res = await fetch(`${process.env.PAYMENT_URL}/v1/charges`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'idempotency-key': idempotencyKey },
        body: JSON.stringify({ amount: amountCents, currency, reference: orderId }),
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000),
      });
      if (res.status === 201) {
        const body = (await res.json()) as { id: string };
        await this.attempts.update({ idempotencyKey }, { status: 'OK', chargeId: body.id });
        return { kind: 'ok', chargeId: body.id };
      }
      if (res.status === 402) {                            // gateway says: declined, definitely not charged
        const body = (await res.json()) as { code: string };
        await this.attempts.update({ idempotencyKey }, { status: 'DECLINED', errorCode: body.code });
        return { kind: 'declined', code: body.code };
      }
      // 5xx: the gateway is unwell; we do not know if the charge landed
      await this.attempts.update({ idempotencyKey }, { status: 'UNKNOWN' });
      return { kind: 'unknown' };
    } catch (err) {
      this.log.warn(`charge unknown order=${orderId}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
      await this.attempts.update({ idempotencyKey }, { status: 'UNKNOWN' });
      return { kind: 'unknown' };                          // never "declined": we do not know
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The attempts table that makes "unknown" visible and reconcilable:

CREATE TABLE payment_attempts (
  idempotency_key text PRIMARY KEY,           -- one row per logical charge, however many retries
  order_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  status          text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('SENT', 'OK', 'DECLINED', 'UNKNOWN')),
  charge_id       text,
  error_code      text,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- The reconciliation job only ever needs the unknowns, so index exactly those.
CREATE INDEX payment_attempts_unknown_idx
  ON payment_attempts (updated_at)
  WHERE status IN ('SENT', 'UNKNOWN');

-- What the reconciler runs every minute: unknowns older than 2 minutes.
SELECT idempotency_key, order_id
FROM payment_attempts
WHERE status IN ('SENT', 'UNKNOWN') AND updated_at < now() - interval '2 minutes'
ORDER BY updated_at
LIMIT 200;

Note SENT is itself an unknown state: if the pod crashed between writing SENT and getting a response, the row stays SENT forever, and the reconciler picks it up. This is the "your own process crashed while waiting" case, which most teams forget.

Production scenario

A marketplace processing 120,000 payments per day measures how often each outcome occurs against their gateway: 97.1% success, 2.7% declined, 0.2% unknown. That 0.2% is 240 unknown outcomes per day. Before they added idempotency keys and a reconciler, roughly a third of those became double charges or lost payments, which is 80 support tickets a day and a chargeback rate that got their account flagged. After: zero double charges, and the reconciler resolves 95% of unknowns within 3 minutes automatically.

Failure scenario

A ride-booking service published RideCompleted to Kafka after the trip ended, then charged the rider. During a broker rolling upgrade, producer.send timed out for 0.5% of events, the code caught the error and re-published. Kafka had already written most of those records. Downstream, the invoicing consumer received two RideCompleted events for the same ride and issued two invoices. The pager went off not because of the duplicates (nobody noticed for a day) but because the finance dashboard showed revenue 0.5% above what the payments table said. The eventual fix was an inbox table in the consumer (Part 29), but the root cause was the producer assuming "timeout means not sent".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The far side succeeded, then crashed before writing its own record of success; both sides believe different things.
  • Timeouts nested inside timeouts: the caller gives up at 3 s while the callee is still retrying its own dependency with a 10 s budget; the callee finishes the work at 8 s into a call nobody is waiting for.
  • The unknown outcome happens on COMMIT itself; the app retries the whole transaction and inserts a second order. Unique constraints on a client-supplied key are the only defense.
  • A load balancer retries a POST on its own after an idle-timeout (some do, by default), so your service receives two requests for one client click.
  • A process crash after the request was sent but before the attempt row was written; the row never says SENT, so nothing reconciles it. Write the attempt row before sending.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior designs every write-side call with three questions: what key makes a repeat harmless, where do I record that I tried, and who cleans up the unknowns. They refuse to write catch (e) { markFailed() } for any call that changes money or stock. They explain to product: "There is a 0.2% of calls where the network does not tell us the answer. We have two choices: build a system that finds the answer later, or accept double charges. We are building the first one; it costs a week."

Common mistakes

  • Mapping every exception to "failed" and showing "please try again", which trains users to create duplicates.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent call because "it's probably fine".
  • Not recording the attempt before sending, so a crash mid-call leaves no trace.
  • Using a fresh idempotency key on each retry (usually by generating it inside the retry loop), which makes the key useless.

Interview questions

  1. A payment call times out. What are the possible states of the world and what do you do? Expected: charged or not charged; retry with the same idempotency key; if still unknown, query the gateway by that key; never tell the user "failed" until you know. Follow-up: what if the gateway does not support idempotency keys?
  2. Why is the unknown outcome the reason idempotency exists? Expected: because the only safe response to "I don't know" is to repeat, and repeating is only safe if repeats are harmless.
  3. Where can the unknown outcome happen inside a single PostgreSQL transaction? Expected: on COMMIT; the transaction may have committed even though the client got an error.
  4. How do you find the requests whose outcome you never learned? Expected: write an attempt record before sending; a reconciler queries old attempts still in SENT/UNKNOWN.

Practical exercise

Wrap one write-side external call in your codebase with an attempt table and an idempotency key. Kill the process (SIGKILL) while a call is in flight, restart it, and run a reconciler. Acceptance criteria: the attempt row exists in a non-final state after the crash, the reconciler resolves it without human help, and repeating the original request creates no second side effect.

28.3 Network partitions and split brain

Concept

A network partition is a period during which some machines can talk to each other and some cannot, while all of them keep running. It is not "the network is down". It is "the network is down between A and B, but fine between B and C". Partitions are dangerous precisely because each side is healthy from its own point of view and keeps working, possibly on the same data.

Split brain is the worst result of a partition: two parts of the system both believe they are in charge (two PostgreSQL primaries, two schedulers running the same cron, two Kafka controllers), and both accept writes that will conflict when the partition heals.

Why does it exist?

Nobody designs partitions; they happen because the network is many physical things (cables, switches, routers, firewalls, DNS, cloud fabric) that fail independently. Typical causes: a switch firmware bug, a misconfigured security group, a saturated link that drops 40% of packets (a "partial partition", even nastier), an availability zone losing connectivity to another, a Kubernetes node losing its network plugin. AWS publishes zone-level networking events a few times a year; within your own cluster, brief partitions happen far more often than that.

Your architecture cannot prevent partitions. It can only decide what to do during one. That decision is the subject of CAP (section 28.4).

Mental model

Back to the bakery. Asha and Ben each keep a copy of the order book and normally phone each other after every change. One afternoon the phone line is dead. Both keep taking orders. Both are right to do so from their own point of view: the customers are standing in front of them. When the line comes back, they discover they both sold the last chocolate cake. The partition did not create the problem; the decision to keep selling during the partition did. The alternative, "stop selling until the phone works", is also a decision, and also has a cost.

How it works

flowchart TB
  subgraph ZoneA
    lb["Load balancer"] --> api1["API pod 1"]
    lb --> api2["API pod 2"]
    api1 --> pgP["PostgreSQL primary"]
    api2 --> pgP
  end
  subgraph ZoneB
    api3["API pod 3"] --> pgS["PostgreSQL standby"]
    etcd3["etcd node 3"]
  end
  etcd1["etcd node 1"] --- etcd2["etcd node 2"]
  pgP -. "replication blocked" .- pgS
  api3 -. "cannot reach primary" .- pgP
  etcd2 -. "cut" .- etcd3

What actually happens, in order, when the link between the two zones dies at t = 0:

  1. t = 0–2 s: nothing looks wrong. In-flight TCP connections just stall. No error yet.
  2. t = 2–5 s: timeouts start. Pod 3's connection pool to the primary begins returning ETIMEDOUT. Pod 3 is healthy, its process is fine, and every request it serves fails. The load balancer, which lives in zone A and can still reach pod 3's health endpoint (or cannot, depending on the exact cut), may or may not stop sending traffic to it.
  3. t = 5–30 s: retries amplify load. Clients of pod 3 retry. Pod 3's outbound requests retry. Each retry holds a socket and a pool slot. Pod 3 runs out of pool connections; now even health checks that touch the database fail; now it is finally taken out of rotation, having served errors for 30 s.
  4. t = 10–30 s: the cluster manager reacts. Patroni on the standby (zone B) cannot see the primary. It asks etcd: is the primary's lease still valid? etcd node 3 in zone B is cut off from nodes 1 and 2, so it has no majority and refuses to answer. The standby correctly does not promote itself. Meanwhile the primary in zone A can still reach etcd nodes 1 and 2 (a majority), renews its lease, and keeps serving. That is a partition handled correctly: one side keeps writing, the other side stops, no split brain.
  5. What split brain would look like: if the standby had a simpler rule, "promote yourself when you cannot see the primary for 10 s", you now have two primaries. Pods in zone B write to the new one, pods in zone A write to the old one. Both accept UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1. When the partition heals there is no way to merge those two histories; one of them is lost, and the order that was accepted from the lost history has no row.
  6. Healing is its own incident. When the link returns, every queued retry fires at once (a retry storm, section 18.18), replication has a backlog to stream, and any caches on the cut-off side hold stale values.

Why "just retry" makes partitions worse: a retry during a partition cannot succeed (the path is cut) but it does consume resources on both sides, holds connections, fills queues, and when the partition heals it arrives as a burst. Retries need a budget (say, at most 10% of requests may be retries), backoff with jitter, and a circuit breaker that stops calling a dependency that has failed N times in a row. Part 30 covers the mechanics; here the point is that retries are a tool for transient errors, and a partition is not transient from the retrier's point of view.

Practical example

Your NestJS service runs in two availability zones with a single PostgreSQL primary in zone A. During a zone-B-to-zone-A partition:

  • Zone B pods cannot write. They can read from the zone B standby, which stops receiving new data, so those reads get staler by the second.
  • The right behavior for zone B pods is usually: fail readiness fast, so the load balancer sends users to zone A, where things work. Serving stale reads for a product catalogue is fine; serving stale account balances is not.
  • The wrong behavior is: keep accepting requests and time out one by one, or, worse, promote the standby.

NestJS example

A readiness check that reflects the database's reachability, so a partitioned pod takes itself out of rotation quickly instead of serving timeouts. Note that this must be readiness, not liveness: restarting a pod does not fix a network partition, and a liveness probe that fails on database errors makes Kubernetes restart every pod in a loop during the incident (CrashLoopBackOff on top of a partition).

// health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator } from '@nestjs/terminus';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  // Liveness: is the process itself alive? Never touch the network here.
  @Get('live')
  live() {
    return { status: 'ok' };
  }

  // Readiness: can this pod do useful work right now? Bounded to 1.5 s so a
  // partition makes us unready quickly instead of hanging the probe.
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1_500 })]);
  }
}

With readinessProbe.periodSeconds: 5 and failureThreshold: 2, a partitioned pod stops receiving traffic within ~10–12 s instead of serving errors for the whole incident.

PostgreSQL example

The tools PostgreSQL gives you to see and control behavior during a partition:

-- On the primary: is the standby still streaming? During a partition this row disappears
-- or its state changes and the lag columns grow.
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_lag_bytes,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- With a synchronous standby, a partition makes every COMMIT wait for an ack that cannot come.
-- This is the "choose consistency" behavior: writes block rather than proceed unreplicated.
SHOW synchronous_standby_names;   -- e.g. 'FIRST 1 (standby_b)'
SHOW synchronous_commit;          -- 'on' means wait for the standby to flush

-- On the standby: am I still receiving WAL? A growing gap means I am cut off.
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS time_since_last_replayed_txn,
       pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby;

If synchronous_standby_names names exactly one standby and that standby is cut off, the primary stops committing. That is correct if your priority is "never lose an acknowledged write", and catastrophic if nobody planned for it. The usual answer is ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c) with standbys in two zones, which is a quorum (section 28.10), or a tool like Patroni that can temporarily switch to async mode by policy.

Production scenario

A payments platform runs PostgreSQL with Patroni across three zones, etcd with three members (one per zone), and API pods in all three zones. They ran a game day and cut zone C from A and B. Measured results: zone C pods went unready in 9 s; the zone C etcd member lost quorum immediately and stopped answering; the primary in zone A kept its lease; write latency rose from 4 ms to 6 ms because the sync standby in zone C was replaced by the one in zone B via ANY 1; zero split brain; 0.3% of requests failed during the 9 s window. When they reconnected zone C, a burst of 14,000 retried requests arrived within 2 s and briefly pushed the primary to 95% CPU. They added retry budgets after that.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 a SaaS company's ops team applied a security-group change that accidentally blocked port 5432 between one subnet and the database subnet. Half of the API pods lost the database. They were on a managed load balancer with health checks pointing at /health, which returned 200 as long as the process was up. For 22 minutes, half of all requests failed with a 30 s timeout, and users who got a working pod on retry then hit a failing one on their next request. The incident review found two mistakes: the readiness check did not reflect dependency health, and the timeout was 30 s where 2 s would have made the failure fast and cheap. The security group was the trigger; the design was the cause.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Partial partitions: 30% packet loss looks like "slow", not "down"; timeouts fire randomly; retries succeed sometimes; the system limps at 5x latency and nobody's alarm has a rule for "slow but alive".
  • Asymmetric partitions: A can send to B but B cannot send to A. Heartbeats in one direction succeed; the other side declares A dead.
  • Load balancer on one side of the cut: it sees pods on the far side as healthy (if health does not touch the database) and keeps sending them traffic that will fail.
  • Cache on the cut-off side serves values that are correct at the moment of the cut and increasingly wrong afterwards, with no error to alert on.
  • Client-side partitions: a mobile app in a tunnel is partitioned from you. If it queues writes and replays them later, you are running a multi-leader system whether you planned to or not (section 28.9).
  • Healing storms: queued retries, replication catch-up and cache refills all hit at once; the recovery can page you harder than the partition did.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior question is never "how do we prevent partitions" but "for each dependency, which side keeps working during a partition, and what do the other side's users see?" They insist on readiness probes that reflect dependency reachability, timeouts measured in low seconds, retry budgets, and a rule that no component promotes itself to leader without a majority agreeing (section 28.11). They also insist on a game day: cut a zone on purpose, in staging first, then in production at a quiet hour, because the first real partition should not be the first time anyone sees the behavior.

Common mistakes

  • Health checks that only say "process is up" while the pod cannot reach anything.
  • Liveness probes that touch the database, so a partition triggers restart loops.
  • Failover rules based on "I cannot see the leader" rather than "a majority agrees the leader is gone".
  • Unbounded retries with no backoff, which turn a 10 s partition into a 5-minute recovery storm.
  • Assuming a single-zone deployment is immune: partitions happen between racks, nodes and even between a pod and its own node's network plugin.

Interview questions

  1. What is split brain and how do you prevent it in a PostgreSQL high-availability setup? Expected: two primaries accepting writes after a partition; prevent with leader leases stored in a majority-based store (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper), fencing of the old primary, and never promoting without quorum. Follow-up: what does Patroni do when it cannot reach the DCS?
  2. Why can retries make a partition worse? Expected: they cannot succeed, they consume resources, and they arrive as a burst when the partition heals. Follow-up: describe a retry budget.
  3. Should a readiness probe check the database? Should a liveness probe? Expected: readiness yes (bounded timeout), liveness no.
  4. Describe a partial partition and why it is harder to handle than a clean one. Expected: packet loss looks like slowness; timeouts and retries behave erratically; alerts based on "down" do not fire.

Practical exercise

Using Docker Compose with a NestJS app, PostgreSQL and a network tool such as Toxiproxy (or iptables inside the containers), inject a full partition between the app and the database for 30 s, then a 40% packet-loss partition for 60 s. Acceptance criteria: the app's readiness endpoint fails within 5 s of the full partition; no request waits longer than 3 s; retries are capped and jittered; when the partition heals, database CPU does not spike above 2x its normal level; and you can describe, from logs alone, which requests ended in each of the three outcomes.

28.4 CAP theorem, explained simply and correctly

Concept

CAP says: during a network partition, a distributed data system must choose between consistency and availability. It cannot give both, because giving both would require the two sides of the partition to agree on data they cannot exchange.

The three letters, with their precise meanings (the theorem uses strict definitions, and most misunderstandings come from using loose ones):

  • C, Consistency: every read returns the most recent write, as if there were a single copy of the data. This is linearizability (section 28.6), not the "C" of ACID.
  • A, Availability: every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, without a guarantee that it contains the latest write.
  • P, Partition tolerance: the system keeps operating when messages between nodes are lost or delayed.

Why does it exist?

CAP exists to kill a fantasy: the fantasy that with enough engineering you can have a multi-node system that is always up and always agrees with itself. Eric Brewer stated it in 2000; Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002. Its practical value is that it forces a question every architecture must answer: when the network breaks, do we stop, or do we go on and risk disagreement?

Mental model

Asha and Ben's bakery, phone line dead. Rule 1: "Only sell a cake if you can confirm with the other shop that it is still available." Under that rule they refuse every sale while the line is down. Consistent, not available. Rule 2: "Sell whatever your copy of the book says is available." They keep selling and may oversell. Available, not consistent. There is no rule 3 that keeps selling and never oversells while the phone is dead. Notice the choice only matters while the phone is dead; when it works, they can have both.

How it works

The three things everyone gets wrong about CAP:

  1. It is not a three-way choice. "Pick two of C, A, P" is how it is usually drawn, and it is misleading. Partitions are not optional in a system that uses a network; you do not "choose P". You get P imposed on you, and the real choice is what you sacrifice when a partition happens: C or A.
  2. "CA" does not exist for a distributed system. A "CA" system is one that never experiences a partition, which means a single node. A single PostgreSQL instance is "CA" in the sense that it is consistent and available until it is down, at which point it is neither. Once you add a second node that must agree with the first, you are choosing C or A during partitions.
  3. The choice applies per operation, not per system. A system can be CP for writes and AP for reads, or CP for one table and AP for another. The letters describe behaviors, not products.
flowchart TB
  P["Network partition happens"] --> Q{"What does the minority side do?"}
  Q -->|"Refuse requests it cannot confirm"| CP["CP behavior: some requests error, no stale or conflicting data"]
  Q -->|"Answer from local copy"| AP["AP behavior: every request answered, some stale or conflicting"]
  CP --> H["Partition heals: replicas catch up, no conflicts to resolve"]
  AP --> H2["Partition heals: conflicts must be detected and resolved"]

How specific systems behave during a partition:

System Behavior during a partition Effective choice
PostgreSQL primary + synchronous standby With synchronous_commit = on and the sync standby unreachable, commits block. With Patroni, a primary that loses its lease in etcd demotes itself; the minority side serves no writes. CP for writes; reads from the primary continue
PostgreSQL primary + asynchronous replicas Primary keeps committing; cut-off replicas serve increasingly stale reads and never error. If you fail over to an async replica you may lose acknowledged writes. Writes: single leader, consistent while the primary is reachable. Replica reads: AP
Redis Cluster Replication is async. The majority side keeps serving; the minority side stops accepting writes after cluster-node-timeout. A failover can lose the last few acknowledged writes. Leans A on the majority side; loses writes on failover, so not C either
DynamoDB Eventually consistent reads succeed from any replica. Strongly consistent reads and writes go through the partition leader and fail if it is unreachable. Per request: eventual reads AP, strong reads and writes CP
Cassandra Tunable per query. ONE answers from any replica. QUORUM needs a majority and errors without it. ONE: AP; QUORUM reads and writes: CP-like
ZooKeeper / etcd Minority side refuses writes and (by default) linearizable reads. Majority side continues. CP
Kafka (acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean leader election off) A partition that leaves fewer than 2 in-sync replicas makes the partition unavailable for writes rather than accepting unreplicated data. CP for writes

How a NestJS system on PostgreSQL behaves during a partition between some pods and the primary: those pods cannot write (connection timeouts, pool exhaustion), and any read they send to a cut-off replica is stale. There is no setting that changes that; the choice you get to make is what the pod does about it. A well-built pod fails readiness so traffic moves to pods that can reach the primary; serves cached catalogue and product pages if it can (accepting staleness there, an AP choice for read-only, low-risk data); and fails checkout and account writes fast with a clear error (a CP choice for money and stock). The system as a whole is CP at the database and can be made partially available at the application layer, on purpose, per endpoint.

Practical example

Inventory for a flash sale. If you keep stock counts in Redis Cluster and a partition splits the cluster, the majority side keeps decrementing, and a failover may lose the last hundred decrements. Result: overselling. If you keep stock in PostgreSQL with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the primary, a partition makes some pods unable to decrement at all. Result: some users see "try again", nobody is oversold. For inventory, the second is the right choice, and the senior engineer makes it knowingly rather than discovering it in a post-mortem.

NestJS example

Choosing the behavior per endpoint, explicitly, with a small guard that decides whether an endpoint may be served from a possibly stale source when the primary is unreachable:

// consistency.decorator.ts
import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
export const CONSISTENCY_KEY = 'consistency';
export type ConsistencyLevel = 'strong' | 'stale-ok';
export const Consistency = (level: ConsistencyLevel) => SetMetadata(CONSISTENCY_KEY, level);

// primary-required.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { PrimaryHealth } from './primary-health.service';

@Injectable()
export class PrimaryRequiredGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector, private readonly primary: PrimaryHealth) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const level = this.reflector.get<ConsistencyLevel>(CONSISTENCY_KEY, ctx.getHandler()) ?? 'strong';
    if (level === 'stale-ok') return true;                 // AP choice for this endpoint
    if (!this.primary.isReachable()) {                     // CP choice: refuse rather than guess
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('Primary database unreachable; try again shortly');
    }
    return true;
  }
}

PrimaryHealth is a small service that pings the primary every 2 s (bounded to 500 ms) and keeps a boolean. Product listing gets @Consistency('stale-ok') and is served from the replica or cache; POST /checkout stays strong and fails fast with a 503 and a Retry-After header instead of a 30 s timeout.

PostgreSQL example

The knob that moves PostgreSQL between "block for safety" and "continue at risk" during a partition:

-- Wait for at least one of two standbys to confirm before COMMIT returns.
-- If both are unreachable, commits block: the CP choice.
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c)';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- Per transaction, a session can opt out for data where losing a few ms of writes is acceptable
-- (audit logs, analytics events), an AP choice made deliberately, per write.
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'local';
INSERT INTO page_views (user_id, path, viewed_at) VALUES ($1, $2, now());
COMMIT;

SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'local' tells the primary to acknowledge as soon as its own WAL is flushed. During a partition those writes succeed while checkout writes (still on) block. Same database, two CAP choices, chosen per transaction.

Production scenario

A ticketing platform sells 40,000 seats in 4 minutes for a concert. Seat holds live in PostgreSQL (CP, FOR UPDATE on the seat row, primary only). The seat map that fans look at is served from Redis with 2 s TTL (AP, stale by design). During the sale a network hiccup partitioned 4 of 30 pods from the primary for 12 s. Those pods went unready in 6 s; fans on them saw a "reconnecting" spinner for about 8 s, then landed on healthy pods. Seat map kept rendering from Redis throughout. Zero double-sold seats. The team's CAP decision was written down before the sale: seat holds are CP, seat map is AP.

Failure scenario

A startup stored shopping carts in a two-node "active-active" key-value store configured to accept writes on either node and merge later with last-writer-wins. A 90-second partition between the nodes, during a promotion, let users add items on both sides. On heal, last-writer-wins discarded 1,900 cart updates. Nobody was paged; there was no error. Support noticed a day later from "my cart lost items" tickets. The store had been chosen for its uptime story ("always available"), and it delivered exactly that, at the price of silently losing data. The fix was not a different store; it was writing down that carts needed a merge strategy (union of items, section 28.9) rather than last-writer-wins.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A system that is "CP" still returns errors during a partition; those errors need a good client experience, or users create retry storms.
  • A system that is "AP" produces conflicts that must be resolved; if nobody wrote the resolution rule, the default (usually last-writer-wins) silently loses data.
  • Partitions between the client and your API are also partitions. A mobile app that queues writes offline is an AP system with the client as a replica.
  • "Strongly consistent reads" in a managed database usually cost more (DynamoDB charges double) and fail during partitions; teams switch them on everywhere for safety and then wonder about the bill and the 5xx spikes.
  • A single PostgreSQL with no replica is not "CA": it is a single point of failure that is neither C nor A when it is down.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior never says "we chose AP" about a whole system. They walk through the data: money and stock are CP; catalogue, search, feeds and analytics are AP; sessions and carts are AP with a merge rule; auth token revocation is CP. Then they check that the storage and the code actually deliver those choices during a partition, ideally with a game day. To a product manager: "When the network breaks, we can either show users an error for a few seconds or risk selling the same seat twice. For seats, we show the error. For the seat map picture, we show a slightly old picture. Both are decisions we made on purpose."

Common mistakes

  • Reading CAP as "pick two" and believing a "CA" database exists.
  • Calling PostgreSQL "CP" or Cassandra "AP" without saying for which operations and which configuration.
  • Choosing an "always available" store for data that actually needs strong consistency, then discovering data loss on the first partition.
  • Enabling strongly consistent reads everywhere "to be safe" and paying in latency, cost and partition-time errors for data that did not need it.

Interview questions

  1. State CAP precisely. Why is "pick two" wrong? Expected: during a partition choose C or A; P is not optional; the choice is per operation. Follow-up: what does "C" mean in CAP versus in ACID?
  2. Is PostgreSQL CP or AP? Expected: depends on replication and failover configuration; sync replication with quorum-based failover is CP for writes; async replicas give AP reads. Follow-up: what happens to commits when a sync standby is unreachable?
  3. How does a NestJS app on PostgreSQL behave during a partition, and what can the app layer do? Expected: pods without the primary cannot write; fail readiness; serve stale reads only for endpoints where that is acceptable; fail writes fast.
  4. Give an example where you would deliberately choose availability over consistency. Expected: product catalogue, feed, seat map preview, analytics; anything where a few seconds of staleness costs less than an error.

Practical exercise

For a system you know, list every table or data type and mark it CP or AP with one sentence of justification. Then, for each AP item, write the conflict rule. Acceptance criteria: money, stock and auth are CP; each AP item has a merge rule other than "last write wins by wall clock" or a written reason why last-writer-wins is acceptable.

28.5 PACELC: the choice you make every day

Concept

PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2012) extends CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. The "else" is the important part, because partitions are rare and "else" is every second of every day. On a normal day, every replicated system still has to decide: do I wait for other replicas before answering (consistent, slower) or answer from the nearest copy (fast, possibly stale)?

Why does it exist?

CAP says nothing about the 99.99% of time when the network works, yet that is when most of your consistency decisions bite: reading from a replica, caching, async versus sync replication, cross-region writes. PACELC gives those decisions a name and puts them next to the partition decision, where they belong.

Mental model

Asha and Ben, phone line working. Before confirming an order, Ben can phone Asha to check her copy (slow, always right) or trust his own copy (fast, sometimes wrong by a minute). He makes that choice a hundred times a day, and nobody calls it a "partition".

How it works

The everyday PACELC choices in a NestJS + PostgreSQL system:

Decision Latency choice (EL) Consistency choice (EC) Typical numbers
Where to read Replica or cache Primary Replica read ~1–3 ms, but 50 ms to several seconds behind; primary ~1–5 ms and always current
Replication mode Async (synchronous_commit = local) Sync (on, or remote_apply) Async commit ~1 ms; sync same-zone adds ~1–2 ms; sync cross-region adds 80–150 ms per commit
Cross-region writes Write locally, replicate later Write to the one primary region Local ~5 ms vs 120 ms round trip
Cache TTL Long TTL, serve possibly stale Short TTL or invalidate on write 0.3 ms cache hit vs 3 ms database read
Kafka producer acks=1 acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 ~2 ms vs ~5–10 ms per batch

Systems by PACELC letter: PostgreSQL with sync replication is PC/EC; with async replicas it is PA/EL for reads; DynamoDB and Cassandra default to PA/EL; etcd and ZooKeeper are PC/EC; MongoDB with majority writes is PA/EC.

Practical example

Order history page: read from the replica (EL). Order confirmation page right after checkout: read from the primary (EC), because the user will notice a missing order much more than 3 ms. Same table, two endpoints, two PACELC choices. Section 28.6 shows how to make that routing automatic.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never enable read replicas fleet-wide with a single switch. They classify reads: "after my own write" reads go to the primary; list and search reads go to replicas; and the replica lag is monitored with an alert at 5 s. They treat sync replication across regions as a per-table decision, not a cluster default, because 120 ms per commit on every table would be a self-inflicted outage.

Common mistakes

  • Turning on TypeORM or Sequelize read replicas globally and getting "I just saved it and it is not there" bugs the same afternoon.
  • Choosing async replication to get fast commits, then promoting a replica during an incident and losing the last seconds of acknowledged orders, without ever having decided that was acceptable.
  • Setting acks=1 for Kafka producers for speed and losing events on broker failover.

Interview questions

  1. What does PACELC add to CAP? Expected: the latency-versus-consistency choice when there is no partition, which is the usual case.
  2. Where does a read-replica setup sit in PACELC, and what bug does it introduce? Expected: EL; stale read-after-write; fix with primary routing for a window after writes.
  3. When would you pay 120 ms per commit for cross-region sync replication? Expected: data whose loss is unacceptable and whose write rate is low (ledger entries, account changes), never for high-volume events.

28.6 Consistency models in plain language

Concept

A consistency model is a contract about what values reads are allowed to return, given the writes that happened. Stronger models make programming easy and cost latency and availability; weaker models are fast and cheap and push complexity into your code. You will meet every model below in an ordinary backend, mostly without anyone naming it.

Why does it exist?

Once data has more than one copy (a replica, a cache, a client), reads can return different values depending on which copy they hit and when. Without a named contract, developers assume the strongest model (a single copy that is always current) and write code that is wrong on replicas and caches. Naming the models lets you say precisely what each endpoint promises.

Mental model

The order status page for order 8813. The status moves PENDING_PAYMENT then PAID then SHIPPED. Ask: what may the page show, to whom, and when? Each model answers differently.

How it works

From strongest to weakest, each with the order status page:

  1. Linearizable (strong consistency): there is effectively one copy. Once any client has seen PAID, every client everywhere sees PAID or later, immediately. Cost: every read must go to the leader or a majority. Example: reading the order row from the PostgreSQL primary.
  2. Sequential consistency: all clients see the same sequence of statuses in the same order, but not necessarily at the same time. Nobody sees SHIPPED then PAID, but a client may still see PAID a while after another client saw SHIPPED. Example: everyone reads from the same single replica that applies WAL in order.
  3. Causal consistency: if SHIPPED was caused by PAID (the shipping service acted because it saw the payment), no client sees SHIPPED without also being able to see PAID. Unrelated updates (a different order, or the customer changing their nickname) may appear in any order. Example: a Kafka consumer that keys all events of one order to one partition sees them in causal order for that order.
  4. Read-your-writes: the client who just clicked "cancel" sees CANCELLED on their next page load. Other clients may see the old status for a while. This is the model users actually notice being broken. Example: route the writing user's reads to the primary for a short window.
  5. Monotonic reads: once a client has seen SHIPPED, a refresh never shows PAID again. Broken when consecutive reads hit different replicas with different lag. Example: pin a user's session to one replica, or carry a "seen up to LSN X" token.
  6. Monotonic writes: a client's own writes are applied in the order it issued them. Broken by fire-and-forget async writes through different paths.
  7. Eventual consistency: if writes stop, all copies eventually show SHIPPED. No promise about when, and no promise about what you see in between. Example: a search index rebuilt by a consumer, a CDN-cached page, a DynamoDB eventually consistent read.

Read-your-writes with a replica, made concrete:

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant API as NestJS
  participant P as Primary
  participant R as Replica
  U->>API: POST /orders/8813/cancel
  API->>P: UPDATE orders SET status = CANCELLED
  P-->>API: committed at LSN 0/9A3F
  API-->>U: 200 plus cookie min_lsn = 0/9A3F
  U->>API: GET /orders/8813 with cookie
  API->>R: SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()
  R-->>API: 0/9A10 which is behind 0/9A3F
  API->>P: SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 8813
  P-->>API: CANCELLED
  API-->>U: 200 CANCELLED

Three ways to achieve read-your-writes with replicas or caches:

  • Time window: after any write by user U, route U's reads to the primary for N seconds (N above your p99 replica lag, usually 2–10 s). Simple, slightly wasteful.
  • LSN token (as in the diagram): after a write, capture pg_current_wal_lsn() and give it to the client (cookie or header). On a read, ask the replica pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(); if it is behind the token, use the primary or wait briefly. Precise, a bit more code.
  • Write-through cache: on write, update the cache entry in the same code path; reads hit the cache first. Works for single-object reads, not for lists or searches.

Practical example

Food-delivery app. Restaurant marks an item "sold out". The restaurant's own tablet must show it sold out immediately (read-your-writes). Customers browsing may see it for a few more seconds (eventual, bounded), but a customer who orders it must be rejected by a strong check on the primary at order time. Three models on one field, each chosen for its cost.

NestJS example

A request-scoped router that decides primary or replica per query, using the LSN token method:

// read-routing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class ReadRouting {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  // Call right after a committing write; returns a token the client stores in a cookie.
  async currentLsn(): Promise<string> {
    const [{ lsn }] = await this.ds.query('SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()::text AS lsn');
    return lsn;
  }

  // Pick a query runner for a read that must include everything up to minLsn.
  async runnerFor(minLsn?: string): Promise<QueryRunner> {
    if (!minLsn) return this.ds.createQueryRunner('slave');          // no freshness requirement
    const replica = this.ds.createQueryRunner('slave');
    const [{ caught_up }] = await replica.query(
      'SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= $1::pg_lsn AS caught_up', [minLsn],
    );
    if (caught_up) return replica;
    await replica.release();
    return this.ds.createQueryRunner('master');                      // replica is behind: go to primary
  }
}

createQueryRunner('master' | 'slave') is TypeORM's real API when the DataSource is configured with replication: { master, slaves }. A controller passes the cookie value as minLsn, and the extra round trip to the replica costs about 1 ms.

PostgreSQL example

Replica lag is the number that decides whether eventual consistency is "50 ms" or "4 minutes". Measure it from both sides:

-- On the primary: per-standby lag in bytes and time.
SELECT application_name,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On the replica: how old is the newest transaction I have applied?
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag;

-- Strongest option: make the primary wait until the standby has APPLIED the commit,
-- so any read from that standby afterwards is read-your-writes without tokens.
-- Costs the full replica apply latency on every commit.
SET synchronous_commit = 'remote_apply';

remote_apply turns a replica into a linearizable read source for committed data, at the price of every commit waiting for apply on that replica. Almost nobody runs it fleet-wide; some run it per transaction for a few critical writes.

TypeORM example

Configuring replication so that createQueryRunner('slave') exists at all, and pinning a read to the primary when needed:

// typeorm.config.ts
import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

export const typeOrmConfig = (): TypeOrmModuleOptions => ({
  type: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    master: { host: process.env.PG_PRIMARY_HOST, port: 5432, username: 'api', password: process.env.PG_PASS, database: 'shop' },
    slaves: [
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA1_HOST, port: 5432, username: 'api', password: process.env.PG_PASS, database: 'shop' },
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA2_HOST, port: 5432, username: 'api', password: process.env.PG_PASS, database: 'shop' },
    ],
  },
  autoLoadEntities: true,
});

// In a service: read after own write must hit the primary.
const runner = dataSource.createQueryRunner('master');
try {
  const order = await runner.manager.findOne(Order, { where: { id } });
  return order;
} finally {
  await runner.release();
}

With replication configured, TypeORM sends plain find and SELECT query-builder calls to a replica and writes to the master; anything that must be fresh needs an explicit master runner or a transaction (transactions always run on the master).

Sequelize example

// sequelize.config.ts
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize('shop', 'api', process.env.PG_PASS, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    write: { host: process.env.PG_PRIMARY_HOST },
    read: [{ host: process.env.PG_REPLICA1_HOST }, { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA2_HOST }],
  },
  pool: { max: 20, min: 2, idle: 10_000 },
});

// Read-your-writes: force the write pool for this one query.
const order = await Order.findByPk(orderId, { useMaster: true });

Sequelize routes SELECTs to the read pool and everything else to write; useMaster: true overrides per query. Queries inside a sequelize.transaction always go to the write pool.

Production scenario

A social app serves 12,000 reads per second from three replicas with p99 lag of 300 ms, occasionally spiking to 20 s during a nightly batch. Without read-your-writes handling, "I posted and it disappeared" tickets arrived every night. They added a 5 s primary-routing window keyed by user id in Redis after any write; primary read load rose from 8% to 11% of total reads; tickets went to zero. They later added an alert on replica lag above 5 s, because a 20 s lag during the day would have broken the window anyway.

Failure scenario

An e-commerce team enabled replica reads for "everything" on a Friday. Checkout wrote the order on the primary, then redirected to /orders/:id, which read from a replica 80 ms behind. One in fifteen users saw "Order not found" on the confirmation page and clicked "Place order" again. Duplicate orders climbed 6% in an hour before someone connected the dashboard to the deploy. Rollback fixed it; the real fix was an explicit consistency level per endpoint.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A replica falls minutes behind during a bulk import; every "eventual" read is now minutes stale and nothing alerts, because "eventual" had no bound.
  • Two consecutive reads hit two replicas with different lag: status goes SHIPPED then PAID on refresh (monotonic reads broken).
  • The LSN cookie is set on one database cluster and presented to another after a failover; compare LSNs only within the same timeline, or fall back to a time window.
  • A cache holds a value written before a concurrent update and then overwritten after it: a stale value with a long TTL. Section 28.16 covers this race.
  • Cross-service reads: order service reads "customer address" from a customer-service cache updated by events; the customer changed their address 2 s ago; the order ships to the old address. Causal consistency between services needs versioning on the event, not luck.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the consistency level into the API contract: "GET /orders/:id returns the order as of at most 1 s ago, except for the user who just modified it, who always sees their own change." They pick the weakest model that satisfies the business, because each stronger level costs latency, load on the primary, or partition-time availability. They ask of every read: who reads it, right after which write, and what happens if it is 5 s stale?

Common mistakes

  • Enabling replica reads globally instead of per endpoint.
  • Believing "eventual" is measured in milliseconds; it is measured in whatever your worst replica lag is.
  • Redirecting to a read endpoint immediately after a write with no read-your-writes mechanism.
  • Relying on wall-clock timestamps to decide which of two replica values is newer.

Interview questions

  1. Explain linearizability, causal consistency and eventual consistency using one order status page. Expected: as in the list above. Follow-up: which does PostgreSQL give a single client on the primary? On a replica?
  2. How do you implement read-your-writes with read replicas? Expected: time window, LSN token, or write-through cache; tradeoffs of each.
  3. A user refreshes and sees an older status than before. Which model is broken and how do you fix it? Expected: monotonic reads; pin to one replica or carry an LSN token.
  4. What is the difference between sequential and causal consistency? Expected: sequential is a single global order for all writes; causal only orders writes that depend on each other.

Practical exercise

Set up PostgreSQL with one streaming replica in Docker, add an artificial delay with recovery_min_apply_delay = '5s' on the replica, and configure TypeORM or Sequelize replication. Acceptance criteria: a test proves that a naive read after write returns stale data; the LSN-token method returns fresh data; the primary receives only reads that need freshness; and replica lag is exposed as a Prometheus gauge.

28.7 Strong versus eventual consistency: which business cases need which

Concept

Strong consistency means every read reflects every completed write, immediately, everywhere. Eventual consistency means copies converge once writes stop, and reads in the meantime may be stale. The choice is not technical taste; it follows from what a stale read costs the business.

Why does it exist?

Strong consistency costs latency (wait for the leader or a majority), scalability (one leader takes all writes and all fresh reads) and availability (no answer during partitions). Eventual consistency gives up freshness to buy all three. Almost every real system uses both, and the engineering skill is knowing where the line goes.

How it works

Business case Needs Why Typical implementation
Payments, ledger, balances Strong A stale balance lets a user spend money twice Single primary, FOR UPDATE, sync replication for durability
Inventory decrement, seat holds Strong at the moment of reservation Overselling costs money and trust Row lock or conditional UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= qty on the primary
Auth: password change, token revocation, permission removal Strong (or eventual with a very short bound) A revoked token that still works for 5 minutes is a security hole Primary reads for auth checks; short-TTL cache with explicit invalidation
Order status for the acting user Read-your-writes "I cancelled and it still says active" Primary routing window or LSN token
Product catalogue, prices shown in lists Eventual, seconds A price stale by 3 s is corrected at checkout, which is strong Replica reads, CDN, cache with TTL
Feeds, timelines, notifications Eventual, seconds to minutes Nobody can tell that a post appeared 4 s late Fan-out workers via Kafka
Search index, recommendations Eventual, minutes Freshness is nice, not required Consumers rebuilding indexes
Analytics, reports, dashboards Eventual, minutes to hours Aggregates are approximations anyway Batch and stream pipelines

UI patterns that make eventual consistency feel fine:

  • Optimistic UI: show the like, the comment, the "added to cart" immediately from the client's own action, then reconcile with the server response. Roll back visibly if the server rejects.
  • Explicit processing states: "Payment processing", "Preparing your order", "Sending". The UI tells the truth about a state machine that has not finished, instead of pretending it is done.
  • Poll or push for the final state: the order page polls GET /orders/:id every 2 s until the status is final, or receives a WebSocket or server-sent event.
  • Read-your-writes for the actor only: the person who made the change sees it at once; everyone else sees it within seconds.
  • Tell users about delays honestly: "Search results update within a few minutes" prevents "the search is broken" tickets.

Practical example

Checkout in an e-commerce app: the "place order" write and stock reservation are strong. The confirmation page says "Order received, confirming payment" (a processing state) and polls. The order appears in the user's order list from a replica (read-your-writes window). The seller's dashboard sees it within seconds (eventual). The recommendations engine sees it within minutes (eventual). The monthly revenue report sees it that night (eventual). One order, five consistency levels, each picked by cost.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They push strong consistency down to the smallest possible operation (the one UPDATE that reserves stock) and let everything around it be eventual. They design the state machine so that "in progress" is a real state the UI can show, not an embarrassment to hide. They explain to product: "The order will always be correct. The seller dashboard will show it within two seconds instead of instantly, and that lets us handle ten times the traffic on the same database."

Common mistakes

  • Making the whole flow strongly consistent (one giant transaction across services) because it feels safer, and then discovering it does not scale and cannot include the payment provider anyway.
  • Making stock decrement eventual "for performance" and overselling.
  • Not designing a "processing" state, so the UI either lies ("Done!") or blocks.
  • Skipping the read-your-writes case and shipping a confirmation page that says "not found".

Interview questions

  1. Which parts of an order flow need strong consistency and which can be eventual? Expected: reservation and payment strong; status propagation, feeds, search, analytics eventual; actor gets read-your-writes.
  2. How do you design a UI for an eventually consistent backend? Expected: optimistic UI, processing states, polling or push, honest messaging.
  3. Can token revocation be eventually consistent? Expected: only with a bound short enough that the business accepts the window; otherwise check the primary or a synchronously invalidated cache.

Practical exercise

Take a feature in your system that currently uses one large transaction across two modules. Split it into a strongly consistent core write and an eventually consistent projection updated by an event, with an explicit processing state visible to the client. Acceptance criteria: the core write's transaction is shorter than before; the client can observe the processing state and the final state; killing the projection worker delays the projection but never corrupts the core.

28.8 Distributed state: where state lives and why services should not hold it

Concept

State is anything the system remembers between two requests: an order, a session, a counter, a lock, a queue of jobs, "which step of checkout this user is on". In a distributed system, state has to live somewhere specific, and the choice of where decides what survives a crash, what other pods can see, and what happens during a partition.

The four places state can live:

Place Survives pod restart? Visible to other pods? Cost per access Typical use
Database (PostgreSQL) Yes, durably Yes 1–5 ms Source of truth: orders, users, balances, saga state
Cache (Redis) Depends (usually treated as no) Yes 0.2–1 ms Sessions, rate limits, locks, hot reads, short-lived coordination
Queue / log (Kafka, RabbitMQ) Yes Yes, to consumers 2–10 ms Work to be done, events that happened
Client (JWT, cookie, local storage) Yes, on that device No 0 ms Identity claims, UI preferences, cart drafts
Process memory (a Map in the pod) No No ~0 Only for caches that may be lost and for per-request scratch

A stateless service is one that keeps nothing important in process memory between requests: every request carries or looks up everything it needs. Stateless does not mean "no state"; it means the state lives in one of the first four rows, not the fifth.

Why does it exist?

If a pod holds state in memory, then only that pod can serve requests that need it. That breaks horizontal scaling (you cannot add pods freely), breaks rolling deploys (killing the pod loses the state), breaks failure recovery (a crash loses in-flight work), and forces the load balancer into sticky sessions: routing each user to "their" pod. Sticky sessions sound harmless and cause: uneven load (one pod gets the busy users), slow drains on deploy (you must wait for sessions to end or lose them), broken failover (a pod death logs out thousands of users), and cache invalidation nightmares (the sticky pod's in-memory copy is the only copy). Avoid them; put the session in Redis or in a signed token.

Mental model

Imagine a call centre where each agent keeps customer notes on their own desk. If you always get the same agent, it works, until that agent is sick. A well-run centre keeps notes in a shared system, and any agent can pick up any call. The agents are stateless; the notes system is the state.

How it works

The senior rule for state: every piece of state has exactly one owner and one home. For a checkout:

  1. The order row in PostgreSQL is the truth about the order. Its status column is a persisted state machine: a fixed set of states and a fixed set of allowed transitions, enforced by the database, not by hoping the code is correct.
  2. The cart, before checkout, lives in Redis keyed by user id (fast, shared across pods, acceptable to lose after 30 days).
  3. The "payment in progress" fact lives in the order row (PENDING_PAYMENT), never in a pod's memory, so any pod can answer "what is happening with order 8813" and any pod can pick up the next step.
  4. Work that must happen later ("send confirmation email") lives in a queue, not in a setTimeout.
  5. The user's identity lives in a signed JWT the client sends; the pod verifies it without any per-pod memory.

Transitions are applied with compare-and-set: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT'. If zero rows are updated, another pod got there first (or the order was cancelled), and the code reacts instead of blindly overwriting.

Practical example

Five NestJS pods handle a payment webhook that can arrive twice (providers retry). Pod 2 and pod 4 each receive a copy at the same time. Both run the compare-and-set update; exactly one changes a row; the other sees affected = 0 and stops. No lock, no coordination between pods, no in-memory "already processed" set that would only exist in one pod.

NestJS example

A state machine service that owns the transition table and applies transitions with compare-and-set:

// order-state.service.ts
import { ConflictException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order, OrderStatus } from './order.entity';

const TRANSITIONS: Record<OrderStatus, OrderStatus[]> = {
  PENDING_PAYMENT: ['PAID', 'PAYMENT_FAILED', 'CANCELLED'],
  PAID: ['STOCK_RESERVED', 'COMPENSATING'],
  STOCK_RESERVED: ['SHIPPING_REQUESTED', 'COMPENSATING'],
  SHIPPING_REQUESTED: ['COMPLETED', 'COMPENSATING'],
  COMPENSATING: ['FAILED'],
  PAYMENT_FAILED: [], CANCELLED: [], COMPLETED: [], FAILED: [],
};

@Injectable()
export class OrderStateService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>) {}

  // Returns true if THIS call performed the transition; false if it had already happened
  // (idempotent replay). Throws only on an illegal transition.
  async transition(orderId: string, from: OrderStatus, to: OrderStatus): Promise<boolean> {
    if (!TRANSITIONS[from].includes(to)) {
      throw new ConflictException(`Illegal transition ${from} -> ${to} for order ${orderId}`);
    }
    const result = await this.orders
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .update(Order)
      .set({ status: to, updatedAt: () => 'now()' })
      .where('id = :orderId AND status = :from', { orderId, from })   // compare-and-set
      .execute();
    if (result.affected === 1) return true;

    const current = await this.orders.findOneOrFail({ where: { id: orderId } });
    if (current.status === to) return false;                          // already done by another pod
    throw new ConflictException(`Order ${orderId} is ${current.status}, expected ${from}`);
  }
}

No pod remembers anything. Any pod, any replica, any time.

PostgreSQL example

Make the state machine a database fact, so a bug in any service cannot produce an impossible state:

CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM (
  'PENDING_PAYMENT', 'PAID', 'PAYMENT_FAILED', 'STOCK_RESERVED',
  'SHIPPING_REQUESTED', 'COMPLETED', 'COMPENSATING', 'FAILED', 'CANCELLED'
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL,
  status      order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING_PAYMENT',
  version     int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Every transition is recorded: who moved it, from what, to what. This is your audit trail
-- and your debugging tool when a saga goes wrong at 3 a.m.
CREATE TABLE order_status_history (
  id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  from_status order_status,
  to_status  order_status NOT NULL,
  reason     text,
  actor      text NOT NULL,        -- 'payment-webhook', 'saga-orchestrator', 'support:alice'
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX order_status_history_order_idx ON order_status_history (order_id, id);

-- Compare-and-set in one statement. affected = 0 means "someone else moved it first".
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'PAID', version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT';

Finding stuck state is a query, not a mystery: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT' AND updated_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'.

TypeORM example

Optimistic locking with @VersionColumn protects whole-row updates where a compare-and-set on one column is not enough:

// order.entity.ts
import { Column, Entity, PrimaryColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column({ type: 'enum', enum: [...] }) status: OrderStatus;
  @VersionColumn() version: number;        // TypeORM adds "AND version = :v" and increments it
}

// Saving an entity read earlier throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError if another pod
// changed it in between. Catch it and reload, or retry the whole operation.

Sequelize example

// order.model.ts
import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Order extends Model {}
Order.init(
  { id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, primaryKey: true }, status: DataTypes.STRING, version: DataTypes.INTEGER },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'orders', version: true },   // version: true enables optimistic locking
);

// order.save() throws OptimisticLockError when the row's version changed since it was loaded.

Production scenario

A ride-booking backend once kept "driver is currently being offered ride X" in memory in the matching service. With one instance, fine. They scaled to three instances behind a load balancer; drivers started receiving two offers at once because instance 2 did not know instance 1 had already offered. The fix moved the offer into a Redis key offer:driver:{id} set with NX and a 20 s TTL, plus an offers table in PostgreSQL for the durable record. Throughput rose from 400 to 1,100 matches per second with three instances, and offers stopped duplicating.

Failure scenario

At 09:00 on a deploy day, a SaaS app with sticky sessions and in-memory session storage rolled out a new version. Kubernetes terminated old pods with a 30 s grace period. Every user on an old pod was logged out mid-work; 14,000 sessions lost; a spreadsheet import that had been running for 20 minutes in one user's session vanished. The post-mortem action items were: sessions to Redis, long-running imports to a queue with progress in PostgreSQL, sticky sessions removed. Deploys became invisible to users.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two pods apply the same transition from a duplicate message; without compare-and-set the second overwrites a later state with an earlier one.
  • A pod caches "current order status" in memory for 60 s "for performance" and serves a cancelled order as active from one pod only; users see different answers on refresh.
  • Redis restarts and all sessions vanish; if that is unacceptable, persist sessions or use signed tokens.
  • A JWT carries a role claim; the role is revoked in the database; the client keeps the old claim until expiry. Client-held state is stale by design; bound its lifetime.
  • Sticky sessions plus autoscaling: new pods sit idle because all sessions are pinned to the old ones.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, for every field: who owns it, where is the single durable copy, which copies are caches, and how long may a cache be wrong? They refuse in-process state that another pod would need. They model every long-running business process as a persisted state machine with recorded transitions, because that turns "what happened to order 8813?" from a debugging session into a SELECT.

Common mistakes

  • Storing "in progress" flags in a module-level variable or Map.
  • Using sticky sessions to paper over in-memory state instead of removing the in-memory state.
  • Modelling status as a free-text column with no constraint and no history.
  • Updating status with SET status = 'PAID' and no WHERE status = ... guard, so replays and races overwrite later states.

Interview questions

  1. What does "stateless service" actually mean, and where does the state go? Expected: nothing needed across requests lives in process memory; state goes to the database, cache, queue or client depending on durability and sharing needs.
  2. Why are sticky sessions a smell? Expected: uneven load, deploy pain, failover logs users out, pinned in-memory state. Follow-up: when are they acceptable? (WebSocket affinity for connection state, with the real state still in Redis.)
  3. How do you make state transitions safe across multiple pods without locks? Expected: compare-and-set on the status column plus a history table; treat affected = 0 as "already done or conflict".
  4. What state can live in a JWT and what cannot? Expected: identity and coarse claims with a short lifetime; never anything that must be revocable immediately or that changes often.

Practical exercise

Find every module-level variable or in-memory Map in a NestJS service that holds data across requests. Classify each as: safe cache (may be lost, never authoritative) or hidden state (other pods would need it). Move every hidden-state item to Redis or PostgreSQL. Acceptance criteria: the service runs correctly with three replicas and a load balancer without session affinity; a pod can be killed at any moment with no lost work.

28.9 Replication

Concept

Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple machines. It exists for three reasons: durability (a disk dies, the data survives), availability (a node dies, another serves), and read scaling (reads spread across copies). Every replication design must answer two questions: who is allowed to write? and when does a write count as done?

Why does it exist?

A single copy of your orders table on a single disk has a measurable annual chance of disappearing, and a single node has planned and unplanned downtime. Replication is the only way to make data survive hardware, and the only way to keep serving during maintenance. The costs: writes take longer (or become unsafe), copies can disagree, and you now have failover, which is a whole class of incidents on its own.

Mental model

Asha and Ben again. Leader-based: only Asha writes in the master notebook; Ben copies from her and only answers questions. Multi-leader: both write in their own notebooks and swap pages every hour; sometimes they wrote conflicting things. Leaderless: there are five notebooks around town; to record a sale you write it into any three; to check a fact you read any three and take the newest entry.

How it works

Leader-based (single-leader) replication. One node, the leader (primary), accepts all writes and streams them to followers (replicas, standbys). PostgreSQL streaming replication ships the WAL; MySQL ships the binlog; Redis ships the replication stream; each Kafka partition has a leader broker and in-sync replicas. Followers can serve reads. Failover means promoting a follower, and the danger is promoting one that is behind (lost writes) or promoting two (split brain, section 28.3).

Multi-leader replication. Two or more nodes accept writes and exchange them. Used for multi-region active-active setups, for offline clients (mobile apps that sync later), and for collaborative editing. The cost: two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same row at the same time, and somebody must decide which wins. PostgreSQL logical replication can be configured in both directions, and tools like pglogical and BDR exist for this, but the conflict problem is yours.

Leaderless replication. Any node accepts writes and reads; the client (or a coordinator) sends each write to several nodes and reads from several nodes, using quorums (section 28.10) to get overlap. Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB's internal design follow this. Stale copies are repaired by read repair (the reader notices a stale copy and updates it) and anti-entropy (background comparison of copies).

When is a write done?

Mode Leader acknowledges when Durability if leader dies right after ack Commit latency cost
Asynchronous Its own WAL is flushed Recent writes may be lost None
Synchronous At least one follower has written/flushed/applied Acknowledged writes survive One round trip to the follower (~1–2 ms same zone, 80–150 ms cross-region)
Semi-synchronous / quorum Any one (or K) of several followers confirmed Survives, and a single slow follower does not block Round trip to the fastest K followers

PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit levels, weakest to strongest: off (do not even wait for local flush), local (local flush only), remote_write (follower received and handed to OS), on (follower flushed to disk), remote_apply (follower applied, so reads there see it).

Conflicts in multi-leader systems and how to resolve them.

  • Last-writer-wins (LWW): each write carries a timestamp; the highest timestamp wins. Simple, and it silently discards the other write. It also depends on clocks that disagree (section 28.13). Cassandra uses LWW per cell; Redis Enterprise CRDBs use it for some types. Acceptable for "user's display name"; unacceptable for "cart items" or "balance".
  • Version vectors: each replica keeps a counter per replica; a write carries the vector. Two writes are concurrent when neither vector dominates the other; the system keeps both (Riak calls them siblings) and asks the application to merge. Correct, and it pushes work to you.
  • CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): data structures designed so that any two concurrent updates merge automatically and deterministically: a grow-only counter (each replica counts its own increments; the total is the sum), an observed-remove set (add and remove with unique tags), an LWW-register. Used in collaborative editors (Yjs, Automerge), Redis Enterprise, and by hand in "merge the cart as a union of items with per-item quantities as max". If you can express your data as a CRDT, multi-leader becomes safe; if not, avoid multi-leader for that data.

Practical example

A cart shared between a user's phone and laptop, both possibly offline. Model it as a set of (sku, quantity, lastChangedAt, deviceId) entries. Merge rule: union of SKUs; for a SKU on both sides, take the entry with the later lastChangedAt, and treat an explicit "removed" tombstone as a change. This is a small LWW-element-set CRDT. It will never lose an item silently, and the only "loss" is choosing between two quantities for the same SKU, which the user can fix in one tap.

NestJS example

Making a Redis write semi-synchronous when it matters. Redis replication is asynchronous by default; the WAIT command blocks until N replicas have acknowledged the preceding writes, or the timeout passes:

// seat-hold.service.ts
import { Injectable, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class SeatHoldService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async hold(eventId: string, seatId: string, userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const key = `hold:${eventId}:${seatId}`;
    const acquired = await this.redis.set(key, userId, 'PX', 120_000, 'NX'); // atomic set-if-absent
    if (acquired !== 'OK') return false;

    // Ask Redis to confirm at least 1 replica has the write, waiting at most 50 ms.
    // Returns the number of replicas that acknowledged.
    const replicas = await this.redis.wait(1, 50);
    if (replicas < 1) {
      await this.redis.del(key);   // do not hand out a hold that a failover could forget
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('Seat hold not replicated; try again');
    }
    return true;
  }
}

WAIT does not make Redis strongly consistent (a failover can still pick a replica that missed the write), but it turns "definitely lost on failover" into "lost only if the replica that acknowledged also dies". Use it for holds and locks, not for every write.

PostgreSQL example

Streaming replication essentials and a check that tells you whether you are one disk failure away from data loss:

-- On the primary: create a physical replication slot so WAL is retained until the
-- standby has consumed it. Without a slot, a standby that falls behind cannot catch up.
SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby_b');

-- Danger check: a slot whose consumer is gone retains WAL forever and fills the disk.
SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;

-- Semi-synchronous: commit waits for any ONE of two standbys. A single slow standby
-- does not block commits; both being unreachable does.
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c)';
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_commit = 'on';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- Logical replication for selective or bidirectional copies (multi-leader building block).
CREATE PUBLICATION orders_pub FOR TABLE orders, order_items;
-- On the other node:
-- CREATE SUBSCRIPTION orders_sub CONNECTION 'host=... dbname=shop' PUBLICATION orders_pub;

An inactive slot with 300 GB of retained WAL is one of the classic 3 a.m. pages: the standby was decommissioned, nobody dropped the slot, the primary's disk filled, PostgreSQL stopped accepting writes.

Production scenario

A payments company runs a primary in zone A, a synchronous standby in zone B (ANY 1 with a third async standby in zone C). Commit latency: 3.8 ms p50 (vs 1.9 ms async). Write throughput: 4,000 transactions per second at peak, well within limits. Read replicas serve 70% of reads. During a zone-B maintenance the sync standby was remote_write-lagging for 20 minutes; ANY 1 transparently used zone C; nobody noticed except the dashboard. Their rule: the money tables run sync; the analytics database is an async logical subscriber, 30 s behind on a bad day.

Failure scenario

A team ran PostgreSQL with one async replica and a script that promoted the replica if the primary was unreachable for 15 s. A network blip triggered promotion while the old primary was alive and 1.2 s (about 900 transactions) ahead. Applications reconnected to the new primary via DNS; the old primary kept accepting writes from pods whose DNS cache had not expired. For 4 minutes there were two primaries (split brain). Merging the two histories took two days of manual work and some orders were lost.
