Lessons: never promote without quorum agreement, fence the old primary (Patroni does both), and if writes must never be lost, replication must be synchronous.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Async replica promoted after leader failure: acknowledged writes disappear; customers who saw "order placed" have no order.
  • Sync standby down and no alternative: commits block; the app looks "down" though the primary is healthy.
  • Replica lag spikes during VACUUM FULL, bulk loads or long-running queries on the replica (which can pause replay); "eventual" becomes minutes.
  • Multi-leader with LWW and clock skew: the write that happened first "wins" because its clock was ahead.
  • Logical replication does not replicate DDL; a migration on one node breaks the subscription on the other.
  • Replication slot with a dead consumer fills the primary's disk.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They decide per dataset how much acknowledged data they are willing to lose (zero for money, seconds for events) and set replication mode from that, not from a benchmark. They never run multi-leader for data without a written merge rule. They monitor replica lag, slot retention and sync-standby health as first-class alerts. And they run failover on purpose, quarterly, because a failover you have never tested is not high availability, it is hope.

Common mistakes

  • Running async replication and assuming failover is lossless.
  • Enabling "active-active" for convenience and letting last-writer-wins silently discard updates.
  • Forgetting replication slots when a standby is removed.
  • Sending all reads to replicas without a read-your-writes plan (section 28.6).

Interview questions

  1. Compare leader-based, multi-leader and leaderless replication. When would you use each? Expected: single-leader for most transactional systems; multi-leader for multi-region or offline clients with CRDT-friendly data; leaderless for high-availability key-value workloads with quorum reads.
  2. What is the difference between synchronous_commit = on and remote_apply? Expected: on waits for the standby's flush; remote_apply waits until the standby has applied, which makes reads there see the commit.
  3. What is a CRDT and where would you use one? Expected: a data type whose concurrent updates merge deterministically; carts, counters, collaborative documents.
  4. How can an async replica setup lose data, and how do you prevent it? Expected: promotion of a lagging replica; prevent with sync or quorum replication and quorum-based failover.

Practical exercise

Build a two-node PostgreSQL setup in Docker with streaming replication and a replication slot. Measure commit latency under synchronous_commit = local, on and remote_apply with pgbench. Then stop the standby under on and observe the primary. Acceptance criteria: you can state the latency cost of each level in milliseconds; you can explain what happened to commits while the standby was down; and you can show the retained WAL growing in pg_replication_slots.

28.10 Quorum

Concept

A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for an operation to count. With N copies of a value, a write that must be confirmed by W nodes and a read that must consult R nodes are guaranteed to overlap in at least one node whenever W + R > N. That overlap is what lets a read find the latest write without asking every node.

Why does it exist?

Waiting for every replica on every write (W = N) means one slow or dead node stops the world. Waiting for none (W = 1) means a write can be lost the moment that one node dies. Quorums give a middle path with a mathematical guarantee: as long as fewer than a certain number of nodes fail, no acknowledged write is lost and no read misses it.

Mental model

Five friends share a notebook policy: to record a fact you must write it into at least three of the five notebooks; to check a fact you must read at least three. Any three you write and any three you read must share at least one notebook (3 + 3 > 5), and that shared notebook has the fact. If two friends are away, you can still write and read. If three are away, you stop, rather than risk missing something.

How it works

flowchart LR
  W["Write: confirmed by W = 2 of N = 3"] --> n1["Node 1: v2"]
  W --> n2["Node 2: v2"]
  W -.->|"slow or down"| n3["Node 3: still v1"]
  R["Read: consult R = 2 of N = 3"] --> n2
  R --> n3
  n2 --> M["Reader sees v2 and v1, picks the newer v2 and repairs Node 3"]
  n3 --> M

With N = 3, W = 2, R = 2:

  1. A write goes to all three nodes; the client waits for two acknowledgements. Node 3 is slow, so the write is acknowledged with nodes 1 and 2 holding version 2.
  2. A read goes to two nodes: say 2 and 3. Node 2 returns v2, node 3 returns v1. The client picks the newest (by version number, not wall clock) and, in a leaderless store, sends v2 back to node 3 (read repair).
  3. Because 2 + 2 > 3, any pair of nodes read overlaps with any pair that acknowledged the write, so v2 is always among the answers.

Common settings: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 (balanced); W = 3, R = 1 (fast reads, slow writes, any single node has everything); W = 1, R = 3 (fast writes, and a single node death can lose acknowledged data, so rarely chosen for important data).

Strict versus sloppy quorum. A strict quorum counts only the N "home" nodes for a key. A sloppy quorum (Dynamo, Cassandra with hinted handoff) lets a write be accepted by other nodes when home nodes are unreachable, storing a "hint" to forward it later. It raises availability during partitions and weakens the overlap guarantee: a read may consult the home nodes while the write sits on a stand-in node, so W + R > N no longer promises the read sees the write until the hint is delivered.

Quorums you already run.

  • PostgreSQL synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c)': a write is acknowledged when the primary plus any one of the two standbys have it. That is W = 2 out of N = 3 copies. FIRST 1 (b, c) is priority-based (wait for b unless b is down), which is not a quorum in the same sense.
  • Kafka acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 and replication factor 3: a produce is acknowledged when at least 2 in-sync replicas have it; reads always come from the leader, so consistency comes from the ISR mechanism rather than a read quorum.
  • etcd, ZooKeeper, Raft in general: a write commits when a majority (floor(N/2) + 1) of members have logged it; reads served by the leader are linearizable.
  • Cassandra QUORUM consistency level: floor(RF / 2) + 1 replicas, per query, for both reads and writes.

Practical example

A geo-distributed order-status service keeps three copies across three zones. With W = 2, R = 2, losing one zone changes nothing: writes and reads proceed with the other two. Losing two zones stops both, on purpose. With W = 1, R = 1 it would keep working with one zone but could return a status that a lost zone alone knew about.

NestJS example

Configuring the producer so a Kafka write is a quorum write, and treating a quorum failure as "unknown" rather than "failed":

// kafka-producer.provider.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Kafka, Producer } from 'kafkajs';

@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsProducer implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderEventsProducer.name);
  private readonly producer: Producer;

  constructor() {
    const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'order-service', brokers: process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS!.split(',') });
    this.producer = kafka.producer({ idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 1 }); // dedup on broker side
  }
  async onModuleInit() { await this.producer.connect(); }
  async onModuleDestroy() { await this.producer.disconnect(); }

  async publish(orderId: string, type: string, payload: unknown): Promise<void> {
    // acks: -1 means "all in-sync replicas"; combined with the topic's min.insync.replicas=2
    // the write must reach a quorum before the broker acknowledges.
    await this.producer.send({
      topic: 'orders.events',
      acks: -1,
      timeout: 5_000,
      messages: [{ key: orderId, value: JSON.stringify({ type, orderId, payload }) }],
    });
    this.log.debug(`published ${type} for ${orderId}`);
  }
}

If send rejects with a timeout, the record may still be on the brokers; the idempotent producer and, downstream, an inbox table (Part 29) make the retry harmless.

PostgreSQL example

Quorum commit and how to confirm it is really in effect:

ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c)';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- sync_state shows 'quorum' for members of an ANY group, 'sync' for FIRST members,
-- 'potential' for FIRST standbys not currently chosen, 'async' for the rest.
SELECT application_name, sync_state, sync_priority, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- A commit that must not be acknowledged unless the quorum has it:
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'on';
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, amount_cents, order_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3);
COMMIT;

Production scenario

An analytics platform ingests 60,000 events per second into Kafka with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2. During a broker's disk failure, partitions led by that broker moved leaders within 10 s; producers with acks=-1 saw a burst of timeouts and retried with idempotence on; no events were lost and no duplicates were written. The same platform once ran acks=1 "for throughput" and lost 40,000 events in a leader failover, which is the incident that made them switch.

Failure scenario

A team set synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (standby_b)' (a single named sync standby) for durability. During a routine standby reboot, every commit on the primary blocked for 9 minutes. The API returned 504s across the board while the database was, technically, perfectly healthy. Moving to ANY 1 (standby_b, standby_c) gave them the same durability with tolerance for one standby being away.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • W + R > N assumes nodes count versions correctly; with wall-clock LWW, the "newest" answer can be an older write from a fast clock.
  • Sloppy quorums can return stale data until hints are delivered; a partition of a few minutes makes "quorum reads" eventual.
  • A quorum write that times out may have reached the quorum; the client must treat it as unknown.
  • Membership changes (adding a node) temporarily change what "majority" means; do it through the system's proper reconfiguration, never by editing config on some nodes.
  • Read repair and anti-entropy add background load that shows up as mysterious latency spikes after a partition heals.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They can say, for every durable store in the system, "how many copies, how many must confirm a write, and what happens when one copy is down". They choose ANY 1 of 2 over FIRST 1 for PostgreSQL, min.insync.replicas=2 for Kafka topics that carry business events, and they know that quorum settings do not remove the unknown outcome; they only shrink the window in which data can be lost.

Common mistakes

  • Believing acks=all alone is a quorum; without min.insync.replicas >= 2 the ISR can shrink to just the leader, and acks=all then means "the leader alone".
  • A single named synchronous standby that turns maintenance into downtime.
  • Treating a quorum-write timeout as a failure and re-sending without idempotence.
  • Confusing "quorum" with "majority": PostgreSQL's ANY 1 (b, c) is 2 of 3 copies including the primary, and the system still has a single leader; it is a durability quorum, not a leader-election quorum.

Interview questions

  1. Explain W + R > N with a three-node example. What does R = 1, W = 3 give you? Expected: overlap guarantee; W = 3 means every node has every write so a single-node read is complete, at the cost of writes blocking when any node is down.
  2. What is a sloppy quorum and what does it cost? Expected: writes accepted by stand-in nodes with hints; higher availability; weaker read guarantee until hints deliver.
  3. How is PostgreSQL's synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (a, b)' a quorum, and how does it differ from FIRST 1? Expected: any one of the listed standbys satisfies the commit; FIRST waits for a specific priority order.
  4. Kafka: what combination of settings gives you "no acknowledged message is lost when one broker dies"? Expected: replication factor 3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean leader election disabled.

Practical exercise

Write a small TypeScript simulation of N = 5 nodes with versioned values, a write(W) and read(R) function, random node unavailability, and a test that asserts reads always return the latest acknowledged version when W + R > N and sometimes do not when W + R <= N. Acceptance criteria: the test passes for (3, 3), (4, 2), (2, 4) and demonstrably fails for (2, 2) and (1, 3) over 10,000 random runs.

28.11 Leader election: one writer at a time

Concept

Leader election is how a group of identical nodes agrees that exactly one of them is, for now, allowed to do a particular job: be the PostgreSQL primary, run the nightly reconciliation, own a Kafka partition, drive a saga. The chosen node holds a lease: permission that expires after a TTL unless renewed. When the leader dies or is cut off, the lease expires and another node takes over.

Why does it exist?

Some jobs are unsafe or wasteful when two nodes do them at once. Two primaries corrupt data. Two cron runners send every customer two invoices. Two saga drivers issue two refunds. Yet you want more than one node available to do the job, so that a crash does not stop it. Leader election gives you both: many candidates, one active.

The NestJS version of this problem is the singleton cron. You write @Cron('0 * * * *') on a method that reconciles payments, deploy five replicas for the API, and at the top of every hour five pods reconcile the same payments concurrently. Every scheduled job in a horizontally scaled service is a leader-election problem.

Mental model

Asha and Ben's bakery, with five staff and one pen for the master notebook. The pen sits in a box with a timer. Whoever takes the pen must press the timer every 30 seconds; if the timer runs out the box unlocks and someone else may take the pen. Now a subtle problem: Asha takes the pen, gets distracted for two minutes, the timer runs out, Ben takes a second pen from the box, and then Asha comes back and keeps writing with hers. Two pens, two writers. The fix is that each pen has a serial number stamped on it, and the notebook refuses any entry whose pen number is lower than the highest number it has already seen. That serial number is the fencing token.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as WorkerA
  participant L as LeaseStore
  participant B as WorkerB
  participant S as Storage
  A->>L: acquire lease reconciler ttl 30s
  L-->>A: granted, token 33
  A->>S: write with token 33
  S-->>A: ok, highest token now 33
  Note over A: long GC pause, lease not renewed
  Note over L: lease expires
  B->>L: acquire lease reconciler
  L-->>B: granted, token 34
  B->>S: write with token 34
  S-->>B: ok, highest token now 34
  Note over A: resumes, still believes it is leader
  A->>S: write with token 33
  S-->>A: rejected, 33 is below 34

The mechanism, step by step:

  1. Acquire: a candidate tries to create the lease record if it does not exist or has expired. Exactly one candidate can succeed, because the store makes the check-and-set atomic.
  2. Renew: the leader refreshes expires_at every TTL / 3 or so. If it fails to renew (network, crash, pause), it must stop acting as leader as soon as it notices, ideally before the lease actually expires.
  3. Expire: after the TTL, any candidate may acquire. The TTL is the time the job can be leaderless after a crash; a shorter TTL means faster failover and more risk of false expiry during pauses.
  4. Fence: each acquisition increments a monotonic token. Every side effect the leader performs carries the token, and the thing being written (database row, file, external API) rejects tokens lower than the highest it has seen. Without fencing, a paused old leader that wakes up after expiry can still write. With fencing, its writes bounce.

Where the lease can live:

Store Mechanism Fencing token Use when
PostgreSQL advisory lock pg_try_advisory_lock(key), held by the session; released on disconnect None built in; add a leases table if you need one The job already uses PostgreSQL; simplest possible singleton cron
PostgreSQL lease table UPDATE ... WHERE expires_at < now() OR holder = me RETURNING token Yes, a bigint column You need fencing or want to see the leader in a table
Redis SET key value NX PX ttl Atomic set-if-absent with expiry No; you must add a counter, and Redis failover can hand out the same lock twice Short critical sections where a rare double-execution is tolerable
etcd / ZooKeeper / Consul Leases with revisions, ephemeral nodes, sessions Yes (etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, Consul lock index) Real leadership for infrastructure (database failover, partition ownership)
Kubernetes Lease object coordination.k8s.io/v1 Lease with holderIdentity and leaseDurationSeconds Via resourceVersion Controllers and operators; it is what kube-controller-manager uses

Advisory-lock caveat: the lock belongs to the session. If your app connects through PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode, the session changes between queries and the lock silently does not do what you think. Use pg_try_advisory_xact_lock inside one transaction that lasts the whole job, or use a lease table.

Practical example

Five NestJS pods, an hourly job that marks unpaid orders as expired and releases their stock. Requirement: run once per hour, keep running if any pod is alive, never run twice concurrently. Solution: each pod fires the cron; each tries pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('expire-orders')) inside a transaction; the one that gets it runs the job in that transaction and commits; the others log "not leader" and return. Failover is automatic (the next hour, any pod can win). Cost: one cheap query per pod per hour.

NestJS example

Singleton cron with a transaction-scoped advisory lock (safe behind PgBouncer), then a lease-table variant with fencing for longer jobs:

// expire-orders.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class ExpireOrdersJob {
  private readonly log = new Logger(ExpireOrdersJob.name);
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_HOUR)
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    const runner = this.ds.createQueryRunner();
    await runner.connect();
    await runner.startTransaction();
    try {
      // Transaction-level advisory lock: released automatically at COMMIT/ROLLBACK,
      // and correct even through PgBouncer transaction pooling.
      const [{ locked }] = await runner.query(
        `SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('expire-orders')) AS locked`,
      );
      if (!locked) {
        this.log.debug('another pod holds expire-orders; skipping');
        await runner.rollbackTransaction();
        return;
      }
      const result = await runner.query(`
        UPDATE orders SET status = 'CANCELLED', updated_at = now()
        WHERE status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT' AND created_at < now() - interval '30 minutes'
        RETURNING id`);
      this.log.log(`expired ${result.length} orders`);
      await runner.commitTransaction();               // lock released here
    } catch (err) {
      await runner.rollbackTransaction();
      throw err;
    } finally {
      await runner.release();
    }
  }
}

For a job that runs for minutes and calls external systems, hold a lease with a fencing token and pass the token to every side effect:

// lease.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class LeaseService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  // Returns the fencing token if acquired or renewed, or null if someone else holds it.
  async acquireOrRenew(name: string, holder: string, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<bigint | null> {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(
      `UPDATE leases
       SET holder = $2,
           expires_at = now() + make_interval(secs => $3),
           fencing_token = CASE WHEN holder = $2 AND expires_at > now() THEN fencing_token ELSE fencing_token + 1 END
       WHERE name = $1 AND (expires_at < now() OR holder = $2)
       RETURNING fencing_token`,
      [name, holder, ttlSeconds],
    );
    return rows.length ? BigInt(rows[0].fencing_token) : null;
  }
}

The job renews every ttl / 3 seconds while it works; if a renewal returns null, it stops immediately. Every write it makes includes WHERE last_fencing_token <= $token (or a check in the receiving service), so a stale leader's writes are rejected.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE leases (
  name          text PRIMARY KEY,
  holder        text,
  expires_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT '-infinity',
  fencing_token bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
INSERT INTO leases (name) VALUES ('reconcile-payments');

-- Protected resource remembers the highest token it has accepted.
ALTER TABLE payment_reconciliations ADD COLUMN applied_by_token bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- A leader's write is fenced: zero rows affected means a newer leader has been here.
UPDATE payment_reconciliations
SET status = 'DONE', applied_by_token = $2
WHERE id = $1 AND applied_by_token <= $2;

-- Session-level advisory lock alternative for simple cases. Key is a bigint; hashtext gives one.
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('expire-orders'));   -- true = you are leader for this session
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(hashtext('expire-orders'));
-- Inspect who holds what:
SELECT pid, objid, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory';

expires_at is compared with the database's now(), never with the application's clock, so five pods with skewed clocks still agree on whether the lease is expired.

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const [[{ locked }]] = await sequelize.query(
    `SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('expire-orders')) AS locked`, { transaction: t },
  );
  if (!locked) return;
  await Order.update({ status: 'CANCELLED' }, {
    where: { status: 'PENDING_PAYMENT', createdAt: { [Op.lt]: new Date(Date.now() - 30 * 60_000) } },
    transaction: t,
  });
});

Production scenario

A subscription-billing service runs 8 pods. The daily invoice run takes 25 minutes and calls the payment gateway 40,000 times. It holds a lease with a 60 s TTL, renewed every 15 s, and every charge request carries an idempotency key that includes the invoice id (not the fencing token, because the gateway does not understand tokens, and the idempotency key already prevents double charges). Over a year: three leader failovers mid-run (two deploys, one node failure), each resumed within 90 s on another pod, zero duplicate invoices. The team's rule: fencing for internal writes, idempotency keys for external ones.

Failure scenario

A team used a Redis lock (SET NX PX 30000) for the leader of a report-generation job that took up to 40 s under load. At 03:00 the job ran long. The lock expired at 30 s; a second pod acquired it and started generating the same report; the first pod finished at 38 s and uploaded its file; the second finished at 70 s and overwrote it with an identical file. Harmless that night. Two weeks later the same race happened with a job that appended to a ledger; the ledger got every row twice. The lock had no fencing and the TTL was shorter than the job. Fixes: TTL renewal from the running job, a fencing token, and idempotent appends keyed by ledger entry id.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GC or event-loop pause longer than the TTL: the leader wakes up believing it still leads. Only fencing protects the data.
  • Clock skew: a lease store that compares the client's clock with expires_at breaks; always compare inside the store.
  • Redis failover: the lock key may not have replicated; the new primary grants it again; two leaders. Use WAIT or a consensus store for anything that matters.
  • Advisory lock through a transaction-pooling proxy: session locks evaporate between statements.
  • Holder crashes without releasing: session locks release on disconnect (once TCP notices, which can take minutes without keepalives); lease rows expire after TTL; Redis keys expire after PX. Every mechanism has a "dead leader" window equal to its detection time.
  • Leader renews but is partitioned from the resource it leads: it holds the lease and cannot do the job; nobody else can either. Renewal should be conditional on being able to do useful work (a health check inside the renew loop).
  • Job runs longer than the cron interval: the next tick tries to acquire while the previous run holds the lock; with try-lock semantics it correctly skips; with blocking lock semantics runs pile up.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask two questions about any "only one should do this" requirement: what is the cost of two doing it, and what is the cost of none doing it for T seconds? If two is merely wasteful, an advisory lock or Redis NX is fine. If two corrupts data, they insist on fencing or on making the work idempotent so a double run is harmless (idempotency is often the better answer than leadership). If none is expensive, they lower the TTL and accept more false failovers. They avoid building "real" leader election themselves and use PostgreSQL for app-level singletons, etcd or Kubernetes leases for infrastructure.

Common mistakes

  • @Cron on a service with replicas and no lock at all.
  • Session-level advisory locks behind PgBouncer transaction pooling.
  • A Redis lock whose TTL is shorter than the job, with no renewal.
  • Relying on lock expiry without fencing for writes that must not be duplicated.
  • Comparing lease expiry using Date.now() in the application.
  • Assuming "I acquired the lock" means "I still hold it" ten minutes later.

Interview questions

  1. You have five replicas of a NestJS service and a nightly cron. How do you make it run exactly once? Expected: advisory lock or lease in PostgreSQL, try-lock semantics, skip if not acquired; discuss PgBouncer and TTLs. Follow-up: what if the job takes 40 minutes and the pod is killed halfway?
  2. What is a fencing token and what problem does it solve? Expected: a monotonic number issued with each lease; storage rejects lower tokens; solves the paused-leader-wakes-up problem.
  3. Why is a Redis SET NX lock not a safe leader election for critical work? Expected: async replication can grant the lock twice on failover; expiry without fencing; the Redlock debate.
  4. Where should lease expiry be evaluated, and why? Expected: in the store (now() in PostgreSQL, the Redis server for TTLs), because client clocks disagree.

Practical exercise

Implement a lease table with fencing tokens, a @Cron job that holds and renews the lease, and a fake "resource" table that rejects stale tokens. Run three instances. Pause one instance with kill -STOP for longer than the TTL, then resume it with kill -CONT. Acceptance criteria: another instance takes over within TTL + renewal interval; the resumed instance's next write is rejected and it logs that it lost leadership; the resource table contains no writes from a stale token.

28.12 Consensus: how machines agree

Concept

Consensus is the problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value (or a single ordered sequence of values) even when some nodes crash and messages are delayed or lost. Leader election, cluster membership, configuration, "which replica has the latest data", and a replicated log are all consensus problems. The famous algorithms are Paxos and Raft; you will use them through etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Kafka's KRaft mode, and Patroni, and you should never write one yourself.

Why does it exist?

Without consensus, "who is the leader" is an opinion each node holds separately, and opinions diverge under partition (section 28.3). Consensus turns it into a fact: a value that a majority has durably recorded and that no future majority can contradict. That property is what makes split brain impossible in systems built on it.

There is also a hard limit to know about: the FLP result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) proves that no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in a fully asynchronous system with even one faulty node. Practical algorithms get around it with timeouts and randomization; the cost is that they can stall (for example during repeated leader elections) but never decide wrongly. Safety is guaranteed; liveness depends on the network behaving reasonably.

Mental model

Five bakery branches must agree on today's special. Each round has a number (a term). One branch proposes; it is accepted when a majority (three of five) have written it in their books. Any later proposal must first ask a majority what they already wrote, and a majority always includes at least one branch that saw the earlier decision, so the decision cannot be reversed. If the proposing branch goes silent, after a random wait another branch starts a new round with a higher number. Two branches proposing at once just waste a round; they never produce two different specials.

How it works

Paxos in one paragraph. Nodes play proposers and acceptors. A proposer picks a ballot number higher than any it has used and asks acceptors to promise not to accept lower ballots (phase 1). Acceptors reply with the highest-ballot value they have already accepted, if any. The proposer must then propose that value (or, if none, its own) and asks acceptors to accept it (phase 2). A value accepted by a majority is chosen. Because every majority overlaps every other, once a value is chosen every later proposer learns it in phase 1 and re-proposes it. Paxos is correct, minimal and notoriously hard to turn into a working system; Multi-Paxos, which elects a stable leader to skip phase 1, is what real systems use, and it is what Raft describes in an understandable way.

Raft, simply. Raft chooses a leader and replicates a log through it.

  1. Terms. Time is divided into numbered terms. Each term has at most one leader. A node that sees a higher term than its own immediately updates and steps down if it was a leader.
  2. Election. Followers expect heartbeats from the leader. If a follower hears nothing for a randomized election timeout (say 150–300 ms), it becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes. A node grants one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A majority of votes makes a leader. Randomized timeouts make split votes rare.
  3. Log replication. Clients send commands to the leader. The leader appends each to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers, including the index and term of the previous entry so followers can check consistency. A follower whose log does not match rejects, and the leader walks back until they agree, then overwrites the follower's divergent tail.
  4. Commit. When a majority has stored an entry, the leader marks it committed, applies it to its state machine, replies to the client, and tells followers the new commit index in the next heartbeat. Followers apply committed entries in order.
  5. Safety. Because a candidate needs votes from a majority, and a majority always includes a node that has every committed entry, a leader always has all committed entries (leader completeness). Committed entries are never lost or reordered.
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant L as Leader
  participant F1 as Follower1
  participant F2 as Follower2
  C->>L: set leader/reconciler = pod-7
  L->>L: append entry index 42 term 5
  L->>F1: AppendEntries prev 41 entry 42
  L->>F2: AppendEntries prev 41 entry 42
  F1-->>L: ok, stored 42
  Note over L: majority has 42, commit index = 42
  L->>L: apply 42 to state machine
  L-->>C: ok, revision 42
  F2-->>L: ok, stored 42 arrives late
  L->>F1: heartbeat commit index 42
  L->>F2: heartbeat commit index 42

Note that the client got its answer after two of three nodes had the entry; the slow follower catches up without holding anything back. That is a quorum write (section 28.10) with a leader enforcing a single order.

Where you meet consensus:

System Uses consensus for Notes
etcd Everything: it is a Raft-replicated key-value store Kubernetes stores all cluster state in it; Patroni can use it as its DCS
ZooKeeper Its Zab protocol (Paxos-like) replicates a hierarchical namespace Used by older Kafka, HBase, many lock services
Consul Raft for the KV store and service catalogue Also a Patroni DCS option
Kafka KRaft Raft among controller nodes for metadata (topics, partitions, leaders) Replaces ZooKeeper in modern Kafka; data replication itself is not Raft but the ISR protocol
Patroni Does not implement consensus; stores the leader lock in etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper and trusts their consensus The primary must renew its lock within ttl; a primary that cannot reach the DCS demotes itself
CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB Raft per data range Consensus per shard of your data

Why you should never implement it. Raft's paper is readable, and a weekend implementation will pass its own tests. Production consensus also needs: log compaction and snapshots, membership changes without losing quorum, disk fsync discipline, handling of clock and pause anomalies, pre-vote to avoid disruptive nodes, read-index for linearizable reads, and years of bug reports. etcd has had serious correctness bugs found by Jepsen after years of use. Use etcd, a managed equivalent, or PostgreSQL-based leases for application singletons, and let consensus experts run the consensus.

Practical example

Kubernetes itself. Every kubectl apply writes to etcd through the API server; etcd's Raft leader replicates to a majority; the write is acknowledged; controllers watching etcd react. When you lose an etcd member, nothing changes. When you lose a majority (two of three), the API server becomes read-only: pods keep running but no new deployments, no scaling, no leader changes. That behavior is CP, on purpose, and every platform team should have experienced it in a drill.

NestJS example

Using etcd directly from a NestJS worker for leadership, which is appropriate when the job coordinates infrastructure rather than application rows (for application singletons, prefer section 28.11's PostgreSQL lease):

// etcd-leader.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Etcd3, Lease } from 'etcd3';

@Injectable()
export class EtcdLeaderService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(EtcdLeaderService.name);
  private readonly client = new Etcd3({ hosts: process.env.ETCD_HOSTS!.split(',') });
  private lease?: Lease;
  isLeader = false;
  private readonly key = 'leaders/partition-rebalancer';
  private readonly podId = process.env.HOSTNAME ?? `pid-${process.pid}`;

  async onModuleInit() {
    this.lease = this.client.lease(15);                        // 15 s TTL, auto-kept-alive by the client
    this.lease.on('lost', () => { this.isLeader = false; this.log.warn('lease lost; stepping down'); });
    // Atomic: create the key only if it does not exist, attached to our lease.
    const txn = await this.client
      .if(this.key, 'Create', '==', 0)
      .then(this.client.put(this.key).value(this.podId).lease(this.lease))
      .commit();
    this.isLeader = txn.succeeded;
    this.log.log(this.isLeader ? 'became leader' : 'standing by');
    // Followers watch the key so they can try again when the leader's lease expires.
    if (!this.isLeader) {
      const watcher = await this.client.watch().key(this.key).create();
      watcher.on('delete', () => this.onModuleInit());
    }
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() { await this.lease?.revoke(); await this.client.close(); }
}

etcd's Raft guarantees that the if ... then ... commit transaction succeeds for exactly one client, and the revision of the write serves as a fencing token if you need one.

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL does not contain a consensus algorithm; Patroni borrows one. The settings that decide how a Patroni primary behaves when it cannot reach the consensus store:

# patroni.yml (excerpt)
ttl: 30              # leader lock TTL in the DCS; primary must renew within this
loop_wait: 10        # how often Patroni runs its loop
retry_timeout: 10    # how long DCS/PG operations may retry
# Rule: ttl > loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout, or the primary can lose its lock while healthy.

When the DCS is unreachable for longer than ttl, the primary demotes itself to read-only, because it can no longer prove it is the only primary. The application sees ERROR: cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction. That is consensus protecting your data, and it is also a page at 3 a.m. if nobody planned for a DCS outage.

Production scenario

A platform team runs a 3-node etcd cluster for Kubernetes and Patroni across three zones. Write latency to etcd: 2–4 ms. A zone outage removed one member; nothing changed. A misconfigured upgrade once took two members down at once; for 11 minutes Kubernetes could not schedule and Patroni demoted the PostgreSQL primary to read-only. The API served reads and failed writes cleanly (section 28.4's per-endpoint choices earned their keep). They moved to 5 etcd members across three zones afterwards, so that losing a zone plus one node still leaves a majority.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: "orders API 100% write errors". PostgreSQL was healthy, CPU idle, disks fine. The logs said read-only transaction. It took 25 minutes to discover that a certificate on the etcd cluster had expired at 02:00, Patroni could not renew its leader lock, and it demoted the primary as designed. Renewing the certificate restored writes in 30 s. The post-mortem noted that consensus did exactly what it promised (no split brain) and that the team had never listed "etcd is a dependency of the database" in their runbooks.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Loss of majority makes the cluster read-only; that is correct and must be in the runbook.
  • Repeated leader elections under a flaky network (election storm) stall progress without ever breaking safety.
  • A node with a slow disk delays every commit because fsync is on the critical path; consensus stores need fast, dedicated disks.
  • Membership changes done by editing config on some nodes can create two clusters that each think they have a majority; always use the reconfiguration API.
  • Clock jumps do not break Raft safety but can break clients that compare lease TTLs with local time.
  • Large values or many watchers make etcd slow; it is a coordination store, not a database.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know which components in their stack contain a consensus store (etcd under Kubernetes, KRaft under Kafka, the DCS under Patroni) and treat those as tier-zero dependencies: monitored, backed up, sized for majority loss, with certificates on a calendar. They use consensus for infrastructure and small coordination state, never as an application database, and they never write consensus code. To a product manager: "There is a small, very reliable committee that decides who is in charge of the database. If more than half the committee is unreachable, the database goes read-only rather than risk two bosses. That is a feature."

Common mistakes

  • Running a 2-member etcd or a 4-member one (even numbers add cost without adding fault tolerance).
  • Placing all consensus members in one zone.
  • Treating etcd as a general key-value store for application data.
  • Not knowing that a Patroni primary depends on the DCS being reachable.
  • Writing a "simple" leader election with timestamps and hoping.

Interview questions

  1. Explain Raft to a colleague in five minutes. Expected: terms, randomized election timeouts, leader-only writes, AppendEntries, majority commit, leader completeness. Follow-up: why must a candidate's log be at least as up to date as the voter's?
  2. What happens to Kubernetes when etcd loses quorum? Expected: API becomes read-only; running pods continue; no scheduling or updates.
  3. Why does Patroni demote a healthy primary when it cannot reach etcd? Expected: it cannot prove uniqueness; demotion prevents split brain.
  4. Should you implement Raft for your service's leader election? Expected: no; use etcd/Kubernetes leases for infrastructure, PostgreSQL leases or advisory locks for application singletons.

Practical exercise

Run a 3-node etcd cluster in Docker. Write a script that performs the compare-and-put leadership transaction from three processes, then kill the leader and observe takeover time. Then stop two of the three etcd nodes and observe what the remaining node does with reads and writes. Acceptance criteria: exactly one process is leader at any time (verified by a shared counter that each leader increments only while holding the lease); takeover happens within the lease TTL plus a few seconds; with two etcd nodes down, writes fail and you can explain why that is correct.

28.13 Time and clocks

Concept

Every machine has a clock, and no two clocks agree. A wall clock (Date.now(), PostgreSQL now()) tells you what time it is according to that machine, and it can be wrong, can be corrected by jumping forwards or backwards, and drifts constantly. A monotonic clock (process.hrtime.bigint(), performance.now()) only ever moves forward and is only meaningful on the machine that produced it. Distributed systems must use each for what it is good for, and must never use wall-clock timestamps from different machines to decide which event happened first.

Why does it exist?

Backends use time for everything: token expiry, lock TTLs, "latest record wins", ordering logs, timeouts, scheduling, rate-limit windows, cache expiry. If two machines disagree by 3 seconds, a token issued by one is "not yet valid" on the other, a lock expires early or late, and a record written first appears to have been written last. Clock skew is invisible until it produces an incident, and then it is very hard to see, because the logs you use to investigate carry the same wrong timestamps.

Mental model

Asha's watch is two minutes fast; Ben's is one minute slow. Asha writes "order 41 cancelled, 10:02". Ben writes "order 41 baked, 10:01". Reading the notebook later, it looks like the cake was baked before the cancellation, so the cancellation must have arrived too late. In reality Ben baked it two minutes after the cancellation, and their watches lied. To know what really happened you need something other than watches: numbered slips ("this is my 17th note, and I had seen your 12th when I wrote it"). That is a logical clock.

How it works

How wrong are clocks? NTP-synchronized servers in one datacenter typically agree within 1–10 ms. Under load, after a VM pause, on a machine whose NTP daemon is broken, or on a laptop, skew of seconds to minutes is routine. Google's Spanner needs custom atomic clocks and GPS to get a known bound of about 7 ms; everyone else has an unknown bound. NTP corrects skew by slewing (speeding the clock slightly) for small errors and by stepping (jumping) for large ones. A step backwards means Date.now() returns a smaller value than it did a moment ago.

Wall clock versus monotonic clock in Node.js:

// Measuring a duration: monotonic, immune to NTP steps.
const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
await paymentClient.charge(orderId, amount);
const elapsedMs = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1_000_000;

// Recording when something happened for humans and for cross-system comparison: wall clock.
const chargedAt = new Date();   // fine as a label; not fine as an ordering key across machines

// Wrong: a duration from the wall clock can be negative or wildly off after a clock step.
const t0 = Date.now();
await doWork();
const badElapsed = Date.now() - t0;

Why timestamps cannot order events across machines. Service A on host 1 writes updated_at = 10:00:00.120. Service B on host 2 writes the same row with updated_at = 10:00:00.090 a moment later, because host 2's clock is 50 ms behind. A "latest timestamp wins" rule keeps A's value and discards the newer write. The error is silent; there is no exception to catch.

Logical clocks. A Lamport clock is a counter per node. Before each local event, increment it. When sending a message, include the counter. On receiving, set your counter to max(own, received) + 1. If event X caused event Y (same node, or through a message chain), then clock(X) < clock(Y). The reverse is not true: two events with different counters may be concurrent and unrelated. Lamport clocks give you a consistent order to break ties deterministically; they do not tell you what really happened first in wall time.

Order service (counter)      Inventory service (counter)
  create order 8813  -> 1
  send "reserve"     -> 2  ----message(2)---->  receive: max(0,2)+1 = 3
                                                 reserve stock       -> 4
  receive "reserved" <-- message(4) ------------- send "reserved"    -> 5
  set clock = max(2,5)+1 = 6
  mark STOCK_RESERVED -> 7

Vector clocks keep one counter per node and can tell "concurrent" apart from "before"; they are what version vectors (section 28.9) are built on. Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine a wall-clock part with a logical counter so that timestamps look like real time, stay close to real time, and still respect causality; CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use them. Google TrueTime returns an interval [earliest, latest] and Spanner waits out the uncertainty before committing; it is the only mainstream system that orders by wall clock safely, and it needs special hardware.

Where skew bites a NestJS backend:

Feature What skew does Defense
JWT exp, nbf, iat A token issued by a server 30 s ahead is "not yet valid" on a server that is behind; a token expires "early" on a server ahead Short skew allowance (clockTolerance of 30–60 s); keep NTP healthy; alert on skew
Redis lock TTL Redis expires the key on its clock; the client computes "I still have 5 s left" on its clock Never reason about remaining time on the client; renew early; use fencing
Lease expires_at in PostgreSQL If the app compares expires_at to Date.now(), skewed pods disagree about expiry Compare in SQL with now()
Cache TTLs Harmless: expiry happens on the cache's clock None needed
"Latest wins" merges Newer write discarded Version numbers, vector clocks, or a single leader
Rate limit windows Pods with skewed clocks put the same second in different windows Compute the window from the Redis server time (TIME command) or use a Lua script on the server
Log correlation Logs from two services appear out of order; investigations chase ghosts Trace ids and spans (OpenTelemetry) carry causal order; timestamps are decoration
Scheduled jobs A cron on a fast clock fires early and "the 09:00 run" happens twice on two pods Leader election plus idempotent runs keyed by the scheduled slot

Practical example

Order service and payment service each set updated_at = now() from their own database connection, and both databases are the same PostgreSQL primary, so their clocks agree. A reporting service joins these with events from Kafka that carry producer-side Date.now() from 40 pods with up to 400 ms of skew between them. Reports show payments "received before the order existed" twice a day. The fix: order events by Kafka offset within a partition (a logical order) and treat the timestamp as a display value.

NestJS example

Allowing a small skew when verifying JWTs, and measuring timeouts with the monotonic clock:

// auth.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtModule } from '@nestjs/jwt';

@Module({
  imports: [
    JwtModule.register({
      secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET,
      signOptions: { expiresIn: '15m' },
      // Passed through to jsonwebtoken: tolerate up to 30 s of skew when checking exp and nbf.
      verifyOptions: { clockTolerance: 30 },
    }),
  ],
  exports: [JwtModule],
})
export class AuthModule {}
// deadline.ts: a request-scoped deadline that survives NTP steps.
export class Deadline {
  private readonly endNs: bigint;
  constructor(budgetMs: number) { this.endNs = process.hrtime.bigint() + BigInt(budgetMs) * 1_000_000n; }
  remainingMs(): number { return Math.max(0, Number(this.endNs - process.hrtime.bigint()) / 1_000_000); }
  signal(): AbortSignal { return AbortSignal.timeout(Math.ceil(this.remainingMs())); }
}

// Usage inside a service: give each downstream call whatever budget is left, never more.
const deadline = new Deadline(2_000);
await fetch(inventoryUrl, { signal: deadline.signal() });
await fetch(pricingUrl, { signal: deadline.signal() });

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has three "now"s, and picking the wrong one causes subtle bugs:

-- now() and transaction_timestamp(): frozen at the START of the transaction. Every row written in
-- a long transaction gets the same timestamp, which is what you usually want for consistency.
-- statement_timestamp(): start of the current statement.
-- clock_timestamp(): the actual current time, changes within a statement. Use for measuring.
SELECT now(), statement_timestamp(), clock_timestamp();

-- Always timestamptz, never timestamp: 'timestamp without time zone' silently depends on the
-- session's TimeZone and turns into a skew bug across pods in different regions.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key         text PRIMARY KEY,
  response    jsonb,
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);

-- Expiry decided by the database clock, the one clock all pods share.
DELETE FROM idempotency_keys WHERE expires_at < now();

-- Ordering events: never by created_at across writers. Use a sequence, which is monotonic
-- within the database regardless of who wrote it.
CREATE TABLE order_events (
  seq        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  type       text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
SELECT * FROM order_events WHERE order_id = $1 ORDER BY seq;

One caution with sequences: bigserial values are assigned at insert time, but a transaction that started earlier may commit later, so a row with seq = 100 can become visible after seq = 101. For a strictly gap-free, commit-ordered stream you need the outbox relay techniques in Part 29.

Production scenario

A fleet of 200 pods across two regions ran NTP against a public pool through a NAT that occasionally rate-limited them. Measured skew: p50 4 ms, p99 180 ms, max observed 41 s on a pod whose NTP daemon had died. Symptoms before they added skew monitoring: sporadic jwt not active errors (0.02% of requests, always from the same few pods), a lock that "expired early" in one region, and analytics with events from the future. They added a node exporter alert on abs(node_timex_offset_seconds) > 0.1 and a startup check that refuses to serve if the offset is above 1 s.

Failure scenario

At 00:00 on a New Year's Eve, a leap second was applied on the hosts as a one-second step backwards, while the cloud provider's NTP servers smeared it over 24 hours. For a few minutes, hosts disagreed by up to a second. A rate limiter computed windows as Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000); requests landed in the "same" second twice; limits were double-counted; 3% of API clients were throttled wrongly for two minutes. The same night a job scheduler fired its 00:00:00 job twice on one pod, because its clock went through midnight twice. Neither was a data-loss incident, both took hours to explain, and both were fixed by moving the window calculation into Redis and by making the job idempotent per scheduled slot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A VM is live-migrated or paused; its clock resumes seconds behind and then steps forward; every timer in the process fires at once.
  • A container image ships with no NTP, and the host clock is fine, so nobody notices until the node is replaced by one with a bad clock.
  • setTimeout(fn, 30_000) in Node uses a monotonic source and is unaffected by steps; new Date(expiresAt) < new Date() comparisons are affected.
  • JWT iat in the future (issuer ahead) is rejected by some libraries unless tolerance is set.
  • A database migration converts timestamp to timestamptz and shifts every historical value by the session offset.
  • Two datacenters observe a daylight-saving change differently because one host has the wrong tzdata; logs are an hour apart.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate three uses of time and use the right clock for each: durations and timeouts use the monotonic clock; labels for humans use wall clock; ordering and conflict resolution use logical order (sequences, offsets, versions, vector clocks) and never wall clock. They put expiry comparisons in the store that owns the data. They monitor clock offset like any other metric, and they design every time-based rule with a tolerance, because the question is never "is the clock right?" but "how wrong can it be before this breaks?"

Common mistakes

  • Using Date.now() differences for timeouts and metrics.
  • "Last updated wins" merges based on timestamps from different machines.
  • Comparing lease or token expiry using the application clock instead of the store's clock.
  • timestamp without time zone columns.
  • No skew alerting, so the first sign of a broken NTP daemon is an authentication outage.

Interview questions

  1. Why can't you use timestamps to order events from two services? Expected: clocks disagree by unknown amounts; a later event can carry an earlier timestamp. Follow-up: what do you use instead? (Sequences, partition offsets, Lamport or vector clocks, HLC.)
  2. Difference between Date.now() and process.hrtime, and when to use each? Expected: wall versus monotonic; durations use monotonic.
  3. A lock in Redis has a 30 s TTL. Can the client know how much time it has left? Expected: not reliably; only Redis knows; renew early and fence writes.
  4. How would you handle JWT verification failures caused by clock skew? Expected: clockTolerance of tens of seconds, NTP monitoring, short-lived tokens with refresh.
  5. What is a hybrid logical clock and why do distributed databases use it? Expected: wall-clock-like timestamps that respect causality without special hardware.

Practical exercise

On a test VM, use date -s to step the clock forward 2 minutes while a NestJS service is running with a Redis lock, a JWT-protected endpoint and a job scheduled with @Cron. Then step it back. Acceptance criteria: you can list every behavior that changed (tokens rejected, cron double-fired or skipped, lock renewal errors), you have fixed each with the techniques above, and after the fix the same clock steps produce no incorrect behavior.

28.14 Failure detection: deciding that something is dead

Concept

Failure detection is how one node decides that another node, process or connection is no longer working. In a distributed system it is always a guess, because "no reply" can mean dead, slow, partitioned, or paused. The tools are heartbeats (periodic "I am alive" messages), timeouts (no reply within T means suspect), and smarter detectors such as the phi accrual detector that turn heartbeat history into a suspicion level rather than a yes/no.

Why does it exist?

Every failover, rebalance and retry starts with a failure detector saying "that one is gone". If the detector is too eager, you get false positives: unnecessary failovers, Kafka consumer group rebalances that stop consumption for seconds, pods restarted while healthy. If it is too patient, you get long outages while a dead leader is still trusted. There is no setting that is right for every case, so the senior job is to understand what each detector is measuring and to pick timeouts on purpose.

Mental model

You phone a friend and get no answer. Are they dead, asleep, in a tunnel, or is your phone broken? You cannot know from one unanswered call. If they normally answer within two rings and have not answered in ten minutes, you start to worry. If they are often slow, ten minutes means nothing. Phi accrual is exactly this: "how unusual is the current silence, given how this friend usually behaves?"

How it works

  1. Heartbeats. The monitored side sends a small message every interval I (Kafka consumers every 3 s by default; Patroni every loop_wait; Kubernetes kubelet posts node status every 10 s).
  2. Timeout. The monitor declares failure after T without a heartbeat (Kafka session.timeout.ms, default 45 s in recent clients; Kubernetes marks a node NotReady after node-monitor-grace-period, 40 s). Rule of thumb: T >= 3 x I so a single lost heartbeat does not trigger.
  3. Phi accrual (Cassandra, Akka). Keep the recent history of inter-arrival times; model their distribution; compute phi = how many "sigmas" late the current heartbeat is. Declare failure when phi crosses a threshold (say 8). The detector adapts to a slow network automatically and reacts fast on a normally quick one.
  4. Action. Failover, rebalance, remove from load balancer, restart. The action's cost determines how confident you must be; removing a pod from a load balancer is cheap and can be eager, promoting a database replica is expensive and must be conservative and quorum-based (section 28.11).

False positives you will actually see:

  • GC pauses. A Node.js process with a 2 GB heap can pause for 200 ms to a few seconds in a major garbage collection; during that pause it sends no heartbeats and answers no probes. A 1 s timeout declares it dead once a day.
  • Event-loop blocking. A synchronous JSON.parse of a 50 MB body, a for loop over a million rows, or bcrypt on the main thread blocks the loop; heartbeats sent from the same loop stop.
  • Rebalance storms. Kafka consumer A pauses for 50 s processing a batch; the broker evicts it; the group rebalances; A returns and rejoins; another rebalance. Consumption stalls for a minute twice.
  • Slow disks and CPU throttling. A container with a CPU limit that is throttled at the wrong moment misses its liveness probe and gets restarted; on restart it is even slower (cold caches), misses again; CrashLoopBackOff on a healthy program.

Where you configure detectors in this stack:

Component Heartbeat Timeout / threshold Consequence of failure
Kubernetes liveness probe periodSeconds (10) failureThreshold (3) x period, plus timeoutSeconds Container restarted
Kubernetes readiness probe same same Pod removed from Service endpoints
Kafka consumer (KafkaJS) heartbeatInterval (3 s) sessionTimeout (30 s); rebalanceTimeout (60 s) Partition reassigned; in-flight work duplicated
PostgreSQL streaming replication WAL sender/receiver status wal_sender_timeout, wal_receiver_timeout (60 s) Replication connection dropped and re-established
PostgreSQL client connections TCP keepalives tcp_keepalives_idle/interval/count; client_connection_check_interval Dead client sessions closed, locks released
Patroni DCS lock renewal every loop_wait ttl (30 s) Primary demoted; replica promoted
Load balancer health check HTTP probe every 5–10 s 2–3 failures Target removed

Practical example

A NestJS worker consumes orders.events, and each message takes up to 20 s (it calls a slow supplier API). With sessionTimeout: 10_000, the consumer is kicked out whenever a message runs long, its partitions move to another worker, that worker processes the same message again (duplicate side effects), and the original worker rejoins and causes another rebalance. The fix is not "raise the timeout to 10 minutes" (that makes real crashes take 10 minutes to detect); it is: keep heartbeats flowing independently of processing (KafkaJS does this from eachMessage via its own heartbeat interval as long as you await inside the handler rather than blocking), bound the per-message work with a timeout, and make the handler idempotent so the occasional duplicate is harmless.

NestJS example

The most common false-positive cause in Node is a blocked event loop. Measure it, expose it, and make readiness reflect it:

// event-loop-health.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { monitorEventLoopDelay, IntervalHistogram } from 'node:perf_hooks';

@Injectable()
export class EventLoopHealth implements OnModuleInit {
  private histogram!: IntervalHistogram;

  onModuleInit() {
    this.histogram = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 }); // sample every 20 ms
    this.histogram.enable();
  }

  // p99 delay over the last window, in ms. A healthy API pod sits under 20 ms.
  p99Ms(): number {
    const p99 = this.histogram.percentile(99) / 1_000_000;
    this.histogram.reset();
    return p99;
  }
}

// health.controller.ts (readiness), extending section 18.3's controller
@Get('ready')
@HealthCheck()
ready() {
  return this.health.check([
    () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1_500 }),
    async () => {
      const p99 = this.loop.p99Ms();
      const healthy = p99 < 250;   // if the loop is stalling, stop taking new traffic
      return { eventLoop: { status: healthy ? 'up' : 'down', p99Ms: p99 } };
    },
  ]);
}

And the Kafka consumer settings that avoid rebalance storms while still detecting real crashes:

const consumer = kafka.consumer({
  groupId: 'shipping-service',
  sessionTimeout: 30_000,      // declare dead after 30 s without heartbeats
  heartbeatInterval: 3_000,    // 10 heartbeats per session timeout
  rebalanceTimeout: 60_000,    // time members get to rejoin after a rebalance starts
});

PostgreSQL example

Detecting dead clients matters because a dead client can hold a lock forever:

-- Server-side TCP keepalives: probe idle client connections so a vanished pod is noticed
-- in ~1 minute instead of the kernel default of ~2 hours.
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_idle = 30;
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_interval = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_count = 3;

-- PostgreSQL 14+: check the client socket during long-running queries so a query whose
-- client is gone is cancelled instead of running to completion for nobody.
ALTER SYSTEM SET client_connection_check_interval = '10s';

-- Replication-side detectors.
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_sender_timeout = '30s';
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_receiver_timeout = '30s';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- Belt and braces: a transaction idle too long is killed, releasing its locks.
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

Production scenario

An API fleet of 60 pods with 1.5 GB heaps saw one liveness-probe restart per pod per day, always during a major GC coinciding with a probe. Each restart caused a 20 s blip of errors on that pod. They changed the liveness probe from periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 1, timeoutSeconds: 1 to periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3, timeoutSeconds: 3, kept readiness eager, and added event-loop lag to readiness. Restarts fell to zero; genuine hangs were still caught within 30 s.

Failure scenario

At 14:20 a marketing team uploaded a 60 MB CSV through an admin endpoint that parsed it synchronously. The event loop blocked for 9 s. During those 9 s: the readiness probe failed (good), the liveness probe failed twice (its threshold was 2, so the pod was killed), the Kafka consumer in the same process missed its heartbeats and was evicted, and a rebalance stalled order processing for 40 s across the whole consumer group. One blocking parse turned into a fleet-wide hiccup. Fixes: streaming CSV parsing, liveness threshold raised, consumers moved to a separate deployment from the API.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Asymmetric detection: A thinks B is dead, B thinks A is fine; B keeps sending work A will never acknowledge.
  • Detector on the wrong side of a partition: the load balancer in zone A cannot reach zone B pods and removes all of them even though zone B users could reach them fine.
  • Cascading detection: a slow database makes every pod's readiness fail at once; the load balancer has zero healthy targets; some balancers then send traffic to all targets ("fail open"), others to none.
  • Timeouts shorter than the p99 of the thing they watch: a 1 s probe timeout on an endpoint whose p99 is 1.2 s restarts healthy pods.
  • Heartbeats that succeed while the work does not: a consumer heartbeats happily while its handler is stuck on a lock; it is "alive" and doing nothing. Watch consumer lag, not just membership.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, for each detector: what does a false positive cost, what does a false negative cost, and what is the normal variance of the signal? They set T from measured p99s plus margin, never from defaults. They keep readiness eager and liveness patient. They move heavy consumers out of API processes so one blocked loop does not trip several detectors. And they know the detector is a guess, so every action it triggers (failover, rebalance, retry) must be safe when the "dead" node turns out to be alive, which brings back fencing and idempotency.

Common mistakes

  • Liveness probes that check dependencies.
  • Kafka session timeouts far below per-message processing time, or far above any reasonable crash-detection time.
  • Health endpoints that do real work (queries, cache warms) and become the thing that is slow.
  • Ignoring event-loop lag and GC pauses as a source of "random" restarts.
  • Fail-open load balancers nobody knew were fail-open.

Interview questions

  1. Why is failure detection in a distributed system always a guess, and what follows from that? Expected: no reply is ambiguous; every action on detection must be safe if the node is actually alive; fencing and idempotency.
  2. How would you set Kafka consumer timeouts for a handler that takes up to 20 s? Expected: heartbeats independent of processing, session timeout around 30 s, bounded processing, idempotent handler.
  3. What should a liveness probe check? A readiness probe? Expected: liveness: process responsive only; readiness: dependencies and event-loop health, bounded timeouts.
  4. Explain the phi accrual failure detector in plain language. Expected: suspicion level based on how unusual the silence is compared to history; adaptive threshold.

Practical exercise

Add event-loop lag measurement to a NestJS service and expose it in readiness. Deliberately block the loop for 2 s and for 20 s from an endpoint. Acceptance criteria: readiness fails within one probe period during both; liveness does not fail during the 2 s block; the Kafka consumer in a separate deployment is unaffected; and a Grafana panel shows event-loop p99 for every pod.

28.15 Distributed caching, locking and rate limiting

Concept

Three things almost every backend team builds in their first year are, without anyone calling them that, distributed systems problems: a cache (a second copy of the truth), a lock (agreement about who may act), and a rate limiter (agreement about how much has happened). Part 26 — Caching and Redis covers how to operate Redis and which data structures to use; Part 30 — Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure covers rate limiting as a protection mechanism. This section looks at the same three through the lens of everything in Part 28: partial failure, asynchrony, clocks you cannot trust, and processes that pause without warning.

Why does it exist?

Because each of the three quietly assumes something the network does not provide. The cache assumes that "invalidate" happens. The lock assumes that "I hold it" is still true when the write lands. The rate limiter assumes that every node sees the same count. Each assumption is false during a partition, a GC pause, or a lost packet, and the failure is not a crash: it is a wrong answer that nobody notices for weeks.

Mental model

Imagine a shared whiteboard in a building with unreliable internal phones. The cache is a photocopy of the board that people keep on their desks: fast, and stale from the moment it is made. The lock is a "do not erase" sign on the board: useful until the person who put it there falls asleep for a minute and someone else, seeing the sign's timer expired, takes over, and then the first person wakes and starts writing as if nothing happened. The rate limiter is a tally of how many times the board has been used today, kept by whoever happens to be standing near it: exact if there is one tally and everyone walks to it, fast but approximate if everyone keeps their own.

How it works

A cache is a second source of truth, and the window is the design. When you write to PostgreSQL and then delete a Redis key, there is a moment between the commit and the delete when the two disagree. That window is normally 0.3–2 ms, and it is unbounded when the delete fails, when the Redis node is partitioned from that pod, or when a concurrent reader repopulates the key with the pre-commit value it read before your commit. The senior questions are always the same three:

  1. How stale can this be before it is wrong? A product description: minutes. An inventory count on a product page: seconds. A payment authorization: never; it is not a cacheable read.
  2. What happens when invalidation is lost? With a delete-only strategy, the key is stale until the TTL. So the TTL is not a performance knob, it is the bound on your incorrectness. A 24-hour TTL on a price is a promise that a price change can be wrong for a day.
  3. Who else writes this key? Two writers plus a cache is a lost-update problem with an extra participant. A read-modify-write through the cache is the same anomaly as in Part 20 — Database Transactions, just harder to see.

The practical consequence: cache-aside with a delete on write and a short TTL is not "eventually consistent" in a comforting sense; it is "consistent within the TTL, and correct only if the delete succeeds". If you need better, you need versioned keys (write product:42:v7 and bump the version pointer transactionally) or a change-data-capture stream driving invalidation, both of which are more machinery than most reads deserve.

A distributed lock is not safe without fencing. Here is the scenario in full, because every senior engineer should be able to draw it.

A worker wants exclusive access to update an order's fulfilment state. It takes a Redis lock: SET lock:order:9001 <uuid> NX PX 30000 (30 second TTL). It gets the lock. Then the Node process enters a major garbage collection, or the container is CPU-throttled by its cgroup quota, or the underlying VM is live-migrated. It stops executing for 40 seconds. It has no idea; from inside the process, no time passed.

At t = 30 s the Redis key expires. A second worker takes the lock legitimately and starts working. At t = 42 s the first worker resumes, exactly at the instruction after the lock acquisition, believing it holds the lock, and writes to the database. Two workers have now written under a lock designed to allow one.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W1 as Worker1
    participant R as Redis
    participant W2 as Worker2
    participant DB as Storage
    W1->>R: SET lock NX PX 30000, token 33
    R-->>W1: OK
    Note over W1: GC pause 40 s, no code runs
    R->>R: key expires at t=30
    W2->>R: SET lock NX PX 30000, token 34
    R-->>W2: OK
    W2->>DB: write with fence 34
    DB-->>W2: accepted, last_fence=34
    Note over W1: resumes at t=42, still believes it holds the lock
    W1->>DB: write with fence 33
    DB-->>W1: rejected, 33 is older than 34

No lock TTL fixes this, because the pause can always exceed the TTL, and shortening the TTL makes false expiry more likely, not less. Adding more Redis nodes does not fix it either: the problem is not availability of the lock service, it is that the holder cannot know it still holds the lock at the moment its write lands.

What fixes it is a fencing token: a number that increases every time the lock is granted, carried with every write, and checked by the storage that performs the write. Worker 1 holds token 33; worker 2 holds token 34; the database has already seen 34, so it rejects 33. The stale write becomes harmless instead of invisible.

The critical part is the last clause: the storage must do the check. A fencing token that only the application compares is worthless, because the paused application is the thing that cannot be trusted. In PostgreSQL this is a WHERE fence_token < $1 on the update, which is exactly optimistic concurrency control with a version column. Which leads to the honest senior conclusion: if your protected resource is a PostgreSQL row, you probably do not need a distributed lock at all. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, a unique constraint, or a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = $1 gives you mutual exclusion enforced by the same component that stores the data, with no clocks and no TTLs. Reach for a Redis lock when the protected resource is outside the database (a third-party API call you must not duplicate, a file in object storage, a singleton scheduler), and then accept that it is an optimization that reduces duplicate work, not a correctness guarantee, unless you can fence.

A distributed rate limiter chooses between exact-and-slow and approximate-and-fast.

Exact: one Redis instance holds the counter, every request from every pod does one atomic round trip (a Lua script or INCR plus EXPIRE). The limit is enforced precisely. Costs: 0.3–1 ms added to every request; a hard dependency on one node for every request (if Redis is unreachable you must decide fail-open or fail-closed, and for a security limit like login attempts the answer is fail-closed while for a capacity limit it is fail-open); and a hot key, because a per-tenant limit for your biggest tenant is a single key handling 20,000 operations per second on one Redis shard, which is fine, and a global limit key at 200,000 operations per second, which is not.

Approximate: each pod keeps a local token bucket sized to its share of the limit (limit ÷ pod count) and periodically syncs its consumption to Redis. Costs: no per-request round trip, so latency is unaffected and Redis being down degrades rather than breaks; but traffic is not evenly distributed across pods, so a tenant whose requests land on three of forty pods gets three-fortieths of their limit, and during a scale-up the divisor is wrong until the next sync. The overshoot is bounded by roughly pods × per-pod bucket size in the worst case, which you can compute and decide to accept.

The hybrid that most teams end up with: a local bucket for the common case plus a Redis check only when the local bucket is nearly exhausted, and a sync interval of 100 ms to 1 s. It costs a round trip for the few percent of requests near the limit, keeps the p99 clean for everyone else, and bounds the error at pods × sync_interval × rate.

Approach Accuracy Added p99 Redis down Hot key risk Use for
Single Redis, atomic script Exact +0.5–1 ms on every request Fail-open or fail-closed decision High on global or big-tenant keys Security limits, billing quotas, small scale
Per-pod local buckets Approximate, pods × overshoot 0 No effect None Coarse capacity protection, very high RPS
Local bucket plus Redis near the limit Near-exact at the boundary +0.5 ms on a few percent Degrades to local Low The default for a 40-pod API

Practical example

An orders API limits each API key to 1,000 requests per minute across 40 pods at 3,000 RPS total. A pure Redis limiter adds 0.6 ms to every request (2 percent of a 30 ms p50, acceptable) and makes Redis a hard dependency for 100 percent of traffic. The team chose the hybrid: each pod holds a bucket of 25 tokens (1,000 ÷ 40), refilled locally, and calls Redis only when its local bucket drops below 20 percent, which happens for about 4 percent of requests. Measured overshoot during a load test was 6 percent above the nominal limit, and the product owner agreed that 1,060 requests per minute is not a business problem while 40 ms of added p99 would have been.

NestJS example

Fencing, done properly: the token comes from Redis, and PostgreSQL enforces it.

// fulfilment/fulfilment.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class FulfilmentService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(FulfilmentService.name);
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, @InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  /** Acquire a lock and a monotonically increasing fence token in one round trip. */
  private async acquire(orderId: string, ttlMs = 30_000): Promise<number | null> {
    // INCR gives a strictly increasing token per lock name; SET NX gives exclusivity.
    const ok = await this.redis.set(`lock:order:${orderId}`, '1', 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');
    if (ok !== 'OK') return null;
    return this.redis.incr(`fence:order:${orderId}`);
  }

  async markShipped(orderId: string, carrierRef: string): Promise<'applied' | 'stale' | 'busy'> {
    const fence = await this.acquire(orderId);
    if (fence === null) return 'busy';

    // The database, not the application, rejects the stale writer. A paused process
    // cannot beat this check no matter how long it slept.
    const result = await this.db.query(
      `UPDATE orders
          SET status = 'shipped', carrier_ref = $2, fence_token = $3, updated_at = now()
        WHERE id = $1 AND fence_token < $3
        RETURNING id`,
      [orderId, carrierRef, fence],
    );

    if (result.length === 0) {
      this.logger.warn(`stale fenced write rejected order=${orderId} fence=${fence}`);
      return 'stale';                      // we were paused; someone newer already acted
    }
    return 'applied';
  }
}

Two details that matter. The UPDATE is the whole critical section, so there is no window between check and write. And we never release the lock by deleting the key blindly; if you do release early, compare the value you wrote (SET lock <uuid> NX PX) inside a Lua script so you cannot delete a lock someone else now holds.

PostgreSQL example

If the resource is a row, skip Redis entirely. This is mutual exclusion with no clock, no TTL and no second system:

-- Option 1: pessimistic, holds a row lock for the transaction
BEGIN;
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'packed';
COMMIT;

-- Option 2: optimistic, no lock held across any I/O
UPDATE orders
   SET status = 'shipped', version = version + 1
 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2;      -- 0 rows means someone else won; re-read and retry

-- Option 3: advisory lock for a non-row resource, scoped to the session or transaction
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('nightly-settlement'));   -- released at COMMIT

Advisory locks are held by a database session, so they are released automatically when the connection dies, which removes the TTL problem entirely. Their limitation is that they are per-database-cluster and do not survive a failover, so treat them as "prevent duplicate work", not "guarantee uniqueness".

Production scenario

A payouts worker ran with a Redis lock and no fencing for eighteen months. It processed 200 payouts a day and the lock "worked".
