Payment Service    consumes OrderCreated       publishes PaymentCaptured / PaymentDeclined
Inventory Service  consumes PaymentCaptured    publishes StockReserved / StockUnavailable
Shipping Service   consumes StockReserved      publishes ShipmentBooked / ShipmentFailed
Order Service      consumes all of the above and updates its own status

Nobody tells anybody what to do. Everybody announces what happened.

Why does it exist?

Because it is the loosest possible coupling. The Order Service does not import a payment client, does not know a payment service exists, and does not change when you add a fifth service. Adding a Loyalty Service that grants points on PaymentCaptured requires zero changes to any existing service — you deploy a new consumer on the existing topic and it works.

For small flows in fast-moving teams, that property is genuinely valuable and should not be dismissed.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen with no head chef. A ticket arrives and is pinned to the rail. The grill cook sees "steak" and starts it. When the steak is done, they call "steak up!" The garnish cook hears that and plates it. When they are done they call "table 6 ready!" and a runner takes it out.

It works. It is fast. Nobody waits for permission. And when something goes wrong — the steak is dropped — nobody is in charge of deciding what happens to table 6. Each person shouts a correction and hopes the others hear it in the right order.

How it works

The happy path, in events:

sequenceDiagram
  participant O as OrderSvc
  participant K as Kafka
  participant P as PaymentSvc
  participant I as InventorySvc
  participant S as ShippingSvc
  O->>K: OrderCreated key=order-7781
  K-->>P: OrderCreated
  P->>K: PaymentCaptured key=order-7781
  K-->>I: PaymentCaptured
  K-->>O: PaymentCaptured
  I->>K: StockReserved key=order-7781
  K-->>S: StockReserved
  K-->>O: StockReserved
  S->>K: ShipmentBooked key=order-7781
  K-->>O: ShipmentBooked
  Note over O: status = COMPLETED

Note the key=order-7781 on every event. In Kafka, the message key determines the partition, and ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Keying every event of an order by the order id is what gives you causal ordering for that order (Part 27 section 27.5 and Part 28 section 28.6). Without it, StockReserved can be consumed before PaymentCaptured and your handlers will see nonsense.

Now the failure paths, which is where choreography earns or loses its keep.

Payment declined — the easy case, because nothing needs undoing yet:

sequenceDiagram
  participant O as OrderSvc
  participant K as Kafka
  participant P as PaymentSvc
  participant N as NotificationSvc
  O->>K: OrderCreated key=order-7782
  K-->>P: OrderCreated
  P->>K: PaymentDeclined reason=insufficient_funds
  K-->>O: PaymentDeclined
  K-->>N: PaymentDeclined
  Note over O: status = PAYMENT_FAILED
  N->>N: send "payment failed, please retry" email

Inventory never heard about this order, so there is nothing to release. Shipping never heard about it either. The failure is cheap because it happened before anything irreversible.

Stock unavailable — the hard case, because the customer's money has already moved:

sequenceDiagram
  participant K as Kafka
  participant P as PaymentSvc
  participant I as InventorySvc
  participant O as OrderSvc
  K-->>I: PaymentCaptured key=order-7783
  I->>K: StockUnavailable sku=BX-19 requested=2 available=0
  K-->>P: StockUnavailable
  K-->>O: StockUnavailable
  P->>P: refund charge ch_71c idempotency=order-7783-refund
  P->>K: PaymentRefunded key=order-7783
  K-->>O: PaymentRefunded
  Note over O: status = FAILED reason=OUT_OF_STOCK

The compensation is itself just an event reaction: the Payment Service subscribes to StockUnavailable and refunds. That is elegant, and it is also where the trouble starts, because now the Payment Service knows about inventory concepts, and the "flow" is spread across four codebases with no single file describing it.

NestJS example

A choreographed consumer, using @nestjs/microservices with the Kafka transport. Note the inbox check (section 29.11) and the transaction boundary.

// inventory.consumer.ts
@Controller()
export class InventoryConsumer {
  private readonly log = new Logger(InventoryConsumer.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly outbox: OutboxService,
  ) {}

  @EventPattern('payments.events')
  async onPaymentEvent(@Payload() msg: PaymentEvent, @Ctx() ctx: KafkaContext): Promise<void> {
    if (msg.type !== 'PaymentCaptured') return;               // topic carries several types

    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      // Deduplicate: same messageId twice is a no-op (see 19.11).
      const dedup = await manager
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .insert().into(InboxMessage)
        .values({ messageId: msg.messageId, consumer: 'inventory' })
        .orIgnore()                                            // -> ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
        .execute();
      if (dedup.identifiers.length === 0) {
        this.log.debug({ messageId: msg.messageId }, 'duplicate, skipping');
        return;
      }

      const ok = await this.tryReserve(manager, msg.orderId, msg.items);

      // The reply event is written in the SAME transaction as the reservation.
      await this.outbox.publish(manager, {
        aggregateType: 'order',
        aggregateId: msg.orderId,
        eventType: ok ? 'StockReserved' : 'StockUnavailable',
        payload: { orderId: msg.orderId, items: msg.items },
      });
    });
  }

  private async tryReserve(manager: EntityManager, orderId: string, items: OrderItem[]) {
    for (const item of items) {
      // Conditional UPDATE: atomic, no read-modify-write race (Part 20, section 13.10).
      const res = await manager.query(
        `UPDATE inventory SET available = available - $2
         WHERE sku = $1 AND available >= $2`,
        [item.sku, item.qty],
      );
      if (res[1] === 0) return false;                          // rowCount 0 means not enough stock
    }
    return true;
  }
}

Two details that separate a working consumer from a demo: the reservation and the outgoing event commit together (so you can never reserve stock without announcing it), and the orIgnore() dedup means a redelivered Kafka message does not double-decrement stock. Both are covered in depth later; they belong in every choreographed handler from day one.

Production scenario

A food-delivery company with three services (Order, Payment, Restaurant) ran a fully choreographed flow at 90 orders per minute for two years and it was the right call. Three events, three consumers, one topic, roughly 400 lines of code total. Adding "notify the driver app" was a new consumer and nothing else changed. Nobody ever wished for an orchestrator.

The same company at 1,400 orders per minute with eleven services was a different story. A single order could touch Order, Payment, Restaurant, Inventory, Driver, Pricing, Loyalty, Fraud, Notification, Analytics and Support. When an order got stuck, answering "which step is it on?" meant a Kibana query joining eleven services by correlation id, and even then the answer was "we saw PaymentCaptured but never saw anything from Restaurant, and we do not know if Restaurant crashed, filtered it out, or is just slow." That is the moment choreography stops paying.

Failure scenario

A retailer's choreographed flow had the Notification Service subscribe to OrderCreated and send "Thanks for your order!" A separate team added a fraud check that consumed OrderCreated and, for suspicious orders, emitted OrderRejected.

Nobody noticed that the notification consumer was faster than the fraud consumer. For six weeks, every fraudulently-flagged order received a cheerful confirmation email 200 ms before being rejected, followed by a rejection email. Customer support handled 340 confused tickets. The bug was not in any one service; it was in the flow, which existed in no file, in no diagram, and in nobody's head completely.

The fix was to make notification consume OrderConfirmed (emitted after the fraud check) instead of OrderCreated. Finding it took three days, because there was no place to look.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No single place shows the flow. The business process exists only as an emergent property of eleven subscriptions. Onboarding a new engineer means reading eleven repositories.
  • Cyclic dependencies. Payment subscribes to inventory events (to refund), inventory subscribes to payment events (to reserve). Now the two services are logically coupled in a cycle even though they never call each other. Change one event schema and both break.
  • Hard to test end to end. A unit test covers one consumer. Testing the flow requires all services plus Kafka, which is a docker-compose with eleven containers that nobody runs locally.
  • Hard to change. Inserting a step in the middle (a fraud check between payment and inventory) means editing the subscription of a service that has nothing to do with fraud.
  • Out-of-order events if the key is missing or the topic is repartitioned: StockReserved arrives before PaymentCaptured.
  • A missing consumer is silent. If the Shipping Service's consumer group is down, StockReserved piles up in the topic and orders quietly stop shipping. There is no timeout, because nothing is waiting.
  • Duplicate reactions. Two services both react to PaymentCaptured by writing to the same aggregate, and now you have a race that neither team knew existed.
  • No timeout anywhere. This is the killer. In choreography, "nothing happened next" is indistinguishable from "it is still working". A saga can hang forever with no alert (section 29.18).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They like choreography for genuinely small, stable flows and reject it for anything a support agent has to reason about. Their test is a question: "When a customer calls and says order 7781 hasn't shipped, how long does it take one person to find out why?" If the answer involves grepping more than two services, choreography has stopped paying.

They also watch for the honest tell: the first time someone builds a dashboard that reconstructs the flow from events across services, the team has already re-invented an orchestrator, badly and after the fact.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing events without a partition key, then being surprised by out-of-order processing.
  • Subscribing to a low-level event (OrderCreated) when you meant a business milestone (OrderConfirmed).
  • Letting compensation logic sprawl: five services each holding a piece of "what happens when it fails".
  • No correlation id in the event envelope, making the flow untraceable.
  • Growing to eight services on choreography because switching later feels expensive. It only gets more expensive.

29.5 Orchestration

Concept

In orchestration, one component owns the flow. The orchestrator holds the saga's state in a database row, sends commands to services ("charge this", "reserve that"), waits for reply events, decides the next step, and drives compensation when something fails.

The services stay dumb and reusable: the Payment Service knows how to charge and refund, and knows nothing about orders, inventory or shipping. All the flow knowledge lives in one file you can read top to bottom.

Why does it exist?

Because sooner or later a human must answer "where is order 7781 stuck?", and the only good answer is a SELECT against one table. Orchestration exists to make that SELECT possible.

It also gives you the two things choreography structurally cannot: timeouts (something is waiting, so something can notice it waited too long) and a single place to change the flow.

Mental model

The kitchen again, now with a head chef. The chef reads the ticket, calls "steak, medium rare, three minutes", waits, hears "steak up", calls "plate table 6". If the steak is dropped, the chef decides: refire the steak, or comp the table and tell the runner to cancel. One person knows the state of every ticket, and if you ask "where is table 6?" they answer instantly.

The cost is obvious: the chef is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Which is exactly the tradeoff in software, and it is why the orchestrator's state must be in PostgreSQL rather than in the chef's head.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant API as CheckoutAPI
  participant OR as Orchestrator
  participant DB as PostgreSQL
  participant P as PaymentSvc
  participant I as InventorySvc
  participant S as ShippingSvc
  API->>DB: INSERT order plus INSERT order_sagas state=STARTED
  OR->>DB: claim saga 7781
  OR->>P: cmd AuthorizePayment
  P-->>OR: evt PaymentAuthorized
  OR->>DB: state=PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED step=RESERVE_STOCK
  OR->>I: cmd ReserveStock
  I-->>OR: evt StockReserved
  OR->>DB: state=STOCK_RESERVED step=CAPTURE_PAYMENT
  OR->>P: cmd CapturePayment
  P-->>OR: evt PaymentCaptured
  OR->>S: cmd RequestShipping
  S-->>OR: evt ShipmentBooked
  OR->>DB: state=COMPLETED

The state row is written before each command is sent and after each reply is received. That ordering matters: if the orchestrator crashes after sending CapturePayment but before recording the reply, the row still says step=CAPTURE_PAYMENT, and on recovery it re-sends the command — which is safe only because the command carries an idempotency key.

PostgreSQL example

The saga table. This DDL is the heart of the whole pattern; every column earns its place.

CREATE TYPE saga_state AS ENUM (
  'STARTED', 'PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED', 'STOCK_RESERVED', 'PAYMENT_CAPTURED',
  'SHIPPING_REQUESTED', 'COMPLETED',
  'COMPENSATING', 'COMPENSATED', 'FAILED', 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW'
);

CREATE TABLE order_sagas (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id      uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- one saga per order, enforced by the database
  state         saga_state NOT NULL DEFAULT 'STARTED',
  step          text NOT NULL,                 -- the step currently in flight
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',   -- refs collected so far: authId, reservationId, chargeId
  attempts      int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_retry_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  step_deadline timestamptz,                   -- when this step is considered timed out
  last_error    text,
  version       int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,       -- optimistic lock against two orchestrators
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- The claim query's index: find runnable sagas cheaply.
CREATE INDEX idx_sagas_runnable ON order_sagas (next_retry_at)
  WHERE state NOT IN ('COMPLETED', 'COMPENSATED', 'FAILED', 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW');

-- The operations index: find stuck sagas.
CREATE INDEX idx_sagas_deadline ON order_sagas (step_deadline)
  WHERE step_deadline IS NOT NULL;

-- Dashboard query, one row per state, cheap because of the partial index above.
CREATE INDEX idx_sagas_state_updated ON order_sagas (state, updated_at DESC);

payload jsonb is where the references accumulate — {"authId":"auth_9f2","reservationId":"res_44a","chargeId":"ch_71c"}. Compensation needs those references, so they must be durable the moment they are known. version is TypeORM's @VersionColumn, and it is what stops two orchestrator pods from advancing the same saga twice (section 29.18).

The query that answers "where is order 7781 stuck?" and the one that finds everything stuck:

SELECT order_id, state, step, attempts, last_error, now() - updated_at AS stuck_for
FROM order_sagas WHERE order_id = '...';

-- Every saga that has not moved in 10 minutes and is not in a terminal state.
SELECT state, step, count(*), min(updated_at) AS oldest
FROM order_sagas
WHERE state NOT IN ('COMPLETED', 'COMPENSATED', 'FAILED')
  AND updated_at < now() - interval '10 minutes'
GROUP BY state, step ORDER BY count DESC;

That second query is the reconciliation job (section 29.15) and the dashboard, in one statement. Choreography has no equivalent.

NestJS example

The state transition table first, because the code is boring once the table is right:

// saga-definition.ts
export type StepName =
  | 'CREATE_ORDER' | 'AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT' | 'RESERVE_STOCK'
  | 'CAPTURE_PAYMENT' | 'REQUEST_SHIPPING'
  | 'RELEASE_STOCK' | 'REFUND_PAYMENT' | 'CANCEL_ORDER';

export interface StepDef {
  readonly kind: 'compensatable' | 'pivot' | 'retryable' | 'compensation';
  readonly onSuccess: StepName | 'DONE';
  readonly onFailure: StepName | 'FAILED' | 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW';
  readonly timeoutMs: number;
  readonly maxAttempts: number;
}

export const ORDER_SAGA: Record<StepName, StepDef> = {
  CREATE_ORDER:      { kind: 'compensatable', onSuccess: 'AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT', onFailure: 'FAILED',              timeoutMs: 5_000,  maxAttempts: 3 },
  AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT: { kind: 'compensatable', onSuccess: 'RESERVE_STOCK',     onFailure: 'CANCEL_ORDER',        timeoutMs: 10_000, maxAttempts: 3 },
  RESERVE_STOCK:     { kind: 'compensatable', onSuccess: 'CAPTURE_PAYMENT',   onFailure: 'REFUND_PAYMENT',      timeoutMs: 5_000,  maxAttempts: 5 },
  CAPTURE_PAYMENT:   { kind: 'pivot',         onSuccess: 'REQUEST_SHIPPING',  onFailure: 'RELEASE_STOCK',       timeoutMs: 15_000, maxAttempts: 5 },
  REQUEST_SHIPPING:  { kind: 'retryable',     onSuccess: 'DONE',              onFailure: 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW', timeoutMs: 20_000, maxAttempts: 12 },
  RELEASE_STOCK:     { kind: 'compensation',  onSuccess: 'REFUND_PAYMENT',    onFailure: 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW', timeoutMs: 5_000,  maxAttempts: 10 },
  REFUND_PAYMENT:    { kind: 'compensation',  onSuccess: 'CANCEL_ORDER',      onFailure: 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW', timeoutMs: 15_000, maxAttempts: 10 },
  CANCEL_ORDER:      { kind: 'compensation',  onSuccess: 'DONE',              onFailure: 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW', timeoutMs: 5_000,  maxAttempts: 10 },
};

Read the onFailure column downwards and you can see the whole compensation chain without reading a line of logic. REQUEST_SHIPPING failing does not refund — it escalates, because it is after the pivot. Compensations have high maxAttempts because giving up on a refund is much worse than giving up on a shipment booking.

Now the orchestrator. It has two entry points: a reply event arrives, or the retry tick fires.

// order-saga.orchestrator.ts
@Injectable()
export class OrderSagaOrchestrator {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderSagaOrchestrator.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    @InjectRepository(OrderSaga) private readonly sagas: Repository<OrderSaga>,
    private readonly commands: CommandBus,           // thin wrapper over the Kafka producer
  ) {}

  /** Advance one saga: record the outcome of the current step, then dispatch the next. */
  async handleReply(orderId: string, step: StepName, outcome: StepOutcome): Promise<void> {
    const next = await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const saga = await manager.findOne(OrderSaga, {
        where: { orderId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' },   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
      });
      if (!saga) throw new NotFoundException(`saga for order ${orderId}`);

      // A reply for a step we already moved past is a duplicate. Ignore it.
      if (saga.step !== step) {
        this.log.warn({ orderId, expected: saga.step, got: step }, 'stale reply ignored');
        return null;
      }

      const def = ORDER_SAGA[step];
      const target = outcome.ok ? def.onSuccess : def.onFailure;

      saga.payload = { ...saga.payload, ...outcome.refs };   // keep chargeId, reservationId, ...
      saga.last_error = outcome.ok ? null : outcome.error ?? 'unknown';
      saga.attempts = 0;
      saga.state = STATE_FOR_STEP[step][outcome.ok ? 'ok' : 'fail'];

      if (target === 'DONE' || target === 'FAILED' || target === 'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW') {
        saga.step = target;
        saga.step_deadline = null;
        await manager.save(saga);
        return null;                                        // terminal, nothing to dispatch
      }

      saga.step = target;
      saga.step_deadline = new Date(Date.now() + ORDER_SAGA[target].timeoutMs);
      saga.next_retry_at = new Date(Date.now() + ORDER_SAGA[target].timeoutMs);
      await manager.save(saga);                             // version column guards concurrency
      return { saga, step: target };
    });

    // Command is sent AFTER the transaction commits. Worst case it is sent twice; the
    // idempotency key on the command makes that harmless.
    if (next) await this.dispatch(next.saga, next.step);
  }

  private async dispatch(saga: OrderSaga, step: StepName): Promise<void> {
    await this.commands.send({
      step,
      orderId: saga.orderId,
      // Deterministic: the same step for the same order always produces the same key.
      idempotencyKey: `${saga.orderId}:${step}`,
      payload: saga.payload,
      replyTo: 'saga.replies',
    });
  }
}

And the tick that handles timeouts and retries — the piece that makes the saga self-healing:

// saga-runner.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class SagaRunner {
  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_10_SECONDS)
  async tick(): Promise<void> {
    // Claim a batch without two pods claiming the same row (Part 27, section 17.9 pattern).
    const due: OrderSaga[] = await this.dataSource.query(
      `SELECT * FROM order_sagas
        WHERE next_retry_at <= now()
          AND state NOT IN ('COMPLETED','COMPENSATED','FAILED','NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW')
        ORDER BY next_retry_at
        LIMIT 50
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
    );

    for (const saga of due) {
      const def = ORDER_SAGA[saga.step as StepName];
      if (saga.attempts >= def.maxAttempts) {
        // Out of retries. A failed step before the pivot compensates; after it, escalate.
        await this.orchestrator.handleReply(saga.order_id, saga.step as StepName, {
          ok: false, error: `max attempts (${def.maxAttempts}) exceeded`, refs: {},
        });
        continue;
      }
      const backoffMs = Math.min(2 ** saga.attempts * 1000, 60_000) + Math.random() * 1000;
      await this.sagas.update(
        { id: saga.id },
        { attempts: saga.attempts + 1, next_retry_at: new Date(Date.now() + backoffMs) },
      );
      await this.orchestrator.dispatchPublic(saga, saga.step as StepName);  // re-send the command
    }
  }
}

Exponential backoff with jitter, capped at 60 s (Part 30 section 30.2). FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED means twenty pods can run this tick concurrently and never collide.

@nestjs/cqrs sagas versus a plain service

NestJS ships a Saga concept in @nestjs/cqrs: you write an RxJS operator that maps a stream of events to a stream of commands.

// order.saga.ts — the @nestjs/cqrs style
@Injectable()
export class OrderSagas {
  @Saga()
  paymentCaptured = (events$: Observable<any>): Observable<ICommand> =>
    events$.pipe(
      ofType(PaymentCapturedEvent),
      map((e) => new ReserveStockCommand(e.orderId, e.items)),
    );
}

It is clean and it is genuinely useful for in-process flows. Be clear-eyed about what it does not do:

Concern @nestjs/cqrs @Saga() Plain service plus PostgreSQL plus Kafka
State persistence None. The stream is in memory A committed row per saga
Survives a pod restart No Yes
Step timeouts You build them with RxJS operators, still in memory step_deadline column plus a cron tick
Retry with backoff RxJS retryWhen, in memory, lost on restart attempts and next_retry_at columns
"Where is order 7781?" Not answerable One SELECT
Cross-process No Yes, via Kafka
Best for Coordinating handlers inside one service Real distributed sagas

Use @nestjs/cqrs sagas to wire up in-process domain events (Part 13 — Domain-Driven Design covers domain events). Use a persisted state machine for anything that crosses a process boundary. Teams that use @Saga() for a distributed flow discover the gap on their first deploy, when every in-flight order stalls silently.

Production scenario

A marketplace runs the orchestrator as three pods behind the same consumer group. Saga volume: 220 per minute at peak, ~12,000 rows in order_sagas in a non-terminal state at any moment, ~9 million rows total (terminal rows archived monthly to a partition). The tick runs every 10 s per pod, claiming up to 50 rows, so worst-case throughput is 900 retries per minute, far above the real retry rate of about 4 per minute.

The dashboard is three panels: count by state, count by step where step_deadline < now(), and the NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW count with a threshold alert at 5. Median time from STARTED to COMPLETED is 2.1 s; p99 is 41 s, dominated by shipping-partner retries. When the shipping partner had a 20-minute outage, REQUEST_SHIPPING backed up to 3,100 sagas, all of which drained automatically in 6 minutes once the partner recovered. No human action, no lost orders, no refunds. That is the payoff for building the state machine.

Failure scenario

An orchestrator was written without the version column and without FOR UPDATE. During a rolling deploy, two pods briefly processed the same reply event for order 4402. Both read step=CAPTURE_PAYMENT, both advanced to REQUEST_SHIPPING, both dispatched the command. The shipping service had no idempotency on the command, so it booked two pickups. The courier collected the parcel twice; the second driver found nothing and charged a failed-pickup fee.

It happened to 31 orders during that deploy. The fix was two lines: lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } on the read and a deterministic idempotencyKey on the command. The lesson the team wrote in the post-mortem: an orchestrator is a distributed system too, and it needs the same defences it provides to others.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two orchestrator instances advancing one saga. Solved by row lock plus optimistic version, and made harmless by idempotent commands.
  • Reply arrives for a step the saga already left. Ignore it (the saga.step !== step check). This happens on every retry that was actually a duplicate.
  • Reply never arrives. step_deadline plus the tick turns silence into a retry, then into a failure, then into compensation or escalation.
  • Command sent, orchestrator crashes before committing the state row. On recovery it re-sends. Safe only because of the idempotency key. This is why the command goes out after commit and why the key is deterministic.
  • Orchestrator becomes a bottleneck. It is stateless apart from PostgreSQL, so scale it horizontally; the contention point becomes the saga table, which SKIP LOCKED handles well up to thousands per second.
  • The saga definition changes while sagas are in flight. A removed step name leaves rows pointing at a step that no longer exists (section 29.18).
  • payload grows unboundedly if you store whole order snapshots in it. Store references, not documents.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the orchestrator as a product feature, not plumbing. It gets a dashboard, an alert, an admin API and a runbook, because the whole point of building it was operability.

They keep the orchestrator thin: it decides the next step and nothing else. Business rules ("is this customer allowed to order?") live in the services. An orchestrator that grows business logic becomes the distributed monolith everyone warns about, and that is a real risk worth naming.

They also make the orchestrator's own database the same one as the order database when possible, so that creating the order and creating the saga row are one local transaction. Otherwise you have added a distributed transaction to solve distributed transactions.

Common mistakes

  • In-memory state, then a deploy.
  • Sending the command inside the transaction, so a rollback leaves a command already published.
  • Non-deterministic idempotency keys (a uuid() per attempt), which makes every retry a new charge.
  • No step_deadline, so a lost reply hangs the saga forever with no alert.
  • Orchestrator that calls services synchronously over HTTP and blocks a request thread for the whole saga. The API returns as soon as the order row exists; the saga runs in the background.
  • Putting business rules in the orchestrator until it knows more about orders than the Order Service.

Interview questions

  1. Design an orchestrated saga for order, payment, inventory, shipping. What is in the state table? Expected: order id (unique), state, current step, payload of references, attempts, next retry, step deadline, version, timestamps; plus the partial index for runnable sagas.
  2. How do you stop two orchestrator instances from double-advancing a saga? Expected: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or optimistic @VersionColumn, plus FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for the claim query, plus idempotent commands so a duplicate dispatch is harmless.
  3. Where do you send the command relative to the transaction commit, and why? Expected: after commit (or via the outbox, section 29.10); sending inside risks publishing a command for a rolled-back state, and the outbox removes even that race.
  4. What does @nestjs/cqrs @Saga() give you and what does it not? Expected: in-process event-to-command mapping with RxJS, no persistence, no timeouts, no cross-process delivery, no resumability.
  5. A saga has been in RESERVE_STOCK for two hours. Walk me through the diagnosis. Expected: check step_deadline and attempts, check last_error, check whether the tick is running and whether the inventory consumer group has lag, check for a poison payload, then resume or compensate via the admin API.

29.6 Choreography versus orchestration

Concept

They are not opposites and you do not have to pick one for the whole system. Most mature systems are orchestrated for the core money flow and choreographed for everything hanging off it.

How it works

Dimension Choreography Orchestration
Where the flow lives Spread across every service's subscriptions One state machine definition, in one file
Coupling Loosest. Services know events, not each other Services know commands; the orchestrator knows everyone
Adding a step New consumer, possibly editing an unrelated service's subscription Edit the step table in one place
Answering "where is order 7781?" Trace across N services by correlation id One SELECT
Timeouts Structurally hard: nothing is waiting Natural: step_deadline per step
Compensation logic Spread across services Centralised in the step table's onFailure
Testing Needs all services plus a broker Orchestrator unit-testable with stubbed commands
Single point of failure None The orchestrator (mitigated: stateless pods plus PostgreSQL)
Risk of distributed monolith Low Real, if business logic creeps into the orchestrator
Debugging a production issue Kibana archaeology Read the row
Good fit 2 to 3 steps, stable flow, loose coupling valued 4 or more steps, compensation matters, humans must inspect it
Typical failure Silent stall nobody notices Orchestrator becomes a god service

The rule of thumb

Use choreography when the flow has two or three steps, changes rarely, and nobody outside engineering ever needs to know where it is. Order created then loyalty points granted then email sent is a perfect choreography. It is three subscriptions and no state machine.

Switch to orchestration the moment a human needs to answer "where is order 7781 stuck?" That question is the tripwire. It arrives from support, or from finance reconciling payments, or from your own on-call at 02:00. If you cannot answer it with one query, you need a saga table.

Two secondary tripwires worth watching for:

  • Money is involved and compensation is required. Refunds spread across four services are a liability. Centralise them.
  • You are drawing the flow on a whiteboard for the third time because nobody can hold it in their head. The whiteboard drawing wants to be a file. That file is the step definition table.

Practical example

A realistic split for our flow at a mid-size retailer:

ORCHESTRATED (the saga table owns this)
  Order -> Payment -> Inventory -> Shipping
  because money moves, compensation is required, support asks about it daily

CHOREOGRAPHED (fire and forget, off the OrderCompleted event)
  OrderCompleted -> loyalty points
  OrderCompleted -> confirmation email
  OrderCompleted -> analytics ingest
  OrderCompleted -> recommendation model update
  because none of these can fail in a way that must undo the order

The rule that separates the two lists: if its failure must change the outcome of the business transaction, it belongs in the saga; if its failure is merely unfortunate, it belongs on an event. Loyalty points failing does not un-place the order. Stock reservation failing does.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make the choice per flow, write it down, and revisit it. They also know the migration path, because "we will refactor later" needs to be true: choreography becomes orchestration by adding a saga table and a service that consumes the same events and issues commands, then flipping services one at a time from event-driven to command-driven. It is incremental, and knowing that removes the fear of starting simple.

The anti-hype line: an orchestrator is not more "enterprise" and choreography is not more "modern". They are two ways to encode a state machine, one implicit and one explicit. Explicit costs a table and buys you operability. For three steps, the table is not worth it. For seven, it is the cheapest thing you will build all quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing choreography for a nine-step money flow because it "decouples", then building a bespoke tracing dashboard that is a worse orchestrator.
  • Choosing orchestration for a two-step flow and writing 600 lines of state machine to send one email.
  • Mixing the two within a single flow without deciding which one owns the outcome, so a failure is handled twice or not at all.
  • Never writing down which flows are which, so the next engineer guesses.

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose choreography over orchestration? Expected: few steps, stable, loose coupling valuable, no compensation, no human inspection needed. Follow-up: what is your tripwire for switching?
  2. What is the biggest operational weakness of choreography? Expected: no timeouts and no single view; a stalled flow is silent because nothing is waiting for anything.
  3. What is the biggest architectural risk of orchestration? Expected: the orchestrator absorbing business logic and becoming a distributed monolith; mitigate by keeping it to routing plus state.
  4. How would you migrate a choreographed flow to an orchestrated one without downtime? Expected: add the saga table and an orchestrator that consumes existing events and records state (shadow mode), verify it matches reality, then move services to command-driven one at a time.

Practical exercise

Implement Order -> Payment -> Inventory -> Shipping twice against the same three stub services: once choreographed on Kafka, once orchestrated with an order_sagas table.

Acceptance criteria: both handle the happy path; both handle a declined payment and unavailable stock; for both, kill the process mid-flow and restart it — the orchestrated version resumes and completes, the choreographed version demonstrates the stall; and write one query per implementation that answers "which orders are stuck and on which step?", then compare how hard each was to write.

29.7 Compensation in practice

Concept

A compensating transaction is a normal, forward-moving local transaction whose business meaning is "undo the effect of an earlier step". It is not a rollback. It runs later, it is visible in history, it can fail, it can be retried, and it sometimes costs money.

For our flow the four compensations are:

C4 Cancel shipment    -> call the courier's cancel API, mark the shipment CANCELLED
C3 Release stock      -> add the reserved quantity back to available, delete the reservation
C2 Refund payment     -> call the gateway's refund API against the charge id
C1 Cancel order       -> UPDATE orders SET status = 'CANCELLED'

They run in reverse order of the forward steps, and every one of them must be safe to run twice.

Why does it exist?

Because the forward steps already committed. Nothing in the database can take them back, and nothing in Stripe or Delhivery can either. If you want the customer to end up whole, you have to write the code that makes them whole, and you have to run it reliably even though the process that started it may be dead.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel where a guest checks out early. The receptionist does not have a time machine. They: cancel the remaining nights in the booking system, issue a refund to the card, notify housekeeping to release the room, and email a revised invoice. Four forward actions, each recorded, each of which can fail on its own.

If the card refund fails because the card expired, the receptionist does not delete the checkout. They put a note in a file: refund pending, contact guest. That file is your manual-intervention queue, and every real system needs one.

How it works

Rule 1: compensations must be idempotent. They will run more than once. The saga runner retries on timeout; a duplicate reply event triggers a second attempt; an operator hits "resume" from the admin API. If releaseStock blindly does available = available + qty, running it three times inflates your stock by 2x the order. That is a real inventory corruption incident and it is very hard to notice.

The correct shape uses a state guard so the second run does nothing:

-- WRONG: additive, not idempotent. Two runs add the quantity twice.
UPDATE inventory SET available = available + 2 WHERE sku = 'BX-19';

-- RIGHT: guarded by the reservation's own state. Only the transition RESERVED -> RELEASED
-- has an effect, and it can only happen once.
WITH released AS (
  UPDATE stock_reservations
     SET status = 'RELEASED', released_at = now()
   WHERE order_id = $1 AND sku = $2 AND status = 'RESERVED'
  RETURNING qty
)
UPDATE inventory i
   SET available = i.available + r.qty
  FROM released r
 WHERE i.sku = $2;

Run that ten times and stock moves exactly once. The WHERE status = 'RESERVED' clause is doing all the work: the second execution updates zero rows in the CTE, so the outer UPDATE touches nothing. This pattern — make the state transition the idempotency mechanism — is the cheapest form of idempotency there is, and section 29.12 comes back to it.

Rule 2: compensations run in reverse order. Not because of elegance, but because of dependencies. Releasing stock before cancelling shipping means a courier can arrive for a parcel whose contents were returned to the shelf. Refunding before releasing stock means a customer sees their money back while the warehouse still shows the item as held, and a second customer cannot buy it. Reverse order keeps every intermediate state explainable.

There is one exception a senior will make deliberately: refund first when the customer is waiting and the internal cleanup is slow. A refund initiated at second 2 rather than second 40 measurably reduces support contacts. If you do this, record it as a deliberate ordering choice in the step table, not as an accident.

Rule 3: compensations can themselves fail. This is the part every tutorial skips. Your refund call gets a 503. Your courier cancel API returns "already dispatched, cannot cancel". What now?

flowchart TB
  F["Step failed after the pivot or during compensation"] --> R["Retry with backoff"]
  R -->|"succeeds"| OK["State advances, saga continues"]
  R -->|"still failing after max attempts"| Q["Insert into manual_interventions, saga state = NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW"]
  Q --> A["Alert fires on queue depth"]
  A --> H["Human opens the admin screen"]
  H --> H1["Resume: retry the step now"]
  H --> H2["Skip: mark done, record why"]
  H --> H3["Cancel: mark the saga failed, handle out of band"]

The manual-intervention queue is a table, not a Slack message:

CREATE TABLE manual_interventions (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  saga_id      uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES order_sagas(id),
  order_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  step         text NOT NULL,
  reason       text NOT NULL,
  context      jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',   -- chargeId, reservationId, last provider response
  money_at_risk_cents int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- lets you sort the queue by customer impact
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN',  -- OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, RESOLVED
  assigned_to  text,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  resolved_at  timestamptz,
  resolution   text
);

CREATE INDEX idx_manual_open ON manual_interventions (created_at)
  WHERE status <> 'RESOLVED';

money_at_risk_cents is the column that makes the queue usable. When 40 items pile up during an outage, the operator works the 12,000-rupee refunds before the 90-rupee ones.

Rule 4: handle the partially-succeeded step. Stock reservation for a 4-line order reserved 3 SKUs and failed on the fourth. The compensation must release exactly what was reserved, no more and no less. That is only possible if the forward step recorded each reservation as it happened:

// inventory.service.ts — record each line as it succeeds, so compensation is exact
async reserve(orderId: string, items: Item[]): Promise<ReserveResult> {
  return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
    const reserved: string[] = [];
    for (const item of items) {
      const res = await manager.query(
        `UPDATE inventory SET available = available - $2
          WHERE sku = $1 AND available >= $2`,
        [item.sku, item.qty],
      );
      if (res[1] === 0) {
        // Whole transaction rolls back: nothing was reserved. This is the easy case,
        // and it is easy ONLY because all lines are in one local database.
        throw new InsufficientStockError(item.sku);
      }
      await manager.insert(StockReservation, {
        orderId, sku: item.sku, qty: item.qty, status: 'RESERVED',
      });
      reserved.push(item.sku);
    }
    return { reservationId: orderId, reserved };
  });
}

Note what makes this clean: all four lines live in one database, so one local transaction covers them and "partially succeeded" cannot happen inside the step. Whenever you can collapse a multi-part step into one local transaction, do it — you delete an entire class of compensation problem. Where you cannot (stock split across two warehouses in two services), you must record each part and compensate part by part.

Rule 5: know the compensation window and what the customer sees in it. This is a product decision with real numbers:

Compensation Technical completion What the customer perceives
Cancel order row ~2 ms Immediate: status flips to Cancelled
Release stock ~5 ms Invisible to them, visible to other shoppers
Cancel courier pickup 200 ms to 2 s Invisible unless the label was already emailed
Void an authorization (not yet captured) Immediate at the gateway Bank hold disappears in 1 to 7 days depending on the issuer
Refund a captured charge 1 to 3 s at the gateway 3 to 7 business days to appear on the statement

That last row is the one product must understand. Your saga completes in 3 seconds; the customer's experience of the compensation lasts a week. Which means the UI must say so explicitly: "We've cancelled your order. Your refund of 4,299 has been issued and will appear on your card within 5 to 7 working days. Reference RF-7781." Silence here generates a support ticket per refund, guaranteed.

NestJS example

The compensation executor, driven by the same step table from section 29.5:

// compensation.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class CompensationService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(CompensationService.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly payments: PaymentGatewayClient,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryClient,
    private readonly shipping: ShippingClient,
    @InjectRepository(ManualIntervention) private readonly manual: Repository<ManualIntervention>,
  ) {}

  async compensate(saga: OrderSaga, step: StepName): Promise<StepOutcome> {
    const key = `${saga.orderId}:${step}`;                 // deterministic, safe to repeat
    try {
      switch (step) {
        case 'CANCEL_SHIPMENT':
          if (!saga.payload.pickupId) return { ok: true, refs: {} };   // nothing to undo
          await this.shipping.cancel(saga.payload.pickupId, { idempotencyKey: key });
          return { ok: true, refs: { shipmentCancelled: true } };

        case 'RELEASE_STOCK':
          if (!saga.payload.reservationId) return { ok: true, refs: {} };
          await this.inventory.release(saga.orderId, { idempotencyKey: key });
          return { ok: true, refs: { stockReleased: true } };

        case 'REFUND_PAYMENT': {
          if (!saga.payload.chargeId) {
            // Authorized but never captured: void the hold instead of refunding.
            if (saga.payload.authId) await this.payments.voidAuth(saga.payload.authId, key);
            return { ok: true, refs: {} };
          }
          const r = await this.payments.refund(saga.payload.chargeId, { idempotencyKey: key });
          return { ok: true, refs: { refundId: r.id } };
        }

        case 'CANCEL_ORDER':
          await this.orders.update(
            { id: saga.orderId, status: Not(OrderStatus.CANCELLED) },
            { status: OrderStatus.CANCELLED, cancelledAt: new Date() },
          );
          return { ok: true, refs: {} };
      }
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof AlreadyDoneError) return { ok: true, refs: {} };  // 409 = success
      this.log.error({ orderId: saga.orderId, step, err: String(err) }, 'compensation failed');
      return { ok: false, error: String(err), refs: {} };
    }
  }

  async escalate(saga: OrderSaga, step: StepName, reason: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.manual.insert({
      sagaId: saga.id,
      orderId: saga.orderId,
      step,
      reason,
      context: saga.payload,
      moneyAtRiskCents: saga.payload.capturedCents ?? 0,
    });
    this.metrics.increment('saga_manual_intervention_total', { step });
  }
}

Three details worth copying. if (!saga.payload.pickupId) return ok — compensating a step that never ran is a success, not an error, and this line prevents an infinite retry loop over a non-existent shipment. AlreadyDoneError mapping a gateway 409 to success — providers return "already refunded" and that is exactly the outcome you wanted. And voidAuth versus refund — the compensation depends on which forward step actually completed, which is why payload must be accurate.

Production scenario

A retailer processes about 480 compensations per day out of 34,000 orders (1.4%). The breakdown:

Trigger Share Typical compensation Auto-resolved
Payment declined at authorization 61% Cancel order only. No money moved 100%
Stock unavailable after payment 22% Release nothing, refund, cancel 99.7%
Customer cancels within the window 12% Cancel shipment, release stock, refund, cancel 98%
Shipping partner rejects the address 4% Refund, cancel; stock stays held for reship 91%
Fraud hold after capture 1% Refund, cancel, flag account 76%

About 6 compensations a day reach NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW. That is a workload one support person absorbs in twenty minutes, which is the correct size for a manual queue. If it were 600 a day, the design would be wrong.

Failure scenario

A refund storm during a gateway incident. The payment provider had a 40-minute degradation where refund requests returned HTTP 500 but actually processed about half the time. The saga runner retried each failed refund with backoff, up to 10 attempts.

Because the refund client generated a fresh idempotency key per attempt (randomUUID()), the provider treated each retry as a new refund. 214 orders were refunded between two and four times. Total over-refund: 780,000 rupees.

Recovery took a week of finance work and re-charging customers who had received money they were not owed, which is a terrible email to send. Two single-line fixes prevented all of it:

// Before: a new key on every attempt. Every retry is a new refund.
const key = randomUUID();

// After: derived from durable identity. Every retry is the SAME refund.
const key = `${orderId}:REFUND_PAYMENT`;

The second fix was reading the provider docs properly: their refund endpoint returns 409 refund_already_exists for a repeated key, and the client was treating 409 as a failure and retrying. Mapping 409 to success would also have prevented the incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Compensating a step that never ran. Guard on the reference in payload; treat it as success.
  • Compensating a step that is still in flight. The forward call timed out but is still executing on the provider; your refund arrives before the charge exists and returns "charge not found". Retry with backoff rather than escalating on the first attempt — and see section 29.18 on compensation racing the original step.
  • Non-refundable amounts. Gateway fees (typically 2% plus 3 rupees) are often not returned. Your ledger must model the difference or your reconciliation will never balance.
  • Cancellation after cut-off. The courier already collected the parcel. Compensation becomes a returns process, which is a different business flow with its own saga. Do not try to force it into the order saga.
  • Compensation for a step whose service is down. The inventory service being down does not permit skipping the release; it must retry until it succeeds or escalate. Skipping silently corrupts stock.
  • Partial refunds. Order of 4 items, 1 out of stock. Compensation is a partial refund, which means the amount is computed, not copied. Compute it from the order lines, never from the request.
  • Currency and rounding. Refunding a converted amount at a different exchange rate leaves a few paise unaccounted for. Always refund in the original charge's currency and amount.
  • Compensation loops. Compensation fails, escalates, an operator hits "retry", it fails again. Cap operator retries too, and require a written resolution note to close the item.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the compensation at the same time as the forward step, in the same pull request, and they refuse to merge a saga step without one. The review question is: if this step succeeds and the next one fails, what exactly runs, with what identifier, and what happens if that also fails?

They treat compensation as a first-class business process, not an error path. It gets a status the customer can see, an email, a ledger entry, a metric and a place in the support tooling. A cancellation is not a failure of the system; it is an outcome of the system.

They also insist on the manual queue existing before it is needed. Building it during an incident, at 03:00, with 400 stuck orders, is the worst time to design a table.

To a product manager: "One in seventy orders will need to be unwound. Almost all of that is automatic and the customer just sees 'cancelled, refund on the way'. About six a day need a person to look, and we will give you a screen for that with the biggest refunds at the top."

Common mistakes

  • Non-idempotent compensations (available = available + qty with no guard).
  • Fresh idempotency keys per retry attempt.
  • Treating a provider's "already done" 409 as a failure.
  • No manual queue, so failed compensations become log lines nobody reads.
  • Compensating in forward order, producing states nobody can explain.
  • Assuming the compensation is instant from the customer's perspective and not telling them about the 5 to 7 day refund window.
  • Compensating a partially-succeeded step by "undoing everything", which undoes things that never happened.

Interview questions

  1. Why must compensations be idempotent, and how do you make them so? Expected: retries and duplicate triggers are guaranteed; use a guarded state transition (WHERE status = 'RESERVED') or a deterministic idempotency key at the provider.
  2. What do you do when a compensation fails permanently? Expected: bounded retries with backoff, then a durable manual-intervention row with money at risk, an alert, and an admin UI with resume/skip/cancel.
  3. In what order do you run compensations and why? Expected: reverse of the forward order so intermediate states stay explainable; refund-first is a deliberate exception for customer experience.
  4. How do you compensate a step that partially succeeded? Expected: the forward step must record what it actually did; compensate exactly that; better, make the step a single local transaction so partial success is impossible.
  5. What is the difference between voiding an authorization and refunding a capture? Expected: void releases a hold before settlement (fast, usually free); refund moves money back after settlement (slow, fees often retained). Your compensation must pick based on what actually happened.

29.8 What happens if every step fails

This section is the centrepiece of Part 29. For each of the four steps, we walk every way it can go wrong and state exactly what the system does and where the order ends up. If you build only one thing from this Part, build a table like this for your own flow.

Two definitions first, because they carry the whole table:

  • Unknown outcome means the request left your process and no answer came back. It may have fully succeeded. Any design that maps "unknown" to "failed" is wrong roughly half the time.
  • End state means the row in orders.status and in order_sagas.state after the system has finished reacting, with no human involved.

The order status enum

CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM (
  'PENDING_PAYMENT',       -- created, payment not yet authorized
  'PAYMENT_UNKNOWN',       -- charge call timed out; outcome being resolved
  'PAYMENT_FAILED',        -- declined or permanently failed; nothing to undo
  'PAID',                  -- authorized and captured
  'STOCK_RESERVED',        -- items held in the warehouse
  'SHIPPING_REQUESTED',    -- pickup booked with the courier
  'COMPLETED',             -- all four steps done
  'COMPENSATING',          -- unwinding: refund and release in progress
  'CANCELLED',             -- unwound cleanly, customer made whole
  'FAILED',                -- terminal, nothing was left behind
  'NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW'    -- automation gave up; a human owns it now
);

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING_PAYMENT';

-- Operational index: everything not finished, cheap to scan even at 40 million rows.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_open ON orders (status, updated_at)
  WHERE status NOT IN ('COMPLETED', 'CANCELLED', 'FAILED');

COMPENSATING and NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW are the two states that separate a real system from a demo. COMPENSATING gives the UI something honest to show while refunds are in flight. NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW gives failure a home instead of a log line.

The saga state machine, with every compensation path

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> PENDING_PAYMENT
  PENDING_PAYMENT --> PAYMENT_UNKNOWN : charge timed out
  PENDING_PAYMENT --> PAYMENT_FAILED : declined
  PENDING_PAYMENT --> PAID : authorized and captured
  PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> PAID : provider says charge exists
  PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> PAYMENT_FAILED : provider says no charge
  PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW : provider unreachable past deadline
  PAYMENT_FAILED --> FAILED : cancel order, nothing to undo
  PAID --> STOCK_RESERVED : reservation succeeded
  PAID --> COMPENSATING : stock unavailable
  STOCK_RESERVED --> SHIPPING_REQUESTED : pickup booked
  STOCK_RESERVED --> COMPENSATING : shipping rejected permanently
  SHIPPING_REQUESTED --> COMPLETED : shipment confirmed
  SHIPPING_REQUESTED --> NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW : courier retries exhausted
  COMPENSATING --> CANCELLED : all compensations succeeded
  COMPENSATING --> NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW : a compensation failed permanently
  NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW --> CANCELLED : operator resolved by refunding
  NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW --> COMPLETED : operator resolved by completing
  COMPLETED --> [*]
  CANCELLED --> [*]
  FAILED --> [*]

Read the arrows into NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW: there are three, and each one is a place where automation has honestly run out. Read the arrows out of it: two, both driven by a human. That is the shape of a complete design.

Step 1 — Order creation

The only step fully inside your database, and therefore the easiest.

Failure mode What actually happened What the system does End state
Fails fast Constraint violation, invalid DTO, customer not found Return 400 or 422 immediately. No saga row is created Nothing exists. Clean
Times out Database unreachable or pool exhausted; the INSERT may have committed Return 503. The client retries with the same Idempotency-Key; the unique index on (customer_id, idempotency_key) returns the existing order One order, no duplicate
Succeeds, acknowledgement lost Row committed, response lost in transit Client retries with the same key, gets the existing order and a 200 PENDING_PAYMENT, one row
Partially succeeds Order header inserted, one line item failed Impossible: one local transaction covers both. Rolls back entirely Nothing exists
Duplicates Two POSTs, one intent (double-click, LB retry) Unique index on the idempotency key rejects the second; return the first order One order
Arrives late The client gave up 30 s ago; the request lands anyway The order is created and enters the saga normally; the customer sees it in their order list and may be surprised PENDING_PAYMENT, then normal flow. Consider rejecting requests older than the client timeout via a Request-Timestamp header
Arrives out of order A cancel for this order arrives before the create The cancel finds no order. Do not create a tombstone silently; park it in a short-lived pending table keyed by order id and apply it when the create lands, or reject it and let the client retry PENDING_PAYMENT then CANCELLED
Compensation fails UPDATE orders SET status = 'CANCELLED' fails Only possible if the database is down. Retry; database availability is a prerequisite for everything COMPENSATING until the database returns

Step 2 — Payment

The expensive step. Every row here is money.

Failure mode What actually happened What the system does End state
Fails fast Card declined, insufficient funds, 3DS rejected. Explicit 402 Mark PAYMENT_FAILED, cancel the order. No compensation needed: nothing moved FAILED. Customer told to try another card
Times out No response after 4 s. The charge may exist Mark PAYMENT_UNKNOWN. Never retry blindly. The reconciler calls GET /charges?idempotency_key=order-7781-charge. If found, move to PAID; if not found after the provider's settlement window, move to PAYMENT_FAILED PAID or FAILED, resolved within minutes
Succeeds, acknowledgement lost Money moved, HTTP response lost Identical to the timeout path. The idempotency-key lookup or the charge.succeeded webhook finds it PAID
Partially succeeds Split payment: 2,000 from wallet succeeded, 2,299 on card declined Record the wallet debit as a real event. Compensation must refund the wallet portion. Model each tender as its own saga step, or you will lose track of it COMPENSATING then CANCELLED with a wallet credit
Duplicates Two charge calls for one order The provider's idempotency key collapses them into one charge. Without the key, two charges and a manual refund PAID, one charge
Arrives late The saga already timed out, compensated and cancelled; the charge lands afterwards The webhook handler sees the order is CANCELLED and triggers an automatic refund saga. This must exist or you keep the money (section 29.18) CANCELLED plus an automatic refund
Arrives out of order charge.refunded webhook is delivered before charge.succeeded Handle by event id and provider timestamp, not arrival order. Store both; apply the latest state per charge id. Never derive state from arrival sequence Correct final state
Compensation fails Refund returns 500 repeatedly Retry 10 times with backoff up to 60 s (about 12 minutes of attempts), then NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW with money_at_risk_cents set. Page if the queue exceeds 5 NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW

Step 3 — Inventory

The step most likely to fail for a business reason rather than a technical one.

Failure mode What actually happened What the system does End state
Fails fast available >= qty is false. Genuinely out of stock Enter COMPENSATING: refund the capture, cancel the order, email "item sold out, refunded" CANCELLED
Times out Inventory service did not answer. Reservation may exist Retry the same command with key order-7781:RESERVE_STOCK. The inventory service's inbox dedups it. After 5 attempts, query reservations by order id; if one exists, treat as success STOCK_RESERVED or COMPENSATING
Succeeds, acknowledgement lost Stock decremented, StockReserved event lost The retry hits the inbox, which returns the existing reservation, and the reply is re-emitted from the outbox STOCK_RESERVED
Partially succeeds 3 of 4 SKUs reserved, then the pod died mid-loop If all lines are in one local transaction, impossible. Across warehouses or services, the saga must release exactly the recorded reservations, line by line COMPENSATING then CANCELLED
Duplicates The reserve command is delivered twice Inbox ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on message_id makes the second a no-op. Without it, stock is double-decremented and you undersell STOCK_RESERVED, decremented once
Arrives late Reserve command processed after the saga already compensated The inventory service accepts it (it has no view of the saga), so stock is now held for a cancelled order. The release compensation must be re-sent, or a nightly reconciler must find reservations whose order is CANCELLED Reconciled within an hour
Arrives out of order ReleaseStock arrives before ReserveStock The release finds no reservation and returns success (nothing to release). Then the reserve lands and holds stock forever. Fix: the release writes a tombstone row (order_id, sku, status='RELEASED'); the later reserve sees the tombstone and refuses Stock correct
Compensation fails Release returns 500 Retry up to 10 times, then NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW. Also caught by the nightly reconciler comparing reservations against cancelled orders NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW, stock corrected by reconciler within 24 h

Step 4 — Shipping

After the pivot. Failure here does not refund; it escalates.

Failure mode What actually happened What the system does End state
Fails fast Courier rejects: undeliverable pin code, oversize parcel Not retryable. Enter COMPENSATING: release stock, refund, cancel, email the customer with the reason CANCELLED
Times out No answer in 20 s. Pickup may be booked Retry with the same idempotency key, backoff to 60 s, 12 attempts (~1 hour). If the courier supports it, query by reference before each retry SHIPPING_REQUESTED or NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW
Succeeds, acknowledgement lost Pickup booked, response lost The idempotent retry returns the same pickup id (or a 409 you map to success). No double booking SHIPPING_REQUESTED
Partially succeeds Multi-parcel order: 2 of 3 parcels booked Record each parcel's booking as it returns. Retry only the unbooked parcels. Never re-book confirmed ones SHIPPING_REQUESTED when all parcels are booked
Duplicates Two RequestShipping commands from two orchestrator pods Deterministic key order-7781:REQUEST_SHIPPING collapses them at the courier. Without it: two pickups, a failed-pickup fee, an annoyed driver One pickup
Arrives late Booking confirmed after the saga escalated and a human cancelled the order The courier webhook finds the order CANCELLED and fires a cancel-pickup compensation automatically CANCELLED, pickup cancelled
Arrives out of order shipment.delivered webhook arrives before shipment.created Apply by the courier's own status timestamp, not arrival order. Store the tracking record with a status_updated_at and only move forward Correct status
Compensation fails Cancel pickup returns "already collected" Not a failure: it is a different business process. Move to the returns saga, notify the customer, keep the refund pending until the parcel is back or write it off NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW linked to a returns case

The pattern across all 32 rows

Read the four tables together and five rules fall out. These are the actual deliverables of this section:

  1. Every remote step needs a deterministic idempotency key derived from durable identity. ${orderId}:${step}. Not a random UUID, not a timestamp. Half the rows above are handled by this one rule.
  2. Every step needs an explicit "unknown" resolution path. Either query the provider by the idempotency key, or wait for a webhook, or both with a deadline. Guessing is not a path.
  3. Every consumer needs an inbox. Duplicates are not exceptional; they are the delivery guarantee (Part 27 section 27.7). ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on message_id handles the whole "duplicates" column.
  4. Every out-of-order pair needs a tombstone or a version. "Release before reserve" and "delivered before created" are the same bug: state derived from arrival order. Fix it by deriving state from data, never from sequence.
  5. Every step needs a bounded number of attempts and a place to land when they run out. NEEDS_MANUAL_REVIEW plus a queue row with money at risk. Unbounded retries are how a saga hangs for three weeks.

Production scenario

A team built exactly this table for their flow, then wrote one integration test per row: 32 tests, each injecting one specific failure with a stub server, asserting the final orders.status and the absence of money discrepancies. The suite ran in 90 seconds in CI.

In the following year they had three provider incidents. In all three the automated compensation handled over 98% of affected orders, and the manual queue peaked at 41 items during the worst one. No customer was charged without an order. The team's own summary: the tests were tedious to write and they are the reason nobody has been paged for a stuck order since.

Failure scenario

The counter-example. A team shipped the same flow with no matrix. Their handling of "payment timed out" was catch (e) { order.status = 'FAILED' }.

For eight months this was invisible, because the timeout rate was 0.04% and the affected customers just re-ordered. Then the gateway had a bad afternoon: 6% timeouts for two hours. 340 orders were marked FAILED while the charges succeeded. Customers saw "Order failed" and re-ordered — many of them twice. 411 duplicate charges, 340 orphaned ones.

Finance found it four days later during settlement reconciliation, when the gateway's total did not match the sum of orders.total_cents WHERE status IN ('PAID','COMPLETED'). That reconciliation query is worth having as a daily job on its own:

-- Daily: charges the provider says exist, that we have no PAID order for.
SELECT p.charge_id, p.amount_cents, p.created_at
FROM provider_charges p
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.payment_ref = p.charge_id
WHERE p.created_at < now() - interval '30 minutes'
  AND (o.id IS NULL OR o.status NOT IN ('PAID','STOCK_RESERVED','SHIPPING_REQUESTED','COMPLETED'))
ORDER BY p.created_at;

If that query ever returns rows and you did not expect it, you have money you should not have.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A failure mode you did not enumerate is a failure mode you handle by accident. The matrix is the deliverable; the code follows from it.
  • The unknown-outcome resolver needs its own deadline. If the provider is unreachable for an hour, PAYMENT_UNKNOWN must eventually escalate rather than spin.
  • Webhook and polling can both resolve the same unknown, at the same time, on two pods. Both paths must be idempotent against the same order row.
  • Refunding a charge you never recorded is possible if the reconciler works from provider data. Always write the charge id into the order before or at the moment you learn it.
  • Time zones and settlement windows. "The provider says no charge exists" can be temporarily true for a charge created 200 ms ago in an eventually consistent provider API. Give the resolver a minimum age before it concludes "no charge".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They build the matrix before the code, on paper, with the product owner in the room for the "end state" column, because half the rows are business decisions, not technical ones. "Charge arrives late for a cancelled order" is a policy question: refund automatically, or hold as store credit? Engineering should not decide that alone.

They then turn each row into a test. The matrix becomes the test plan, which becomes the regression suite, which becomes the reason the next gateway incident is boring.

And they keep a single number on the dashboard that summarises the whole table: orders in a non-terminal state older than 15 minutes. If that number is zero, all 32 rows are being handled. If it climbs, exactly one of them is not.

Common mistakes

  • Mapping every exception to FAILED.
  • No PAYMENT_UNKNOWN state, so an unknown outcome must be forced into a lie.
  • Testing only the happy path and the "declined" path, which are the two cheapest rows in the table.
  • Assuming internal services do not need the duplicate and out-of-order columns. They do; Kafka rebalances and Kubernetes restarts guarantee it.
  • No daily reconciliation against the provider, so discrepancies are found by finance rather than by monitoring.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through every way a payment step can fail and what your system does for each. Expected: the eight rows above, with "unknown" handled by idempotency-key lookup or webhook, not by guessing.
  2. A charge succeeds after the order was already cancelled. What happens? Expected: the webhook handler detects the cancelled order and triggers an automatic refund saga; without that path you silently keep the money.
  3. ReleaseStock arrives before ReserveStock. What breaks and how do you fix it? Expected: the release is a no-op, then the reserve holds stock forever; fix with a tombstone row or a per-order version, never with arrival ordering.
  4. How do you bound the time an order can stay in a non-terminal state? Expected: per-step deadline, a reconciliation job scanning for stale sagas, a hard escalation to manual review, and a dashboard metric with an alert.
  5. What single query would tell you your saga implementation is broken in production? Expected: count of non-terminal orders older than N minutes; or the provider-charges-without-a-paid-order reconciliation query.

Practical exercise

Build the 32-row matrix for your own flow and turn it into 32 integration tests using a stub provider you can command to fail, hang, respond twice or respond out of order.

Acceptance criteria: every test asserts the final orders.status, the final saga state, and that the sum of money held by the provider matches the sum implied by your order statuses; at least six tests fail on your current code before you fix them; and the whole suite runs in under three minutes so it can live in CI.

29.9 The dual-write problem

Concept

A dual write is when one logical operation writes to two systems that cannot commit together. The canonical example, and the one every backend eventually writes:

await this.orders.save(order);                  // write 1: PostgreSQL
await this.kafka.emit('orders.events', event);  // write 2: Kafka

Two writes. Two systems. No shared transaction. There is no ordering of those two lines that is correct, and that is not a figure of speech — it is provable by enumerating the interleavings.

Why does it exist?

It exists because the code looks obviously fine. Save the order, tell the world. Every team writes it, most teams ship it, and it works 99.9% of the time. The 0.1% is where orders exist that nobody downstream ever heard about, or events exist for orders that do not.

At 500 orders per minute, 0.1% is 30 broken orders per hour. In our flow, an OrderCreated event that never gets published means the payment service never charges, and the order sits in PENDING_PAYMENT forever with no error anywhere.

Mental model

Imagine posting a cheque and separately phoning the bank to say "I've posted a cheque." If your phone dies after posting, the bank does not know. If the postbox is emptied late but you already phoned, the bank expects a cheque that has not arrived. The only reliable design is to put the note inside the same envelope as the cheque, and let the person who opens the envelope handle both. That envelope is the outbox.

How it works

There are exactly two orderings, and both are broken. Here is each one, with the failure drawn.

Ordering A: database first, then Kafka.

sequenceDiagram
  participant S as OrderService
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  participant K as Kafka
  S->>PG: BEGIN, INSERT orders, COMMIT
  PG-->>S: committed
  Note over S: Pod is OOMKilled here
  S--xK: OrderCreated never published
  Note over PG,K: Order exists but the payment service never hears about it, so it sits in PENDING_PAYMENT forever

Failure: lost event. The order is real; nothing downstream happens. No error is logged because the process died. The order is invisible to every metric except "orders stuck in PENDING_PAYMENT", which you only have if you built it.

Ordering B: Kafka first, then database.

sequenceDiagram
  participant S as OrderService
  participant K as Kafka
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  participant P as PaymentSvc
  S->>K: OrderCreated order-7781
  K-->>S: ack
  K-->>P: OrderCreated order-7781
  P->>P: charge the customer
  S->>PG: BEGIN, INSERT orders, COMMIT
  PG--xS: constraint violation, rollback
  Note over PG,P: Customer charged and the order row does not exist. This is the 02:14 incident from section 19.1

Failure: phantom event. Downstream acted on something that never became real. This is strictly worse than ordering A, because money moved.

Ordering C: the "clever" one — publish inside the transaction.

sequenceDiagram
  participant S as OrderService
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  participant K as Kafka
  S->>PG: BEGIN
  S->>PG: INSERT orders
  S->>K: OrderCreated order-7781
  K-->>S: ack
  S->>PG: COMMIT
  PG--xS: deadlock detected, ROLLBACK
  Note over PG,K: Event published and row rolled back. Same phantom as ordering B, plus the transaction was held open across a network call

Failure: phantom event, plus the connection-pinning problem from section 29.1. Kafka has no ROLLBACK you can call from a PostgreSQL transaction. Publishing inside a transaction does not make the publish transactional; it just makes the transaction longer.

The three interleavings side by side:

Ordering Crash point Result Severity
A: DB then Kafka After commit, before publish Order exists, no event. Flow stalls silently High: silent stall
A: DB then Kafka Kafka broker unavailable Same as above, but you get an error you can log and retry in-process (which fails on pod death) High
B: Kafka then DB After publish, before commit Event exists, no order. Downstream acts on nothing Critical: money moves
C: publish inside txn Commit fails after publish Same as B, plus pool exhaustion Critical

Retrying does not fix it. If you retry the publish in a catch block, the retry loop dies with the pod. If you retry with a background job, you have just started building an outbox — you simply have not persisted the intent yet, which is the whole trick.

Practical example

The three "solutions" teams try before finding the outbox, and why each fails:

// Attempt 1: try/catch and log. Loses the event on pod death, and the log line
// helps nobody because there is no process that reads logs and republishes.
try { await this.kafka.emit(topic, event); }
catch (e) { this.log.error({ e, event }, 'failed to publish'); }

// Attempt 2: in-memory retry queue. Dies with the pod. Also unbounded memory.
this.pendingEvents.push(event);
setInterval(() => this.drain(), 1000);

// Attempt 3: publish first, "compensate" the database. Now you need a compensating
// event, and the compensating publish has exactly the same problem, recursively.
await this.kafka.emit(topic, event);
try { await this.orders.save(order); }
catch (e) { await this.kafka.emit(topic, { ...event, type: 'OrderCreationFailed' }); }

Every attempt fails for the same reason: the intent to publish is not durable. Fix that one thing and everything else follows.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They spot a dual write in code review from the shape alone: an await to an external system immediately after or before a database write, with no durable record connecting them. The review comment is one line: "this is a dual write; use the outbox."

They also apply the test in reverse. When someone proposes any cross-system consistency mechanism, the senior asks: what is the single atomic thing that makes this reliable? For the outbox the answer is "one PostgreSQL transaction writes both rows". If a proposal has no such single atomic thing, it is a dual write wearing a costume.

Common mistakes

  • Believing a try/catch around the publish makes it reliable.
  • Believing Kafka's producer acks=all helps. It guarantees the broker stored the message; it says nothing about whether your database committed.
  • Believing Kafka transactions solve it. Kafka transactions give exactly-once within Kafka (consume-process-produce). They do not span PostgreSQL.
  • Reordering the two writes and thinking the problem is now solved because the failure changed shape.

Interview questions

  1. What is the dual-write problem? Expected: one logical operation, two systems, no shared transaction; every ordering has a crash window that loses or fabricates an event.
  2. Which ordering is worse, database-first or broker-first? Expected: broker-first, because downstream acts on something that never became real; database-first only stalls.
  3. Does acks=all or a Kafka transaction fix it? Expected: no; both are about durability and atomicity inside Kafka, not across Kafka and your database.

29.10 The transactional outbox

Concept

The transactional outbox removes the second write. Instead of publishing to Kafka, you INSERT the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business row. One transaction, one commit, atomic.

A separate process — the relay — reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, then marks them published. If the relay crashes, the rows are still there. If Kafka is down, the rows wait. Nothing is ever lost, because the intent was committed with the data.

BEGIN
  INSERT INTO orders (...)                 <- business fact
  INSERT INTO outbox (...)                 <- intent to tell the world
COMMIT                                     <- both or neither

[relay, separate process]
  SELECT unpublished FROM outbox FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  publish to Kafka
  UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now()

Why does it exist?

Because your database already has exactly one thing you can trust absolutely: atomic local commit. The outbox pattern is the trick of routing all cross-system communication through that one trustworthy mechanism. It is the single most valuable pattern in this Part, and it is about forty lines of code.

Mental model

Imagine a busy office. Instead of each employee running to the post office whenever they write a letter (and sometimes forgetting, or dropping it in the rain), they put finished letters in a tray on their desk. Once a letter is in the tray, it is going to be sent — the office runner comes by every few minutes and takes everything.

The employee's job ends at the tray. The runner's job is to get things posted, retrying if the post office is closed. Two simple jobs instead of one unreliable one.

PostgreSQL example

The table, with every column justified:

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id             bigserial PRIMARY KEY,      -- monotonic: preserves insertion order
  aggregate_type text        NOT NULL,       -- 'order', 'payment', 'shipment'
