  if (['ECONNRESET', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'EPIPE', 'EAI_AGAIN', 'ETIMEDOUT'].includes(e.code ?? '')) return true;
  if (e.name === 'TimeoutError' || e.name === 'AbortError') return true; // only safe with idempotency key
  return [429, 502, 503, 504].includes(e.statusCode ?? 0);
}

export function retryAfterMsFrom(err: unknown): number | undefined {
  const h = (err as { headers?: Record<string, string> }).headers?.['retry-after'];
  if (!h) return undefined;
  const secs = Number(h);
  if (!Number.isNaN(secs)) return Math.min(secs * 1000, 30_000);   // cap what we will honour
  const date = Date.parse(h);
  return Number.isNaN(date) ? undefined : Math.max(0, Math.min(date - Date.now(), 30_000));
}

Using p-retry instead, the same policy is:

import pRetry, { AbortError } from 'p-retry';

const result = await pRetry(
  () => this.inventory.reserve(items, deadline),
  {
    retries: 2,                 // 3 attempts in total
    factor: 2,
    minTimeout: 100,
    maxTimeout: 2_000,
    randomize: true,            // multiplies the delay by a random factor in [1, 2)
    shouldRetry: (err) => isRetryableHttpError(err) && this.budget.canRetry(),
    onFailedAttempt: (err) => this.log.warn({ attempt: err.attemptNumber, left: err.retriesLeft }),
  },
);
// Throw `new AbortError(err)` from inside the function to stop retrying immediately.

PostgreSQL example

The most legitimate retry in a database-backed service is the serialization failure. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL will abort a transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 when it cannot guarantee isolation; the entire transaction must be rerun. Deadlocks (40P01) are the same: one victim is chosen and must retry.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT on_hand, reserved FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 'p_123';
UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + 1 WHERE product_id = 'p_123';
COMMIT;
-- ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update  (SQLSTATE 40001)
-- Correct response: re-run the whole transaction from BEGIN, a few times, with a tiny jitter.

TypeORM example

async function withSerializableRetry<T>(ds: DataSource, work: (m: EntityManager) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await ds.transaction('SERIALIZABLE', work);
    } catch (err) {
      const code = (err as { code?: string }).code;
      const retryable = code === '40001' || code === '40P01';
      if (!retryable || attempt >= 3) throw err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 25 * attempt)); // tiny jitter
    }
  }
}

// usage
await withSerializableRetry(this.dataSource, async (m) => {
  const inv = await m.findOneByOrFail(Inventory, { productId });
  if (inv.onHand - inv.reserved < qty) throw new OutOfStockError(productId);
  await m.increment(Inventory, { productId }, 'reserved', qty);
});

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(
  { isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.SERIALIZABLE },
  async (t) => {
    const inv = await Inventory.findOne({ where: { productId }, transaction: t, rejectOnEmpty: true });
    if (inv.onHand - inv.reserved < qty) throw new OutOfStockError(productId);
    await inv.increment('reserved', { by: qty, transaction: t });
  },
);
// Wrap the call above in the same 40001/40P01 retry loop; Sequelize surfaces the
// PostgreSQL code at err.original.code (or err.parent.code).

Sequelize also has a retry option on the constructor (retry: { max: 3, match: [/SequelizeConnectionError/] }) which retries individual queries on connection errors; it does not rerun whole transactions, so do not rely on it for serialization failures.

Production scenario

An orders service processes 800 RPS. Inventory reservation fails transiently 0.3% of the time (mostly ECONNRESET during inventory deploys, which happen 10 times a day). With 3-attempt retries and 100 ms base backoff, the user-visible failure rate drops from 0.3% to 0.002%, and the retry budget usage sits around 0.4%. During a real inventory outage the picture changes: the first attempt fails for 100% of calls, retries push the ratio toward 10%, the budget trips, and subsequent failures are returned immediately without retries. Inventory receives 1.1x normal load during its outage instead of 3x, which is the difference between recovering in 30 seconds and staying down because it is being hammered.

Failure scenario

At 11:03 a marketing push doubled traffic to a ride-booking API. The pricing service, a little under-provisioned, started returning 503 for 5% of requests. The booking service retried 503 five times with no backoff; the mobile app retried the booking call three times; the gateway retried 502 twice. Pricing went from 105% load to a computed worst case of 30x on the failing fraction, in practice about 4x overall, and fell over completely. Bookings dropped to zero for 22 minutes. The post-mortem action items: retry at one layer only (booking service), 3 attempts max, exponential backoff with full jitter, a 10% retry budget, and Retry-After headers from pricing that the booking service honours. In the load test that followed, the same traffic spike produced a 4% error rate for 90 seconds and then recovered on its own.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Retrying a non-idempotent write after a timeout double-executes it. A POST /charges timeout followed by a retry without an idempotency key is a double charge.
  • Retry storms (the 27x math). Retry at one layer; enforce budgets.
  • Retries eating the deadline. Three attempts of a 2 s call take 6 s inside a 3 s budget. Check remaining time before each attempt.
  • Retrying 400/404. You will never succeed; you only add latency and load.
  • Retrying 500. Sometimes transient, often a bug. At most one retry, and only for idempotent reads.
  • Ignoring Retry-After. The downstream told you exactly when to come back; anything else is rude and counterproductive.
  • Synchronized retries. Without jitter, all clients that failed at the same instant retry at the same instant (30.4).
  • Retries inside retries: p-retry around an axios instance that has axios-retry configured, inside a BullMQ job with attempts: 5. Know every retry layer in the path.
  • Retrying inside a transaction holds locks across the backoff. Retry the whole transaction, not a statement inside it.
  • Successful retry after partial success. Attempt 1 wrote 3 of 5 rows and failed; attempt 2 writes 5. Without a transaction or idempotent upserts you now have 8.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior engineer's first question about any retry is "is this operation idempotent, and how do I know?" If the answer is "I think so", there is no retry until it is proven. Their second question is "who else in this path retries?" and they draw the layers to compute the amplification. They put retries as close to the failure as possible and as far from the user as possible, and they make the count small (2–3) because the data says almost all transient failures resolve on the first retry. They add a retry budget because they have watched a retry storm take down a database. And they make every retry visible: retries_total{dependency, reason} and retry_budget_exhausted_total are on the dashboard, because a rising retry rate is the earliest warning that a dependency is unhealthy.

To a product manager: "We automatically try again when a partner has a brief hiccup, so the customer never sees it. But we cap how often we do that, so a partner's bad day cannot become our bad day."

Common mistakes

  • Blanket retry(3) around everything, including POSTs.
  • Retrying immediately with no delay ("it's just a network blip").
  • Not distinguishing timeouts (unknown outcome) from connection refusals (known not to have happened).
  • Copying axios-retry defaults, which retry on network errors and idempotent methods only, then wondering why POST is not retried; or, worse, forcing retryCondition: () => true.
  • Forgetting that BullMQ attempts is itself a retry layer with its own backoff.

Interview questions

  1. Which HTTP status codes do you retry and which do you never retry? Why is 429 special? Expected: retry 502/503/504/429 and connection errors; never 4xx client errors; 429 is retried only after Retry-After and does not count against the breaker.
  2. Explain retry amplification with three layers and three attempts each. Expected: 3^3 = 27x on the failing fraction; fix with single-layer retries and budgets.
  3. What is a retry budget and how would you implement one? Expected: ratio of retries to requests per window; refuse retries when exceeded; token bucket or counters.
  4. A payment call timed out. Do you retry it? Expected: only if the request carried an idempotency key the gateway honours; otherwise mark pending and reconcile.
  5. How do you retry a PostgreSQL serialization failure correctly? Expected: rerun the whole transaction from BEGIN, small number of attempts, jitter; never retry a single statement inside the failed transaction.

Practical exercise

Build a Retrier provider with a RetryBudget and the classification table above. Write a Jest test with a fake dependency that fails with 503 for the first N calls. Acceptance criteria: a POST without an idempotency key is never retried on timeout; 429 with Retry-After: 2 waits 2 s; when the budget ratio exceeds 10% over 200 calls, no further retries are attempted and a retry_budget_exhausted_total counter increments.

30.4 Exponential backoff and jitter

Concept

Backoff is the wait between retry attempts. Exponential backoff makes each wait roughly double the previous one (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms), so a struggling dependency gets progressively more breathing room. Jitter adds randomness to each wait so that many clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment. The two together are the standard, and the standard exists because each on its own is not enough.

Why does it exist?

Picture 2,000 NestJS pods, each with a Redis client, when Redis restarts. Every pod loses its connection at the same millisecond. With a fixed 1 s retry, all 2,000 reconnect at exactly t+1 s, Redis is still initialising, all 2,000 fail, and all 2,000 come back at t+2 s. That is a thundering herd: synchronized retries that arrive as a spike. Exponential backoff spaces the rounds out but does nothing about the synchronization; at t+1, t+3, t+7 you still get 2,000 simultaneous connections. Jitter breaks the synchronization by spreading each client's wait over an interval, so the 2,000 reconnects arrive as a smooth trickle over several seconds instead of as a wall.

Mental model

Imagine a stadium exit after a match. If everyone counts to ten and then walks to the gate at the same time, there is a crush. If everyone picks a random number between zero and ten, the crowd flows. Doubling the count each time the gate is found blocked (exponential) means people stop crowding a broken gate; picking a random number (jitter) means they do not all arrive together.

How it works

Let base be the initial delay (say 100 ms), cap the maximum delay (say 10 s), and attempt the retry number starting at 1.

Exponential:          sleep = min(cap, base * 2^attempt)
Full jitter:          sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
Equal jitter:         temp  = min(cap, base * 2^attempt)
                      sleep = temp / 2 + random(0, temp / 2)
Decorrelated jitter:  sleep = min(cap, random(base, prev_sleep * 3))
  • Full jitter spreads the wait uniformly from zero to the exponential value. It gives the best load smoothing (the AWS Architecture Blog analysis found it minimizes total work and completion time in contention). The cost is that a client may retry almost immediately, which is fine when the failure is contention and less fine when the downstream needs a guaranteed pause.
  • Equal jitter guarantees at least half the exponential wait, then randomizes the other half. Choose it when the downstream genuinely needs a minimum pause (a restarting broker) and you still want de-synchronization.
  • Decorrelated jitter uses the previous sleep as the input, producing a random walk that grows on average. It is a good default for long-lived reconnection loops (database, Kafka).

Attempt-by-attempt with base 100 ms, cap 10 s:

Attempt Exponential Full jitter range Equal jitter range
1 200 ms 0–200 ms 100–200 ms
2 400 ms 0–400 ms 200–400 ms
3 800 ms 0–800 ms 400–800 ms
4 1,600 ms 0–1,600 ms 800–1,600 ms
5 3,200 ms 0–3,200 ms 1,600–3,200 ms
7 10,000 ms (capped) 0–10 s 5–10 s

Retry-After takes precedence. If the response carries Retry-After (seconds or an HTTP date), the downstream is telling you exactly when it will be ready. Honour it (with a sanity cap so a malicious or buggy Retry-After: 86400 does not park your request for a day), and add a small jitter on top so that all your clients do not return at the same second.

Practical example

The Redis reconnection strategy in ioredis takes a function of the attempt number. Decorrelated or full jitter with a 5 s cap means 40 pods reconnect over a spread of several seconds after a Redis failover, rather than in one wall. For the payment gateway, equal jitter with base 200 ms and cap 2 s keeps retries inside the 3 s handler budget while guaranteeing the gateway at least 100 ms of quiet per client.

NestJS example

/** Backoff strategies. All return milliseconds. `attempt` starts at 1. */
export type JitterMode = 'none' | 'full' | 'equal' | 'decorrelated';

export function computeBackoff(
  attempt: number,
  baseMs: number,
  capMs: number,
  mode: JitterMode = 'full',
  prevMs = baseMs,
): number {
  const exp = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
  switch (mode) {
    case 'none':
      return exp;
    case 'full':
      return Math.floor(Math.random() * exp);
    case 'equal':
      return Math.floor(exp / 2 + Math.random() * (exp / 2));
    case 'decorrelated':
      return Math.floor(Math.min(capMs, baseMs + Math.random() * (prevMs * 3 - baseMs)));
  }
}

/** ioredis retryStrategy using decorrelated jitter, capped at 5 s, give up after 30 tries. */
let prev = 100;
export const redisRetryStrategy = (times: number): number | null => {
  if (times > 30) return null;                       // stop; let the health check fail the pod
  prev = computeBackoff(times, 100, 5_000, 'decorrelated', prev);
  return prev;
};

Wiring it into a NestJS Redis provider:

import { Provider } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

export const REDIS = Symbol('REDIS');

export const redisProvider: Provider = {
  provide: REDIS,
  useFactory: () =>
    new Redis({
      host: process.env.REDIS_HOST,
      port: 6379,
      connectTimeout: 1_000,
      commandTimeout: 300,          // a Redis call slower than 300 ms is a problem, not a wait
      maxRetriesPerRequest: 1,      // per-command retry while reconnecting
      enableOfflineQueue: false,    // fail fast instead of queueing commands while disconnected
      retryStrategy: redisRetryStrategy,
    }),
};

enableOfflineQueue: false deserves a note: with the default true, commands issued while Redis is down are queued in memory and replayed on reconnect. That is a hidden retry buffer with no bound, and during a long outage it grows until the pod runs out of memory. Failing fast is what you want in a request path; a cache miss is cheaper than an OOM.

PostgreSQL example

Reconnection to PostgreSQL after a failover follows the same logic. pg.Pool does not reconnect a broken client; it discards it and creates a new one on the next connect(). Your application-level "wait for the database" loop at startup should use jittered backoff so that 40 pods restarting after a database failover do not open 40 x 20 connections in the same 100 ms:

async function waitForDatabase(ds: DataSource, maxAttempts = 20): Promise<void> {
  let prev = 200;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      await ds.query('SELECT 1');
      return;
    } catch (err) {
      prev = computeBackoff(attempt, 200, 5_000, 'decorrelated', prev);
      console.warn(`db not ready (attempt ${attempt}), waiting ${prev} ms`);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, prev));
    }
  }
  throw new Error('database unavailable after retries');
}

Production scenario

A Kafka cluster with 12 brokers performs a rolling restart. 300 consumer pods each lose one broker connection in turn. kafkajs defaults (initialRetryTime: 300, factor: 0.2, multiplier: 2, maxRetryTime: 30000, retries: 5) already include randomization; the effect is that reconnections to each restarted broker arrive spread over 1–3 s instead of as a spike, and broker CPU during the rolling restart shows small bumps rather than the vertical lines that used to precede a cascade of leader elections.

Failure scenario

A team replaced a library's default backoff with a fixed 500 ms retry "to make things faster". The next Redis failover (Redis replica promotion takes 1–3 s) produced 1,200 pods reconnecting in the same 50 ms window every 500 ms. The new primary spent its first 6 seconds accepting and dropping connections instead of serving traffic, redis_connected_clients sawtoothed, and the API error rate hit 40% for 90 seconds. Reverting to jittered exponential backoff cut the same failover's error window to under 8 seconds.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Backoff without a cap grows to minutes; requests hang past every deadline. Always cap, and always check the deadline before sleeping.
  • Jitter with Math.random() per process seeded identically is not an issue in Node (V8 seeds from entropy), but in some container images with a fixed seed environment you can see synchronized "random" values. Verify once.
  • Retry-After longer than your deadline: fail fast; do not wait.
  • Retry-After in the past (clock skew): treat as zero.
  • Backoff inside a database transaction holds locks while sleeping. Never sleep inside a transaction.
  • Backoff in BullMQ: backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 } has no jitter; supply a custom backoffStrategy on the worker if you have thousands of jobs failing together.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that the shape of the retry curve matters more than the exact numbers. They default to full jitter for request-path retries and decorrelated jitter for long-lived reconnection loops. They cap delays below the deadline. They read the downstream's Retry-After and treat ignoring it as a bug. And they test backoff behaviour under simulated mass failure (kill Redis in staging with 50 pods connected and watch connected_clients), because backoff bugs only show up under synchronized failure.

Common mistakes

  • Exponential backoff with no jitter ("we have backoff" while the herd still thunders).
  • Jitter with no exponential (random 0–100 ms forever, hammering the dependency).
  • Not capping the delay.
  • Sleeping past the deadline.
  • Applying Retry-After without a maximum.

Interview questions

  1. Why is exponential backoff alone insufficient? What does jitter add? Expected: exponential spaces rounds but keeps clients synchronized; jitter de-synchronizes them.
  2. Compare full jitter and equal jitter. When would you choose each? Expected: full for maximum smoothing; equal when a minimum quiet period is needed.
  3. Write the formula for decorrelated jitter and explain why it uses the previous sleep. Expected: min(cap, random(base, prev*3)); grows on average without a fixed schedule.
  4. A downstream returns 429 with Retry-After: 120. Your request deadline is 3 s. What do you do? Expected: do not wait; fail fast with a clear error, optionally enqueue for later.

Practical exercise

Implement computeBackoff with all four modes and write a simulation: 1,000 clients fail at t=0 and retry up to 5 times against a dependency that recovers at t=2 s. Plot (or tabulate per 100 ms bucket) the number of retry arrivals per bucket for each mode. Acceptance criteria: the fixed-delay and no-jitter modes show spikes of near 1,000 in single buckets; full jitter's largest bucket is under 150; every mode's maximum delay never exceeds the cap.

30.5 Circuit breakers

Concept

A circuit breaker is a stateful wrapper around calls to one dependency. It watches the recent failure rate. While the dependency is healthy the breaker is closed and calls pass through. When failures cross a threshold the breaker opens: for a cooling-off period every call fails immediately without touching the dependency. After the cooling-off period the breaker goes half-open and lets a small number of probe calls through; if they succeed it closes, if they fail it opens again.

The name comes from the electrical device: when current exceeds a limit the breaker trips, cutting the circuit so the wiring does not melt. A software breaker cuts the circuit so a failing dependency is not buried under load, and so your service stops burning its own resources waiting on something that is not going to answer.

Why does it exist?

Timeouts bound each call. Retries handle transient blips. Neither handles a dependency that is down for minutes. With only timeouts, every request to a dead payment gateway still waits the full 2 s before failing; at 500 RPS that is 1,000 in-flight requests holding memory, sockets and possibly DB connections, all to learn what the previous 10,000 calls already learned. And every one of those calls is load on a gateway that is trying to recover. A breaker learns the lesson once, fails fast for a while (microseconds instead of 2 s), and periodically checks whether the dependency has recovered. It converts "slow failure under load" into "fast failure with automatic recovery".

Mental model

Imagine a receptionist at a clinic. Normally when you ask for Dr. Patel she rings his office. If she rings ten times in a row and gets no answer, she stops ringing and tells everyone who asks "he is not available, try again in a few minutes" without picking up the phone. Every few minutes she tries once; if he answers, she goes back to normal. The receptionist is the breaker: she protects the waiting room from pointless queuing and protects the doctor from a phone that never stops ringing.

How it works

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open : failure rate over threshold with enough volume
    Open --> HalfOpen : resetTimeout elapsed
    HalfOpen --> Closed : probe call succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open : probe call fails
    Closed --> Closed : success or isolated failure
    Open --> Open : call rejected immediately
  1. Closed. Calls pass through. The breaker records each outcome in a rolling window (for example 10 buckets of 1 s each). Timeouts count as failures. Errors you choose to filter out (a 400 is the caller's fault, not the dependency's) do not.
  2. Trip condition. Two thresholds together: a failure percentage (say 50%) and a volume threshold (say at least 20 calls in the window). The volume threshold prevents a breaker from opening because 1 of 2 calls failed at 03:00 on a quiet night.
  3. Open. Every call is rejected instantly with a specific error (BreakerOpenError) and the fallback runs if one is configured. No traffic reaches the dependency. This state lasts resetTimeout (say 10–30 s).
  4. Half-open. One (or a few) real calls are allowed. Success closes the breaker and clears the stats; failure reopens it and restarts the resetTimeout.
  5. Metrics and events. State transitions are logged and exported (circuit_breaker_state{name} as a gauge 0/1/2, circuit_breaker_transitions_total{name, to}), because an open breaker is often the first alert of a downstream outage.

Two design decisions matter as much as the thresholds:

  • One breaker per dependency (and usually per operation class within a dependency: reads and writes to the same service can have different health). A single global breaker means a dead email provider blocks payments.
  • Fallback behaviour is a product decision: fail the request, return cached data, return a degraded answer, or queue the work for later. Section 30.10 covers the choices; the breaker is where you plug them in.

Practical example

Checkout calls the payment gateway. Normal error rate is under 0.5%. The breaker is configured to open when the failure rate exceeds 50% over at least 20 calls in a 10 s window, stay open 15 s, then probe. When the gateway has an outage, within 10 s the breaker opens on every pod; checkout returns a 503 with a friendly message and a Retry-After: 15 header in about 1 ms instead of 2 s; the gateway gets a few probe calls per pod every 15 s instead of 500 RPS; and the on-call sees circuit_breaker_state{name="payment-gateway"} = 1 in the alert. Meanwhile the catalog and cart features are untouched, because their dependencies have their own breakers.

NestJS example

opossum is the standard breaker library for Node. Here it wraps a payment gateway client inside a NestJS provider, with Prometheus metrics via prom-client and an error filter that keeps client-side mistakes from tripping the breaker.

import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import CircuitBreaker from 'opossum';
import { Counter, Gauge } from 'prom-client';
import { PaymentGatewayHttp, ChargeRequest, ChargeResult } from './payment-gateway.http';

const stateGauge = new Gauge({
  name: 'circuit_breaker_state', help: '0=closed 1=open 2=half-open', labelNames: ['name'],
});
const transitions = new Counter({
  name: 'circuit_breaker_transitions_total', help: 'state changes', labelNames: ['name', 'to'],
});

@Injectable()
export class PaymentBreaker implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PaymentBreaker.name);
  private readonly breaker: CircuitBreaker<[ChargeRequest], ChargeResult>;

  constructor(private readonly http: PaymentGatewayHttp) {
    this.breaker = new CircuitBreaker((req: ChargeRequest) => this.http.charge(req), {
      name: 'payment-gateway',
      timeout: 2_500,                 // opossum's own timer; counts as a failure
      errorThresholdPercentage: 50,   // trip when >= 50% of calls fail...
      volumeThreshold: 20,            // ...and at least 20 calls were made in the window
      rollingCountTimeout: 10_000,    // window length
      rollingCountBuckets: 10,        // 1 s buckets
      resetTimeout: 15_000,           // open -> half-open after 15 s
      capacity: 200,                  // max concurrent in-flight calls (a bulkhead, see 20.6)
      // Return true to NOT count this error as a dependency failure.
      errorFilter: (err: { statusCode?: number }) =>
        err.statusCode !== undefined && err.statusCode >= 400 && err.statusCode < 500 && err.statusCode !== 429,
    });

    this.breaker.on('open', () => this.onState('open', 1));
    this.breaker.on('halfOpen', () => this.onState('half-open', 2));
    this.breaker.on('close', () => this.onState('closed', 0));
    this.breaker.on('reject', () => this.log.warn('payment call rejected: breaker open'));
    this.breaker.on('semaphoreLocked', () => this.log.warn('payment call rejected: capacity exhausted'));
    stateGauge.set({ name: 'payment-gateway' }, 0);
  }

  async charge(req: ChargeRequest): Promise<ChargeResult> {
    try {
      return await this.breaker.fire(req);
    } catch (err) {
      if ((err as Error).message === 'Breaker is open' || (err as { code?: string }).code === 'EOPENBREAKER') {
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException('payments temporarily unavailable');
      }
      throw err;
    }
  }

  private onState(to: string, value: number) {
    stateGauge.set({ name: 'payment-gateway' }, value);
    transitions.inc({ name: 'payment-gateway', to });
    this.log.warn({ msg: 'breaker state change', name: 'payment-gateway', to });
  }

  onModuleDestroy() { this.breaker.shutdown(); }
}

A few notes on the real behaviour of opossum:

  • In half-open state it lets one call through; the outcome decides the next state. That is deliberately conservative: it avoids a herd of probes hitting a recovering service.
  • breaker.fallback(fn) registers a function called whenever the action fails or is rejected; the fallback's return value becomes the result of fire(). Use it for cached or degraded answers; do not use it to hide errors you need to see.
  • breaker.stats exposes the rolling counts (fires, failures, timeouts, rejects, successes), which you can export as metrics.
  • An open breaker does not stop the resetTimeout timer from firing if the process is under heavy event-loop lag; the transition may be late by the lag amount, which is another reason to keep the event loop healthy (30.8).

PostgreSQL example

Breakers around your primary database are usually a mistake: if the primary is down you have nothing to fall back to, and failing fast is what connectionTimeoutMillis already does. Breakers around read replicas are useful: when a replica lags badly or goes away, you route reads to the primary (or another replica) for a while.

// Two DataSources: primary and replica. The breaker guards the replica.
const replicaBreaker = new CircuitBreaker(
  (sql: string, params: unknown[]) => replica.query(sql, params),
  { timeout: 800, errorThresholdPercentage: 40, volumeThreshold: 30, resetTimeout: 20_000, name: 'pg-replica' },
);
replicaBreaker.fallback((sql: string, params: unknown[]) => primary.query(sql, params));

// A lag check that counts as failure if the replica is more than 5 s behind.
await replicaBreaker.fire(
  `SELECT CASE WHEN now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() > interval '5 seconds'
          THEN pg_terminate_backend(pg_backend_pid()) END`, [],
);

The lag check above is intentionally blunt: it turns "too laggy" into an error the breaker can see. In practice you would measure pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() in a health probe every second and feed the breaker's decision from that.

Production scenario

A marketplace API has breakers on: payment gateway, tax-calculation SaaS, address-validation SaaS, recommendations service, search cluster, and email provider. In one quarter the breakers opened 31 times. 27 of those were third-party outages lasting 2–40 minutes that customers never noticed because each dependency had a fallback (tax: last known rate table; address validation: accept as entered and flag for review; recommendations: bestsellers; search: database ILIKE on the first 100 products of the category; email: queue). The 4 remaining were the payment gateway, where there is no fallback; checkout showed a "please try again in a moment" screen and conversion dipped for the duration. Total engineering time spent on those 31 incidents: near zero. Before breakers, each third-party outage was a page.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday the on-call was paged for elevated checkout latency. Dashboards showed the payment breaker flapping: open, half-open, closed, open, every 20 seconds. The gateway was healthy for 90% of calls but returned 500 for a specific card BIN range after a change on their side. Every time the breaker closed, the 10% failures accumulated, the breaker tripped, and all checkouts failed for 15 s, including the 90% that would have succeeded. The threshold of 50% was correct; the problem was that a partial, deterministic failure looked like a transient outage. The fix was twofold: treat the gateway's 500 with a specific error.code = "unsupported_card" as a non-counting error (it is a per-card business outcome, not a dependency failure), and raise volumeThreshold so the window needed 50 calls. Lesson: breakers reason about dependency health; feed them only errors that mean the dependency is unhealthy.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Flapping. A dependency that is partially failing pushes the breaker across the threshold repeatedly. Tune volume thresholds, lengthen resetTimeout, and filter deterministic errors out of the count.
  • Half-open herd. If your breaker allows N probes and you run 50 pods, the recovering service gets 50N probes at once. Keep probes to 1 per pod and stagger resetTimeout with a little jitter per instance.
  • Breaker per process. Each pod has its own breaker with its own view; during a partial outage some pods are open and some closed. This is normal and usually fine. A shared breaker in Redis is possible but adds a dependency to your reliability layer; do it only if the per-pod divergence hurts.
  • Timeouts counted twice. If your HTTP client has a 2 s timeout and the breaker has a 2.5 s timeout, the client's timeout fires first and is counted as a failure; fine. If the breaker timeout is shorter, the breaker gives up while the HTTP call continues; set the breaker timeout above the client timeout, or leave the breaker timeout off and rely on the client.
  • Counting the wrong errors. 400, 404, 422, business declines, validation errors: none of these mean the dependency is down. Filter them.
  • Breaker with no fallback and no Retry-After. Clients retry an open breaker in a loop; add Retry-After to the 503.
  • Breaker hiding a real outage. Fallbacks are so smooth nobody notices the dependency has been down for three days. Alert on circuit_breaker_state == 1 for more than N minutes.
  • Breaker around a non-idempotent call with retries inside it. The breaker sees one failure but the retries hit the dependency three times; keep retries inside the breaker action and count them as one fire, or put retries outside and count each attempt.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They add a breaker to every third-party call and to every cross-service call that has a sensible fallback. They do not add one where fast failure has no benefit (the primary database) or where the call is so rare the volume threshold is never met (a monthly report). They think carefully about the error filter, because a breaker fed with business errors becomes a random outage generator. They put the breaker state on the main dashboard and alert on "open for more than 2 minutes". And they treat an opened breaker as a successful outcome: the system did what it was designed to do.

To a product manager: "When a partner goes down, the breaker lets us instantly switch to Plan B for a few minutes and keep checking whether the partner is back, instead of making every customer wait and fail."

Common mistakes

  • One breaker for all outbound HTTP.
  • Trip thresholds with no volume floor (breaker opens on the first two errors of the day).
  • Counting 4xx as failures.
  • No metrics on state; discovering the breaker was open for six hours from a customer complaint.
  • Wrapping a call that has no timeout: the breaker never sees a failure because nothing ever returns.
  • Using the fallback to return "success" for a write that did not happen.

Interview questions

  1. Describe the three states of a circuit breaker and what triggers each transition. Expected: closed/open/half-open; failure rate plus volume threshold; reset timeout; probe result.
  2. Why do breakers need a volume threshold in addition to a failure percentage? Expected: to avoid tripping on small samples at low traffic.
  3. Your breaker keeps flapping. What do you look at? Expected: which errors are counted; partial deterministic failures; window and volume; reset timeout; jitter.
  4. Where would you NOT use a circuit breaker? Expected: primary database with no alternative; extremely low-volume calls; calls where fast failure gives no benefit.
  5. How does a per-pod breaker behave differently from a shared one, and which do you prefer? Expected: per-pod diverges but has no extra dependency; prefer per-pod unless divergence is harmful.

Practical exercise

Wrap a fake payment gateway (an Express or NestJS stub that can be toggled between healthy, 50% 500, and 100% timeout) with opossum in a NestJS provider, export circuit_breaker_state to Prometheus, and drive 50 RPS at it with autocannon. Acceptance criteria: within 10 s of switching the stub to timeout mode the breaker opens and p99 latency drops below 5 ms; within 20 s of restoring the stub the breaker closes; 400 responses from the stub never open the breaker.

30.6 Bulkheads

Concept

A bulkhead is an isolation boundary that limits how many resources one workload or one dependency can consume, so that its failure cannot take resources from the others. In practice: separate connection pools, separate socket pools, separate worker processes, separate Kubernetes deployments, separate per-tenant quotas. The word comes from ship design: a hull divided into watertight compartments stays afloat when one compartment floods.

Why does it exist?

Shared resources fail together. If all outbound HTTP calls share one socket pool of 100 sockets and the email provider hangs, 100 sockets are soon held by email calls and the payment gateway, which is perfectly healthy, cannot get a socket. If the API and the nightly reporting job share one PostgreSQL pool of 20 connections, a report that runs 10 concurrent 5-minute queries leaves the API with 10 connections during its peak hour. If one tenant sends 10,000 requests a second, every other tenant's requests queue behind them. Bulkheads make sure a problem in one compartment stays in that compartment.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital with one waiting room for everything. A flu outbreak fills every chair, and the person with a broken arm cannot get in. A hospital with separate emergency, outpatient and paediatric departments keeps functioning during the flu outbreak because the flu patients only fill their department. Bulkheads are the separate departments.

How it works

flowchart LR
    subgraph NestJS pod
        API["API handlers"]
        HA1["undici Agent\npayments: 50 sockets"]
        HA2["undici Agent\nemail: 10 sockets"]
        HA3["undici Agent\ninventory: 100 sockets"]
        P1["pg pool\napi: 20 conns"]
        P2["pg pool\nbatch: 5 conns"]
    end
    API --> HA1 --> PG1["Payment gateway"]
    API --> HA2 --> EM["Email provider"]
    API --> HA3 --> INV["Inventory svc"]
    API --> P1 --> DB["PostgreSQL"]
    JOB["Batch job"] --> P2 --> DB

The levels at which you can draw a bulkhead, from smallest to largest:

  1. Concurrency limit per dependency in-process. opossum's capacity, a p-limit or bottleneck limiter around the client. When exhausted, calls are rejected immediately instead of queuing.
  2. Socket pool per dependency. One undici.Agent (or https.Agent) per downstream host with its own connections limit. A hung email provider holds at most its 10 sockets.
  3. Database pool per workload. Two DataSources: api (small, short statement_timeout) and batch (small too, long timeout). PostgreSQL-side CONNECTION LIMIT per role enforces the split even if the app misbehaves.
  4. Process/deployment per workload. API pods, worker pods and cron pods are separate Kubernetes deployments with their own resource requests, replica counts and autoscaling. A memory leak in the PDF-generating worker cannot OOMKill the API.
  5. Per-tenant quotas. A Bottleneck.Group keyed by tenant, or gateway-level rate limits per API key, so one tenant cannot consume the whole capacity.
  6. Per-priority queues. Separate Kafka topics or BullMQ queues for critical and bulk work, with separate consumers, so a million bulk emails do not delay the password-reset email.

Practical example

A SaaS invoicing API serves 200 tenants. Three bulkheads: (1) per-dependency undici agents so the tax SaaS hanging cannot starve the PDF renderer's sockets; (2) api and batch PostgreSQL pools with role-level connection limits so month-end batch invoicing cannot starve interactive requests; (3) per-tenant concurrency of 20 via Bottleneck.Group, so one tenant's script that fires 5,000 invoice creations queues in their lane, and the other 199 tenants see normal latency.

NestJS example

Two TypeORM connections registered under different names, injected where needed:

// app.module.ts
@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
      name: 'default',                 // API pool: small, fast, short timeouts
      type: 'postgres', url: process.env.PG_URL_API,
      extra: { max: 20, connectionTimeoutMillis: 1_000, statement_timeout: 2_000 },
      entities: [Order, Invoice],
    }),
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
      name: 'batch',                   // batch pool: separate role, long timeouts
      type: 'postgres', url: process.env.PG_URL_BATCH,
      extra: { max: 5, connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000, statement_timeout: 300_000 },
      entities: [Order, Invoice],
    }),
    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Invoice], 'batch'),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

// month-end.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class MonthEndService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Invoice, 'batch') private readonly invoices: Repository<Invoice>) {}
}

Per-tenant concurrency with bottleneck:

import Bottleneck from 'bottleneck';

@Injectable()
export class TenantLimiter {
  // Each tenant gets its own limiter: at most 20 in flight, at most 200 queued.
  private readonly group = new Bottleneck.Group({
    maxConcurrent: 20,
    highWater: 200,
    strategy: Bottleneck.strategy.OVERFLOW,  // reject when the queue is full instead of growing
  });

  run<T>(tenantId: string, fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    return this.group.key(tenantId).schedule(fn);
  }
}

With strategy: OVERFLOW, a job added beyond highWater is dropped and schedule() rejects; that rejection becomes a 429 for that tenant only. Other strategies (LEAK, BLOCK) exist; OVERFLOW is the one that behaves like a bulkhead.

PostgreSQL example

Enforce the pool split on the server side, so that a misconfigured pod cannot exceed its share:

CREATE ROLE app_api   LOGIN PASSWORD '...' CONNECTION LIMIT 400;  -- 20 pods x 20
CREATE ROLE app_batch LOGIN PASSWORD '...' CONNECTION LIMIT 20;   -- 4 pods x 5
ALTER ROLE app_api   SET statement_timeout = '2s';
ALTER ROLE app_batch SET statement_timeout = '5min';

-- Watch the split in production:
SELECT usename, state, count(*)
  FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE datname = 'shop'
 GROUP BY usename, state
 ORDER BY usename, state;

If you run PgBouncer, define separate pools per user in pgbouncer.ini ([databases] with pool_size per entry, and max_user_connections per user) for the same effect one layer up.

Sequelize example

export const apiDb = new Sequelize(process.env.PG_URL_API!, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  pool: { max: 20, acquire: 1_000 },
  dialectOptions: { statement_timeout: 2_000 },
});
export const batchDb = new Sequelize(process.env.PG_URL_BATCH!, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  pool: { max: 5, acquire: 5_000 },
  dialectOptions: { statement_timeout: 300_000 },
});
// Register with @nestjs/sequelize using SequelizeModule.forRoot({ name: 'batch', ... })
// and inject the model with @InjectModel(Invoice, 'batch').

Production scenario

Kubernetes deployments as bulkheads for a food-delivery platform:

# api: latency-sensitive, autoscaled on CPU and RPS
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: orders-api }
spec:
  replicas: 12
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: orders:1.42.0
          args: ["node", "dist/main.js"]           # boots only the HTTP app
          resources: { requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }, limits: { memory: "768Mi" } }
---
# worker: throughput-oriented, scaled on queue depth
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: orders-worker }
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: orders:1.42.0
          args: ["node", "dist/worker.js"]         # boots only queue consumers
          resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: "1Gi" }, limits: { memory: "1536Mi" } }

Same image, different entrypoints, different resource envelopes, different scaling rules. When a bad deploy of the PDF worker leaks memory and is OOMKilled every 10 minutes, the API deployment does not notice.

Failure scenario

At 00:05 on the first of the month, a reporting query started on the same pool as the API. It ran 8 concurrent SELECT ... GROUP BY statements over 400 million rows, each for about 6 minutes. The API pool had 20 connections; 8 were now busy for 6 minutes. At 00:06 a traffic spike (push notifications go out at midnight) needed 18 connections; 12 were available; connectionTimeoutMillis was 30 s; requests queued; p99 went to 30 s; the gateway timed out at 10 s; users retried; the pool never recovered until the reports finished. Post-mortem: batch work moved to a separate role with CONNECTION LIMIT 6 and a separate pool, connectionTimeoutMillis on the API pool cut to 1 s so that pool exhaustion turns into a fast 503 instead of a 30 s hang, and an alert on pg_pool_waiting_requests > 0 for more than 10 s.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Too many small pools. 15 dependencies x 50 sockets each x 40 pods = 30,000 sockets. Size each pool from its measured concurrency, not from a default.
  • Bulkhead that only queues. A concurrency limit with an unbounded queue is not a bulkhead; it is a memory leak with a delay. Bound the queue and reject when full.
  • Batch role too generous. CONNECTION LIMIT counts all sessions for the role including idle ones; a leaked connection reduces the effective limit.
  • Cross-pool transactions. You cannot span a transaction across two DataSources; pick the pool per unit of work, not per table.
  • Per-tenant limiter memory. Bottleneck.Group keeps a limiter per key; set timeout on the group so idle tenant limiters are garbage-collected.
  • Deployment bulkheads without PodDisruptionBudgets. A node drain can take out all worker pods at once even though the API is fine.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask: "if this dependency hangs completely, what is the maximum amount of my resources it can hold?" and make sure the answer is a number they chose (50 sockets, 5 connections, 200 queued jobs) rather than "all of them". They separate latency-sensitive work from throughput work at the deployment level early, because it is cheap when the codebase is small and painful later. They enforce limits on both sides where possible (pool max in the app and CONNECTION LIMIT in PostgreSQL). And they resist the urge to make every limit generous; a bulkhead that never fills is not protecting anything.

Common mistakes

  • One shared axios instance with one https.Agent for every outbound host.
  • Running cron jobs and batch processing inside the API process "because it's simpler".
  • Pools sized "to be safe" (max: 100) on 40 pods against a PostgreSQL with max_connections = 200.
  • Per-tenant fairness implemented in the database (ORDER BY tenant_id) instead of at admission.

Interview questions

  1. What is a bulkhead and give three concrete examples in a Node/PostgreSQL system. Expected: per-dependency socket pools, per-workload DB pools/roles, separate deployments; per-tenant limiters.
  2. How would you stop a monthly batch job from starving the API's database connections? Expected: separate role with CONNECTION LIMIT, separate pool, short connectionTimeoutMillis on the API pool, alerts on waiting requests.
  3. Why is an unbounded queue in front of a concurrency limiter dangerous? Expected: memory growth, latency without rejection; bound it and shed.
  4. One tenant floods your API. Where do you isolate them and why there? Expected: at admission (gateway or a per-tenant limiter), before the shared resources are touched.

Practical exercise

Split an existing NestJS app's PostgreSQL access into api and batch DataSources with different roles and CONNECTION LIMITs. Run a batch job that holds 5 connections for 2 minutes while autocannon drives the API at 200 RPS. Acceptance criteria: API p99 stays under 100 ms during the batch; pg_stat_activity shows the batch role never exceeding its limit; the API pool's waitingCount stays at 0.

30.7 Rate limiting

Concept

Rate limiting caps how many operations a caller may perform in a time window. It appears in two directions. Inbound rate limiting protects you from clients (abusive, buggy, or simply enthusiastic). Outbound (client-side) rate limiting protects downstreams from you, and protects you from being cut off by a third party whose contract says "100 requests per second".

Part 14 — API Design (REST first) covers token bucket and sliding window in detail; here we recap just enough to place rate limiting in the reliability toolbox.

Why does it exist?

Capacity is finite. A NestJS pod can serve maybe 1,500 simple requests per second; a PostgreSQL primary maybe 20,000 small queries per second; a payment gateway contract may allow 50 charges per second. Without a limit, one client's loop, one misconfigured retry, or one scraper decides how the rest of your capacity is spent. Rate limiting makes the decision yours, and makes it before the expensive work happens.

Mental model

Imagine a nightclub with a bouncer counting people in. The room holds 300; the bouncer lets in 300 and then admits one for each person who leaves. Nobody inside notices the queue outside. The alternative, letting everyone in, is a fire hazard for the people already inside and a worse night for everyone. Rate limiting is the bouncer, and the point is that the people inside keep having a good time.

How it works

  • Token bucket: a bucket of capacity B refills at R tokens per second; each request takes one token; empty bucket means reject. Allows bursts up to B, sustained rate R. This is what most APIs want.
  • Sliding window log/counter: count requests in the last W seconds; reject above N. Smoother than fixed windows (no double-burst at window edges), a little more memory.
  • Where the counter lives: in-process (per pod, fast, inconsistent across pods) or in Redis (shared, one INCR + EXPIRE or a Lua script per request, roughly 0.3–1 ms). Use in-process limits for coarse self-protection and Redis for per-user quotas that must be consistent.
  • What to key on: user id or API key for authenticated traffic, IP as a fallback, tenant for multi-tenant, route for expensive endpoints.
  • What to return: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining, so well-behaved clients back off correctly (30.4).

Practical example

An e-commerce API applies three inbound limits: 600 requests per minute per user for general endpoints, 10 per minute per user for POST /orders, and 5 per minute per IP for POST /auth/login. Outbound, it limits calls to the SMS provider to 20 per second globally (their contract) using a Redis-backed limiter shared across pods, and calls to the tax SaaS to 50 per second.

NestJS example

Inbound, with @nestjs/throttler and a Redis storage so the count is shared across pods:

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { APP_GUARD } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ThrottlerModule, ThrottlerGuard, seconds } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ThrottlerStorageRedisService } from '@nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
      throttlers: [
        { name: 'default', ttl: seconds(60), limit: 600 },
        { name: 'strict',  ttl: seconds(60), limit: 10 },
      ],
      storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL!)),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }],
})
export class AppModule {}

// orders.controller.ts
@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  @Post()
  @Throttle({ strict: { limit: 10, ttl: seconds(60) } })   // override for this route
  create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) { /* ... */ }
}

ThrottlerGuard keys on IP by default; override getTracker(req) in a subclass to key on the authenticated user id, which is what you want behind a load balancer where many users share an egress IP. When the limit is hit the guard throws ThrottlerException (HTTP 429) and sets Retry-After.

Outbound, a client-side limiter honouring a third-party contract, shared across pods through Redis:

import Bottleneck from 'bottleneck';

@Injectable()
export class SmsClient {
  // 20 per second across ALL pods: Bottleneck's Redis datastore coordinates the reservoir.
  private readonly limiter = new Bottleneck({
    id: 'sms-provider',
    datastore: 'ioredis',
    clientOptions: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST, port: 6379 },
    reservoir: 20,                       // tokens available now
    reservoirRefreshAmount: 20,          // refill to 20...
    reservoirRefreshInterval: 1_000,     // ...every second
    maxConcurrent: 10,
    highWater: 500,                      // bounded queue: beyond this, reject
    strategy: Bottleneck.strategy.OVERFLOW,
  });

  send(to: string, body: string): Promise<void> {
    return this.limiter.schedule(() => this.http.post('/messages', { to, body }));
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Rate limiting inside PostgreSQL is not a thing you should build, but PostgreSQL gives you a related protection: per-role connection limits and statement_timeout (30.2), which bound the cost a role can impose. For per-user quotas that must survive Redis being down, some teams keep a small api_quota table updated with UPDATE ... SET used = used + 1 WHERE used < quota RETURNING used; it works, and it costs a row lock per request, so use it only for low-rate, high-value limits (e.g. 100 exports per day).

Production scenario

A public API gets 4,000 RPS. In-process token buckets (per pod, keyed on API key, 200 tokens, 100/s refill) reject 0.8% of traffic from two keys running unthrottled scrapers, and cost about 5 microseconds per request. Redis-backed per-user quotas for POST /orders cost 0.6 ms per call on the 30 RPS that reach that route. Outbound, the SMS limiter queues about 400 messages during a promotion burst and drains them over 20 s, well inside the "delivered within a minute" SLA, while never exceeding the provider's 20/s.

Failure scenario

A team added a Redis-backed rate limiter to every route with no fallback for Redis failures. When Redis had a 40 s failover, every request waited on a Redis INCR that timed out after 5 s (the client had no commandTimeout), then the guard threw and returned 500. An availability control took availability to zero. Fix: commandTimeout: 200 on the limiter's Redis client, and a fail-open policy for the limiter (if Redis is unreachable, allow the request and increment a rate_limiter_fail_open_total metric). Fail-open is the right default for a limiter guarding capacity; fail-closed is right for a limiter guarding security (login attempts).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Limiter depends on Redis with no timeout (above).
  • Keying on IP behind a NAT rate-limits an entire office or mobile carrier.
  • Fixed windows allow 2x bursts at the boundary; prefer token bucket or sliding window.
  • Per-pod limits multiplied by pod count: "100/s per pod" becomes 4,000/s after a scale-out.
  • Unbounded outbound queue: a client-side limiter with no highWater turns a downstream slowdown into memory growth.
  • 429 without Retry-After leaves clients guessing and retrying too soon.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate self-protection limits (cheap, in-process, generous, fail-open) from business quota limits (Redis, exact, fail-open for capacity and fail-closed for security). They key on identity, not IP, wherever there is identity. They put outbound limiters on every third party with a contract, because being cut off by a provider is an outage nobody can fix quickly. And they make 429 responses helpful: Retry-After, remaining counts, and a documented policy.

Common mistakes

  • Rate limiting after doing the expensive work (the guard is placed after a database call in a service method).
  • Fail-closed on Redis failure for a capacity limit.
  • Forgetting outbound limits and getting the company's API key revoked by a provider.

Interview questions

  1. Token bucket vs sliding window: how do they differ in burst behaviour and memory? Expected: bucket allows bursts up to capacity with O(1) state; sliding window is smoother, slightly more state.
  2. Where should a rate limiter fail open and where fail closed? Expected: capacity protection fails open; security limits (login, OTP) fail closed.
  3. How do you enforce a third party's "50 requests per second" across 30 pods? Expected: shared limiter in Redis (reservoir) or a single outbound proxy; bounded queue; metrics.

Practical exercise

Add @nestjs/throttler with Redis storage keyed on user id to an existing API, plus a Bottleneck outbound limiter (20/s, Redis datastore) around a fake SMS provider. Acceptance criteria: two pods together never exceed 20 SMS calls per second under a 200 RPS burst; a user exceeding 10 POST /orders per minute receives 429 with Retry-After; stopping Redis causes the inbound limiter to fail open (requests succeed, metric increments) within 200 ms.

30.8 Load shedding

Concept

Load shedding is deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so that the requests you do accept complete within their deadline. It is rate limiting driven by your own health rather than by a caller's quota. The name comes from power grids: when demand exceeds supply, the grid cuts power to some neighbourhoods so it does not collapse for everyone.

Why does it exist?

Every server has a throughput cliff. Below capacity, latency is flat. Just above capacity, queues form: requests wait for the event loop, wait for a DB connection, wait for a socket. Latency climbs, clients time out, clients retry, load rises further, and goodput (requests that complete usefully, within their deadline) falls to zero even though the server is 100% busy. This is congestion collapse. Shedding at the door keeps the queues short, so the requests inside finish on time and goodput stays near capacity. Rejecting 10% of traffic quickly is far better than serving 100% of traffic 10 s late, because the 10 s late responses are worthless to a client that gave up at 5 s.

Mental model

Imagine a bakery with one oven. Orders arrive faster than loaves can be baked. Option A: take every order, tell everyone "30 minutes", and watch the queue grow to three hours while customers leave without paying for loaves that are still baking. Option B: put up a sign, "we are full, back in 15 minutes", once the queue reaches 20 minutes. Option B sells the same number of loaves and disappoints fewer people. Load shedding is the sign.

How it works

flowchart TB
    R["Incoming request"] --> A{"Admission check"}
    A -->|"event loop lag under 100 ms\nand queue under limit"| H["Handler runs"]
    A -->|"overloaded and request\nis low priority"| S["503 + Retry-After\nin under 1 ms"]
    A -->|"overloaded but request\nis critical"| H
    H --> D["DB / downstreams"]
    S --> M["shed_requests_total metric"]

Signals you can shed on, cheapest first:

  1. Event-loop lag. In Node, perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() gives a histogram of how late timers are firing; p99 above 50–100 ms means the loop is saturated. This is the best single overload signal for a Node process.
  2. In-flight request count per pod, compared to a known limit.
  3. Queue depth: pending DB pool acquisitions (pool.waitingCount), pending outbound calls, BullMQ queue length.
  4. Memory (process.memoryUsage().heapUsed approaching the limit).
  5. Gateway-level admission control: the load balancer or gateway drops or queues requests when the backend reports unhealthy, or based on concurrency limits per backend.

And what to shed: low-priority first. Classify requests (a header from the gateway, the route, or the client type): critical (checkout, payment webhooks, auth), normal (browse, search), bulk (analytics events, prefetching, bots). Shed bulk at mild overload, normal at severe overload, critical never (or only when the process is about to die).

The rejection itself must be cheap (no DB calls, no logging per request beyond a counter) and informative (503 with Retry-After and a stable error code), otherwise shedding costs almost as much as serving.

Practical example

A ride-booking API distinguishes POST /rides (critical), GET /drivers/nearby (normal, polled every 3 s by the app), and POST /telemetry (bulk, sent every second by driver phones). During a stadium-exit surge the event-loop lag on the API pods hits 120 ms. Telemetry is shed first (the phones buffer and resend later); if lag stays above 200 ms, nearby-driver polls get a 503 with Retry-After: 5 and the app shows the last known map. Ride creation keeps working throughout.

NestJS example

A middleware that sheds based on event-loop delay and a request priority header. It runs before routing, before guards, before any database access.

import { Injectable, NestMiddleware, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { monitorEventLoopDelay, IntervalHistogram } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { Counter } from 'prom-client';

const shed = new Counter({ name: 'shed_requests_total', help: 'requests shed', labelNames: ['priority'] });

type Priority = 'critical' | 'normal' | 'bulk';

@Injectable()
export class LoadShedMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  private readonly log = new Logger(LoadShedMiddleware.name);
  private readonly h: IntervalHistogram = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 });
  private lagMs = 0;
  private inFlight = 0;

  constructor() {
    this.h.enable();
    // Sample every 500 ms; the histogram is in nanoseconds.
    setInterval(() => { this.lagMs = this.h.percentile(99) / 1e6; this.h.reset(); }, 500).unref();
  }

  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    const priority = (req.header('x-priority') as Priority) ?? this.classify(req);
    const limit = this.lagLimitFor(priority);

    if (this.lagMs > limit || this.inFlight > this.inFlightLimitFor(priority)) {
      shed.inc({ priority });
      res.setHeader('Retry-After', priority === 'bulk' ? '30' : '5');
      res.status(503).json({ code: 'OVERLOADED', message: 'try again shortly' });
      return;
    }

    this.inFlight++;
    res.on('finish', () => this.inFlight--);
    res.on('close', () => { if (!res.writableFinished) this.inFlight--; });
    next();
  }

  private classify(req: Request): Priority {
    if (req.path.startsWith('/rides') || req.path.startsWith('/payments')) return 'critical';
    if (req.path.startsWith('/telemetry') || req.path.startsWith('/events')) return 'bulk';
    return 'normal';
  }
  private lagLimitFor(p: Priority) { return p === 'critical' ? 500 : p === 'normal' ? 150 : 60; }
  private inFlightLimitFor(p: Priority) { return p === 'critical' ? 2_000 : p === 'normal' ? 800 : 200; }
}

Register it first in AppModule (consumer.apply(LoadShedMiddleware).forRoutes('*')). Note two details: the histogram is reset every sample so the reading reflects the last 500 ms, not the process lifetime; and in-flight accounting handles aborted connections via the close event, otherwise the counter drifts upward and the middleware sheds forever.

Also give Kubernetes a way to help: report 503 from the readiness probe (30.12) when the pod is shedding normal traffic for more than a few seconds, so the Service stops routing new connections to it until it recovers. Do this cautiously: if every pod is overloaded, marking them all unready removes all capacity.

PostgreSQL example

The database sheds on your behalf if you let it: a short connectionTimeoutMillis (1 s) on the pool turns "wait forever for a connection" into a fast error you can map to 503; lock_timeout turns "queue behind a lock" into an error; statement_timeout bounds the cost of any one query. Check pool pressure explicitly before expensive work:

// pg.Pool exposes counts you can shed on.
const pool = (this.dataSource.driver as { master: Pool }).master;
if (pool.waitingCount > 10) {
  throw new ServiceUnavailableException('database busy'); // shed before joining the queue
}

Production scenario

A social-media feed API is provisioned for 12,000 RPS and receives 30,000 RPS after a celebrity post. Without shedding: p99 climbs to 20 s, the mobile app's 10 s timeout fires for most requests, users pull-to-refresh, load doubles again, and the service serves nothing useful for 15 minutes. With event-loop-lag shedding: 55% of GET /feed requests receive a 503 in under a millisecond, the app shows a "busy, tap to retry" banner honouring Retry-After: 5, and the remaining 45% complete with p99 of 350 ms. Goodput stays at roughly 12,000 RPS throughout. The incident is a graph, not a page.

Failure scenario

A team shipped load shedding keyed on CPU usage from os.loadavg(). On a 32-core node with 8 pods each pinned to one core, load average reflected the whole node and the shedder fired whenever a neighbouring pod was busy. Their API returned 503 for 30% of requests while its own event loop was idle. Post-mortem: shed on per-process signals (event-loop lag, own in-flight count), never on host-wide signals a container cannot interpret.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shedding the wrong traffic: rejecting payment webhooks while serving analytics. Priority classification must be explicit and reviewed.
  • Shedding too late: measuring lag over 60 s averages; by the time it triggers, the queue is already enormous. Use short windows (500 ms to 2 s).
  • Shedding that costs as much as serving: logging a full request per shed, or computing priority via a database lookup.
  • All pods unready at once because readiness reflects overload; the service loses all capacity. Prefer 503 on the request path over unready status for pure overload.
  • Oscillation: shed at 100 ms lag, recover at 99 ms, shed again. Add hysteresis (start shedding at 100, stop at 60).
  • Clients that ignore Retry-After and retry immediately, keeping you overloaded. Combine with per-client rate limits.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that a system without load shedding has a shedding policy anyway: it sheds everything, by falling over. They would rather choose. They classify traffic by business value and make the classification a first-class concept (a header set at the gateway, propagated downstream). They shed as early as possible (gateway, then middleware) and as cheaply as possible. And they load-test past capacity on purpose, because the shape of the latency curve beyond the cliff is what determines whether an incident lasts 2 minutes or 2 hours.

Common mistakes

  • No shedding at all; discovering the cliff in production.
  • Shedding on host metrics inside a container.
  • Shedding without priorities, so critical traffic is dropped at the same rate as bulk.
  • Returning 500 instead of 503 with Retry-After, so clients treat it as a bug and retry aggressively.

Interview questions

  1. What is congestion collapse and how does load shedding prevent it? Expected: queues grow past deadlines, goodput falls to zero; shedding keeps queues short so accepted work completes.
  2. Which signal would you shed on in a Node process and why? Expected: event-loop lag via monitorEventLoopDelay; it reflects the process's own saturation.
  3. How do you decide what to shed? Expected: explicit priorities by business value; bulk first, critical never.
  4. What is the danger of using readiness probes to shed load? Expected: all pods unready removes all capacity; use it only as a last resort and prefer request-level 503.

Practical exercise

Add the LoadShedMiddleware to a NestJS app with a CPU-heavy route (e.g. bcrypt with cost 12). Drive it with autocannon -c 500. Acceptance criteria: with shedding disabled, p99 exceeds 5 s; with shedding enabled, p99 for accepted critical requests stays under 500 ms, shed_requests_total{priority="bulk"} rises first, and no critical request is shed.

30.9 Backpressure

Concept

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer tells a fast producer to slow down. Load shedding rejects work at the edge; backpressure propagates the "I'm full" signal upstream so that producers stop generating work faster than it can be handled. In Node it shows up as stream highWaterMark and drain, as bounded queues that block or reject when full, as Kafka consumers that pause fetching, and as concurrency limiters that make a loop wait for a slot.

Why does it exist?

Without backpressure, the only place for excess work to go is memory. Promise.all(tenThousandItems.map(x => db.query(...))) fires 10,000 queries at once: 20 get a connection, 9,980 wait in the pool's queue, each holding its closure, its promise, and its parameters in memory. If the items were 1,000,000 the process dies. Reading a 4 GB CSV with fs.readFileSync and splitting it puts 4 GB in the heap. Consuming Kafka at 50,000 messages per second while your handler manages 5,000 per second grows an in-memory backlog by 45,000 per second until OOM. Backpressure ties the rate of intake to the rate of completion.

Mental model

Imagine a sink. The tap is the producer; the drain is the consumer. If the tap runs faster than the drain, the sink fills and eventually overflows onto the floor. A sink with backpressure has a float valve: when the water reaches a line, the tap closes until the level drops. Nothing overflows, and the tap simply runs in bursts at the rate of the drain.

How it works

  1. Bounded buffers. Every hand-off between a producer and a consumer has a buffer with a maximum size (stream highWaterMark in bytes or objects; a queue with maxSize; a limiter's highWater).
  2. A full signal. When the buffer is full, writable.write() returns false; queue.push() rejects or blocks; consumer.pause() stops fetching.
  3. The producer waits or stops. It listens for drain (streams), awaits a slot (p-limit), or resumes fetching when depth drops (consumer.resume()).
  4. Batching reduces per-item overhead so the consumer drains faster: 1,000 single-row INSERTs cost about 1 s; one INSERT ... VALUES with 1,000 rows costs about 20 ms.

Concrete forms in our stack:

Layer Backpressure mechanism
Node streams highWaterMark, write() returning false, drain, pipeline(), for await
Async loops p-limit/p-map with concurrency, bounded in-memory queues
PostgreSQL reads Cursors (pg-query-stream), LIMIT/keyset pagination instead of SELECT *
PostgreSQL writes Batched inserts, COPY, pool max as the hard ceiling
Kafka consumer consumer.pause()/resume(), maxBytesPerPartition, eachBatch with manual commit
BullMQ Worker concurrency, queue limiter, producers checking queue.count()
HTTP 429/503 with Retry-After (backpressure across a network boundary)

Practical example

A nightly job exports every order of the day (2 million rows) to a warehouse. The naive version loads all rows with find(), maps them, and Promise.alls 2 million HTTP PUTs. The correct version streams rows from PostgreSQL with a cursor in batches of 1,000, transforms them, and uploads with concurrency 8 via p-limit; memory stays flat at about 60 MB, and the warehouse sees a steady 8 concurrent uploads instead of a wall of 2 million.

NestJS example

Bounded concurrency over a large set with p-limit and batching:

import pLimit from 'p-limit';

@Injectable()
export class OrderExportService {
  private readonly limit = pLimit(8);   // at most 8 uploads in flight

  async exportDay(day: Date): Promise<void> {
    const pageSize = 1_000;
    let lastId = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
    for (;;) {
      // Keyset pagination: bounded memory per page, no OFFSET scans.
      const page = await this.orders.createQueryBuilder('o')
        .where('o.created_at >= :from AND o.created_at < :to', { from: day, to: nextDay(day) })
        .andWhere('o.id > :lastId', { lastId })
        .orderBy('o.id', 'ASC').take(pageSize).getMany();
      if (page.length === 0) break;

      // One upload per 100 orders (batching), at most 8 uploads concurrently (bounded).
      const chunks = chunk(page, 100);
      const results = await Promise.allSettled(
        chunks.map((c) => this.limit(() => this.warehouse.putBatch(c))),
      );
      for (const r of results) if (r.status === 'rejected') this.log.error(r.reason);

      lastId = page[page.length - 1].id;
    }
  }
}

Streams with real backpressure, reading a large upload, parsing, and writing to PostgreSQL through a Transform with bounded concurrency:

import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import { Transform } from 'node:stream';
import { parse } from 'csv-parse';

async importProducts(file: NodeJS.ReadableStream): Promise<void> {
  const batch: ProductRow[] = [];
  const flush = async () => {
    if (batch.length === 0) return;
    await this.products.createQueryBuilder().insert().values(batch.splice(0)).orIgnore().execute();
  };

  await pipeline(
    file,                                              // network read, 64 KB highWaterMark
    parse({ columns: true }),                          // one object per row
    new Transform({
      objectMode: true,
      highWaterMark: 500,                              // at most 500 rows buffered here
      transform: async (row, _enc, cb) => {
        batch.push(toProductRow(row));
        if (batch.length >= 500) await flush();        // awaiting here is backpressure:
        cb();                                          // upstream pauses until we call cb()
      },
      flush: async (cb) => { await flush(); cb(); },
    }),
  );
}

pipeline wires up drain handling and error propagation for you; because the transform does not call cb() until the batch insert completes, the CSV parser and the socket read stop when the database is the bottleneck. Memory stays bounded by highWaterMark at each stage regardless of file size.

Kafka consumer backpressure with @nestjs/microservices:

@Controller()
export class OrderEventsConsumer {
  private paused = false;

  @EventPattern('orders.created')
  async onOrderCreated(@Payload() event: OrderCreatedEvent, @Ctx() ctx: KafkaContext) {
    const consumer = ctx.getConsumer();
    const depth = await this.enrichmentQueue.count();    // BullMQ queue depth downstream

    if (depth > 10_000 && !this.paused) {
      consumer.pause([{ topic: 'orders.created' }]);       // stop fetching; offsets are not advanced
      this.paused = true;
      this.scheduleResume(consumer);
    }
    await this.enrichmentQueue.add('enrich', event, { jobId: event.orderId });
  }

  private scheduleResume(consumer: Consumer) {
    const t = setInterval(async () => {
      if ((await this.enrichmentQueue.count()) < 2_000) {
        consumer.resume([{ topic: 'orders.created' }]);
        this.paused = false;
        clearInterval(t);
      }
    }, 1_000);
    t.unref();
  }
}

Pausing a Kafka consumer is safe: the broker keeps the messages, the consumer keeps its partitions (as long as it keeps heartbeating, which kafkajs does in the background), and lag grows in Kafka rather than in your heap. That is exactly where lag belongs.

PostgreSQL example

Streaming reads with a cursor keep memory flat for arbitrarily large results:

import QueryStream from 'pg-query-stream';

const qr = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await qr.connect();
const client = (await (qr as any).connect()) as import('pg').PoolClient; // underlying pg client
const stream = client.query(new QueryStream(
  'SELECT id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE created_at >= $1 ORDER BY id',
  [since], { batchSize: 1_000 },                     // rows fetched per round trip
));
for await (const row of stream) { await this.sink.write(row); }
await qr.release();

For writes, the equivalent is batching: INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...) in groups of 500–1,000, or COPY ... FROM STDIN through pg-copy-streams for bulk loads (10–50x faster than row-by-row inserts).

Production scenario

An analytics ingest consumes a Kafka topic at 40,000 events per second and writes to PostgreSQL. Row-by-row inserts managed 6,000 per second and the in-memory backlog grew until pods were OOMKilled every 20 minutes. Rewritten with eachBatch, 1,000-row multi-value inserts, p-limit(4) around the inserts, and consumer.pause() when more than 5 batches are pending: throughput 55,000 per second, memory flat at 180 MB, and during a PostgreSQL maintenance window the consumer simply paused, Kafka lag grew to 12 million, and it drained in 6 minutes afterward with no data loss.

Failure scenario

At 03:20 a "resend all failed notifications" admin action loaded 480,000 notification rows and ran Promise.all(rows.map(r => this.push.send(r))). Within 2 s the push provider's socket pool (maxSockets: 50) had 50 in flight and 479,950 queued in the http.Agent request queue, each holding a serialized payload. Heap hit 2 GB, the pod was OOMKilled, and because the job was not idempotent and had no checkpoint, the retry started from row 1 and OOMKilled again. Three iterations later someone killed the job. Fix: p-limit(20), batches of 500 marked as sent per batch, and a checkpoint column so a restart resumes where it stopped.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Promise.all over unbounded input (the canonical Node memory bug).
  • Backpressure that stops at a boundary. A stream with proper backpressure feeding a function that pushes into an unbounded array.
  • Pausing Kafka but not heartbeating (custom consumers) leads to a rebalance and duplicate delivery; kafkajs handles heartbeats while paused.
  • Batches that partially fail: a 1,000-row insert with one bad row fails the whole statement; use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for duplicates and validate rows before batching.
  • Cursor held open across an await of an external call keeps a transaction open; consume the cursor into bounded batches, then call out.
  • highWaterMark in object mode counts objects, not bytes; 500 objects of 1 MB each is 500 MB.
  • Consumer paused forever because the resume condition never triggers (downstream queue stuck). Add a maximum pause duration and an alert.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They look at every loop over data of unknown size and ask "what bounds the memory here?" If the answer is "nothing", it is a bug even if it works today. They think in pipelines with bounded buffers between stages, and they place the buffer where the cheapest waiting happens: in Kafka, in the database cursor, in a bounded queue, never in an unbounded JavaScript array. They batch to make the consumer faster before they add concurrency to make the producer slower. And they know that Promise.all is a fan-out, not a queue; it belongs on a handful of things, never on a list from the database.

Common mistakes

  • Promise.all over a database result set.
  • find() with no take followed by processing in memory.
  • Reading a whole file into memory to "parse it".
  • Adding more consumers instead of batching, which just moves the bottleneck to the database.
  • Ignoring write() returning false on a stream.

Interview questions

  1. What is backpressure and how does Node implement it in streams? Expected: bounded buffers with highWaterMark; write() returns false; wait for drain; pipeline handles it.
  2. Why does Promise.all over 10,000 DB calls hurt the pool, and what do you use instead? Expected: all 10,000 queue in memory for 20 connections; use p-limit/p-map with bounded concurrency and batching.
  3. How do you apply backpressure to a Kafka consumer whose downstream is slow? Expected: pause()/resume() based on downstream depth; lag stays in Kafka.
  4. A batch insert of 1,000 rows fails because of one bad row. What now? Expected: validate before batching; ON CONFLICT for duplicates; fall back to smaller batches or per-row for the failing batch.

Practical exercise

Write a NestJS job that reads 1 million orders via a cursor, groups them into batches of 500, and uploads each batch to a stub HTTP endpoint with p-limit(8). Run it under node --max-old-space-size=256.
