Acceptance criteria: the job completes without OOM; process.memoryUsage().heapUsed never exceeds 150 MB (log it every 5 s); the stub never sees more than 8 concurrent connections; killing the stub mid-run causes the job to pause (not crash) and resume when the stub returns.

30.10 Graceful degradation

Concept

Graceful degradation is the practice of keeping the core of a product working when a non-core part fails, by substituting a cheaper, older or simpler answer for the one you cannot produce right now. The recommendations service is down: show bestsellers. The tax service is down: use yesterday's rate table and flag the order for review. The search cluster is down: fall back to a database ILIKE. The write path to the database is down: switch to read-only mode and let people browse. Each of those is a fallback, and the sum of them is a product that bends instead of breaking.

Why does it exist?

A checkout page calls eight things. If any one failure fails the page, the page's availability is the product of eight availabilities: eight dependencies at 99.9% each give you 99.2%, which is 7 hours of downtime a month. If only two of the eight are truly required and the other six degrade, the page's availability is the product of two: 99.8%, or 90 minutes a month, and those 90 minutes are the payment gateway's problem, not yours. Degradation is how you stop paying for other people's downtime.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that runs out of a side dish. A badly run one closes for the night. A well-run one tells you "no fries tonight, would you like a salad?" and keeps serving. The kitchen decided in advance which items are essential (the grill) and which have substitutes (the sides). Graceful degradation is the substitute menu, decided in advance.

How it works

  1. Classify each feature as core or non-core with the product owner, per page or per flow. Core means "without this, the flow cannot complete correctly". Everything else is non-core and needs a fallback.
  2. Design the fallback per feature. The options, roughly in order of preference:
    • Stale data: serve the last successful result from a cache with a longer TTL than normal (stale-while-revalidate / stale-if-error semantics).
    • Default data: bestsellers instead of recommendations; a default shipping estimate instead of a live one.
    • Deferred work: accept the request, queue the non-core step (email, analytics, loyalty points) for later.
    • Reduced function: read-only mode; search without facets; checkout without promo-code validation (or with an allow-list of known codes).
    • Honest absence: hide the widget; the page renders without the "people also bought" row.
  3. Trigger it automatically, from a circuit breaker fallback, a timeout, or a feature flag an operator can flip.
  4. Make it visible: a metric per fallback (fallback_served_total{feature}) and, where the customer is affected, a UI hint ("estimated delivery times are temporarily unavailable").
  5. Degrade non-core first, and in order. Under overload, shed the cheapest-to-lose feature first (see 30.8): recommendations, then reviews, then live inventory badges, then search facets, and only in the last resort the checkout itself.
flowchart TB
    T0["Tier 0 - Core\ncheckout, payment, auth, order status"] --> K0["Never degraded\nfull timeout, retry, breaker, no fallback"]
    T1["Tier 1 - Important\nsearch, live inventory, shipping estimate"] --> K1["Degrade to cached or\ndefault values"]
    T2["Tier 2 - Nice to have\nrecommendations, reviews, related items"] --> K2["Hide widget or\nshow bestsellers"]
    T3["Tier 3 - Background\nanalytics, loyalty points, emails"] --> K3["Queue and process later"]

The core vs non-core table for an e-commerce checkout:

Step Core? Dependency Fallback
Authenticate user Yes Auth service / session store None (fail request); but cache public keys for JWT verification so auth works while the auth service is down
Load cart Yes PostgreSQL None
Validate promo code No Promo service Accept known codes from cache; reject unknown codes with "try again later"
Calculate tax Semi Tax SaaS Last known rate table (max 24 h old); flag order tax_estimated = true
Shipping estimate No Carrier API Static estimate ("3–5 days")
Reserve inventory Yes Inventory service / PostgreSQL None
Charge card Yes Payment gateway None; but if the gateway supports it, "authorize now, capture later"
Create order Yes PostgreSQL None; if primary is down, read-only mode for the whole site
Send confirmation email No Email provider Queue via outbox; retry for hours
Award loyalty points No Loyalty service Queue; eventual consistency
Recommendations on the thank-you page No Recommendations service Bestsellers from cache; or hide
Analytics event No Kafka Buffer locally and drop after a bound

Practical example

Recommendations are computed by a separate service with a p99 of 400 ms and an availability of 99.5%. The product page calls it with a 500 ms timeout inside a breaker. On timeout, on error, or when the breaker is open, the page uses a bestsellers:{category} key in Redis (refreshed hourly by a job). If Redis is also down, the page renders without the row. None of those three states produces an error for the customer, and all three are counted.

NestJS example

A fallback chain using the breaker's fallback hook and a cache with a long "stale" TTL:

@Injectable()
export class RecommendationsService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(RecommendationsService.name);
  private readonly breaker: CircuitBreaker<[string, string], Product[]>;

  constructor(
    private readonly http: RecommendationsHttp,
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
  ) {
    this.breaker = new CircuitBreaker(
      (userId: string, category: string) => this.http.forUser(userId, category, { timeoutMs: 500 }),
      { name: 'recommendations', timeout: 600, errorThresholdPercentage: 50, volumeThreshold: 20, resetTimeout: 20_000 },
    );
    // Called on failure, timeout, or when the breaker is open.
    this.breaker.fallback((_userId: string, category: string) => this.bestsellers(category));
    this.breaker.on('fallback', () => fallbackServed.inc({ feature: 'recommendations' }));
  }

  forUser(userId: string, category: string): Promise<Product[]> {
    return this.breaker.fire(userId, category);
  }

  private async bestsellers(category: string): Promise<Product[]> {
    try {
      const cached = await this.redis.get(`bestsellers:${category}`);   // refreshed hourly by a job
      return cached ? (JSON.parse(cached) as Product[]) : [];
    } catch (err) {
      this.log.warn({ msg: 'bestsellers cache unavailable', err: String(err) });
      return [];                                                          // honest absence
    }
  }
}

Read-only mode, the whole-site degradation for a primary database outage, as a guard driven by a flag that the failover watcher (30.11) or an operator can set:

@Injectable()
export class ReadOnlyModeGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly flags: FeatureFlagsService) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const mutating = !['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS'].includes(req.method);
    if (mutating && this.flags.isOn('read_only_mode')) {
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException({ code: 'READ_ONLY', message: 'Ordering is paused for maintenance. Browsing still works.' });
    }
    return true;
  }
}

FeatureFlagsService should read from an in-memory copy refreshed every few seconds from Redis or a config service, so that flipping the flag does not itself depend on the thing that is down.

PostgreSQL example

Read-only mode has a database-level counterpart. When the primary is unavailable and a replica is promoted with a delay, or when you deliberately fail reads to a replica during maintenance:

-- On a replica, writes fail with SQLSTATE 25006 (read_only_sql_transaction).
-- The app maps 25006 to the READ_ONLY response instead of a 500.
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, total_cents) VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 'u1', 4200);
-- ERROR:  cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

-- Detect where you are:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();   -- true on a replica

And "stale but present" has a database form too: a materialized view refreshed periodically serves a dashboard when the live aggregation query is too expensive or its source is unavailable:

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW category_bestsellers AS
SELECT category_id, product_id, count(*) AS sales
  FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
 WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
 GROUP BY category_id, product_id;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON category_bestsellers (category_id, product_id);
-- Hourly: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY category_bestsellers;

Production scenario

A grocery-delivery app's home page composes 11 backend calls. After a degradation review, 3 are core (session, cart, store hours) and 8 have fallbacks. Over six months, the fallback metrics show: recommendations fallback served 2.1% of the time; delivery-slot estimate fallback 0.4%; promo banner fallback 6% (the marketing service is flaky); nothing else above 0.1%. Page availability as measured by synthetic checks: 99.97%, against a raw dependency-product availability of about 99.3%. The degradation work was two engineer-weeks.

Failure scenario

A fallback that was too graceful: the tax service fallback used "last known rates" with no age limit. The tax SaaS API key expired silently; the breaker opened; the fallback served rates from the day the key expired, for five weeks, during which a state changed its rate. Nobody noticed because nothing was failing; fallback_served_total had been rising, but no alert was attached. The company under-collected tax on 40,000 orders. Fixes: a maximum age on stale fallbacks (24 h for tax, then fail the step and route orders to manual review), and an alert whenever any fallback rate exceeds 1% for more than 15 minutes. Degradation must be visible, and stale data must have an expiry.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Fallback with no age limit serves data that is wrong, not just old.
  • Fallback that depends on the same failed dependency (bestsellers from the recommendation service's own cache).
  • Silent degradation: no metrics, no alert, no UI hint; the business runs degraded for weeks.
  • Fallback that changes semantics: "accept unknown promo codes" is a revenue leak, "reject unknown codes" is a conversion hit; the product owner must choose.
  • Degrading core by accident because the classification was never written down.
  • Read-only mode that is not enforced at the database: a background job still writes to the primary while the site shows "maintenance".
  • Fallback that is slower than the real thing (a database ILIKE on 5 million rows as a search fallback) and takes the database down too. Bound the fallback's cost.
  • Queued work from a degradation replayed all at once on recovery: 200,000 emails in five minutes. Rate-limit the drain.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They run the core/non-core classification as a workshop with product, because it is a product decision with an engineering implementation. They design the fallback before the feature ships, since bolting it on later means touching every caller. They make stale data carry its age and enforce a maximum. They alert on fallback rates, not just on errors, because "everything is green and we are serving garbage" is the worst incident type. And they prefer honest absence over a fake answer: hiding a widget is fine; inventing a delivery date is not.

To a product manager: "If the recommendations engine breaks, customers see bestsellers instead of an error. If the payment provider breaks, there is no substitute, so we tell them clearly and ask them to try again in a minute. We decide together which features get a Plan B."

Common mistakes

  • Treating every dependency as core, so any failure fails the page.
  • Fallbacks with no observability.
  • Caching stale data without recording when it was cached.
  • A feature-flag system for degradation that lives in the database that is down.

Interview questions

  1. How do you decide which features to degrade and in what order? Expected: core/non-core classification with product; degrade cheapest-to-lose first; never core.
  2. What are the main fallback strategies, in order of preference? Expected: stale data, defaults, deferred work, reduced function, honest absence.
  3. What went wrong in the "five weeks of stale tax rates" story and how would you prevent it? Expected: unbounded staleness and no alert on fallback rate; add max age and alerts.
  4. How would you implement site-wide read-only mode in NestJS, and where must it also be enforced? Expected: a guard on mutating methods driven by an in-memory flag; also stop writers (jobs, consumers); map PostgreSQL 25006.

Practical exercise

For a product page that calls recommendations, reviews and live inventory, implement fallbacks (bestsellers from Redis, hide reviews, "in stock" from a 10-minute cache with cached_at), each with a fallback_served_total{feature} metric and a max age. Use toxiproxy to take each dependency down in turn. Acceptance criteria: the page returns 200 in every case; the response includes a degraded: ["recommendations"] field listing active fallbacks; a fallback older than its max age causes the widget to be hidden rather than shown stale.

30.11 Failover

Concept

Failover is switching to a standby copy of a component when the primary copy fails. It happens on the server side (a database promotes a replica; a load balancer stops sending traffic to a dead node; a Multi-AZ deployment moves to the surviving zone) and on the client side (your application detects that its connection is dead and reconnects to whatever is now primary; it retries against a second endpoint; it sends reads to a replica when the primary is busy). Server-side failover is mostly infrastructure work. Client-side failover is your code, and it is where most failover incidents actually happen.

Why does it exist?

Hardware dies, zones lose power, kernels panic, and cloud providers reboot instances for maintenance. A single-copy component has the availability of the single machine, which is roughly 99.5–99.9%. A primary with a synchronous standby in another availability zone can reach 99.95–99.99%, if the switch happens automatically and if clients follow it correctly. The second "if" is the one this section is about.

Mental model

Imagine a shop with a main phone line and a backup line. When the main line goes dead, the phone company reroutes the number to the backup within a minute. But a customer who is mid-call gets cut off and has to redial; and a customer whose phone has cached the old routing keeps calling a dead line until the cache expires. Server-side failover is the phone company's rerouting. Client-side failover is the customer knowing to redial, and not having a stale cache.

How it works

Server side (PostgreSQL on RDS Multi-AZ, or Patroni on Kubernetes):

  1. Health monitoring detects the primary is unresponsive (typically 10–30 s of failed checks).
  2. A standby is promoted. With synchronous replication, no committed transaction is lost; with asynchronous, the last few hundred milliseconds of commits may be lost.
  3. The DNS name (RDS endpoint) or virtual IP is repointed to the new primary. DNS TTL for RDS endpoints is 5 s; on Kubernetes, the Service endpoints update within a few seconds.
  4. Total: typically 30–120 s from failure to writable-again.

Client side (your NestJS pods): during and after that window, this is what your process sees and must handle:

Moment What the app sees What the app must do
Primary dies In-flight queries error with ECONNRESET / 57P01 (admin shutdown) / socket hang up Fail the in-flight request as unknown outcome; do not retry non-idempotent writes
Standby not yet promoted New connections: ECONNREFUSED or connect timeout Fail fast (1 s connect timeout); return 503 with Retry-After; enter read-only mode if replicas are reachable
DNS repointed Existing pooled connections are dead; new ones go to the new primary Discard dead pooled connections; do not cache DNS beyond TTL; reconnect with jittered backoff
New primary writable Writes succeed again Leave read-only mode; drain deferred work slowly
Old primary comes back as a replica Nothing, if DNS is right; 25006 read-only errors if a client cached the old IP Treat 25006 on the "primary" as "I am on the wrong host": drop the connection and re-resolve

The three client-side failures that matter most:

  • DNS caching. Node does not cache DNS by itself, but dns.lookup uses the OS resolver, and some base images and some libraries (or a cacheable-lookup you added for performance) cache for longer than the TTL. Respect TTL; on ECONNREFUSED force a re-resolve.
  • Pool holding dead connections. pg.Pool discovers a connection is dead only when a query fails on it. After failover, the next N queries (one per pooled connection) each fail once. Handle this by retrying connection-level errors once on a fresh connection for idempotent operations, and by letting the pool's idleTimeoutMillis and error handling evict the dead ones.
  • Writes during the window. Anything that must not be lost goes to the outbox/queue (Part 29), not to a "retry later in memory" list that dies with the pod.

Practical example

An orders service on RDS Multi-AZ. The pool has connectionTimeoutMillis: 1000, idleTimeoutMillis: 10000, and an error handler that logs and discards. A DatabaseHealthWatcher runs SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() every 2 s; if the query fails for 3 consecutive checks the service flips read_only_mode on (browsing still works via the replica pool); when a check succeeds and returns false, it flips the flag off. During a 70 s RDS failover the site served browsing throughout, returned 503 READ_ONLY for 61 s of checkout attempts, and lost zero orders.

NestJS example

A watcher that drives read-only mode from the primary's reachability, and a wrapper that retries idempotent reads once on a fresh connection after a connection-level error:

@Injectable()
export class DatabaseFailoverWatcher implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DatabaseFailoverWatcher.name);
  private failures = 0;
  private timer?: NodeJS.Timeout;

  constructor(
    @InjectDataSource() private readonly primary: DataSource,
    private readonly flags: FeatureFlagsService,
  ) {}

  onModuleInit() { this.timer = setInterval(() => void this.probe(), 2_000); this.timer.unref(); }
  onModuleDestroy() { if (this.timer) clearInterval(this.timer); }

  private async probe() {
    try {
      const [{ pg_is_in_recovery }] = await this.primary.query('SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()');
      if (pg_is_in_recovery) throw new Error('connected to a replica as primary');  // stale DNS
      if (this.failures > 0) this.log.warn({ msg: 'primary reachable again', after: this.failures });
      this.failures = 0;
      this.flags.set('read_only_mode', false);
    } catch (err) {
      this.failures++;
      if (this.failures === 3) {
        this.log.error({ msg: 'primary unreachable, entering read-only mode', err: String(err) });
        this.flags.set('read_only_mode', true);
      }
    }
  }
}

const CONNECTION_ERRORS = new Set(['ECONNRESET', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'EPIPE', '57P01', '57P02', '57P03', '08006', '08001']);

/** Retry idempotent reads once when the pooled connection turned out to be dead. */
export async function readWithFailover<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  try { return await fn(); }
  catch (err) {
    const code = (err as { code?: string }).code ?? '';
    if (!CONNECTION_ERRORS.has(code)) throw err;
    return fn();   // pool hands out a fresh connection; the dead one was discarded on error
  }
}

The two TypeOrmModule.forRoot registrations for primary and replica pools were shown in 30.6; the replica pool is what keeps GET routes alive in read-only mode. TypeORM also supports replication: { master, slaves } in the DataSource options, routing find/SELECT to replicas automatically and writes to the master. It is convenient, but keep in mind that automatic routing sends every read to a replica, including reads inside a write flow that must see the latest data; use queryRunner with 'master' explicitly for those.

PostgreSQL example

What the database shows during and after a failover, and the settings that make clients behave:

-- On the newly promoted primary:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();                 -- false
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();            -- null on a primary

-- On a client that is still talking to the demoted old primary (now replica):
INSERT INTO orders ...;                     -- ERROR 25006: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

-- libpq/pg connection option that helps (supported by node-postgres via the connection string):
-- postgresql://host1:5432,host2:5432/shop?target_session_attrs=read-write
-- With two hosts and target_session_attrs=read-write, the client tries each host and
-- keeps only the one that accepts writes: client-side failover without DNS.

Also relevant: synchronous_commit = on with a synchronous standby (synchronous_standby_names) ensures zero data loss at the cost of write latency (typically +1–3 ms in-region), while remote_apply additionally guarantees the standby has applied the change before commit returns, which makes replica reads consistent immediately after failover.

Sequelize example

export const sequelize = new Sequelize('shop', null as unknown as string, null as unknown as string, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    write: { host: process.env.PG_PRIMARY_HOST, username: 'app_api', password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD },
    read: [
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA_1, username: 'app_ro', password: process.env.PG_RO_PASSWORD },
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA_2, username: 'app_ro', password: process.env.PG_RO_PASSWORD },
    ],
  },
  pool: { max: 20, acquire: 1_000, idle: 10_000 },
});
// Sequelize routes SELECT to a read replica (round-robin) and everything else to write.
// Force a read to the primary inside a write flow with { useMaster: true } on the query options.

Production scenario

Redis Sentinel or Elasticache with automatic failover promotes a replica in 5–30 s. ioredis with Sentinel configuration (sentinels: [...], name: 'mymaster') re-resolves the master from the sentinels on reconnect; with a plain host it reconnects to the same DNS name, which Elasticache repoints. During the window, commands fail with READONLY You can't write against a read only replica if a client lands on the old master, and ioredis treats READONLY as a reason to reconnect. With enableOfflineQueue: false and commandTimeout: 300 (30.4) the cache returns fast errors for the window and the app treats every read as a miss; database load rises about 2.5x for 20 s and returns to normal. That is the designed behaviour, and the capacity plan accounts for it.

Failure scenario

At 04:31 RDS performed an unplanned Multi-AZ failover. The service recovered in 90 s, except one pod that stayed broken for 40 minutes, returning 500 on every write. Its logs showed 25006 cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. That pod's base image ran nscd with a 30-minute positive DNS cache; it kept connecting to the old primary, now a replica, on every new connection. The other pods, on a newer image without nscd, followed the RDS endpoint's 5 s TTL. Fixes: remove nscd, treat 25006 on the primary pool as "wrong host" (drop the pool and re-resolve), and make the readiness probe fail if pg_is_in_recovery() is true on the primary connection so Kubernetes stops routing to a confused pod.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Split brain: the old primary still accepts writes because it did not notice it was demoted; a client with a cached address writes to it; those writes are lost. Fencing (Patroni, RDS) prevents this on the server side; target_session_attrs=read-write and pg_is_in_recovery() checks protect you on the client side.
  • Asynchronous replication loses the tail. Orders committed in the last 200 ms before the crash may not exist on the new primary. The outbox and idempotent clients let them be safely re-submitted.
  • Replica lag after failover: the new primary's replicas re-sync; reads may be stale for minutes. Route consistency-critical reads to the primary.
  • Connection storm on recovery: 40 pods x 20 connections reconnect at once; jittered backoff (30.4) and max on each pool bound it.
  • In-flight transactions during failover are lost; the app must treat the error as unknown outcome.
  • Client library "reconnect" that replays buffered commands (Redis offline queue) executes stale writes after failover.
  • Health checks that depend on the primary mark every pod unready during failover and remove all capacity (30.12); readiness should reflect "can I serve something", not "is every dependency perfect".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume the database will fail over, and they test it: a game day (30.15) where someone triggers an RDS reboot-with-failover in staging while load runs. They watch for the three client-side sins (stale DNS, dead pooled connections, non-idempotent retries) and fix them before production finds them. They use target_session_attrs=read-write or a proxy (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) to make client-side failover boring. They keep a read-only mode ready because it turns a 90 s outage into a 90 s "browsing only" period. And they know the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication in terms of which orders they might lose, and have written that down for the business.

Common mistakes

  • Never testing failover, so the first real one is a surprise.
  • Retrying writes after a connection error without idempotency keys.
  • DNS caches (nscd, cacheable-lookup, custom lookup functions) that outlive the TTL.
  • Reading your own writes from a replica immediately after failover.
  • Assuming a pooled connection is alive because it was five seconds ago.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what your NestJS pods see during an RDS Multi-AZ failover and what they must do at each step. Expected: the table above; unknown-outcome handling; pool eviction; DNS TTL; read-only mode.
  2. What is target_session_attrs=read-write and why does it help? Expected: libpq tries multiple hosts and keeps the writable one; client-side failover without DNS dependency.
  3. Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: what does each mean for data loss at failover? Expected: sync loses nothing but adds write latency; async can lose the last few hundred milliseconds.
  4. A pod keeps getting 25006 after failover while others are fine. What happened? Expected: stale DNS cache; connected to the demoted primary; fix DNS and detect the condition.

Practical exercise

Run PostgreSQL primary and replica in Docker with repmgr or Patroni (or simulate with two containers and manual promotion). Point a NestJS app at a DNS name (or a pg multi-host connection string with target_session_attrs=read-write). While autocannon drives 50 RPS of writes, kill the primary and promote the replica. Acceptance criteria: the app enters read-only mode within 6 s, GET routes keep returning 200 from the replica pool, no write returns 500 (only 503 READ_ONLY), and the app resumes writes within 10 s of promotion without a restart.

30.12 Health checks

Concept

A health check is an endpoint (or command) that the platform calls to ask your process a question. Kubernetes asks three different questions, and confusing them is the source of most health-check incidents:

  • Liveness: "Are you alive at all, or should I kill and restart you?" A failing liveness probe causes a restart.
  • Readiness: "Can you take traffic right now?" A failing readiness probe removes the pod from the Service's endpoints; traffic stops, but the pod keeps running.
  • Startup: "Have you finished booting?" Until the startup probe passes, liveness and readiness are not evaluated, which protects slow-starting processes from being killed mid-boot.

Why does it exist?

A process can be running and useless: deadlocked event loop, out of file descriptors, unable to reach its database, still loading a 2 GB model. Without health checks the load balancer keeps sending traffic to it and every request fails. With health checks the platform can route around a sick pod (readiness) and replace a dead one (liveness). The distinction matters because the two remedies have very different blast radii: removing a pod from rotation is cheap and reversible; restarting it destroys in-flight work and, if the cause is external, restarts every pod in a loop.

Mental model

Imagine a taxi rank. Liveness asks the driver "are you conscious?" If not, tow the car away. Readiness asks "are you free to take a passenger right now?" If not (refuelling, on a break), skip them for this fare but leave them in the rank. You would never tow a car because the driver is refuelling. And you would never decide a driver is unconscious because the petrol station is closed, which is exactly what a liveness check that pings the database does.

How it works

  1. Kubernetes calls the probe on a schedule (periodSeconds), with its own timeoutSeconds, and counts consecutive failures against failureThreshold.
  2. Your endpoint runs a set of indicators and returns 200 if all pass, 503 otherwise, with a JSON body describing each.
  3. Readiness failure: the endpoint controller removes the pod IP from the Service; the pod continues running; when the probe passes again the pod is re-added.
  4. Liveness failure: the kubelet kills the container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period) and restarts it, with CrashLoopBackOff delays if it keeps failing.

What each probe must and must not check:

Probe Must check Must NOT check Why
Liveness The process can respond at all: event loop responsive, no fatal internal state Database, Redis, any network dependency If the DB is down and liveness pings it, every pod restarts forever; restarts do not fix the DB
Readiness Things without which this pod cannot serve anything: DB pool can get a connection (fast ping, short timeout), required config loaded, warm caches if mandatory Third-party APIs, non-core dependencies, replicas, anything with a fallback A readiness check on the payment gateway marks all pods unready when the gateway is down, taking the whole site down instead of just checkout
Startup Migrations applied, config loaded, first DB connection made Anything slow that happens repeatedly It only runs at boot

The rule of thumb: liveness checks the process, readiness checks the pod's ability to do its core job, and neither checks anything you have a fallback for. If the readiness probe includes something, a failure of that thing removes all your capacity. Ask for each indicator: "when this is down, do I want zero pods in rotation?" Usually the answer is no.

Practical example

A NestJS orders API exposes /health/live (returns 200 if the event loop responds; nothing else), /health/ready (PostgreSQL ping with a 300 ms timeout on the API pool, plus "migrations are at the expected version", plus "not shutting down"), and /health/startup (same as ready, but Kubernetes gives it 60 s x 5 attempts). Redis, Kafka and the payment gateway are not in readiness, because the service has fallbacks for Redis (cache miss), buffers for Kafka (outbox), and a 503 path for payments.

NestJS example

Using @nestjs/terminus with built-in indicators and one custom indicator via HealthIndicatorService:

import { Controller, Get, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  MemoryHealthIndicator, HealthIndicatorService, HealthIndicatorResult,
} from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { ShutdownState } from './shutdown-state';

@Injectable()
export class AppStateIndicator {
  constructor(private readonly hi: HealthIndicatorService, private readonly shutdown: ShutdownState) {}

  notShuttingDown(): HealthIndicatorResult {
    const ind = this.hi.check('app_state');
    return this.shutdown.isShuttingDown ? ind.down({ reason: 'draining' }) : ind.up();
  }
}

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly memory: MemoryHealthIndicator,
    private readonly appState: AppStateIndicator,
  ) {}

  /** Liveness: is the process able to respond at all? No dependencies. */
  @Get('live')
  live() { return { status: 'ok' }; }

  /** Readiness: can this pod do its core job right now? */
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 300 }),          // fast ping on the API pool
      () => this.memory.checkHeap('heap', 900 * 1024 * 1024),           // shed traffic near the limit
      () => this.appState.notShuttingDown(),                           // fail fast during drain
    ]);
  }
}

HealthCheckService.check runs the indicators, returns { status: 'ok' | 'error', info, error, details }, and Terminus sets the HTTP status to 503 when any indicator is down. TerminusModule.forRoot({ gracefulShutdownTimeoutMs: 5000 }) makes readiness fail for 5 s before the app closes on SIGTERM, which is what lets Kubernetes stop routing before the server stops listening (next section).

The Kubernetes side, with values that match the probes:

containers:
  - name: app
    ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 24            # up to 120 s to boot (migrations, warmup)
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 5
      timeoutSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 3             # 15 s of failures before removal from the Service
      successThreshold: 1
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 3             # 30 s of no response before restart

The liveness timeout is the important part: a Node process whose event loop is blocked (a synchronous 5 s JSON parse, a CPU-bound loop) will fail to answer in 2 s, and that is the condition you actually want a restart for.

PostgreSQL example

The readiness ping should be the cheapest possible statement on the pool the API actually uses, with a server-side timeout so it cannot hang:

-- What Terminus' TypeOrmHealthIndicator runs:
SELECT 1;

-- A slightly richer readiness check that also detects "I am connected to a replica by mistake"
-- and "migrations are behind", both in one cheap round trip:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery,
       (SELECT max(id) FROM migrations) AS migration_version;

Never put an expensive query in readiness (SELECT count(*) FROM orders). At periodSeconds: 5 across 40 pods that is 8 count-scans per second, forever.

Production scenario

A payments service with 20 pods runs readiness every 5 s, with a 300 ms DB ping. During a PostgreSQL primary failover (60 s), readiness fails on all pods for the duration: the Service has zero endpoints, and the gateway returns 503 for the payments route for 60 s. That is acceptable for payments, because payments cannot work without the database. The catalog service, on the same database, has a replica pool and a read-only mode, so its readiness only checks the replica ping; it stays in rotation and serves browsing throughout. Same infrastructure event, two correct and different readiness policies.

Failure scenario

At 14:02 the entire e-commerce site went down for 25 minutes because of a health check. The readiness probe on the api deployment included an HttpHealthIndicator.pingCheck('reviews', 'http://reviews.svc/health') added by a well-meaning engineer "to make sure the whole system is healthy". The reviews service had a slow deploy: its own readiness took 8 s. The API's readiness probe had timeoutSeconds: 3, so it failed on every pod, every pod was removed from the Service, and the gateway had nothing to route to. Reviews were a non-core feature with a fallback that already worked. The check had turned a 0% impact event into a 100% outage. Post-mortem rule, now enforced in code review: readiness may only include dependencies the pod cannot serve any traffic without, and every one of them needs a timeout under 500 ms.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Liveness that pings a dependency: restart loop across all pods for an external cause.
  • Readiness that includes a non-core dependency: total outage from a partial failure.
  • Probe timeout longer than the probe interval: overlapping probes pile up on a slow pod.
  • Flapping readiness (DB ping at exactly its timeout): pods bounce in and out of the Service, connection churn everywhere. Add hysteresis via failureThreshold and successThreshold.
  • Expensive readiness multiplies with pod count.
  • Health endpoint behind auth or rate limiting: the kubelet gets 401/429 and restarts the pod. Exclude /health/* from guards and throttling.
  • Health endpoint that allocates (creates a new DB connection per probe instead of using the pool): pool exhaustion caused by monitoring.
  • Liveness during garbage collection pauses longer than the timeout on huge heaps; raise the timeout or shrink the heap.
  • Startup probe missing: slow boots (migrations) get killed by liveness before they finish, and the migration is left half-applied unless it is transactional.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design health checks from the remedy backward: "if this check fails, Kubernetes will do X; is X the right response to this condition?" Restarting a pod is the right response to a hung event loop and to nothing else. Removing a pod from rotation is the right response to "this pod cannot get a database connection", and the wrong response to "a partner API is slow". They keep the probes fast, dependency-light and unauthenticated, and they review every added indicator with the question "when this is down, do I want zero pods?"

Common mistakes

  • One /health endpoint used for both liveness and readiness.
  • Checking every dependency because "more checks is more safety".
  • No startup probe on a service that runs migrations at boot.
  • Health checks that hit the primary database when the pod could serve from a replica.

Interview questions

  1. Explain liveness, readiness and startup probes and what Kubernetes does when each fails. Expected: restart / remove from Service / defer other probes.
  2. Should a readiness probe check the payment gateway? Why not? Expected: no; a gateway outage would remove all pods; checkout has its own 503 path.
  3. Why should liveness never check the database? Expected: an external failure becomes a restart loop; restarts cannot fix it.
  4. Tell me about a health check that caused an outage. Expected: the non-core dependency in readiness story or similar; rule derived.

Practical exercise

Add /health/live, /health/ready, and /health/startup to a NestJS app with @nestjs/terminus. Deploy to a local Kubernetes (kind or minikube) with the probe configuration above. Acceptance criteria: blocking the event loop for 40 s (a synchronous loop triggered by a debug endpoint) causes a restart within 45 s; stopping PostgreSQL removes the pod from the Service within 20 s without a restart; adding 3 s latency to a third-party dependency with toxiproxy changes nothing about the pod's readiness.

30.13 Graceful shutdown

Concept

Graceful shutdown is the sequence a process follows when asked to stop, so that no in-flight work is lost, no client sees a connection reset, and no resource (database connection, Kafka partition, lock) is left dangling. The platform asks by sending SIGTERM. The process has a grace period (Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30 s) to finish; then it is killed with SIGKILL, which cannot be caught.

Why does it exist?

Pods stop all the time: every deploy, every scale-down, every node upgrade, every spot-instance reclaim. If stopping a pod loses the 40 requests it was serving, the 3 Kafka messages it was processing, and the transaction it had open, then every deploy is a small incident. At 10 deploys a day across 30 services, that is 300 small incidents a day. Graceful shutdown makes stopping a pod a non-event, which is the precondition for deploying often.

Mental model

Imagine closing a shop for the night. You do not turn off the lights with customers still at the till. You lock the front door (stop accepting new customers), serve everyone already inside (finish in-flight work), close the registers (commit and close connections), and then turn off the lights (exit). If the landlord gives you 30 minutes to be out, you plan to be done in 20.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Kubernetes
    participant P as Pod
    participant LB as Service endpoints
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant KF as Kafka
    K->>P: preStop hook runs, e.g. sleep 5
    K->>LB: remove pod IP from endpoints
    Note over LB: propagation takes 1 to 5 s
    K->>P: SIGTERM
    P->>P: readiness returns 503, stop accepting new connections
    P->>P: finish in-flight HTTP requests
    P->>KF: stop fetching, finish current batch, commit offsets, leave group
    P->>DB: finish or roll back open transactions, close pool
    P->>K: exit 0
    Note over K: SIGKILL only if grace period expires

Step by step, in a NestJS process:

  1. Kubernetes decides to stop the pod. It runs the preStop hook and starts removing the pod from Service endpoints in parallel. Endpoint removal takes a few seconds to propagate to every kube-proxy and ingress. A preStop of sleep 5 gives that propagation time before the process is told anything; during those 5 s the pod is still serving normally.
  2. SIGTERM arrives. NestJS, with app.enableShutdownHooks(), catches it and begins app.close().
  3. Stop accepting new work. The readiness endpoint starts returning 503 (ShutdownState, or Terminus' gracefulShutdownTimeoutMs). The HTTP server stops listening. Keep-alive connections that are idle are closed; ones with a request in progress are allowed to finish.
  4. Finish in-flight work. HTTP requests complete. BullMQ workers finish their active jobs (worker.close() waits). Kafka consumers stop fetching, finish the current eachMessage/eachBatch, commit offsets, and leave the group (consumer.disconnect()), which triggers a rebalance so other pods pick up the partitions.
  5. Release resources. OnModuleDestroy -> BeforeApplicationShutdown(signal) -> OnApplicationShutdown(signal) run in that order across modules (destroy hooks run in reverse dependency order). Close the DataSource (returns pooled connections cleanly, so PostgreSQL does not log connection resets), quit Redis, close the Kafka producer.
  6. Exit 0. Well within the grace period. If you cannot finish (a 5-minute job is running), you have two choices: make the grace period long enough, or make the work resumable and abort it cleanly.

Practical example

An orders API with a Kafka consumer and a BullMQ worker in the same process (not ideal, but common). Deploy rolls 12 pods one at a time. Each old pod: preStop sleep 5; SIGTERM; readiness 503; HTTP server closes (in-flight p99 is 800 ms, so this takes under a second); the Kafka consumer finishes its current batch of 100 messages (about 2 s), commits, leaves the group; the BullMQ worker finishes its 1–2 active jobs (up to 10 s); the pool closes; exit. Total: 8–18 s, under a 30 s grace period. Zero 502s during the deploy, zero duplicate Kafka processing beyond the at-least-once baseline, zero lost jobs.

NestJS example

Bootstrap with shutdown hooks and correct HTTP server timeouts, plus a ShutdownState provider the health check reads:

// main.ts
async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true });
  app.enableShutdownHooks();                       // listen for SIGTERM/SIGINT and call app.close()

  const server = app.getHttpServer() as import('node:http').Server;
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;                // > ALB idle timeout (60 s)
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000;                  // > keepAliveTimeout
  server.requestTimeout = 30_000;

  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

// shutdown-state.ts
@Injectable()
export class ShutdownState implements BeforeApplicationShutdown {
  isShuttingDown = false;
  private readonly log = new Logger(ShutdownState.name);

  async beforeApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.isShuttingDown = true;                    // readiness now returns 503
    this.log.warn({ msg: 'shutdown started', signal });
    // Give the load balancer a moment to see the failing readiness probe
    // before the HTTP server actually closes (in addition to the preStop sleep).
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2_000));
  }
}

Draining the Kafka consumer and BullMQ worker, and closing the database, in the right order:

@Injectable()
export class KafkaConsumerLifecycle implements OnModuleInit, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly log = new Logger(KafkaConsumerLifecycle.name);
  constructor(@Inject(KAFKA_CONSUMER) private readonly consumer: Consumer) {}

  async onModuleInit() {
    await this.consumer.connect();
    await this.consumer.subscribe({ topic: 'orders.created' });
    await this.consumer.run({ eachMessage: (p) => this.handle(p) });
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.log.warn({ msg: 'draining kafka consumer', signal });
    // kafkajs: stops the fetch loop, waits for the in-flight handler to return,
    // commits offsets, leaves the group. Bounded by the caller's grace period.
    await this.consumer.disconnect();
  }
}

@Injectable()
export class WorkerLifecycle implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  constructor(private readonly worker: Worker) {}                 // BullMQ Worker
  async onApplicationShutdown() {
    await this.worker.close();      // waits for active jobs to finish; close(true) would abort them
  }
}

@Injectable()
export class DatabaseLifecycle implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}
  async onApplicationShutdown() {
    if (this.ds.isInitialized) await this.ds.destroy();   // returns connections cleanly, closes pool
  }
}

Order matters: consumers and workers stop before the database closes, otherwise a job finishes its last step against a closed pool. NestJS runs onApplicationShutdown hooks module by module; put the database module at the root so its hook runs last, or explicitly sequence the drain inside one lifecycle provider.

The Kubernetes side:

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45          # must exceed preStop + drain + close
  containers:
    - name: app
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] # let endpoint removal propagate before SIGTERM

terminationGracePeriodSeconds counts from the moment termination starts, including the preStop sleep. With sleep 5 and a 45 s period, the process has 40 s after SIGTERM.

Two Node details that bite people: SIGTERM has no default handler that runs your cleanup (the default is to exit immediately), which is why enableShutdownHooks() is required; and process.exit() anywhere in your shutdown path skips every pending await. Let the event loop drain and exit naturally.

PostgreSQL example

What a graceful close looks like versus an abrupt one, from the database's point of view:

-- Abrupt (SIGKILL, or process.exit before pool.end()): server log shows
-- LOG:  could not receive data from client: Connection reset by peer
-- LOG:  unexpected EOF on client connection with an open transaction
-- Open transactions are rolled back; locks are released; but only after TCP notices, which
-- can take tcp_keepalives_idle (default 2 h!) if the client vanished without a FIN.

-- Protect yourself server-side regardless of client behaviour:
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_idle = 60;             -- detect dead clients in ~1–2 minutes
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_interval = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET tcp_keepalives_count = 3;
ALTER ROLE app_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';

-- During a drain, watch for stuck sessions from the pod being terminated:
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS tx_age, left(query, 60)
  FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE usename = 'app_api' AND state <> 'idle'
 ORDER BY tx_age DESC;

Production scenario

A deploy of 30 pods with a 4 s p99 request, a Kafka consumer, and a terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30. Before graceful shutdown was implemented: each deploy produced 200–400 502s at the ALB (requests on connections Node had already closed), and Kafka consumer lag spiked for 90 s per pod because partitions were reassigned only after the session timeout (sessionTimeout: 30000) expired for the dead consumer. After: 502s per deploy fell to 0–3 (all from clients with their own broken keep-alive handling), and lag during deploys became invisible because the consumer left the group explicitly, triggering an immediate rebalance.

Failure scenario

At 16:45 a routine deploy of the billing worker double-charged 212 customers. The worker processed "capture payment" jobs in batches of 50 and marked them as captured only at the end of the batch. The deploy sent SIGTERM; the process had no shutdown hooks, so Node exited immediately mid-batch; the batch was 30 jobs in, so 30 captures had happened at the gateway and none were marked. The new pod re-ran the batch. Two fixes: per-job completion marking inside the same transaction as the capture record (so a restart resumes at job 31), and graceful shutdown that finishes the current job and stops. A third, from Part 29: an idempotency key on every capture call so that even an ungraceful exit cannot double-charge.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shutdown killing in-flight transactions: process.exit() or a missing hook. Transactions roll back; the client sees an error for work that must be redone.
  • Draining longer than the grace period: a 5-minute job; Kubernetes sends SIGKILL. Either raise the period (up to a few minutes is fine), or make jobs resumable and abort on SIGTERM via an AbortSignal passed into the job.
  • Readiness still passing during drain: the LB keeps sending requests to a server that is closing; 502s. Flip readiness first, wait a beat, then close.
  • Keep-alive connections not closed: Node's server.close() waits for idle keep-alive connections until they time out. Node 19+ closes idle connections in close(); on older versions call server.closeIdleConnections().
  • Consumer leaves without committing: at-least-once redelivery of the last batch; handlers must be idempotent (Part 29).
  • Pool closed before workers finish: "Cannot use a pool after calling end on the pool". Order the hooks.
  • Two SIGTERM handlers (yours and Nest's) racing; use Nest's hooks only.
  • Health probe removed pod, but a sticky ingress still routes to it: some ingress controllers hold connections; the preStop sleep plus draining covers most; for stubborn cases, return Connection: close on responses once draining starts.
  • CronJobs and one-shot pods that ignore SIGTERM during a node drain.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat "can this pod be killed at any moment without harm?" as a requirement, because it is the property that makes autoscaling, spot instances, node upgrades and frequent deploys safe. They implement the drain once, in a shared lifecycle module, and they test it: kubectl delete pod during a load test, watching 502 counts and consumer lag. They size the grace period from the measured drain time with margin. And they combine graceful shutdown with idempotency, because graceful shutdown is what makes deploys clean and idempotency is what makes crashes survivable; you need both.

Common mistakes

  • No enableShutdownHooks(); the process dies instantly on SIGTERM.
  • process.on('SIGTERM', () => process.exit(0)), which is the same as no handler.
  • No preStop sleep, so the server closes before the load balancer stops sending.
  • Closing the database pool first.
  • Grace period shorter than the longest job.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what happens from kubectl rollout restart to the old pod exiting, and what your NestJS app must do at each step. Expected: endpoint removal + preStop, SIGTERM, readiness 503, server close, drain consumers/workers, close pools, exit.
  2. Why is a preStop sleep needed even though the app handles SIGTERM correctly? Expected: endpoint removal propagates asynchronously; without the sleep, traffic arrives at a closing server.
  3. How do you drain a Kafka consumer safely? Expected: stop fetching, finish the in-flight batch, commit, leave the group (disconnect()), before closing the database.
  4. A job takes 5 minutes; your grace period is 30 s. What do you do? Expected: make the job resumable and abort on SIGTERM, or extend the grace period; never let SIGKILL cut it.

Practical exercise

Implement graceful shutdown in a NestJS app with an HTTP server, a BullMQ worker and a TypeORM DataSource, deployed to kind with a preStop sleep and a 45 s grace period. Drive 100 RPS with autocannon and a steady stream of 3 s jobs, then kubectl rollout restart three times. Acceptance criteria: zero non-2xx responses at the client during rollouts; every job completes exactly once (verify with a unique constraint on job_results.job_id); PostgreSQL logs show no "connection reset by peer" from the app; each old pod exits within 20 s.

30.14 Idempotency as a reliability primitive

Concept

An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. In reliability terms, idempotency is what makes every other pattern in this part safe. Timeouts leave you with unknown outcomes; retries re-send; failover reconnects mid-write; graceful shutdown re-delivers the last Kafka batch; degradation queues work for later replay. Every one of those produces duplicates, and idempotency is the property that turns a duplicate from a double charge into a no-op. Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency covers the mechanics in depth; this section places it in the reliability toolbox.

Why does it exist?

Because "exactly once" does not exist across a network. A request either arrives zero, one, or many times, and the sender cannot tell which. The only way to get exactly-once effects is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. Without it, a senior engineer cannot safely enable retries on any write, and without retries the system's user-visible error rate is the raw transient failure rate of every dependency.

Mental model

Imagine a light switch versus a "toggle" button. Pressing "on" twice leaves the light on. Pressing "toggle" twice leaves it off. Reliability patterns keep pressing buttons on your behalf; make the buttons switches.

How it works

  1. The caller generates a unique key per logical operation (Idempotency-Key: order_8842_capture), once, before the first attempt, and reuses it on every retry.
  2. The callee records the key with the outcome, atomically with the side effect (same transaction, or a unique constraint that fails the duplicate insert).
  3. A repeated key returns the recorded outcome instead of re-executing.
  4. For your own writes, prefer naturally idempotent statements: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, UPDATE ... SET status = 'paid' WHERE status = 'pending', upserts keyed by a business id.

NestJS example

A minimal idempotency guard for POST /orders/:id/capture, backed by a PostgreSQL table so that it survives Redis outages and pod restarts:

@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Returns the stored response if this key was already completed; otherwise claims it. */
  async claim(key: string, scope: string): Promise<{ replay?: unknown }> {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(
      `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, scope, status, created_at)
       VALUES ($1, $2, 'in_progress', now())
       ON CONFLICT (key, scope) DO UPDATE SET key = EXCLUDED.key   -- no-op update to RETURNING
       RETURNING status, response, (xmax = 0) AS inserted`,
      [key, scope],
    );
    const row = rows[0];
    if (row.inserted) return {};                                        // first time: proceed
    if (row.status === 'completed') return { replay: row.response };    // duplicate: replay
    throw new ConflictException('request with this key is still in progress');
  }

  async complete(key: string, scope: string, response: unknown): Promise<void> {
    await this.ds.query(
      `UPDATE idempotency_keys SET status = 'completed', response = $3, completed_at = now()
        WHERE key = $1 AND scope = $2`, [key, scope, JSON.stringify(response)],
    );
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key          text NOT NULL,
  scope        text NOT NULL,                 -- e.g. 'capture', so keys cannot collide across operations
  status       text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('in_progress', 'completed')),
  response     jsonb,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  completed_at timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (key, scope)
);
-- Expire old keys with a nightly job: DELETE ... WHERE created_at < now() - interval '7 days'.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They refuse to enable retries on a write until the write is idempotent, and they refuse to accept a webhook without deduplicating on the provider's event id. They design idempotency keys from business identity (order id + operation) rather than random UUIDs, so that a client that crashed and restarted still produces the same key. And they see idempotency as the foundation, not a feature: it is what allows the rest of this part to be switched on safely.

Interview questions

  1. Why is idempotency a reliability concern and not just an API-design concern? Expected: every reliability pattern introduces duplicates; idempotency makes them harmless.
  2. How do you make a payment capture idempotent end-to-end? Expected: business-derived key, sent to the gateway and stored locally atomically with the outcome; replay on duplicate.

30.15 Chaos testing

Concept

Chaos testing (or chaos engineering) is deliberately injecting failures into a running system to verify that the reliability patterns actually work. You kill a pod and check that requests are not lost. You add 3 s of latency to the payment gateway and check that the timeout, breaker and fallback behave. You partition Redis and check that the cache degrades to misses instead of errors. A game day is a scheduled exercise where the team runs several of these against staging (or, carefully, production) and practises the response.

Why does it exist?

Every pattern in this part is a hypothesis: "if the gateway hangs, the breaker opens in 10 s and checkout returns a friendly 503." Hypotheses that have never been tested are usually wrong in some detail: the timeout is on the wrong client, the breaker's error filter counts the wrong errors, the health check includes the dependency, the fallback depends on the failed thing. Chaos testing finds these in the afternoon instead of at 02:14.

Mental model

Imagine a fire drill. Everyone knows where the exits are, in theory. The drill reveals that one exit is locked, the alarm cannot be heard in the basement, and nobody knows who counts heads. Chaos testing is the fire drill for your reliability design.

How it works

  1. State the hypothesis. "With inventory-service latency at 3 s, checkout p99 stays under 4 s and returns 503 INVENTORY_UNAVAILABLE for the affected requests; no request exceeds 5 s; no pod restarts."
  2. Pick the smallest blast radius that tests it: one dependency, one pod, staging first.
  3. Inject the failure. Tools:
    • Kill pods: kubectl delete pod (tests graceful shutdown, consumer rebalancing, retries), or a chaos controller (Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos) for scheduled random kills.
    • Latency and faults: toxiproxy sits between your app and a dependency as a TCP proxy; you add "toxics" (latency, bandwidth limit, connection reset, slow close, timeout) at runtime via its API.
    • Resource pressure: stress-ng in a sidecar for CPU/memory; tc netem for packet loss.
    • Dependency outage: scale a service to zero; block a security group; stop Redis.
  4. Observe with the same dashboards and alerts you would use in a real incident. If an alert should have fired and did not, that is a finding.
  5. Fix, then repeat. Keep a runbook of the experiments and their last result.

Practical example

toxiproxy in docker-compose for local and CI chaos, proxying PostgreSQL and the payment gateway stub:

services:
  toxiproxy:
    image: ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.9.0
    ports: ["8474:8474", "15432:15432", "18080:18080"]
  app:
    environment:
      PG_HOST: toxiproxy
      PG_PORT: "15432"
      PAYMENT_URL: http://toxiproxy:18080
# Create proxies (once), then inject failures on demand.
toxiproxy-cli create -l 0.0.0.0:15432 -u postgres:5432 pg
toxiproxy-cli create -l 0.0.0.0:18080 -u payment-stub:8080 payment

# 2 s latency with 500 ms jitter on responses from the payment gateway
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=2000 -a jitter=500 payment
# Reset connections to PostgreSQL after 1 KB (simulates a failover mid-query)
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t limit_data -a bytes=1024 pg
# Full outage
toxiproxy-cli toggle payment
# Remove all toxics
toxiproxy-cli toxic remove -n latency_downstream payment

NestJS example

A Jest integration test that turns a reliability hypothesis into an assertion, using the toxiproxy-node-client API:

import { Toxiproxy, Toxic } from 'toxiproxy-node-client';

describe('checkout under payment gateway latency', () => {
  const tp = new Toxiproxy('http://localhost:8474');
  let proxy: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof tp.get>>;

  beforeAll(async () => { proxy = await tp.get('payment'); });
  afterEach(async () => { for (const t of await proxy.getToxics()) await t.remove(); });

  it('opens the breaker and returns 503 within the budget', async () => {
    await proxy.addToxic(new Toxic(proxy, {
      name: 'slow', type: 'latency', stream: 'downstream', toxicity: 1, attributes: { latency: 5_000, jitter: 0 },
    }));

    // 30 requests: enough to cross volumeThreshold=20 with 100% failures.
    const results = await Promise.all(
      Array.from({ length: 30 }, () => request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/orders/o1/capture').send({})),
    );
    expect(results.every((r) => r.status === 503)).toBe(true);
    expect(Math.max(...results.map((r) => Number(r.header['x-response-time'])))).toBeLessThan(3_200);

    const metrics = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/metrics');
    expect(metrics.text).toMatch(/circuit_breaker_state\{name="payment-gateway"\} 1/);
  });
});

Production scenario

A quarterly game day for a ride-booking platform, run in staging with production-shaped load: (1) delete 3 of 12 API pods during a load test; (2) add 4 s latency to the maps provider; (3) stop Redis for 2 minutes; (4) trigger an RDS reboot with failover; (5) fill the notifications queue with 500,000 jobs. Findings from the last one: experiment 2 revealed that the maps fallback (cached ETAs) had a bug that returned ETAs for the wrong city; experiment 4 revealed that one service's DNS cache was 5 minutes; experiment 5 revealed that the queue consumer had no p-limit and OOMKilled. Three real bugs, no customers involved.

Failure scenario

A team ran its first chaos experiment in production with a "random pod killer" at 10% of pods per hour, without first testing graceful shutdown. Every kill dropped 30–50 in-flight requests and caused a Kafka rebalance that reprocessed the last batch, which was not idempotent. Customers received duplicate order confirmations for a week before anyone connected the two. Chaos testing found the problem, as designed, but in the wrong environment. Blast radius first, always.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Chaos in production without a kill switch. Every experiment needs a one-command abort.
  • Chaos that tests the wrong layer: adding latency at the proxy when the real failure is a slow TLS handshake that a proxy hides.
  • Latency injection that also delays the health check (same proxy), so the pod is removed from rotation and the experiment measures nothing.
  • Staging that does not resemble production (1 pod, no load): experiments pass trivially.
  • No observability during the experiment: you cannot tell if the system did the right thing.
  • Experiments that never get repeated after fixes, so regressions return silently.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see every reliability control as untested until chaos has exercised it. They automate the cheap experiments into CI (a toxiproxy latency test per critical dependency) and schedule the expensive ones as game days with the on-call rotation present, because the drill is as much about people as about code. They start in staging, they start small, and they write down the hypothesis before injecting anything.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping chaos because "we have unit tests for the retry logic".
  • Running chaos in production before staging.
  • Injecting failures without watching the dashboards.
  • Testing only outages, never slowness (slowness is more common and more damaging).

Interview questions

  1. How would you verify that your circuit breaker actually works? Expected: inject latency or errors with toxiproxy under load; assert state metric and response times.
  2. What is a game day and what makes a good one? Expected: scheduled, hypothesis-driven, bounded blast radius, on-call participates, findings become tickets.
  3. Why is latency injection more valuable than outage injection? Expected: slow dependencies cause resource exhaustion and cascades; outages fail fast.

Practical exercise

Add toxiproxy to your local docker-compose, route PostgreSQL and one HTTP dependency through it, and write three Jest integration tests: (a) 5 s latency on the HTTP dependency opens the breaker; (b) a PostgreSQL connection reset mid-transaction results in a rollback and a 503, never a 500 or a partial write; (c) killing the app process (SIGTERM) mid-request completes the in-flight request. Acceptance criteria: all three pass in CI and each asserts on a metric as well as on the HTTP response.

30.16 Putting it together: a resilient PaymentGatewayClient

Concept

This section assembles the patterns into one production-grade client for the most sensitive dependency in an e-commerce system: the payment gateway. The client applies, in order from the outside in: deadline (the caller's remaining budget), circuit breaker (fail fast when the gateway is down), bulkhead (bounded concurrency and a dedicated socket pool), retry with jitter (only when an idempotency key makes it safe), timeout (per attempt, from the remaining deadline), response validation (a 200 with the wrong shape is a failure), plus metrics and structured logs on every path.

flowchart LR
    S["OrdersService\ndeadline 3 s"] --> B["Circuit breaker\nopossum, per gateway"]
    B --> K["Bulkhead\ncapacity 200, agent 50 sockets"]
    K --> R["Retry\n2 attempts, jitter,\nidempotency-key aware"]
    R --> T["Timeout per attempt\nfrom remaining deadline"]
    T --> H["undici request\nvalidate response"]
    H --> G["Payment gateway"]
    B -.->|"open"| F["503 + Retry-After"]

How it works

The order of layers is deliberate. The breaker is outermost so that when the gateway is down we do not even consume a bulkhead slot or wait for a retry. The bulkhead is next so that an open-for-business gateway cannot hold more than 200 of our requests. Retries sit inside the bulkhead so that one logical call occupies one slot regardless of attempts. The timeout is innermost and is recomputed per attempt from the deadline, so that attempts never overrun the caller's budget. Validation happens on every successful response before it is returned or counted as a success.

NestJS example

Types, errors and the response DTO with validation:

import { IsIn, IsInt, IsString, Min, validateOrReject } from 'class-validator';
import { plainToInstance } from 'class-transformer';

export interface ChargeRequest {
  orderId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  currency: string;
  paymentMethodId: string;
  idempotencyKey?: string;      // present => retries are safe
}

export class ChargeResponseDto {
  @IsString() id!: string;
  @IsIn(['succeeded', 'pending', 'failed']) status!: 'succeeded' | 'pending' | 'failed';
  @IsInt() @Min(0) amountCents!: number;
  @IsString() currency!: string;
}

export class GatewayError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, readonly statusCode?: number, readonly code?: string,
              readonly retryAfterMs?: number, readonly outcome: 'failed' | 'unknown' = 'failed') {
    super(message);
  }
}

export async function parseChargeResponse(json: unknown, expected: ChargeRequest): Promise<ChargeResponseDto> {
  const dto = plainToInstance(ChargeResponseDto, json);
  await validateOrReject(dto, { whitelist: true });                   // shape check
  if (dto.amountCents !== expected.amountCents || dto.currency !== expected.currency) {
    throw new GatewayError('response does not match request', 200, 'MISMATCH'); // business check
  }
  return dto;
}

The HTTP layer: dedicated agent (bulkhead), per-attempt timeout from the deadline, error classification and response validation:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Agent, request } from 'undici';
import { Deadline } from '../reliability/deadline';

@Injectable()
export class PaymentGatewayHttp {
  private readonly agent = new Agent({
    connections: 50, connect: { timeout: 1_000 }, headersTimeout: 2_500, bodyTimeout: 2_500,
  });

  constructor(private readonly baseUrl = process.env.PAYMENT_URL!, private readonly apiKey = process.env.PAYMENT_KEY!) {}

  async charge(req: ChargeRequest, deadline: Deadline): Promise<ChargeResponseDto> {
    const budget = deadline.child(2_500);
    if (budget <= 0) throw new GatewayError('no time left', undefined, 'DEADLINE');

    let res: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof request>>;
    try {
      res = await request(`${this.baseUrl}/v1/charges`, {
        method: 'POST', dispatcher: this.agent, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(budget),
        headers: {
          'content-type': 'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${this.apiKey}`,
          ...(req.idempotencyKey ? { 'idempotency-key': req.idempotencyKey } : {}),
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ amount: req.amountCents, currency: req.currency,
                               payment_method: req.paymentMethodId, metadata: { orderId: req.orderId } }),
      });
    } catch (err) {
      const e = err as { name?: string; code?: string };
      if (e.name === 'TimeoutError' || e.name === 'AbortError')
        throw new GatewayError('timeout', undefined, 'TIMEOUT', undefined, 'unknown'); // may have charged
      if (e.code === 'ECONNREFUSED' || e.code === 'ENOTFOUND')
        throw new GatewayError(e.code, undefined, e.code, undefined, 'failed');         // never reached
      throw new GatewayError(String(err), undefined, e.code, undefined, 'unknown');
    }

    const body = (await res.body.json()) as Record<string, unknown>;
    if (res.statusCode >= 500 || res.statusCode === 429) {
      const ra = res.headers['retry-after'];
      throw new GatewayError(`gateway ${res.statusCode}`, res.statusCode, String(body.code ?? ''),
        ra ? Number(ra) * 1000 : undefined, res.statusCode === 429 ? 'failed' : 'unknown');
    }
    if (res.statusCode >= 400) throw new GatewayError(String(body.message ?? 'rejected'), res.statusCode, String(body.code ?? ''));
    return parseChargeResponse(body, req);
  }
}

The client: breaker, bulkhead, idempotency-aware retry, metrics and logs:

import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy } from '@nestjs/common';
import CircuitBreaker from 'opossum';
import { Counter, Histogram } from 'prom-client';
import { computeBackoff } from '../reliability/backoff';

const latency = new Histogram({ name: 'payment_gateway_seconds', help: 'charge latency',
  labelNames: ['outcome'], buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3] });
const attempts = new Counter({ name: 'payment_gateway_attempts_total', help: 'attempts', labelNames: ['result'] });

@Injectable()
export class PaymentGatewayClient implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PaymentGatewayClient.name);
  private readonly breaker = new CircuitBreaker(
    (req: ChargeRequest, deadline: Deadline) => this.chargeWithRetry(req, deadline),
    { name: 'payment-gateway', errorThresholdPercentage: 50, volumeThreshold: 20, rollingCountTimeout: 10_000,
      resetTimeout: 15_000, capacity: 200,
      // 4xx (except 429) and validation mismatches are not gateway health signals.
      errorFilter: (e: GatewayError) => (e.statusCode ?? 500) >= 400 && (e.statusCode ?? 500) < 500 && e.statusCode !== 429 });

  constructor(private readonly http: PaymentGatewayHttp) {
    this.breaker.on('open', () => this.log.error({ msg: 'payment breaker open' }));
    this.breaker.on('close', () => this.log.warn({ msg: 'payment breaker closed' }));
  }

  async charge(req: ChargeRequest, deadline: Deadline): Promise<ChargeResponseDto> {
    try {
      return await this.breaker.fire(req, deadline);
    } catch (err) {
      if ((err as { code?: string }).code === 'EOPENBREAKER')
        throw new GatewayError('breaker open', 503, 'BREAKER_OPEN', 15_000, 'failed');
      throw err;
    }
  }

  private async chargeWithRetry(req: ChargeRequest, deadline: Deadline): Promise<ChargeResponseDto> {
    const maxAttempts = req.idempotencyKey ? 2 : 1;                // no key => never retry a charge
    for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
      const end = latency.startTimer();
      try {
        const res = await this.http.charge(req, deadline);
        end({ outcome: 'success' }); attempts.inc({ result: 'success' });
        this.log.log({ msg: 'charge ok', orderId: req.orderId, chargeId: res.id, status: res.status, attempt });
        return res;
      } catch (err) {
        const e = err as GatewayError;
        end({ outcome: e.outcome }); attempts.inc({ result: e.code ?? 'error' });
        const retryable = e.code === 'TIMEOUT' || e.code === 'ECONNREFUSED' || e.statusCode === 503 || e.statusCode === 429;
        const delay = e.retryAfterMs ?? computeBackoff(attempt, 200, 1_500, 'equal');
        if (attempt >= maxAttempts || !retryable || delay > deadline.remainingMs() - 300) {
          this.log.warn({ msg: 'charge failed', orderId: req.orderId, code: e.code, status: e.statusCode, outcome: e.outcome, attempt });
          throw e;
        }
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
      }
    }
  }

  onModuleDestroy() { this.breaker.shutdown(); }
}

And the caller, handling the three outcomes correctly (success, known failure, unknown):

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  async capture(orderId: string): Promise<CaptureResult> {
    const deadline = Deadline.in(3_000);
    const order = await this.orders.findOneByOrFail({ id: orderId, status: 'pending_payment' });
    const req: ChargeRequest = { orderId, amountCents: order.totalCents, currency: order.currency,
      paymentMethodId: order.paymentMethodId, idempotencyKey: `capture:${orderId}` };

    try {
      const res = await this.gateway.charge(req, deadline);
      await this.orders.update({ id: orderId }, { status: res.status === 'succeeded' ? 'paid' : 'payment_pending', chargeId: res.id });
      return { status: res.status };
    } catch (err) {
      const e = err as GatewayError;
      if (e.outcome === 'unknown') {
        // Do NOT mark failed: the charge may exist. Park it and let the reconciler query by idempotency key.
        await this.orders.update({ id: orderId }, { status: 'payment_unknown' });
        await this.reconcileQueue.add('reconcile', { orderId }, { delay: 30_000, jobId: `reconcile:${orderId}` });
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException({ code: 'PAYMENT_PENDING', retryAfter: 30 });
      }
      if (e.statusCode === 503 || e.code === 'BREAKER_OPEN')
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException({ code: 'PAYMENTS_UNAVAILABLE', retryAfter: Math.ceil((e.retryAfterMs ?? 15_000) / 1000) });
      await this.orders.update({ id: orderId }, { status: 'payment_failed', failureCode: e.code });
      throw new UnprocessableEntityException({ code: e.code ?? 'PAYMENT_DECLINED' });
    }
  }
}

Notice what is not here: the charge is not inside a database transaction (a transaction held across an HTTP call is the classic pool killer), the order is never marked failed on an unknown outcome, and the reconciler (a BullMQ job that queries the gateway by idempotency-key) is what eventually resolves payment_unknown orders, which in practice is a handful per day.

Production scenario

With this client in front of a gateway at 200 charges per second: p50 380 ms, p99 1.4 s; timeouts 0.05%; retries 0.08% of calls (nearly all timeouts, all safe under the idempotency key); breaker opened 4 times in a quarter, each for under 3 minutes; payment_unknown orders averaged 6 per day and all reconciled within 2 minutes. The dashboard shows payment_gateway_seconds by outcome, payment_gateway_attempts_total by result, and circuit_breaker_state. The alert is "breaker open for 2 minutes" or "unknown outcome rate above 0.5%".

30.17 Edge cases & failure modes across the reliability toolbox

The patterns interact. Each of these is a real failure mode of the combination, with the mechanism and the fix:

  • Retry storm. Retries at multiple layers multiply load on a struggling dependency (3 layers x 3 attempts = 27x). Retry at one layer, cap attempts at 2–3, enforce a retry budget, and make the deepest layer fail fast with 503 + Retry-After.
  • Thundering herd on recovery. When a dependency comes back, every waiting client and every open breaker probes at once; the dependency falls over again. Jittered backoff, one probe per breaker, resetTimeout jitter per instance, and rate-limited replay of queued work.
  • Circuit breaker flapping. A partially failing dependency crosses the threshold, opens, half-opens, closes, and repeats, taking the healthy 80% down with the failing 20%. Filter deterministic errors out of the count, raise the volume threshold, lengthen resetTimeout, and consider per-operation breakers.
  • Half-open probes overwhelming a recovering service. 60 pods x N probes at the same instant. Keep probes to one per instance, jitter the reset, and let the dependency's own Retry-After slow you down.
  • Timeout shorter than the downstream's p99. You cancel 1% of healthy calls, retry them, and add 1–2% load to a healthy system; under mild slowness this becomes a self-inflicted outage. Set timeouts from latency histograms, above p99 for the normal state, and revisit them when the dependency's latency profile changes.
  • Retries of non-idempotent calls. A POST /charges timed out and was retried without a key: double charge. Never retry writes without idempotency keys; classify timeouts as unknown, not failed.
  • Health checks flapping causing restart loops. A liveness probe that touches a dependency, or a readiness probe with a timeout near its own latency; pods restart or bounce in and out of rotation. Liveness checks only the process; readiness checks only core dependencies with sub-500 ms timeouts; add failureThreshold hysteresis.
