  • Load shedding rejecting the wrong traffic. No priorities, or priorities derived from something expensive: payment webhooks are shed while analytics gets through. Explicit, reviewed priority classes propagated in a header; critical never shed.
  • Shutdown killing in-flight transactions. SIGTERM handled by immediate exit; transactions rolled back; half-finished jobs re-run. Shutdown hooks, readiness 503 first, drain, close pools last, grace period sized from measured drain time.
  • Cascading failure across services. Service A's slowness exhausts B's pool, B's slowness exhausts C's, and the whole graph stalls. Every hop needs a timeout budget that shrinks inward, bulkheads per dependency, and shedding at each layer; the first service to fail fast stops the cascade.
  • Dependency returning 200 with wrong data. A schema change, a bug, or a proxy error page with a 200. Validate every response's shape and its business content (amount, currency, ids) before acting on it; treat validation failure as a dependency error for logging but not for the breaker's count unless it is systematic.
  • Partial success in batch calls. A batch of 100 items returns 207 or 200 with per-item results; 97 succeeded and 3 failed; the caller treats the whole batch as success or as failure. Process per-item results, retry only the failed items (idempotently), and never re-send the whole batch.

Dependency decision table. The values below are starting points for an e-commerce API; measure and adjust.

Dependency Timeout Retries Breaker Fallback
PostgreSQL primary (API pool) connect 1 s, statement 2 s, lock 500 ms, idle-in-tx 10 s Transaction-level for 40001/40P01 only, 3 attempts; connection errors once for reads No (nothing to fall back to); fail fast via pool timeout Read-only mode via replica pool
PostgreSQL replica connect 1 s, statement 2 s Once on connection error Yes, fallback to primary or another replica Route to primary
Redis cache connect 1 s, command 200–300 ms, enableOfflineQueue: false 1 per command (client-level) Optional; the cache-miss path is the fallback Treat as miss; guard the DB against stampede
Redis for locks or rate limits command 200 ms 1 No Fail open for capacity limits; fail closed for security limits
Kafka producer connection 3 s, request 10 s, producer timeout 5 s Built-in with idempotent producer No Outbox table; produce later
Payment gateway per attempt 2.5 s inside a 3 s deadline 2 attempts, only with idempotency key, timeouts treated as unknown Yes, 50% over 20 calls, 15 s reset, capacity 200 None; 503 + Retry-After; unknown outcomes parked for reconciliation
Email or SMS provider 3 s 3 attempts with jitter (idempotent by message id) Yes Queue via outbox, retry for hours
Inventory service (internal) 800 ms 2 attempts (idempotent reservation id) Yes None for reservation; stale count for display
Recommendations or search 300–500 ms 0–1 Yes Bestsellers from cache; hide widget; DB ILIKE with a bound
Tax or address SaaS 1.5 s 1 Yes Last known table with max age 24 h, flag for review

Senior Checklist — Part 30

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I run the six-question dependency interrogation on every network call in code review
  • I can design a timeout budget that shrinks from the edge to each DB call, and I set timeouts at every layer including statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
  • I can classify errors into retryable and non-retryable, and I never retry a non-idempotent write without an idempotency key
  • I can implement full, equal and decorrelated jitter and explain when each applies
  • I can wire an opossum breaker with correct error filtering, volume thresholds and state metrics
  • I can isolate dependencies with separate socket pools, separate DB pools and roles, and separate deployments
  • I can implement load shedding on event-loop lag with explicit priorities and Retry-After
  • I can bound memory in any loop over unknown-size data with cursors, batching and p-limit, and pause a Kafka consumer under backpressure
  • I can classify features as core or non-core with product and design bounded-staleness fallbacks with metrics
  • I know what my pods see during a database failover and how they must respond
  • I can write liveness, readiness and startup probes that never include a non-core dependency
  • I can implement graceful shutdown in NestJS with preStop, readiness 503, drain order and a sized grace period
  • I have exercised at least one reliability control with toxiproxy or a pod kill

Part 30 — Key Takeaways

  • Every network dependency can time out, fail, slow down, duplicate, lie, or half-succeed; the code must answer all six before it ships.
  • A timeout is a budget, not a number: it shrinks from the edge inward, and each layer's timeout must be shorter than its caller's remaining time.
  • A timeout means "unknown outcome"; only idempotency turns unknown into safe-to-retry.
  • Retries multiply load; retry at one layer, cap at 2–3 attempts, enforce a retry budget, and honour Retry-After.
  • Exponential backoff spaces retries out; jitter de-synchronizes clients; you need both.
  • A circuit breaker turns slow failure into fast failure and probes for recovery; feed it only errors that mean the dependency is unhealthy.
  • Bulkheads make sure a dead dependency can hold a number of your resources that you chose, not all of them.
  • A system without load shedding sheds anyway, by falling over; choose what to reject and reject it cheaply with 503 + Retry-After.
  • Unbounded Promise.all is a memory bug waiting for a large input; bound concurrency, batch, and let lag live in Kafka or the database, not in the heap.
  • Degrade non-core features first, with stale data that carries its age, and alert on fallback rates, not just errors.
  • Liveness checks the process, readiness checks the pod's core job, and neither checks anything you have a fallback for.
  • Graceful shutdown (readiness off, drain, close pools last) is what makes deploys, scale-downs and spot instances safe; idempotency is what makes crashes safe.
  • Reliability controls are hypotheses until chaos testing has exercised them.

Part 31 — Concurrency in Node.js and NestJS

"Node is single-threaded, so I don't have to think about race conditions." Every backend engineer has heard this, and most have believed it at some point. It is wrong in a way that costs money: oversold inventory, double payments, duplicated emails, cron jobs that run five times because there are five pods. Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, but it runs many requests at once on that thread, switching between them at every await. And your NestJS process is one of many identical pods talking to the same database. Concurrency is everywhere in a Node backend; it is just not called threads.

This part teaches concurrency the way it actually shows up: two customers buying the last item, two pods claiming the same job, a cache being rebuilt by 500 requests at once, a transaction waiting for a connection that will never come. For each problem we look at the mechanism, the fix in PostgreSQL, TypeORM and Sequelize, the NestJS wiring, and the incident that made someone learn it. The lens throughout is one rule: every await is a point where the world can change.

31.1 The Node.js concurrency model

Concept

A Node.js process executes JavaScript on a single thread. It achieves concurrency, meaning many operations in progress at once, by never waiting: when your code asks for something slow (a database query, an HTTP call, a file read, a timer), it hands the work to the operating system or to libuv's worker pool, registers a callback, and moves on to run other JavaScript. When the slow thing finishes, its continuation is queued and run when the thread is free. async/await is syntax over that mechanism: the code after an await is the callback.

Concurrency is many things in progress, interleaved. Parallelism is many things executing at the same instant on different cores. A single Node process gives you concurrency for I/O and no parallelism for JavaScript. Parallelism comes from running several processes (Kubernetes replicas, the cluster module) or from worker_threads, each with its own event loop.

Why does it exist?

A thread-per-request server (classic Java, Apache prefork) spends most of its threads waiting: on the database, on the network, on the disk. Each waiting thread costs a stack (about 1 MB) and context switches. Node's model was designed for I/O-heavy servers, where a single thread can keep 10,000 sockets in flight because it never blocks on any of them. The cost is that the one thread must never be held: a 200 ms synchronous computation freezes every one of those 10,000 requests for 200 ms.

Mental model

Imagine a single chef in a kitchen with twenty pots on the stove. The chef never stands and watches a pot boil; they stir one, move to the next, plate a third, and come back when a timer rings. Twenty dishes are "in progress" with one pair of hands. That is concurrency without parallelism. Now imagine the chef stops to hand-grind spices for five minutes: every pot burns. That is a blocked event loop. And if you hire a second chef, you have parallelism, but now two people can reach for the same pot at the same time, and that is where the rest of this part begins.

How it works

  1. A request arrives on the socket. libuv notices and the event loop calls the HTTP parser, which calls your NestJS route handler. This runs synchronously until the first await.
  2. At await this.repo.findOne(...), the query is written to the PostgreSQL socket and the handler returns a pending promise. The thread is free.
  3. Another request arrives and its handler runs until its first await. Now two requests are in flight, both parked.
  4. PostgreSQL replies to the first query. libuv queues the callback; when the current synchronous work finishes, the promise resolves and the first handler's continuation runs (as a microtask) until its next await.
  5. This repeats. At any moment exactly one piece of JavaScript is running; between awaits, any other request may have run and changed the database, the cache, or in-memory state.
Event loop tick (simplified)
  timers        -> setTimeout / setInterval callbacks
  pending I/O   -> completed socket / fs callbacks
  poll          -> wait for new I/O, run callbacks
  check         -> setImmediate callbacks
  close         -> socket close callbacks
  (after every callback: drain ALL microtasks: resolved promises, process.nextTick)

libuv thread pool (default 4 threads, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE up to 1024):
  fs.*, dns.lookup, crypto.pbkdf2 / randomBytes / scrypt, zlib
  -> these are parallel, but their callbacks still run on the one JS thread

Practical example

An orders API handler does: read the cart (5 ms DB), call the pricing service (40 ms HTTP), write the order (5 ms DB), publish an event (2 ms Kafka). Total 52 ms of waiting and about 1 ms of JavaScript. One pod handles 500 such requests per second with the event loop busy about 50% of the time; around 26 requests are in flight at any moment, interleaved at their awaits.

NestJS example

The same handler with the interleaving points marked. Each comment is a place where other requests run.

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(
    private readonly carts: CartsRepository,
    private readonly pricing: PricingClient,
    private readonly orders: OrdersRepository,
    private readonly events: OrderEventsPublisher,
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(userId: string, dto: PlaceOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
    const cart = await this.carts.findActive(userId);        // yield: other requests run here
    if (!cart) throw new NotFoundException('cart');

    const quote = await this.pricing.quote(cart);             // yield: 40 ms; the cart may change meanwhile
    const order = await this.orders.create({                  // yield
      userId, items: cart.items, totalCents: quote.totalCents,
    });
    await this.events.publish('orders.created', order);       // yield
    return order;
  }
}

Nothing here is wrong yet. The point is that between reading the cart and creating the order, 40 ms pass during which the same user can add an item, a different request can place the same cart, and inventory can be sold to someone else. Section 31.2 turns that observation into a bug.

A blocked event loop, for contrast:

@Post('import')
import(@Body() body: { csv: string }) {
  const rows = parseCsvSync(body.csv);       // 30 MB CSV: ~800 ms of pure JavaScript
  return { rows: rows.length };               // every other request on this pod waited 800 ms
}

At 500 RPS, that one call delays about 400 other requests by up to 800 ms, and if the liveness probe was among them and its timeout is 2 s, three such imports in a row restart the pod. CPU-bound work belongs in a worker thread or a separate worker process (31.9, 31.10).

Production scenario

A NestJS API with 8 pods serves 4,000 RPS with p99 of 45 ms. Event-loop lag p99 is 3 ms. One deploy introduces a synchronous JSON.stringify of a 12 MB report response on one route called 2 times per minute. Event-loop lag p99 rises to 180 ms on every route, because for 150 ms twice a minute nothing else runs. The route was "fast" in isolation (150 ms) and invisible in its own latency metrics; the damage showed up in everyone else's. monitorEventLoopDelay (Part 30 — Reliability Engineering, load shedding) is the metric that catches this.

Failure scenario

At 09:12 the auth service began restarting in a loop. Liveness probes were timing out. CPU was at 100% on one core per pod. The cause: password hashing with bcrypt.hashSync at cost factor 12 (about 250 ms of CPU) on a login endpoint that had just received a credential-stuffing attack at 40 logins per second per pod. 40 x 250 ms = 10 s of CPU demanded per second of wall clock; the event loop never came up for air; liveness failed; Kubernetes restarted the pod; the attack continued. Fix: bcrypt.hash (async; runs in the libuv thread pool), a rate limit on login per IP and per account, and UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 so four hashes could run in parallel without starving fs and dns.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Synchronous CPU work on the request path: JSON.parse of large bodies, bcrypt.hashSync, regex catastrophes, sorting a million items, image processing.
  • await inside a loop over thousands of items serializes them (slow but safe) versus Promise.all (fast but unbounded; Part 30, backpressure).
  • The libuv thread pool is shared: dns.lookup, fs, crypto.pbkdf2 and zlib compete for 4 threads; a burst of fs.readFile delays DNS resolution for your HTTP clients.
  • Microtask starvation: a promise chain that never yields to the event loop (while (true) await Promise.resolve()) blocks I/O just like a synchronous loop.
  • Unhandled promise rejection crashes the process on Node 15+ (31.11).
  • process.nextTick recursion starves I/O entirely.
  • Timers are not precise: setTimeout(fn, 100) fires at least 100 ms later, and later still under lag.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never say "single-threaded" without adding "with many requests interleaved". They watch event-loop lag as a first-class metric. They keep CPU-bound work off the request path, either in worker threads for latency-sensitive cases or in worker deployments for everything else. They size the process count to cores (one Node process per core via replicas, not one giant pod) and they know the libuv pool size and what runs on it. And they treat every await as a place where state must be re-validated, which is the subject of the rest of this part.

Common mistakes

  • Believing single-threaded means race-free.
  • Doing CPU work in the API process because "it's only 100 ms".
  • Using *Sync APIs in request handlers.
  • Assuming setTimeout or setInterval runs on time under load.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between concurrency and parallelism in Node.js. How do you get each? Expected: concurrency via the event loop for I/O; parallelism via replicas, cluster, or worker_threads.
  2. What happens to other requests when one handler runs 500 ms of synchronous code? Expected: they all wait; latency and health probes suffer; move the work to a worker.
  3. What runs on the libuv thread pool, and why does its size matter? Expected: fs, dns.lookup, some crypto, zlib; default 4; contention between them.
  4. If Node is single-threaded, where can a race condition come from? Expected: interleaving at awaits across in-flight requests; multiple pods; the database as shared state.

Practical exercise

Write a NestJS route that computes a SHA-256 over a 50 MB buffer synchronously, and a /ping route. Drive /ping at 200 RPS with autocannon and call the hashing route once every 2 s. Record /ping p99 and event-loop lag. Then move the hash to crypto.subtle.digest (async) or a worker thread and repeat. Acceptance criteria: with the synchronous version, /ping p99 exceeds 100 ms; with the async version it stays under 10 ms and event-loop lag p99 under 5 ms.

31.2 How race conditions happen in single-threaded Node.js

Concept

A race condition is a bug whose outcome depends on the relative timing of two or more operations. In Node, the operations are requests (or jobs, or timers), and the timing is decided by which promise resolves first. Two requests each read a value, each compute a new value from what they read, and each write it back; the second write silently overwrites the first, and the state is wrong even though every line of code "worked".

Why does it exist?

Because the sequence read, think, write is not atomic when there is an await inside it. The await releases the thread; another request performs its own read before the first request's write lands; both requests now hold the same stale value. The database sees two separate, individually valid transactions. Nothing errors. The inventory says 1, two customers each buy it, the inventory says 0, and two shipments are promised.

Mental model

Imagine two bank tellers with one shared ledger page. Teller A reads "balance: 100", walks to the back office to get a form (that is the await), and comes back to write "balance: 90" after a 10 withdrawal. While A was away, Teller B read "balance: 100", walked away, and came back to write "balance: 70" after a 30 withdrawal. The final page says 70; the customer withdrew 40. The tellers never worked at the same instant. They interleaved.

How it works

The canonical oversell, in NestJS with TypeORM:

// THIS IS THE BUG. Do not copy it.
@Injectable()
export class InventoryService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Inventory) private readonly repo: Repository<Inventory>) {}

  async reserve(productId: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
    const inv = await this.repo.findOneByOrFail({ productId });   // (1) read
    if (inv.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException('out of stock'); // (2) think
    inv.stock -= qty;
    await this.repo.save(inv);                                      // (3) write: UPDATE ... SET stock = <computed>
  }
}

Two requests for the last unit arrive within a few milliseconds:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Request A
    participant L as Event loop
    participant B as Request B
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    A->>DB: SELECT stock WHERE product = p1
    Note over L: A awaits, thread free
    B->>DB: SELECT stock WHERE product = p1
    Note over L: B awaits, thread free
    DB-->>A: stock = 1
    A->>A: 1 >= 1, ok, stock = 0
    A->>DB: UPDATE SET stock = 0
    DB-->>B: stock = 1
    B->>B: 1 >= 1, ok, stock = 0
    B->>DB: UPDATE SET stock = 0
    Note over DB: stock = 0, two reservations succeeded

Both requests read 1. Both pass the check. Both write 0. One unit, two sales. The interleaving that produced this needs no threads: it needs only two awaits and a few milliseconds.

The rule: every await is a point where the world can change. Whatever you read before an await may be stale after it. If your write depends on what you read, and something else could have written in between, you have a race. The fix is always one of:

  • Make the read-think-write atomic in the database (UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= qty; 31.6).
  • Lock the row for the duration (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; 31.8).
  • Detect the change and retry (version column; 31.7).
  • Serialize through a single owner (a queue with one consumer per key; 31.10).

In-memory state is shared mutable state. A module-level Map, a property on a singleton NestJS provider, a closure captured by a route: all of these are shared across every in-flight request in the process. The classic version:

@Injectable()
export class CouponService {
  private redeemed = new Set<string>();          // shared by every request in this pod

  async redeem(code: string, userId: string) {
    if (this.redeemed.has(code)) throw new ConflictException('already used');
    const coupon = await this.coupons.findOne({ where: { code } });   // await: another request can pass the check
    await this.orders.applyDiscount(userId, coupon);
    this.redeemed.add(code);                                          // too late
  }
}

Between the has check and the add, there are two awaits. Two requests with the same code both pass. And even if you moved add before the first await (which would make the in-process check correct, because there is no await between has and add), it would still be wrong, because:

Multiple pods make it worse. Your process's memory is invisible to the other 11 pods. An in-process check, mutex, or Set protects against interleaving within one pod and nothing else. Two requests for the same coupon land on two different pods and both pass. Any correctness guarantee for a multi-pod deployment must live in a shared system: PostgreSQL (constraints, locks, atomic updates), Redis (SET NX, Lua), or a queue with partitioning by key. In-process locks are for protecting in-process resources (a cache entry being rebuilt, a file handle), never for business invariants.

Practical example

A flash sale: 5,000 units of a product, 60,000 shoppers hitting "buy" in the first 10 seconds across 20 pods. The naive findOne / check / save sells 5,600 units. Each oversold order costs a cancellation email, a refund, and a customer who tweets about it.

PostgreSQL example

The same race, shown as two sessions so you can reproduce it in psql. Open two terminals.

-- Session A                                   -- Session B
BEGIN;
SELECT stock FROM inventory
 WHERE product_id = 'p1';   -- 1
                                                BEGIN;
                                                SELECT stock FROM inventory
                                                 WHERE product_id = 'p1';   -- 1 (READ COMMITTED sees the same)
UPDATE inventory SET stock = 0
 WHERE product_id = 'p1';
COMMIT;
                                                UPDATE inventory SET stock = 0
                                                 WHERE product_id = 'p1';   -- waits for A, then proceeds
                                                COMMIT;                     -- stock = 0, both "sold"

Under the default READ COMMITTED, B's UPDATE waits for A's lock, re-reads the row (sees 0), and applies SET stock = 0 anyway, because the value was computed in the application, not in SQL. The database did everything right; the application wrote a stale computation. Under SERIALIZABLE, B's commit would fail with 40001 and could be retried, which is one valid fix (31.7 discusses the tradeoffs).

TypeORM example

The same bug and its smallest fix side by side:

// Bug: read, compute in JS, write.
const inv = await repo.findOneByOrFail({ productId });
if (inv.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException();
inv.stock -= qty;
await repo.save(inv);

// Fix: let PostgreSQL do read-check-write in one statement (details in 21.6).
const result = await repo.createQueryBuilder()
  .update(Inventory)
  .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
  .where('product_id = :productId AND stock >= :qty', { productId, qty })
  .execute();
if (result.affected === 0) throw new ConflictException('out of stock');

Sequelize example

// Bug
const inv = await Inventory.findOne({ where: { productId }, rejectOnEmpty: true });
if (inv.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException();
await inv.update({ stock: inv.stock - qty });

// Fix
const [affected] = await Inventory.update(
  { stock: sequelize.literal(`stock - ${Number(qty)}`) },        // qty validated as a positive integer by the DTO
  { where: { productId, stock: { [Op.gte]: qty } } },
);
if (affected === 0) throw new ConflictException('out of stock');

Production scenario

An e-commerce API at 300 RPS, with 2% of requests touching a "hot" product during promotions. With the naive code, oversells occurred about 15 times a day, always on hot products, always during the first minute of a promotion. After the atomic UPDATE, zero oversells in six months, and no measurable latency change (the conditional UPDATE is one round trip instead of two).

Failure scenario

At 20:00 a sneaker drop began. 1,000 pairs. Inventory service on 16 pods. The code was findOne, check, save. By 20:00:14 the site showed "sold out". By 20:01 the orders table had 1,312 paid orders for that SKU. The team discovered it at 20:30 from the warehouse. 312 refunds, 312 apology emails, a social-media storm, and a post-mortem whose root cause was written as: "await between read and write; no atomic guard; in-process checks on 16 pods." The fix (one conditional UPDATE) took 30 minutes. The refund processing took a week.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Read-modify-write via ORM save(): every ORM save of a loaded entity is a stale write unless guarded.
  • Two awaits far apart (an HTTP call between read and write) widen the window from milliseconds to seconds.
  • Retries widen the window further: a retried request re-reads and re-races.
  • Multi-pod defeats every in-process guard.
  • Replica reads make the initial read stale by replication lag before the race even begins.
  • Caches are another read of stale state; check-then-act against a cached value is the same bug with extra steps.
  • Event handlers (@OnEvent, Kafka consumers) race with HTTP handlers on the same rows.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Their reflex on seeing findOne followed by save is to ask "what happens if two of these run at once?" and then "on two pods?". They push invariants into the database, where atomicity and constraints are free, and they keep in-memory state out of request handling entirely unless it is explicitly a per-process cache. They know that SERIALIZABLE is correct but pays a retry tax, that atomic updates are cheapest when the invariant is a simple predicate, and that row locks are the tool when the critical section has several steps. And they reproduce the race in a test with two concurrent requests before they believe the fix (31.16).

To a product manager: "Two customers can click 'buy' on the last item within the same millisecond. Unless the database itself refuses the second one, we sell it twice."

Common mistakes

  • findOne then save for anything that is a counter, a balance, a stock level or a status transition.
  • "I added an if check" as a fix.
  • An in-process Map or Set as a lock or a deduplication table.
  • Testing with one request at a time and calling it verified.

Interview questions

  1. Show me how a race condition can happen in single-threaded Node.js. Expected: read-await-write interleaving; two requests both see the old value; multi-pod.
  2. Why does an in-memory lock not fix an oversell in Kubernetes? Expected: each pod has its own memory; the shared state is the database.
  3. What are the four families of fixes for a read-modify-write race? Expected: atomic statement, row lock, optimistic version, serialize by key through a queue.
  4. Under READ COMMITTED, why does the second UPDATE not "see" the first one's change? Expected: it does see it (re-reads the row), but applies a value computed in the application from stale data.

Practical exercise

Reproduce the oversell: seed inventory(product_id='p1', stock=1), start a NestJS app with the buggy reserve, and fire 50 concurrent POST /reserve requests with Promise.all from a script. Acceptance criteria: with the buggy code, more than one request returns 200; after replacing the body with the conditional UPDATE, exactly one returns 200 and 49 return 409, over 20 repeated runs.

31.3 A catalogue of race conditions

Concept

The oversell is one instance of a small family of shapes. Once you can recognise the shape, you can see the race in code review before it ships. Each shape has a standard fix.

Shape Looks like Standard fix
Check-then-act if (!exists) create() Unique constraint + ON CONFLICT; let the database refuse
Read-modify-write x = read(); write(x - 1) Atomic UPDATE ... SET x = x - 1 WHERE x >= 1
TOCTOU on files if (!fs.exists(p)) fs.write(p) Open with exclusive flags (wx); atomic rename; use the OS as the arbiter
Double submit Same request twice (double click, retry) Idempotency key with unique constraint; disable the button too, but never rely on it
Duplicate job across pods Two workers pick the same job SKIP LOCKED claim, or unique constraint on (job_id) in a results table, or lease with heartbeat
Cache stampede Key expires; 500 requests rebuild at once Single-flight per key (in-process mutex) plus a distributed lock or early refresh

How it works

Check-then-act. "Create the user if the email is not taken."

// Bug: two signups for the same email both pass the check.
const existing = await this.users.findOneBy({ email });
if (existing) throw new ConflictException('email taken');
await this.users.insert({ email, passwordHash });

// Fix: the unique index is the check. Catch the violation and map it.
try {
  await this.users.insert({ email, passwordHash });
} catch (err) {
  if ((err as { code?: string }).code === '23505') throw new ConflictException('email taken');
  throw err;
}
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_uq ON users (lower(email));
-- Or make it idempotent: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (lower(email)) DO NOTHING RETURNING id;
-- zero rows returned means "already existed".

Read-modify-write. Counters, balances, stock, "likes". The fix is the conditional atomic update (31.6). For balances that must never go negative, add a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint as a backstop so that even a buggy code path cannot violate it.

TOCTOU on files. Time-of-check to time-of-use. existsSync then writeFileSync lets another process create the file in between; on shared volumes across pods it is worse.

import { open, rename, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

// Exclusive create: fails with EEXIST if the file appeared between your check and your write.
const fh = await open(path, 'wx');
try { await fh.writeFile(data); } finally { await fh.close(); }

// Atomic replace: write to a temp file, then rename (rename is atomic on POSIX within a filesystem).
await writeFile(`${path}.tmp-${process.pid}`, data);
await rename(`${path}.tmp-${process.pid}`, path);

Double submit. The user double-clicks "Place order", or the mobile app retries a timed-out POST. Two orders. The fix is the idempotency key (Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency): the client generates a key per intent, the server stores it with a unique constraint, and the second request replays the first response. UI tricks (disabling the button) reduce the frequency; only the constraint removes the bug.

Duplicate job execution across pods. A "send reminder emails" job runs on every worker pod at 09:00, or two BullMQ workers process the same job after a lock expiry, or a Kafka rebalance redelivers a batch. Fixes, in order of strength: make the job handler idempotent (a sent_reminders(user_id, date) unique constraint; sending twice fails the second insert before the email goes out), claim work with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (31.8), and use a lease with heartbeat for long jobs (31.14).

Cache stampede. A popular key (homepage:deals) expires. In the next 50 ms, 500 requests miss, and all 500 run the 300 ms database query. The database sees 500 identical heavy queries; the cache is written 500 times. Fixes:

import { Mutex } from 'async-mutex';

@Injectable()
export class DealsCache {
  private readonly inflight = new Map<string, Promise<Deal[]>>();   // single-flight within this pod

  async get(key: string): Promise<Deal[]> {
    const cached = await this.redis.get(key);
    if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

    // Coalesce concurrent misses for the same key in this process.
    let p = this.inflight.get(key);
    if (!p) {
      p = this.rebuild(key).finally(() => this.inflight.delete(key));
      this.inflight.set(key, p);
    }
    return p;
  }

  private async rebuild(key: string): Promise<Deal[]> {
    // Cross-pod: only one pod rebuilds; others serve stale or wait briefly.
    const token = await this.redis.set(`lock:${key}`, process.pid, 'PX', 5_000, 'NX');
    if (token !== 'OK') {
      const stale = await this.redis.get(`${key}:stale`);           // keep a longer-lived stale copy
      if (stale) return JSON.parse(stale);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));                  // brief wait then re-check
      return this.get(key);
    }
    const deals = await this.dealsRepo.findActive();
    await this.redis.multi().set(key, JSON.stringify(deals), 'EX', 60)
                            .set(`${key}:stale`, JSON.stringify(deals), 'EX', 600).exec();
    return deals;
  }
}

Single-flight in-process (the Map of in-flight promises) removes the 500-to-1 amplification within a pod; the Redis NX lock removes the 20-pods-to-1 amplification across pods; the stale copy means nobody waits. Note this is one of the legitimate uses of in-memory state in a request path: it protects a process-local resource (the right to issue a rebuild query from this process), not a business invariant.

Production scenario

A media site's homepage cache expired every 60 s. At 2,000 RPS, each expiry produced a 60–120 ms spike of 100–200 identical queries; the database's p99 doubled every minute like clockwork. With single-flight plus a distributed rebuild lock plus a 10-minute stale copy, the spike disappeared: one query per pod per minute at worst, usually one per cluster.

Failure scenario

At 09:00 sharp, 5 worker pods each ran the "daily digest" cron. Each pod queried "users who have not received today's digest", got the same 40,000 users, and started sending. The sent flag was written after each email. 200,000 emails for 40,000 users. The unsubscribe rate that day was 4%. Fixes: INSERT INTO digest_sends (user_id, day) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING user_id before sending, so only the pod that wins the insert sends; and a leader-elected cron (31.15) so only one pod runs the job at all. Two layers, because belt and braces are cheap compared with 160,000 unwanted emails.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unique constraint on the wrong columns (email case-sensitive) lets A@x.com and a@x.com both in.
  • ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING hides real errors if you do not check the returned row count.
  • Single-flight without a timeout parks every request behind one hung rebuild; wrap the rebuild in a deadline.
  • Stale cache copy served forever when the rebuild keeps failing; add a max age and an alert (Part 30 — degradation).
  • Idempotency keys scoped too broadly (the same key reused for a different amount) replay the wrong response; include the operation and a hash of the payload.
  • File TOCTOU on NFS or object storage: rename is not atomic across every filesystem; on S3 use conditional writes (If-None-Match: *).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They name the shape out loud in review ("this is check-then-act") because naming it makes the fix obvious. They prefer constraints to code: a unique index cannot be bypassed by a future refactor, an if can. They reserve in-process coordination for in-process resources. And they layer fixes for the expensive cases (idempotent handler and single execution) because the cost of one duplicate can exceed the cost of both layers for a year.

Common mistakes

  • Checking existence in code instead of enforcing it with a constraint.
  • Catching 23505 and retrying the same insert.
  • Setting the "done" flag after the side effect instead of claiming before it.
  • Fixing a stampede with a longer TTL (it just makes the stampede rarer and the data staler).

Interview questions

  1. Name five common race-condition shapes and the standard fix for each. Expected: the table above.
  2. How do you prevent a cache stampede across 20 pods? Expected: single-flight per process, distributed rebuild lock, stale-while-revalidate copy, or probabilistic early refresh.
  3. Why is "check in code, then insert" wrong even with a unique index present? Expected: it is not wrong for correctness once the index exists, but the check is redundant and gives a false sense of safety; the index is the real guard, and the code must handle 23505.
  4. Your daily job ran on every pod. What are the two layers of fix? Expected: claim-before-act with a unique constraint, and single-execution via leader election or a scheduler.

Practical exercise

Implement DealsCache with single-flight and a Redis rebuild lock. Write a test that fires 200 concurrent get('deals') calls against an empty cache with a rebuild that sleeps 200 ms and counts invocations. Acceptance criteria: rebuild runs exactly once per process; with two app instances against one Redis, it runs at most twice; after the first rebuild completes, all 200 calls resolve with identical data within 250 ms.

31.4 Deadlocks

Concept

A deadlock is a cycle of waiting. Transaction A holds a lock that transaction B wants, and B holds a lock that A wants. Neither can proceed, and neither will ever give up voluntarily. Unlike a slow query, a deadlock does not resolve itself with patience: it is a permanent state until something outside the cycle intervenes.

In a Node backend you meet deadlocks in three very different places, and they behave differently:

  • Database deadlocks. Two PostgreSQL transactions lock the same rows in opposite orders. PostgreSQL detects this and kills one of them with an error. Annoying, recoverable, retryable.
  • Application-level deadlocks. Two in-process locks (async-mutex mutexes, a semaphore, a lock keyed by entity id) acquired in inconsistent order. Nothing detects this. The requests hang until their timeout, or forever.
  • Resource deadlocks. The most common one in real Node services: a transaction is holding one database connection while awaiting a second connection from an exhausted pool. Nobody is holding a row lock. Nothing is deadlocked in the database. The pool is deadlocked.

The first has a built-in escape hatch. The other two do not, which is exactly why they cause the worse incidents.

Why does it exist?

Deadlock is the price of locking. Any system that lets one actor exclusively hold a resource while requesting another can form a cycle. You could eliminate deadlocks by never holding two things at once, but real work needs to: debiting one account and crediting another, decrementing stock on three SKUs in a basket, updating an order and its lines.

The alternative to locking is not "no deadlocks", it is "wrong data". So the engineering question is never "how do I avoid all locks", it is "how do I take locks in a way that either cannot cycle, or cycles rarely enough that a retry is cheap".

Mental model

Imagine two people in a narrow corridor carrying furniture. A holds the left half of a sofa and needs the right half; B holds the right half and needs the left. Neither will put their half down, because putting it down means starting over. They stand there.

Now change the rule: everyone always picks up the left half first. A grabs the left half. B tries to grab the left half, cannot, and waits. A grabs the right half, walks out, and B proceeds. No cycle is possible, because there is a global order. That single rule — always acquire locks in a consistent, globally agreed order — prevents more deadlocks in production than every retry wrapper ever written.

How it works

PostgreSQL takes a row-level exclusive lock when a transaction updates a row, and holds it until commit or rollback. A second transaction updating the same row blocks on tuple / transactionid wait events.

When a transaction has waited longer than deadlock_timeout (default 1s), PostgreSQL runs its deadlock detector:

  1. It builds a wait-for graph: an edge from each waiting transaction to the transaction it is waiting on.
  2. It looks for a cycle.
  3. If it finds one, it picks a victim (in practice the transaction that ran the check, i.e. the one that just blocked and triggered detection) and aborts it.
  4. The victim's client gets SQLSTATE 40P01, message deadlock detected, with a helpful DETAIL naming both processes and both statements.
  5. The other transaction is unblocked immediately and proceeds.

Note the timing: PostgreSQL waits a full second before even looking. That is deliberate; running the detector on every lock wait would be expensive, and the vast majority of lock waits clear in milliseconds. It also means a deadlock costs you at least one second of latency for the victim, and one second of a held connection.

Here is the classic two-session example. An order has three lines. Two workers update the lines of the same order, one iterating ascending by line id, the other descending — because one of them used ORDER BY created_at DESC in a query somewhere and nobody thought about it.

-- Session A: repricing job, iterates lines ascending
BEGIN;
UPDATE order_lines SET unit_price_cents = 1990
 WHERE id = 'line-1';        -- A now holds the row lock on line-1
                                    -- Session B: tax recalculation, iterates descending
                                    BEGIN;
                                    UPDATE order_lines SET tax_cents = 358
                                     WHERE id = 'line-3';   -- B holds line-3

UPDATE order_lines SET unit_price_cents = 2490
 WHERE id = 'line-3';        -- A blocks: waiting for B
                                    UPDATE order_lines SET tax_cents = 298
                                     WHERE id = 'line-1';   -- B blocks: waiting for A
                                    -- after deadlock_timeout (1s), PostgreSQL detects the cycle
                                    -- ERROR:  deadlock detected
                                    -- DETAIL: Process 4412 waits for ShareLock on transaction 88201;
                                    --         blocked by process 4398.
                                    --         Process 4398 waits for ShareLock on transaction 88214;
                                    --         blocked by process 4412.
                                    -- HINT:   See server log for query details.
COMMIT;                             ROLLBACK;   -- B was the victim; its whole transaction is gone
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as TxA
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant B as TxB
    A->>PG: UPDATE line-1
    PG-->>A: lock granted
    B->>PG: UPDATE line-3
    PG-->>B: lock granted
    A->>PG: UPDATE line-3
    Note over PG: A waits for B
    B->>PG: UPDATE line-1
    Note over PG: B waits for A, cycle formed
    Note over PG: after deadlock_timeout, detector runs
    PG-->>B: ERROR 40P01 deadlock detected
    PG-->>A: lock granted, A proceeds

The important detail: the victim loses its entire transaction, not just the statement. Everything it did since BEGIN is rolled back. That is why the fix has two halves — prevent most of them with lock ordering, and survive the rest with a retry.

Practical example

An order-fulfilment service updates order lines in whatever order the client sent them in the request body. Two support agents edit the same order at the same moment, one from a list sorted by SKU, one from a list sorted by price. Deadlock. The fix is one line:

// Deterministic lock order: sort by primary key before touching anything.
const lines = [...dto.lines].sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
for (const line of lines) {
  await manager.update(OrderLine, { id: line.id }, { unitPriceCents: line.unitPriceCents });
}

Sorting by the primary key (or by any total order that every code path agrees on) means two concurrent transactions always request locks in the same sequence. The second one blocks at the first contended row and simply waits. A wait is not a deadlock; a wait finishes.

NestJS example

The retry wrapper. This belongs in a shared module, not copy-pasted into services.

import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

// 40P01 deadlock_detected, 40001 serialization_failure (SERIALIZABLE / REPEATABLE READ).
const RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES = new Set(['40P01', '40001']);

export interface RetryOptions {
  attempts?: number;   // total tries, including the first
  baseMs?: number;     // first backoff delay
  maxMs?: number;      // cap on backoff
}

@Injectable()
export class TransactionRunner {
  private readonly log = new Logger(TransactionRunner.name);

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async runWithRetry<T>(
    work: (manager: EntityManager) => Promise<T>,
    opts: RetryOptions = {},
  ): Promise<T> {
    const attempts = opts.attempts ?? 5;
    const baseMs = opts.baseMs ?? 20;
    const maxMs = opts.maxMs ?? 500;

    for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
      try {
        return await this.dataSource.transaction(work);
      } catch (err) {
        const code = (err as { code?: string }).code;
        if (!code || !RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES.has(code) || attempt >= attempts) throw err;

        // Exponential backoff with full jitter: without jitter, both victims retry
        // at the same instant and deadlock again.
        const ceiling = Math.min(maxMs, baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
        const delay = Math.random() * ceiling;
        this.log.warn(`sqlstate=${code} attempt=${attempt} retrying in ${Math.round(delay)}ms`);
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
      }
    }
  }
}

Three things make this correct rather than decorative:

  • The whole transaction is retried, because the whole transaction was rolled back. Retrying only the failed statement inside a dead transaction gets you 25P02 current transaction is aborted.
  • Full jitter. Two victims that retry after exactly 20 ms collide again. Randomising the delay across [0, ceiling) spreads them.
  • work must be a pure function of its inputs. If it sends an email or charges a card, a retry sends two. Side effects go outside the retried block, or behind an idempotency key (Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency).

Usage:

await this.txRunner.runWithRetry(async (manager) => {
  const lines = [...dto.lines].sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
  for (const line of lines) {
    await manager.update(OrderLine, { id: line.id }, { taxCents: line.taxCents });
  }
  await manager.update(Order, { id: dto.orderId }, { recalculatedAt: new Date() });
});

PostgreSQL example

Deadlocks are counted, so you can alert on them:

-- Cumulative deadlocks for this database since the last stats reset.
SELECT datname, deadlocks, xact_commit, xact_rollback
  FROM pg_stat_database
 WHERE datname = current_database();
--  datname | deadlocks | xact_commit | xact_rollback
-- ---------+-----------+-------------+---------------
--  shop    |      1483 |   402881904 |         51022

A non-zero, growing deadlocks counter is a design smell, not a fact of life. Healthy OLTP services run months at zero. Rate-alert it: more than ~1 per minute means a code path is taking locks in inconsistent order.

To see who is blocking whom right now:

SELECT a.pid, a.wait_event_type, a.wait_event, a.state,
       cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) AS blockers,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by,
       left(a.query, 80) AS query,
       now() - a.xact_start AS tx_age
  FROM pg_stat_activity a
 WHERE a.datname = current_database()
   AND cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) > 0
 ORDER BY tx_age DESC;

Set log_lock_waits = on and keep deadlock_timeout = 1s; then every wait longer than a second is logged with the blocking query, which is the single most useful lock-debugging setting in PostgreSQL.

Application-level deadlocks

PostgreSQL has a detector. Your process does not. Two async-mutex locks acquired in different orders hang forever:

import { Mutex } from 'async-mutex';

const walletLock = new Mutex();
const ledgerLock = new Mutex();

// Path 1: transfer
await walletLock.runExclusive(async () => {
  await ledgerLock.runExclusive(async () => { /* ... */ });
});

// Path 2: reconciliation  <-- opposite order. This deadlocks.
await ledgerLock.runExclusive(async () => {
  await walletLock.runExclusive(async () => { /* ... */ });
});

Two requests, one on each path, interleaving at their first await: request 1 holds walletLock and waits for ledgerLock; request 2 holds ledgerLock and waits for walletLock. There is no timeout by default, no error, no log line. The two requests hang until the client gives up, and both mutexes stay held forever, so every subsequent request on either path also hangs. One deadlock takes down the whole pod.

Two defences, and you want both:

import { Mutex, withTimeout, E_TIMEOUT } from 'async-mutex';

// 1. Every application lock has a timeout. A hang becomes an error you can see.
const walletLock = withTimeout(new Mutex(), 2_000);

try {
  await walletLock.runExclusive(async () => { /* ... */ });
} catch (err) {
  if (err === E_TIMEOUT) throw new ServiceUnavailableException('wallet busy');
  throw err;
}
// 2. Never nest application locks. If you truly must, define one global order
//    and enforce it with a helper that sorts the keys for you.
async function withLocks<T>(keys: string[], fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const ordered = [...new Set(keys)].sort();          // global order: lexicographic key
  const releases: Array<() => void> = [];
  try {
    for (const key of ordered) releases.push(await locks.get(key).acquire());
    return await fn();
  } finally {
    for (const release of releases.reverse()) release();
  }
}

The promise deadlock

A subtler version: a request awaits a promise that nothing will ever resolve.

// A worker with BullMQ concurrency 1 that waits for another job on the same queue.
@Processor('reports')
export class ReportProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  async process(job: Job) {
    // The child job is queued on the SAME queue this worker serves, with concurrency 1.
    // This worker is the only consumer, and it is busy waiting here.
    const child = await this.reportsQueue.add('render-page', { page: 1 });
    await child.waitUntilFinished(this.queueEvents);  // never resolves
  }
}

The parent job occupies the only worker slot; the child can never be picked up; the parent waits for the child forever. The same shape appears with an in-process Map<string, Deferred> where the resolving code path is guarded by an if that turned out to be false, and with request/response over a message broker when the reply topic has no consumer.

The defences are structural: never wait on work that your own capacity is required to perform, always put a deadline on any promise that depends on an external event, and use a separate queue (and separate worker) for child jobs.

export function withDeadline<T>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number, label: string): Promise<T> {
  return new Promise<T>((resolve, reject) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`timeout after ${ms}ms: ${label}`)), ms);
    p.then(resolve, reject).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
  });
}

The connection-pool deadlock

This is the one that will actually page you. It is not a database deadlock and pg_stat_database.deadlocks stays at zero.

pg (and TypeORM and Sequelize on top of it) hands each transaction a dedicated connection from a fixed-size pool. If code inside a transaction asks the pool for a second connection — because a nested service call does this.repo.find() on the default DataSource instead of the transaction's EntityManager — then that request now needs two connections and holds one while waiting for the other.

// THE BUG. Do not copy it.
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {          // holds connection #1
  await manager.update(Order, { id }, { status: 'PAID' });
  await this.pricingService.recalculate(id);                     // <-- uses this.repo (a NEW connection)
});
flowchart TB
    subgraph Pool
      c1["connection 1"]
      c2["connection 2"]
    end
    A["Request A: transaction holding connection 1"] --> c1
    B["Request B: transaction holding connection 2"] --> c2
    A -->|"nested call asks for a connection"| W["Pool wait queue"]
    B -->|"nested call asks for a connection"| W
    W --> D["No connection can be released until A and B finish"]
    D --> E["Both time out after connectionTimeoutMillis"]

The arithmetic. Let P be the pool size and D the maximum number of connections a single request may hold simultaneously (its nesting depth: 1 for a plain query, 2 for a transaction that makes a nested non-transactional query, 3 if that call transacts again). With N concurrent requests all at depth D:

  • Total connections needed to guarantee progress for at least one request: each of the N requests may hold D - 1 connections and still be stuck. If P = N * (D - 1), every request is stuck holding its share with none left. So you need one more.
  • P >= N * (D - 1) + 1.

That is the HikariCP deadlock-avoidance formula and it applies unchanged to pg. Concretely, with a pool of 10 and D = 2: as soon as 10 concurrent requests are inside a transaction and each wants a second connection, the pool is empty and nothing can finish. P >= 10 * 1 + 1 = 11 would guarantee one request completes, then the next, then the next — slowly, serially, but without deadlock. With D = 1 the formula collapses to P >= 1: a request that never nests can never pool-deadlock.

So there are two fixes, and they rank very differently:

  1. Make D = 1. Pass the transaction's EntityManager (or the Sequelize transaction object) down through every call inside a transaction, so nested work reuses the same connection. This is the real fix. See 31.11 for propagating it automatically with AsyncLocalStorage instead of threading a parameter through eight layers.
  2. Raise the pool so P >= N * (D - 1) + 1. This is a mitigation that buys you time and costs you database connections. It does not remove the bug; it moves the cliff.
// FIXED: the nested call receives the same EntityManager, so D stays at 1.
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  await manager.update(Order, { id }, { status: 'PAID' });
  await this.pricingService.recalculate(id, manager);   // reuses connection #1
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize has exactly the same trap, and its CLS integration is the standard cure:

// BUG: the inner query opens a second connection from the pool.
await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await Order.update({ status: 'PAID' }, { where: { id }, transaction: t });
  await Payment.findAll({ where: { orderId: id } });     // no `transaction: t` -> new connection
});

// FIX A: pass the transaction explicitly.
await Payment.findAll({ where: { orderId: id }, transaction: t });

// FIX B: enable CLS so the transaction is picked up automatically by every query
// in the same async context. Do this once, before models are defined.
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
Sequelize.useCLS(new AsyncLocalStorage());

Production scenario

A payments API runs 6 pods, max: 20 connections per pod (120 total against a max_connections = 200 PostgreSQL). Normal load is 400 RPS with p99 of 55 ms and waitingCount at 0. During a promotion, traffic hits 1,200 RPS. A settlement endpoint that opens a transaction and then calls a nested service (depth 2) is 8% of traffic. At 1,200 RPS with 90 ms of latency there are ~108 in-flight requests, ~9 per pod on that endpoint. With a pool of 20 that is survivable. The next release adds a second level of nesting: depth 3. Required pool becomes 9 * 2 + 1 = 19. Add the other endpoints competing for the same 20 connections and the pool tips over: waitingCount climbs to 40, connectionTimeoutMillis fires, and the API returns 500s at 30% while PostgreSQL sits at 4% CPU with 118 idle connections. The database was never the bottleneck. The nesting was.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: checkout p99 > 30s, error rate 22%. PostgreSQL CPU 6%, deadlocks counter unchanged, no slow queries in pg_stat_statements, no lock waits in pg_locks. Every symptom pointed away from the database. The clue was pg_stat_activity: 118 connections, 116 of them idle in transaction with xact_start up to 40 seconds old.

Root cause: a refactor three days earlier had moved a loyalty-points lookup into OrdersService.finalize(), which runs inside the checkout transaction. The lookup used the injected repository, not the transaction manager. Depth went from 1 to 2. Under normal load nothing happened; under the 3x Tuesday-night batch of retried webhooks, more than 20 concurrent checkouts were inside a transaction on the same pod, the pool emptied, and every one of them waited for a connection that only another waiter could release.

Mitigation at 02:31: pool raised from 20 to 45, which restored service by pure arithmetic. Real fix shipped next morning: the loyalty lookup took the EntityManager, and a lint rule was added forbidding injected repositories inside a transaction() callback. The permanent guard was a dashboard panel for pool.waitingCount with an alert at > 5 for 1 minute (31.12).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • deadlock_timeout is also the lock-wait logging threshold. Lowering it to 200 ms detects faster but runs the detector more often; leave it at 1s unless you have measured a reason.
  • Foreign keys cause surprising deadlocks. Inserting a child row takes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent. Two transactions inserting children of two parents, in opposite order, deadlock on rows nobody explicitly locked.
  • Unique indexes cause deadlocks on concurrent INSERT ... ON CONFLICT of the same key from three or more sessions.
  • Retry storms. Every victim retrying immediately re-forms the cycle. Jitter is not optional.
  • Retrying a transaction with side effects sends the email twice, charges twice.
  • Long-running transactions widen every window. A transaction that awaits an HTTP call holds its locks and its connection for the duration of that call. Never do I/O to a third party inside a transaction.
  • SERIALIZABLE turns some deadlocks into 40001 instead, which is cheaper (no 1-second wait) but more frequent.
  • A pool deadlock looks like a database problem in every dashboard except waitingCount and idle in transaction.
  • PgBouncer in transaction mode adds a second pool with its own exhaustion behaviour; a client-side pool of 20 per pod against a PgBouncer default_pool_size of 25 will queue at PgBouncer instead.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat deadlocks as a design signal, not a runtime nuisance. The first question is "what order are we taking locks in, and is that order the same everywhere?" Sorting by primary key before a multi-row update costs nothing and removes the whole class. The retry wrapper is the seatbelt, not the brakes.

They insist that transactions be short and pure: open late, commit early, no HTTP calls, no queue publishes, no await sleep. They know the pool-deadlock formula and can recite what D is for their hottest endpoint. They watch deadlocks, waitingCount and idle in transaction count as three separate signals, because each one points at a different bug.

And they refuse a certain kind of fix. "Just increase the pool" is accepted only as an incident mitigation with a follow-up ticket, never as a design. Connections are a shared, finite resource across every pod; the pod that fixes its problem by taking 45 connections is stealing them from the other five.

To a product manager: "Two operations grabbed the same two records in opposite order and each is waiting for the other. The database noticed and cancelled one. We retry it automatically, so the user sees a slightly slower request instead of an error. But the fact that it happens at all means we're doing the work in an inconsistent order, and we should fix that."

Common mistakes

  • Retrying only the failed statement instead of the whole transaction.
  • Retrying without jitter, producing a synchronised second collision.
  • Retrying a transaction that has already sent a notification or charged a card.
  • Calling an injected repository inside a transaction() callback.
  • Making an HTTP call inside a transaction ("it's only 200 ms").
  • Nesting in-process mutexes without a global order or a timeout.
  • Treating a rising pool waitingCount as "the database is slow".
  • Fixing a pool deadlock by raising max and closing the ticket.

Interview questions

  1. Two transactions deadlock in PostgreSQL. What exactly happens, and what does the application see? Expected: wait-for graph checked after deadlock_timeout; one transaction aborted with 40P01; the entire transaction is rolled back; the other proceeds; the client must retry the whole unit of work.
  2. How do you prevent database deadlocks rather than survive them? Expected: consistent lock ordering (sort by primary key), short transactions, fewer rows locked, atomic single-statement updates where possible. Follow-up: why does sorting work? Because a cycle requires two actors requesting in opposite orders.
  3. Explain the connection-pool deadlock and give the sizing formula. Expected: a request holding a connection while waiting for a second; P >= N * (D - 1) + 1; the real fix is reducing D to 1 by propagating the transaction's manager.
  4. Your service hangs but PostgreSQL shows zero deadlocks and no lock waits. Where do you look? Expected: pool waitingCount, idle in transaction sessions, in-process mutexes, promises that can never resolve.
  5. Why is a retry wrapper dangerous around code with side effects? Expected: at-least-once execution; duplicate emails/charges; side effects must be idempotent or moved outside the retried block.
  6. When would you deliberately accept deadlocks instead of preventing them? Expected: when the ordering constraint would serialise an otherwise parallel workload and deadlocks are rare (say < 0.01% of transactions), a jittered retry is cheaper than the lost concurrency.

Practical exercise

Build a reproducible deadlock. Create order_lines with 3 rows. Write two NestJS endpoints, POST /reprice (updates lines ascending by id) and POST /retax (updates lines descending by id), each inside a transaction with a 300 ms await between the two updates. Fire both concurrently in a loop.

Acceptance criteria: (a) you observe 40P01 and pg_stat_database.deadlocks incrementing; (b) after wrapping both handlers in TransactionRunner.runWithRetry, both endpoints return 200 and the deadlock counter still increments; (c) after sorting the ids in both handlers, the deadlock counter stops incrementing entirely over 200 iterations. Then reproduce the pool deadlock: set max: 3, add a nested non-transactional query inside the transaction, fire 5 concurrent requests, and confirm the failure is a pool acquisition timeout while pg_stat_database.deadlocks stays flat.

31.5 Locks

Concept

A lock is a way of saying "only one actor at a time may be inside this section". It converts concurrent access to a resource into serial access, which is exactly what you want when the operation is not naturally atomic.

The question is never "should I use a lock" in the abstract. It is "what is the scope of the thing I am protecting?" — because that determines which lock can possibly work:

Scope of shared state Lock that works Lock that does not
A variable, cache entry or file handle in one process in-process mutex (async-mutex) anything, this is the cheapest correct answer
A row in PostgreSQL SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, advisory lock in-process mutex (other pods bypass it)
A logical operation with no row yet, e.g. "run the nightly settlement" PostgreSQL advisory lock, or Redis lock in-process mutex
A resource outside your database, e.g. an SFTP upload slot Redis lock with fencing token PostgreSQL row lock

Get the scope wrong and the lock is decoration. An async-mutex protecting an inventory decrement on a 12-pod deployment prevents exactly one twelfth of the races and gives the team confidence it has solved the problem.

Why does it exist?

Because some critical sections cannot be expressed as a single atomic statement. If your invariant is "decrement stock if it is at least qty", 31.6 shows you never need a lock: one UPDATE ... WHERE does it. But if the critical section is "read three rows, call a pricing function, decide, then write two rows and enqueue a job", there is no single statement. You need to hold something for the duration.

Mental model

Imagine the single key to a meeting room, hanging on a hook. To enter, you take the key. Anyone else who wants the room stands at the hook and waits. When you leave, you hang the key back.

Now add the three failure modes that every lock design must answer:

  • You take the key and have a heart attack inside the room. Nobody can ever enter again. That is why distributed locks have a TTL.
  • The TTL expires while you are still in the room. Someone else takes the key and walks in on you. That is why you need a fencing token: the resource itself must refuse the older key-holder.
  • You leave, come back, and hang up a key that is now someone else's. That is why the release must be a compare-and-delete, not a delete.

How it works

In-process: async-mutex. A mutex here is a promise queue. acquire() returns a promise that resolves when it is your turn; release() resolves the next waiter. There is no OS involvement and no blocking; the event loop keeps serving other requests while a handler waits.

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Mutex, withTimeout, E_TIMEOUT } from 'async-mutex';

@Injectable()
export class PricingCache {
  // One mutex per key, created lazily. Without the per-key split, an expensive
  // rebuild of key A would block every request for key B.
  private readonly locks = new Map<string, ReturnType<typeof withTimeout>>();
  private readonly cache = new Map<string, { value: PriceTable; expiresAt: number }>();

  private lockFor(key: string) {
    let m = this.locks.get(key);
    if (!m) { m = withTimeout(new Mutex(), 5_000); this.locks.set(key, m); }
    return m;
  }

  async get(key: string): Promise<PriceTable> {
    const hit = this.cache.get(key);
    if (hit && hit.expiresAt > Date.now()) return hit.value;

    try {
      return await this.lockFor(key).runExclusive(async () => {
        // Re-check inside the lock: a previous waiter may have already rebuilt it.
        const again = this.cache.get(key);
        if (again && again.expiresAt > Date.now()) return again.value;

        const value = await this.pricingRepo.loadTable(key);   // ~300 ms
        this.cache.set(key, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + 60_000 });
        return value;
      });
    } catch (err) {
      if (err === E_TIMEOUT) throw new ServiceUnavailableException('price table unavailable');
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

Note the double-checked pattern: check, lock, check again. Without the second check, 50 queued waiters each run the 300 ms rebuild in turn, serially, for a total of 15 seconds. With it, one rebuilds and 49 return the fresh value instantly.

This is the entire legitimate domain of an in-process mutex: protecting a process-local resource (a cache slot, a file handle, a rate-limited outbound client, an in-memory batch buffer). It is correct on one pod and on fifty pods, because the thing it protects exists once per pod. The moment the invariant is about shared data, it stops being correct.

Cross-process, in PostgreSQL: row locks. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes an exclusive lock on the selected rows until the transaction ends. Covered in depth in 31.8. Use it when the thing you want to protect is a row.

Cross-process, in PostgreSQL: advisory locks. These lock an arbitrary 64-bit number that means whatever you decide. Nothing is checked; it is a pure mutual-exclusion primitive that happens to live in your database, which means it inherits your database's availability, transactions and connection handling. Perfect for "only one pod may run the nightly settlement".

There are four variants and choosing wrong causes real bugs:

Function Scope Blocks? Released by
pg_advisory_lock(k) session yes, waits forever pg_advisory_unlock(k) or session end
pg_try_advisory_lock(k) session no, returns false pg_advisory_unlock(k) or session end
pg_advisory_xact_lock(k) transaction yes automatically at COMMIT / ROLLBACK
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(k) transaction no, returns false automatically at COMMIT / ROLLBACK

Prefer the xact variants. A session-level lock is released only when you explicitly unlock or the connection closes. With a connection pool, "the connection closes" may be never, and a handler that throws between lock and unlock leaks the lock permanently — the classic "the nightly job stopped running two weeks ago and nobody noticed". The transaction-scoped variant is released by the database no matter how your code exits.

Prefer the try variants for anything where waiting is pointless. If four pods want to run the same cron, three of them should discover that instantly and go back to sleep, not queue up to run it again afterwards.

-- Turn a business key into the bigint the lock functions want.
-- Two-argument form: (namespace int4, key int4). Keeps different lock families apart.
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(4711, hashtext('settlement:2026-09-09'));
--  pg_try_advisory_xact_lock
-- ---------------------------
--  t          <- this session won; another session gets f until this tx ends

-- Who holds advisory locks right now:
SELECT pid, classid, objid, granted
  FROM pg_locks
 WHERE locktype = 'advisory';
// NestJS: run a block only if this pod wins the lock; skip silently otherwise.
async runExclusively<T>(key: string, work: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T | null> {
  return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
    const [{ locked }] = await manager.query<[{ locked: boolean }]>(
      'SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock($1, hashtext($2)) AS locked',
      [4711, key],
    );
    if (!locked) return null;             // someone else has it; do nothing
    return work();                        // lock is held until this transaction commits
  });
}

The catch: the lock lives for the length of the transaction, and the transaction holds a connection. A 20-minute settlement run holds a pool connection for 20 minutes. That is acceptable for one job on a dedicated connection; it is not acceptable as a general-purpose lock for request handling. Also note hashtext is a 32-bit hash: distinct keys can collide, which means an unrelated job might be blocked. With the namespace form and a handful of job names, the risk is negligible; with millions of per-entity keys, it is not — use row locks for per-entity work.

Cross-process, in Redis. The standard pattern is a single command:

SET lock:settlement:2026-09-09 <random-token> NX PX 30000

NX means "only if it does not exist" — that is what makes acquisition atomic. PX 30000 sets a 30-second expiry so a crashed holder cannot block forever. The token is a random value unique to this acquisition, and it is the whole point of the design.

Release must be a compare-and-delete, in Lua so it is atomic:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

const RELEASE = `
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end`;

const EXTEND = `
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
else
  return 0
end`;

@Injectable()
export class RedisLock {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async acquire(key: string, ttlMs: number): Promise<string | null> {
    const token = randomUUID();
    const ok = await this.redis.set(`lock:${key}`, token, 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');
    return ok === 'OK' ? token : null;
  }

  // Compare-and-delete: never delete a lock that is no longer yours.
  async release(key: string, token: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const deleted = await this.redis.eval(RELEASE, 1, `lock:${key}`, token);
    return deleted === 1;
  }

  // Heartbeat: extend only while we still hold it.
  async extend(key: string, token: string, ttlMs: number): Promise<boolean> {
    const ok = await this.redis.eval(EXTEND, 1, `lock:${key}`, token, String(ttlMs));
    return ok === 1;
  }
}

Why the plain DEL is a bug: suppose the TTL is 30 s, your work takes 35 s, and at t=30 the lock expires and pod B acquires it. At t=35 pod A finishes and calls DEL. It has just deleted pod B's lock, and now pod C acquires it while B is still working. One naive release turns a single overrun into an unbounded cascade. The Lua compare-and-delete makes A's release a no-op.

TTL versus work duration is the hardest number in the design:

  • TTL too short: the lock expires mid-work and two workers run concurrently. Silent corruption.
  • TTL too long: a crashed pod blocks the resource for that long. A 10-minute TTL means a 10-minute outage for that key after a pod is OOMKilled.

The rule of thumb: TTL = p99 work duration x 3, plus a heartbeat that extends the lock every TTL / 3 while the work is still running, plus a hard local deadline that aborts the work when it exceeds the TTL. If the work cannot be bounded, a Redis lock is the wrong tool — use a claim row in PostgreSQL with a lease and a version (31.14).

Fencing tokens. Even with heartbeats, a lock can be lost without the holder noticing: a 40-second GC pause, a network partition, a pod frozen by the CPU scheduler. Distributed locks over an unreliable network cannot provide mutual exclusion by themselves. The only complete answer is to make the protected resource reject stale writers.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as PodA
    participant R as Redis
    participant B as PodB
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    A->>R: INCR fence:settlement
    R-->>A: 17
    A->>R: SET lock NX PX 30000
    R-->>A: OK
    Note over A: 40s GC pause, lock expires
    B->>R: INCR fence:settlement
    R-->>B: 18
    B->>R: SET lock NX PX 30000
    R-->>B: OK
    B->>DB: UPDATE row WHERE fence below 18
    DB-->>B: ok, fence = 18
    A->>DB: UPDATE row WHERE fence below 17
    DB-->>A: 0 rows, write rejected
-- The resource enforces the ordering. A stale holder's write affects 0 rows.
UPDATE settlement_runs
   SET status = 'DONE', fence = $1
 WHERE run_date = $2
   AND fence < $1;

fence comes from a monotonic counter (INCR fence:settlement in Redis, or a PostgreSQL sequence). Every acquisition gets a strictly larger number; the resource only accepts writes from the highest number it has seen. Now the lock is an optimisation that stops most contention, and the fence is the correctness guarantee. That is the right division of labour, and it is why "we use Redlock" is not an answer to "is this correct".

Practical example

A payouts service must not run two settlement batches for the same day. The state is a row in settlement_runs. Three viable designs:

  1. INSERT INTO settlement_runs (run_date) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id — the unique constraint is the lock, it never expires, and it is a permanent record. Best when the operation should happen exactly once ever.
  2. pg_try_advisory_xact_lock around the whole batch — best when the job is repeatable and you just want one runner at a time.
  3. Redis lock with fence — best when the batch talks to an external system that you can fence, and you do not want a 20-minute PostgreSQL transaction.

Design 1 is the strongest and the least fashionable. Reach for it first.

Decision table: which lock for which problem

Problem Use Why not the others
Rebuild one cache key once per pod async-mutex per key Distributed locks add latency for a per-pod resource
Decrement stock No lock: atomic UPDATE ... WHERE available >= qty (31.6) Any lock is slower and can be forgotten
Multi-step edit of one order SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the order row (31.8) Advisory locks do not tie to the row's lifetime
Admin edits a product form open for 4 minutes Version column, optimistic (31.7) Holding a row lock for 4 minutes blocks everyone
Only one pod runs the nightly cron pg_try_advisory_xact_lock, or a replicas: 1 deployment Redis lock works but adds a dependency for zero benefit
Claim one of 100,000 pending jobs FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (31.14) A single global lock serialises all workers
Serialise access to a third-party API with a per-account limit Redis lock + fencing token PostgreSQL locks cannot fence an external system
Guarantee an action happens at most once, forever Unique constraint / idempotency key Every TTL-based lock eventually expires

Lock scope, hold time, and the one rule

Two numbers decide whether a lock is a tool or a bug: how much it covers and how long it is held. Throughput through a lock is roughly 1 / hold_time operations per second per lock key. A lock held for 5 ms gives 200 ops/s. A lock held for 500 ms gives 2 ops/s. If 40 requests per second need that key, you have built a queue that grows forever.

So:

  • Narrow the scope. Lock per entity (lock:order:${id}), never a global lock, unless the operation truly is global.
  • Shorten the hold. Do all the reading, computing, formatting and validating outside the lock. Inside it, only the read-decide-write that must be atomic.
  • Acquire late, release early. Not "at the top of the handler, in a finally at the bottom".
  • Always set a timeout on acquisition. Waiting forever converts a slow path into a hung pod.
  • Always release in finally (and for Redis, with compare-and-delete).

And the rule that saves the most incidents:

Never call an external API while holding a lock.

A payment gateway that normally responds in 300 ms will one day respond in 30 seconds, or not at all. If that call is inside your lock, the lock is held for 30 seconds, every other request for that key queues behind it, the pool fills with waiters, and one slow third party becomes your outage. The same applies to holding a database transaction across an HTTP call — the transaction is a lock on every row it has touched, plus a connection.

The correct shape is: lock, write a PENDING row, release, call the external API, then lock again (or use an atomic conditional update) to record the result. That is the outbox/state-machine pattern from Part 29, and concurrency is one of the main reasons it exists.

Production scenario

A wallet service on 8 pods handles 900 RPS of balance operations. Per-user Redis locks (lock:wallet:${userId}, TTL 5 s) around a read-compute-write. Median hold time 6 ms, p99 22 ms. Redis adds ~0.4 ms per acquire and ~0.4 ms per release, so the lock costs about 1 ms on a 14 ms endpoint.
