  • No attempt cap: a poison-pill job kills every pod in rotation.
  • Ordering is not guaranteed with SKIP LOCKED; if you need per-entity ordering, partition by a key (claim only jobs whose entity_id is not already RUNNING) or use a broker with per-key partitions.
  • Claiming a huge batch loses a lot of work when a pod dies and holds locks longer.
  • DONE rows growing forever slow every query; partition by month or delete after N days.
  • Clock skew between pods makes lease_until comparisons wrong; always compute times with the database's now(), never with new Date() in Node.
  • The takeover sweep running on every pod re-queues jobs concurrently; elect a leader for it (31.13).
  • Long transactions during processing hold connections; claim in a short transaction, then process outside it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the queue table before the handler, because the table is where all the concurrency lives. They insist on SKIP LOCKED and a partial index, and they can explain why each is load-bearing.

They accept at-least-once as a fact and put the effort into idempotent handlers rather than trying to achieve exactly-once, which is not available. Their rule: claim the side effect, not just the job — insert the email_sends row before sending, pass an idempotency key to the payment provider, use a conditional state transition for status changes.

They choose lease duration from the p99 job duration, not the median, and they alert on three things: queue depth, oldest pending job age, and lease-takeover rate. A rising takeover rate means pods are dying or jobs are exceeding their lease, and both are worth knowing before the queue backs up.

And they ask whether they need a queue table at all: if BullMQ or SQS is already in the stack, those solve claiming, leases, retries and dead-lettering for you. A hand-rolled table is right when you want the jobs in the same transaction as your data (the outbox pattern) and wrong when you just want a queue.

To a product manager: "Ten machines share one to-do list. Each one takes the next item nobody else has taken, and writes down that it is working on it with a deadline. If a machine dies, its item goes back on the list after the deadline. And every task is written so that doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once."

Common mistakes

  • Omitting SKIP LOCKED.
  • SELECT then UPDATE ... SET status='RUNNING' in separate statements.
  • No lease, so a dead pod's jobs are stuck forever.
  • No attempt cap, so a poison pill takes down the fleet.
  • Marking a job DONE without checking you still own it.
  • Handlers that are not idempotent, relying on the lease for correctness.
  • Computing lease times in Node instead of with the database's now().
  • Never archiving completed jobs.

Interview questions

  1. Ten workers poll a jobs table. How do you ensure each gets different rows? Expected: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a claiming UPDATE ... RETURNING, in one statement.
  2. What happens without SKIP LOCKED? Expected: every worker blocks on the same row; fleet throughput collapses to one worker; invisible until jobs get slow.
  3. A pod is OOMKilled mid-job. Walk me through recovery. Expected: the lease expires; a sweep re-queues it with backoff and an incremented attempt count; the handler is idempotent so partial work is safe; after N attempts it is dead-lettered.
  4. Why can you not achieve exactly-once here? Expected: a paused pod can lose its lease and still complete its work; at-least-once plus idempotent handlers is the achievable design.
  5. How do you set the lease duration? Expected: from p99 job duration, with a heartbeat at a third of it; too short causes double execution, too long delays recovery.
  6. How would you guarantee per-customer ordering across 10 workers? Expected: partition by key — only claim a job whose entity has no other RUNNING job, or use a broker with per-key partitions and one consumer per partition.
  7. What indexes does the jobs table need and why? Expected: partial index on the claim predicate (priority DESC, run_after) WHERE status = 'PENDING', unique partial index on dedupe_key for pending/running; plus archiving so the table does not grow forever.

Practical exercise

Build the jobs table with the partial indexes above, a claim query with SKIP LOCKED, a heartbeat, and a leader-elected takeover sweep. Seed 10,000 jobs and run 6 worker processes.

Acceptance criteria: (a) all 10,000 jobs complete exactly once, verified by a unique constraint on a job_results table; (b) with SKIP LOCKED removed and a 500 ms artificial delay per job, measured throughput drops to roughly one worker's rate; (c) kill -9 on a worker mid-batch results in its jobs being re-run after the lease expires, with no duplicate rows in job_results; (d) a job that always throws is dead-lettered after 5 attempts and does not block the queue; (e) claim query p99 stays under 5 ms after 500,000 DONE rows accumulate, or you can explain why and fix it with archiving.

31.15 Testing concurrency

Concept

A concurrency bug is a bug about timing between two actors. A unit test has one actor. It runs the function, the function runs to completion, the assertion passes. There is no second request to interleave with, no second pod, no second connection. A single-threaded unit test cannot fail on a race condition, no matter how buggy the code is.

That is why oversells reach production. The code was tested. It was tested wrong.

Testing concurrency needs two different techniques, and you need both:

  • Stochastic tests: fire N real concurrent operations at a real database and assert an invariant. These prove your fix works under realistic interleavings, and they catch bugs you did not think of. They are non-deterministic, so a passing run is weak evidence and a failing run is strong evidence.
  • Deterministic tests: force a specific interleaving by controlling when promises resolve. These prove a specific window is closed, they never flake, and they document the bug in code. They only test the interleaving you thought of.

Why does it exist?

Because "we fixed it" is a hypothesis until something demonstrates the race is gone. The atomic UPDATE fix in 31.2 is three lines; the argument that it is correct depends on READ COMMITTED re-evaluation semantics, which most reviewers cannot verify by reading. A test that fires 50 concurrent requests at 10 units of stock and asserts exactly 10 succeed converts that argument into evidence.

It also exists because concurrency fixes regress silently. A future refactor replaces the conditional UPDATE with an ORM save() because it "reads better", and every existing test still passes. Only a concurrency test fails.

Mental model

Imagine testing a revolving door by walking through it alone. It works every time. The failure only appears when two people push at once from opposite sides. You cannot discover that by testing more carefully alone; you have to bring a second person.

How it works

The stochastic test needs three things to be trustworthy:

  1. A real PostgreSQL, not a mock and not SQLite. The bug lives in the database's concurrency semantics; a mock has none. Testcontainers gives you a real one per test run.
  2. Genuinely parallel requests. Promise.all over 50 supertest calls does this within one process — all 50 start before any completes.
  3. An invariant assertion, not a count of successes. Assert "successes equal stock" and "final stock is zero" and "order rows equal successes". A single assertion can pass for the wrong reason.
// test/inventory.concurrency.e2e-spec.ts
import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import request from 'supertest';

jest.setTimeout(180_000);   // container pull + boot

describe('POST /orders under concurrency', () => {
  let container: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;
  let app: INestApplication;
  let ds: DataSource;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine').start();

    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] })
      .overrideProvider(DATABASE_URL)
      .useValue(container.getConnectionUri())
      .compile();

    app = moduleRef.createNestApplication();
    await app.init();
    ds = app.get(DataSource);
    await ds.runMigrations();
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await app?.close();
    await container?.stop();
  });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    await ds.query('TRUNCATE orders, order_lines, inventory RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE');
    await ds.query(
      `INSERT INTO inventory (sku, available, reserved) VALUES ('SKU-1', 10, 0)`,
    );
  });

  it('sells exactly 10 units to 50 concurrent buyers', async () => {
    const attempts = 50;

    // All 50 start before any completes: this is the interleaving that matters.
    const responses = await Promise.all(
      Array.from({ length: attempts }, (_, i) =>
        request(app.getHttpServer())
          .post('/orders')
          .set('Idempotency-Key', `test-${i}`)
          .send({ sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 1 }),
      ),
    );

    const created = responses.filter((r) => r.status === 201);
    const conflicts = responses.filter((r) => r.status === 409);

    // Three independent assertions. Any one alone can pass for the wrong reason.
    expect(created).toHaveLength(10);
    expect(conflicts).toHaveLength(40);

    const [inv] = await ds.query(`SELECT available, reserved FROM inventory WHERE sku = 'SKU-1'`);
    expect(Number(inv.available)).toBe(0);
    expect(Number(inv.reserved)).toBe(10);

    const [{ count }] = await ds.query(`SELECT count(*)::int AS count FROM orders`);
    expect(count).toBe(10);           // no phantom orders for failed reservations
  });

  // Run it repeatedly: one pass proves little, twenty passes prove something.
  it.each([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])('is stable across repeated runs (%i)', async () => {
    const responses = await Promise.all(
      Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) =>
        request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/orders')
          .set('Idempotency-Key', `rep-${Date.now()}-${i}`)
          .send({ sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 1 }),
      ),
    );
    expect(responses.filter((r) => r.status === 201)).toHaveLength(10);
  });
});

Three practical notes. Run the test against the buggy code first — if it passes with findOne + save, your test is not concurrent and you are about to ship a false sense of safety. Repeat it: a race with a 5% window passes 95% of single runs. Truncate, do not drop and recreate, between tests; container startup is 3-8 seconds and you only want to pay it once.

If you want the multi-pod dimension too, boot two INestApplication instances against the same container. That catches in-process locks masquerading as fixes.

Deterministic interleaving

Stochastic tests find bugs; deterministic tests pin them down and stop them coming back. The technique is to replace the slow dependency with a promise you resolve, so you control exactly where the code parks.

// A deferred you can resolve from the test.
function deferred<T>() {
  let resolve!: (v: T) => void;
  let reject!: (e: unknown) => void;
  const promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; });
  return { promise, resolve, reject };
}
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Test
    participant A as CallA
    participant B as CallB
    participant R as FakeRepo
    T->>A: reserve SKU-1
    A->>R: findOne
    R-->>T: gate1 pending, A parked at the await
    T->>B: reserve SKU-1
    B->>R: findOne
    R-->>T: gate2 pending, B parked at the same await
    T->>R: resolve gate1 with stock 1
    T->>R: resolve gate2 with stock 1
    Note over A,B: both now hold stock = 1, the window is forced open
    T->>T: await both, assert exactly one succeeded
describe('reserve: forced check-then-act window', () => {
  it('does not oversell when both callers read the same stock value', async () => {
    const gateA = deferred<Inventory>();
    const gateB = deferred<Inventory>();
    const findOne = jest.fn()
      .mockReturnValueOnce(gateA.promise)     // first caller parks here
      .mockReturnValueOnce(gateB.promise);    // second caller parks here too

    const updates: Array<{ qty: number }> = [];
    const repo = {
      findOneByOrFail: findOne,
      // Simulate PostgreSQL's conditional update: only the first one that finds
      // enough stock succeeds. This is the contract we are asserting on.
      conditionalDecrement: jest.fn(async ({ qty }: { qty: number }) => {
        if (stock < qty) return { affected: 0 };
        stock -= qty;
        updates.push({ qty });
        return { affected: 1 };
      }),
    };
    let stock = 1;

    const service = new InventoryService(repo as never);

    // Start both. Neither can proceed past findOne yet.
    const a = service.reserve('SKU-1', 1);
    const b = service.reserve('SKU-1', 1);
    await Promise.resolve();       // let both reach the await

    // Force the exact interleaving: both read stock = 1.
    gateA.resolve({ sku: 'SKU-1', available: 1 } as Inventory);
    gateB.resolve({ sku: 'SKU-1', available: 1 } as Inventory);

    const results = await Promise.allSettled([a, b]);
    const fulfilled = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'fulfilled');

    expect(fulfilled).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(updates).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(stock).toBe(0);
  });
});

This test is deterministic: it passes or fails the same way every run, in milliseconds, with no container. It documents the exact scenario in code, which is worth as much as the assertion. Use deterministic tests for the races you have already found and stochastic tests to find new ones.

The await Promise.resolve() line is doing real work: it yields one microtask turn so both reserve calls actually reach their await before you resolve the gates. Without it you may resolve gateA before the second call has started.

Testing deadlock retry

You do not need a real deadlock. You need to prove that a 40P01 error causes a full retry of the transaction and that the retry succeeds.

it('retries the whole transaction on 40P01 and succeeds', async () => {
  const deadlock = Object.assign(new Error('deadlock detected'), { code: '40P01' });
  const work = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(deadlock)
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(deadlock)
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('ok');

  const ds = { transaction: (fn: (m: unknown) => Promise<unknown>) => fn({}) } as DataSource;
  const runner = new TransactionRunner(ds);

  const result = await runner.runWithRetry(work as never, { attempts: 5, baseMs: 1 });

  expect(result).toBe('ok');
  expect(work).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);       // the WHOLE unit of work re-ran
});

it('gives up after the attempt limit and rethrows', async () => {
  const deadlock = Object.assign(new Error('deadlock detected'), { code: '40P01' });
  const work = jest.fn().mockRejectedValue(deadlock);
  const runner = new TransactionRunner({ transaction: (fn: never) => (fn as never)({}) } as never);

  await expect(runner.runWithRetry(work as never, { attempts: 3, baseMs: 1 }))
    .rejects.toMatchObject({ code: '40P01' });
  expect(work).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});

it('does not retry a non-retryable error', async () => {
  const notNull = Object.assign(new Error('null value'), { code: '23502' });
  const work = jest.fn().mockRejectedValue(notNull);
  const runner = new TransactionRunner({ transaction: (fn: never) => (fn as never)({}) } as never);

  await expect(runner.runWithRetry(work as never, { attempts: 5, baseMs: 1 })).rejects.toThrow();
  expect(work).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);       // fail fast on real bugs
});

For a genuine end-to-end deadlock test, run two transactions that update two rows in opposite orders with an await between, against a real container, and assert that both eventually succeed and the deadlock counter incremented. Keep it in a separate, slower suite.

Testing the advisory-lock cron

The point is that only one of N callers runs the work, and that a failure still releases the lock.

it('runs the job on exactly one of five concurrent callers', async () => {
  const ran: string[] = [];

  // Five independent LeaderElection instances, each with its own connection
  // from a real pool, exactly like five pods.
  const results = await Promise.all(
    ['pod-1', 'pod-2', 'pod-3', 'pod-4', 'pod-5'].map((pod) =>
      new LeaderElection(ds).runIfLeader('daily-settlement', async () => {
        ran.push(pod);
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200));   // hold the lock
      }),
    ),
  );

  expect(ran).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(results.filter(Boolean)).toHaveLength(1);
});

it('releases the lock when the work throws, so the next run can proceed', async () => {
  await expect(
    new LeaderElection(ds).runIfLeader('job-x', async () => { throw new Error('boom'); }),
  ).rejects.toThrow('boom');

  // If the lock had leaked, this would return false.
  const ran = await new LeaderElection(ds).runIfLeader('job-x', async () => undefined);
  expect(ran).toBe(true);
});

The second test is the one that would have caught the eleven-day silent failure in 31.5. It is four lines.

Do not use fake timers for these. jest.useFakeTimers() and real database round trips do not mix — the timers your ORM and driver use will not fire. Trigger the scheduled method directly instead of waiting for the cron to fire; @nestjs/schedule's SchedulerRegistry lets you fetch and invoke a job by name if you want the wiring covered too.

Production scenario

A payments team added a "concurrency suite" to CI: 14 tests, all against Testcontainers PostgreSQL, running on every PR. Total runtime 95 seconds (one container, TRUNCATE between tests). Over 18 months it caught 6 regressions before merge, including two where someone replaced an atomic update with an ORM save() during a refactor and every other test still passed.

Cost: 95 seconds per PR and one engineer-week to build. Value: the two save() regressions alone would each have been an oversell incident.

The one operational lesson: they had to pin the container image tag and set maxWorkers: 2 for that suite, because 8 Jest workers each starting a PostgreSQL container exhausted the CI runner's memory.

Failure scenario

At 11:00 a "fix" for an oversell shipped with a passing test. The test fired 50 concurrent requests and asserted 10 succeeded. It passed in CI. It passed locally. Oversells continued in production.

The test used a mocked repository whose decrement was implemented as stock -= qty in JavaScript — with no guard, but also with no await inside it, so it was atomic in the mock. The test was proving that JavaScript's -= is not interruptible, which is true and irrelevant. The production repository issued a real conditional UPDATE whose guard someone had accidentally deleted in the same PR.

Fix: the concurrency suite was moved to Testcontainers with the real repository, and a rule was added that any test with "concurrency" or "race" in its name must not mock the database layer. The retro's one-liner: a concurrency test that mocks the shared resource tests nothing.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mocking the database in a concurrency test removes the thing under test.
  • SQLite or an in-memory shim has different locking and isolation semantics; the test lies.
  • Running the test once and calling it proof; repeat 20 times.
  • Not running it against the buggy code first, so you never verify the test can fail.
  • Promise.all over supertest with agent.keepAlive off can serialise connections; check that requests really overlap.
  • Fake timers plus real I/O deadlock the test.
  • Shared state between tests (a container that is not truncated) makes failures look random.
  • Jest parallel workers each starting a container exhausts CI memory; cap maxWorkers for that suite.
  • Testing only the happy interleaving — also test that the loser gets a clean 409, not a 500.
  • Flaky assertions on timing (expect(duration).toBeLessThan(50)) fail on loaded CI; assert on invariants, not on speed.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They will not accept a concurrency fix without a concurrency test, and they check that the test fails against the old code. That check is non-negotiable, because a test that cannot fail is documentation with a false badge.

They keep two suites: fast deterministic tests in the main run, slower container-backed tests in a separate CI job. They assert invariants — sums, counts, constraints — rather than sequences, because the sequence is legitimately non-deterministic and only the invariant is guaranteed.

They add a database CHECK constraint alongside the test, because the constraint tests every code path forever, including ones written after they leave. And they treat a flaky concurrency test as a bug in the system, not in the test, until proven otherwise — flakiness under concurrency is usually the system telling you something.

To a product manager: "We wrote a test that pretends fifty customers click buy at the same instant on ten items. It runs on every change. If someone ever breaks the protection, the build fails instead of the warehouse."

Common mistakes

  • Unit-testing a race condition.
  • Mocking the shared resource.
  • One run, one assertion, done.
  • Never verifying the test detects the original bug.
  • Testing the winner's path and not the loser's error response.
  • Timing-based assertions that flake in CI.
  • No test at all because "it's hard to test concurrency".

Interview questions

  1. How do you test a race condition? Expected: real database, N genuinely concurrent operations, invariant assertions, repeated runs; plus deterministic tests with controlled promise resolution.
  2. Why does a unit test never catch an oversell? Expected: one actor, no interleaving, no second pod, and the shared resource is usually mocked away.
  3. How do you force a specific interleaving deterministically? Expected: replace the awaited dependency with deferreds you resolve from the test; yield a microtask so both callers reach the await.
  4. How do you know your concurrency test is any good? Expected: it fails against the pre-fix code; it passes 20 consecutive runs after the fix.
  5. How would you test deadlock retry? Expected: inject an error with code: '40P01' and assert the whole unit of work re-ran, that non-retryable codes do not retry, and that the attempt limit is honoured.
  6. How do you test that a cron runs on only one of five pods? Expected: five concurrent runIfLeader calls against one real database; assert exactly one ran; and a separate test that a throwing job still releases the lock.

Practical exercise

Add a concurrency suite to an existing NestJS service. Include: (1) a Testcontainers test firing 50 concurrent reservations against 10 units, (2) a deterministic test using deferreds that forces both callers to read the same stock value, (3) a deadlock-retry unit test, (4) a leader-election test with five concurrent callers plus a lock-release-on-throw test.

Acceptance criteria: every test fails against the pre-fix code and passes against the fixed code; the suite runs in under 2 minutes with one container; maxWorkers is configured so CI does not OOM; and a CHECK (available >= 0) constraint exists so the invariant is also enforced outside the tests.

31.16 Edge cases and failure modes

This is the reference section. Each entry is a real production failure: what you see, why it happens, what you do about it.

Oversell

  • Symptom. More orders than stock. The site shows "sold out" while paid orders keep arriving. Discovered by the warehouse, not by monitoring.
  • Cause. findOne -> check in JavaScript -> save. Two requests both read the old value across an await. Multi-pod makes any in-process guard useless.
  • Fix. One atomic statement: UPDATE inventory SET available = available - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND available >= $1, and treat affected === 0 as a 409. Add CHECK (available >= 0) so no future code path can violate it. Add a 50-concurrent-request test.

Double payment

  • Symptom. One customer charged twice for one order. Two payments rows, two provider charge ids.
  • Cause. Double-clicked button, or a client retry after a timeout where the first request actually succeeded. Two requests both see status = 'PENDING' and both charge.
  • Fix. Three layers. Idempotency key with a unique constraint, stored before calling the provider. A conditional state transition (UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=$1 AND status='PENDING') so only one request proceeds. And the provider's own idempotency key so even a duplicate call is deduplicated on their side.

Duplicate cron execution

  • Symptom. Five settlement runs, five digest emails per user, five reports. Always exactly N times, where N is your replica count.
  • Cause. @Cron is a per-process timer. Every replica has one.
  • Fix. Leader election with pg_try_advisory_xact_lock, or BullMQ repeatable jobs, or a replicas: 1 scheduler deployment with strategy: Recreate. Plus a unique constraint on (job_name, run_date) as the second layer, and a staleness alert so a silently-stopped job is noticed.

A job lost when a pod restarts mid-processing

  • Symptom. Queue depth looks fine; individual jobs never complete. A customer's export never arrives. No error anywhere.
  • Cause. The job was marked RUNNING, the pod was OOMKilled or evicted, and nothing ever reclaims a RUNNING row.
  • Fix. A lease (lease_until) with a heartbeat, and a leader-elected sweep that re-queues expired leases with backoff and an incremented attempt count. Cap attempts so a poison pill is dead-lettered instead of killing every pod in rotation. Make handlers idempotent, because takeover means at-least-once. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds high enough for a job to finish, and stop claiming new work on SIGTERM.

Unhandled rejection crashing the process

  • Symptom. Pods restart with no stack trace in the request logs. CrashLoopBackOff. Every in-flight request on that pod fails.
  • Cause. A promise rejected with no .catch() — almost always fire-and-forget (this.email.send(order) with no await). Node 15+ terminates the process by default.
  • Fix. Never fire-and-forget work that matters: use a transactional outbox or a queue. Where it truly does not matter, attach .catch() explicitly with void. Install a process.on('unhandledRejection') handler that logs fatally, closes the app gracefully and exits non-zero — so Kubernetes restarts you cleanly instead of mid-transaction. Enable @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises so the linter catches it.

Event listener leaks on a long-lived emitter

  • Symptom. MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 error listeners added. Memory climbs slowly. Eventually one emitted event runs the handler thousands of times.
  • Cause. A per-request or per-job emitter.on('x', handler) on a singleton emitter, with no off. Common with @nestjs/event-emitter, Redis clients, and stream error handlers registered inside a handler.
  • Fix. Register listeners once at module init, not per request. If you must register per operation, use once() and always remove in finally, or use AbortSignal with { signal } on addEventListener. Alert on the warning; do not raise setMaxListeners to silence it.

Memory growth from unbounded Promise.all

  • Symptom. RSS climbs to the pod limit during a batch job. OOMKilled, restart, job restarts from the beginning, OOMKilled again.
  • Cause. Promise.all(rows.map(...)) where rows came from a query. Every task starts immediately and retains its payload and closure. 10,000 x 14 KB is 140 MB before the actual data.
  • Fix. p-map or p-limit with concurrency chosen from the scarcest downstream (usually the connection pool). Stream the source with pg-query-stream instead of loading it. Checkpoint progress so a restart resumes. Bound the worker-pool queue (maxQueue) so a burst is rejected rather than buffered.

Nested-transaction deadlock (connection pool)

  • Symptom. Requests hang and then fail with timeout exceeded when trying to connect. PostgreSQL CPU is low, pg_stat_database.deadlocks is flat, no lock waits. Every dashboard says the database is healthy.
  • Cause. Code inside a transaction calls an injected repository, which takes a second connection. With N concurrent requests each holding one and wanting another, the pool is deadlocked.
  • Fix. Propagate the transaction's EntityManager (or Sequelize transaction) so nesting depth stays 1 — best done with AsyncLocalStorage (@nestjs-cls/transactional, or Sequelize's useCLS) so it is automatic. As a mitigation only, size the pool to P >= N * (D - 1) + 1. Alert on pool.waitingCount > 0 and on idle in transaction sessions.

AsyncLocalStorage context lost

  • Symptom. Log lines with an empty or wrong correlation id. cls.get('userId') returns undefined in a background handler. Audit rows with a null actor. Traces that break at a queue boundary.
  • Cause. Three distinct boundaries. setTimeout scheduled outside the context runs in whatever context existed when it was scheduled. Event-emitter listeners registered at startup run in the startup context, not the emitter's caller's. Queue and process boundaries (BullMQ, Kafka, HTTP to another service) do not carry in-process state at all.
  • Fix. For timers and emitters, capture and re-enter: const store = cls.get(); setTimeout(() => cls.run(store, work), 1000) — or better, avoid detaching from the request in the first place. For queues, serialise the ids into the job payload and re-enter the context at the top of the processor:
@Processor('emails')
export class EmailProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  constructor(private readonly cls: ClsService) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<{ correlationId: string; userId: string; to: string }>) {
    // Re-establish the context on the other side of the boundary.
    await this.cls.run(async () => {
      this.cls.set('correlationId', job.data.correlationId);
      this.cls.set('userId', job.data.userId);
      await this.mail.send(job.data);       // logs and audits now carry the right ids
    });
  }
}

For HTTP, propagate x-correlation-id (or W3C traceparent) as a header. The rule: ALS is a within-process convenience; across any boundary you must carry the value explicitly.

Request-scoped providers collapsing throughput

  • Symptom. Throughput drops 30-60% after a refactor. p99 doubles. GC time rises. No individual endpoint looks slower in traces.
  • Cause. Someone made one provider Scope.REQUEST, and scope bubbled up the injection chain, making the controller and its whole subtree per-request. NestJS now builds an object graph on every request.
  • Fix. Move the request data to AsyncLocalStorage (nestjs-cls) and keep providers singleton. Where per-request instances are genuinely needed for multi-tenancy, use durable providers with a ContextIdStrategy keyed on tenant, and bound the tenant map. Measure before and after; do not accept scope changes without a benchmark.

A Redis lock expiring while the work is still running

  • Symptom. Two workers processing the same job. Duplicate side effects despite "having a lock". Logs show both holding it, both convinced they are exclusive.
  • Cause. TTL shorter than the work. Or a GC pause / network partition froze the holder past its TTL. A TTL-based lock cannot provide mutual exclusion by itself.
  • Fix. Three things together. Set TTL from p99 work duration x 3 and heartbeat-extend at TTL/3 with a Lua compare-and-extend. Release with a Lua compare-and-delete so you never delete someone else's lock. And make the protected resource enforce ordering with a fencing token: INCR a counter per acquisition and write UPDATE ... WHERE fence < $token, so a stale holder's write affects zero rows. The fence is the correctness guarantee; the lock is the optimisation.

setInterval pile-up

  • Symptom. Increasing concurrent runs of a poll loop. Connection pool exhaustion at a regular cadence. Memory climbing in a sawtooth that never fully returns.
  • Cause. setInterval(fn, 30_000) schedules starts 30 s apart regardless of duration. Work that takes 45 s overlaps; work that takes 90 s triples up and grows without bound.
  • Fix. Self-schedule from the end of each run with setTimeout and reschedule in finally, so a gap is guaranteed. Or add a re-entrancy guard that skips the tick and increments a cron.skipped counter — silence here is dangerous, so always count skips. Remember the guard is per pod: on multiple replicas you also need leader election. Clear the timer in onModuleDestroy or shutdown hangs.

Two workers claiming the same row without SKIP LOCKED

  • Symptom. Queue depth grows while all workers show as busy. Fleet throughput equals one worker's throughput. Adding pods changes nothing.
  • Cause. The claim query is SELECT ... ORDER BY priority LIMIT 25 FOR UPDATE with no SKIP LOCKED. Every worker blocks on the same top row. Invisible while jobs are fast; catastrophic the moment a downstream slows down.
  • Fix. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a claiming UPDATE ... RETURNING, so each worker takes a disjoint batch. Add a partial index on the claim predicate. Put a timeout on every downstream call so slowness degrades throughput proportionally. Alert on "oldest pending job age", which catches this shape long before queue depth does.

Replication lag reading stale state

  • Symptom. A user creates a resource, immediately reads it, and gets a 404. Or a balance check passes against a replica that has not seen the debit.
  • Cause. Reads routed to a replica that is seconds behind. The race is between your write and the replica's replay.
  • Fix. Route reads that follow a write in the same user flow to the primary (read-your-writes). Never make a decision on replica data — validation, authorisation and money checks go to the primary. Monitor pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() lag and fail over reads to the primary when lag exceeds a threshold.

Cache stampede on a hot key

  • Symptom. Database p99 spikes at a fixed cadence matching a TTL. Hundreds of identical expensive queries in pg_stat_statements within a few milliseconds.
  • Cause. A popular key expires and every concurrent request misses and rebuilds.
  • Fix. Single-flight per process (a Map of in-flight promises), a distributed rebuild lock so one pod rebuilds, and a longer-lived stale copy served while the rebuild happens. Add jitter to TTLs so keys do not expire together. Covered in full in 31.3.

31.17 A concurrency review checklist

Use this on any pull request that touches shared state — a database row, a cache key, a queue, an in-memory field, or a scheduled task.

# Question to ask What a good answer looks like Red flag
1 What happens if two of these run at the same instant? A specific mechanism: atomic statement, row lock, version check, unique constraint "It won't"
2 What happens on twelve pods? Same answer as #1, because the guard lives in PostgreSQL or Redis An in-process Map, Set or mutex
3 Is there an await between a read and a write that depends on it? No, or the write is guarded by the value read Yes, unguarded
4 Is the row count of every UPDATE checked? affected === 0 maps to a 409/404 await repo.update(...) with the result discarded
5 Could this be a single atomic statement instead? Yes, and it is A lock or transaction wrapping one logical decision
6 Is the invariant also a database constraint? UNIQUE, CHECK or EXCLUDE backs the code Code-only enforcement
7 Are locks taken in a consistent order? Sorted by primary key, with ORDER BY on the locking select Client-supplied order
8 Is there any external call inside a transaction or lock? No fetch, queue publish, or S3 inside the critical section
9 What is the p99 hold time, and what throughput does 1/hold allow? A measured number that exceeds peak demand Unknown
10 If this is retried, what happens twice? Nothing harmful: idempotency key or claim-before-act An email, a charge, a webhook
11 Does the retry re-read state and use jitter? Yes, bounded attempts, full jitter Fixed delay, or reuses stale data, or unbounded
12 Is any request data stored on a provider field? No; parameters or AsyncLocalStorage this.currentUser, this.tenantId
13 Is any new provider Scope.REQUEST? No, or benchmarked and justified Added "to be safe"
14 How many concurrent operations can this generate, and does the pool fit? pods x concurrency computed against max_connections Promise.all over a query result
15 Is every Promise.all bounded? p-limit/p-map with a justified concurrency Unbounded over a variable-length array
16 Does every remote call have a timeout and a decreasing budget? Yes, shorter than the caller's No signal, no statement_timeout
17 Is there a @Cron or @Interval here? How many replicas? Leader-elected or scheduler-owned, plus a unique constraint @Cron with replicas > 1
18 Can this scheduled work overlap with its previous run? No: self-scheduling, or a guard that counts skips @Interval shorter than p99 duration
19 If a pod dies mid-operation, what is left behind and who cleans it? A lease with heartbeat and a takeover sweep A RUNNING row nobody reclaims
20 Is the ALS context re-entered after a queue or timer boundary? Ids carried in the payload and cls.run() at the top of the handler Correlation ids that vanish
21 Is there a concurrency test, and does it fail against the old code? Testcontainers, N concurrent calls, invariant assertions, repeated A unit test with a mocked repository
22 What is the metric that would show this failing in production? pg_pool_waiting, deadlock rate, lease-takeover rate, oldest pending job, idle in transaction "We'd see the errors"

If a PR cannot answer #1, #2 and #10, it is not ready, regardless of how clean the code reads.

Senior Checklist — Part 31

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain why single-threaded Node still has race conditions, and point at the await that causes one
  • I can name the five race-condition shapes and the standard fix for each
  • I can write the atomic conditional UPDATE for a stock decrement and explain why the row count is the business answer
  • I can choose between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency and defend the choice with a conflict rate
  • I can write a correct Redis lock with a Lua compare-and-delete release, and explain why a fencing token is still required
  • I can explain the connection-pool deadlock and compute P >= N * (D - 1) + 1 for my own service
  • I can size a database pool across pods, workers and cron against max_connections, including what the HPA does to it
  • I can spot request data stored on a singleton NestJS provider and know two ways to fix it
  • I can make a @Cron job run exactly once across a fleet, and know how I would find out if it silently stopped
  • I can build a PostgreSQL job queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, leases, heartbeats and dead-lettering
  • I can write a concurrency test that fails against the buggy code and passes against the fix
  • I know which metrics tell me a concurrency problem is happening right now

Part 31 — Key Takeaways

  • Node is single-threaded but not race-free: every await is a point where the world can change, and every pod is another actor doing the same thing.
  • In-process guards — a Map, a Set, an async-mutex — protect process-local resources only. Business invariants must live in PostgreSQL or Redis, where every pod can see them.
  • Push the decision into the layer that serialises it for you. A conditional UPDATE whose row count is the answer beats every lock, and a constraint beats every code path, including the ones not written yet.
  • Optimistic when conflicts are rare and the think-time is long; pessimistic when contention is high, transactions are short, and the work must not be redone. Above both: if the write is relative, use an atomic statement and choose neither.
  • Deadlocks are prevented by consistent lock ordering and survived by a jittered retry of the whole transaction. Sorting by primary key removes the entire class.
  • The connection-pool deadlock is the one that will page you: a transaction holding one connection while awaiting a second. Fix it by propagating the transaction's manager, not by raising the pool.
  • Never hold a lock or a transaction across an external call. Throughput through a lock is 1 / hold_time, and a third party's bad day becomes your outage.
  • A NestJS provider is a singleton shared by every concurrent request. Request data on a provider field is a data-leak bug, not a style issue.
  • Bound every fan-out. Promise.all over a query result is unbounded on memory, connections and downstream rate limits; p-map with a justified concurrency is the fix.
  • @Cron runs on every replica. Elect a leader with pg_try_advisory_xact_lock, and add a unique constraint as the second layer, and alert on staleness so a silently-stopped job is noticed the next day.
  • Distributed job processing is at-least-once. SKIP LOCKED for claiming, leases with heartbeats for recovery, attempt caps for poison pills, and idempotent handlers because none of the above is exactly-once.
  • A concurrency fix without a concurrency test is a hypothesis. Run N real requests against a real database, assert the invariant, repeat twenty times, and verify the test fails against the old code.
  • The metrics that tell the truth: event-loop lag, pg_pool_waiting, pg_stat_database.deadlocks, idle in transaction age, lease-takeover rate, and oldest pending job.

Part 32 — File Storage and Uploads

32.1 Why file storage is its own discipline

Every product eventually stores files. Profile pictures, invoices as PDF, product images, KYC documents, CSV imports, chat attachments, voice notes. Most developers meet this the same way: multer writes the upload to ./uploads, a column stores the path, and it works on the laptop. Then the app gets a second pod and half the images return 404.

Files are different from rows. A row is 200 bytes and lives in PostgreSQL where transactions, backups and replication are already solved. A file is 5 MB to 5 GB, it is written once and read many times, it must survive pod restarts, it must be served fast from anywhere in the world, and it is the most common way attackers get executable content into your system. Files need their own storage tier, their own upload path, their own metadata, their own lifecycle and their own security review.

This part follows the life of a file through a NestJS system: where the bytes live, how they get there without going through your API pods, how the database tracks them, how they are processed and delivered, and every way the whole thing goes wrong.

32.2 The local filesystem

Concept

Local file storage means the NestJS process writes uploaded bytes to a directory on the disk of the machine (or container) it is running on, and reads them back from the same path later. The database stores the path.

It is the simplest possible storage: fs.createWriteStream('/data/uploads/abc.jpg'). No SDK, no credentials, no network. That simplicity is exactly why it breaks in production.

Why does it exist?

Local storage exists because it is the default. Every language has a filesystem API, every tutorial uses it, and for a single-server application it is genuinely fine. The engineering problem it fails to solve is sharing: the moment two processes on two machines must see the same file, a local disk is the wrong abstraction.

Mental model

Imagine a shop where each cashier keeps customer receipts in the drawer of their own till. It works with one cashier. Hire a second cashier and a customer who paid at till 1 cannot get a copy of their receipt from till 2. Replace till 1 overnight and every receipt in its drawer is gone. The fix is not a better drawer; it is a filing cabinet in the back office that every cashier walks to.

How it works

  1. The HTTP request carries multipart/form-data. A parser (multer, busboy) reads the body stream and writes the file part to disk.
  2. The service records the path (/data/uploads/2026/09/abc.jpg) in PostgreSQL.
  3. A download request looks up the path and streams the file back with res.sendFile or a read stream.

Where it fails:

Situation What happens
Two or more pods behind a load balancer Upload lands on pod A; download request hits pod B; 404
Container restart or redeploy Container filesystem is ephemeral; every upload since the last deploy is gone
Kubernetes node failure The pod is rescheduled elsewhere; the volume, if any, may not follow
Backups Your database backup does not include the disk; you now need a second backup system
Disk full The whole pod fails, including unrelated endpoints, because logs and temp files share the disk
Serving large files Node.js pods spend CPU and memory shuffling bytes that a CDN could serve for free

Shared network volumes (NFS, AWS EFS mounted into every pod) fix the "which pod" problem but bring their own: EFS latency for small files is 1 to 3 ms per operation instead of microseconds, throughput is provisioned and can throttle, and you still own backups and serving.

Practical example

A food-delivery back office lets restaurant owners upload menu photos. The first version stores them under ./public/menus and serves them with ServeStaticModule. It runs on one EC2 instance for a year. Then the team moves to Kubernetes with three replicas. Within an hour, support tickets say "my photo uploaded but disappears when I refresh". The upload went to replica 2; the refresh was served by replica 1. Rolling back does not help because the deploy replaced the containers and the photos uploaded during the last hour are gone with them.

NestJS example

When local storage is genuinely fine (a single-instance internal tool, or a temp staging area before pushing to S3), keep it explicit and bounded:

// upload.controller.ts
import {
  Controller, Post, UploadedFile, UseInterceptors,
  ParseFilePipe, MaxFileSizeValidator, FileTypeValidator,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { FileInterceptor } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { diskStorage } from 'multer';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { extname } from 'node:path';

@Controller('internal/imports')
export class ImportController {
  @Post('csv')
  @UseInterceptors(FileInterceptor('file', {
    storage: diskStorage({
      destination: process.env.IMPORT_TMP_DIR ?? '/tmp/imports',
      // never trust the client filename for the path; generate our own
      filename: (_req, file, cb) => cb(null, `${randomUUID()}${extname(file.originalname).toLowerCase()}`),
    }),
    limits: { fileSize: 20 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 }, // 20 MB, one file
  }))
  async importCsv(
    @UploadedFile(new ParseFilePipe({
      validators: [
        new MaxFileSizeValidator({ maxSize: 20 * 1024 * 1024 }),
        new FileTypeValidator({ fileType: /text\/csv|application\/vnd\.ms-excel/ }),
      ],
    }))
    file: Express.Multer.File,
  ) {
    // file.path is on THIS pod's disk. Process it now, in this request or a
    // same-pod job, then delete it. Do not store file.path in the database.
    return { received: file.size, tmpPath: file.path };
  }
}

ParseFilePipe, MaxFileSizeValidator and FileTypeValidator are real @nestjs/common exports. Note that FileTypeValidator checks the client-declared mimetype in older versions; treat it as a first filter, not as proof (see 32.12 on magic bytes).

Production scenario

When is local disk acceptable?

  • A single-replica internal tool where losing uploads on redeploy is fine.
  • A temp directory for a file that is fully processed within the same request or same pod (CSV import parsed and rows inserted), then deleted.
  • A build cache or scratch space that is explicitly disposable.

In each case, the rule is: the path never leaves the pod's memory, and the disk is never the system of record.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday, after a deploy that scaled the API from one pod to three, the on-call sees a spike in 404s on /files/:id. The database has 12,000 rows with paths that exist on no current pod. The previous pod's disk was emptyDir and was deleted with the pod. There is no backup. The team recovers 9,000 files from a stale staging sync and asks 3,000 users to re-upload. The postmortem action item is a single line: "Files live in S3. Local disk is temp only."

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Disk fills with orphaned temp files from crashed requests; add a cleanup cron and a per-pod size cap.
  • multer default memory storage buffers the whole file in RAM; a 2 GB upload OOM-kills the pod.
  • Symlinks in an upload path let an attacker read /etc/passwd if you ever serve by client-supplied name.
  • hostPath volumes tie a pod to one node and break scheduling.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks one question: "If this pod disappears in the next second, what is lost?" If the answer includes user files, the design is wrong. Local disk is a buffer, not storage. They also ask about the download path: serving bytes through Node.js is the most expensive way to serve bytes on the planet.

Common mistakes

  • Storing file.path in the database and calling it "the file service".
  • Mounting one shared PVC into three pods with ReadWriteOnce and wondering why two pods will not start.
  • Using ServeStaticModule for user uploads in production, so every image request occupies a Node.js event loop tick and a socket.

Interview questions

  1. Why does local file storage break with multiple replicas? Expected: each replica has its own disk; uploads are not visible across pods; containers are ephemeral. Follow-up: how would you fix it with zero code change? Answer: shared volume like EFS, then explain its limits.
  2. When is local disk fine? Expected: temp files consumed within the same pod and deleted; disposable caches.
  3. What is the cost of serving files through Node.js? Expected: event loop time, memory for buffers, sockets held open for slow clients, no caching; a CDN serves them cheaper and faster.

Practical exercise

Take a NestJS app that stores uploads locally. Run two instances behind nginx with round-robin. Upload a file and download it ten times; measure the failure rate. Then move the write to S3 (next sections) and repeat. Acceptance criteria: 0 percent failure with two instances; a pod restart loses no files.

32.3 Object storage: the S3 model

Concept

Object storage stores files as objects: an opaque blob of bytes, a key (its name), and metadata (content type, size, custom tags). Objects live in a bucket, which is a globally named container. You talk to it over HTTPS with PUT, GET, HEAD, DELETE and LIST. There are no directories, no file handles, no partial writes and no locks. Amazon S3 defined this model; Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, MinIO and Cloudflare R2 follow it closely.

Why does it exist?

A filesystem promises things that are expensive to keep at scale: hierarchical directories, in-place modification, byte-range writes, POSIX locks, consistent metadata across every reader. Object storage drops all of them. In exchange, it can replicate every object across multiple data centers, scale to trillions of objects, serve them from any pod in any region, and charge about $0.023 per GB-month (approximate US list price) with no capacity planning on your side.

The engineering problem it solves: durable, shared, cheap, infinitely wide storage for write-once-read-many blobs. That is exactly what user files are.

Mental model

Imagine a giant warehouse with numbered shelves but no rooms. You hand the clerk a box and a label (the key). The clerk copies the box three times and puts the copies in three different buildings. When you come back with the label you get the box. You cannot open the box on the shelf and change one page inside; you hand over a whole new box with the same label and the clerk replaces it. Labels can contain slashes, invoices/2026/09/abc.pdf, but that is only a naming convention; there is no invoices room.

How it works

The parts of the model you must know:

  1. Bucket. A namespace with a globally unique name, in one region. Holds unlimited objects. Policies, encryption defaults, versioning and lifecycle rules are set per bucket.
  2. Key. A UTF-8 string up to 1,024 bytes. Slashes are ordinary characters. The console draws folders by splitting on /; the service does not care.
  3. Flat namespace. LIST takes a Prefix and a Delimiter. Listing Prefix=tenants/42/ with Delimiter=/ gives you the "folder view". Listing is paginated at 1,000 keys and is slower than a GET; never design a hot path that needs to list.
  4. Metadata. System metadata (Content-Type, Content-Length, ETag, Last-Modified) and user metadata (x-amz-meta-* headers, up to 2 KB total). Metadata is set at write time; changing it requires a copy of the object onto itself.
  5. Durability. S3 is designed for 99.999999999 percent (eleven nines) annual durability. Objects are stored redundantly across at least three Availability Zones. In plain terms: if you store 10 million objects, you can expect to lose one every 10,000 years. Durability is not availability; the SLA for availability is 99.9 to 99.99 percent depending on class.
  6. Consistency. Since December 2020, S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for all operations: after a successful PUT, every subsequent GET, HEAD or LIST sees the new object. Before that, overwrites and deletes were eventually consistent, which is why older advice talks about "wait and retry". You no longer need that inside S3. You still need it for CDN caches in front of S3 (see 32.9).
  7. Versioning. When enabled on a bucket, every overwrite and delete keeps the previous version. A delete adds a delete marker instead of removing bytes. This is your undo button for accidental deletes and ransomware, and a cost trap if you never expire old versions.
  8. Storage classes. Same API, different price and retrieval behavior:
Class Approx. $/GB-month (US) Retrieval Use for
Standard 0.023 Instant Active user files, product images
Intelligent-Tiering 0.023 then auto-lowers Instant Unknown access pattern
Standard-IA 0.0125 plus per-GB retrieval Instant Files older than 30 days rarely read
One Zone-IA 0.01 Instant, one AZ only Re-creatable derived files
Glacier Instant Retrieval 0.004 Milliseconds Archives read a few times a year
Glacier Flexible Retrieval 0.0036 Minutes to hours Compliance archives
Glacier Deep Archive 0.00099 12 hours Seven-year legal retention

Prices are approximate list prices and change; the shape matters more than the digits. Cheaper classes charge more per request and per GB retrieved, and some have minimum storage durations (30, 90, 180 days) so moving a file in and out quickly costs more than leaving it.

flowchart LR
  APP["NestJS pod"] -->|"PUT key, bytes, metadata"| S3["S3 bucket in region"]
  S3 --> AZ1["Copy in AZ a"]
  S3 --> AZ2["Copy in AZ b"]
  S3 --> AZ3["Copy in AZ c"]
  APP2["Any other pod or Lambda"] -->|"GET key"| S3
  CDN["CloudFront edge"] -->|"GET on cache miss"| S3

Practical example

An e-commerce catalog has 2 million products with an average of 4 images each at 300 KB. That is 8 million objects and about 2.4 TB. In S3 Standard that is roughly $55 per month for storage. The same data on provisioned EBS volumes with replication and backups would be several times that, and you would still have to build the serving layer. Product images are read 50 million times a day, which is why they must go through a CDN (32.9) rather than being fetched from S3 per request: S3 GET requests cost about $0.0004 per 1,000, so 50 million per day is about $600 per month just in request fees, and CloudFront's cache eliminates most of that.

NestJS example

The S3 client is a singleton provider configured from the environment. Credentials come from the IAM role attached to the pod (IRSA on EKS, task role on ECS), never from static keys in config.

// s3.module.ts
import { Module, Global } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { NodeHttpHandler } from '@smithy/node-http-handler';

export const S3_CLIENT = Symbol('S3_CLIENT');

@Global()
@Module({
  imports: [ConfigModule],
  providers: [
    {
      provide: S3_CLIENT,
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) =>
        new S3Client({
          region: config.getOrThrow<string>('AWS_REGION'),
          // No explicit credentials: the default provider chain picks up the
          // pod's IAM role (IRSA / task role) or local env in development.
          maxAttempts: 4, // SDK retries with backoff on 5xx and SlowDown
          requestHandler: new NodeHttpHandler({
            connectionTimeout: 3_000,
            requestTimeout: 30_000, // per request; multipart parts are smaller
          }),
          // Optional: point at MinIO / LocalStack in tests
          ...(config.get('S3_ENDPOINT')
            ? { endpoint: config.get('S3_ENDPOINT'), forcePathStyle: true }
            : {}),
        }),
    },
  ],
  exports: [S3_CLIENT],
})
export class S3Module {}

A minimal write and read, used for small server-generated files such as invoices:

// invoice-storage.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand, GetObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { S3_CLIENT } from './s3.module';

@Injectable()
export class InvoiceStorageService {
  private readonly bucket = process.env.INVOICE_BUCKET!;
  constructor(@Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  async putInvoice(orderId: string, pdf: Buffer): Promise<string> {
    const key = `invoices/${orderId.slice(0, 2)}/${orderId}.pdf`;
    await this.s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: this.bucket,
      Key: key,
      Body: pdf,
      ContentType: 'application/pdf',
      ContentDisposition: `attachment; filename="invoice-${orderId}.pdf"`,
      ServerSideEncryption: 'aws:kms', // SSE-KMS; bucket default may already do this
      Metadata: { orderId }, // becomes x-amz-meta-orderid
      ChecksumAlgorithm: 'SHA256', // SDK computes and S3 verifies integrity
    }));
    return key;
  }

  async getInvoiceStream(key: string) {
    const res = await this.s3.send(new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key }));
    // res.Body is a Node.js Readable in Node runtimes
    return { stream: res.Body as NodeJS.ReadableStream, size: res.ContentLength, type: res.ContentType };
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The database never stores bytes; it stores the pointer and the facts you need to query:

CREATE TABLE files (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  owner_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  bucket      text NOT NULL,
  key         text NOT NULL,
  size_bytes  bigint,
  mime_type   text,
  checksum_sha256 text,
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (bucket, key)
);
CREATE INDEX files_owner_created_idx ON files (owner_id, created_at DESC);

We expand this table into a full state machine in 32.8.

Production scenario

Throughput: S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix, and partitions scale automatically. A single GET from a same-region pod takes 10 to 30 ms first byte for a small object, and streams at hundreds of MB/s for large ones. Multi-GB downloads are best done in parallel byte ranges. Monitoring: watch 4xxErrors, 5xxErrors, FirstByteLatency, and bucket size and object count from CloudWatch; alert on 503 SlowDown in your own client metrics.

When should you not use object storage? When you need in-place random writes (a database file), POSIX semantics (a legacy app that fopens files), sub-millisecond reads on the hot path (use Redis or memory), or transactional coupling with row data (store the small blob in a bytea column instead if it is under a few hundred KB and always read with the row).

Failure scenario

A team migrates from local disk to S3 and keeps the old code path: every product page does GetObject for four images and streams them through NestJS. Traffic is 400 requests per second, so 1,600 S3 GETs per second at 20 ms each. The Node.js pods spend most of their event loop time copying buffers, p99 climbs to 900 ms, and the monthly S3 request bill is $1,700 for something CloudFront would serve for a fraction. Fix: public product images served by CDN URL directly; NestJS never touches image bytes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Keys are case sensitive and byte-exact; Invoice.pdf and invoice.pdf are different objects.
  • Object size limits: 5 GB per single PUT, 5 TB with multipart.
  • A PUT to an existing key overwrites atomically; readers see either the old or the new object, never a mix.
  • LIST is eventually expensive: listing a prefix with 10 million keys takes 10,000 paginated calls. Keep an index in PostgreSQL instead.
  • Bucket names are global; prod-uploads is taken. Use company-env-purpose-random.
  • Cross-region reads cost egress and add 80 to 150 ms.
  • 11 nines durability does not protect against you deleting the object. Versioning and Object Lock do.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Object storage is where files live; everything else is a cache or a pointer. The senior separates three concerns: bytes (S3), facts about bytes (PostgreSQL), and delivery (CDN). They refuse to let the API pods be a byte pipe for anything large, and they refuse to put file paths in the database without a status that says whether the bytes actually exist.

Common mistakes

  • Treating prefixes as folders and "creating a folder" by uploading a zero-byte object.
  • Using LIST to find a user's files instead of querying PostgreSQL.
  • Storing the full https://bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/key URL in the database instead of bucket plus key; the URL format changes when you add a CDN or move regions.
  • Assuming durability means "cannot be lost"; a bad lifecycle rule deletes with 11 nines of reliability.

Interview questions

  1. What does eleven nines of durability actually mean, and what does it not protect against? Expected: expected annual loss of one object in 10 billion; does not protect against deletion, bad lifecycle rules, account compromise, region-wide disaster without replication.
  2. Is S3 strongly consistent? Expected: yes, since December 2020, for all operations; caches in front of it are not.
  3. How would you store 8 million product images and serve 50 million views a day? Expected: S3 Standard, unique keys per version, CloudFront with long cache TTL, no NestJS in the read path.
  4. Why store bucket and key rather than a URL? Expected: URL is a delivery detail; CDN, region, signing all change it.

Practical exercise

Stand up MinIO in Docker (minio/minio server /data), point the S3Client at it with forcePathStyle: true, and write an integration test that uploads an invoice PDF, reads it back, verifies the ContentType, and confirms that a second PUT to the same key replaces it atomically. Acceptance criteria: the test passes against MinIO and against a real S3 bucket with only environment variables changed.

32.4 S3 usage patterns: keys, encryption, policies and IAM

Concept

Four decisions shape every S3 integration: how you name keys, how objects are encrypted, who can reach the bucket (bucket policy and Block Public Access), and how your code authenticates (IAM roles). Get them right at the start; changing key layout or encryption for millions of objects later is a migration project.

Why does it exist?

A bucket with a bad key scheme cannot be lifecycle-managed per tenant. A bucket without encryption fails every compliance review. A bucket with a permissive policy becomes tomorrow's data breach headline. Static access keys in a config file become a leaked credential in a Git history.

Mental model

Imagine the warehouse again. Key design is how you write the labels so a forklift can find "everything for customer 42 from last September" without reading every label. Encryption is the lock on each box. The bucket policy is the guard at the door with a list of who may enter. IAM roles are the ID badges your workers wear instead of a shared key hidden under the mat.

How it works

Key design. Historical advice (before 2018) said to put random characters at the start of keys so that S3's internal partitions would not get hot. That advice is obsolete: S3 now scales partitions per prefix automatically and sustains thousands of requests per second per prefix. Design keys for humans and lifecycle rules instead:

{purpose}/{tenant_id}/{yyyy}/{mm}/{file_uuid}.{ext}

uploads/tenant-42/2026/09/9c1f2a7e-....jpg      user uploads, raw
derived/tenant-42/2026/09/9c1f2a7e-..._thumb.webp  generated thumbnails
exports/tenant-42/2026/09/orders-2026-09-01.csv  temp exports, expire 7 days

Rules that pay off:

  • The key contains a UUID you generated. Never the client's filename. Never a sequential integer (enumerable, hot).
  • The prefix groups by purpose and tenant so a lifecycle rule can say "expire exports/ after 7 days" and a deletion request for tenant 42 can list one prefix.
  • Never overwrite a key with different content. A new version of the avatar gets a new UUID. This is what makes CDN caching safe (32.9).
  • Store the extension for humans, but set Content-Type explicitly from validated detection, never from the extension.

Encryption at rest. Since January 2023 every new object is encrypted with SSE-S3 (AES-256, keys managed by S3) by default. SSE-KMS uses a key in AWS KMS instead: you get an audit trail of every decrypt in CloudTrail, the ability to revoke access by disabling the key, and per-tenant keys if you want them. SSE-KMS costs about $0.03 per 10,000 requests to KMS; enabling S3 Bucket Keys cuts that by 99 percent by caching a data key per bucket. For regulated data (KYC documents, medical files) use SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key. For product images, SSE-S3 is fine. Encryption in transit is HTTPS, enforced by a bucket policy that denies aws:SecureTransport = false.

Bucket policy and Block Public Access. Turn on all four Block Public Access settings at the account level and never turn them off for buckets holding user data. Public read is only ever appropriate for a dedicated public-assets bucket, and even that is better served through CloudFront with an Origin Access Control so the bucket itself stays private.

A private uploads bucket policy that only allows the app role and CloudFront:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-uploads", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-uploads/*"],
      "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontRead",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-uploads/*",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::123456789012:distribution/E1ABCDEF" } }
    }
  ]
}

IAM roles for the application. The NestJS pod gets a role via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) on EKS or a task role on ECS. The SDK's default credential chain picks it up with no code. The role's policy is scoped to the exact bucket and actions:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:HeadObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload", "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-uploads/uploads/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["kms:GenerateDataKey", "kms:Decrypt"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd-1234"
    }
  ]
}

No s3:ListBucket unless you need it, no s3:*, no wildcard resource. A pre-signed URL (32.7) inherits exactly these permissions, so a narrow role limits the blast radius of a leaked URL.

flowchart TB
  POD["NestJS pod with IAM role"] -->|"SigV4 signed HTTPS"| S3["Private bucket, Block Public Access ON"]
  S3 -->|"SSE-KMS encrypt on write"| KMS["KMS customer managed key"]
  CF["CloudFront distribution"] -->|"Origin Access Control"| S3
  USER["Browser"] -->|"HTTPS"| CF
  USER -.->|"Direct URL blocked 403"| S3

Practical example

A multi-tenant SaaS stores customer documents. Key layout docs/{tenant_id}/{yyyy}/{mm}/{uuid}.pdf, SSE-KMS with one key per region, bucket policy denying non-TLS, Block Public Access on, IRSA role scoped to docs/*. When a tenant leaves, the offboarding job lists docs/{tenant_id}/ (bounded, one tenant) and deletes; the lifecycle rule moves objects older than 90 days to Standard-IA. Every decrypt lands in CloudTrail, which satisfies the auditor's "who accessed this document" question.

NestJS example

Key generation lives in one place so nobody improvises:

// object-key.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export type Purpose = 'uploads' | 'derived' | 'exports';

@Injectable()
export class ObjectKeyService {
  build(purpose: Purpose, tenantId: string, ext: string, now = new Date()): string {
    const safeExt = ext.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '').toLowerCase().slice(0, 8);
    const yyyy = now.getUTCFullYear();
    const mm = String(now.getUTCMonth() + 1).padStart(2, '0');
    // UUID guarantees uniqueness; tenant prefix enables scoped lifecycle and deletion.
    return `${purpose}/${tenantId}/${yyyy}/${mm}/${randomUUID()}${safeExt ? '.' + safeExt : ''}`;
  }

  tenantPrefix(purpose: Purpose, tenantId: string): string {
    return `${purpose}/${tenantId}/`;
  }
}

Production scenario

Auditors ask: "Show me every access to document X in the last 90 days." With SSE-KMS and CloudTrail data events on the bucket, that is one Athena query. Without them, the answer is "we do not know". Cost of CloudTrail data events for a bucket with 20 million requests per month is roughly $20; most teams find that cheap relative to the audit finding.

Failure scenario

A developer testing a CDN change disables Block Public Access on the uploads bucket "for five minutes" and adds a Principal: * read statement. The change is never reverted. Four months later a security researcher finds 300,000 KYC documents enumerable by guessing keys that used a sequential order id. The company reports a breach. Two controls would have stopped it: account-level Block Public Access that a single developer cannot disable, and UUID keys that are not enumerable.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • KMS key deleted or disabled: every object encrypted with it becomes unreadable. Deletion has a mandatory 7 to 30 day waiting period; alert on ScheduleKeyDeletion.
  • KMS throttling: default 5,500 to 50,000 requests per second per region depending on region; bucket keys avoid it.
  • Cross-account access needs both the bucket policy and the caller's IAM policy to allow; either missing gives an opaque 403.
  • Bucket policy size limit is 20 KB; per-tenant statements do not scale, use prefix conditions.
  • s3:PutObject permission without kms:GenerateDataKey gives a confusing AccessDenied on SSE-KMS buckets.
  • Keys with characters that need URL encoding (+, spaces, %) break naive URL construction; the SDK encodes correctly, string concatenation does not.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the key scheme on a whiteboard with the lifecycle and deletion stories written next to it. They assume any URL will leak and any credential will be pasted into Slack, so they scope the role to the narrowest prefix and actions. They pick SSE-KMS for anything the compliance team would call "personal data" and SSE-S3 for the rest, and they turn on Block Public Access at the account level as an organization guardrail, not a per-bucket setting.

Common mistakes

  • Random prefixes at the start of keys "for performance", which makes lifecycle rules and tenant deletion impossible.
  • Static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in a .env file committed to Git.
  • One IAM role with s3:* on * shared by every service.
  • Overwriting avatars/{user_id}.jpg on every change, then fighting CDN staleness forever.

Interview questions

  1. Is the "random prefix" advice for S3 still valid? Expected: no; S3 scales per prefix automatically since 2018; design keys for lifecycle and tenancy.
  2. SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS: when do you choose which? Expected: KMS for audit trail, revocation, per-tenant keys, compliance; S3 for everything else; bucket keys to reduce KMS cost.
  3. How does a pod authenticate to S3 without keys? Expected: IAM role via IRSA or task role; SDK default credential chain; short-lived STS credentials.
  4. How do you make it impossible for a developer to make a bucket public? Expected: account-level Block Public Access plus an SCP in the organization denying changes to it.

Practical exercise

Write the key scheme, bucket policy and IAM policy for a ride-booking app that stores driver license photos (regulated), trip receipts (user-visible) and nightly CSV exports (temp). Acceptance criteria: a reviewer can, from the key alone, tell purpose, tenant and month; the license bucket uses SSE-KMS; the export prefix expires in 7 days; the role for the API cannot list the whole bucket.

32.5 Small uploads through NestJS: FileInterceptor and busboy

Concept

There are two ways bytes can enter your system: through your API pods, or directly into S3 with your API only issuing permission. This section covers the first, because it is right for small files (a 200 KB avatar, a 2 MB CSV) and because you need to understand its cost to appreciate why large files must not use it.

multer (wrapped by NestJS's FileInterceptor) parses multipart/form-data and gives you the file as a buffer or a temp file. busboy is the streaming parser underneath multer; using it directly lets you pipe the incoming stream straight to S3 without buffering the whole file.

Why does it exist?

Sometimes the server must see the bytes before they are stored: to validate a CSV's header row, to strip EXIF GPS data from a photo, to scan a document synchronously, or because the client is a legacy integration that can only POST to your API. For files under a few megabytes, the simplicity of "one request, done" beats the pre-signed dance.

Mental model

Imagine a receptionist who accepts parcels. For a letter, the receptionist opens it, checks it, and files it: fast and safe. For a refrigerator, the receptionist should not carry it through the lobby; they should hand the courier a key to the loading dock. FileInterceptor is the receptionist opening letters. Pre-signed URLs are the loading-dock key.

How it works

  1. The browser sends Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=.... The body is a sequence of parts, each with headers and bytes.
  2. busboy reads the request stream, finds boundaries, and emits field and file events. The file event hands you a readable stream of that part's bytes while they are still arriving.
  3. multer on top of busboy collects each file into memory (memoryStorage) or a temp file (diskStorage) and calls your handler when the whole body has been read.
  4. Your service validates, then writes to S3 with PutObjectCommand (buffer) or the Upload helper (stream, see 32.6).

Cost per upload through a pod: the request occupies a socket and a worker for the whole transfer; on a slow mobile connection a 5 MB upload can hold that for 30 seconds. Memory storage holds the whole file in the heap. Twenty concurrent 50 MB uploads through memoryStorage is 1 GB of heap and an OOMKilled pod.

Practical example

A ride-booking app lets drivers upload a profile photo (max 2 MB, JPEG or PNG). Requirements: strip EXIF metadata (GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken), resize to 512 by 512, store in S3, update the driver record. The server must see the bytes to strip and resize, the file is small, so FileInterceptor with memory storage is a reasonable choice.

NestJS example

// driver-photo.controller.ts
import {
  Controller, Post, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, UploadedFile, UseInterceptors,
  ParseFilePipe, MaxFileSizeValidator, BadRequestException, UseGuards,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { FileInterceptor } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { memoryStorage } from 'multer';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { DriverPhotoService } from './driver-photo.service';
import { sniffImageType } from '../files/magic-bytes';

@Controller('drivers')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class DriverPhotoController {
  constructor(private readonly photos: DriverPhotoService) {}

  @Post(':id/photo')
  @UseInterceptors(FileInterceptor('photo', {
    storage: memoryStorage(),
    limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1, fields: 0 }, // multer aborts the stream past 2 MB
  }))
  async upload(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) driverId: string,
    @UploadedFile(new ParseFilePipe({
      fileIsRequired: true,
      validators: [new MaxFileSizeValidator({ maxSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024 })],
    }))
    file: Express.Multer.File,
  ) {
    // Client mimetype is a hint; magic bytes are the truth.
    const detected = sniffImageType(file.buffer);
    if (detected !== 'image/jpeg' && detected !== 'image/png') {
      throw new BadRequestException('Only JPEG or PNG images are accepted');
    }
    return this.photos.replacePhoto(driverId, file.buffer, detected);
  }
}
// driver-photo.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import sharp from 'sharp';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';
import { ObjectKeyService } from '../s3/object-key.service';
import { DriverRepository } from './driver.repository';

@Injectable()
export class DriverPhotoService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DriverPhotoService.name);
  constructor(
    @Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client,
    private readonly keys: ObjectKeyService,
    private readonly drivers: DriverRepository,
  ) {}

  async replacePhoto(driverId: string, input: Buffer, mime: string) {
    // sharp re-encodes the image: this drops EXIF (GPS) and neutralizes
    // polyglot files that are both a valid image and a valid script.
    const webp = await sharp(input).rotate().resize(512, 512, { fit: 'cover' }).webp({ quality: 82 }).toBuffer();
    const key = this.keys.build('derived', driverId, 'webp'); // new key every time, never overwrite
    await this.s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET!, Key: key, Body: webp,
      ContentType: 'image/webp', CacheControl: 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable',
    }));
    const previousKey = await this.drivers.setPhotoKey(driverId, key); // returns old key
    this.log.log({ msg: 'driver photo replaced', driverId, key, previousKey, inMime: mime });
    // previousKey is deleted by a scheduled job after 24 h, not here, so CDN edges
    // and in-flight pages that still reference it do not break.
    return { key };
  }
}

When the server needs to see the bytes but must not hold them all in memory (a 200 MB CSV whose rows are inserted as they stream), use busboy directly and pipe to S3 and a parser at the same time:

// stream-upload.controller.ts
