import { Controller, Post, Req, BadRequestException, PayloadTooLargeException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';
import busboy from 'busboy';
import { PassThrough } from 'node:stream';
import { Upload } from '@aws-sdk/lib-storage';
import { Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';

@Controller('imports')
export class StreamUploadController {
  constructor(@Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  @Post('stream')
  async stream(@Req() req: Request): Promise<{ key: string; bytes: number }> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const bb = busboy({ headers: req.headers, limits: { fileSize: 200 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 } });
      let handled = false;

      bb.on('file', (_name, fileStream, info) => {
        handled = true;
        const key = `imports/${Date.now()}-${info.filename.replace(/[^\w.-]/g, '_').slice(0, 80)}`;
        const pass = new PassThrough();
        let bytes = 0;
        fileStream.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => { bytes += chunk.length; });
        fileStream.on('limit', () => { pass.destroy(new PayloadTooLargeException('File exceeds 200 MB')); });
        fileStream.pipe(pass);

        // lib-storage Upload streams to S3 in 5 MB+ parts as bytes arrive.
        new Upload({ client: this.s3, params: { Bucket: process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET!, Key: key, Body: pass, ContentType: 'text/csv' }, partSize: 8 * 1024 * 1024, queueSize: 3 })
          .done()
          .then(() => resolve({ key, bytes }))
          .catch(reject);
      });
      bb.on('error', reject);
      bb.on('finish', () => { if (!handled) reject(new BadRequestException('No file part')); });
      req.pipe(bb);
    });
  }
}

Memory stays flat regardless of file size because PassThrough applies backpressure: if S3 is slow, the request stream pauses.

PostgreSQL example

Store the outcome, not the bytes, and do it after S3 confirms the write:

UPDATE drivers
   SET photo_key = $2, photo_updated_at = now()
 WHERE id = $1
RETURNING (SELECT photo_key FROM drivers WHERE id = $1) AS previous_key;

The subselect runs before the update within the same statement, so you get the old key back for deferred deletion.

Production scenario

A pod handling 50 concurrent avatar uploads at 2 MB uses about 100 MB of extra heap for buffers plus sharp working memory (roughly 3 to 4 times the decoded image size per operation). Set container memory limits accordingly and cap concurrent uploads per pod with limits and a rate limiter (@nestjs/throttler) on the upload route. Upload latency end to end: 300 ms network plus 60 ms sharp plus 40 ms S3 PUT plus 3 ms PostgreSQL.

When not to do this: any file that can exceed 10 MB, any client on a slow network, any endpoint that is hot. Go to pre-signed URLs (32.7).

Failure scenario

A marketing team adds "upload your video testimonial" to the same FileInterceptor endpoint with fileSize: 500 MB and memoryStorage. During a campaign, 40 users upload at once. Each pod has a 1 GB memory limit. Three pods are OOMKilled within two minutes, Kubernetes restarts them, in-flight uploads fail, users retry, and the retry storm keeps the pods in CrashLoopBackOff. The API is down for everything, including checkout, because uploads share the deployment. Fix: pre-signed URLs for video, and a separate deployment for any endpoint that streams bytes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • limits.fileSize exceeded: multer emits an error mid-stream; make sure your exception filter maps LIMIT_FILE_SIZE to 413 and that the client sees it rather than a socket reset.
  • Client sends Content-Length smaller than actual body; the parser hangs waiting; set server.requestTimeout and headersTimeout.
  • Missing boundary in Content-Type: busboy throws synchronously in the constructor; wrap it.
  • Nginx or ALB in front has its own body limit (client_max_body_size defaults to 1 MB in nginx); the 413 arrives before NestJS sees anything.
  • sharp on a crafted image (decompression bomb: 1 KB PNG that decodes to 20,000 by 20,000 pixels) allocates 1.6 GB; set sharp({ limitInputPixels }).
  • Two uploads for the same driver at the same time: last write wins on photo_key; the loser's object is orphaned until cleanup.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Through-the-API uploads are a budgeted resource, not a default. The senior sets a hard size ceiling (typically 5 to 10 MB), isolates upload endpoints into their own deployment or at least their own rate-limit bucket, always re-encodes images, and never lets a client filename touch a path or a key.

Common mistakes

  • memoryStorage with no limits.
  • Trusting file.mimetype (set by the browser from the extension).
  • Doing image processing in the request when a queue would do; a 20 MB PNG resize blocks the event loop's thread pool for seconds.
  • Deleting the old object synchronously before the CDN has moved on.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between multer and busboy? Expected: busboy is the streaming parser; multer wraps it and buffers into memory or disk; use busboy directly to stream to S3 with bounded memory.
  2. Why re-encode uploaded images? Expected: strips EXIF and metadata, defeats polyglot files, normalizes format; costs CPU.
  3. How do you protect a pod from a large upload? Expected: size limits at LB, parser and validator; streaming; separate deployment; rate limiting; pre-signed URLs for anything big.
  4. What is backpressure and why does it matter here? Expected: a slow consumer pauses the producer; without it buffers grow unbounded.

Practical exercise

Implement the streaming CSV import above and prove that memory stays flat: upload a 500 MB file while watching process.memoryUsage().rss. Acceptance criteria: RSS growth under 100 MB during the upload; the S3 object size equals the file size; a client disconnect at 50 percent aborts the multipart upload (check ListMultipartUploads is empty afterwards).

32.6 Multipart upload

Concept

Multipart upload splits one object into parts (5 MB to 5 GB each, up to 10,000 parts), uploads them independently, and then asks S3 to assemble them into a single object. Parts can be uploaded in parallel, retried individually, and the whole upload can be paused and resumed. It is mandatory above 5 GB and recommended above about 100 MB.

Why does it exist?

A single 3 GB PUT over a flaky connection fails at 2.9 GB and must restart from zero. It also uses one TCP connection, which on a high-latency link caps throughput. Multipart turns one fragile transfer into 300 small, retryable, parallel ones.

Mental model

Imagine shipping a car overseas. You could build one giant crate and hope the crane does not drop it. Or you ship it as numbered boxes on several trucks; if box 47 falls off, you resend box 47. The receiving dock reassembles the car when all boxes have arrived, and if you stop halfway the dock keeps the boxes in a corner until you either finish or tell them to throw them away. That corner costs rent every day.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S3 as S3
  C->>S3: CreateMultipartUpload key
  S3-->>C: UploadId
  par parallel parts
    C->>S3: UploadPart 1 with UploadId
    S3-->>C: ETag 1
    C->>S3: UploadPart 2 with UploadId
    S3-->>C: ETag 2
    C->>S3: UploadPart N with UploadId
    S3-->>C: ETag N
  end
  C->>S3: CompleteMultipartUpload with list of part numbers and ETags
  S3-->>C: 200 object exists
  Note over C,S3: If the client vanishes, parts stay and cost money until AbortMultipartUpload or a lifecycle rule
  1. CreateMultipartUpload returns an UploadId. The object does not exist yet.
  2. UploadPart for each part number 1..N, each returning an ETag. Parts can arrive in any order and be re-uploaded (the last one for a part number wins).
  3. CompleteMultipartUpload sends the ordered list of { PartNumber, ETag }. S3 assembles the object. Only now does the key become visible.
  4. AbortMultipartUpload discards parts. If nobody calls it, the parts sit in the bucket, billed at Standard rates, invisible to LIST and to the console's size view. A lifecycle rule AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload with DaysAfterInitiation: 3 is mandatory hygiene.

Resuming: keep the UploadId and the list of ETags you have. ListParts tells you which part numbers S3 already has. Upload the missing ones and complete.

The ETag of a multipart object is not the MD5 of the content; it is the MD5 of the concatenated part MD5s followed by -N. If you need a content checksum, use ChecksumAlgorithm: 'SHA256' on each part and the object gets a composite checksum, or compute your own SHA-256 as you stream (32.11).

Practical example

A video platform accepts 4 GB raw uploads from creators. Requirements: uploads from a browser, resumable after a laptop sleeps, no bytes through the API. The browser asks the API for an UploadId and a batch of pre-signed UploadPart URLs (32.7), uploads 8 parts at a time, stores progress in localStorage, and asks the API to complete when done. The API is involved for three tiny requests; the 4 GB go straight to S3.

NestJS example

Server side, when the server itself has the stream (an export generated by a worker, or the busboy case above), @aws-sdk/lib-storage's Upload handles the whole multipart protocol:

// export-writer.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { Upload } from '@aws-sdk/lib-storage';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';

@Injectable()
export class ExportWriterService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(ExportWriterService.name);
  constructor(@Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  async writeCsv(key: string, rows: AsyncIterable<string>): Promise<{ key: string; etag?: string }> {
    const body = Readable.from(rows); // rows streamed from a PostgreSQL cursor
    const upload = new Upload({
      client: this.s3,
      params: { Bucket: process.env.EXPORTS_BUCKET!, Key: key, Body: body, ContentType: 'text/csv' },
      partSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024, // 10 MB parts; 5 MB is the minimum
      queueSize: 4,               // 4 parts in flight in parallel
      leavePartsOnError: false,   // abort the multipart upload if anything fails
    });
    upload.on('httpUploadProgress', (p) => this.log.debug({ key, loaded: p.loaded, part: p.part }));
    const result = await upload.done();
    return { key, etag: result.ETag };
  }
}

Client-driven multipart, where the API only coordinates:

// multipart.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  S3Client, CreateMultipartUploadCommand, UploadPartCommand,
  CompleteMultipartUploadCommand, AbortMultipartUploadCommand, ListPartsCommand,
} from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { getSignedUrl } from '@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';

@Injectable()
export class MultipartService {
  private readonly bucket = process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET!;
  constructor(@Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  async start(key: string, contentType: string) {
    const res = await this.s3.send(new CreateMultipartUploadCommand({
      Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, ContentType: contentType,
    }));
    return { uploadId: res.UploadId! };
  }

  // Issue a batch of part URLs; the browser PUTs each part directly to S3.
  async signParts(key: string, uploadId: string, from: number, to: number) {
    const urls: { partNumber: number; url: string }[] = [];
    for (let n = from; n <= to; n++) {
      const url = await getSignedUrl(this.s3, new UploadPartCommand({
        Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, UploadId: uploadId, PartNumber: n,
      }), { expiresIn: 3600 });
      urls.push({ partNumber: n, url });
    }
    return urls;
  }

  async listUploadedParts(key: string, uploadId: string) {
    const res = await this.s3.send(new ListPartsCommand({ Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, UploadId: uploadId }));
    return (res.Parts ?? []).map((p) => ({ partNumber: p.PartNumber!, etag: p.ETag!, size: p.Size! }));
  }

  async complete(key: string, uploadId: string, parts: { partNumber: number; etag: string }[]) {
    return this.s3.send(new CompleteMultipartUploadCommand({
      Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, UploadId: uploadId,
      MultipartUpload: { Parts: parts.sort((a, b) => a.partNumber - b.partNumber).map((p) => ({ PartNumber: p.partNumber, ETag: p.etag })) },
    }));
  }

  async abort(key: string, uploadId: string) {
    await this.s3.send(new AbortMultipartUploadCommand({ Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, UploadId: uploadId }));
  }
}

The browser reads the ETag response header from each part PUT; the bucket's CORS configuration must include ExposeHeaders: ["ETag"] or the browser cannot read it.

PostgreSQL example

Track in-progress multipart uploads so you can abort them when the user gives up, and so a restart of the API does not lose the UploadId:

CREATE TABLE multipart_uploads (
  file_id     uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES files(id),
  upload_id   text NOT NULL,
  parts_total int  NOT NULL,
  started_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- A janitor job: abort uploads idle for 24 h and mark the file FAILED.
SELECT file_id, upload_id FROM multipart_uploads WHERE last_seen_at < now() - interval '24 hours';

Production scenario

Throughput: a browser uploading 8 parts of 10 MB in parallel to same-continent S3 typically reaches 50 to 150 Mbit/s on a home connection, limited by the uplink, not S3. From an EC2 instance in the same region, Upload with queueSize: 8 pushes 500 MB/s or more. Monitoring: count of in-progress uploads (from your table), age of the oldest, AbortMultipartUpload rate, and a monthly check of ListMultipartUploads on each bucket, which should be near empty if the lifecycle rule works.

Failure scenario

A data team runs a nightly job that streams 40 GB of Parquet to S3 with a home-grown multipart client. On failure it logs and exits without aborting. Nine months later the finance team asks why the "empty" analytics bucket costs $900 per month. ListMultipartUploads shows 38 TB of orphaned parts. A single lifecycle rule would have cost nothing.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Part smaller than 5 MB that is not the last part: CompleteMultipartUpload fails with EntityTooSmall.
  • Same part number uploaded twice: the later one wins; make sure your retry uses the newest ETag.
  • CompleteMultipartUpload can take seconds for thousands of parts and may return 200 with an error in the body; the SDK handles this, hand-rolled clients often do not.
  • The completed object's ETag is not an MD5; do not use it for dedup.
  • Abandoned uploads are invisible in normal listings and cost money forever without a lifecycle rule.
  • Pre-signed part URLs that expire mid-upload: issue in batches and re-sign on 403.
  • Client clock skew invalidates SigV4 signatures with RequestTimeTooSkewed (tolerance 15 minutes).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Multipart is the default for anything above 100 MB, and the abort story is designed before the upload story. The senior insists on the lifecycle rule as a Terraform-managed bucket default, tracks UploadIds in the database, and never lets a browser hold the only copy of state needed to finish.

Common mistakes

  • Uploading a 2 GB file with a single PutObject from a browser and calling the failure "network issues".
  • Forgetting ExposeHeaders: ETag in CORS, so the browser cannot complete.
  • No abort path, no lifecycle rule, no monitoring of orphaned parts.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through multipart upload and where its state lives. Expected: create, parts with ETags, complete; state is the UploadId plus ETags, kept by the client and preferably mirrored in your database.
  2. What happens to parts if the client disappears? Expected: billed until abort; lifecycle AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload.
  3. Why is the ETag of a multipart object not usable as a checksum? Expected: it is an MD5 of part MD5s with a part count suffix.
  4. How do you resume an upload after a browser restart? Expected: persist UploadId and key; ListParts to find what S3 has; upload the rest; complete.

Practical exercise

Build a resumable browser upload: the API issues UploadId and signed part URLs in batches of 10; the browser uploads 4 parts in parallel and stores progress in localStorage; a "resume" button calls ListParts via the API and continues. Acceptance criteria: killing the tab at 60 percent and resuming uploads only the missing parts; abandoning the upload and waiting for the janitor produces zero entries in ListMultipartUploads.

32.7 Pre-signed URLs

Concept

A pre-signed URL is a normal S3 URL with a signature attached that grants whoever holds it the right to perform exactly one operation (PUT this key, or GET this key) until an expiry time. Your API creates it using its own IAM credentials and hands it to the browser. The browser then talks to S3 directly. Your pods never see the bytes.

A pre-signed POST (a "POST policy") is the same idea for HTML form uploads, with the extra ability to constrain content length range and content type in the signed policy.

Why does it exist?

Every byte that passes through a NestJS pod costs event-loop time, memory, a socket, and a load balancer's bandwidth, and adds a hop's worth of latency and failure. S3 can absorb terabytes per second; your pod can absorb maybe 100 MB/s. Pre-signed URLs let S3 do the byte work while your API keeps control of who may upload what, where, and how big.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel that gives guests a key card valid for one room for one night. The front desk (your API) checks identity, decides which room (the key), programs the expiry, and hands over the card. The guest walks to the room on their own; the receptionist does not carry the luggage. If the card is lost, the finder can open that one room until midnight, which is why the card is scoped and short-lived.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant API as NestJS API
  participant DB as PostgreSQL
  participant S3 as S3
  B->>API: POST /files with name, size, mime
  API->>API: authorize, validate size and type, generate key
  API->>DB: INSERT files status PENDING
  API->>S3: sign PUT for key, expires 15 min
  API-->>B: 201 with fileId and uploadUrl
  B->>S3: PUT uploadUrl with bytes and Content-Type
  S3-->>B: 200 ETag
  B->>API: POST /files/:id/confirm
  API->>S3: HeadObject key
  S3-->>API: size, content type, checksum
  API->>DB: UPDATE files status UPLOADED
  API-->>B: 200
  1. Issue. The client asks the API for permission, sending the intended content type and size. The API authorizes the user, checks quotas, generates a key, writes a PENDING row, and signs a PutObjectCommand for that key with expiresIn of a few minutes. If ContentType (and optionally ContentLength) are in the signed command, the browser must send exactly those headers or S3 rejects with 403.
  2. Upload. The browser PUTs to the signed URL. S3 verifies the signature, expiry and any signed headers, stores the object, returns 200.
  3. Confirm. The browser tells the API it is done. The API runs HeadObject to verify the object exists with the expected size and type, then moves the row to UPLOADED and enqueues processing (32.11). Without this step the database believes in files that may never have arrived.

Expiry: the URL is valid until expiresIn seconds after signing, and never longer than the signing credentials are valid. A pod using an IAM role has STS credentials that rotate (typically valid up to 6 to 12 hours). Signing with expiresIn: 7 days using role credentials produces a URL that silently dies when the role credentials expire. Keep upload URLs to 5 to 15 minutes and download URLs to minutes, not days.

POST policies: createPresignedPost from @aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post builds a set of form fields and a policy document. Conditions like ['content-length-range', 1, 10485760] and ['starts-with', '$Content-Type', 'image/'] are enforced by S3 at upload time. This is the only way to enforce a size cap on a browser upload; a pre-signed PUT can pin an exact Content-Length but cannot say "at most".

Practical example

An e-commerce seller portal lets sellers upload product images up to 10 MB. Flow: POST /products/:id/images returns a fileId and POST policy fields; the browser submits the form to S3; then POST /files/:fileId/confirm. The API pods handle two tiny JSON requests per image. At 5,000 image uploads per hour, that is nothing; the same traffic through the pods would be 50 GB per hour of body streaming.

NestJS example

// create-upload.dto.ts
import { IsIn, IsInt, IsString, Max, MaxLength, Min } from 'class-validator';

export class CreateUploadDto {
  @IsString() @MaxLength(255) filename!: string;      // display only, never used in the key
  @IsIn(['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp', 'application/pdf']) mimeType!: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(10 * 1024 * 1024) sizeBytes!: number;
}
// presign.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand, GetObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { getSignedUrl } from '@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner';
import { createPresignedPost } from '@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';

@Injectable()
export class PresignService {
  private readonly bucket = process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET!;
  constructor(@Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client) {}

  // Pre-signed PUT: simplest; pins Content-Type and exact Content-Length.
  async signPut(key: string, mimeType: string, sizeBytes: number) {
    const cmd = new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, ContentType: mimeType, ContentLength: sizeBytes });
    return getSignedUrl(this.s3, cmd, { expiresIn: 15 * 60 });
  }

  // POST policy: enforces a size RANGE and a content-type prefix at S3.
  async signPost(key: string, mimePrefix: string, maxBytes: number) {
    return createPresignedPost(this.s3, {
      Bucket: this.bucket,
      Key: key,
      Conditions: [
        ['content-length-range', 1, maxBytes],
        ['starts-with', '$Content-Type', mimePrefix],
        { 'x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'aws:kms' },
      ],
      Fields: { 'x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'aws:kms' },
      Expires: 15 * 60,
    }); // returns { url, fields }; the browser posts fields plus the file as multipart form
  }

  // Download: short expiry; force a safe filename and disposition.
  async signGet(key: string, downloadName: string, inline = false) {
    const disposition = `${inline ? 'inline' : 'attachment'}; filename="${downloadName.replace(/["\r\n]/g, '')}"`;
    const cmd = new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, ResponseContentDisposition: disposition });
    return getSignedUrl(this.s3, cmd, { expiresIn: 5 * 60 });
  }
}
// files.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Post, Req, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CreateUploadDto } from './create-upload.dto';
import { FilesService } from './files.service';

@Controller('files')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class FilesController {
  constructor(private readonly files: FilesService) {}

  @Post()
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 30, ttl: 60_000 } }) // 30 URL issuances per minute per user
  create(@Req() req: { user: { id: string; tenantId: string } }, @Body() dto: CreateUploadDto) {
    return this.files.createPendingUpload(req.user, dto); // { fileId, upload: { url, fields } }
  }

  @Post(':id/confirm')
  confirm(@Req() req: { user: { id: string } }, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    return this.files.confirmUpload(req.user.id, id);
  }
}

FilesService is shown in full in 32.14.

PostgreSQL example

Issuing URLs is cheap for you and useful for an abuser (they can fill your bucket). Track issuance:

-- Per-user pending quota check inside createPendingUpload
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 hour') AS pending_last_hour,
       coalesce(sum(size_bytes) FILTER (WHERE status IN ('UPLOADED','PROCESSED')), 0) AS stored_bytes
  FROM files
 WHERE owner_id = $1;

Refuse to issue a new URL when pending_last_hour exceeds a threshold (say 100) or stored_bytes exceeds the plan's quota.

Production scenario

A document-heavy SaaS issues 200,000 pre-signed URLs per day. Signing is local CPU work (HMAC-SHA256), about 0.2 ms, no network call, so the API cost is the JSON request itself. The bucket's CORS rule allows PUT and POST from the app origin only, with MaxAgeSeconds: 3000 so the browser does not preflight every upload. Observability: a metric for URLs issued vs confirmed per hour; if the confirm ratio drops below 90 percent, something in the browser flow is broken (CORS change, expired URLs, S3 outage).

When not to use pre-signed URLs: when the server must transform or inspect the bytes synchronously before storing (rare; usually async processing is fine), or when the client cannot reach S3 directly (locked-down corporate networks that only allow your domain; a CloudFront distribution in front of the upload bucket with signed URLs solves that too).

Failure scenario

At 11:05 a deploy changes the bucket CORS configuration while tightening security and drops PUT from AllowedMethods. Every browser upload fails with a CORS error, which the browser reports as a generic network failure. The API sees nothing: URLs are issued fine, confirm calls never arrive. Only the "issued vs confirmed" metric moves. The on-call notices 40 minutes later from a support ticket. Action items: alert on confirm ratio, test the full browser flow in CI against a staging bucket, manage CORS in Terraform with review.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • URL leaked: anyone with it can upload to that key (PUT) or read that object (GET) until expiry. Mitigation: short expiry, per-file keys, confirm step, and the fact that a PUT URL cannot be used to write anywhere else.
  • URL reused: a PUT URL can be used many times until expiry; the last body wins. The confirm step and processing pipeline should treat the object as untrusted until scanned; after PROCESSED, the object should be copied to a final key or the upload URL long expired.
  • Signed headers mismatch: signing with ContentType but the browser sending a different one gives a 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch; the error is opaque, log the signed headers.
  • Clock skew on the client's machine affects nothing (the signature carries the server's time), but skew on the signing pod does; keep NTP healthy.
  • Credential expiry shorter than expiresIn silently kills long URLs.
  • S3 returns SlowDown (503) under burst; the browser must retry with backoff.
  • Presigned GET of a non-existent key returns a valid-looking URL that 404s; check the row status before signing downloads.
  • User deleted between issue and confirm: confirm must re-authorize, not trust the row.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats a pre-signed URL as a bearer token with a narrow scope and a short life. They put the size constraint in the POST policy where S3 enforces it, they never trust an upload that has not been confirmed and scanned, and they measure the issue-to-confirm funnel because it is the only visibility they have into a flow that bypasses their servers.

Common mistakes

  • expiresIn: 604800 (7 days) "so the link in the email keeps working"; use a short-lived redirect endpoint instead (32.13).
  • Issuing PUT URLs with no size constraint and no quota.
  • Skipping the confirm step and marking the file as uploaded when the URL is issued.
  • Using one wildcard key like uploads/${userId}/* in the policy; a POST policy can require an exact key or a prefix, choose exact.

Interview questions

  1. Why should large uploads not pass through the API? Expected: pod CPU, memory, sockets, LB bandwidth, latency, failure surface; S3 scales, pods do not.
  2. How do you cap upload size for a browser upload that goes directly to S3? Expected: POST policy content-length-range; pre-signed PUT can pin an exact Content-Length only.
  3. What happens if a pre-signed URL leaks? Expected: scoped to one operation and key until expiry; keep expiry short; confirm and scan; do not put secrets in keys.
  4. Why do you need a confirm endpoint? Expected: the API otherwise cannot know whether the upload happened; HeadObject verifies; it triggers processing and prevents orphans.
  5. What limits the maximum expiry of a pre-signed URL? Expected: 7 days hard limit for SigV4, and the lifetime of the credentials used to sign; role credentials are hours.

Practical exercise

Implement the issue, upload and confirm flow with a POST policy limiting uploads to 10 MB and image/ types. Acceptance criteria: an 11 MB upload is rejected by S3 (not by your API); a text/html upload is rejected by S3; a confirm on a file that was never uploaded returns 409 and leaves the row PENDING; the confirm ratio metric appears in Prometheus.

32.8 File metadata: the files table and its state machine

Concept

S3 knows bytes. PostgreSQL knows facts: who owns the file, what it is for, whether it has been scanned, whether it is safe to show, which product it belongs to. The files table is the system of record for those facts, and its status column is a state machine that tells the rest of the application what it may do with the object.

Why does it exist?

Without a metadata table you end up listing S3 to answer "what files does this user have", trusting S3 metadata that the uploader controlled, and having no way to say "this file exists but has not been virus-scanned yet". The state machine is what makes a direct-to-S3 upload safe: the object can land in the bucket at any time, but nothing in the app treats it as real until the row says so.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel locker at a post office. Anyone with a code can drop a parcel in a locker (the upload). But the parcel is not "delivered" until a clerk opens the locker, checks the label and weight, scans it for anything dangerous, and writes it into the ledger. The ledger, not the locker, is what the counter staff look at when a customer asks "did my parcel arrive?".

How it works

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> PENDING: URL issued, row inserted
  PENDING --> UPLOADED: confirm verified HeadObject
  PENDING --> EXPIRED: no confirm within 1 h, janitor
  UPLOADED --> SCANNING: worker picked job
  SCANNING --> PROCESSED: clean, derived files written
  SCANNING --> QUARANTINED: malware or invalid content
  SCANNING --> FAILED: processing error after retries
  PROCESSED --> DELETED: user delete or retention
  QUARANTINED --> DELETED: security review
  EXPIRED --> [*]
  DELETED --> [*]

Rules that the state machine enforces:

  1. Only PROCESSED files can be delivered to other users. UPLOADED files can be shown back to the uploader as "processing".
  2. Transitions are made with a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'expected' so two workers cannot both process the same file, and a late confirm cannot resurrect an EXPIRED file.
  3. PENDING rows older than the URL expiry plus a grace period are the orphan candidates: either the upload never happened (delete the row) or it happened and confirm was lost (a janitor calls HeadObject, and if the object exists, promotes to UPLOADED).
  4. Every transition writes updated_at and, for failures, a failure_reason, so support can answer "why is my file stuck".

Practical example

A marketplace stores seller documents (business license, ID). Sellers upload, see "under review", and the compliance team sees only PROCESSED documents with a clean scan and extracted text. A document whose scan flags malware goes to QUARANTINED, the seller sees "rejected", and security gets a ticket. A document uploaded but never confirmed (seller closed the tab) is cleaned up after an hour.

NestJS example

Transitions are centralized so no controller changes status directly:

// file-status.ts
export enum FileStatus {
  PENDING = 'PENDING', UPLOADED = 'UPLOADED', SCANNING = 'SCANNING',
  PROCESSED = 'PROCESSED', QUARANTINED = 'QUARANTINED', FAILED = 'FAILED',
  EXPIRED = 'EXPIRED', DELETED = 'DELETED',
}

export const ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS: Record<FileStatus, FileStatus[]> = {
  [FileStatus.PENDING]: [FileStatus.UPLOADED, FileStatus.EXPIRED],
  [FileStatus.UPLOADED]: [FileStatus.SCANNING],
  [FileStatus.SCANNING]: [FileStatus.PROCESSED, FileStatus.QUARANTINED, FileStatus.FAILED],
  [FileStatus.PROCESSED]: [FileStatus.DELETED],
  [FileStatus.QUARANTINED]: [FileStatus.DELETED],
  [FileStatus.FAILED]: [FileStatus.SCANNING, FileStatus.DELETED], // manual retry
  [FileStatus.EXPIRED]: [],
  [FileStatus.DELETED]: [],
};

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TYPE file_status AS ENUM ('PENDING','UPLOADED','SCANNING','PROCESSED','QUARANTINED','FAILED','EXPIRED','DELETED');

CREATE TABLE files (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  owner_id         uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  bucket           text NOT NULL,
  key              text NOT NULL,
  original_name    text NOT NULL,             -- display only, sanitized
  declared_mime    text NOT NULL,             -- what the client said
  detected_mime    text,                      -- what magic bytes said, set by worker
  size_bytes       bigint,
  checksum_sha256  text,
  status           file_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  scan_status      text,                      -- 'clean', 'infected:Trojan.X', null
  failure_reason   text,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (bucket, key)
);

CREATE INDEX files_owner_idx    ON files (owner_id, created_at DESC) WHERE status <> 'DELETED';
CREATE INDEX files_pending_idx  ON files (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';   -- janitor scan
CREATE INDEX files_checksum_idx ON files (tenant_id, checksum_sha256) WHERE checksum_sha256 IS NOT NULL; -- dedup

-- Derived files (thumbnails, extracted text) point at their source.
CREATE TABLE file_derivatives (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  file_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES files(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  kind       text NOT NULL,       -- 'thumb_256', 'thumb_1024', 'pdf_text'
  bucket     text NOT NULL,
  key        text NOT NULL,
  size_bytes bigint,
  UNIQUE (file_id, kind)
);

The conditional transition:

UPDATE files
   SET status = 'UPLOADED', size_bytes = $2, detected_mime = $3, updated_at = now()
 WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'PENDING'
RETURNING id;
-- zero rows returned means someone else moved it or it expired: do not proceed

TypeORM example

// file.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, CreateDateColumn, UpdateDateColumn, Index, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { FileStatus } from './file-status';

@Entity('files')
@Unique(['bucket', 'key'])
@Index(['ownerId', 'createdAt'])
export class FileRecord {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'tenant_id' }) tenantId!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'owner_id' }) ownerId!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) bucket!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) key!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text', name: 'original_name' }) originalName!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text', name: 'declared_mime' }) declaredMime!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text', name: 'detected_mime', nullable: true }) detectedMime!: string | null;
  @Column({ type: 'bigint', name: 'size_bytes', nullable: true }) sizeBytes!: string | null; // bigint comes back as string
  @Column({ type: 'text', name: 'checksum_sha256', nullable: true }) checksumSha256!: string | null;
  @Column({ type: 'enum', enum: FileStatus, default: FileStatus.PENDING }) status!: FileStatus;
  @Column({ type: 'text', name: 'failure_reason', nullable: true }) failureReason!: string | null;
  @CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'created_at' }) createdAt!: Date;
  @UpdateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'updated_at' }) updatedAt!: Date;
}
// file.repository.ts (transition helper)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { FileRecord } from './file.entity';
import { FileStatus, ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS } from './file-status';

@Injectable()
export class FileRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(FileRecord) private readonly repo: Repository<FileRecord>) {}

  /** Returns true if the transition happened; false if the row was not in `from`. */
  async transition(id: string, from: FileStatus, to: FileStatus, patch: Partial<FileRecord> = {}): Promise<boolean> {
    if (!ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS[from].includes(to)) throw new Error(`Illegal transition ${from} -> ${to}`);
    const result = await this.repo.createQueryBuilder()
      .update(FileRecord)
      .set({ ...patch, status: to })
      .where('id = :id AND status = :from', { id, from })
      .execute();
    return (result.affected ?? 0) === 1;
  }
}

Sequelize example

// file.model.ts
import { Table, Column, Model, DataType, PrimaryKey, Default } from 'sequelize-typescript';

@Table({ tableName: 'files', underscored: true, timestamps: true })
export class FileModel extends Model {
  @PrimaryKey @Default(DataType.UUIDV4) @Column(DataType.UUID) id!: string;
  @Column(DataType.UUID) tenantId!: string;
  @Column(DataType.UUID) ownerId!: string;
  @Column(DataType.TEXT) bucket!: string;
  @Column(DataType.TEXT) key!: string;
  @Column(DataType.BIGINT) sizeBytes!: number | null;
  @Column(DataType.TEXT) checksumSha256!: string | null;
  @Column(DataType.ENUM('PENDING','UPLOADED','SCANNING','PROCESSED','QUARANTINED','FAILED','EXPIRED','DELETED')) status!: string;
}

// Conditional transition: affected-row count is the truth.
const [affected] = await FileModel.update(
  { status: 'UPLOADED', sizeBytes: head.ContentLength },
  { where: { id: fileId, status: 'PENDING' } },
);
if (affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('File is not pending');

Production scenario

A files table for a mid-size SaaS: 40 million rows, 25 GB. The partial index on PENDING rows stays tiny (a few thousand rows) so the janitor query runs in milliseconds every minute. The dedup index on (tenant_id, checksum_sha256) lets a second upload of the same invoice reuse the existing object: the new row points at the same key, and a reference count (or a DELETE guarded by "no other row uses this key") governs physical deletion.

Orphan cleanup, two directions:

  • Rows without objects: PENDING older than 1 hour, HeadObject says 404, mark EXPIRED.
  • Objects without rows: a weekly S3 Inventory report (a CSV of every key) joined against the files table in a batch job; unknown keys older than 7 days are deleted. Never do this with LIST at scale.

Failure scenario

A confirm endpoint bug marks files PROCESSED directly, skipping the scan. Three weeks later an uploaded "invoice.pdf" that is actually a malware dropper is downloaded by 200 customer-support agents from the admin panel. The state machine existed but was bypassed by one repo.save({ status: 'PROCESSED' }). The fix is the transition() helper as the only write path to status, with a database-level check: a trigger that rejects PROCESSED unless scan_status = 'clean'.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Confirm called twice: second call finds UPLOADED, returns 200 idempotently instead of 409.
  • Confirm called before the browser's PUT finished (a client bug): HeadObject 404s; return 409 and let the client retry after upload.
  • Row deleted while the worker processes it: the worker's transition affects 0 rows; it must abort and delete any derivative it wrote.
  • Same checksum, different tenants: never dedup across tenants (cross-tenant existence leak).
  • bigint in TypeORM is returned as a string; compare as strings or BigInt.
  • Janitor and confirm race: both try PENDING -> X; the conditional update guarantees exactly one wins.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The row is the truth, the object is a payload. The senior designs the state machine first, makes status writable only through a guarded transition, adds the janitor on day one, and refuses to serve any file the pipeline has not blessed.

Common mistakes

  • No status column: "if the row exists the file exists".
  • Storing the CDN URL in the row.
  • Physical delete in S3 inside the HTTP request that deletes the row; if the S3 call fails the row is gone and the object lingers forever. Mark DELETED, let a job delete bytes.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a status column necessary when uploads go directly to S3? Expected: the API cannot see the upload happen; the object is untrusted until confirmed and scanned.
  2. How do you find orphaned objects in a bucket with 50 million keys? Expected: S3 Inventory joined with the table in a batch job.
  3. How do you prevent two workers processing the same file? Expected: conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'UPLOADED' claiming into SCANNING.

Practical exercise

Implement the state machine with the transition() helper and a database trigger enforcing PROCESSED requires scan_status = 'clean'. Acceptance criteria: an attempt to save PROCESSED without a clean scan fails at the database; running two workers against the same UPLOADED row results in exactly one processing.

32.9 CDN delivery

Concept

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a fleet of caching proxies at the edge of the internet, close to users. CloudFront in front of S3 means a user in Mumbai fetches a product image from an edge in Mumbai (10 ms) instead of from a bucket in Virginia (250 ms), and S3 sees one request per edge per cache lifetime instead of one per user.

Why does it exist?

Latency (distance), cost (S3 request fees and egress are higher than CloudFront's), and load (S3 and your origin see a fraction of requests). Also security: the bucket stays private, CloudFront is the only principal allowed to read it (Origin Access Control), and private content is gated with CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies.

Mental model

Imagine a publisher with one printing press in one city. Instead of mailing every copy from the press, they stock copies in every city's bookshop. The shop only orders from the press when it runs out. For members-only books, the shop asks to see a membership card (signed cookie) before handing the book over.

How it works

  1. DNS points cdn.example.com at the CloudFront distribution.
  2. The distribution has the S3 bucket as origin, with OAC so S3 accepts requests only from this distribution.
  3. On a request, the edge checks its cache by URL (and any headers or query strings you configured as part of the cache key). Miss: fetch from S3, cache according to Cache-Control or the distribution's default TTL, return.
  4. Private content: your API generates a CloudFront signed URL (different from an S3 pre-signed URL) with an expiry, using a private key registered in a CloudFront key group. Or it sets signed cookies so a whole set of paths (/tenants/42/*) becomes accessible for a session.
  5. Invalidation: CreateInvalidation with paths purges them from every edge. It takes seconds to minutes and costs about $0.005 per path beyond 1,000 per month. The correct design makes invalidation unnecessary: every new version of a file gets a new key and long Cache-Control: immutable.
  6. Image resizing on the fly: a small service (Lambda@Edge, or a NestJS image service behind CloudFront) that takes /img/{key}?w=400 and produces a resized variant; CloudFront caches the result so the resize happens once per size per image.
flowchart LR
  U["User in Mumbai"] -->|"GET cdn.example.com/derived/.../abc.webp"| E["CloudFront edge Mumbai"]
  E -->|"cache hit 10 ms"| U
  E -->|"miss, OAC signed request"| S3["S3 bucket us-east-1"]
  S3 -->|"object plus Cache-Control"| E
  API["NestJS API"] -->|"CloudFront signed URL for private files"| U

Practical example

Product images: public, immutable, new key per version, Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, served via cdn.example.com. Cache hit ratio above 95 percent. Invoices: private, Cache-Control: private, no-store, served via CloudFront signed URLs that expire in 5 minutes, issued by the API after an authorization check.

NestJS example

// cdn-url.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { getSignedUrl } from '@aws-sdk/cloudfront-signer';

@Injectable()
export class CdnUrlService {
  private readonly base = process.env.CDN_BASE_URL!;            // https://cdn.example.com
  private readonly keyPairId = process.env.CF_KEY_PAIR_ID!;
  private readonly privateKey = process.env.CF_PRIVATE_KEY!;    // from a secret manager, PEM

  /** Public immutable asset: plain URL, cached for a year at the edge. */
  publicUrl(key: string): string {
    return `${this.base}/${encodeURI(key)}`;
  }

  /** Private file: CloudFront signed URL, 5 minute expiry. */
  privateUrl(key: string, ttlSeconds = 300): string {
    return getSignedUrl({
      url: `${this.base}/${encodeURI(key)}`,
      keyPairId: this.keyPairId,
      privateKey: this.privateKey,
      dateLessThan: new Date(Date.now() + ttlSeconds * 1000).toISOString(),
    });
  }
}

Production scenario

A catalog serving 50 million image views per day: with a 96 percent hit ratio, S3 sees 2 million GETs per day (about $25 per month in requests) and CloudFront delivers roughly 15 TB per month at about $0.085 per GB for the first 10 TB (approximate US pricing, S3 to CloudFront transfer is free). Median image latency drops from 180 ms to 25 ms worldwide. Monitor: cache hit ratio, 4xx and 5xx rates per distribution, origin latency.

Failure scenario

A team stores avatars at avatars/{userId}.jpg and overwrites on change, with a 24-hour CDN TTL. A user uploads a new photo and sees the old one. Support says "clear your cache". The team adds an invalidation call per upload; at 20,000 avatar changes per day the invalidation bill is $100 per day and edges still lag by a minute. The fix, in one line: new key per version, immutable caching, invalidation removed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CDN caches a 403 or 404 from a not-yet-available object (Error Caching Minimum TTL defaults to 10 seconds for some codes, configurable); set error TTL low for private paths.
  • Query strings ignored in the cache key by default; if ?w=400 matters, add it to the cache policy.
  • Vary: Origin and CORS headers must be forwarded and cached correctly or the browser blocks image drawing to canvas.
  • Signed cookies do not work cross-domain; the CDN must be on a subdomain of the app.
  • A CloudFront private key leak lets anyone sign; rotate via key groups.
  • Regional S3 outage: CloudFront origin failover to a replica bucket in another region using an origin group.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Immutable keys plus long TTLs is the whole strategy; invalidation is a sign the design is wrong. The senior keeps the bucket private, puts CloudFront in the read path for everything users see, and keeps the API out of the byte path entirely.

Common mistakes

  • Serving S3 pre-signed URLs to browsers for public images (no caching, request fees, slow).
  • Overwriting keys and fighting the cache.
  • One distribution and one cache policy for public and private content.

Interview questions

  1. S3 pre-signed URL vs CloudFront signed URL: when each? Expected: S3 pre-signed for uploads and rare downloads; CloudFront signed for delivery of private content at the edge with caching.
  2. How do you handle a replaced image without invalidation? Expected: new key per version, immutable cache headers.
  3. What is OAC and why does it matter? Expected: lets CloudFront read a private bucket; users cannot bypass the CDN.

Practical exercise

Put CloudFront with OAC in front of a private bucket; serve public images with immutable caching and invoices with signed URLs. Acceptance criteria: direct bucket URL returns 403; a replaced image is visible worldwide immediately because its key changed; a signed invoice URL stops working after 5 minutes.

32.10 Lifecycle policies

Concept

A lifecycle policy is a set of rules on a bucket that S3 applies automatically: move objects matching a prefix or tag to a cheaper storage class after N days, expire them after M days, delete old non-current versions, and abort incomplete multipart uploads. It is how you keep storage cost from growing forever without writing cleanup code.

Why does it exist?

Files accumulate. Temp exports, abandoned uploads, superseded versions, logs, thumbnails for deleted products. Nobody is paid to delete them. Lifecycle rules encode the retention decision once and run daily, for free.

Mental model

Imagine a records office with a written policy: "paperwork under a year old stays in the front cabinets; one to seven years goes to the basement; after seven years it is shredded; abandoned half-filled forms are binned after three days." The clerks follow it every night without being told.

How it works

Rules are evaluated once a day per object. A rule has a filter (prefix, tags, size range), and actions:

Action Typical setting Why
Transition to Standard-IA 30 days after creation Reads drop off after a month; IA is about half the price
Transition to Glacier Instant 180 days Compliance archives that are rarely read
Expiration 7 days for exports/, 1 day for tmp/ Temp files
NoncurrentVersionTransition and NoncurrentVersionExpiration Expire after 30 non-current days, keep 3 newer versions Versioning as undo, not as infinite history
AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload 3 days after initiation Orphaned parts
ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker true Cleans delete markers with no versions left

Minimum billable durations matter: Standard-IA charges for at least 30 days and Glacier classes for 90 or 180 days, plus a per-object transition request fee; transitioning millions of tiny thumbnails to IA can cost more than it saves. Objects under 128 KB are not transitioned to IA by default for this reason.

A Terraform-flavored expression of the rules (shown as the JSON the API accepts):

{
  "Rules": [
    { "ID": "abort-mpu", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {}, "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 3 } },
    { "ID": "exports-expire", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": { "Prefix": "exports/" }, "Expiration": { "Days": 7 } },
    { "ID": "uploads-tier", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": { "Prefix": "uploads/" },
      "Transitions": [ { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" }, { "Days": 365, "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR" } ],
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30, "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3 } }
  ]
}

Practical example

An e-commerce platform's uploads bucket holds 12 TB: 3 TB of product images (hot), 8 TB of order documents older than 90 days (cold), 1 TB of abandoned uploads and old versions. After lifecycle rules: images stay Standard ($70 per month), documents move to Glacier Instant ($32 per month instead of $184), the junk is gone. Savings roughly $170 per month for a one-time configuration.

PostgreSQL example

Lifecycle deletes objects; it does not update your table. Keep them consistent by making the database drive retention where the rule is data-dependent, and letting S3 handle the pure time-based cases:

-- Nightly: files whose product was deleted more than 30 days ago
SELECT f.id, f.bucket, f.key
  FROM files f
  JOIN products p ON p.image_file_id = f.id
 WHERE p.deleted_at < now() - interval '30 days'
   AND f.status = 'PROCESSED'
 LIMIT 5000;
-- worker deletes objects and derivatives, then marks rows DELETED

Production scenario

Storage classes and lifecycle are the single biggest lever on the S3 bill; a bucket with mixed hot and cold data typically drops 40 to 70 percent in cost after tiering. Monitor with S3 Storage Lens: bytes per storage class, incomplete multipart bytes, non-current version bytes. Alert if non-current bytes exceed 20 percent of current.

Failure scenario

A rule intended for tmp/ is written with an empty filter ("Filter": {}) and Expiration: 1 day. The next morning every object in the production uploads bucket older than a day is gone. Versioning was enabled, so the objects are behind delete markers and can be restored by removing the markers, which takes a scripted afternoon. Without versioning it would have been total loss. Two controls: lifecycle rules in Terraform with review and a plan diff, and versioning on every bucket that holds user data.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rules apply per bucket, not per key; a prefix typo affects nothing (silent no-op) or everything.
  • Expiration is asynchronous: objects past their date may be visible for hours.
  • Transition to Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive makes GetObject fail until a restore is requested; the app must handle InvalidObjectState.
  • Versioned buckets with no non-current expiration double or triple storage silently.
  • Objects with Object Lock (compliance mode) cannot be expired until the retention date.
  • Lifecycle does not delete the row; the app sees a PROCESSED row and a 404 object.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Retention is a product decision written as code. The senior asks "how long must we keep this, legally and for users?" per prefix, encodes the answers as lifecycle rules in infrastructure code, turns on versioning as the undo button, and reconciles the table against S3 Inventory monthly.

Common mistakes

  • No AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload rule.
  • Transitioning millions of small objects to IA and paying more.
  • Enabling versioning without a non-current expiration.

Interview questions

  1. Which lifecycle rule should exist on every bucket? Expected: abort incomplete multipart uploads.
  2. Why can moving data to a cheaper class cost more? Expected: minimum storage durations, per-object transition fees, retrieval fees, small objects.
  3. How do you keep the database consistent with lifecycle deletions? Expected: DB-driven retention for data-dependent rules; S3 Inventory reconciliation.

Practical exercise

Write lifecycle rules for a bucket with uploads/, derived/, exports/ and tmp/ prefixes and versioning on. Acceptance criteria: a reviewer can state, per prefix, when objects are tiered and deleted; the rules are in Terraform; Storage Lens shows non-current bytes trending down after 30 days.

32.11 The processing pipeline

Concept

After an upload is confirmed, work happens: virus scan, magic-bytes validation, thumbnail generation, PDF text extraction, EXIF stripping, transcoding. None of this belongs in the HTTP request. It runs in a background worker triggered by an event, is idempotent, writes derived files under their own keys, and moves the files row through the state machine.

Why does it exist?

Processing is slow (seconds to minutes), CPU heavy, failure prone (corrupt files, third-party scanner timeouts), and must not block the user. It must also be authoritative: the file is not safe until the pipeline says so.

Mental model

Imagine airport baggage. You drop the bag at the counter (upload), get a receipt (file id), and walk away. Behind the wall, the bag goes through the X-ray (scan), gets a tag (metadata), maybe gets opened (extraction), and only then is loaded on the plane (PROCESSED). If the X-ray flags it, it goes to a separate room (QUARANTINED). You never wait at the counter for the X-ray.

How it works

flowchart LR
  B["Browser PUT to S3"] --> S3["S3 uploads bucket"]
  API["NestJS confirm endpoint"] -->|"enqueue file.uploaded"| Q["SQS or BullMQ queue"]
  S3 -.->|"optional S3 event notification"| Q
  Q --> W["Worker pod"]
  W -->|"GetObject stream"| S3
  W -->|"scan"| AV["ClamAV service"]
  W -->|"PutObject derived keys"| S3D["S3 derived prefix"]
  W -->|"transition SCANNING to PROCESSED"| PG["PostgreSQL files"]
  W -->|"failed after retries"| DLQ["Dead letter queue"]
  1. Trigger. Either the confirm endpoint enqueues a job (deterministic, carries the fileId), or an S3 event notification (s3:ObjectCreated:*) to SQS or EventBridge fires on the object itself. Prefer the confirm-driven job as the primary trigger and S3 events as a safety net for lost confirms; both must be idempotent because you will sometimes get both.
  2. Claim. The worker runs transition(UPLOADED -> SCANNING). If 0 rows are affected, another worker has it or it is not in a processable state; ack the message and stop.
  3. Fetch and validate. Stream the object, read the first bytes for magic-byte detection, compute SHA-256 while streaming, compare size to HeadObject.
  4. Scan. Send the stream to ClamAV (or a managed scanner). Infected: transition(SCANNING -> QUARANTINED), optionally copy to a quarantine bucket with restricted access, delete from uploads.
  5. Derive. Thumbnails via sharp, PDF text via pdf-parse or a Textract call, each written to derived/... keys. Record in file_derivatives. Writes are idempotent because keys are deterministic (derived/{tenant}/{fileId}_thumb256.webp).
  6. Finish. transition(SCANNING -> PROCESSED) with checksum_sha256, detected_mime. Emit file.processed for the rest of the app (attach to product, notify user).
  7. Fail. Exceptions retry with backoff (3 to 5 attempts); then transition(SCANNING -> FAILED) with the reason and the message goes to a dead-letter queue for a human.

Practical example

A legal-tech product ingests contracts as PDFs up to 50 MB. Pipeline per file: magic bytes (must be %PDF), scan (1 to 4 seconds), text extraction (2 to 20 seconds), page thumbnails (1 second per page). The worker pool is 6 pods with concurrency 2, sized for the p95 of 40 seconds per file and a target of 30 files per minute. The user sees "processing" for under a minute.

NestJS example

// file-processing.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Job } from 'bullmq';
import { Inject, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client, GetObjectCommand, PutObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import sharp from 'sharp';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';
import { FileRepository } from './file.repository';
import { FileStatus } from './file-status';
import { sniffMime } from './magic-bytes';
import { ClamAvClient } from './clamav.client';

@Processor('file-processing', { concurrency: 2 })
export class FileProcessingProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  private readonly log = new Logger(FileProcessingProcessor.name);
  constructor(
    @Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client,
    private readonly files: FileRepository,
    private readonly clamav: ClamAvClient,
  ) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<{ fileId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    const { fileId } = job.data;
    const claimed = await this.files.transition(fileId, FileStatus.UPLOADED, FileStatus.SCANNING);
    if (!claimed) { this.log.warn({ fileId, msg: 'not claimable, skipping' }); return; } // idempotent no-op

    const rec = await this.files.findOrFail(fileId);
    const obj = await this.s3.send(new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: rec.bucket, Key: rec.key }));
    const bytes = await obj.Body!.transformToByteArray(); // fine up to tens of MB; stream for larger
    const buf = Buffer.from(bytes);

    const detected = sniffMime(buf);
    if (!detected || !['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'application/pdf'].includes(detected)) {
      await this.files.transition(fileId, FileStatus.SCANNING, FileStatus.QUARANTINED, { failureReason: `bad content type ${detected ?? 'unknown'}` });
      return;
    }
    const verdict = await this.clamav.scanBuffer(buf); // { clean: boolean; signature?: string }
    if (!verdict.clean) {
      await this.files.transition(fileId, FileStatus.SCANNING, FileStatus.QUARANTINED, { failureReason: `infected:${verdict.signature}` });
      return;
    }

    const sha256 = createHash('sha256').update(buf).digest('hex');
    if (detected.startsWith('image/')) {
      const thumb = await sharp(buf, { limitInputPixels: 50_000_000 }).rotate().resize(256, 256, { fit: 'inside' }).webp().toBuffer();
      const thumbKey = rec.key.replace(/^uploads\//, 'derived/').replace(/\.[^.]+$/, '') + '_thumb256.webp';
      await this.s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: rec.bucket, Key: thumbKey, Body: thumb, ContentType: 'image/webp', CacheControl: 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable' }));
      await this.files.upsertDerivative(fileId, 'thumb_256', rec.bucket, thumbKey, thumb.length);
    }
    const done = await this.files.transition(fileId, FileStatus.SCANNING, FileStatus.PROCESSED, { checksumSha256: sha256, detectedMime: detected });
    if (!done) this.log.error({ fileId, msg: 'row changed under us during processing' });
  }
}

The job is enqueued from the confirm endpoint with jobId: fileId so BullMQ deduplicates a double confirm, and with attempts: 4, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5000 }. For the S3-event safety net, an SQS consumer maps key to fileId via the table and enqueues the same job id.

PostgreSQL example

Deduplicate content by hash after processing, within a tenant:

-- Does an identical file already exist for this tenant?
SELECT id, key FROM files
 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND checksum_sha256 = $2 AND status = 'PROCESSED' AND id <> $3
 LIMIT 1;
-- If yes: point the new row at the existing key, delete the new object, mark the new row PROCESSED.

Production scenario

Sizing: a sharp thumbnail of a 12-megapixel JPEG takes 80 to 150 ms and about 60 MB of RAM; ClamAV scanning a 10 MB file takes 1 to 3 seconds. A worker pod with 1 CPU and 1 GB handles about 2 files concurrently. Queue depth and job age are the key metrics; alert when the oldest waiting job exceeds 5 minutes. When a processing bug ships, the DLQ fills; the replay tool re-enqueues by fileId after the fix.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged: file processing DLQ depth 4,000 and climbing. A vendor update changed the ClamAV daemon's socket path; every scan throws ECONNREFUSED, every job retries four times, and the queue is saturated with retries. Uploads still work (users see "processing"), which is the point of the design: the user-facing path is unaffected. The on-call rolls back the ClamAV deployment, replays the DLQ, and the backlog drains in 20 minutes. Action items: a health check on the scanner in the worker's readiness probe, and a circuit breaker so a dead scanner fails fast instead of retrying slowly.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Job runs twice (at-least-once delivery): the claim transition makes the second run a no-op; derived keys are deterministic so a partial first run is overwritten cleanly.
  • File replaced under the same key mid-processing (should be impossible with immutable keys; another reason never to overwrite).
  • Huge file loaded into memory: switch to streaming for anything above a few tens of MB; scan via stream, hash via stream.
  • Scanner false positive quarantines a legitimate invoice: support flow to review and re-run.
  • Worker crash after writing thumbnails but before the final transition: the row stays SCANNING; a janitor moves rows SCANNING older than 30 minutes back to UPLOADED for a retry.
  • Processing reads a file before the scan verdict and passes extracted text to a downstream system: order the steps so nothing downstream sees content until PROCESSED.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The pipeline is the trust boundary. The senior orders steps so untrusted bytes touch as little as possible before the scan, makes every step idempotent, keys derived objects deterministically, keeps the DLQ and replay tooling ready before launch, and treats "user waits for processing" as a UX state, not a bug.

Common mistakes

  • Processing inside the confirm request.
  • Non-deterministic derived keys, so retries create duplicates.
  • Trusting the client's declared mime type in the pipeline.
  • No DLQ, so a poison file blocks the queue forever.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make file processing idempotent? Expected: claim via conditional transition, deterministic derived keys, job id equals file id.
  2. Confirm-driven vs S3-event-driven processing? Expected: confirm is deterministic and carries context; S3 events are a safety net; both must be idempotent.
  3. What must happen before any part of the system reads uploaded content? Expected: magic-byte validation and malware scan; state PROCESSED gates delivery.

Practical exercise

Build the BullMQ processor with ClamAV in Docker (clamav/clamav). Acceptance criteria: uploading the EICAR test string as invoice.pdf ends in QUARANTINED; a JPEG produces a 256 px WebP thumbnail under derived/; running the job twice produces no duplicate derivatives; killing the worker mid-job leaves the row in a state the janitor recovers within 30 minutes.

32.12 Security of file handling

Concept

File upload is the one feature where you invite strangers to hand you arbitrary bytes and then store, process and re-serve them. Every part of that sentence is an attack surface: the bytes (malware, polyglots, decompression bombs), the name (path traversal, encoding tricks), the type (HTML disguised as an image), the storage (public buckets), the delivery (signed URL leakage), and the API that hands out permission (abuse of URL issuance).

Why does it exist?

Because "it is just a file" is how most storage breaches start. The controls are individually simple; the discipline is applying all of them, every time, in the right layer.

Mental model

Imagine airport security for luggage. The bag is X-rayed (scan), the tag is printed by the airline, not written by the passenger (server-generated keys), the bag goes into the hold, not the cabin (private bucket, no execution), and the baggage claim ticket is single-use and expires (signed URLs). Any one of these being skipped is a story on the news.

How it works

1. Content-type validation by magic bytes. The browser sets Content-Type from the file extension; an attacker sets it to whatever they like. The only trustworthy signal is the first bytes of the content:

// magic-bytes.ts
export function sniffMime(buf: Buffer): string | null {
  if (buf.length < 12) return null;
  if (buf[0] === 0xff && buf[1] === 0xd8 && buf[2] === 0xff) return 'image/jpeg';
  if (buf.subarray(0, 8).equals(Buffer.from([0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a]))) return 'image/png';
  if (buf.subarray(0, 4).toString('ascii') === 'RIFF' && buf.subarray(8, 12).toString('ascii') === 'WEBP') return 'image/webp';
  if (buf.subarray(0, 5).toString('ascii') === '%PDF-') return 'application/pdf';
  if (buf.subarray(0, 4).toString('ascii') === 'GIF8') return 'image/gif';
  return null; // unknown: reject, do not guess
}
export const sniffImageType = (buf: Buffer) => { const m = sniffMime(buf); return m?.startsWith('image/') ? m : null; };

The file-type package covers hundreds of formats and is the practical choice; the point is that detection happens on bytes, in the pipeline, and the detected type is what gets written as Content-Type on the final object. A file whose detected type does not match an allow-list is quarantined, not stored with a guessed type.

2. Size limits at every layer. Load balancer or ingress body limit, POST policy content-length-range, multer limits, ParseFilePipe validators, and a per-user quota in the database. Each layer catches what the previous missed and each costs less than the next.

3. Path traversal and filename handling. The client's filename is display data. It never becomes part of a key, a path, or a header without sanitization. ../../etc/passwd, null bytes, and 10,000-character names are all normal inputs. Keys are server-generated UUIDs; the original name is stored in a text column and re-emitted only inside a quoted, sanitized Content-Disposition (RFC 5987 filename*=UTF-8''... for non-ASCII).

4. No execution, no HTML. Never serve user uploads from the same origin as your app. If evil.html (or an SVG with a <script>) is served from app.example.com, it runs with your users' cookies: stored XSS via S3. Serve uploads from a separate domain (cdn-usercontent.example.com), set Content-Type from detection, add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Disposition: attachment for anything not in a small inline allow-list (JPEG, PNG, WebP, PDF), and consider a CSP sandbox header on the CDN response. SVG is executable content; treat it as such (rasterize or forbid).

5. Private buckets, always. Block Public Access at the account level. Delivery goes through CloudFront with OAC and signed URLs or cookies for anything non-public.

6. PII and regulated data. Separate buckets for regulated content (KYC, medical) with SSE-KMS and a customer-managed key, CloudTrail data events, and tighter lifecycle. Never put PII in keys or in user metadata (both appear in logs and inventories). Deletion requests must cover derivatives and backups.

7. Signed URL leakage. Short expiry (minutes), per-object scope, never in query strings that get logged by third parties (referrer headers leak them; use Referrer-Policy: no-referrer on pages that embed them). For shareable links, issue a redirect endpoint under your control (GET /files/:id/download) that checks authorization and returns a fresh short-lived URL each time (32.13).

8. Rate limiting URL issuance. Signing costs you nothing and costs the attacker nothing; the bucket fill and the request bill are yours. @nestjs/throttler on the issue endpoint, per-user pending quota, and an alert on issuance spikes.

flowchart TB
  IN["Untrusted upload"] --> L1["Size cap at LB and POST policy"]
  L1 --> L2["Server-generated key, client name is display only"]
  L2 --> L3["Worker: magic bytes and allow-list"]
  L3 --> L4["Malware scan"]
  L4 --> L5["Re-encode images, set Content-Type from detection"]
  L5 --> L6["Private bucket, separate delivery origin, nosniff, attachment"]
  L6 --> OUT["PROCESSED and deliverable"]
  L3 -->|"unknown or forbidden type"| Q["QUARANTINED"]
  L4 -->|"infected"| Q

Practical example

A social app allows image posts. Attack attempts seen in a typical month: SVGs with embedded scripts (rejected: SVG not on the allow-list), a GIF with an HTML payload appended (re-encoded through sharp, payload gone), a 900 by 900 pixel PNG that decompresses to 4 GB (limitInputPixels rejects it), a filename "><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>.png (stored as text, HTML-escaped when rendered, never in a header unquoted), and 40,000 pre-signed URL requests in an hour from one account (throttled at 30 per minute, account flagged).

NestJS example

A response interceptor for the download path that hardens every file response:

// file-response-headers.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable } from 'rxjs';
import { tap } from 'rxjs/operators';
import { Response } from 'express';

const INLINE_OK = new Set(['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp', 'application/pdf']);

export function contentDisposition(name: string, mime: string): string {
  const ascii = name.replace(/[^\x20-\x7e]/g, '_').replace(/["\\]/g, '_').slice(0, 150);
  const utf8 = encodeURIComponent(name.slice(0, 150));
  const type = INLINE_OK.has(mime) ? 'inline' : 'attachment';
  return `${type}; filename="${ascii}"; filename*=UTF-8''${utf8}`;
}

@Injectable()
export class FileResponseHeadersInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    res.setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff');
    res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', "default-src 'none'; sandbox");
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store');
    res.setHeader('Referrer-Policy', 'no-referrer');
    return next.handle().pipe(tap(() => { /* headers already set before the stream starts */ }));
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Per-tenant quotas and abuse detection live next to the data:

-- Issuance velocity per user over the last 10 minutes (for throttling beyond the in-memory limiter)
SELECT count(*) FROM files WHERE owner_id = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval '10 minutes';

-- Tenants with an unusual quarantine ratio today (abuse signal)
SELECT tenant_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'QUARANTINED') AS quarantined,
       count(*) AS total
  FROM files
 WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
 GROUP BY tenant_id
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'QUARANTINED') > 5;

Production scenario

A security review of a file feature takes an afternoon with a checklist: where does the client name go, what sets Content-Type, which origin serves the bytes, which bucket setting blocks public access, how long do URLs live, what is the allow-list, where is the scan, what is the quota. The controls cost almost nothing at runtime: magic-bytes detection is microseconds, scanning is seconds in a worker, headers are free.

Failure scenario

A support portal lets customers attach files to tickets and serves them from app.example.com/attachments/:id with the client-declared Content-Type. An attacker uploads screenshot.png that is actually HTML with Content-Type: text/html, then opens a ticket asking an agent to "look at the screenshot". The agent clicks; the page runs in the app's origin with the agent's session and calls the admin API to export customer data. Root causes: trusted declared type, same-origin serving, no nosniff, no sandbox. Each control alone would have stopped it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Polyglot files that are both a valid JPEG and a valid ZIP or script: re-encoding images destroys the second personality; for PDFs, sanitize or serve only as attachment with sandbox.
  • Filenames with RTL override characters that make invoice.exe display as invoice.pdf; strip Unicode control characters.
  • Zip bombs in "import" features: cap decompressed size and entry count before extracting.
  • Scanner signatures lag zero-day malware; scanning is necessary, not sufficient; sandboxed delivery is the second layer.
  • A signed URL embedded in an email is forwarded; the recipient gets the file until expiry. Use the redirect endpoint for anything user-shared.
  • EXIF GPS in photos leaks the uploader's home address; strip on ingest.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Untrusted bytes stay untrusted until the pipeline says otherwise, and even trusted bytes are served from an origin where they cannot hurt anyone. The senior chooses the delivery origin and the Content-Type policy before writing the upload code, because those two decisions determine whether an XSS is possible at all.

Common mistakes

  • Using the client's Content-Type when writing to S3.
  • Serving uploads from the app origin because "the CDN was extra work".
  • Allowing SVG "because it is an image".
  • Long-lived signed URLs stored in the database as "the file URL".

Interview questions

  1. How can an image upload become an XSS? Expected: HTML or SVG stored with a permissive type served from the app origin; fixes are detection, separate origin, nosniff, sandbox, attachment.
  2. Where should upload size be enforced? Expected: every layer, cheapest first: LB, POST policy at S3, parser limits, validators, quotas.
  3. What is the risk of a leaked pre-signed GET URL and how do you contain it? Expected: anyone can read that object until expiry; short expiry, redirect endpoint, no-referrer, do not store URLs.
  4. Why is the client filename dangerous? Expected: traversal, header injection, encoding tricks; keep it as display data only.

Practical exercise

Write a security test suite for an upload feature: HTML-as-PNG, SVG with script, path traversal filename, 1 KB decompression bomb PNG, EICAR in a PDF, 50,000 URL issuance requests. Acceptance criteria: each is rejected or quarantined at the documented layer; the delivered files carry nosniff, sandbox CSP and the correct Content-Disposition; no test file is ever served with text/html.

32.13 Downloads

Concept

There are two ways to deliver a file: redirect the client to a signed URL (S3 or CloudFront) so the bytes flow from storage to the client directly, or stream the bytes through NestJS. The first is the default. The second is for when the server must do something to the bytes or the headers that the storage layer cannot: transform on the fly, apply complex authorization per byte range, or hide the storage entirely.

Why does it exist?

Downloads are where authorization meets bandwidth. You want the authorization decision in your code and the bandwidth on S3 and CloudFront. The redirect pattern gives you both: GET /files/:id/download runs your guard and returns a 302 to a URL that expires in a minute.

Mental model

Imagine a library. The redirect model: you show your card at the desk, the librarian hands you a slip with a shelf code valid for five minutes, and you fetch the book yourself. The streaming model: the librarian walks to the shelf, brings the book, and reads it to you. The second is only worth it if the librarian has to translate it as they go.

How it works

Redirect model:

  1. GET /files/:id/download with the user's session.
  2. Guard checks the user may read this file (owner, share, tenant admin). Row must be PROCESSED.
  3. Sign a GetObjectCommand (or a CloudFront URL) with ResponseContentDisposition and ResponseContentType overrides, expiring in 60 seconds.
  4. Return 302 Location: <signed url> (or 200 { url } for API clients that need the URL in JSON).
  5. The client fetches from S3 or the CDN. Range requests, resume, and parallel chunks work natively because S3 supports Range and returns 206 Partial Content with Content-Range and Accept-Ranges: bytes.

Streaming model:

  1. Same guard.
  2. GetObjectCommand with the client's Range header forwarded.
  3. Pipe Body to the response with StreamableFile, forwarding Content-Length, Content-Range, Content-Type, ETag, Last-Modified, and setting Content-Disposition yourself.
  4. Handle client disconnect by destroying the S3 stream so you do not keep pulling bytes for nobody.

Cost comparison for a 100 MB file at 1,000 downloads per day: through NestJS, 100 GB per day through the load balancer and pods, roughly 30 seconds of pod socket time per download, and ALB processing fees. Redirected to CloudFront: zero pod time, cached at the edge for popular files, and CloudFront's per-GB price is lower than ALB plus EC2 egress.

Practical example

An invoice download in an e-commerce account page uses the redirect model. A "watermarked preview" of a stock photo uses the streaming model because the watermark is applied per user on the fly (and cached in Redis by {fileId, userId} for repeat views). A video course player uses CloudFront signed cookies so the <video> element can issue range requests to the CDN directly.

NestJS example

// download.controller.ts
import {
  Controller, Get, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Req, Res, UseGuards, UseInterceptors,
  NotFoundException, ForbiddenException, StreamableFile, Headers,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { S3Client, GetObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { FileRepository } from './file.repository';
import { FileAccessService } from './file-access.service';
import { PresignService } from './presign.service';
import { FileStatus } from './file-status';
import { FileResponseHeadersInterceptor, contentDisposition } from './file-response-headers.interceptor';

@Controller('files')
