@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class DownloadController {
  constructor(
    @Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client,
    private readonly files: FileRepository,
    private readonly access: FileAccessService,
    private readonly presign: PresignService,
  ) {}

  /** Default: authorize, then redirect to a 60 s signed URL. Bytes never touch this pod. */
  @Get(':id/download')
  async download(@Req() req: Request & { user: { id: string } }, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Res() res: Response) {
    const rec = await this.files.findOrFail(id);
    if (rec.status !== FileStatus.PROCESSED) throw new NotFoundException();
    if (!(await this.access.canRead(req.user.id, rec))) throw new ForbiddenException();
    const url = await this.presign.signGet(rec.key, rec.originalName, false, 60);
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store');
    res.redirect(302, url);
  }

  /** Streaming variant: only when the server must control headers or transform bytes. */
  @Get(':id/stream')
  @UseInterceptors(FileResponseHeadersInterceptor)
  async stream(
    @Req() req: Request & { user: { id: string } },
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
    @Headers('range') range: string | undefined,
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ): Promise<StreamableFile> {
    const rec = await this.files.findOrFail(id);
    if (rec.status !== FileStatus.PROCESSED) throw new NotFoundException();
    if (!(await this.access.canRead(req.user.id, rec))) throw new ForbiddenException();

    const obj = await this.s3.send(new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: rec.bucket, Key: rec.key, Range: range }));
    const body = obj.Body as Readable;
    res.status(range ? 206 : 200);
    res.setHeader('Accept-Ranges', 'bytes');
    if (obj.ContentRange) res.setHeader('Content-Range', obj.ContentRange);
    if (obj.ETag) res.setHeader('ETag', obj.ETag);
    res.setHeader('Content-Disposition', contentDisposition(rec.originalName, rec.detectedMime ?? 'application/octet-stream'));
    // Stop pulling from S3 if the client goes away mid-transfer.
    req.on('close', () => body.destroy());
    return new StreamableFile(body, { type: rec.detectedMime ?? 'application/octet-stream', length: obj.ContentLength });
  }
}

Note the Content-Type comes from detectedMime, set by the pipeline, never from the client's declaration.

PostgreSQL example

Authorization for downloads is a query, and it should be indexed:

-- Can user U read file F? Owner, or file shared with U, or U is admin of the tenant.
SELECT 1
  FROM files f
 WHERE f.id = $2 AND f.status = 'PROCESSED'
   AND (
        f.owner_id = $1
     OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM file_shares s WHERE s.file_id = f.id AND s.user_id = $1 AND (s.expires_at IS NULL OR s.expires_at > now()))
     OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tenant_members m WHERE m.tenant_id = f.tenant_id AND m.user_id = $1 AND m.role = 'admin')
   );
CREATE INDEX file_shares_user_idx ON file_shares (user_id, file_id);

Production scenario

Download authorization at 200 requests per second: the query above is 1 to 2 ms with warm indexes; signing is 0.2 ms; the redirect response is under 5 ms total. The same 200 requests per second streamed through pods at an average of 5 MB each is 1 GB/s through Node.js, which is a different and much larger deployment. Monitor: redirect count, 403 rate (authorization failures, often a bug after a permissions change), and for the streaming route, bytes served and concurrent streams per pod.

Failure scenario

A product team wants "download all attachments as a zip". The first version streams every S3 object through the pod, zips in memory, and returns the archive. A customer with 4,000 attachments totaling 9 GB clicks it; the pod is OOM-killed and the ALB returns 502 to every other user on that pod. The second version enqueues a job, a worker streams objects one at a time into a zip stream that is multipart-uploaded to exports/, and the user gets an email with a redirect link that expires in 24 hours. The API never touches the bytes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Range header with an invalid range: S3 returns 416; forward it rather than crashing.
  • Client aborts: without body.destroy() the pod keeps downloading from S3 and pays egress for nothing.
  • A redirect URL cached by a browser or proxy: Cache-Control: no-store on the redirect response.
  • Content-Disposition with non-ASCII names breaks in older clients without the filename* form.
  • Signed URL expires while a slow client is mid-download: S3 checks the signature at request start, so an in-progress transfer completes; a resume after expiry fails, and the client must re-request the redirect.
  • Files in Glacier classes return InvalidObjectState; surface a "restore requested, try again in N hours" response rather than a 500.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Authorization in the API, bytes on the edge. The senior reaches for the streaming route only with a specific reason and a size cap, and they put a job and an email between the user and any "download everything" feature.

Common mistakes

  • Streaming everything through NestJS "so we can log downloads" (log the redirect instead).
  • Returning a 24-hour signed URL from the download endpoint and calling it a share link.
  • Forgetting Accept-Ranges and 206 handling so video scrubbing does not work.

Interview questions

  1. When do you stream a file through the API instead of redirecting? Expected: transform on the fly, header control, hide storage, tiny files; otherwise redirect.
  2. How do range requests work with S3? Expected: Range header, 206, Content-Range; S3 supports natively; forward when streaming.
  3. How do you implement "download as zip" for thousands of files? Expected: async job, streaming zip into multipart upload, link by email; never in the request.

Practical exercise

Implement both routes. Acceptance criteria: a curl -r 0-1023 against the stream route returns 206 with 1,024 bytes and a correct Content-Range; the redirect route returns 302 with a URL that fails after 60 seconds; aborting a 1 GB stream at 10 percent stops S3 egress within 2 seconds (check bytes read on the pod).

32.14 NestJS upload architecture: the full worked example

This section assembles everything above into one coherent flow for a product-image upload in an e-commerce seller portal. Requirements: images up to 10 MB, JPEG/PNG/WebP, direct-to-S3, scanned and thumbnailed before they appear on the storefront, delivered by CDN.

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant API as NestJS API
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  participant S3 as S3
  participant Q as BullMQ
  participant W as Worker
  participant CDN as CloudFront
  B->>API: POST /files name, mime, size
  API->>PG: INSERT files PENDING
  API-->>B: fileId, POST policy url and fields
  B->>S3: POST form with file
  S3-->>B: 204
  B->>API: POST /files/:id/confirm
  API->>S3: HeadObject
  S3-->>API: 200 size, type
  API->>PG: UPDATE PENDING to UPLOADED
  API->>Q: add job fileId
  API-->>B: 202 status UPLOADED
  W->>PG: UPDATE UPLOADED to SCANNING
  W->>S3: GetObject
  W->>W: magic bytes, scan, sha256, thumbnails
  W->>S3: PutObject derived keys
  W->>PG: UPDATE SCANNING to PROCESSED
  B->>API: GET /files/:id
  API-->>B: status PROCESSED, cdn urls
  B->>CDN: GET thumbnail
  CDN->>S3: on miss

The service that ties the pieces together:

// files.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException, NotFoundException, ForbiddenException, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';
import { S3Client, HeadObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';
import { ObjectKeyService } from '../s3/object-key.service';
import { PresignService } from './presign.service';
import { FileRepository } from './file.repository';
import { FileRecord } from './file.entity';
import { FileStatus } from './file-status';
import { CreateUploadDto } from './create-upload.dto';
import { CdnUrlService } from '../cdn/cdn-url.service';

const MAX_PENDING_PER_HOUR = 100;

@Injectable()
export class FilesService {
  private readonly bucket = process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET!;
  constructor(
    @Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client,
    private readonly keys: ObjectKeyService,
    private readonly presign: PresignService,
    private readonly files: FileRepository,
    private readonly cdn: CdnUrlService,
    private readonly ds: DataSource,
    @InjectQueue('file-processing') private readonly queue: Queue,
  ) {}

  async createPendingUpload(user: { id: string; tenantId: string }, dto: CreateUploadDto) {
    const pending = await this.files.countPendingSince(user.id, new Date(Date.now() - 3600_000));
    if (pending >= MAX_PENDING_PER_HOUR) throw new ConflictException('Too many uploads in progress');

    const ext = dto.mimeType.split('/')[1] === 'jpeg' ? 'jpg' : dto.mimeType.split('/')[1];
    const key = this.keys.build('uploads', user.tenantId, ext);

    const rec = await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => em.save(FileRecord, em.create(FileRecord, {
      tenantId: user.tenantId, ownerId: user.id, bucket: this.bucket, key,
      originalName: dto.filename.slice(0, 255), declaredMime: dto.mimeType, status: FileStatus.PENDING,
    })));

    const upload = await this.presign.signPost(key, dto.mimeType.split('/')[0] + '/', dto.sizeBytes);
    return { fileId: rec.id, upload }; // { url, fields } for the browser form POST
  }

  async confirmUpload(userId: string, fileId: string) {
    const rec = await this.files.findOrFail(fileId);
    if (rec.ownerId !== userId) throw new ForbiddenException();
    if (rec.status === FileStatus.UPLOADED || rec.status === FileStatus.PROCESSED) return { status: rec.status }; // idempotent
    if (rec.status !== FileStatus.PENDING) throw new ConflictException(`File is ${rec.status}`);

    let head;
    try {
      head = await this.s3.send(new HeadObjectCommand({ Bucket: rec.bucket, Key: rec.key }));
    } catch (e: any) {
      if (e?.$metadata?.httpStatusCode === 404) throw new ConflictException('Object not uploaded yet');
      throw e;
    }
    if ((head.ContentLength ?? 0) === 0 || (head.ContentLength ?? 0) > 10 * 1024 * 1024) {
      throw new ConflictException('Object size out of range'); // janitor will expire it
    }
    const moved = await this.files.transition(fileId, FileStatus.PENDING, FileStatus.UPLOADED, {
      sizeBytes: String(head.ContentLength),
    });
    if (!moved) throw new ConflictException('File state changed');

    // jobId = fileId makes a double confirm enqueue once; attempts and backoff handle transient failures.
    await this.queue.add('process', { fileId }, { jobId: fileId, attempts: 4, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5000 }, removeOnComplete: true });
    return { status: FileStatus.UPLOADED };
  }

  async describe(userId: string, fileId: string) {
    const rec = await this.files.findWithDerivatives(fileId);
    if (!rec) throw new NotFoundException();
    if (rec.ownerId !== userId) throw new ForbiddenException();
    const thumb = rec.derivatives.find((d) => d.kind === 'thumb_256');
    return {
      id: rec.id, status: rec.status, size: rec.sizeBytes, mime: rec.detectedMime,
      urls: rec.status === FileStatus.PROCESSED
        ? { original: this.cdn.privateUrl(rec.key), thumb: thumb ? this.cdn.publicUrl(thumb.key) : null }
        : null,
    };
  }
}

The janitor that closes the loop on orphans:

// file-janitor.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { S3Client, HeadObjectCommand, DeleteObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';
import { S3_CLIENT } from '../s3/s3.module';
import { FileRepository } from './file.repository';
import { FileStatus } from './file-status';

@Injectable()
export class FileJanitorService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(FileJanitorService.name);
  constructor(
    @Inject(S3_CLIENT) private readonly s3: S3Client,
    private readonly files: FileRepository,
    @InjectQueue('file-processing') private readonly queue: Queue,
  ) {}

  @Cron('*/5 * * * *') // every 5 minutes; single instance via a leader lock in production
  async sweepPending() {
    const stale = await this.files.findPendingOlderThan(new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60_000), 500);
    for (const rec of stale) {
      try {
        await this.s3.send(new HeadObjectCommand({ Bucket: rec.bucket, Key: rec.key }));
        // Object exists but confirm was lost: promote and process instead of losing the upload.
        if (await this.files.transition(rec.id, FileStatus.PENDING, FileStatus.UPLOADED)) {
          await this.queue.add('process', { fileId: rec.id }, { jobId: rec.id, attempts: 4 });
        }
      } catch (e: any) {
        if (e?.$metadata?.httpStatusCode === 404) {
          await this.files.transition(rec.id, FileStatus.PENDING, FileStatus.EXPIRED);
        } else {
          this.log.warn({ fileId: rec.id, msg: 'head failed, will retry', err: e?.name });
        }
      }
    }
    // SCANNING rows stuck for 30+ minutes: worker died; put them back for a retry.
    const stuck = await this.files.findScanningOlderThan(new Date(Date.now() - 30 * 60_000), 100);
    for (const rec of stuck) {
      if (await this.files.transition(rec.id, FileStatus.SCANNING, FileStatus.UPLOADED)) {
        await this.queue.add('process', { fileId: rec.id }, { jobId: `${rec.id}:retry:${Date.now()}`, attempts: 2 });
      }
    }
  }
}

(SCANNING -> UPLOADED must be added to ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS for the janitor's use.)

Deployment shape: the API deployment handles the JSON endpoints and never streams bytes; the worker deployment runs the BullMQ processor with ClamAV as a sidecar or a shared service; the CDN sits in front of the bucket with OAC; lifecycle rules abort multipart after 3 days and expire uploads/ objects whose rows are EXPIRED via a nightly DB-driven job. Dashboards: URLs issued, confirmed, processed, quarantined per hour; queue depth and oldest job age; DLQ depth; CDN hit ratio.

32.15 Edge cases & failure modes

  • Upload succeeded but confirm never called (orphans). The browser closed after the S3 POST. The row is PENDING, the object exists. The janitor's HeadObject promotes it to UPLOADED and processing continues; without a janitor the object costs money and the user thinks the upload failed. The S3 event notification safety net catches the same case faster.
  • Duplicate uploads (content hash dedup). The same PDF uploaded twice by the same tenant. The worker computes SHA-256, finds a PROCESSED row with the same hash in the same tenant, points the new row at the existing key and deletes the new object. Never dedup across tenants; the existence check itself would leak information.
  • Huge files timing out through the API. A 3 GB upload through FileInterceptor hits the ALB idle timeout (60 seconds default) or the pod's memory limit. Fix is architectural: pre-signed multipart, not a bigger timeout.
  • Multipart parts left forever (cost). Every abandoned multipart upload bills at Standard rates and is invisible to normal listings. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload at 3 days, plus the multipart_uploads table janitor.
  • Pre-signed URL reused or leaked. A PUT URL can be used repeatedly until expiry; the last body wins. The pipeline treats every object as untrusted until scanned, expiry is minutes, and after PROCESSED the original upload URL has long expired. A leaked GET URL exposes one object until expiry; the redirect endpoint keeps that window to a minute.
  • Wrong content type sniffed as HTML (stored XSS via S3). Client declares text/html or the browser sniffs it; served from the app origin it executes. Detection sets the type, uploads are served from a separate origin with nosniff and a sandbox CSP, and HTML and SVG are not on the allow-list.
  • CDN eventual consistency after replace. Overwriting a key leaves stale copies at edges for the TTL; invalidations are slow and cost money. Never overwrite; every version is a new key with immutable caching.
  • S3 throttling (503 SlowDown). Bursts above the per-prefix rate return SlowDown. The SDK retries with backoff (maxAttempts); browsers need retry logic in the upload code; spread hot writes across prefixes only if you actually exceed 3,500 writes per second on one prefix.
  • Region outage. Uploads fail, downloads fail unless CloudFront has cached them. Mitigation is Cross-Region Replication to a second bucket and a CloudFront origin group with failover; RPO is replication lag (typically seconds to minutes) and it doubles storage cost. Decide per bucket whether that is worth it (see Part 49 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery).
  • Lifecycle deleting needed files. A rule with a wrong prefix or empty filter deletes production data; versioning turns that into a delete-marker cleanup instead of a loss. Lifecycle rules live in infrastructure code with review.
  • Bucket public by mistake. A developer disables Block Public Access for a test and forgets; enumerable keys make it a breach. Account-level Block Public Access plus an organization policy that denies changing it; UUID keys so nothing is guessable even if it happens.
  • Clock skew invalidating signatures. SigV4 tolerates 15 minutes between the signer's clock and S3's. A pod with broken NTP produces URLs that fail with RequestTimeTooSkewed, which looks like a permissions error. Alert on NTP drift on nodes.
  • Filename encoding issues. Names with emoji, RTL overrides, quotes or newlines break Content-Disposition and log lines. Keys are UUIDs; display names are sanitized for headers with filename*=UTF-8'' encoding and stripped of control characters.
  • Virus in file processed before scan. A pipeline that extracts PDF text and indexes it before the scan verdict has already handed malicious content to a downstream system. The scan is the first step after magic-byte detection; nothing reads deeper into the bytes until it passes.
  • Confirm called before the upload finished. HeadObject 404s; the API returns 409 and the client retries after the PUT completes. Never mark UPLOADED optimistically.
  • KMS key disabled or throttled. Every read fails with KMS.DisabledException or ThrottlingException; alert on KMS key state changes and enable bucket keys.
  • Disk-based temp files piling up on API pods. For the small through-the-API path with diskStorage, a crashed request leaves a temp file. Use emptyDir with a size limit and a cleanup on startup.

Senior Checklist — Part 32

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain why local disk fails with multiple pods and when it is still acceptable
  • I can design an S3 key scheme that supports lifecycle rules and tenant deletion
  • I can implement a pre-signed upload flow with a confirm endpoint and a files state machine
  • I can implement resumable multipart uploads and know the abort and lifecycle story
  • I can explain why uploads are served from a separate origin with detected content types
  • I can design an idempotent processing pipeline with scan, derivatives and a DLQ
  • I can put CloudFront in front of a private bucket with OAC and signed URLs
  • I can list the lifecycle rules every bucket needs and the cost traps of storage classes
  • I can choose between redirect-to-signed-URL and streaming through NestJS for downloads

Part 32 — Key Takeaways

  • Bytes live in object storage; facts about bytes live in PostgreSQL; delivery is the CDN's job. NestJS pods coordinate and never carry large files.
  • Local disk is a buffer, not storage. If a pod vanishing loses a user file, the design is wrong.
  • S3 is strongly consistent and eleven-nines durable, but durability does not protect against your own deletes; versioning and reviewed lifecycle rules do.
  • Keys are server-generated UUIDs under purpose and tenant prefixes; never overwrite a key with new content.
  • Pre-signed URLs are short-lived, narrowly scoped bearer tokens; the POST policy is where S3 enforces size and type; the confirm endpoint is how your database learns the truth.
  • The files.status state machine, written only through guarded conditional updates, is what makes direct-to-S3 uploads safe.
  • Nothing reads uploaded content before magic-byte detection and a malware scan; nothing is delivered before PROCESSED.
  • Serve user content from a separate origin with detected Content-Type, nosniff, a sandbox CSP and attachment for anything not on a small inline allow-list.
  • Multipart uploads need an abort path and an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule, or they bill forever invisibly.
  • Downloads are authorization in the API plus a redirect to a one-minute signed URL; stream through NestJS only with a reason and a size cap.
  • Measure the issue-to-confirm funnel and the processing queue; they are the only visibility into a flow that bypasses your servers.

Part 33 — Search: PostgreSQL Full-Text to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch

33.1 Search, filtering and lookup: three different problems

Concept

Developers use the word "search" for three things that have almost nothing in common:

  • Lookup. "Give me order ORD-2026-4471." One key, one row, exact match. A B-tree index answers it in microseconds.
  • Filtering. "Show me shoes, size 42, under 80 euros, in stock, sorted by price." Structured predicates on typed columns. Indexes, WHERE clauses, ORDER BY. The result set is exactly defined; there is no notion of "better" or "worse" matches, only in or out.
  • Search. "running shoes for flat feet." Free text against free text. The user does not know the exact words in the product name; the product description was written by someone else; "running" should match "run", "runner" and "runs"; a typo should still find something; and the results must be ranked, because the user will look at the first five and no more.

Relevance is the thing that separates search from filtering. Relevance is a score that estimates how well a document answers a query, so the results can be ordered by that score. Filtering has no score. Lookup has no ordering. Search is the only one where the correct answer is fuzzy and "good enough, fast" beats "exact, slow".

Why does it exist?

Because humans do not know your schema. A user typing "iphone charger cable usb c" is not going to select category = 'Cables' and connector_type = 'USB-C'. They type words; the system must map words to products. Every product with a catalog, every app with user-generated content, every back office with tickets eventually needs this, and the naive answer, WHERE name ILIKE '%iphone%charger%', is both wrong (no ranking, no stemming, no typo tolerance) and, on a large table, catastrophically slow (a sequential scan of every row for every keystroke).

Mental model

Imagine a library. Lookup is asking for a book by its catalog number: the librarian walks straight to the shelf. Filtering is asking for "all hardback history books published after 2010": the librarian uses the card catalog's categories. Search is walking in and saying "something about how the Romans built roads"; the librarian has to understand what you mean, recall which books talk about that, and hand you the best three first, not all four hundred that mention Rome.

How it works

A search system, at any scale, has the same four pieces:

  1. Analysis. Text is broken into tokens (words), normalized (lowercased, stemmed, accents removed, stop words dropped). "Running Shoes" becomes run, shoe.
  2. Indexing. An inverted index maps each token to the list of documents containing it. shoe -> [12, 99, 4410, ...].
  3. Matching. The query is analyzed the same way and the token lists are intersected or unioned.
  4. Ranking. Each matching document gets a score (how many query terms, how rare they are, where they appear, how long the document is), and results are sorted by score.

PostgreSQL does all four inside the database with tsvector, tsquery, GIN indexes and ts_rank. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch do the same four with Lucene, at much larger scale, with far more control over analysis and ranking, at the cost of running a separate cluster and keeping it in sync.

"Running Shoes for Flat Feet"
        |  analysis: lowercase, stop words, stemming
        v
   [run, shoe, flat, feet]
        |  indexing: inverted index
        v
   run  -> {p12, p99, p4410}
   shoe -> {p12, p99, p777}
   flat -> {p12, p2}
   feet -> {p12, p2, p99}
        |  matching + ranking
        v
   p12 (4 terms, short title)  score 0.91
   p99 (3 terms)               score 0.63
   p2  (2 terms)               score 0.20

Practical example

An e-commerce catalog with 2 million products. Three endpoints, three problems:

  • GET /products/:sku is lookup: primary key, 1 ms.
  • GET /products?category=shoes&size=42&maxPrice=80&sort=price is filtering: composite index, 3 to 10 ms.
  • GET /search?q=running+shoes+flat+feet is search: full-text index plus ranking, 10 to 40 ms in PostgreSQL for this data size, 5 to 20 ms in Elasticsearch, and the results must be good, which is measured by whether users click them.

Mixing them up costs real money. A team that implements search as ILIKE '%running%' AND ILIKE '%shoes%' returns "Running Shoes Cleaning Kit" above actual running shoes and burns a CPU core per query.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The first question is always "which of the three is this?" The second is "what does the user do with the result?" If they look at the top five, relevance is the product. If they page through everything, it is filtering and ranking is a distraction. The senior refuses to build a search engine for what is actually a filter, and refuses to fake search with ILIKE.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between search and filtering? Expected: filtering is exact predicates with no ranking; search is free text with relevance scoring; they need different indexes and different APIs.
  2. What does "relevance" mean technically? Expected: a score estimating how well a document matches the query, used to order results; computed from term frequency, rarity, field weights and business signals.

33.2 Full-text search in PostgreSQL

Concept

PostgreSQL has a complete full-text search engine built in. It has been there since version 8.3 and it is good: dictionaries for two dozen languages, stemming, stop words, weighted fields, phrase queries, ranking functions, result highlighting, and a GIN index type that makes queries fast. For most products, it is all the search you need, and it comes with transactions, backups and the operational knowledge you already have.

The two core types:

  • tsvector: a sorted list of normalized words (lexemes) with their positions in the original text. 'brown':3 'dog':9 'fox':4 'jump':5.
  • tsquery: a boolean expression over lexemes. 'run' & 'shoe' & !'nike'.

The @@ operator matches a tsvector against a tsquery.

Why does it exist?

Because LIKE cannot stem, cannot rank, cannot ignore stop words, cannot do phrase queries, and cannot use a B-tree index for %term%. Full-text search is a different data structure (the inverted index) and a different query language, packaged into the database so you do not need a second system.

Mental model

Imagine the index at the back of a textbook. It does not list every word; it lists the important words in their base form ("running" is filed under "run"), and for each one the pages where it appears. to_tsvector builds that index for one document. to_tsquery turns your question into the same base-form words. @@ checks whether the pages overlap. ts_rank decides which page is the best answer, by counting how many of your words appear and how close together.

How it works

Step 1: the text search configuration. A configuration (for example english) defines a parser (splits text into tokens: words, numbers, emails, URLs) and a chain of dictionaries per token type. The english configuration maps normal words through a Snowball stemmer that also drops stop words.

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The quick brown foxes jumped over the lazy dogs');
--  'brown':3 'dog':9 'fox':4 'jump':5 'lazi':8 'quick':2

The, over and the are gone (stop words). foxes became fox, jumped became jump, lazy became lazi (stems are not always English words; they only need to be consistent between indexing and querying). Positions are kept so phrase queries and proximity ranking work.

Step 2: the query. Four constructors, from strictest to friendliest:

SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'running & shoes');          -- 'run' & 'shoe'   (you write the operators)
SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'running shoes');       -- 'run' & 'shoe'   (words ANDed)
SELECT phraseto_tsquery('english', 'running shoes');      -- 'run' <-> 'shoe' (adjacent, in order)
SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"running shoes" -nike or adidas');
--  'run' <-> 'shoe' & !'nike' | 'adida'                   (Google-like syntax, never throws on bad input)

websearch_to_tsquery is the one to expose to users: it accepts quoted phrases, - for negation, or, and never raises a syntax error on garbage input, which to_tsquery does.

Step 3: weights. A product's name matters more than its description. setweight tags lexemes with A, B, C or D, and ts_rank weights them (default weights 1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1):

SELECT setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'Trail Running Shoes'), 'A')
    || setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'Lightweight shoes for running on trails'), 'B');
-- 'lightweight':4B 'run':2A,7B 'shoe':3A,5B 'trail':1A,9B

Step 4: ranking. ts_rank(vector, query) scores by term frequency and weights. ts_rank_cd (cover density) additionally rewards query terms appearing close together, which is usually what you want for product search. Both accept a normalization bitmask; 1 divides by 1 + log(document length) so long descriptions do not win by repetition, 32 scales the score into 0..1.

Step 5: the index. A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) on the tsvector column. GIN stores, for each lexeme, a posting list of the row locations that contain it; the @@ operator becomes a lookup of a few posting lists and an intersection. Section 33.3 explains the structure.

Step 6: keeping the vector current. Since PostgreSQL 12, a GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED column recomputes the vector on every insert and update, with no trigger code. The expression must be immutable, which means you must pass the configuration explicitly (to_tsvector('english', ...), never to_tsvector(...) relying on the session default).

Step 7: highlighting. ts_headline returns a fragment of the original text with query terms wrapped in markers, for search result snippets.

flowchart LR
  T["Raw text: Trail Running Shoes"] --> P["Parser: tokens"]
  P --> D["Dictionaries: lowercase, stop words, stem"]
  D --> V["tsvector: run:2A shoe:3A trail:1A"]
  V --> G["GIN index posting lists"]
  Q["User query: running shoe"] --> QP["websearch_to_tsquery: run and shoe"]
  QP --> M["@@ match via GIN"]
  G --> M
  M --> R["ts_rank_cd ordering"]
  R --> H["ts_headline snippet"]

Practical example

Product search for an e-commerce catalog. Requirements: search name, brand, description and SKU; name and brand count more; users type natural queries with typos handled elsewhere (33.6); results ranked; snippets highlighted; filters (category, price) combined with search; 20 results per page.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE products (
  id           bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id    uuid   NOT NULL,
  sku          text   NOT NULL,
  name         text   NOT NULL,
  brand        text,
  description  text,
  category_id  int    NOT NULL,
  price_cents  int    NOT NULL,
  in_stock     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  language     text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'english',   -- per-row config name
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  -- Weighted, generated, stored. 'simple' for SKU and brand so they are matched exactly, not stemmed.
  search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
       setweight(to_tsvector('simple',  coalesce(sku, '')),          'A')
    || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')),         'A')
    || setweight(to_tsvector('simple',  coalesce(brand, '')),        'B')
    || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')),  'C')
  ) STORED
);

CREATE INDEX products_search_gin ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
CREATE INDEX products_tenant_cat_price ON products (tenant_id, category_id, price_cents);

The query, with a filter, ranking and a headline:

WITH q AS (SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1) AS query)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.brand, p.price_cents,
       ts_rank_cd(p.search_vector, q.query, 1) AS rank,
       ts_headline('english', coalesce(p.description, ''), q.query,
                   'StartSel=<mark>, StopSel=</mark>, MaxFragments=2, MaxWords=18, MinWords=6') AS snippet
  FROM products p, q
 WHERE p.tenant_id = $2
   AND p.search_vector @@ q.query
   AND ($3::int IS NULL OR p.category_id = $3)
   AND p.in_stock
 ORDER BY rank DESC, p.id
 LIMIT 20 OFFSET $4;

What the planner does for 2 million products and the query running shoes:

Limit  (cost=1843.21..1843.26 rows=20 width=120) (actual time=18.402..18.409 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=2311
  ->  Sort  (cost=1843.21..1851.70 rows=3396 width=120) (actual time=18.400..18.403 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (ts_rank_cd(p.search_vector, q.query, 1)) DESC, p.id
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 41kB
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on products p  (cost=71.32..1752.85 rows=3396 width=120) (actual time=1.912..15.877 rows=3412 loops=1)
              Recheck Cond: (search_vector @@ '''run'' & ''shoe'''::tsquery)
              Filter: (in_stock AND (tenant_id = '...'::uuid))
              Rows Removed by Filter: 188
              Heap Blocks: exact=2204
              Buffers: shared hit=2311
              ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_search_gin  (cost=0.00..70.47 rows=3600 width=0) (actual time=1.402..1.402 rows=3600 loops=1)
                    Index Cond: (search_vector @@ '''run'' & ''shoe'''::tsquery)
                    Buffers: shared hit=18
Planning Time: 0.412 ms
Execution Time: 18.501 ms

Read it bottom up: the GIN index found 3,600 candidate rows in 1.4 ms by intersecting two posting lists. The heap scan fetched those rows (2,204 pages) and applied the remaining filters. ts_rank_cd ran on 3,412 rows and a top-N heapsort kept 20. Total 18 ms. Note the cost of ranking scales with the number of matches, not the table size: a query for a very common word (shoes alone, 400,000 matches) will take hundreds of milliseconds because every match is ranked. That is the fundamental limit of PostgreSQL FTS and the first reason teams move to Elasticsearch, which ranks with early termination and skip lists.

Multi-language: the generated column above uses one config. For per-row language, the expression must remain immutable; a CASE over a small set of literal configurations is:

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
  setweight(to_tsvector(CASE language WHEN 'german' THEN 'german'::regconfig
                                      WHEN 'french' THEN 'french'::regconfig
                                      ELSE 'english'::regconfig END, coalesce(name, '')), 'A')
  || setweight(to_tsvector(CASE language WHEN 'german' THEN 'german'::regconfig
                                         WHEN 'french' THEN 'french'::regconfig
                                         ELSE 'english'::regconfig END, coalesce(description, '')), 'C')
) STORED;

And the query must use the same configuration as the row's language, which means either you know the user's language or you run the query against the configuration that matches the catalog segment. Accent-insensitive search uses the unaccent extension as a dictionary in a custom configuration:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent;
CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION english_unaccent (COPY = english);
ALTER TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION english_unaccent
  ALTER MAPPING FOR hword, hword_part, word WITH unaccent, english_stem;
SELECT to_tsvector('english_unaccent', 'Café Crème');  -- 'cafe':1 'creme':2

Stop words deserve a warning here: to_tsvector('english', 'IT services') yields only 'servic':2 because it is a stop word. A brand called "IT" or a product called "The The" is unfindable through the english config. That is why the sku and brand columns above use simple (lowercase only, no stemming, no stop words), and why the query side should try simple as a fallback when the english query comes back empty (33.14 covers this failure).

TypeORM example

Full-text queries are parameterized raw SQL or QueryBuilder with setParameters. Never interpolate the user's string.

// product-search.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export interface ProductHit { id: string; name: string; brand: string | null; priceCents: number; rank: number; snippet: string }

@Injectable()
export class ProductSearchRepository {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async search(tenantId: string, q: string, categoryId: number | null, limit = 20, offset = 0): Promise<ProductHit[]> {
    // QueryBuilder keeps the SQL readable and parameters bound.
    const rows = await this.ds.createQueryBuilder()
      .select('p.id', 'id')
      .addSelect('p.name', 'name')
      .addSelect('p.brand', 'brand')
      .addSelect('p.price_cents', 'priceCents')
      .addSelect(`ts_rank_cd(p.search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q), 1)`, 'rank')
      .addSelect(`ts_headline('english', coalesce(p.description, ''), websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q), 'StartSel=<mark>, StopSel=</mark>, MaxWords=18, MinWords=6')`, 'snippet')
      .from('products', 'p')
      .where('p.tenant_id = :tenantId', { tenantId })
      .andWhere(`p.search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q)`, { q })
      .andWhere('p.in_stock = true')
      .andWhere(categoryId === null ? '1=1' : 'p.category_id = :categoryId', { categoryId })
      .orderBy('rank', 'DESC')
      .addOrderBy('p.id', 'ASC')
      .limit(limit)
      .offset(offset)
      .getRawMany<ProductHit>();
    return rows.map((r) => ({ ...r, rank: Number(r.rank), priceCents: Number(r.priceCents) }));
  }
}

The entity can declare the generated column so migrations create it; TypeORM supports asExpression with generatedType: 'STORED':

@Column({
  type: 'tsvector', select: false, insert: false, update: false,
  generatedType: 'STORED',
  asExpression: `setweight(to_tsvector('simple', coalesce(sku, '')), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('simple', coalesce(brand, '')), 'B') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'C')`,
})
searchVector!: string;

And the GIN index in a migration, because @Index cannot express the access method:

await queryRunner.query(`CREATE INDEX products_search_gin ON products USING GIN (search_vector)`);

Sequelize example

// product-search.sequelize.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectModel } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { Sequelize, QueryTypes } from 'sequelize';
import { Product } from './product.model';

@Injectable()
export class ProductSearchSequelize {
  constructor(@InjectModel(Product) private readonly products: typeof Product, private readonly sequelize: Sequelize) {}

  // Model-based with literal fragments; replacements are bound, never concatenated.
  async search(tenantId: string, q: string, limit = 20, offset = 0) {
    const query = `websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q)`;
    return this.products.findAll({
      attributes: [
        'id', 'name', 'brand', 'priceCents',
        [Sequelize.literal(`ts_rank_cd("Product"."search_vector", ${query}, 1)`), 'rank'],
        [Sequelize.literal(`ts_headline('english', coalesce("Product"."description", ''), ${query}, 'MaxWords=18, MinWords=6')`), 'snippet'],
      ],
      where: Sequelize.and(
        { tenantId, inStock: true },
        Sequelize.literal(`"Product"."search_vector" @@ ${query}`),
      ),
      order: [[Sequelize.literal('rank'), 'DESC'], ['id', 'ASC']],
      limit, offset,
      replacements: { q },
    });
  }

  // Raw variant when the query outgrows the model API.
  async searchRaw(tenantId: string, q: string) {
    return this.sequelize.query(
      `SELECT id, name, ts_rank_cd(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q), 1) AS rank
         FROM products WHERE tenant_id = :tenantId AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q)
        ORDER BY rank DESC, id LIMIT 20`,
      { replacements: { q, tenantId }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
    );
  }
}

NestJS example

The controller validates the query DTO and delegates. The full search module with a provider port is in 33.11; the DTO is worth seeing now because it is where injection and abuse are stopped:

// search-products.dto.ts
import { IsInt, IsOptional, IsString, Max, MaxLength, Min, MinLength, IsIn, Matches } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';

export class SearchProductsDto {
  @IsString() @MinLength(1) @MaxLength(200)
  @Matches(/^[^\x00-\x1f]+$/, { message: 'control characters are not allowed' })
  q!: string;

  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) categoryId?: number;
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(0) minPriceCents?: number;
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(0) maxPriceCents?: number;
  @IsOptional() @IsIn(['relevance', 'price_asc', 'price_desc', 'newest']) sort: 'relevance' | 'price_asc' | 'price_desc' | 'newest' = 'relevance';
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(50) limit = 20;
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(0) @Max(2000) offset = 0; // hard cap on deep paging
}

Production scenario

A marketplace with 3 million products, 120 search requests per second at peak, PostgreSQL on a 16 vCPU instance. FTS query p50 is 9 ms, p95 is 45 ms, p99 is 140 ms (the p99 is queries with common terms that match 100,000 or more rows and have to be ranked). CPU for search sits at 25 percent of the instance. The GIN index is 1.1 GB and fits in shared buffers. Inserts and updates on products cost an extra 0.3 ms each for the vector recompute and GIN entry. This is a perfectly healthy setup and it costs nothing beyond the database you already run.

Monitoring: pg_stat_statements for the search query's mean and p99, the ratio of zero-result searches (from your application logs), GIN index size, and the pending list size (33.14). When should you not use PostgreSQL FTS? When you need per-field analyzers with synonyms and n-grams, when ranking must combine text score with popularity and recency in tunable ways, when facet counts over millions of matches must be under 50 ms, or when the search load would take more than a third of the primary's CPU. The full decision table is in 33.12.

Failure scenario

At 14:20 on Black Friday, PostgreSQL CPU hits 95 percent. pg_stat_statements shows the search query at 800 ms mean. The cause: the marketing team added "shoes" as a suggested search on the home page, and "shoes" alone matches 600,000 products. Every one of those rows is fetched from the heap and ranked before the top 20 are picked. Mitigations that day: cap the candidate set by adding AND category_id = ANY($1) from the suggested link (so it becomes a filter plus search) and put a 60-second Redis cache on the top 100 queries. The longer-term fix was to route the top 1 percent of common single-word queries to a pre-computed "popular in category" result and keep FTS for the long tail. The lesson: FTS cost is proportional to matches, so common terms are your hot keys.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Empty tsquery: websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'the it') returns an empty query with a NOTICE and @@ matches nothing; detect and fall back to simple.
  • Generated column with a non-immutable expression fails at CREATE TABLE; to_tsvector(text) without a config is the usual culprit.
  • Changing the text search configuration (adding synonyms, switching stemmer) does not rebuild stored vectors; you must UPDATE products SET name = name (or recreate the column) and reindex.
  • ts_headline is expensive (it re-parses the document); only compute it for the 20 rows you return, never in a subquery over all matches.
  • OFFSET 10000 still ranks all matches and then skips; deep pagination is as expensive as page one plus the skip. Cap it.
  • Prefix matching ('run':*) works in to_tsquery but not through websearch_to_tsquery; autocomplete is a separate design (33.7).
  • Large documents (a 5 MB PDF text) produce huge vectors; tsvector is limited to 1 MB and positions to 16,383; truncate or split.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior starts with PostgreSQL FTS because it is transactional, backed up, and already operated. They design the weights and configurations deliberately (simple for identifiers, language config for prose), put the vector in a generated column with a GIN index, expose websearch_to_tsquery to users, and watch two metrics from day one: p99 latency and zero-result rate. They know the cost model (proportional to matches) and plan a cache and a candidate cap for common terms before the traffic arrives.

Common mistakes

  • ILIKE '%term%' on a large table and calling it search.
  • Computing to_tsvector in the WHERE clause at query time instead of indexing a stored column, so the GIN index is never used.
  • Using english for SKUs and brand names, which stems Nike to nike (fine) but IT to nothing (not fine).
  • Ranking with ts_rank on the full match set and then OFFSET 5000.
  • Forgetting coalesce in the generated expression, so one NULL description makes the whole vector NULL.

Interview questions

  1. Explain tsvector, tsquery and @@. Expected: normalized lexemes with positions; boolean lexeme expression; match operator that a GIN index accelerates.
  2. Why does FTS latency depend on the query and not the table size? Expected: GIN finds matches fast; ranking touches every match; common terms are slow. Follow-up: how do you mitigate? Candidate caps via filters, caching hot queries, or move ranking to Elasticsearch.
  3. How do you keep the search vector up to date? Expected: generated stored column with an immutable expression and explicit config; trigger in older versions.
  4. What is the role of setweight? Expected: tags lexemes by field importance so ts_rank weights title matches above description matches.
  5. A brand named "IT" cannot be found. Why, and what do you do? Expected: stop word in english; index identifiers with simple and fall back to simple on empty queries.
  6. Which tsquery constructor do you expose to users and why? Expected: websearch_to_tsquery, because it accepts natural syntax and never throws.

Practical exercise

Build product search on a 1 million row products table (generate with generate_series and a word list). Acceptance criteria: a weighted generated tsvector column with a GIN index; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows a Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index; a query with two rare terms returns in under 20 ms; a query for the most common word returns in under 300 ms with a category filter applied; the query IT returns the brand "IT" products via the simple fallback; highlighted snippets are computed only for the returned page.

33.3 Inverted indexes

Concept

An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents that contain it. A normal ("forward") index goes from document to its contents; the inverted one goes from content to documents. Every full-text search engine, from PostgreSQL's GIN to Lucene inside Elasticsearch, is an inverted index plus a ranking function.

Why does it exist?

To answer "which documents contain the word shoe?" without reading every document. With 2 million products, a sequential scan reads 2 million descriptions per query. An inverted index reads one short list. The cost moves from query time to index time, which is the right trade for data that is written once and searched thousands of times.

Mental model

Imagine the index at the back of a cookbook. Instead of flipping through 400 pages to find recipes with saffron, you look up "saffron" and find "pages 12, 88, 301". Two ingredients? Look up both and keep the page numbers in both lists. The book is the forward representation; the back-of-book index is the inverted one.

How it works

  1. Dictionary. A sorted structure (B-tree in GIN, a finite state transducer in Lucene) of every distinct term. Lookup by term is a logarithmic or better search.
  2. Posting lists. For each term, the sorted list of document ids (in PostgreSQL, heap tuple ids) that contain it, optionally with positions and frequencies. shoe -> [12, 99, 777, 4410, ...].
  3. Compression. Posting lists are stored as deltas between sorted ids and compressed, so a term in 500,000 documents takes a few hundred KB, not megabytes.
  4. Boolean operations. run AND shoe is the intersection of two sorted lists, done with a merge walk; OR is a union; NOT is a difference. Skip pointers let the engine jump over long stretches of one list when the other is sparse.
  5. Scoring. Lucene stores term frequency per posting so BM25 can be computed while walking; PostgreSQL's GIN stores only locations, and ts_rank re-reads the tsvector of each candidate row from the heap. That difference is why PostgreSQL ranking is proportional to match count while Lucene can stop early.
Documents
  p12:  "trail running shoes"
  p99:  "running socks"
  p777: "leather shoes"

Inverted index (after stemming)
  leather -> [p777]
  run     -> [p12, p99]
  shoe    -> [p12, p777]
  sock    -> [p99]
  trail   -> [p12]

Query "running shoes" = run AND shoe
  [p12, p99] intersect [p12, p777] = [p12]

Why GIN is an inverted index. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is PostgreSQL's generic implementation of exactly this: a B-tree over keys (lexemes for tsvector, trigrams for pg_trgm, keys and values for jsonb), each pointing to a posting list (or a posting tree when the list is large) of heap tuple ids. The "generalized" part means the index does not know what a key is; the operator class (tsvector_ops, gin_trgm_ops, jsonb_path_ops) tells it how to extract keys from a value and from a query.

GIN has one notable optimization with an operational cost: the pending list. Because adding one row may touch dozens of keys (one per lexeme), GIN by default (fastupdate = on) appends new entries to an unsorted pending list and merges them into the main structure later, during VACUUM or when the list exceeds gin_pending_list_limit (default 4 MB). Inserts get faster; searches must scan the pending list linearly, so if it grows (heavy inserts, lazy autovacuum), search latency creeps up. Section 33.14 covers the failure.

Practical example

The products_search_gin index from 33.2 on 2 million products: about 180,000 distinct lexemes, index size 1.1 GB. The term shoe has a posting tree with 600,000 entries; merino has a posting list of 340. A query for merino shoe reads the short list, then probes the long one with the 340 candidates, and returns in 2 ms. A query for shoe alone returns 600,000 candidates and the ranking is what takes 400 ms.

PostgreSQL example

-- Inspect a GIN index: size and pending list
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('products_search_gin')) AS index_size;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT * FROM gin_metapage_info(get_raw_page('products_search_gin', 0));
-- n_pending_pages and n_pending_tuples show pending list growth

-- Flush the pending list without a full VACUUM
SELECT gin_clean_pending_list('products_search_gin');

-- Turn fastupdate off for a search-heavy, insert-light table
ALTER INDEX products_search_gin SET (fastupdate = off);

Production scenario

Index build time: creating a GIN index on 2 million rows of product text takes 1 to 3 minutes with maintenance_work_mem = 1GB; use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production so writes are not blocked. Write amplification: each inserted product adds 20 to 60 entries; on a table receiving 200 inserts per second that is around 10,000 index entries per second, comfortably handled with the pending list on. Monitor pending pages and autovacuum activity on the table.

Failure scenario

A nightly catalog import inserts 400,000 products in ten minutes. autovacuum is tuned to run rarely on this table because "it is mostly reads". The pending list grows to hundreds of MB. From 03:10 onwards every search scans the pending list linearly and p95 goes from 40 ms to 900 ms; the on-call gets paged for the search SLO. SELECT gin_clean_pending_list(...) takes 40 seconds and fixes it. Permanent fix: run the import with fastupdate = off for that index, or run gin_clean_pending_list at the end of the import, and give the table its own autovacuum settings.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GIN cannot do ordered scans; ORDER BY always needs a sort of the candidates.
  • A GIN index on a very high-cardinality key set (unique ids) is a waste; use B-tree.
  • Posting trees for extremely common terms are large; VACUUM must clean dead entries or bloat grows.
  • Concurrent index creation can fail and leave an INVALID index that must be dropped.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Understanding the posting list model tells you the cost of every query before you run it: rare terms are cheap, common terms are expensive, and PostgreSQL pays that cost in ranking. The senior uses that to decide where a candidate cap, a cache or a move to Lucene is needed.

Interview questions

  1. What is an inverted index and how does it answer an AND query? Expected: term to sorted posting list; intersection by merge walk with skip pointers.
  2. Why is GIN called "generalized"? Expected: same structure for tsvector lexemes, trigrams, jsonb keys via operator classes.
  3. What is the GIN pending list and how can it hurt? Expected: unsorted buffer of new entries for insert speed; searches scan it linearly; grows without vacuum.

Practical exercise

Insert 500,000 rows into a GIN-indexed table with fastupdate on, measure search latency before and after gin_clean_pending_list, then repeat with fastupdate = off. Acceptance criteria: a written table of insert throughput and search p95 under both settings, and a recommendation for your workload.

33.4 Tokenization and analysis

Concept

Analysis is the pipeline that turns raw text into index terms. It runs at index time on documents and at query time on the user's input, and the two must agree, or nothing matches. The steps: tokenize (split into words), normalize (lowercase, strip accents), filter (drop stop words), transform (stem, apply synonyms), and optionally expand (n-grams for partial matching).

Why does it exist?

Because "Running", "running", "runs", "ran" and "runner" are the same idea to a shopper and five different strings to a computer. Analysis collapses the variations into one term at both ends so a query for any of them finds all of them. Every relevance problem you will ever debug is, at its root, an analysis question: "what terms did this document produce, and what terms did this query produce?"

Mental model

Imagine two people who must agree on how to file paperwork so that either can find it later. They agree on rules: everything in lowercase, plural becomes singular, "Ltd." and "Limited" are the same, ignore "the" and "of". The rules matter less than the fact that both follow identical rules. A single mismatch ("she files under plural, I search singular") makes documents disappear.

How it works

Step What it does PostgreSQL Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
Tokenizer Splits text into tokens; recognizes emails, URLs, numbers Built-in parser, token types (asciiword, email, url, numword) standard, whitespace, keyword, pattern, edge_ngram, ngram tokenizers
Lowercase Shoe = shoe Always, in dictionaries lowercase token filter
Accent folding café = cafe unaccent dictionary in a custom config asciifolding filter
Stop words Drop the, a, of Part of language dictionaries (Snowball) stop filter with a word list
Stemming running = run Snowball stemmers per language snowball, porter_stem, kstem, language analyzers
Synonyms sneaker = trainer = running shoe synonym dictionary file, thesaurus dictionary for phrases synonym and synonym_graph filters
N-grams shoe becomes sh, sho, hoe, shoe; for partial and fuzzy pg_trgm (trigrams) as a separate index ngram filter
Edge n-grams shoe becomes s, sh, sho, shoe; for prefix autocomplete Not built in; trigram or B-tree prefix instead edge_ngram filter, index-time only

Two rules the mechanisms enforce:

  1. Same analyzer both sides, with one deliberate exception: edge n-grams are applied at index time only. If you edge-n-gram the query too, shoe becomes s and matches everything starting with s. Elasticsearch has analyzer and search_analyzer on a field for exactly this.
  2. Analysis is baked into the index. Changing the stemmer, adding a synonym, or turning on accent folding does not change existing index entries. You must reindex. In PostgreSQL that is rewriting the generated column; in Elasticsearch it is a new index and an alias swap (33.10).

Practical example

A food-delivery search: "biryani" is spelled "biriyani", "briyani" and "biryaani" by users. Synonyms map the variants to one term at both index and query time. "veg" and "vegetarian" are synonyms. "chicken" should not stem to "chick". A restaurant_names field uses a keyword analyzer with lowercase only so "Burger King" stays one token; a dishes field uses the language analyzer with the synonym filter; a dishes.autocomplete sub-field uses edge n-grams for the search box.

PostgreSQL example

A custom configuration with synonyms and accent folding. Synonym dictionaries read a file in $SHAREDIR/tsearch_data:

# /usr/share/postgresql/16/tsearch_data/shop_synonyms.syn
sneaker trainer
sneakers trainer
trainers trainer
tee tshirt
t-shirt tshirt
CREATE TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY shop_syn (TEMPLATE = synonym, SYNONYMS = shop_synonyms);
CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION shop_en (COPY = english);
ALTER TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION shop_en
  ALTER MAPPING FOR asciiword, asciihword, hword_asciipart, word, hword, hword_part
  WITH unaccent, shop_syn, english_stem;

SELECT to_tsvector('shop_en', 'Running Sneakers');   -- 'run':1 'trainer':2
SELECT to_tsvector('shop_en', 'Running Trainers');   -- 'run':1 'trainer':2

Both products now share the lexeme trainer, and so does the query. Rebuild stored vectors after changing a configuration.

NestJS example

The analysis contract belongs in code review, so encode it as a test that runs against the database:

// search-analysis.spec.ts (integration test against a real PostgreSQL)
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

describe('shop_en text search configuration', () => {
  let ds: DataSource;
  beforeAll(async () => { ds = new DataSource({ type: 'postgres', url: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL! }); await ds.initialize(); });
  afterAll(() => ds.destroy());

  const lexemes = async (text: string) => {
    const [{ v }] = await ds.query(`SELECT to_tsvector('shop_en', $1)::text AS v`, [text]);
    return v as string;
  };

  it('maps synonyms and stems consistently', async () => {
    expect(await lexemes('Running Sneakers')).toBe(await lexemes('running trainer'));
  });
  it('folds accents', async () => {
    expect(await lexemes('Café crème')).toContain("'cafe'");
  });
  it('keeps identifiers findable via simple config', async () => {
    const [{ v }] = await ds.query(`SELECT to_tsvector('simple', $1)::text AS v`, ['IT']);
    expect(v).toBe("'it':1");
  });
});

Production scenario

Analysis choices are relevance choices, and they need a feedback loop: a "query to terms" debugging endpoint (33.11) and a list of the top 200 queries with their zero-result rate. A synonym file grows from real query logs, five to twenty entries a month, reviewed by whoever owns search. Reindexing after each change is a scheduled job, not an emergency.

Failure scenario

A team switches the product name field from the english analyzer to a standard analyzer with no stemming "to make exact matches rank higher". They reindex. Searches for "running shoes" now miss every product named "Running Shoe" (singular). Zero-result rate doubles overnight; conversion from search drops 8 percent. Rolled back in a day; the postmortem introduces the analysis test above and an A/B process for analyzer changes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stemmers over-stem: universe, university and universal all become univers. Use a lighter stemmer (kstem) or a keyword marker for protected terms.
  • Compound words in German, Dutch and Scandinavian languages need decompounding or n-grams.
  • CJK languages have no spaces; the standard tokenizer splits into single characters; use icu or language-specific plugins (kuromoji, nori, smartcn).
  • Emojis and symbols are dropped by most tokenizers; a product named "#1 Fan Tee" loses the #1.
  • Synonym expansion at index time bloats the index; at query time it slows the query; choose per synonym set.
  • Multi-word synonyms with synonym_graph must be applied at query time to keep positions consistent.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before touching ranking, the senior asks "what tokens exist in the index for this document, and what tokens does this query produce?" They write those down (with to_tsvector or the _analyze API), and most "search is broken" tickets end there. They keep analyzers per field, not per index, and they have a reindex process ready before changing any of them.

Common mistakes

  • Different analyzers at index and query time by accident (index built with english, query built with the session default simple).
  • Applying edge n-grams to the query.
  • Stemming identifiers and codes.
  • Changing an analyzer without reindexing and being surprised nothing changed.

Interview questions

  1. Why must the query and the index use the same analysis? Expected: terms must match byte for byte; different stems or case produce no matches. Follow-up: when do they intentionally differ? Edge n-grams for autocomplete.
  2. What is the difference between n-grams and edge n-grams? Expected: all substrings of length n vs prefixes; fuzzy and infix vs prefix autocomplete.
  3. How do synonyms work and what is the index-time vs query-time trade-off? Expected: index-time expands stored terms (bigger index, changes need reindex); query-time expands the query (slower queries, changes are instant).
  4. How would you debug "this product does not show up for this query"? Expected: analyze both sides, compare terms, check filters, then check ranking.

Practical exercise

Create a custom PostgreSQL configuration with unaccent and a synonym dictionary of ten domain terms; write the analysis test; rebuild the stored vectors. Acceptance criteria: the test passes; a query for a synonym finds products indexed under the other term; EXPLAIN shows the GIN index still used.

33.5 Ranking: TF-IDF, BM25, boosting and business signals

Concept

Ranking assigns a score to each matching document and sorts by it. The classic score is TF-IDF: a term counts more when it appears often in this document (term frequency, TF) and when it is rare across all documents (inverse document frequency, IDF). BM25 is the modern refinement used by Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch by default; it caps the benefit of repeating a term and normalizes for document length. On top of the text score, real systems add field boosts, recency, popularity and business rules.

Why does it exist?

Because a query for "wireless mouse" matches 4,000 products and the user will look at five. If the five are wrong, the search is useless regardless of how fast it is. Ranking is the difference between a search engine and a filter that happens to accept text.

Mental model

Imagine asking a librarian for books about "Roman roads". A book that mentions "Roman" once in a footnote scores low. A book with "roads" in the title scores high. A word like "the" appears in every book, so matching it means nothing; a word like "aqueduct" appears in few, so matching it means a lot. And a 900-page encyclopedia that mentions everything once should not beat a 90-page book that is entirely about the topic. BM25 is those instincts written as a formula.

How it works

In simple language:

  1. Term frequency. More occurrences of the query term in the document is better, but with diminishing returns: the tenth mention adds far less than the second. BM25's k1 parameter (default 1.2) controls how fast the curve flattens.
  2. Inverse document frequency. A term that appears in 1 percent of documents is worth much more than one in 60 percent. IDF is roughly log(total_docs / docs_with_term).
  3. Length normalization. A match in a short document is worth more than the same match in a long one, because the long one is less about the term. BM25's b parameter (default 0.75) controls how strongly length counts.
  4. Sum over query terms. The document's score is the sum of its per-term scores. Documents matching more of the query's rare terms rise to the top.

PostgreSQL's ts_rank and ts_rank_cd are simpler: they use term frequency, field weights and (for _cd) proximity of query terms, with optional length normalization; they do not use IDF, because a tsvector has no view of the whole corpus. In practice that means a query with one rare term and one common term ranks the common term as heavily as the rare one. For product catalogs this is usually acceptable; for large heterogeneous text (support tickets, articles) it is the most visible quality gap versus Elasticsearch.

Boosting fields. A match in name should outrank a match in description. PostgreSQL: setweight A/B/C/D and the weights array in ts_rank. Elasticsearch: multi_match with fields: ["name^3", "brand^2", "description"].

Recency and popularity. Text score alone ranks a 2019 product with a keyword-stuffed description above the 2026 bestseller. Real ranking blends signals: final = text_score * (1 + log(1 + sales_30d)) * recency_decay. In PostgreSQL that is arithmetic in ORDER BY; in Elasticsearch it is function_score with field_value_factor and gauss decay, or a rank_feature field.

Business rules. Sponsored products pinned to slot 1 and 4; out-of-stock demoted, not hidden; a brand the user has bought before boosted. These are explicit, not learned, and they belong in a layer over the search provider so they can be changed without touching the index.

flowchart LR
  Q["Query terms"] --> TS["Text score: BM25 or ts_rank_cd"]
  TS --> FB["Field boosts: name x3, brand x2"]
  FB --> SIG["Signals: popularity, recency, in stock"]
  SIG --> BR["Business rules: pins, demotions, personalization"]
  BR --> OUT["Final ordering, top 20"]

Practical example

An e-commerce catalog blends three signals: ts_rank_cd with weights {0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, a popularity factor from 30-day sales, and a small in-stock bonus. Sponsored placements are injected by the API layer after the search returns, so they do not distort the organic ranking or the analytics.

PostgreSQL example

-- Materialized popularity, refreshed hourly, so ranking does not join sales at query time
CREATE TABLE product_signals (
  product_id  bigint PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES products(id),
  sales_30d   int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  rating      numeric(3,2),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

WITH q AS (SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('shop_en', $1) AS query)
SELECT p.id, p.name,
       ts_rank_cd('{0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}', p.search_vector, q.query, 1) AS text_score,
       coalesce(s.sales_30d, 0) AS sales_30d,
       ts_rank_cd('{0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}', p.search_vector, q.query, 1)
         * (1 + ln(1 + coalesce(s.sales_30d, 0)))               -- popularity, log-damped
         * (CASE WHEN p.in_stock THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.6 END)          -- demote, do not hide
         * (1 + 0.2 * exp(-extract(epoch FROM now() - p.created_at) / 86400 / 60)) AS final_score  -- 60 day recency decay
  FROM products p
  JOIN q ON true
  LEFT JOIN product_signals s ON s.product_id = p.id
 WHERE p.tenant_id = $2 AND p.search_vector @@ q.query
 ORDER BY final_score DESC, p.id
 LIMIT 20;

NestJS example

Business rules sit in a service that decorates provider results, so the same rules apply whether the provider is PostgreSQL or OpenSearch:

// ranking-rules.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface RankedHit { id: string; score: number; inStock: boolean; brand: string | null; sponsored?: boolean }

@Injectable()
export class RankingRulesService {
  apply(hits: RankedHit[], ctx: { preferredBrands: Set<string>; sponsoredIds: string[] }): RankedHit[] {
    const boosted = hits.map((h) => ({
      ...h,
      score: h.score * (h.brand && ctx.preferredBrands.has(h.brand) ? 1.15 : 1) * (h.inStock ? 1 : 0.6),
    }));
    boosted.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.id.localeCompare(b.id)); // stable tiebreak
    // Pin up to two sponsored results at positions 0 and 3 without removing organic ones.
    const sponsored = boosted.filter((h) => ctx.sponsoredIds.includes(h.id)).slice(0, 2).map((h) => ({ ...h, sponsored: true }));
    const organic = boosted.filter((h) => !ctx.sponsoredIds.includes(h.id));
    const out = [...organic];
    if (sponsored[0]) out.splice(0, 0, sponsored[0]);
    if (sponsored[1]) out.splice(3, 0, sponsored[1]);
    return out;
  }
}

Production scenario

Ranking quality is measured, not argued: click-through rate on the first result, the position of the first click, zero-click searches, and conversion after search. A relevance change ships behind a flag to 10 percent of traffic and is compared on those metrics for a week. Latency cost of the blended PostgreSQL query above versus pure text ranking: about 15 percent, from the join and the arithmetic over the candidate set.

Failure scenario

A "boost by popularity" change multiplies the text score by raw sales_30d. A phone case with 40,000 sales now appears first for every query containing "phone", including "phone" itself, "phone charger", and "phone stand". Search conversion drops 12 percent in two days. The fix is the log damping shown above. Lesson: every signal needs a ceiling.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Scores are not comparable across queries (a 0.9 for one query and 0.9 for another mean nothing together); never threshold on absolute score.
  • BM25 IDF is per shard in Elasticsearch by default; small indices with few shards get inconsistent scores; use one shard or dfs_query_then_fetch when testing.
  • Ties: always add a deterministic tiebreak or pagination will show duplicates and skips.
  • Keyword stuffing in seller-written descriptions games TF; length normalization and field caps help.
  • Personalization signals leak across users if cached without the user in the key.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior separates text relevance (the engine's job), signals (data, refreshed on a schedule) and rules (product decisions, in application code). They insist on a measurement loop before tuning anything, and they treat every multiplier as something that needs a cap.

Common mistakes

  • Sorting by created_at DESC and calling it search.
  • Joining live sales counts into every search query.
  • Hiding out-of-stock items instead of demoting them, so users think the product does not exist.
  • Tuning ranking by looking at three queries the product manager typed.

Interview questions

  1. Explain BM25 in plain words. Expected: term frequency with diminishing returns, rarity across the corpus, shorter documents win ties; k1 and b.
  2. What does ts_rank lack compared to BM25? Expected: IDF; it has no corpus-wide view.
  3. How do you combine text relevance with popularity without one dominating? Expected: log or bounded transforms, multiplicative with caps, measured by CTR.
  4. How do you measure whether a ranking change was good? Expected: online metrics (CTR at rank 1, zero-click rate, conversion) with a controlled rollout; offline judgments for regression.

Practical exercise

Add a product_signals table and the blended ranking query. Acceptance criteria: for the query "phone", the top 20 contain at most 3 accessories; latency increase under 20 percent versus text-only; a Jest test asserts that a sponsored pin never removes an organic result.

33.6 Fuzzy search

Concept

Fuzzy search matches strings that are almost equal: "adidas" for "addidas", "iphone" for "ipohne". Two techniques dominate: trigram similarity (compare the sets of three-character substrings; PostgreSQL pg_trgm) and edit distance (count the character insertions, deletions and substitutions between strings; Levenshtein; Elasticsearch fuzziness).

Why does it exist?

Users misspell. Product names contain brand words no dictionary stems. Full-text search is exact at the lexeme level: addida and adida are different terms and nothing matches. Fuzzy matching closes the gap for short strings like names, brands and SKUs, at a cost in precision and CPU.

Mental model

Imagine recognizing a friend's handwriting. Trigrams: you compare overlapping three-letter chunks; if most chunks of "addidas" and "adidas" agree, it is probably the same word. Edit distance: you count how many pen strokes would turn one into the other; one extra "d" is one edit.

How it works

pg_trgm. The extension splits a string into trigrams, padding with two spaces at the start and one at the end:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
SELECT show_trgm('adidas');     -- {"  a"," ad","ada","adi","as ","das","did","ida","s  "}
SELECT similarity('adidas', 'addidas');   -- 0.5833
SELECT similarity('adidas', 'nike');      -- 0

similarity(a, b) is the size of the intersection of trigram sets divided by the size of the union, from 0 to 1. The % operator is similarity(a, b) >= pg_trgm.similarity_threshold (default 0.3, session-settable). word_similarity and <% handle a short query against a long string (the query appearing as a word inside the text). The <-> operator returns the distance 1 - similarity, and a GiST trigram index can order by it (a KNN scan), which is how you get "top 10 closest names" cheaply.

The trigram index also accelerates LIKE and ILIKE with a leading wildcard, which no B-tree can:

CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm ON products USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);
-- Now these use the index:
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%adidas%';
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name % 'addidas';
-- Ordered by closeness needs GiST:
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm_gist ON products USING GIST (name gist_trgm_ops);
SELECT id, name, name <-> 'addidas' AS dist FROM products ORDER BY name <-> 'addidas' LIMIT 10;

EXPLAIN for the ILIKE on 2 million rows: Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm with a Recheck (the index finds rows containing all the pattern's trigrams; the heap check confirms the actual pattern). A pattern shorter than three characters yields no trigrams and falls back to a sequential scan.

Levenshtein. The fuzzystrmatch extension provides levenshtein(a, b) (and soundex, metaphone, dmetaphone for phonetic matching). It cannot use an index; it is a per-row computation, fine on a candidate set of a few hundred rows produced by a trigram index first, catastrophic on the whole table.

Elasticsearch fuzziness. A match or multi_match with "fuzziness": "AUTO" allows 0 edits for terms up to 2 characters, 1 edit for 3 to 5, and 2 edits above. Lucene builds a finite automaton for the term and walks the dictionary, so it is index-accelerated. Costs: fuzzy matches score lower than exact ones by default, and prefix_length: 1 avoids matching every term with a different first letter.

flowchart LR
  Q["User types addidas"] --> F["FTS exact lexeme: 0 results"]
  F --> T["pg_trgm: name % 'addidas'"]
  T --> C["Candidates ordered by name <-> 'addidas'"]
  C --> R["Top 10 suggestions, did you mean adidas"]

Practical example

The catalog search runs FTS first. If it returns zero results (or fewer than 3), the API runs a trigram query against name and brand to produce "Did you mean adidas?" and also to show the closest products. This two-step keeps the fast, precise path for 95 percent of queries and spends trigram CPU only on the misses.

PostgreSQL example

-- Fallback for zero-result searches: closest brand and closest product names
SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = 0.35;

SELECT 'brand' AS kind, brand AS value, similarity(brand, $1) AS sim
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT brand FROM products WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND brand IS NOT NULL) b
 WHERE brand % $1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'product', name, similarity(name, $1)
  FROM products
 WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND name % $1
 ORDER BY sim DESC
 LIMIT 10;

A common trick for multi-word queries: split into words, trigram-match each against a distinct_terms table (built from the catalog nightly), and reassemble the corrected query for FTS.

CREATE TABLE search_terms (term text PRIMARY KEY, doc_count int NOT NULL);
CREATE INDEX search_terms_trgm ON search_terms USING GIST (term gist_trgm_ops);
-- For each misspelled word: the closest known term weighted by how common it is
SELECT term FROM search_terms WHERE term % $1 ORDER BY (term <-> $1) - ln(doc_count) / 100 LIMIT 1;

TypeORM example

async didYouMean(tenantId: string, q: string): Promise<string | null> {
  const words = q.toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter((w) => w.length >= 3);
  const corrected: string[] = [];
  for (const w of words) {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(
      `SELECT term FROM search_terms WHERE term % $1 ORDER BY (term <-> $1) - ln(doc_count) / 100 LIMIT 1`, [w],
    );
    corrected.push(rows[0]?.term ?? w);
  }
  const suggestion = corrected.join(' ');
  return suggestion !== q.toLowerCase() ? suggestion : null;
}

Production scenario

Trigram index size is large: on a 2 million row name column it is roughly 400 MB (GIN), more for GiST. A % query against name costs 5 to 30 ms depending on how common the trigrams are; ILIKE '%ab%' on a two-letter pattern cannot use the index. Keep fuzzy matching on short columns (name, brand, SKU) and a terms table, never on descriptions. Zero-result fallback adds one query to about 5 percent of searches.

Failure scenario

A support tool searches tickets with WHERE subject ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' OR body ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' and no trigram index. It works at 100,000 tickets. At 50 million tickets each search is a 40-second sequential scan of a 60 GB table; agents fire off several searches while waiting, and the database's connection pool fills with scans. The fix is FTS on a generated column for body and a trigram index on subject, and a rewrite of the query. See 33.14 for the incident shape.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • similarity is symmetric; word_similarity is not; choose deliberately for "query inside text".
  • Threshold too low returns junk; too high misses; tune per column from real misspellings.
  • Trigram indexes on long text explode in size; index short fields only.
  • Non-Latin scripts: trigrams work on characters, so they work for CJK, but similarity thresholds differ.
  • levenshtein on strings over 255 characters raises an error in fuzzystrmatch.
