        cfg.get('SEARCH_ENGINE') === 'opensearch' ? os : pg },
  ],
  exports: [SEARCH_PROVIDER],
})
export class SearchModule {}

The same contract test suite runs against both providers. If a test passes on PostgreSQL and fails on OpenSearch, the port is leaking engine semantics and needs tightening - which is exactly the signal you want before the migration, not during it.

Production scenario

A team ships PostgreSQL search on day one behind this port. Eighteen months and 1.4 million products later, faceted category pages breach the 300 ms budget. They write the OpenSearch adapter in two weeks, run both providers in parallel behind a flag comparing results for 5% of traffic, find eleven ranking differences, fix nine and accept two, then flip the flag per tenant over a month. Application code changed in zero places outside src/search/providers/.

Failure scenario

The search cluster's p99 rises to 4 seconds during a shard relocation. The API has no timeout on the search call. Node's HTTP agent keeps 200 sockets open waiting; incoming requests queue on the event loop; the readiness probe times out; Kubernetes restarts pods; the restarts drop in-flight requests and increase load on the remaining pods. A slow dependency has become a full outage of the whole API, including endpoints that have nothing to do with search.

The withTimeout plus degraded fallback above is the fix, along with a bulkhead: search calls run against their own bounded concurrency so they cannot consume every socket. The lesson is the senior mantra applied to a dependency: can it become slow? is a more dangerous question than can it fail?, because failure is fast and slowness is contagious.

Common mistakes

  • A port that exposes the engine's query DSL, so it abstracts nothing.
  • Tenant id as an optional parameter, or read from the query string.
  • Free-text sort or filter field names reaching a query builder.
  • No timeout on the search call.
  • Ranking weights scattered across three files and a database table.
  • A public debug endpoint.

Interview questions

  1. Why put search behind a port, and what belongs in the port versus the adapter? Expected: engine choice must be reversible; the port speaks business terms (query, filters, sort, cursor, facets); the adapter owns DSL, analysis and pagination mechanics.
  2. How do you guarantee tenant isolation in search? Expected: required non-optional field, sourced from auth context, enforced in a single base method every query passes through, plus a test that a missing tenant throws.
  3. What do you do when the search backend is slow? Expected: hard timeout, degrade to a simpler query without facets, bulkhead the concurrency, surface a degraded-mode metric; never let it queue.
  4. What does a relevance-debugging endpoint return and who may call it? Expected: parsed query, document terms, score breakdown, applied filters, position; support and admin roles only.

Practical exercise

Implement the port, both adapters and one shared contract test suite. Acceptance criteria: the suite passes against both providers; removing the tenant filter from either adapter fails a test; a forced 2-second delay in the provider produces a degraded result within 900 ms rather than an error; the debug endpoint returns 403 for a normal user.

33.12 When PostgreSQL search is enough, and when it is not

Concept

The decision is not "which is better". PostgreSQL full-text plus trigram is a genuinely good search engine for a large class of products, and it comes with zero additional operational surface. A search cluster is more capable and costs you a distributed stateful system. The question is whether your requirements have crossed the line.

How it works

Dimension PostgreSQL is comfortable Reach for a search engine
Document count Up to a few million searchable rows Tens of millions, or growing fast
Index size GIN index fits in RAM alongside the working set Index alone exceeds the database's memory budget
Query complexity Terms, phrases, prefix, filters, simple boolean Multi-field cross-field matching, nested documents, "more like this", vectors
Relevance Field weights and a couple of business signals are enough Tuned BM25, per-field analyzers, synonym sets you iterate on weekly, learning to rank
Facets Worst-case candidate set in the tens of thousands Hundreds of thousands of candidates, many facets, sub-100 ms
Latency budget 50 to 300 ms acceptable Consistent sub-50 ms p95 at high concurrency
Concurrency Under ~100 searches per second, or heavily cached Hundreds to thousands per second
Write rate Steady updates; GIN pending list manageable Very high update rates alongside heavy search
Languages One or two, Snowball stemmers suffice Many languages, CJK, decompounding, ICU
Operational cost Free: it is the database you already run and back up A cluster, upgrades, snapshots, heap tuning, on-call
Consistency Read-your-writes for free, always current Eventual, 1 to 5 seconds, plus a sync pipeline to own
Team skill Everyone knows SQL Someone must know Lucene, JVM and cluster operations

Concrete thresholds, stated as honestly as such numbers can be. PostgreSQL full-text with a GIN index plus pg_trgm comfortably serves a catalogue into the low millions of documents with simple relevance, worst-case candidate sets in the tens of thousands, and a p95 budget above about 100 ms with caching in front. You start genuinely needing a search engine when any of these is true:

  • you need tuned relevance you will iterate on: BM25 with per-field analyzers, synonym sets updated weekly, and the ability to measure a change;
  • you need heavy faceting over hundreds of thousands of candidates on every request;
  • you need multi-language analysis beyond one or two Snowball languages;
  • you need sub-50 ms p95 at high concurrency, and caching cannot save you because the query space is too diverse;
  • search load is starting to compete with transactional load on the same database, and a read replica is not enough because GIN index maintenance is on the primary;
  • you need capabilities PostgreSQL does not have at all: nested document queries, "more like this", significant-terms, or dense-vector semantic search at scale.

Notice what is not on that list: "we have a lot of data" on its own, or "search feels slow" before anyone has run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Most search performance problems at small and medium scale are a missing index, a LIKE '%x%' without trigrams, ranking over an unbounded candidate set, or facets computed five times.

flowchart TB
    A["Do you need search, or a filter?"] -->|"filter or exact lookup"| B["B-tree index. Not search."]
    A -->|"ranked text search"| C{"More than a few million docs?"}
    C -->|"no"| D{"Tuned relevance or heavy facets or many languages?"}
    C -->|"yes"| G["Search engine"]
    D -->|"no"| E{"p95 budget under 50 ms at high RPS?"}
    D -->|"yes"| G
    E -->|"no"| F["PostgreSQL FTS plus pg_trgm. Start here."]
    E -->|"yes"| H{"Can caching absorb it?"}
    H -->|"yes"| F
    H -->|"no"| G
    G --> I["Behind the port from 34.11, fed by outbox or CDC"]

The honest recommendation: start with PostgreSQL. Not because it is always right, but because of what each choice costs when it is wrong. Starting with PostgreSQL and migrating later costs you two weeks of adapter work, done at a time when you know exactly what your relevance requirements are, because you have real query logs. Starting with a cluster you did not need costs you an ongoing operational burden, a sync pipeline, a consistency window in the UI, and a second thing to be woken up for - paid every month, starting immediately, in exchange for capabilities you may never use.

The migration path, when you do outgrow it:

  1. Put the port from 33.11 in place first, while PostgreSQL is still the only provider. This is the whole trick: the migration is only cheap if the seam already exists.
  2. Build the sync pipeline (33.10) and let it run for a week. Verify with reconciliation before anyone searches against it.
  3. Write the second adapter and run the shared contract tests against it.
  4. Shadow mode: for a sample of traffic, run both providers, serve PostgreSQL's results, and log the differences - overlap in the top 10, rank correlation, latency of each. Fix the differences you care about; document the ones you accept.
  5. Roll out per tenant or per percentage behind a flag, watching zero-result rate and click-through on the first three results, not just latency.
  6. Keep the PostgreSQL adapter working as a fallback for at least a quarter, and run its tests in CI. The day the cluster is red, a degraded search is much better than none.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask what the worst realistic query looks like - the empty search on the biggest category, with all facets - and size the decision on that, not on the average. They separate "search is slow" from "this query is slow" and refuse to buy infrastructure before reading a query plan. They build the seam early and the cluster late. And they say out loud, in the proposal, who will be on call for the cluster, because that sentence has ended more premature Elasticsearch projects than any benchmark.

Interview questions

  1. When is PostgreSQL full-text search not enough? Expected: tuned relevance you iterate on, heavy facets over large candidate sets, many languages, sub-50 ms at high concurrency, search competing with transactional load, capabilities PostgreSQL lacks.
  2. Roughly how far does PostgreSQL FTS scale? Expected: low millions of documents with simple relevance and candidate sets in the tens of thousands; the binding constraint is the worst-case candidate set, not the row count.
  3. How would you migrate from PostgreSQL search to a cluster with no downtime? Expected: port first, sync pipeline, reconciliation, shadow mode with result comparison, flagged rollout by tenant, keep the old adapter as fallback.
  4. What does adopting a search cluster cost beyond the instances? Expected: sync pipeline, consistency window in the UI, upgrades, snapshots, heap and shard tuning, monitoring, and on-call expertise.

Practical exercise

Write the decision for your own system as a one-page document: worst-case candidate set measured with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), current and projected document counts, latency budget, facet requirements, languages, and the operational owner. Acceptance criteria: the recommendation is supported by measured numbers rather than adjectives, and names the specific requirement that would trigger a move.

33.13 Observability, security and cost of search

Concept

Search fails in ways that produce no errors. A relevance regression, a stale index, a stop word swallowing a product name - all return HTTP 200 with a plausible-looking empty page. So search needs its own metrics, and the most important ones are about results, not about latency.

How it works

The metrics that matter:

Metric Why Alert on
Latency p50 / p95 / p99, split by "with facets" and "without" The two have completely different distributions; averaging them hides both p95 over budget for 5 minutes
Zero-result rate The single best proxy for search quality. A step change means analysis, indexing or a data problem Absolute above ~8%, or a 2x jump day over day
Click-through on the top 3 results Tells you whether the ranking is right, which latency never does 20% relative drop week over week
Position of the first click Rising means users are scrolling to find what they wanted trend
Query volume by normalized term Finds the head you should optimize and the terms that suddenly spike anomaly
Index lag - seconds between the source row's commit and its visibility in the index The user-visible symptom of a broken pipeline p95 over 30 s
Drift count from reconciliation Correctness of the derived copy any sustained non-zero
Degraded-mode rate How often the fallback fires above 1%
Cache hit ratio for facets and autocomplete Directly drives database load below the expected floor
Timeouts and provider errors Distinguish "slow" from "broken" any sustained

Zero-result rate deserves the emphasis. It is cheap to compute, it catches analyzer mistakes, index outages, a mis-parsed query, a filter applied twice, and a bad synonym file - and it does all of that before a customer emails you. Track it overall and per top-200 query.

Logging queries safely. Query strings are user input, and users type surprising things into a search box: their own email address, an order number, a phone number, occasionally a password they meant to type elsewhere. So:

  • Log the normalized query (lowercased, whitespace collapsed, truncated to 100 characters), not the raw one.
  • Redact patterns that look like PII - email addresses, long digit runs, card-shaped numbers - before the string leaves the process.
  • Do not put the query in a URL path or in a metric label. Metric labels with unbounded cardinality will take down your metrics backend faster than search will take down your database.
  • Keep the aggregate long-term (query term plus daily count, for the suggestion corpus and analytics) and the per-request log short - 7 to 30 days.
  • Never join the search log to a user id in a table that outlives your retention policy.

Preventing injection when building a query DSL. The concern is real and it is not "SQL injection" in the classic sense; it is query injection - user input changing the structure of the query rather than being data within it.

  • SQL: always parameterize. websearch_to_tsquery('shop_en', $1) is safe; string-concatenating into to_tsquery is not, and it will also throw syntax errors on ordinary user input containing &, |, ! or :. Prefer websearch_to_tsquery or plainto_tsquery precisely because they tolerate arbitrary text. Escape %, _ and \ before they reach a LIKE pattern.
  • Search DSL: build objects, never strings. { match: { name: userInput } } is safe because the input is a value in a JSON document. Concatenating user input into a query string template is how you get structure injection.
  • Never expose query_string to user input. It accepts Lucene syntax, so a user can write field names they should not reach, regular expressions, or wildcard-prefixed terms that scan the entire dictionary - a cheap denial of service. If you need operator syntax, use simple_query_string with an explicit flags allow-list and an explicit fields list.
  • Disable scripting in queries built from user input, and reject any request whose payload contains a script key if you build DSL from client-supplied structures at all. Better: do not accept client-supplied DSL. The DTO allow-list in 33.11 means the client sends values, never query shapes.
  • Bound everything: limit maximum, filter array sizes, query length, facet count, and a server-side timeout so an expensive query cannot run forever.

Tenant isolation in the index. Three models, with honest tradeoffs:

  • Shared index with a tenant_id filter. Simplest, most efficient, one mapping to maintain. The risk is that one forgotten filter leaks data - which is why the enforcement lives in one method in one adapter, and why a test asserts it. Add routing by tenant so a tenant's documents live on one shard and searches touch fewer shards.
  • Index per tenant. Strong isolation, per-tenant mappings and reindexing. Falls apart past a few hundred tenants because of shard-count limits and cluster-state size. Reasonable for tens of large tenants; wrong for thousands of small ones.
  • Alias per tenant over a shared index with a filtered alias: the filter is defined in cluster state rather than in your query, so application code cannot forget it. A good middle ground.

Whichever you choose, remember that facets and suggestions leak too. A brand facet computed before the tenant filter, an autocomplete corpus built from all tenants' queries, a cardinality aggregation, even a doc_count - each can reveal the existence of data the caller may not see. Apply the tenant filter first, always, and put it in the cache key.

Cost drivers. What actually moves the bill:

  • Index size times (1 + replicas), which is storage and, more importantly, the RAM you need for the page cache. Denormalized fields you never query are pure cost - "index": false for display-only fields, and do not store the full description twice.
  • Refresh interval: a 1-second refresh on a high-write index creates many small segments and constant merge CPU. Raising it to 5 or 30 seconds where visibility allows is often the single cheapest win.
  • Node count driven by peak concurrency, not by data size, once the data fits.
  • Reindex compute, which is a periodic doubling of write load; schedule it off-peak.
  • Autocomplete traffic, which is 5 to 10 times search traffic and must be cached or it dominates everything (33.7).
  • Facets, which add 50 to 70% to every search that computes them; cache them separately from results so the results can be fresher.
  • Cross-AZ data transfer for replication in a multi-zone cluster - real money, invisible until the bill arrives.
  • On the PostgreSQL side: GIN index size in shared buffers, the maintenance cost of the pending list, and the CPU of ranking over large candidate sets.

Common mistakes

  • Alerting on latency only, so a relevance regression ships silently.
  • Logging raw query strings forever.
  • Query text as a Prometheus label.
  • Exposing query_string or accepting client-supplied DSL.
  • Tenant filter applied to results but not to facets or suggestions.
  • A 1-second refresh interval on an index nobody reads in real time.

Interview questions

  1. What is the most useful single search metric and why? Expected: zero-result rate; cheap, catches analysis, indexing and data problems before users report them.
  2. How do you log search queries without creating a privacy problem? Expected: normalize, truncate, redact PII patterns, short per-request retention, aggregate long-term, never as a metric label.
  3. How do you prevent query injection into a search DSL? Expected: build objects not strings, allow-list filters and sorts, never expose query_string or scripts, parameterize SQL, bound every limit.
  4. Compare tenant isolation strategies in a search index. Expected: shared with filter (efficient, one mistake leaks), index per tenant (isolated, does not scale past hundreds), filtered alias (filter in cluster state, good middle ground); facets and suggestions leak too.
  5. What drives the cost of a search cluster? Expected: index size times replicas and the RAM behind it, refresh and merge, peak concurrency, reindex compute, autocomplete traffic, facets, cross-AZ transfer.

33.14 Edge cases and failure modes

The index is out of sync after a failed publish. The outbox relay crashes between publishing and marking rows published, so a batch is republished - harmless with external versioning, catastrophic without. Or it marks rows published and then crashes before the broker accepted them, so those changes are lost forever and no error is ever raised. Mark published only after a confirmed broker acknowledgement, accept duplicates, and let reconciliation catch the rest.

A reindex doubles cluster load at peak. Someone starts a rebuild at 11:00 because the mapping change is ready. Indexing and search share thread pools and page cache; search p95 triples; the store degrades while every dashboard on the database side is green. Rate-limit reindexing, run it off-peak, and wire an automatic pause when search p95 breaches its SLO.

Mapping explosion from dynamic fields. Dynamic mapping is on, and a supplier feed contains per-product attribute objects with the attribute name as a key: attributes.shoe_size_eu_42, attributes.thread_count_400. Each new key becomes a new field in the mapping. At 12,000 fields the cluster state is megabytes, every node must hold it, updates take seconds, and eventually the field limit trips and indexing stops. Fix: "dynamic": "strict", and model attributes as a nested array of { name, value } pairs instead of as keys. Prevention is entirely at mapping-design time; recovery requires a reindex.

Deep pagination. A crawler walks to page 900. from: 21600 forces every shard to sort and return 21,600 hits to the coordinating node; in PostgreSQL the equivalent OFFSET 21600 sorts the entire candidate set every time. Both degrade smoothly right up to the point where they do not. Use search_after or keyset cursors, cap the maximum page for anonymous traffic, and remember that the result window default of 10,000 exists to protect you.

A stop word removes a meaningful term. A product is literally called "IT" - an IT support service, a book titled It, a brand named "The". The english configuration drops it as a stop word, the document's vector contains nothing for it, and searching for the exact name returns zero results. The customer is certain your search is broken, and they are right. Fixes: index the name field with the simple configuration as well as the language one and search both, or use a keyword sub-field for exact name matching, or maintain a protected-terms list. Related: single-character and two-character queries produce no trigrams either.

Language mismatch. A German product description is analysed with the english stemmer. "Laufschuhe" is not decompounded into "Lauf" and "Schuhe", so a search for "Schuhe" misses it. Symptom: a per-locale zero-result rate that is fine for one market and terrible for another - which nobody notices until that market's revenue is questioned. Detect the document's language at index time, store it, and route to a per-language field (name.de, name.en); at query time use the user's locale, falling back to a multi-language field.

ILIKE '%term%' sequentially scanning 50 million rows. The support tool from 33.6, at scale: no trigram index, so every search is a full scan of a 60 GB table taking 40 seconds. Agents get impatient and fire three more searches; the connection pool fills with sequential scans; unrelated queries queue behind them and the whole application slows down. A pattern shorter than three characters cannot use a trigram index at all, so even after adding one, ILIKE '%it%' still scans. Enforce a minimum query length, add the trigram index, and put a statement_timeout on the search role so a runaway query dies at 3 seconds instead of 40.

GIN pending-list growth slowing inserts and searches. Covered in 33.3: fastupdate buffers new entries in an unsorted list that every search must scan linearly. A bulk import plus lazy autovacuum grows it to hundreds of megabytes and search p95 goes from 40 ms to 900 ms with no code change and no plan change - which is what makes it hard to diagnose. Watch gin_metapage_info, run gin_clean_pending_list after bulk loads, or set fastupdate = off on search-heavy tables.

A relevance regression after an analyzer change, with no way to measure it. Someone swaps a stemmer or adds twenty synonyms. Nothing errors. Conversion drops 6% over the following week and is attributed to seasonality. Without a measurement loop you cannot even have the argument. The minimum viable loop: a golden set of 200 query-and-expected-result pairs run in CI as a regression test, plus zero-result rate and click-through at rank 1-3 compared before and after, plus a flagged rollout so you have a control group. Relevance changes without a control group are guesses with a deploy attached.

Hot shards. Routing by tenant id puts one enormous tenant entirely on one shard; that node's CPU sits at 90% while others idle. Or a date_histogram-partitioned index sends all of today's writes to one shard. Symptom: cluster-wide averages look fine and p99 is terrible. Fix: do not route by a skewed key, split the giant tenant into its own index, or use a routing key with more entropy.

Oversized documents. A product with 5,000 review texts denormalized into one document; a document with a 12 MB description. Large documents slow indexing, blow up highlighting, break bulk batching, and can exceed the HTTP payload limit. Keep documents to what search needs: index the fields you match and filter on, store an id, and fetch the rest from PostgreSQL for display. Cap field lengths at index time (ignore_above for keywords, an explicit truncation for text).

PII in the search index. Denormalization pulls in a customer's email or phone number "because it might be useful for admin search". Now personal data lives in a second system with its own backups, snapshots and access controls - and a deletion request must be honoured there too, in every snapshot. Rules: index the minimum, keep PII out of any index that a customer-facing endpoint queries, use a separate admin index with its own access control if you truly need it, and make sure your data-deletion job covers the search index and its retention.

Tenant leakage in results. The worst failure in this part. A missing filter on one code path, a facet computed before the filter, an autocomplete corpus built from every tenant's queries, a cached result keyed without the tenant, or an admin endpoint that "temporarily" skips the filter. It is a data breach, it is usually found by a customer, and it is entirely preventable by the three-layer enforcement in 33.11 plus a test that asserts tenant B's document can never appear for tenant A - on results, facets and suggestions.

Two more that bite in practice. Highlighting on a huge field re-analyses the entire text per hit and can dominate query time; cap it with fragment_size and number_of_fragments, or highlight a truncated copy. A synonym file that fails to load after a config change silently starts a node with the previous analyzer definition, so half your shards analyse differently from the other half and results depend on which replica served the request.

Senior Checklist — Part 33

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can tell search apart from filtering and lookup, and pick the right index for each
  • I can build PostgreSQL full-text search with weights, a generated tsvector column and a GIN index
  • I can explain an inverted index, posting lists and the GIN pending list
  • I can debug "this document does not match this query" by comparing the terms on both sides
  • I can explain BM25 in plain words and why ts_rank differs
  • I can implement fuzzy matching and "did you mean" with pg_trgm, and know when not to
  • I can build autocomplete within a 50 ms budget and explain the cache design
  • I can compute correct multi-select facets in one scan and explain why counts ignore their own filter
  • I can explain shards, replicas, refresh, and filter versus query context
  • I can size shards and say what a cluster costs to operate
  • I can keep an index in sync with PostgreSQL using an outbox or CDC, with idempotent, version-guarded writes
  • I can run a zero-downtime reindex behind an alias and roll it back
  • I can detect drift with bucketed counts and checksums
  • I can put search behind a port so the engine choice is reversible
  • I can guarantee tenant isolation across results, facets and suggestions
  • I can name the metrics that catch a relevance regression before a customer does

Part 33 — Key Takeaways

  • Search is ranking; filtering is exclusion; lookup is exact. Confusing them produces both bad relevance and bad plans.
  • Every relevance bug is an analysis question first: what terms did the document produce, and what terms did the query produce? Answer that before touching ranking.
  • PostgreSQL full-text plus pg_trgm is a real search engine that comfortably serves catalogues into the low millions of documents with simple relevance. Start there.
  • The binding constraint is the worst-case candidate set, not the row count. Broad queries and empty category pages are what break you.
  • Facet counts must ignore their own filter, or multi-select is impossible. Compute the base set once and aggregate over it many times.
  • In a search cluster, put every yes/no condition in filter context: unscored and cached. Only the user's text belongs in must.
  • Never dual-write to the database and the index. Use an outbox or CDC, partition by entity id, and guard every write with an external version so replay is safe.
  • The index is a derived read model, never the source of truth. A full rebuild behind an alias must be routine, rehearsed and reversible.
  • Design the UI around the one-to-five-second consistency window instead of pretending it is not there: read the detail page from PostgreSQL, and publish index lag as a metric.
  • Put search behind a port on day one. The migration to a cluster is cheap only if the seam already exists.
  • Tenant isolation must be enforced in one place that no query can bypass, and it must cover facets and suggestions, not just results.
  • Zero-result rate and click-through at ranks one to three catch the failures that latency graphs never will. A relevance change without a control group is a guess with a deploy attached.
  • Before buying a cluster, answer the question that ends most premature migrations: who is on call for it, and what do they do when it goes red?

Part 34 — Real-Time Systems: WebSockets, SSE and Pub/Sub

34.1 Choosing a real-time transport

HTTP was built for a client that asks and a server that answers. Real-time features invert that: the server has something to say and the client is waiting. A driver moved 200 metres, a payment was captured, a colleague typed a character. This part is about how to push those facts to thousands of connected clients from a NestJS backend, keep the connections alive, survive restarts, and not lose or duplicate messages while doing it.

34.1.1 WebSockets, SSE, long polling and polling compared

Concept

There are four mainstream ways to get server-originated data to a browser or mobile client:

  • Polling: the client asks every N seconds. Simple, wasteful, delayed by up to N seconds.
  • Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request open until it has something to say or a timeout passes. Then the client immediately asks again.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long-lived HTTP response that the server keeps writing to. One direction only: server to client.
  • WebSockets: a TCP connection that starts as HTTP, upgrades to a bidirectional message protocol, and stays open. Either side can send at any time.

Why does it exist?

Each transport exists because the previous one was not enough for some use case. Polling is fine for a dashboard that refreshes every 30 seconds. It is useless for chat, where a 30 second delay is a broken product and a 1 second poll from 100,000 clients is 100,000 requests per second to serve mostly "nothing new". Long polling fixes the latency but still pays for a full HTTP request per message. SSE removes the per-message HTTP cost but cannot carry client-to-server messages. WebSockets remove every limitation at the price of a stateful connection you must manage.

Mental model

Imagine waiting for a parcel. Polling is walking to the door every five minutes to check. Long polling is standing at the door until the courier arrives or your legs give out, then standing again. SSE is a delivery slot under the door: parcels arrive without you doing anything, but you cannot send anything back through it. WebSockets is a phone call with the courier: either of you can talk whenever you want, as long as the line stays up.

How it works

flowchart TB
    Q1{"Does the server need to push data to the client?"}
    Q1 -->|"No"| REST["Plain request and response"]
    Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"Does the client need to send many small messages back?"}
    Q2 -->|"No, mostly server to client"| Q3{"Is HTTP streaming allowed through your proxies?"}
    Q3 -->|"Yes"| SSE["SSE: notifications, order tracking, live dashboards"]
    Q3 -->|"No, proxies buffer"| LP["Long polling as fallback"]
    Q2 -->|"Yes, bidirectional and low latency"| Q4{"Can you operate stateful connections and a Pub/Sub layer?"}
    Q4 -->|"Yes"| WS["WebSockets: chat, collaborative editing, games, driver location"]
    Q4 -->|"Not yet"| SSEPOST["SSE for downstream plus REST POST for upstream"]

The decision table a senior engineer keeps in their head:

Polling Long polling SSE WebSockets
Direction Client to server, server replies Same, but replies are delayed until data exists Server to client only Both directions
Protocol HTTP HTTP HTTP, text/event-stream HTTP upgrade then ws:// or wss:// framing
Browser support Universal Universal All modern browsers via EventSource All modern browsers via WebSocket
Passes through proxies and load balancers Always Always, if timeouts are long enough Usually; some proxies buffer the response Needs explicit upgrade support and long idle timeouts
Auto-reconnect You write it You write it Built into EventSource, with Last-Event-ID You write it, or Socket.IO does
Connection cost One request per poll One open request per client One open response per client One TCP connection per client
Latency of a push Up to the poll interval Near zero while a poll is pending Near zero Near zero
Scaling shape Stateless; scales like REST Stateful while held; needs Pub/Sub to wake waiters Stateful; needs Pub/Sub for fan-out Stateful; needs Pub/Sub for fan-out
Connections per domain in the browser Not a concern HTTP/1.1 limit of 6 per host bites HTTP/1.1 limit of 6 per host bites; fine on HTTP/2 No practical per-host limit
Binary payloads Yes Yes No, text only Yes, native binary frames
Best for Slow dashboards, admin screens Fallback when nothing else works Notifications, order status, price tickers, progress bars, log tails Chat, presence, collaborative editing, multiplayer, high-frequency telemetry

Two things people forget. First, SSE is a normal HTTP response, so everything you already have for REST works: cookies, JWT in headers, the same guards, the same load balancer, HTTP/2 multiplexing. Second, WebSockets are not HTTP after the handshake, so your interceptors, your API gateway's rate limiter and your CDN's rules may not apply. That difference is why SSE is the right default for "server pushes updates" and WebSockets are the right choice only when the client genuinely needs to talk back at high frequency.

Practical example

A food-delivery app has three real-time features. Order status for the customer ("preparing", "on the way", "delivered") is server-to-client, a few messages per order, and must survive a flaky mobile network: SSE. The driver's location on the map is server-to-client at 1 message per 2 seconds: SSE works, WebSockets work equally well. The in-app chat between customer and driver is bidirectional with typing indicators: WebSockets. Most teams pick one transport for all three (usually WebSockets via Socket.IO) to avoid running two systems, and that is a reasonable engineering trade as long as they understand that they took on connection state management for a feature that did not require it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "who initiates?" before anything else. If only the server initiates, they reach for SSE and keep the stateless REST path for client actions, because a POST /orders/:id/messages that goes through the usual guards, validation and rate limiting is simpler to secure than a WebSocket message handler. They pick WebSockets when a product needs sub-100 ms bidirectional traffic or binary payloads, and they accept the operational cost consciously. They refuse to add a WebSocket server to a monolith that has no Pub/Sub layer, because the first time it runs on two pods the messages stop arriving.

34.2 WebSockets

34.2.1 The upgrade handshake, frames and ping/pong

Concept

A WebSocket connection starts as an ordinary HTTP GET with an Upgrade: websocket header. If the server agrees, it replies 101 Switching Protocols, and from that moment the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames instead of HTTP. A frame has a small header (2 to 14 bytes) with an opcode (text, binary, close, ping, pong), a payload length and, for client-to-server frames, a masking key. Messages can be split across frames. Ping and pong frames are the protocol's built-in heartbeat.

Why does it exist?

Before WebSockets, bidirectional real-time in the browser meant hacks: hidden iframes, long polling, Flash sockets. The upgrade handshake exists so a WebSocket can reuse port 443, pass through TLS and look like HTTP to firewalls for its first packet, and then become a lean framed protocol with 2 bytes of overhead per message instead of 500 bytes of HTTP headers.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant LB as LoadBalancer
    participant S as NestJSGateway
    B->>LB: GET /socket.io/ HTTP/1.1 with Upgrade websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Key
    LB->>S: forwards upgrade request, keeps the TCP connection pinned
    S-->>LB: 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept
    LB-->>B: 101 Switching Protocols
    Note over B,S: TCP connection now carries WebSocket frames both ways
    B->>S: text frame: auth token in first message or handshake auth
    S-->>B: text frame: connected, session id
    loop every 25 seconds
        S->>B: ping frame
        B-->>S: pong frame
    end
    B->>S: text frame: join room order 8812
    S-->>B: text frame: ack joined
    S->>B: text frame: driver location update
    B->>S: close frame with code 1000
    S-->>B: close frame
  1. The client sends GET with Connection: Upgrade, Upgrade: websocket, Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key.
  2. The server hashes the key with a fixed GUID, base64-encodes it and returns it as Sec-WebSocket-Accept. This proves the server understood the upgrade and prevents a caching proxy from replaying an old response.
  3. Both sides now exchange frames. Text frames carry UTF-8, typically JSON; binary frames carry bytes, typically MessagePack or Protobuf.
  4. Either side may send a ping; the other must answer with a pong carrying the same payload. Libraries do this for you: Socket.IO sends a ping every 25 seconds (pingInterval) and drops the connection if no pong arrives within 20 seconds (pingTimeout). The ws library exposes socket.ping() and a pong event and leaves the schedule to you.
  5. A close frame carries a status code (1000 normal, 1001 going away, 1008 policy violation, 1011 server error) and an optional reason. A clean close is a two-way exchange; a TCP reset is not, and detection then depends on the heartbeat.

Message formats. Raw WebSockets give you frames with no structure; you design the envelope. A common one is { "type": "order.status", "id": 1842, "data": { ... } } where id is a monotonically increasing sequence number per stream (used for gap detection in 34.10). Socket.IO adds its own layer on top: named events, acknowledgements, rooms, namespaces and automatic fallback to long polling, at the cost of a Socket.IO-specific protocol that plain WebSocket clients cannot speak. Choose Socket.IO when the clients are yours (web and mobile SDKs exist) and you want rooms and acks; choose raw ws when third parties connect or you need every byte.

34.2.2 Authentication and authorization on WebSockets

Concept

A WebSocket connection is authenticated once, at connect time, and then trusted for its lifetime. There is no per-message Authorization header. That single fact drives every design decision here.

How it works

Three places to put the credential:

Method How Pros Cons
Cookie The browser sends cookies on the upgrade request Works with existing session auth; not visible to JavaScript if HttpOnly CSRF-like risk: any site can open a WebSocket to your origin and the cookie goes along, so you must check Origin
Query string or handshake auth io(url, { auth: { token } }) puts the token in the handshake payload; raw ws clients often use ?token= Works for mobile and non-browser clients Query strings end up in proxy and access logs; prefer the Socket.IO auth object or a header when the client can set one
First message Connect unauthenticated, send { type: "auth", token } within 5 seconds or be disconnected Keeps tokens out of URLs The server must hold an unauthenticated connection briefly; needs a timeout

Authorization is a second, separate step. "This is user 41" does not mean "user 41 may join room order:8812". Every join is checked against the database or a cached ownership record, and every server-side emit goes to a room, never to "everyone who asked".

NestJS example

@nestjs/websockets with @nestjs/platform-socket.io gives you a gateway class: a provider that owns a Socket.IO namespace, with decorated handlers for events. Guards work on gateways, but they run on message handlers, not on the connection itself, so connection auth lives in handleConnection.

// realtime/orders.gateway.ts
import {
  ConnectedSocket, MessageBody, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect,
  SubscribeMessage, WebSocketGateway, WebSocketServer, WsException,
} from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { UseGuards, UsePipes, ValidationPipe, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Server, Socket } from 'socket.io';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { WsAuthGuard } from './ws-auth.guard';
import { JoinOrderDto } from './dto/join-order.dto';

@WebSocketGateway({
  namespace: '/orders',
  cors: { origin: ['https://app.example.com'], credentials: true },
  pingInterval: 25_000,
  pingTimeout: 20_000,
  maxHttpBufferSize: 64 * 1024,   // reject any single message over 64 KB
})
export class OrdersGateway implements OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect {
  @WebSocketServer() server: Server;
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrdersGateway.name);

  constructor(private readonly jwt: JwtService, private readonly orders: OrdersAccessService) {}

  async handleConnection(client: Socket) {
    try {
      // Socket.IO clients send { auth: { token } } in the handshake; never read it from the query string.
      const token = client.handshake.auth?.token as string | undefined;
      if (!token) throw new Error('missing token');
      const payload = await this.jwt.verifyAsync<{ sub: string; exp: number }>(token);
      client.data.userId = payload.sub;
      client.data.tokenExp = payload.exp * 1000;
      client.join(`user:${payload.sub}`);        // personal room for notifications
    } catch (err) {
      this.log.warn({ err: (err as Error).message, ip: client.handshake.address }, 'ws auth failed');
      client.emit('error', { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED' });
      client.disconnect(true);                   // close the socket, do not keep an unauthenticated peer
    }
  }

  handleDisconnect(client: Socket) {
    this.log.debug({ userId: client.data.userId, reason: client.disconnected }, 'ws disconnected');
  }

  @UseGuards(WsAuthGuard)
  @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }))
  @SubscribeMessage('order.join')
  async joinOrder(@ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() dto: JoinOrderDto) {
    // Authorization per room: only the customer or the assigned driver may watch this order.
    const allowed = await this.orders.canView(client.data.userId, dto.orderId);
    if (!allowed) throw new WsException('FORBIDDEN');
    await client.join(`order:${dto.orderId}`);
    // Returning a value sends it as the acknowledgement if the client passed a callback.
    return { ok: true, room: `order:${dto.orderId}` };
  }

  @UseGuards(WsAuthGuard)
  @SubscribeMessage('order.leave')
  async leaveOrder(@ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() dto: JoinOrderDto) {
    await client.leave(`order:${dto.orderId}`);
    return { ok: true };
  }
}

The guard for message handlers reads the user the connection handler stored and rejects expired tokens, which matters because a connection can outlive its token (see 34.15).

// realtime/ws-auth.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { WsException } from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { Socket } from 'socket.io';

@Injectable()
export class WsAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const client = ctx.switchToWs().getClient<Socket>();
    if (!client.data.userId) throw new WsException('UNAUTHORIZED');
    if (client.data.tokenExp && Date.now() > client.data.tokenExp) {
      client.emit('auth.expired');            // tell the client to refresh and reconnect
      client.disconnect(true);
      throw new WsException('TOKEN_EXPIRED');
    }
    return true;
  }
}

// realtime/dto/join-order.dto.ts
import { IsUUID } from 'class-validator';
export class JoinOrderDto {
  @IsUUID() orderId: string;
}

Emitting from anywhere else in the application goes through the gateway's server reference and always targets a room:

// realtime/order-events.publisher.ts
@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsPublisher {
  constructor(private readonly gateway: OrdersGateway) {}

  statusChanged(orderId: string, status: string, seq: number) {
    // Every payload carries a sequence number so clients can detect gaps after a reconnect.
    this.gateway.server.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('order.status', { orderId, status, seq, at: Date.now() });
  }
}

Rooms and namespaces. A namespace (/orders, /chat) is a logical channel with its own handlers and middleware over the same physical connection. A room is a named set of sockets inside a namespace; sockets join and leave freely, and emitting to a room fans out to every member. Rooms are the unit of authorization and the unit of fan-out: order:8812, user:41, restaurant:77. They exist in memory on the pod that holds the socket, which is why multi-pod deployments need the Redis adapter from 34.5.

Acknowledgements. A Socket.IO client can pass a callback as the last argument to emit; the server's return value from the @SubscribeMessage handler is delivered to that callback. Use acks for anything the client must know succeeded (joining a room, sending a chat message) and add a client-side timeout, because an ack never arrives if the pod restarts mid-handler.

If you prefer the lighter ws library, @nestjs/platform-ws provides WsAdapter; you lose rooms, namespaces and acks and gain a smaller protocol and lower per-connection memory. The gateway decorators are the same.

Production scenario

A gateway service with 8 pods, each holding 25,000 Socket.IO connections. Handshake rate during the evening peak is 400 per second, each verifying a JWT (about 0.1 ms of CPU) and one Redis lookup for the ownership cache (0.3 ms). Message rate is 6,000 outbound per second across the fleet, mostly location updates of 180 bytes each. CPU per pod sits at 30 to 40 percent of one core, almost entirely JSON serialization and socket writes; memory is about 20 KB per connection in Node.js plus kernel socket buffers, so 25,000 connections cost roughly 500 MB heap plus 200 MB of socket buffers.

Failure scenario

At 19:40, a developer ships a gateway change that reads the token from client.handshake.query.token "for the mobile app". The API gateway's access logs now contain every user's JWT in the URL. The logs ship to a third-party log vendor with 30 day retention. Security finds it in a routine scan a week later; every token has to be revoked and every user signed out. The rule that came out of the incident: tokens live in the Socket.IO auth object or an Authorization header, and the load balancer's log format strips query strings on upgrade requests.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A client connects, never authenticates and never sends anything; without a timeout the socket sits forever. Disconnect unauthenticated sockets after 5 seconds.
  • A valid token for a deleted or banned user still connects if you only verify the signature. Check a revocation list or the user's status on connect and on a periodic re-check.
  • client.join is asynchronous with the Redis adapter; emitting to the room in the same tick can miss the joining socket. await it.
  • An exception thrown inside handleConnection does not automatically disconnect the socket; catch and disconnect(true) explicitly.
  • Payloads over maxHttpBufferSize disconnect the client; choose the limit deliberately and tell the client team.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting Origin implicitly. Configure cors.origin to the exact list; a wildcard with credentials is a cross-site WebSocket hijack waiting to happen.
  • Emitting to this.server.emit(...) (everyone) because it was easier than rooms. Every customer sees every order.
  • Doing database writes inside message handlers without the same validation, transactions and idempotency you would use in a REST controller.

34.3 Server-Sent Events

34.3.1 One-way streaming over plain HTTP

Concept

SSE is a response that never ends. The server sets Content-Type: text/event-stream, keeps the connection open, and writes events as small text blocks: id: 42, event: order.status, data: {...}, then a blank line. The browser's EventSource parses them, fires onmessage or a named listener, and, if the connection drops, reconnects automatically and sends the last id it saw in a Last-Event-ID header so the server can resume.

Why does it exist?

Most real-time features are one-way. Notifications, order status, price tickers, build logs, progress bars. Running a WebSocket infrastructure for those means paying for bidirectional connection management you never use. SSE gives you push over HTTP with everything HTTP already has: TLS, HTTP/2 multiplexing, cookies, the same guards and interceptors, the same load balancer rules, and a client that reconnects itself.

Mental model

Imagine a stock ticker tape machine in an old trading office. A paper strip comes out continuously; each printed line is an event. If the machine jams, you tear off the tape, note the last number printed, and ask the exchange to resend from there. You never type into the ticker.

How it works

  1. The client opens new EventSource('/orders/8812/events'), with cookies, or with a token via a small polyfill that allows custom headers (the native EventSource cannot set headers, which pushes browser auth towards cookies).
  2. The server responds 200 with Content-Type: text/event-stream, Cache-Control: no-cache, Connection: keep-alive, and for nginx, X-Accel-Buffering: no so the proxy does not hold the response until it is "complete".
  3. Each event is written as text. id: sets the value the browser will send back as Last-Event-ID. retry: tells the browser how many milliseconds to wait before reconnecting.
  4. The server writes a comment line (: keepalive) every 15 to 30 seconds so intermediaries do not close an idle connection.
  5. On disconnect, the browser waits retry ms (default about 3 seconds), reconnects with Last-Event-ID, and the server replays anything after that id from its buffer (Redis Stream, database, or in-memory ring).

NestJS example

NestJS supports SSE with the @Sse() decorator on a controller method that returns an RxJS Observable<MessageEvent>. Each emitted MessageEvent (from @nestjs/common) becomes one event on the wire.

// orders/order-events.controller.ts
import { Controller, Headers, MessageEvent, Param, Sse, UseGuards, ParseUUIDPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, merge, interval, map, filter, from, concatWith } from 'rxjs';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { OrderOwnerGuard } from './order-owner.guard';
import { OrderEventStream } from './order-event.stream';

@Controller('orders')
export class OrderEventsController {
  constructor(private readonly stream: OrderEventStream) {}

  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, OrderOwnerGuard)          // the same guards as REST
  @Sse(':id/events')
  events(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) orderId: string,
    @Headers('last-event-id') lastEventId?: string,   // the browser sends this on reconnect
  ): Observable<MessageEvent> {
    // 1. Replay anything the client missed, from the Redis Stream for this order.
    const replay$ = from(this.stream.replaySince(orderId, lastEventId ?? '0')).pipe(
      map((ev) => this.toMessage(ev)),
    );
    // 2. Then live events published for this order.
    const live$ = this.stream.subscribe(orderId).pipe(map((ev) => this.toMessage(ev)));
    // 3. Keepalive comments so proxies and mobile networks do not close the idle connection.
    const keepalive$ = interval(20_000).pipe(map(() => ({ type: 'keepalive', data: '' }) as MessageEvent));
    return replay$.pipe(concatWith(merge(live$, keepalive$)));
  }

  private toMessage(ev: { id: string; type: string; payload: unknown }): MessageEvent {
    return { id: ev.id, type: ev.type, data: ev.payload, retry: 3_000 };
  }
}

OrderEventStream wraps a Redis Stream per order: XADD order:8812 MAXLEN ~ 500 * type order.status payload {...} on publish, XRANGE order:8812 (lastId + for replay, and a Redis Pub/Sub or XREAD BLOCK loop for live events. The Redis Stream id (1725630131483-0) doubles as the SSE id, so Last-Event-ID maps directly to XRANGE.

The response headers NestJS sets for @Sse() are correct out of the box; add the nginx header with an interceptor or at the ingress:

# ingress annotation for nginx: do not buffer streaming responses, keep long connections
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"

Production scenario

An order tracking page opened by 40,000 customers during the dinner peak, each holding one SSE connection for the 30 to 45 minutes of a delivery. With HTTP/2, all of a customer's streams share one TCP connection. Each connection costs about 8 KB in Node.js (less than a Socket.IO socket, because there is no protocol state) and the fleet emits 5 events per order on average, so the total message rate is tiny; the cost is entirely in holding 40,000 open responses, which 3 pods handle comfortably. The 30 day p99 for "status change visible to the customer" is 180 ms, dominated by Kafka consumer latency, not by SSE.

Failure scenario

At 12:05 the platform team upgrades the ingress controller. The new config enables response buffering by default. SSE connections open fine, but customers see no events until the server closes the connection, because nginx is waiting for the "complete" response before forwarding it. Nothing errors; the order tracking page simply stops updating. The on-call notices only when support tickets arrive. The fix is the proxy-buffering: "off" annotation on the SSE route, and the lesson is a synthetic check that opens an SSE stream and asserts an event arrives within 30 seconds.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Browser connection limits. On HTTP/1.1, browsers allow about 6 connections per host. Six SSE tabs and the seventh request to the same host hangs. HTTP/2 removes the limit; if you cannot use HTTP/2, share one stream per origin via a SharedWorker or BroadcastChannel.
  • Proxies buffering. nginx, some CDNs and some corporate proxies buffer or refuse text/event-stream. Send a 2 KB padding comment at the start for old proxies, set X-Accel-Buffering: no, and test through the real ingress.
  • No custom headers in EventSource. Browser auth must be cookies or a query token; mobile clients using a raw HTTP client can send Authorization.
  • Replay without bounds. A client reconnecting with a Last-Event-ID from a week ago asks for everything since; cap replay to the stream's MAXLEN and tell the client to refetch state via REST if the id is older than the buffer.
  • Event loop blocking on a slow client. res.write returns false when the socket buffer is full; the Observable keeps emitting. A slow client on a tiny mobile link can accumulate memory in Node.js. Track res.writableLength or drop the connection when it exceeds a limit.
  • Text only. Binary data must be base64 encoded, a 33 percent size penalty.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They choose SSE for every server-to-client feature until a product requirement forces bidirectional traffic, because it reuses the entire HTTP stack and the client reconnects itself. They put the replay buffer in Redis Streams, never in pod memory, so a reconnect to a different pod still resumes. They treat the ingress config as part of the feature and add a synthetic SSE check to the uptime monitor.

34.4 Long polling

34.4.1 How it works and why it is only a fallback

Concept

The client sends GET /orders/8812/events?since=42. The server checks for events after 42. If there are any, it responds immediately. If not, it holds the request open, up to a timeout (typically 20 to 30 seconds, under the load balancer's idle limit), responding as soon as an event arrives or with an empty 204 at the timeout. The client immediately sends the next request. The client never waits more than one round trip to learn about an event, but every event costs a full HTTP request and response.

Why does it exist?

Because some network paths break everything else. A corporate proxy that strips Upgrade headers, a mobile carrier that buffers streaming responses, an old embedded browser. Socket.IO starts with long polling and upgrades to WebSocket exactly because long polling works everywhere.

How it works in NestJS

// orders/order-poll.controller.ts
@Controller('orders')
export class OrderPollController {
  constructor(private readonly stream: OrderEventStream) {}

  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, OrderOwnerGuard)
  @Get(':id/events/poll')
  async poll(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) orderId: string,
    @Query('since') since = '0',
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ) {
    const events = await this.stream.replaySince(orderId, since);
    if (events.length > 0) return { events };
    // Nothing yet: wait for the first event or the timeout, whichever comes first.
    const next = await this.stream.waitForNext(orderId, 25_000);   // resolves null on timeout
    if (!next) { res.status(204); return; }
    return { events: [next] };
  }
}

waitForNext subscribes to the Redis Pub/Sub channel for the order and resolves on the first message or a timer. Keep the timeout below the load balancer's idle timeout (60 seconds on an AWS ALB by default) or the balancer closes the request first and the client sees an error instead of a 204.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Every waiting request holds a Node.js promise and a Redis subscription; 50,000 clients polling is 50,000 pending handlers, the same memory as WebSockets plus a request object each.
  • The gap between one poll's response and the next poll's arrival is a window where events must be buffered server-side, which is why since exists. Without it, events in the gap are lost.
  • HTTP/1.1 connection limits apply; a page with three long polls to the same host has three of its six connections permanently busy.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never design for long polling; they design for SSE or WebSockets with a since or Last-Event-ID resume contract, and long polling falls out of that same contract as a fallback. If a product asks "just poll every 2 seconds", they do the arithmetic aloud: 100,000 clients at 0.5 requests per second is 50,000 RPS of mostly-empty responses, which costs more than the entire real-time stack.

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose SSE over WebSockets? Expected: server-to-client only, wants HTTP stack reuse, built-in reconnect with Last-Event-ID; WebSockets when bidirectional or binary. Follow-up: how do you handle client actions with SSE? (REST POST.)
  2. Walk through the WebSocket upgrade handshake. Expected: GET with Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-Key, 101 with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, then frames; why the key exists.
  3. How do you authenticate a WebSocket connection, and why is it different from REST? Expected: once at connect, via handshake auth or cookie with Origin check; no per-message headers; must handle token expiry mid-connection.
  4. What breaks SSE in production? Expected: proxy buffering, HTTP/1.1 connection limits, no custom headers in EventSource, unbounded replay.
  5. Why does Socket.IO start with long polling? Expected: works through every proxy; upgrades opportunistically.
  6. Where does room authorization happen and why is it separate from authentication? Expected: on every join, against ownership; identity is not permission.

Practical exercise

Build both transports for order tracking:

  1. A NestJS OrdersGateway on namespace /orders with handshake JWT auth, order.join with ownership check and ack, and order.status emits to order:{id} rooms with a sequence number.
  2. An @Sse(':id/events') endpoint on the same service, with replay from a Redis Stream via Last-Event-ID and a 20 second keepalive comment.
  3. A long-poll fallback endpoint with since and a 25 second server timeout.
  4. Acceptance: a browser client on the WebSocket path receives status updates within 100 ms of a PATCH /orders/:id/status; killing the SSE client mid-stream and reconnecting delivers exactly the missed events and no duplicates; an unauthenticated WebSocket is disconnected within 5 seconds; a user who does not own the order receives FORBIDDEN on join; running the SSE endpoint through a local nginx with buffering enabled fails your synthetic check and passes with buffering off.

34.5 Pub/Sub for fan-out across pods

34.5.1 Why a message on pod A must reach a client on pod B

Concept

A WebSocket connection lives on exactly one process. When your gateway runs as 8 pods behind a load balancer, the customer watching order 8812 is connected to pod 3, and the Kafka consumer that learns the driver moved is running on pod 6. Pod 6 calling server.to('order:8812').emit(...) reaches only the sockets that pod 6 holds. The customer sees nothing. Fan-out across pods needs a shared channel that every pod subscribes to: a Pub/Sub layer.

Why does it exist?

Rooms are in-memory data structures. Horizontal scaling is the whole reason you have more than one pod. The two are in direct conflict unless something carries "emit this to room X" from the pod that knows to the pods that hold the sockets. Every real-time system that runs on more than one process has this layer; the only question is whether it is Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams, Kafka, NATS or a vendor.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel with eight reception desks, each with its own list of guests who asked to be woken at 7 a.m. A wake-up call for room 812 must go to the desk that has 812 on its list. Instead of each desk phoning the other seven, they all listen to one intercom: whoever learns about 812 announces it, and the desk that has 812 acts. The intercom is Pub/Sub. If the intercom is broken, every desk is an island.

How it works

flowchart LR
    K["Kafka topic driver.locations"] --> C6["Consumer on gateway pod 6"]
    C6 -->|"PUBLISH socket.io#orders# with room order:8812"| R["Redis Pub/Sub"]
    R --> P1["Gateway pod 1"]
    R --> P3["Gateway pod 3"]
    R --> P6["Gateway pod 6"]
    P3 -->|"local room lookup finds socket"| S3["Customer 41 on pod 3"]
    P1 -->|"no members, ignored"| N1["nothing"]
    P6 -->|"driver app on pod 6"| S6["Driver 77 on pod 6"]

With the Socket.IO Redis adapter:

  1. Every pod, on startup, opens two Redis connections: one to publish, one subscribed to the adapter's channels (a subscribed connection cannot run other commands, so a second connection is mandatory).
  2. server.to('order:8812').emit('driver.location', payload) on pod 6 emits locally and publishes a compact message (rooms, event, payload, and the origin pod's id) to Redis.
  3. Every other pod receives it, looks up the room in its own memory, and emits to its own matching sockets. Pods with no members do nothing.
  4. client.join and client.leave stay local; membership never leaves the pod. That is why the adapter is cheap: it broadcasts intent, not state.
  5. Adapter requests that need cluster-wide answers (fetchSockets(), serverSideEmit, counting sockets in a room) use a request-response protocol over the same channels with a timeout. They are slow (a Redis round trip plus the slowest pod) and should not be on a hot path.

Three backends for the channel:

Backend Durability Ordering Throughput Use when
Redis Pub/Sub None; a message published while a pod is disconnected is gone Per channel, per publisher Very high, sub-millisecond, but every subscriber receives every message The default. Live fan-out where a missed message is recovered by the client's resume logic, not by the channel
Redis Streams Persistent up to MAXLEN; consumers read from an id Per stream High Replay on reconnect (XRANGE since the last id), and as the source of Last-Event-ID for SSE
Kafka Durable, partitioned, retained for days Per partition Very high but with 5 to 50 ms latency The upstream source of truth for events (driver locations, order status). Gateways consume it; they do not use it as the pod-to-pod channel because a rebalance across 8 gateway pods on every deploy is painful

The common production shape is all three: Kafka carries the business events from producers to the gateway fleet; the gateway consumer writes the last N events per room to a Redis Stream for replay; the Socket.IO Redis adapter (Pub/Sub) does the live fan-out between pods.

NestJS example

NestJS lets you replace the Socket.IO server factory with a custom adapter class. This is where the Redis adapter is installed.

// realtime/redis-io.adapter.ts
import { IoAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-socket.io';
import { INestApplicationContext } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ServerOptions } from 'socket.io';
import { createAdapter } from '@socket.io/redis-adapter';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

export class RedisIoAdapter extends IoAdapter {
  private adapterConstructor?: ReturnType<typeof createAdapter>;

  constructor(app: INestApplicationContext, private readonly redisUrl: string) {
    super(app);
  }

  async connectToRedis(): Promise<void> {
    const pub = new Redis(this.redisUrl, { maxRetriesPerRequest: 3, enableOfflineQueue: false });
    const sub = pub.duplicate();            // subscriber connection must be separate
    await Promise.all([pub.connect?.(), sub.connect?.()].filter(Boolean));
    pub.on('error', (err) => console.error('redis pub error', err.message));
    sub.on('error', (err) => console.error('redis sub error', err.message));
    this.adapterConstructor = createAdapter(pub, sub, {
      requestsTimeout: 5_000,               // fetchSockets and friends give up after 5 s
      publishOnSpecificResponseChannel: true,
    });
  }

  createIOServer(port: number, options?: ServerOptions) {
    const server = super.createIOServer(port, {
      ...options,
      transports: ['websocket', 'polling'],
      allowEIO3: false,
    });
    server.adapter(this.adapterConstructor);
    return server;
  }
}
// main.ts
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
const ioAdapter = new RedisIoAdapter(app, process.env.REDIS_URL!);
await ioAdapter.connectToRedis();
app.useWebSocketAdapter(ioAdapter);
app.enableShutdownHooks();
await app.listen(3000);

After this change, nothing in the gateway code changes; server.to(room).emit is cluster-wide. That transparency is a trap as well as a gift, because the failure modes of Redis become the failure modes of your rooms (see 34.15).

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL has its own Pub/Sub, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and it is tempting for small systems: a trigger on orders runs pg_notify('order_events', json) and each gateway pod runs LISTEN order_events. It works for tens of events per second across a handful of pods. It does not scale: every listener holds a dedicated connection, NOTIFY payloads are capped at 8,000 bytes, notifications are queued per connection and dropped if the queue (8 GB by default, but shared) overflows, and a long transaction delays every notification issued inside it until commit. Use it for admin dashboards and internal tools, not for customer-facing fan-out.

-- Fire an event on status change; the gateway's LISTEN picks it up within a few ms of commit.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION notify_order_status() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  PERFORM pg_notify('order_events', json_build_object('orderId', NEW.id, 'status', NEW.status, 'seq', NEW.version)::text);
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_status_notify AFTER UPDATE OF status ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_order_status();

Production scenario

A gateway fleet of 8 pods, 200,000 connections, 6,000 emits per second, each to a room with 1 to 3 members. Redis Pub/Sub receives 6,000 publishes per second and delivers 48,000 messages per second (one per pod), each about 300 bytes: 15 MB per second of Redis output, comfortably within one Redis instance's capacity and well under 1 ms per message. CPU on each pod for the adapter is under 5 percent. The first thing that breaks as this grows is not Redis throughput; it is that every pod pays to receive every message, so at 80 pods the adapter traffic is 480,000 deliveries per second and the design needs sharded channels (the adapter supports a sharded mode on Redis 7 with SSUBSCRIBE) or a partitioning scheme where a room's members are pinned to a subset of pods.

Failure scenario

At 21:10 the Redis instance backing the adapter is failed over by the cloud provider's maintenance. For 40 seconds each pod's subscriber connection is dead. The adapter emits locally only, so a customer connected to pod 3 receives updates only if the Kafka partition with their driver's location happens to be consumed by pod 3, about one in eight. The dashboard's messages_emitted_total looks normal because emits are counted at the publisher. Nobody notices for 6 minutes until a support ticket says "my driver is not moving". The retrospective adds a Redis adapter health check to the readiness probe, a metric for adapter publish failures, and a synthetic test that connects to two different pods and asserts a message published via one arrives at the other.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The subscriber connection drops and reconnects. ioredis resubscribes automatically, but messages published in between are gone. Pub/Sub has no memory. The client's resume-by-sequence logic (34.9) is what covers the gap; if you do not have that, you have a silent data loss window on every Redis blip.
  • fetchSockets across a large fleet is a scatter-gather with a 5 second timeout; a slow pod makes the call slow for everyone. Use it for admin tooling, not for authorization checks.
  • Serialization cost. The adapter serializes the payload once per publish, and every pod deserializes it. A 50 KB payload emitted 100 times per second is 40 MB per second of Redis traffic across 8 pods.
  • Room names with user input. order:${dto.orderId} where orderId is validated as a UUID is safe; a free-form room name lets a client join admin or *.
  • A pod that publishes but cannot subscribe (a firewall rule that allows one connection but rate-limits the second) is the hardest to spot: it sends everyone's messages and receives none.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They install the Redis adapter on day one, before the second pod exists, because the cost is thirty lines and the alternative is a production bug that appears exactly when traffic grows. They keep Kafka as the source of truth and Redis as the transport, and never make the client's correctness depend on Pub/Sub delivering every message. They put the adapter's Redis in the readiness probe and its publish errors on the dashboard. They plan for the day one Redis is not enough by using room names that could be sharded (order:{id} hashes evenly) and by keeping the gateway stateless enough to run as a separate deployment with its own scaling rules.

Common mistakes

  • Running two gateway pods without an adapter and debugging "messages arrive sometimes".
  • Using the Pub/Sub channel as the replay buffer. It has none.
  • Holding room membership in Redis "so it is shared" and then doing a Redis round trip per emit to look it up. Membership belongs on the pod; intent goes through Redis.
  • Reusing the application's main ioredis connection for the subscriber. A subscribed connection cannot run GET, and every cache read starts failing.

34.6 Presence

34.6.1 Online, offline, last seen and multiple devices

Concept

Presence is the answer to "is user 41 online right now, and on which devices?" It looks trivial (set a flag on connect, clear it on disconnect) and is one of the most bug-prone features in real-time systems, because disconnects are not always observed, users have several devices, and the pod that saw the connection may die without saying goodbye.

Why does it exist?

Chat shows a green dot. A dispatch system routes an order only to drivers who are actually connected. A collaborative editor shows who is in the document. A notification service decides between a WebSocket push and a mobile push notification based on whether the user is reachable. All of these need a presence answer that is correct within a few seconds and does not go stale when a pod crashes.

Mental model

Imagine a building's sign-in sheet, but every visitor must re-sign every minute. If a name has not been re-signed for two minutes, the visitor is assumed to have left, whether or not they signed out. Crashed pods, dead phones and NAT timeouts all look the same: the name stops being refreshed.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Device
    participant G as GatewayPod
    participant R as Redis
    participant N as NotificationService
    D->>G: connect with token
    G->>R: SET presence:u41:d-phone pod3 EX 60
    G->>R: SADD presence:u41:devices d-phone
    G->>R: PUBLISH presence u41 online
    loop every 25 seconds while the socket is alive
        G->>R: EXPIRE presence:u41:d-phone 60
    end
    D-->>G: TCP connection lost, no close frame
    Note over G: pingTimeout fires after 20 s
    G->>R: DEL presence:u41:d-phone and SREM devices
    Note over R: if the pod itself died, the key simply expires after 60 s
    N->>R: EXISTS presence:u41:* via SMEMBERS devices then EXISTS
    R-->>N: 0 devices alive
    N->>N: send mobile push instead of WebSocket message
  1. On connect, the gateway writes a key per device: presence:{userId}:{deviceId} with the pod id as the value and a TTL of 60 seconds. It adds the device id to a set presence:{userId}:devices, and publishes an online event if this is the user's first live device.
  2. Every 25 seconds (the same cadence as the ping), while the socket is alive, the gateway refreshes the TTL. The refresh is the heartbeat; it proves the pod and the socket both still exist.
  3. On a clean disconnect, the gateway deletes the key, removes the device from the set, and publishes offline if no devices remain. It also records last_seen:{userId} with a timestamp.
  4. On a pod crash, nothing is deleted, and the keys expire on their own within 60 seconds. Presence is eventually correct, with a bounded staleness of one TTL.
  5. A reader asks "is u41 online" by reading the devices set and checking which device keys still exist. A read that finds a device in the set whose key is gone cleans the set up lazily.

Why a TTL and not a "connected" flag: a flag set on connect and cleared on disconnect is wrong forever after a single pod crash. The TTL makes the absence of a heartbeat the source of truth, which matches reality.

NestJS example

// realtime/presence.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

const TTL_SECONDS = 60;
const REFRESH_MS = 25_000;

@Injectable()
export class PresenceService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PresenceService.name);
  private readonly timers = new Map<string, NodeJS.Timeout>();   // socketId -> refresh timer

  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly podId: string) {}

  async connected(socketId: string, userId: string, deviceId: string): Promise<void> {
    const key = `presence:${userId}:${deviceId}`;
    const wasOnline = await this.isOnline(userId);
    await this.redis.multi()
      .set(key, this.podId, 'EX', TTL_SECONDS)
      .sadd(`presence:${userId}:devices`, deviceId)
      .expire(`presence:${userId}:devices`, TTL_SECONDS * 2)
      .exec();
    if (!wasOnline) await this.redis.publish('presence', JSON.stringify({ userId, state: 'online' }));

    // Heartbeat: refresh the TTL while this socket lives. If the pod dies, the key expires on its own.
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      this.redis.expire(key, TTL_SECONDS).catch((err) => this.log.warn({ err: err.message }, 'presence refresh failed'));
    }, REFRESH_MS);
    this.timers.set(socketId, timer);
  }

  async disconnected(socketId: string, userId: string, deviceId: string): Promise<void> {
    clearInterval(this.timers.get(socketId));
    this.timers.delete(socketId);
    await this.redis.multi()
      .del(`presence:${userId}:${deviceId}`)
      .srem(`presence:${userId}:devices`, deviceId)
      .set(`last_seen:${userId}`, Date.now().toString())
      .exec();
    if (!(await this.isOnline(userId))) {
      await this.redis.publish('presence', JSON.stringify({ userId, state: 'offline', lastSeen: Date.now() }));
    }
  }

  async isOnline(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const devices = await this.redis.smembers(`presence:${userId}:devices`);
    if (devices.length === 0) return false;
    const alive = await this.redis.mget(devices.map((d) => `presence:${userId}:${d}`));
    const stale = devices.filter((_, i) => alive[i] === null);
    if (stale.length) await this.redis.srem(`presence:${userId}:devices`, ...stale);   // lazy cleanup
    return alive.some((v) => v !== null);
  }

  onModuleDestroy() {
    for (const t of this.timers.values()) clearInterval(t);
  }
}

Wire it into the gateway's handleConnection and handleDisconnect. The device id comes from the client (a stable id per install, sent in the handshake auth), and socketId is client.id.

PostgreSQL example

Presence itself never lives in PostgreSQL; a UPDATE users SET online = true per connect is a write per socket event and a hot row per active user. What does belong in PostgreSQL is last_seen_at, written lazily (at most once per minute per user, from the disconnect path or a periodic flush), because product features like "active in the last 7 days" need durable history and are queried by cohort, not by socket.

-- Written at most once per minute per user; never on every heartbeat.
UPDATE users SET last_seen_at = GREATEST(last_seen_at, $2) WHERE id = $1;
CREATE INDEX users_last_seen_idx ON users (last_seen_at DESC);

Production scenario

A chat product with 300,000 online users across 12 gateway pods. Each connection refreshes its TTL every 25 seconds: 12,000 EXPIRE commands per second on Redis, trivially cheap. isOnline is called by the notification service about 2,000 times per second; each call is SMEMBERS plus one MGET, about 0.6 ms. Presence staleness after a pod crash is bounded at 60 seconds, which product accepted after being shown the alternative (a distributed sweep that costs more than the feature).

Failure scenario

The first version of presence used a plain SET presence:u41 true on connect and DEL on disconnect. A gateway pod was OOMKilled at 14:00. Every user connected to it stayed "online" in Redis forever; the notification service kept trying WebSocket delivery to 25,000 users who were not reachable and never fell back to mobile push. Users missed messages for six hours until someone ran FLUSHDB on the presence keyspace. The rewrite to TTL-refreshed keys took one afternoon and the bug class disappeared.

Edge cases & failure modes
