  • Multi-device. A user with a phone and a laptop must stay online when the laptop closes. Key per device, set of devices per user; offline only when the set is empty of live keys.
  • Reconnect flapping. A mobile user on a train produces connect and disconnect every few seconds; publishing online/offline each time floods the presence channel. Debounce the offline event: wait 10 seconds and re-check before publishing.
  • Clock skew is irrelevant here because TTLs are relative and computed by Redis, one of the reasons to prefer TTLs over stored timestamps compared against local clocks.
  • The refresh timer keeps running after a disconnect if the disconnect handler throws before clearInterval. Clear timers first, then do I/O.
  • Redis restart without persistence empties presence; everyone appears offline until the next refresh cycle repopulates within 25 seconds. Acceptable; document it.
  • Privacy. Presence and last-seen are personal data in many jurisdictions; expose them only to contacts the user has allowed, and never broadcast them to a room.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They define presence as "has heartbeated within the last N seconds" and refuse any design where correctness depends on observing a disconnect. They put the TTL in the product conversation: "you will see someone as online for up to 60 seconds after their phone dies; is that acceptable, or do you want a 20 second TTL at three times the Redis load?" They keep presence in Redis and history in PostgreSQL, and they debounce the visible state so a flapping network does not make the green dot blink.

34.7 Connection management

34.7.1 Limits, memory, file descriptors and load balancers

Concept

A long-lived connection is a resource on every hop: a file descriptor and socket buffers in the kernel, a socket object and its buffers in Node.js, a connection table entry in the load balancer, and NAT state in the client's network. Managing connections means knowing those limits, staying inside them, and getting connections off a pod cleanly when it must go away.

How it works

Per-pod limits. A Node.js process holding 50,000 idle Socket.IO connections uses roughly 1 to 1.5 GB of heap (about 20 to 30 KB per socket for the objects, buffers and room maps) and a similar amount in kernel socket buffers. The container also needs enough file descriptors: the default ulimit -n of 1,024 in many base images means the 1,025th connection fails with EMFILE. Set it to at least 2 times the connection target (ulimit -n 131072 in the entrypoint, or the container runtime's nofile limit). A practical per-pod target is 10,000 to 30,000 connections, sized so a single pod's loss is a manageable reconnect wave (34.9).

Sticky sessions versus stateless with the Redis adapter. Socket.IO's long-polling transport requires that every HTTP request of one session hits the same pod, so with polling enabled you need sticky sessions at the load balancer (cookie-based or IP hash). With transports: ['websocket'] only, there is one TCP connection per client and stickiness is irrelevant: the connection is pinned to a pod by nature. The Redis adapter handles fan-out. The tradeoff is that clients behind a proxy that blocks WebSocket upgrades cannot connect at all. Most teams run websocket-only on the mobile apps and websocket-with-polling-fallback on the web, and enable stickiness at the ingress for the polling path.

Load balancer and ingress configuration. Three settings break WebSockets when wrong:

Layer Setting Safe value Symptom when wrong
AWS ALB idle_timeout.timeout_seconds 300 or more, above the ping interval Connections closed every 60 s with no close frame; clients reconnect in a wave
AWS NLB Idle timeout is fixed at 350 s Ping at least every 60 s so the flow stays alive Same as above after 350 s of silence
nginx ingress proxy-read-timeout, proxy-send-timeout 3600 Connections dropped at 60 s
nginx ingress Upgrade and Connection headers passed through On by default in the ingress-nginx controller; manual nginx needs proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade and Connection "upgrade" Handshake returns 400 or 502
Cloudflare and other CDNs WebSocket support enabled; timeouts around 100 s Ping under the timeout Periodic drops

Graceful shutdown. A pod that receives SIGTERM must drain, not vanish. The order matters: fail readiness first so the load balancer stops sending new upgrades, tell connected clients to reconnect with a spread of delay, close sockets, then exit before the termination grace period ends.

// realtime/orders.gateway.ts (shutdown handling)
import { BeforeApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';

export class OrdersGateway implements BeforeApplicationShutdown {
  @WebSocketServer() server: Server;

  async beforeApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.log.warn({ signal, clients: this.server.engine.clientsCount }, 'draining websocket connections');
    this.health.markNotReady();                          // readiness returns 503 from now on
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5_000));      // let the LB observe the readiness change
    const sockets = await this.server.local.fetchSockets();
    for (const socket of sockets) {
      // Tell each client when to reconnect; spread over 0 to 10 seconds to avoid a stampede.
      socket.emit('server.reconnect', { afterMs: Math.floor(Math.random() * 10_000) });
    }
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2_000));      // give the emits time to flush
    this.server.local.disconnectSockets(true);           // close what is left
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => this.server.close(() => resolve()));
  }
}

Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds on the pod to more than the sum of those waits (30 seconds here is safe). server.local restricts fetchSockets and disconnectSockets to this pod, which is what you want during a shutdown; without it, the Redis adapter would ask the whole fleet.

Backpressure on slow clients. A client on a bad mobile link cannot read as fast as you write. Every emit to it appends to the socket's write buffer in Node.js; nothing stops the buffer growing until the process runs out of memory. For high-frequency streams, prefer the newest message over the complete history: coalesce (keep only the latest driver location per client, not the last 50), or use Socket.IO's volatile flag, which drops the emit when the underlying transport is not writable.

// Coalescing location updates: only the latest position per order is kept for a slow client.
this.server.to(`order:${orderId}`).volatile.emit('driver.location', { orderId, lat, lng, seq });

// Detecting a slow client on raw ws: check the buffered amount before writing.
if (ws.bufferedAmount > 256 * 1024) {
  ws.close(1008, 'slow consumer');   // or skip this message and let the client refetch
}

For Socket.IO, socket.conn.transport.writable and the Engine.IO writeBuffer length tell you whether the client is keeping up; a bounded policy ("drop the connection when the buffer exceeds 1 MB") protects the pod from one bad client.

Production scenario

A gateway deployment of 10 pods at 20,000 connections each, 2 CPU and 3 GB memory per pod, ulimit -n 65536, websocket-only transport, ALB idle timeout 600 seconds, ping every 25 seconds. A rolling deploy with maxSurge: 2, maxUnavailable: 0 replaces one pod at a time; each drain moves 20,000 clients over 10 seconds, about 2,000 reconnects per second across the remaining 11 pods, each costing one JWT verify and one Redis round trip. The deploy of 10 pods takes 8 minutes and never exceeds 3,000 handshakes per second fleet-wide.

Failure scenario

At 10:00 a cost-saving change lowers the ALB idle timeout from 600 to 60 seconds. The ping interval is 25 seconds, so connections should survive. But the mobile client has a battery optimization that pauses timers in the background, so backgrounded apps stop answering pings and the ALB closes them at 60 seconds instead of the server's 45. Every backgrounded app now reconnects every minute: 150,000 extra handshakes per minute, JWT verification CPU triples, and the p99 of the REST API on the shared pods goes from 80 to 900 ms. The fix was the timeout back to 600 seconds and a separate gateway deployment so that WebSocket handshake load can never affect the REST path again.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • EMFILE when the file descriptor limit is hit; the process keeps running but every new connection and every outbound HTTP call fails.
  • Kernel net.core.somaxconn and tcp_max_syn_backlog too low for a reconnect wave; connections are refused at the TCP level before Node.js sees them.
  • A pod at 95 percent memory during a reconnect wave gets OOMKilled, which triggers another wave on the other pods: a cascade. Keep 40 percent headroom on gateway pods.
  • SIGTERM handled but readiness not failed first; the load balancer keeps sending upgrades to a pod that is closing them.
  • disconnectSockets() without server.local during shutdown disconnects every socket on every pod.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They run the gateway as its own deployment with its own HPA scaled on connection count and CPU, never inside the REST API pods, so a reconnect storm cannot take down checkout. They set the per-pod connection ceiling from the reconnect arithmetic ("if this pod dies, can the others absorb 20,000 handshakes in 10 seconds?") rather than from memory alone. They put every timeout in a table, from the client's ping to the CDN's idle limit, and make sure each layer's timeout is longer than the one below it.

34.8 Heartbeats

34.8.1 Detecting dead connections

Concept

TCP does not tell you a peer is gone. A phone that loses signal, a laptop that closes its lid, a NAT gateway that forgets a mapping, a pod that is killed: none of them send a close frame. The server keeps the socket, keeps the room membership, keeps counting the client as online, and keeps writing into a buffer nobody reads. Heartbeats exist to turn silence into a decision.

How it works

  • Server ping, client pong (Socket.IO's default): the server sends a ping every pingInterval (25 seconds); if no pong arrives within pingTimeout (20 seconds), the server closes the socket and fires disconnect with reason ping timeout. Cost: one tiny frame per connection per 25 seconds; at 200,000 connections that is 8,000 frames per second fleet-wide, negligible.
  • Client ping as well, for detecting a dead server from the client side: a client that has not received anything (including pings) within pingInterval + pingTimeout assumes the connection is dead and reconnects. Socket.IO clients do this automatically.
  • Protocol-level ping/pong frames on raw ws: call ws.ping() on a timer, mark the socket alive on pong, and terminate sockets that missed two consecutive pings.
// Raw ws heartbeat: terminate sockets that did not answer the previous ping.
const interval = setInterval(() => {
  for (const ws of wss.clients) {
    if ((ws as any).isAlive === false) { ws.terminate(); continue; }   // missed a ping
    (ws as any).isAlive = false;
    ws.ping();
  }
}, 30_000);
wss.on('connection', (ws) => {
  (ws as any).isAlive = true;
  ws.on('pong', () => { (ws as any).isAlive = true; });
});

NAT and idle timeouts are why the interval is what it is. Home routers and mobile carrier NATs drop idle TCP mappings after somewhere between 30 seconds and a few minutes; once the mapping is gone, the next server-to-client frame vanishes, and the client only finds out when it tries to send. A ping every 25 seconds keeps the mapping alive on almost every network. Below 15 seconds you waste battery on mobile; above 60 seconds you start losing connections on aggressive carriers.

Choose the numbers as a table, with each layer's timeout larger than the one it wraps: ping interval 25 s, pong timeout 20 s (so detection takes at most 45 s), load balancer idle timeout at least 120 s, ingress read timeout 3,600 s. Detection latency is the sum of interval and timeout; a product that needs "offline within 10 seconds" needs a 5 second interval and pays for it in traffic and battery.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A pong is answered by the client's network stack even when the application is frozen (protocol-level pong is automatic in browsers). If you need "the app is alive", send an application-level heartbeat message and have the app respond.
  • Mobile OS background restrictions suspend JavaScript timers; the client cannot ping, and the server sees a timeout. Treat mobile background as an expected disconnect, keep the presence TTL, and let the client reconnect on foreground.
  • Ping frames count as traffic to some load balancers' idle timers and not to others; test yours.
  • A ping timeout during a GC pause or event loop stall on the server disconnects healthy clients in bulk; the event loop lag metric from Part 42 tells you that this is what happened.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a WebSocket message emitted on one pod not reach a client on another, and how do you fix it? Expected: rooms are in-memory per process; a Pub/Sub adapter broadcasts emit intent to every pod. Follow-up: what happens when Redis is down? (Pods become islands; readiness should fail.)
  2. Design presence for a chat app with multiple devices per user. Expected: TTL key per device refreshed on heartbeat, device set per user, offline only when no live devices, lazy cleanup, last-seen in PostgreSQL. Follow-up: what is the staleness bound after a pod crash?
  3. How do you drain a WebSocket pod during a deploy? Expected: fail readiness, wait, tell clients to reconnect with jitter, close local sockets, exit within the grace period.
  4. What is backpressure on a WebSocket and how do you handle it? Expected: slow client, write buffer grows; coalesce, volatile, drop the connection at a threshold.
  5. Why 25 seconds for a ping interval? Expected: NAT mapping timeouts and load balancer idle timeouts versus battery; detection latency is interval plus timeout.
  6. Sticky sessions or not? Expected: required only for long-polling; websocket-only plus the Redis adapter is stateless from the LB's point of view.

Practical exercise

Make the order gateway safe to run as three pods:

  1. Install the Redis adapter; run three instances of the gateway behind a local nginx with WebSocket upgrade support and a 60 second read timeout.
  2. Implement PresenceService with 60 second TTL keys and 25 second refresh; expose GET /presence/:userId for the notification service.
  3. Implement graceful drain on SIGTERM with a jittered server.reconnect message.
  4. Acceptance: a message published through pod 1 reaches a client on pod 3 within 50 ms; killing pod 2 with SIGKILL leaves its users online in Redis for at most 60 seconds; sending SIGTERM to pod 2 reconnects its clients to the other pods spread over 10 seconds with no client seeing an error; a client that stops answering pings is disconnected within 45 seconds and its presence key deleted; with the nginx read timeout at 60 seconds and pings at 25 seconds, no connection drops over a 10 minute idle test.

34.9 Reconnection and resume

34.9.1 Exponential backoff with jitter, and resuming from a sequence number

Concept

Connections drop. Trains go through tunnels, pods roll, load balancers time out. Reconnection is the client's job; resume is the shared contract that makes a reconnect invisible to the user: the client tells the server the last event it saw, and the server replays what was missed. Without resume, every reconnect is a data loss window; without backoff, every mass disconnect is a self-inflicted denial of service.

Why does it exist?

When a pod holding 20,000 connections dies, 20,000 clients notice within 45 seconds and all try to reconnect. If they retry immediately and at the same cadence, the remaining pods see a synchronized wave every second until it succeeds, and each wave costs 20,000 TLS handshakes and JWT verifications. A pod that was fine at 2,000 handshakes per second falls over at 20,000, its clients disconnect, and the wave grows. This is the thundering herd, and jitter is the cure.

Mental model

Imagine a fire alarm in a stadium and one exit. If everyone runs to it at once, nobody gets out. If people leave section by section with a few seconds between them, the same exit clears the stadium. Exponential backoff is "wait longer each time the door is blocked"; jitter is "and do not all wait the same amount".

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as GatewayFleet
    participant S as RedisStream
    C->>G: connected, receives events seq 40, 41, 42
    Note over C: stores lastSeq 42 per stream
    G--xC: connection lost, pod restarted
    Note over C: attempt 1 after 1 s plus random 0 to 1 s
    C->>G: reconnect fails, fleet still absorbing wave
    Note over C: attempt 2 after 2 s plus jitter, attempt 3 after 4 s plus jitter, cap 30 s
    C->>G: connect with auth token and resume order:8812 from seq 42
    G->>S: XRANGE order:8812 after id for seq 42
    S-->>G: events seq 43, 44
    G-->>C: replay 43, 44 then live from 45
    Note over C: if gap too large the server says RESYNC and client fetches state via REST
  1. Detect. The client learns the connection is dead from a close event or a missed ping.
  2. Back off. Attempt n waits min(cap, base * 2^n) plus random jitter. With base 1 second, cap 30 seconds and full jitter, attempts land at roughly 0 to 1 s, 0 to 2 s, 0 to 4 s, and so on. Socket.IO's client implements exactly this with reconnectionDelay, reconnectionDelayMax and randomizationFactor.
  3. Reconnect and authenticate. A fresh handshake; the token may need refreshing first if it expired during the outage.
  4. Resume. The client sends, per stream it cares about, the last sequence number or event id it processed. The server replays from the buffer (a Redis Stream per room, capped at a few hundred entries or a few minutes), then switches to live.
  5. Resync when the buffer cannot cover the gap. If the last id is older than the buffer, the server replies RESYNC; the client fetches the full current state via REST and starts fresh from the current sequence. This is the fallback that makes the whole design safe: the replay buffer is an optimization, and REST is the source of truth.
// Client side (browser or React Native) with the Socket.IO client
const socket = io('https://rt.example.com/orders', {
  transports: ['websocket'],
  auth: (cb) => cb({ token: getFreshAccessToken() }),   // called on every (re)connect, so expired tokens are refreshed
  reconnection: true,
  reconnectionDelay: 1_000,
  reconnectionDelayMax: 30_000,
  randomizationFactor: 0.5,                             // jitter: each delay is multiplied by a random factor in 0.5 to 1.5
});

socket.on('connect', () => {
  for (const [orderId, lastSeq] of lastSeqByOrder) {
    socket.emit('order.resume', { orderId, lastSeq }, (ack: { status: 'OK' | 'RESYNC' }) => {
      if (ack.status === 'RESYNC') refetchOrderState(orderId);   // buffer could not cover the gap
    });
  }
});

socket.on('order.status', (ev) => {
  if (ev.seq <= (lastSeqByOrder.get(ev.orderId) ?? 0)) return;   // duplicate after replay: ignore
  applyEvent(ev);
  lastSeqByOrder.set(ev.orderId, ev.seq);
});

NestJS example

The server side of resume reads the Redis Stream for the room. Each business event written to the stream carries a monotonically increasing seq from PostgreSQL (the order's version column is a natural choice), so the client's lastSeq maps to a stream position.

// realtime/order-stream.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

export interface OrderEvent { seq: number; type: string; payload: unknown; }

@Injectable()
export class OrderStreamService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  // Called by the Kafka consumer for every business event, before emitting to the room.
  async append(orderId: string, ev: OrderEvent): Promise<void> {
    // Cap the stream at roughly 500 entries; older entries are trimmed lazily.
    await this.redis.xadd(`stream:order:${orderId}`, 'MAXLEN', '~', '500', '*',
      'seq', String(ev.seq), 'type', ev.type, 'payload', JSON.stringify(ev.payload));
    await this.redis.expire(`stream:order:${orderId}`, 6 * 3600);   // no order is tracked for more than 6 h
  }

  // Returns events after lastSeq, or null when the buffer no longer covers that point.
  async replaySince(orderId: string, lastSeq: number): Promise<OrderEvent[] | null> {
    const raw = await this.redis.xrange(`stream:order:${orderId}`, '-', '+');
    const events = raw.map(([, fields]) => this.parse(fields));
    if (events.length === 0) return lastSeq === 0 ? [] : null;
    if (events[0].seq > lastSeq + 1) return null;         // the client's position was trimmed away
    return events.filter((e) => e.seq > lastSeq);
  }

  private parse(fields: string[]): OrderEvent {
    const f: Record<string, string> = {};
    for (let i = 0; i < fields.length; i += 2) f[fields[i]] = fields[i + 1];
    return { seq: Number(f.seq), type: f.type, payload: JSON.parse(f.payload) };
  }
}

// In the gateway
@UseGuards(WsAuthGuard)
@SubscribeMessage('order.resume')
async resume(@ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() dto: ResumeOrderDto) {
  if (!(await this.orders.canView(client.data.userId, dto.orderId))) throw new WsException('FORBIDDEN');
  await client.join(`order:${dto.orderId}`);            // join first so live events are not missed during replay
  const missed = await this.stream.replaySince(dto.orderId, dto.lastSeq);
  if (missed === null) return { status: 'RESYNC' };
  for (const ev of missed) client.emit('order.status', { orderId: dto.orderId, ...ev });
  return { status: 'OK', replayed: missed.length };
}

Joining the room before replaying means a live event that arrives during the replay is delivered too, possibly twice (once from replay, once live). The client's seq check makes the duplicate harmless. That is the at-least-once plus dedup pattern from 34.10.

Production scenario

A gateway fleet loses one pod of ten at 20:00 during peak: 20,000 clients disconnect. With full jitter and a 30 second cap, the remaining nine pods see about 4,000 reconnects in the first second, 2,500 in the second, and the wave is fully absorbed in 12 seconds with p99 handshake latency staying under 150 ms. Without jitter, the same fleet saw 20,000 reconnects in the first 200 ms, two more pods hit their file descriptor limit, and the cascade took 4 minutes to settle. Resume replayed on average 1.3 events per client from Redis Streams; 0.2 percent of clients got RESYNC because their last event was more than 500 events back (long-running admin dashboards).

Failure scenario

At 03:30 a Redis maintenance failover clears the Streams (the instance was configured without persistence, which was fine for the adapter but not for the replay buffer that had been added to the same instance). Every reconnecting client sends order.resume with a real lastSeq, the stream is empty, and the server, following the code above, returns RESYNC. Ten thousand clients refetch order state via REST within 30 seconds, a 100x spike on GET /orders/:id. The API survived because the endpoint was cached, but the retrospective moved the replay stream to a persistent Redis with AOF enabled and added a small random delay to the client's resync fetch.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Token expired during the outage. The reconnect fails with UNAUTHORIZED and the naive client retries forever with the same token. Refresh the token in the auth callback and stop retrying after a 401.
  • Reconnect to the same dead pod because the load balancer has not yet noticed it is gone; the first attempt fails, backoff handles it.
  • Replay before join misses live events emitted during the replay; join first, dedup by sequence.
  • Buffers per room grow without bound if MAXLEN and EXPIRE are forgotten; 200,000 orders times 10,000 events is Redis out of memory.
  • Clients that never reset their backoff after a successful connection start the next outage at the 30 second cap. Reset on connect.
  • A client that resumes with a lastSeq from a different stream (a bug in client state) receives nothing or RESYNC; never trust it for authorization, only for positioning.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the resume contract before the first message is sent: every stream has a monotonically increasing sequence, every client stores the last sequence it applied, every reconnect carries it, and REST remains the source of truth for a full resync. They insist on jitter in every client library and test it by killing a pod under load. They keep the replay buffer on persistent Redis, separate from the adapter's Pub/Sub instance if budget allows, because the two have different durability needs.

34.10 Ordering and delivery guarantees

34.10.1 Per-connection ordering, cross-pod ordering and at-least-once plus dedup

Concept

A single TCP connection delivers bytes in order, so messages written to one socket by one process arrive in the order written. Everything beyond that single socket is unordered by default: two pods emitting to the same room, a replay racing a live event, a Kafka topic with several partitions, a retry after a timeout. Delivery guarantees are the promises you make on top of that: at-most-once (fire and forget), at-least-once (retry until acknowledged, accept duplicates), exactly-once (which in practice means at-least-once plus deduplication at the receiver).

Why does it exist?

An order status stream that shows "delivered" then "on the way" is a bug the customer notices immediately. A chat that shows a reply before the message it answers is unusable. A driver location that jumps backwards makes the map twitch. Ordering matters to humans in ways it never mattered to log lines.

Mental model

Imagine numbered pages of a report arriving by several couriers. Each courier hands over their pages in order, but couriers arrive in any order. If every page has a number, the reader can put them in order, notice that page 7 is missing and ask for it, and throw away a second copy of page 5. Sequence numbers are the page numbers; gap detection is noticing page 7 is missing.

How it works

  1. Assign a sequence at the source of truth. The number must be assigned where the order of events is decided, which for an order is the database transaction that changes its state. PostgreSQL's version column (incremented on every update, or a @VersionColumn in TypeORM) gives a strictly increasing per-order sequence for free, and it is assigned under the row lock so two concurrent updates cannot share a number.
  2. Carry the sequence end to end. Into the outbox row, the Kafka message, the Redis Stream entry and the WebSocket payload.
  3. Preserve order per key upstream. Kafka keeps order per partition; publish every event for one order with the order id as the message key so they land on the same partition, and consume each partition with one consumer at a time. This gives per-order ordering across the whole pipeline without global ordering (which does not scale).
  4. Client applies events in sequence. It keeps lastSeq per stream, ignores seq <= lastSeq (duplicates) and, on seq > lastSeq + 1 (a gap), either waits briefly for the missing event or asks for a replay from lastSeq.
  5. Server emits are at-least-once by construction whenever replay exists, and the client's dedup makes the visible result exactly-once.
// Client-side ordering and gap detection for one stream
function onEvent(ev: { seq: number }, state: { lastSeq: number; pending: Map<number, unknown> }) {
  if (ev.seq <= state.lastSeq) return;                 // duplicate
  if (ev.seq === state.lastSeq + 1) {
    apply(ev); state.lastSeq = ev.seq;
    while (state.pending.has(state.lastSeq + 1)) {     // drain buffered out-of-order events
      apply(state.pending.get(state.lastSeq + 1)); state.pending.delete(++state.lastSeq);
    }
    return;
  }
  state.pending.set(ev.seq, ev);                       // gap: hold it
  if (state.pending.size > 20) requestReplay(state.lastSeq);   // gap is not closing; refetch
}

Cross-pod ordering. Two pods emitting to the same room can interleave in any order at the client; nothing in Redis Pub/Sub prevents it. If a room's events come from one Kafka partition consumed by one consumer, this cannot happen for that room, because only one pod emits for it at a time. If several producers can emit for the same room (an order updated by the customer service and the driver service), the sequence number is the only thing that makes the client's view consistent, and the client-side reorder buffer above is what applies it.

Delivery guarantee decision table.

Guarantee Server does Client does Use for
At-most-once Emit once, no buffer, volatile Nothing Typing indicators, cursor positions, high-frequency telemetry where the next value supersedes
At-least-once Emit and keep in a replay buffer; replay on resume Dedup by sequence Order status, chat messages, notifications
Effectively exactly-once At-least-once, plus idempotent server-side handling of client messages by clientMessageId Dedup incoming by sequence; attach a unique id to every outgoing message; retry until acked Chat sends, collaborative edits, anything a user would notice twice

PostgreSQL example

The sequence comes from the row. With optimistic locking it is also the concurrency guard.

-- version increments on every state change and becomes the event sequence
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  version     integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Update under the row lock; the returned version is the seq for the emitted event.
UPDATE orders SET status = 'on_the_way', version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'preparing'
RETURNING version AS seq;

The outbox row for this change stores seq, the Kafka message carries it, and the client sees seq: 5 after seq: 4 no matter which pod delivered it.

TypeORM example

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column() status: string;
  @VersionColumn() version: number;   // incremented automatically on save; used as the event seq
}

// In the service, after save(), order.version is the new sequence.
const saved = await manager.save(order);
await outbox.insert({ aggregateId: saved.id, seq: saved.version, type: 'order.status', payload: { status: saved.status } });

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Sequence assigned in the gateway instead of at the source: two pods assign overlapping numbers and the client's dedup discards real events.
  • Kafka key missing: events for one order spread across partitions and arrive out of order at the gateway.
  • Consumer rebalance: for a few seconds two consumers may process the same partition's tail; at-least-once semantics and client dedup cover it.
  • Retrying a client message without an id: a chat message sent, timed out and re-sent appears twice for everyone. Every client-originated message carries a UUID and the server dedups on it (a Redis SET NX with a 10 minute TTL, or a unique constraint).
  • Reorder buffer that never drains because the gap event was genuinely lost upstream: cap the buffer and request replay.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never promise global ordering; they promise per-key ordering and design the keys (order id, conversation id, document id). They put the sequence where the truth is decided, the database row, and carry it everywhere. They accept at-least-once as the honest guarantee and put deduplication at the edges, because "exactly-once" in a distributed system is at-least-once wearing a costume.

34.11 Security

34.11.1 Origin, auth, rate limits and payload limits

Concept

A WebSocket server is an open port that accepts long-lived connections from anyone who can reach it, holds memory per connection, runs code per message and can broadcast to thousands of clients per emit. Every one of those properties is an attack surface: connection floods, message floods, oversized payloads, cross-site connection hijacking, unauthorized room joins, and data leaks through broadcasts.

How it works

Threat Control
Cross-site WebSocket hijacking (a malicious page opens a socket to your origin and the browser sends your cookies) Check Origin on the upgrade against an allowlist; Socket.IO's cors.origin does this. Prefer token auth over cookies for WebSockets
Unauthenticated connections held open Authenticate in the handshake or within 5 seconds of connect; disconnect otherwise
Expired or revoked tokens on long connections Store exp on the socket, check it on every message and on a periodic timer; on expiry emit auth.expired and disconnect; check a revocation set on connect
Unauthorized room joins Every join validates ownership against the database or an ownership cache; room names are built server-side from validated ids
Message floods from one client Per-socket token bucket: for example 20 messages per second burst, 5 per second sustained; disconnect on repeated violation
Connection floods from one IP Rate limit upgrades per IP at the ingress or load balancer; the API gateway's WAF can do this before the pod sees it
Oversized payloads maxHttpBufferSize in Socket.IO (default 1 MB; set 64 KB for most apps); maxPayload in ws
Malformed payloads ValidationPipe with whitelist: true on every @SubscribeMessage handler, DTOs with class-validator
PII in broadcasts Rooms carry only what every member may see; a driver's location goes to the order room, the driver's phone number never does
Information leakage in errors WsException messages are codes (FORBIDDEN), not stack traces
Server-side request forgery via user-supplied URLs in messages Never fetch a URL from a message payload without an allowlist 
// realtime/ws-rate-limit.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { WsException } from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { Socket } from 'socket.io';

const BURST = 20;
const REFILL_PER_SEC = 5;

@Injectable()
export class WsRateLimitGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const client = ctx.switchToWs().getClient<Socket>();
    const now = Date.now();
    const bucket = (client.data.bucket ??= { tokens: BURST, updatedAt: now });
    bucket.tokens = Math.min(BURST, bucket.tokens + ((now - bucket.updatedAt) / 1000) * REFILL_PER_SEC);
    bucket.updatedAt = now;
    if (bucket.tokens < 1) {
      client.data.violations = (client.data.violations ?? 0) + 1;
      if (client.data.violations > 10) client.disconnect(true);   // persistent abuser
      throw new WsException('RATE_LIMITED');
    }
    bucket.tokens -= 1;
    return true;
  }
}

Apply it with @UseGuards(WsAuthGuard, WsRateLimitGuard) on every handler. The bucket lives on the socket, so a reconnect resets it; the ingress-level per-IP limit covers reconnect abuse.

Failure scenario

A penetration test connects to the chat gateway with a valid user token and sends { "conversationId": "*" } to the join handler. The handler built the room name as conv:${dto.conversationId} with no validation, and Socket.IO happily joined the socket to conv:*. Nothing was emitted to that literal room, so the tester found nothing, but the next test sent a conversation id belonging to another user, and the handler had no ownership check. Every message of every conversation was readable with one guessable id. Both bugs are one line each: @IsUUID() on the DTO and canView before join.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat every @SubscribeMessage handler like a POST endpoint: validated DTO, guard, rate limit, authorization, audit log. They keep secrets out of URLs and logs, bound every buffer, and assume a client will connect ten thousand times and send a megabyte per message until told otherwise. They ask the security team to test the WebSocket path explicitly, because most scanners only cover REST.

34.12 Scaling

34.12.1 Numbers, topology and protocol cost

Concept

Scaling real-time is about three limits: connections per pod (memory and file descriptors), messages per second per pod (CPU, mostly serialization and socket writes), and fan-out traffic through the Pub/Sub layer (Redis throughput and the per-pod cost of receiving every publish).

How it works

Connections per pod. With Socket.IO on Node.js, 20,000 to 30,000 mostly idle connections per 2 CPU, 3 GB pod is comfortable; 50,000 is possible with tuning; beyond that, single-process limits and GC pauses hurt tail latency. With raw ws and a binary protocol, 100,000 per pod is achievable. The number that actually bounds you is usually the reconnect wave a pod's death causes, not memory.

Messages per pod. JSON serialization is the CPU cost. JSON.stringify of a 200 byte object costs about 1 to 2 microseconds; emitting it to 1,000 sockets in a room costs one serialization (Socket.IO encodes once per emit) plus 1,000 socket writes at roughly 5 to 10 microseconds each. A pod can push 50,000 to 100,000 small messages per second before CPU saturates. Large payloads change the arithmetic: a 20 KB JSON to 1,000 sockets is 20 MB of writes per emit.

Dedicated gateway versus embedded. Embedding the gateway in the API pods is simplest and correct for small systems. It couples two very different workloads: a reconnect storm or a slow-client memory leak takes down checkout; scaling the API for CPU also scales the number of pods that must subscribe to Pub/Sub; rolling the API for a bug fix disconnects every real-time client. Past a few thousand connections, split the gateway into its own deployment with its own HPA, its own memory headroom and its own rollout schedule. The gateway then consumes Kafka and talks to Redis; it does not talk to PostgreSQL at all except for authorization lookups, which are cached.

Horizontal scaling with the Redis adapter. Each pod receives every publish. At N pods and P publishes per second, Redis delivers N times P messages per second and each pod deserializes P messages per second regardless of whether it has a member for the room. That is fine to about 20 pods and 10,000 publishes per second (200,000 deliveries per second, 10 to 20 percent CPU per pod on the adapter). Beyond that: shard rooms across Redis channels with the sharded adapter, or partition rooms by hash across gateway groups so a group only subscribes to its share, or use a message bus with real subscriptions (NATS, or Kafka with one consumer group per gateway group and topic partitioning by room hash).

Binary protocols. MessagePack or Protobuf cut payload size by 30 to 70 percent and serialization CPU by a similar factor; Socket.IO supports a MessagePack parser as a drop-in. The cost is debuggability (you cannot read the frames in the browser's network tab) and client complexity. Reach for it when messages per second per pod is your bottleneck and the payload is numeric (locations, telemetry, game state).

flowchart LR
    subgraph Producers
        OS["Order service"] --> OB["Outbox"] --> K["Kafka topic order.events keyed by orderId"]
        DS["Driver service"] --> K2["Kafka topic driver.locations keyed by orderId"]
    end
    subgraph GatewayFleet["Gateway deployment, own HPA"]
        G1["Gateway pod 1"]
        G2["Gateway pod 2"]
        GN["Gateway pod N"]
    end
    K --> G1
    K --> G2
    K --> GN
    K2 --> G1
    K2 --> G2
    K2 --> GN
    G1 <--> R["Redis: adapter Pub/Sub plus replay Streams plus presence"]
    G2 <--> R
    GN <--> R
    LB["Load balancer with long idle timeout"] --> G1
    LB --> G2
    LB --> GN
    C1["Customers and drivers"] --> LB

The Kafka consumer group across the gateway pods means each order's events are consumed by exactly one pod, which then publishes to the room through Redis. That pod may hold none of the room's sockets; the adapter handles it.

Production scenario

A ride-hailing product at evening peak: 400,000 concurrent riders and drivers, 20 gateway pods at 20,000 connections each, driver locations at one message per 3 seconds per active trip (60,000 trips: 20,000 messages per second), fan-out of one message to one rider each. Kafka partitions: 48 for driver.locations, consumed by 20 pods. Redis adapter traffic: 20,000 publishes per second, 400,000 deliveries per second across the fleet; each pod spends 15 percent of one core on the adapter and 25 percent on socket writes. The team is planning the sharded adapter for when the fleet passes 30 pods.

Failure scenario

An engineering team embeds the WebSocket gateway in the main API. A marketing push brings 80,000 users at once; each opens a socket. The API pods, sized for REST CPU, hit their file descriptor limit at 65,536 combined connections and start failing REST calls with EMFILE. Checkout is down because the tracking page is popular. The gateway was split out the following week, with ulimit set from the connection target and an HPA on a websocket_connections custom metric.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • HPA on CPU alone scales the gateway down during a quiet period and then a single pod holds 80,000 connections; the next scale-up event drains them in a wave. Scale on connection count with a minimum replica floor.
  • Kafka consumer group with more gateway pods than partitions leaves pods idle for consumption but still serving sockets; that is fine and expected.
  • The adapter's request-response calls (fetchSockets) at 30 pods take seconds; anything on the hot path that uses them is a latency bug.
  • A single 1 MB message to a room with 5,000 members is 5 GB of writes across the fleet. Cap payloads and send references (an id to fetch), not documents.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start embedded, with the Redis adapter, and split the gateway out at the first sign of interference between workloads. They size pods by reconnect arithmetic, scale on connections, and keep the gateway ignorant of PostgreSQL. They resist binary protocols until serialization CPU is measured as the bottleneck. They explain to product that "one event to a million clients" is not a WebSocket problem but a fan-out problem that needs a hierarchy, batching or a CDN-style push, and they size the promise accordingly.

Interview questions

  1. A pod holding 20,000 connections dies. What happens and how do you make it survivable? Expected: reconnect wave; exponential backoff with jitter on the client; resume by sequence with a bounded replay buffer; RESYNC via REST; pods sized with headroom.
  2. How do you guarantee ordering for one order's events across Kafka, Redis and several pods? Expected: sequence assigned at the database row, Kafka keyed by order id, per-partition consumption, client dedup and reorder by sequence.
  3. What is the honest delivery guarantee of a WebSocket system and how do you get to effectively exactly-once? Expected: at-least-once with replay; dedup by sequence downstream and by client message id upstream.
  4. List five security controls specific to WebSockets. Expected: origin allowlist, handshake auth with expiry handling, per-room authorization, per-socket rate limiting, payload size limits, DTO validation.
  5. When do you split the gateway out of the API? Expected: when connection-driven load (handshakes, memory, FDs) can interfere with REST, or rollouts of the API would disconnect clients; typically past a few thousand connections.
  6. What limits the Redis adapter, and what comes next? Expected: every pod receives every publish; sharded adapter, room partitioning, or a bus with real subscriptions.

Practical exercise

Add resume, ordering and security to the order gateway:

  1. Add a version-based sequence to order status events, carried through the outbox, Kafka (keyed by order id) and the Redis Stream.
  2. Implement order.resume with replay from the stream and RESYNC when the gap exceeds the buffer.
  3. Implement the client with full-jitter backoff, per-stream lastSeq, and a reorder buffer capped at 20 events.
  4. Add WsRateLimitGuard, maxHttpBufferSize: 65536, an Origin allowlist and token expiry checks.
  5. Acceptance: with the gateway running as three pods, killing one under a load of 5,000 connected clients results in every client reconnecting within 30 seconds with no missed or duplicated status events (verified by comparing each client's applied sequence list against the database); a client sending 100 messages in one second is rate limited and disconnected after repeated violations; a connection from a disallowed origin is refused at the handshake; a token that expires during the connection triggers auth.expired and a clean reconnect with a fresh token.

34.13 Worked example: live order tracking for food delivery

34.13.1 The requirement and the architecture

Concept

A customer places an order and opens the tracking screen. They must see the order's status changes (accepted, preparing, picked_up, on_the_way, delivered) within a second of them happening, and the driver's position on a map, updated every few seconds while the order is on_the_way. The driver's app sends its GPS position every 3 seconds to the driver service. Restaurants and support agents may also watch orders. There are 60,000 concurrent orders at peak, roughly 250,000 connected clients, and the gateway must survive deploys and pod failures without the customer noticing.

The flow

flowchart LR
    DA["Driver app"] -->|"POST /locations every 3 s"| DS["Driver service"]
    DS -->|"produce keyed by orderId"| KL["Kafka driver.locations"]
    OSvc["Order service"] -->|"outbox then produce keyed by orderId"| KO["Kafka order.events"]
    KL --> GC["Gateway Kafka consumer, one partition per pod at a time"]
    KO --> GC
    GC -->|"XADD replay stream"| RS["Redis Streams stream:order:id"]
    GC -->|"server.to room order:id emit"| AD["Redis adapter Pub/Sub"]
    AD --> P1["Gateway pod 1"]
    AD --> P2["Gateway pod 2"]
    P1 --> CA["Customer app in room order:8812"]
    P2 --> SA["Support dashboard in room order:8812"]
    CA -->|"reconnect with lastSeq"| P2
    P2 -->|"XRANGE replay"| RS

Design decisions, each with the reason:

  • Kafka is the source of events, not the gateway. The order service writes an outbox row in the same transaction as the status change and a relay publishes it; the driver service publishes locations directly because losing one location is acceptable. Both topics are keyed by orderId so each order's events stay ordered on one partition.
  • The gateway is a separate NestJS deployment that consumes both topics, writes the replay stream, and emits to rooms. It reads PostgreSQL only through a cached canView check on join.
  • Rooms are order:{id}. Customers, drivers, restaurant staff and support join the same room with different authorization rules; the payload carries nothing the least-privileged member may not see (no phone numbers, no addresses; those are fetched via REST with their own guards).
  • Status events are at-least-once with replay; location events are at-most-once and coalesced (volatile), because the next one supersedes.
  • Presence tracks drivers so dispatch can tell "connected" from "app killed", and tracks customers so the notification service can fall back to push.

34.13.2 The code

NestJS example: module and adapter

// realtime/realtime.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtModule } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { OrdersGateway } from './orders.gateway';
import { OrderStreamService } from './order-stream.service';
import { PresenceService } from './presence.service';
import { OrderEventsConsumer } from './order-events.consumer';
import { OrdersAccessService } from './orders-access.service';
import { RealtimeMetrics } from './realtime.metrics';
import { REDIS } from '../redis/redis.module';

@Module({
  imports: [JwtModule.register({ secret: process.env.JWT_PUBLIC_KEY, verifyOptions: { algorithms: ['RS256'] } })],
  providers: [
    OrdersGateway, OrderStreamService, OrdersAccessService, OrderEventsConsumer, RealtimeMetrics,
    { provide: PresenceService, inject: [REDIS], useFactory: (redis) => new PresenceService(redis, process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local') },
  ],
})
export class RealtimeModule {}

The RedisIoAdapter from 34.5 is installed in main.ts exactly as shown there; nothing in this module needs to know about it.

NestJS example: the gateway

// realtime/orders.gateway.ts
import {
  ConnectedSocket, MessageBody, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect, OnGatewayInit,
  SubscribeMessage, WebSocketGateway, WebSocketServer, WsException,
} from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { BeforeApplicationShutdown, Logger, UseGuards, UsePipes, ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { Server, Socket } from 'socket.io';
import { WsAuthGuard } from './ws-auth.guard';
import { WsRateLimitGuard } from './ws-rate-limit.guard';
import { OrdersAccessService } from './orders-access.service';
import { OrderStreamService } from './order-stream.service';
import { PresenceService } from './presence.service';
import { RealtimeMetrics } from './realtime.metrics';
import { ResumeOrderDto } from './dto/resume-order.dto';

interface Handshake { token: string; deviceId: string; role: 'customer' | 'driver' | 'staff'; }

@WebSocketGateway({
  namespace: '/tracking',
  cors: { origin: (process.env.WS_ORIGINS ?? '').split(','), credentials: true },
  transports: ['websocket'],
  pingInterval: 25_000,
  pingTimeout: 20_000,
  maxHttpBufferSize: 32 * 1024,
})
export class OrdersGateway implements OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect, BeforeApplicationShutdown {
  @WebSocketServer() server: Server;
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrdersGateway.name);
  private draining = false;

  constructor(
    private readonly jwt: JwtService,
    private readonly access: OrdersAccessService,
    private readonly stream: OrderStreamService,
    private readonly presence: PresenceService,
    private readonly metrics: RealtimeMetrics,
  ) {}

  afterInit(server: Server) {
    // Refuse new upgrades while draining; the LB will route elsewhere once readiness flips.
    server.use((socket, next) => (this.draining ? next(new Error('DRAINING')) : next()));
  }

  async handleConnection(client: Socket) {
    const hs = client.handshake.auth as Partial<Handshake>;
    try {
      if (!hs.token || !hs.deviceId) throw new Error('missing credentials');
      const payload = await this.jwt.verifyAsync<{ sub: string; exp: number; role: string }>(hs.token);
      client.data.userId = payload.sub;
      client.data.role = payload.role;
      client.data.deviceId = hs.deviceId;
      client.data.tokenExp = payload.exp * 1000;
      await this.presence.connected(client.id, payload.sub, hs.deviceId);
      this.metrics.connections.inc({ role: payload.role });
      this.log.log({ userId: payload.sub, role: payload.role, deviceId: hs.deviceId }, 'ws connected');
    } catch (err) {
      this.metrics.authFailures.inc();
      client.emit('error', { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED' });
      client.disconnect(true);
    }
  }

  async handleDisconnect(client: Socket) {
    if (!client.data.userId) return;
    this.metrics.connections.dec({ role: client.data.role });
    this.metrics.disconnects.inc({ reason: (client as any).disconnectReason ?? 'unknown' });
    await this.presence.disconnected(client.id, client.data.userId, client.data.deviceId);
  }

  // Join or resume: the client always sends its lastSeq (0 for a fresh open).
  @UseGuards(WsAuthGuard, WsRateLimitGuard)
  @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }))
  @SubscribeMessage('order.watch')
  async watch(@ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() dto: ResumeOrderDto) {
    const allowed = await this.access.canView(client.data.userId, client.data.role, dto.orderId);
    if (!allowed) throw new WsException('FORBIDDEN');
    await client.join(`order:${dto.orderId}`);
    const missed = await this.stream.replaySince(dto.orderId, dto.lastSeq);
    if (missed === null) { this.metrics.resyncs.inc(); return { status: 'RESYNC' }; }
    for (const ev of missed) client.emit('order.event', { orderId: dto.orderId, ...ev });
    this.metrics.replayed.inc(missed.length);
    return { status: 'OK', replayed: missed.length };
  }

  @UseGuards(WsAuthGuard)
  @SubscribeMessage('order.unwatch')
  async unwatch(@ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() dto: ResumeOrderDto) {
    await client.leave(`order:${dto.orderId}`);
    return { status: 'OK' };
  }

  // Called by the Kafka consumer. Status events are durable and sequenced.
  emitStatus(orderId: string, ev: { seq: number; type: string; payload: unknown }) {
    this.server.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('order.event', { orderId, ...ev });
    this.metrics.emitted.inc({ kind: 'status' });
  }

  // Location events are best-effort: volatile drops them for clients whose transport is not writable.
  emitLocation(orderId: string, loc: { lat: number; lng: number; heading: number; at: number }) {
    this.server.to(`order:${orderId}`).volatile.emit('driver.location', { orderId, ...loc });
    this.metrics.emitted.inc({ kind: 'location' });
  }

  async beforeApplicationShutdown() {
    this.draining = true;
    this.log.warn({ clients: this.server.engine.clientsCount }, 'draining');
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5_000));                    // readiness has flipped; LB stops routing
    const sockets = await this.server.local.fetchSockets();
    for (const s of sockets) s.emit('server.reconnect', { afterMs: Math.floor(Math.random() * 10_000) });
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2_000));
    this.server.local.disconnectSockets(true);
  }
}
// realtime/dto/resume-order.dto.ts
import { IsInt, IsUUID, Min } from 'class-validator';
export class ResumeOrderDto {
  @IsUUID() orderId: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(0) lastSeq: number;
}

NestJS example: authorization with a cache

// realtime/orders-access.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { Order } from '../orders/order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersAccessService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>, private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async canView(userId: string, role: string, orderId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    if (role === 'staff') return true;                       // support and restaurant staff: role-based
    const key = `order:${orderId}:viewers`;
    let viewers = await this.redis.smembers(key);
    if (viewers.length === 0) {
      const order = await this.orders.findOne({ where: { id: orderId }, select: ['customerId', 'driverId'] });
      if (!order) return false;
      viewers = [order.customerId, order.driverId].filter(Boolean) as string[];
      await this.redis.multi().sadd(key, ...viewers).expire(key, 300).exec();   // 5 minute cache; driver reassignment invalidates it
    }
    return viewers.includes(userId);
  }

  async invalidate(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.del(`order:${orderId}:viewers`);
  }
}

The order service calls invalidate (through an event) when a driver is reassigned, so the old driver loses access within one event rather than five minutes. That still leaves the old driver in the room until their socket rejoins; 34.15 covers evicting them.

NestJS example: the Kafka consumer

// realtime/order-events.consumer.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Consumer, Kafka } from 'kafkajs';
import { OrdersGateway } from './orders.gateway';
import { OrderStreamService } from './order-stream.service';
import { OrdersAccessService } from './orders-access.service';

@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsConsumer implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderEventsConsumer.name);
  private consumer: Consumer;

  constructor(
    private readonly gateway: OrdersGateway,
    private readonly stream: OrderStreamService,
    private readonly access: OrdersAccessService,
  ) {}

  async onModuleInit() {
    const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'tracking-gateway', brokers: process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS!.split(',') });
    this.consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: 'tracking-gateway', sessionTimeout: 30_000 });
    await this.consumer.connect();
    await this.consumer.subscribe({ topics: ['order.events', 'driver.locations'] });
    await this.consumer.run({
      eachMessage: async ({ topic, message }) => {
        const orderId = message.key!.toString();
        const body = JSON.parse(message.value!.toString());
        if (topic === 'order.events') {
          const ev = { seq: body.seq as number, type: body.type as string, payload: body.payload };
          await this.stream.append(orderId, ev);          // durable replay first, then live emit
          this.gateway.emitStatus(orderId, ev);
          if (body.type === 'order.driver_assigned') await this.access.invalidate(orderId);
        } else {
          // Drop stale locations: if the message is older than 15 s the next one is already on its way.
          if (Date.now() - body.at > 15_000) return;
          this.gateway.emitLocation(orderId, { lat: body.lat, lng: body.lng, heading: body.heading, at: body.at });
        }
      },
    });
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    await this.consumer?.disconnect();   // leave the group cleanly so the rebalance is fast
  }
}

Writing to the replay stream before emitting means a client that reconnects during the emit finds the event in the stream. The order (stream first, then emit) is what makes the at-least-once promise true.

PostgreSQL example

The order service's side of the contract: the status change, its sequence and its outbox row commit together.

BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'on_the_way', version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'picked_up'
RETURNING version;                                     -- suppose it returns 4

INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, seq, payload, created_at)
VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 'order', $1, 'order.status', 4,
        jsonb_build_object('status', 'on_the_way', 'eta', $2), now());
COMMIT;

The relay publishes to order.events with key = aggregate_id and seq in the body. See Part 27 — Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS for the outbox relay itself.

Client behaviour summary

The customer app opens the socket with { token, deviceId, role: 'customer' }, emits order.watch { orderId, lastSeq } on every connect (including reconnects), applies order.event in sequence with dedup, applies driver.location immediately (latest wins, no sequence), and on server.reconnect closes and reconnects after the given delay. On RESYNC it calls GET /orders/:id and resets lastSeq to the returned version.

Production scenario

Peak numbers for this design: 60,000 active orders, 250,000 sockets on 12 gateway pods, 20,000 location messages per second and 300 status events per second consumed from Kafka across 48 partitions, Redis adapter at 20,300 publishes and 244,000 deliveries per second, replay streams totalling 1.2 GB in Redis (60,000 orders times about 20 KB), presence at 10,000 EXPIREs per second. p99 from Kafka produce to customer screen is 220 ms for status and 90 ms for location. A rolling deploy of the gateway takes 9 minutes and produces zero customer-visible errors.

34.14 Observability for real-time systems

34.14.1 The gauges and rates that matter

Concept

Real-time systems fail quietly. A REST API that breaks returns 500s and the error ratio alert fires. A WebSocket gateway that breaks keeps connections open and simply stops delivering, or delivers to half the clients, and nothing in the standard RED metrics changes. The metrics here are chosen to make silence visible.

How it works

// realtime/realtime.metrics.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Counter, Gauge, Histogram } from 'prom-client';
import { registry } from '../metrics/registry';

@Injectable()
export class RealtimeMetrics {
  readonly connections = new Gauge({ name: 'ws_connections', help: 'Open sockets on this pod', labelNames: ['role'], registers: [registry] });
  readonly emitted = new Counter({ name: 'ws_messages_emitted_total', help: 'Room emits by kind', labelNames: ['kind'], registers: [registry] });
  readonly disconnects = new Counter({ name: 'ws_disconnects_total', help: 'Disconnects by reason', labelNames: ['reason'], registers: [registry] });
  readonly authFailures = new Counter({ name: 'ws_auth_failures_total', help: 'Handshakes rejected', registers: [registry] });
  readonly replayed = new Counter({ name: 'ws_events_replayed_total', help: 'Events replayed on resume', registers: [registry] });
  readonly resyncs = new Counter({ name: 'ws_resyncs_total', help: 'Resumes that fell back to REST', registers: [registry] });
  readonly handshakeDuration = new Histogram({ name: 'ws_handshake_duration_seconds', help: 'Connect to authenticated', buckets: [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1], registers: [registry] });
  readonly slowClients = new Gauge({ name: 'ws_slow_clients', help: 'Sockets with a write backlog over the threshold', registers: [registry] });
  readonly deliveryLag = new Histogram({ name: 'ws_delivery_lag_seconds', help: 'Kafka message timestamp to emit', buckets: [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5], registers: [registry] });
}
Metric What it catches
ws_connections per pod Uneven distribution (one pod at 60,000 while others idle), a pod silently losing all clients, HPA input
rate(ws_disconnects_total[5m]) by reason A reconnect storm (transport close spikes), a load balancer timeout (ping timeout every N seconds), a deploy
rate(ws_messages_emitted_total[5m]) versus Kafka consume rate Emits dropping while consumption continues means the adapter or rooms are broken
ws_delivery_lag_seconds p99 Consumer lag plus processing delay, the customer-facing latency
ws_events_replayed_total and ws_resyncs_total Reconnect health; resyncs rising means the replay buffer is too small or Redis lost data
ws_slow_clients Backpressure building; a precursor to memory growth
ws_auth_failures_total Token rollout problems or an attack
Kafka consumer lag for tracking-gateway The gateway is behind; delivery lag will follow
Redis adapter publish errors (from ioredis error events, counted) The cluster is splitting into islands

Alerts, symptom-based as always: delivery lag p99 above 2 seconds for 5 minutes; disconnect rate above 5 times the 1 hour baseline; emitted rate dropping below 50 percent of the consumed rate; any pod at more than 80 percent of its connection ceiling. Plus a synthetic end-to-end check: a probe connects to the gateway, publishes a test event to a test order through the real Kafka path, and asserts it arrives within 3 seconds. That single check catches every "everything is green but nothing arrives" failure in this part.

Traces cross this system too. The Kafka message carries traceparent from the order service; the consumer span in the gateway is the child of the outbox relay's produce span; the emit is an event on that span with the room and member count. A customer complaint with an order id becomes a trace search on order.id, showing the status change, the outbox relay delay, the consumer lag and the emit, in one timeline.

34.15 Edge cases & failure modes

  • Load balancer killing idle connections. An ALB with a 60 second idle timeout and a client that stops answering pings in the background produces a disconnect every minute per backgrounded app. Symptom: ws_disconnects_total{reason="transport close"} at a steady rate that matches the timeout. Fix: idle timeout well above the ping interval, and treat backgrounded mobile as expected disconnect.
  • Pod restart dropping 50,000 connections at once. Without jitter, the reconnect wave overloads the survivors and cascades. With full-jitter backoff (1 s base, 30 s cap) and pods at 60 percent capacity, the wave drains in 10 to 20 seconds. Keep per-pod connection counts low enough that any single pod's loss is absorbable, and scale on connections with a replica floor.
  • Messages lost during reconnect. Anything emitted between the disconnect and the rejoin is gone unless it went to the replay stream first. The consumer writes the stream before emitting; the client resumes with lastSeq; a gap larger than the buffer triggers RESYNC via REST.
  • Duplicate delivery after replay. Joining the room before replaying means a live event can arrive during replay and again from it. The client's sequence dedup makes this harmless; without sequences, the customer sees "on the way" twice and support gets a ticket.
  • Slow consumer memory growth. One client on a congested link stops reading; every emit to its room appends to its buffer. With volatile for high-frequency events and a per-socket backlog limit that disconnects the client at 1 MB, the pod is protected. Without either, one bad client can take a pod to OOMKilled, which drops the other 20,000.
  • Redis adapter down, cluster splits. Each pod keeps serving its own sockets but only sees events its own consumer processed. Readiness must include the adapter's Redis so the pod is removed from rotation, the synthetic check must fail loudly, and the client's resume covers the gap once Redis returns.
  • Auth token expiring mid-connection. The connection was authenticated an hour ago; the token expired 30 minutes ago; the user was disabled 10 minutes ago. Check exp on every message and on a periodic timer, emit auth.expired and disconnect; subscribe to a user.disabled event and disconnect that user's sockets fleet-wide with server.in(user:${id}).disconnectSockets().
  • Room membership stale after user removal. A driver reassigned away from an order is still in order:8812 and keeps receiving events until they disconnect. Authorization on join is not enough; on a reassignment event, make the old driver leave: server.in(user:${oldDriverId}).socketsLeave(order:${orderId}), which the Redis adapter propagates across pods.
  • Message ordering across pods. Two pods emitting for the same room interleave arbitrarily. Kafka keyed by order id and one consumer per partition means one pod emits per order at a time; the sequence number covers the rebalance windows where two might.
  • Huge fan-out: one event to 1,000,000 clients. A "restaurant closed" broadcast to a city, or a system-wide notice. One emit becomes one million socket writes across the fleet, tens of seconds of CPU, and a reply storm if clients react by fetching something. Batch by pod and spread over 30 to 60 seconds; send a reference the client fetches from a cached endpoint rather than the content; use a CDN-cached poll for truly global notices.
  • Sticky sessions breaking on deploy. With long-polling enabled and cookie-based stickiness, a rolling deploy makes each client's next poll land on a different pod that does not know its session; Socket.IO reports Session ID unknown and the client reconnects, paying the full handshake. Prefer websocket-only, or accept the reconnect and make sure resume covers it.
  • Proxies buffering SSE. Covered in 34.3: the stream opens fine and nothing arrives. Ingress annotations plus a synthetic SSE check.
  • Consumer group rebalance on every gateway deploy. With 12 pods and a rolling deploy, the tracking-gateway group rebalances 12 times, each pausing consumption for a few seconds; delivery lag spikes to 3 to 5 seconds during the deploy. Use cooperative sticky assignment where the client supports it, or a slower rollout, and put the deploy annotation on the lag panel so nobody pages for it.
  • Replay stream on a non-persistent Redis. A failover wipes the buffer; every resume becomes a RESYNC; REST takes a 100x spike. Persist the replay Redis (AOF), and add jitter to the client's resync fetch.
  • JSON serialization CPU at scale. A pod at 100,000 emits per second spends most of its CPU in JSON.stringify and socket writes. Measure before optimizing; then binary encoding, coalescing, and reducing payload size, in that order.
  • The disconnect handler never runs for sockets killed by the process dying; presence keys expire on their own, room membership evaporates with the process, and nothing needs cleanup. Designs that require the handler to run are the designs that break.

34.15.1 How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the real-time path as an optimization over a REST path that must work on its own: every screen can be reloaded, every client can resync, and the WebSocket only makes it faster. They pick SSE when the server is the only talker, WebSockets when both sides talk, and they never let the choice leak state into the API pods. They assume every connection will drop, every pod will die and every Redis will fail over, and they make each of those events boring: jittered reconnect, sequence-based resume, TTL-based presence, symptom-based alerts and one synthetic check that proves messages actually arrive.

34.15.2 Common mistakes

  • Emitting from the API pod that handled the PATCH, skipping Kafka, so the event exists only if that pod also held the socket.
  • Storing room membership or presence in the process and being surprised after the first deploy.
  • No sequence numbers, then trying to debug "sometimes the status goes backwards".
  • A single Redis for adapter, replay and cache with no persistence and no memory limit.
  • Treating the WebSocket handler as trusted because "the user is authenticated".
  • Alerting only on REST metrics for a system whose failure mode is silence.

34.15.3 Interview questions

  1. Design live order tracking for 250,000 concurrent clients. Expected: Kafka keyed by order id as the event source, a separate gateway deployment consuming it, Redis adapter for fan-out, Redis Streams for replay, rooms per order with authorization on join, sequence numbers from the database, jittered reconnect with resume, presence with TTL keys, synthetic end-to-end check. Why it matters: covers every concept in the part in one answer.
  2. How do you evict a user from a room across all pods? Expected: server.in(userRoom).socketsLeave(room) through the adapter, triggered by a domain event; authorization on join alone is insufficient.
  3. What breaks when the Redis adapter's Redis fails, and how do you detect it? Expected: pods become islands, emits still counted; readiness on Redis, publish error counter, synthetic check.
  4. Why write to the replay stream before emitting? Expected: a client that reconnects during the emit must find the event in the stream; ordering makes at-least-once true.
  5. What metrics make a silent gateway failure visible? Expected: emitted versus consumed rate, delivery lag, disconnect rate by reason, connections per pod, synthetic check.
  6. How do you handle a broadcast to a million clients? Expected: it is a fan-out problem: batch and spread, send references not content, CDN-cached polling for global notices.

34.15.4 Practical exercise

Build the tracking gateway end to end:

  1. A NestJS tracking-gateway deployment with the module, gateway, consumer, access service, presence and metrics from this section; the Redis adapter from 34.5; the drain logic from 34.7.
  2. An orders service that changes status via PATCH /orders/:id/status, writing the order and an outbox row in one transaction, and a relay that publishes to order.events keyed by order id with seq.
  3. A driver simulator that publishes locations for 200 orders every 3 seconds.
  4. A browser client with jittered reconnect, order.watch with lastSeq, sequence dedup and reorder, RESYNC handling, and a map.
  5. Acceptance: with three gateway pods, status changes appear on the map within 500 ms; killing a pod under 3,000 connections produces no missed or duplicated status events on any client; reassigning a driver removes the old driver's socket from the room within one event; the synthetic check fails within 30 seconds when the adapter's Redis is stopped and the pod's readiness flips to 503; Grafana shows connections per pod, delivery lag p99, disconnect rate by reason and resync count; the ws_slow_clients gauge rises and the offending socket is disconnected when a client is throttled to 1 KB per second while receiving locations.

Senior Checklist — Part 34

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can choose between WebSockets, SSE, long polling and polling from the direction of traffic and the proxy path, and defend the choice
  • I can implement a NestJS gateway with handshake authentication, per-room authorization, validated DTOs, guards and acknowledgements
  • I can implement an @Sse() endpoint with Last-Event-ID replay from a Redis Stream and the ingress settings it needs
  • I can install the Socket.IO Redis adapter and explain what it does and does not carry between pods
  • I can implement presence with TTL keys refreshed by heartbeat, multi-device sets and lazy cleanup, and state the staleness bound
  • I can size a gateway pod from memory, file descriptors and reconnect arithmetic, and configure the load balancer's timeouts
  • I can drain a pod on SIGTERM without a visible client error
  • I can implement client reconnect with full-jitter backoff and resume by sequence with a RESYNC fallback
  • I can explain per-key ordering from the database version column through Kafka keys to client-side dedup
  • I can list the WebSocket-specific security controls and the metrics that make silent failures visible
  • I can design fan-out for a million clients without taking the fleet down

Part 34 — Key Takeaways

  • Ask who initiates. Server-only pushes are SSE over plain HTTP; bidirectional, low-latency or binary traffic is WebSockets; long polling is the fallback you get for free from a good resume contract.
  • A WebSocket is authenticated once at the handshake; token expiry, revocation and room authorization are your problem on every message and every join.
  • Rooms live in one process. Two pods need a Pub/Sub adapter, and Kafka stays the source of truth for events; Redis Pub/Sub carries intent, not state, and remembers nothing.
  • Presence is "has heartbeated recently", implemented as TTL keys, never as a flag that depends on observing a disconnect.
  • Size gateway pods by the reconnect wave their death would cause; keep them out of the API pods; make every layer's idle timeout longer than the one below it.
  • Every stream has a sequence assigned where truth is decided (the database row); clients dedup and reorder by it, resume from it, and fall back to REST when the buffer cannot cover the gap.
  • Write the replay buffer before emitting live; join the room before replaying; accept at-least-once and dedup at the edge.
  • Reconnect with exponential backoff and full jitter; a synchronized retry is a self-inflicted outage.
  • Bound everything: payload size, per-socket message rate, write backlog, replay stream length, connections per pod.
  • Real-time systems fail silently. Alert on delivery lag, emitted-versus-consumed ratio and disconnect rate, and run a synthetic check that proves a message actually arrives.
  • The REST path must work on its own; the real-time path only makes it faster.

Part 35 — Background Jobs and Schedulers

35.1 Why background jobs exist

There is a moment in every backend engineer's career when a POST /orders endpoint that used to answer in 90 ms starts answering in 6 seconds, and nobody changed the order logic. What changed is that somebody added "send the confirmation email" to it, then "generate the invoice PDF", then "push the order to the warehouse system", then "notify the loyalty service". Each addition was small. Each one was synchronous. Together they turned a fast, reliable endpoint into a slow, fragile one.

This part is about the machinery that fixes that: queues, workers, schedulers, retries, dead-letter queues, and the operational discipline that keeps them honest. The main example is NestJS with @nestjs/bullmq (BullMQ on Redis), with a PostgreSQL-backed queue using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED as the durable alternative, and @nestjs/schedule for cron.

35.1.1 Moving work out of the request path

Concept

A background job is a unit of work that is recorded now and executed later, by a different process, outside the HTTP request that asked for it. The request records an intent ("this order needs a confirmation email") and returns. Some other process picks that intent up and does the work.

The word "later" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. "Later" can mean 20 milliseconds later on an idle worker, or 15 minutes later for a deliberately delayed job, or three attempts and four hours later after a third-party outage. The point is that the user is not waiting.

Why does it exist?

Two reasons, and they are different. Confusing them leads to bad architecture.

Latency. The user is holding a phone. Every millisecond your endpoint spends on something they do not need in the response is a millisecond of their attention you are burning. Checkout conversion drops measurably as latency rises; the industry rule of thumb is roughly 1 to 2 percent of conversions lost per extra 100 ms on a checkout flow. If your order endpoint spends 4.5 s generating a PDF, you are paying for that PDF in lost revenue.

Reliability. This is the bigger one. When you call a third-party email API inside your HTTP handler, you have welded their availability to yours. If SendGrid has a bad ten minutes, your POST /orders returns 500, the customer's card was charged, and the order was never created because your transaction rolled back. Your availability is now the product of your own availability and every synchronous dependency's availability. Four dependencies at 99.9 percent give you 99.6 percent (we do this arithmetic properly in Part 48 — Site Reliability Engineering).

A queue breaks that welding. The email API being down becomes "some emails are delayed by eleven minutes", which is an inconvenience, not an outage.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. The waiter takes your order and walks away in 40 seconds. They do not stand at your table while the chef cooks, while the dishwasher runs, while the accountant files the receipt. The order ticket goes on a rail in the kitchen; cooks pull tickets off the rail at their own pace; if the dessert station is backed up, your main course still arrives.

The ticket rail is the queue. The ticket is the job. The cooks are the workers. And critically: the ticket contains a table number, not the food. The chef looks up what is needed. We will come back to that when we talk about payload design, because it is the single most common mistake.

How it works

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"POST /orders"| API["NestJS API pod"]
    API --> DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    API -->|"enqueue job"| Q["Queue: Redis or PostgreSQL"]
    API -->|"201 Created in 95 ms"| C
    W1["Worker pod 1"] -->|"pull"| Q
    W2["Worker pod 2"] -->|"pull"| Q
    W1 --> Mail["Email provider"]
    W2 --> PDF["PDF renderer"]
    W1 --> DB
  1. The request handler does only the work whose result the client needs: validate, write the order row, reserve stock, take payment authorization.
