  2. It appends a job record to a queue. On Redis with BullMQ that is a few Lua-scripted commands, roughly 0.3 to 1 ms. On PostgreSQL it is one INSERT, roughly 0.5 to 2 ms.
  3. It returns 201 Created.
  4. Workers, running in separate pods with their own scaling and their own memory limits, pull jobs and execute them. If they fail, the queue retries them.

Practical example

Here is the real arithmetic for a checkout endpoint at an e-commerce company doing 400 orders per minute at peak.

Step Synchronous cost Failure probability Belongs in the request?
Validate DTO 1 ms ~0 Yes
Load cart, price it 12 ms low Yes
Reserve inventory (UPDATE ... RETURNING) 8 ms low Yes — the user must know if it is out of stock
Authorize payment 350 ms p50, 2.5 s p99 0.4 percent Yes — the user must know if the card failed
Write order + items 9 ms low Yes
Send confirmation email 220 ms p50, 8 s p99, provider outages 0.6 percent No
Generate invoice PDF 1.4 s, 180 MB peak RSS 0.2 percent No
Push to warehouse API 400 ms, their maintenance window is Sunday 02:00 1.1 percent No
Recalculate loyalty tier 90 ms low No
Reindex the product in search 40 ms low No

Synchronous everything: p50 around 2.5 s, p99 around 12 s, and the endpoint fails whenever any of five dependencies fails — a combined failure rate around 2.3 percent. Move the bottom five to a queue and the endpoint is p50 380 ms, p99 2.6 s, failing only when payment or the database fails.

That is the whole argument. It is not about elegance. It is 2.3 percent of orders versus 0.4 percent.

What must stay synchronous

Junior engineers, having discovered queues, try to move everything. Do not. Work belongs in the request path when the client's next decision depends on its result, or when not doing it immediately would let the system enter an inconsistent state a user can observe.

Stays synchronous:

  • Anything whose result is in the response body. If the response says orderId, the order row must exist.
  • Authorization and authentication checks. Never "we will check permissions later".
  • Inventory reservation for a purchasable item. If you queue it, you will oversell.
  • Payment authorization, because the user must be told their card was declined now.
  • Any write that a subsequent read in the same user flow will look for. Queue the write, and the user's "My Orders" page shows nothing, and they order again.

Goes to a queue:

  • Notifications of all kinds: email, SMS, push, webhooks to partners.
  • Document generation: invoices, shipping labels, statements, exports.
  • Media processing: image resizing, video transcoding, virus scanning.
  • Third-party synchronization: ERP, warehouse, accounting, CRM, tax service.
  • Analytics, search index updates, cache warming, recommendation refreshes.
  • Reports and aggregations over large row counts.
  • Anything that takes longer than about 200 ms and is not in the response.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on a Sunday, the warehouse partner starts a maintenance window and their API begins returning 503. Because the previous team called it inside OrdersService.create() inside the order transaction, every checkout now takes 30 s (their client timeout) and then returns 500. The order transaction rolls back. But payment was already authorized, because the payment call happened before the warehouse call. Ninety-one customers are charged with no order. Support spends Monday issuing refunds, and finance spends the week reconciling.

The fix that shipped that week was four lines: remove the warehouse call from the transaction, enqueue a warehouse.sync job after commit. The partner's next maintenance window produced zero customer impact and a queue depth graph that rose to 1,100 and drained in eight minutes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, for every line in a request handler: does the caller need this to have happened before I answer? If the answer is no, it is a job. Then they ask the second question, which juniors skip: what happens if this job runs twice, or runs three hours late, or never runs? If any of those answers is "we lose money silently", the job needs idempotency, a dead-letter queue and an alert — which is the rest of this part.

They also refuse to use a queue as an excuse for not fixing slow code. A 4-second query does not become fast by moving it to a worker; it becomes invisible. Sometimes that is right. Often it hides a missing index.

35.2 Job queues

35.2.1 Producer, queue, worker

Concept

Three roles, and you should be able to name which process plays which in your system.

  • Producer — the code that creates a job. Usually an API request handler, sometimes a scheduler, sometimes another worker.
  • Queue — durable storage that holds jobs and hands each one to exactly one consumer at a time. It provides ordering (loosely), visibility (a job being processed is not handed to someone else), and persistence.
  • Worker — a long-running process that pulls jobs, runs a handler, and reports success or failure.

The queue is the boundary. Producers do not know who consumes. Workers do not know who produced. That decoupling is the point.

Mental model

Imagine a post office sorting shelf with numbered pigeonholes. Anyone can drop a letter in. Sorters take letters one at a time, and while a sorter is holding a letter, nobody else can take it. If a sorter drops dead mid-letter, the letter falls back on the shelf after a while — that "after a while" is the visibility timeout or lock duration, and it is why a job can genuinely run twice. Hold that thought; it is section 35.7.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant API as OrdersApi
    participant R as Redis
    participant W as Worker
    participant M as MailProvider
    API->>R: LPUSH job to wait list
    API-->>API: return 201
    W->>R: BRPOPLPUSH wait to active, take lock
    R-->>W: job payload
    W->>M: POST /send
    M-->>W: 202 Accepted
    W->>R: move job to completed, release lock

BullMQ implements this with Redis lists and sorted sets, driven by Lua scripts so that "move from waiting to active and take the lock" is a single atomic operation. The important structures:

Redis key Type Holds
bull:<queue>:wait list jobs ready to run, FIFO
bull:<queue>:active list jobs currently held by a worker
bull:<queue>:delayed sorted set jobs scored by their run-at timestamp
bull:<queue>:prioritized sorted set jobs scored by priority
bull:<queue>:completed / :failed sorted set finished jobs, trimmed by removeOnComplete
bull:<queue>:<jobId> hash the job's data, options, attempt count, stacktrace

Knowing this is not trivia. When somebody says "Redis memory went from 400 MB to 9 GB overnight", you will know to look at the completed sorted set and the job hashes, and you will know the fix is removeOnComplete.

35.2.2 Payload design: pass ids, never whole objects

Concept

A job payload should be the smallest identifier the handler needs to find the truth, plus anything genuinely not derivable later.

// Good
{ orderId: 'ord_8812', attemptReason: 'created' }

// Bad
{ order: { id, userId, items: [...42 items...], address: {...}, totals: {...} } }

Why does it exist?

Four concrete reasons, all of which you will meet.

  1. Staleness. A job enqueued at 14:02 may run at 14:09 after a retry. Between those times the order was cancelled, the address was corrected, the price was adjusted. A payload-carrying job emails the customer the old address. An id-carrying job reloads the row and sees the truth.
  2. Size. Redis holds every job in memory. A 40 KB payload times 200,000 queued jobs is 8 GB of RAM, and Redis is not a database you want to run at 8 GB for this. An id is 24 bytes.
  3. Schema evolution. Payloads are serialized contracts. If you change the shape of order and deploy, the jobs already sitting in the queue carry the old shape, and your new worker code crashes on all of them. Ids never change shape. (This is the same compatibility problem as Part 24 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients.)
  4. Secrets. Whole objects tend to carry emails, phone numbers, addresses. Redis is often less protected than PostgreSQL, is dumped to RDB files, and appears in Bull Board screenshots pasted into Slack. Do not put personal data in job payloads.

Practical example

// jobs/order-jobs.types.ts
// Payloads are versioned, tiny, and contain no personal data.
export interface SendOrderConfirmationJob {
  v: 1;                 // payload version, so a handler can branch during a rollout
  orderId: string;      // the only thing we need; everything else is loaded fresh
  correlationId: string; // Part 42: the request id that caused this job
}

export interface ReindexProductJob {
  v: 1;
  productId: string;
  reason: 'price_change' | 'stock_change' | 'content_edit';
}

The one legitimate exception: data that cannot be reconstructed later. If the job's purpose is "record that the user saw variant B of the banner at 14:02", the timestamp and variant must be in the payload, because nothing in the database will tell you afterwards. Snapshot-style jobs (audit, analytics, "email exactly this rendered content") carry data by design. Everything else carries ids.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an entire TypeORM entity in the payload. It serializes lazily-loaded relations as undefined, or worse, triggers loads and serializes half your schema.
  • Putting a Date object in and being surprised it arrives as a string. JSON has no date type. Always toISOString() and parse explicitly.
  • Putting a file buffer in the payload. Upload to S3 first, pass the key (Part 32 — File Storage).
  • Putting an access token in the payload so the worker can "act as the user". Pass the user id and let the worker mint its own service credential.

35.2.3 Job options

Every serious queue library gives you the same handful of knobs. Knowing what each one does in production is what separates a working queue from a queue that pages you.

Option What it does Sensible default Gotcha
attempts total tries including the first 3 to 5 for network work, 1 for non-idempotent work attempts: 1 means no retry at all, not one retry
backoff delay between attempts { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 } without jitter, all retries from an outage fire together
delay milliseconds before the job becomes runnable 0 delayed jobs sit in a sorted set; a million of them is a memory problem
priority lower number runs first leave unset priorities move jobs to a different structure and can starve low-priority work
jobId explicit id; a duplicate id is silently ignored derive it for dedupe only dedupes while the job still exists in Redis
removeOnComplete drop or cap finished jobs { age: 3600, count: 1000 } leaving it false is the classic Redis OOM
removeOnFail same for failures { age: 604800 } (7 days) never true; you lose your dead letters
lifo push to the front rarely useful for interactive "retry now" buttons
timeout (worker-side) abort a stuck handler set it BullMQ v5 has no per-job timeout option; enforce it in your handler

A note on that last row, because it trips people up: in BullMQ v5 the old timeout job option was removed. You enforce time limits yourself, which is honest — only your handler knows how to abort safely.

// common/with-timeout.ts
export async function withTimeout<T>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number, label: string): Promise<T> {
  let timer: NodeJS.Timeout;
  const guard = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`${label} timed out after ${ms}ms`)), ms);
  });
  try {
    return await Promise.race([p, guard]);
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer!);
  }
}

Pair it with an AbortSignal on your HTTP client so the underlying socket actually closes; a raced Promise alone leaves the request running and the socket held.

35.2.4 BullMQ in NestJS

NestJS example

Registration. Note the shared defaultJobOptions — this is where you stop the Redis-OOM class of incident once, for the whole app.

// queues/queues.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { BullModule } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Module({
  imports: [
    BullModule.forRootAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
        connection: {
          host: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('REDIS_HOST'),
          port: cfg.getOrThrow<number>('REDIS_PORT'),
          // BullMQ requires this; ioredis would otherwise retry commands forever.
          maxRetriesPerRequest: null,
          enableReadyCheck: false,
        },
        // Keys are prefixed per environment so staging can never eat prod jobs.
        prefix: `bull:${cfg.getOrThrow<string>('NODE_ENV')}`,
        defaultJobOptions: {
          attempts: 5,
          backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2_000 },
          removeOnComplete: { age: 3_600, count: 1_000 }, // keep 1h or 1000, whichever first
          removeOnFail: { age: 7 * 24 * 3_600 },          // keep failures for a week
        },
      }),
    }),
    BullModule.registerQueue(
      { name: 'notifications' },
      { name: 'documents' },
      { name: 'integrations' },
    ),
  ],
  exports: [BullModule],
})
export class QueuesModule {}

Producing. The producer is a thin service, not raw queue.add calls scattered through controllers, so that payload shape and job naming stay in one place.

// notifications/notification-jobs.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class NotificationJobsService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(NotificationJobsService.name);

  constructor(@InjectQueue('notifications') private readonly queue: Queue) {}

  async enqueueOrderConfirmation(orderId: string, correlationId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.queue.add(
      'order.confirmation',                      // job name, used to route inside the processor
      { v: 1, orderId, correlationId },          // payload: ids only
      {
        // Deterministic id: enqueueing twice for the same order is a no-op.
        jobId: `order-confirmation:${orderId}`,
        attempts: 5,
        backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5_000 },
      },
    );
    this.log.log({ orderId, correlationId }, 'enqueued order.confirmation');
  }
}

Consuming. @Processor plus WorkerHost is the modern @nestjs/bullmq pattern; the class is the worker.

// notifications/notification.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost, OnWorkerEvent } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Job, UnrecoverableError } from 'bullmq';

@Processor('notifications', {
  concurrency: 10,        // how many jobs this single worker process runs at once
  lockDuration: 30_000,   // how long the worker owns a job before it is considered stalled
  limiter: { max: 100, duration: 1_000 }, // queue-level: at most 100 jobs/second
})
export class NotificationProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  private readonly log = new Logger(NotificationProcessor.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrdersService,
    private readonly mail: MailService,
  ) {
    super();
  }

  async process(job: Job): Promise<unknown> {
    switch (job.name) {
      case 'order.confirmation':
        return this.sendOrderConfirmation(job);
      default:
        // An unknown name means a deploy skew or a typo. Do not retry it forever.
        throw new UnrecoverableError(`unknown job name ${job.name}`);
    }
  }

  private async sendOrderConfirmation(job: Job<{ orderId: string; correlationId: string }>) {
    const { orderId, correlationId } = job.data;

    // Reload the truth. Never trust the payload's view of the world.
    const order = await this.orders.findForNotification(orderId);
    if (!order) throw new UnrecoverableError(`order ${orderId} no longer exists`);
    if (order.status === 'cancelled') {
      this.log.warn({ orderId }, 'order cancelled before confirmation was sent, skipping');
      return { skipped: true };
    }

    await this.mail.sendOrderConfirmation(order, { correlationId });
    return { sent: true, attempt: job.attemptsMade + 1 };
  }

  @OnWorkerEvent('failed')
  onFailed(job: Job | undefined, err: Error) {
    this.log.error(
      { jobId: job?.id, name: job?.name, attempt: job?.attemptsMade, err },
      'job failed',
    );
  }
}

Three things in that code are load-bearing and easy to miss:

  1. process() dispatches on job.name. One processor class per queue, many job names inside it. Do not create a queue per job type; queues are not free (each one costs connections, dashboards and alerts) and you lose the ability to reason about a single depth number.
  2. The handler reloads the order. The payload said orderId, not "here is the order".
  3. UnrecoverableError stops retries immediately. Retrying "this order does not exist" five times with exponential backoff wastes 90 seconds of worker capacity and adds five stack traces to your log budget for no possible benefit.

35.2.5 Flows and parent-child jobs

Concept

A flow is a tree of jobs where a parent job does not become runnable until all its children have completed. BullMQ implements this natively with FlowProducer.

Why does it exist?

Because real pipelines have fan-out and a join. "Generate the invoice, send the email, notify the warehouse — and when all three are done, mark the order as fulfilment_started and emit an analytics event." Without flows you either chain jobs manually (each handler enqueues the next, which serializes work that could be parallel and scatters the pipeline across five files) or you invent a counter in Redis and reinvent the join badly.

Mental model

Imagine assembling a bicycle. Wheels, frame and handlebars can be built in parallel by three people. Final assembly cannot start until all three are on the bench. The flow is the work order; the parent job is final assembly; it becomes runnable exactly when the last child reports done.

How it works

flowchart TB
    P["parent: order.finalize"]
    C1["child: invoice.generate"]
    C2["child: email.confirmation"]
    C3["child: warehouse.notify"]
    C1 --> P
    C2 --> P
    C3 --> P
    P --> D["order.status = fulfilment_started"]

Children are added to their own queues (so they scale independently), each with its own retry policy. The parent sits in a waiting-children state, invisible to normal workers, until the last child completes. If a child exhausts its attempts and fails, the parent stays waiting forever unless you configure failParentOnFailure — which is exactly the "orphaned parent flow" failure mode we cover in 35.13.

// orders/order-flow.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectFlowProducer } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { FlowProducer } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class OrderFlowService {
  constructor(@InjectFlowProducer('orders') private readonly flow: FlowProducer) {}

  async startFulfilment(orderId: string, correlationId: string) {
    await this.flow.add({
      name: 'order.finalize',
      queueName: 'orders',
      data: { v: 1, orderId, correlationId },
      opts: { jobId: `finalize:${orderId}`, attempts: 3 },
      children: [
        {
          name: 'invoice.generate',
          queueName: 'documents',
          data: { v: 1, orderId, correlationId },
          // If the invoice can never be produced, the parent must not hang forever.
          opts: { jobId: `invoice:${orderId}`, attempts: 5, failParentOnFailure: true },
        },
        {
          name: 'order.confirmation',
          queueName: 'notifications',
          data: { v: 1, orderId, correlationId },
          opts: { jobId: `confirm:${orderId}`, attempts: 5 },
        },
        {
          name: 'warehouse.notify',
          queueName: 'integrations',
          data: { v: 1, orderId, correlationId },
          opts: { jobId: `wh:${orderId}`, attempts: 8, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 10_000 } },
        },
      ],
    });
  }
}

Register the flow producer alongside the queues with BullModule.registerFlowProducer({ name: 'orders' }).

The parent reads its children's return values with job.getChildrenValues(), which is how the invoice's S3 key reaches the finalize step without a database round trip.

35.2.6 Rate limiting and concurrency

These two are constantly confused, and confusing them causes both wasted money and third-party bans.

  • Concurrency is per worker process: how many jobs this process runs at the same time. It is a resource control. Ten concurrent jobs each holding a 40 MB PDF buffer is 400 MB of RSS; that is how workers get OOMKilled.
  • Rate limiting is per queue, coordinated across all worker processes through Redis: how many jobs may start per time window in total. It is a politeness control, for third parties who will ban you.
@Processor('integrations', {
  concurrency: 20,                          // this pod runs 20 at once
  limiter: { max: 50, duration: 1_000 },    // all pods together: 50 jobs/second
})
export class IntegrationProcessor extends WorkerHost { /* ... */ }

With three pods at concurrency 20 you have 60 potential parallel jobs, but the limiter guarantees the start rate never exceeds 50 per second across the fleet. If the partner's contract says 3,000 requests per minute, set { max: 45, duration: 1_000 } and sleep well.

For per-tenant fairness — "no single merchant may consume more than 20 percent of the warehouse worker" — a global limiter is not enough. Use BullMQ's group rate limiting if you have it available, or shard by tenant into several queues, or implement a token bucket in Redis inside the handler and call job.moveToDelayed() when the tenant is over budget. The last option is the most portable and is worth knowing:

const allowed = await this.tokenBucket.tryConsume(`tenant:${tenantId}`, 1);
if (!allowed) {
  // Put the job back with a short delay; do not burn an attempt.
  await job.moveToDelayed(Date.now() + 2_000, token);
  // Signal BullMQ that this worker deliberately released the job.
  throw new DelayedError();
}

DelayedError and the token argument (available as the second parameter of process(job, token)) are real BullMQ APIs and exist precisely for this pattern.

Interview questions

  1. Why do we pass ids in job payloads instead of the full object? Expected: staleness, memory, schema evolution, PII. Follow-up: name a case where you would embed data anyway (audit or snapshot jobs).
  2. What is the difference between worker concurrency and a queue limiter? Expected: per-process resource control versus fleet-wide start-rate control coordinated in Redis. Follow-up: which one protects a third-party API?
  3. Your Redis memory grew 20x in a week with no traffic change. Where do you look? Expected: removeOnComplete/removeOnFail unset, large payloads, a huge delayed set, a repeatable job creating jobs faster than they drain.
  4. What is a flow, and what breaks if a child fails permanently? Expected: parent waits on children; without failParentOnFailure the parent stalls in waiting-children forever and needs monitoring.
  5. Why does attempts: 1 surprise people? Expected: it means one total attempt, so no retries at all.

Practical exercise

Take an existing POST /orders handler that does five things synchronously. Measure it with autocannon at 50 RPS for 60 seconds and record p50/p99. Then:

  1. Move email, PDF and warehouse sync to a notifications, documents and integrations queue with deterministic jobIds.
  2. Set defaultJobOptions with retention limits and exponential backoff.
  3. Re-run the load test.

Acceptance criteria: p99 drops by at least 60 percent; killing the mail provider container causes zero HTTP 5xx and a visible rise in notifications queue depth that drains within two minutes of the provider returning; redis-cli MEMORY USAGE on the completed set stays under 5 MB after 3,000 jobs.

35.3 Workers as a separate deployment

35.3.1 Why workers do not belong in the API pods

Concept

A worker is a process that runs Worker instances and no HTTP server. It ships from the same repository and the same Docker image as the API, but it is a different Kubernetes Deployment, with a different command, different replica count, different resource limits and different scaling rules.

The tempting alternative is to let the API pods also run the processors. It works on day one. It is one of the most reliable ways to cause a checkout outage on day 200.

Why does it exist?

Four independent reasons, and any one of them is sufficient.

Resource contention. Node.js is single-threaded for your JavaScript. A worker rendering a PDF with a CPU-bound library blocks the event loop for 400 ms. If that process is also serving HTTP, every request queued behind it waits 400 ms. Your p99 becomes a function of PDF sizes. We measured this once: adding image thumbnailing to API pods moved p99 from 210 ms to 3.4 s while p50 barely moved, which is the signature of event-loop blocking.

Different scaling signals. The API scales on requests per second and CPU. The worker scales on queue depth. These move independently: at 03:00 the API is idle and the nightly report queue has 12,000 jobs. If they share a Deployment you either over-provision the API all night or under-provision the workers.

Different failure blast radius. A worker that leaks memory gets OOMKilled. If it is an API pod, you just dropped in-flight customer requests. If it is a worker pod, BullMQ's stalled-job detection re-queues the job and nobody notices.

Different deploy risk. You often want to pause workers during a risky migration while keeping the API serving reads. You cannot do that if they are the same pods.

Mental model

Imagine a shop with a counter and a back room. The counter serves customers: fast, interruptible, always staffed. The back room does stock-taking, packing and paperwork: slow, batched, can be paused. Putting both in the same person means every customer waits while that person counts boxes. Every business that has ever existed separates them. Do the same.

How it works

flowchart TB
    subgraph API_Deployment
        A1["api pod 1"]
        A2["api pod 2"]
        A3["api pod 3"]
    end
    subgraph Worker_Deployment
        W1["worker pod 1"]
        W2["worker pod 2"]
    end
    LB["Ingress"] --> A1
    LB --> A2
    LB --> A3
    A1 --> R[("Redis")]
    A2 --> R
    A3 --> R
    R --> W1
    R --> W2
    W1 --> PG[("PostgreSQL")]
    A1 --> PG
    KEDA["KEDA ScaledObject on queue depth"] -.-> W1

One image, two entrypoints. The API bootstraps the HTTP server; the worker bootstraps a Nest application context with the processor modules and no listener.

// main.worker.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Logger } from 'nestjs-pino';
import { WorkerAppModule } from './worker-app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  // createApplicationContext: DI, config, database, processors -- but no HTTP listener.
  const app = await NestFactory.createApplicationContext(WorkerAppModule, { bufferLogs: true });
  app.useLogger(app.get(Logger));

  // Kubernetes sends SIGTERM; enableShutdownHooks wires it into onModuleDestroy.
  app.enableShutdownHooks();

  const log = new Logger('worker');
  log.log(`worker started, queues=${process.env.WORKER_QUEUES}`);
}
bootstrap();
# One image, two commands.
# api:    CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
# worker: CMD ["node", "dist/main.worker.js"]

Which queues a pod serves comes from configuration, so you can split hot queues onto their own Deployment later without a code change:

// worker-app.module.ts (fragment)
const enabled = (process.env.WORKER_QUEUES ?? 'notifications,documents,integrations').split(',');

@Module({
  imports: [
    QueuesModule,
    ...(enabled.includes('notifications') ? [NotificationModule] : []),
    ...(enabled.includes('documents') ? [DocumentModule] : []),
    ...(enabled.includes('integrations') ? [IntegrationModule] : []),
  ],
})
export class WorkerAppModule {}

35.3.2 Scaling on queue depth

CPU is the wrong signal for a worker that spends 95 percent of its time waiting on a third-party HTTP call. The right signal is how much work is waiting and, better, how old the oldest waiting job is.

With KEDA on Kubernetes:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: notifications-worker
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: notifications-worker
  minReplicaCount: 2      # never zero for a queue with an SLA on latency
  maxReplicaCount: 20
  pollingInterval: 15
  cooldownPeriod: 120     # do not thrash; workers are expensive to start
  triggers:
    - type: redis
      metadata:
        address: redis.prod.svc.cluster.local:6379
        listName: "bull:prod:notifications:wait"
        listLength: "200"   # target: 200 waiting jobs per replica

Two production notes. First, minReplicaCount: 0 is attractive for cost but means the first job after a quiet period waits for a cold start, which for a Node image with a database connection pool is 8 to 25 seconds. For anything user-visible, keep at least one. Second, cooldownPeriod matters more than you think: a queue that spikes and drains every 30 seconds will otherwise start and kill pods continuously, and a pod killed mid-job produces a stalled job.

35.3.3 Graceful shutdown

Concept

When Kubernetes wants a pod gone it sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), then sends SIGKILL. A worker that ignores SIGTERM gets killed mid-job. That job is not lost — BullMQ will eventually detect it as stalled and retry it — but "eventually" is up to stalledInterval (default 30 s) times maxStalledCount, and the retry may duplicate side effects.

Correct behaviour on SIGTERM: stop taking new jobs, finish the current ones, then exit.

NestJS example

@nestjs/bullmq closes its workers in onModuleDestroy, and worker.close() in BullMQ waits for active jobs to finish by default. So app.enableShutdownHooks() plus a correct grace period is most of the work. Make it explicit and observable:

// common/worker-lifecycle.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class WorkerLifecycleService implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly log = new Logger(WorkerLifecycleService.name);

  constructor(@InjectQueue('documents') private readonly queue: Queue) {}

  async onApplicationShutdown(signal?: string) {
    this.log.warn({ signal }, 'shutdown signal received, draining worker');
    // Nest closes the Worker for us; this hook is where we flush metrics,
    // close the tracer and log how long the drain took.
    const t0 = Date.now();
    await this.queue.close();
    this.log.warn({ drainMs: Date.now() - t0 }, 'worker drained');
  }
}
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      # Must be longer than your longest job, plus a margin.
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: orders:2.14.3
          command: ["node", "dist/main.worker.js"]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }

The rule: terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed your p99 job duration. If your PDF job takes 90 seconds at p99 and your grace period is 30, every deploy kills roughly one PDF job per pod and produces a duplicate invoice on retry. That is a real incident I have watched happen, and the fix was a one-line YAML change.

For very long jobs (a 40-minute export), do not raise the grace period to 40 minutes. Make the job checkpointed and resumable instead — see 35.10.

35.3.4 CPU-bound jobs and worker threads

Node.js runs your JavaScript on one thread. A job that spends 3 seconds in sharp, pdfkit, zlib.gzipSync, JSON.parse of a 60 MB string, or a crypto loop blocks that thread. With concurrency: 10, the other nine jobs are frozen. Worse, BullMQ's own heartbeat — the timer that renews the job lock — is also frozen, so a long synchronous block causes your own job to be declared stalled and re-run by another worker. That is the mechanism behind "the report generated three times".

Three fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Use the async API. sharp is async and does its work on libuv's threadpool. zlib.gzip is async. crypto.pbkdf2 is async. Most heavy native libraries have a non-blocking variant, and it uses the threadpool for free. Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (default 4) to about your concurrency if you lean on it.
  2. Move the work to a worker_thread. BullMQ supports a sandboxed processor: pass a file path instead of a function and each job runs in a separate process. In a NestJS app that means giving up DI inside the handler, so many teams instead use a small typed pool.
  3. Move the work out of Node entirely. Image and video processing at scale belongs in a dedicated service (or a Lambda, or ffmpeg in its own container). Node is a poor CPU host and an excellent orchestrator.
// documents/pdf.worker.ts  (runs inside a worker_thread)
import { parentPort, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';
import { renderInvoicePdf } from './render-invoice';

(async () => {
  const buffer = await renderInvoicePdf(workerData.invoice);
  parentPort!.postMessage(buffer, [buffer.buffer]); // transfer, do not copy
})();
// documents/pdf-pool.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';
import { join } from 'node:path';

@Injectable()
export class PdfPoolService {
  render(invoice: InvoiceView, timeoutMs = 20_000): Promise<Buffer> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const w = new Worker(join(__dirname, 'pdf.worker.js'), { workerData: { invoice } });
      const timer = setTimeout(() => { w.terminate(); reject(new Error('pdf render timeout')); }, timeoutMs);
      w.once('message', (buf: Buffer) => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(buf); });
      w.once('error', (err) => { clearTimeout(timer); reject(err); });
      w.once('exit', (code) => { if (code !== 0) reject(new Error(`pdf worker exit ${code}`)); });
    });
  }
}

Spawning a thread costs 10 to 30 ms, so for jobs under about 100 ms of CPU it is not worth it. Above that it is the difference between a healthy worker and a stalled one.

35.3.5 Memory per job

Budget memory as concurrency x peak RSS per job + baseline. A Node process baseline with a Nest app, TypeORM and a connection pool is 120 to 200 MB. A PDF job peaks at 180 MB. At concurrency: 10 you are asking for 2 GB, and your limit is 1 Gi, so the pod is OOMKilled roughly every 40 minutes and you get duplicate invoices.

The senior move is to size concurrency per queue rather than globally:

Queue Work Concurrency Memory limit Why
notifications HTTP call to a mail provider 30 512 Mi I/O bound, tiny heap per job
integrations HTTP call to partner APIs 20 512 Mi I/O bound, rate-limited anyway
documents PDF render 3 1 Gi 180 MB peak per job
exports CSV of 2M rows, streamed 2 1 Gi streamed, but holds a DB cursor

Also set --max-old-space-size a little below the container limit (for a 1 Gi limit, use --max-old-space-size=768). Otherwise V8 happily grows past the cgroup limit and the kernel kills the process without a JavaScript heap error, giving you an OOMKilled with no stack trace and no clue.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Worker pod killed mid-job because the grace period is shorter than the job.
  • Autoscaler scaling to zero and the first job of the morning waiting 20 s for a cold start.
  • A CPU-bound job freezing the lock heartbeat and causing self-inflicted stalls.
  • UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE of 4 throttling ten concurrent sharp calls to four at a time.
  • Workers sharing a database connection pool sized for the API, exhausting PostgreSQL max_connections when the autoscaler adds ten pods (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals; use PgBouncer).
  • One worker Deployment serving all queues, so a poison job in documents starves notifications.

35.4 Scheduled jobs

35.4.1 Cron in a single process

Concept

A scheduled job runs on a clock rather than in response to an event: the nightly settlement at 02:00, the hourly stock sync, the every-five-minutes retry sweep. @nestjs/schedule gives you @Cron, @Interval and @Timeout decorators backed by an in-process timer.

// billing/settlement.scheduler.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';

@Injectable()
export class SettlementScheduler {
  private readonly log = new Logger(SettlementScheduler.name);

  @Cron('0 2 * * *', { name: 'nightly-settlement', timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' })
  async runNightlySettlement() {
    this.log.log('starting nightly settlement');
    await this.settlement.run();
  }
}

This is correct, simple and completely wrong in production the moment you have more than one replica.

Failure scenario

At 02:00 on 14 March, the nightly settlement ran. It ran five times, because the orders-api Deployment had five replicas and @Cron fires in every process. Each run read the day's unsettled orders, created payout rows and called the payment provider's payout API. The provider is idempotent per idempotency key, and the code did not send one. Three of the five runs raced past the WHERE settled = false check before any of them wrote settled = true. Merchants were paid three times, totalling about 4.1 crore rupees. Recovery took nine days and a lot of apologetic phone calls.

The bug was one line: a cron decorator in a module that was imported by the API, which runs with replicas: 5.

The three correct answers

Answer 1: run the scheduler in exactly one process. Put ScheduleModule.forRoot() and every @Cron class in a dedicated Deployment with replicas: 1 and strategy: Recreate. Simple, obvious, and it has a real weakness: during a rolling deploy or a node failure there is a window with zero schedulers, so a job scheduled in that window never fires. Acceptable for "refresh the cache" and unacceptable for "settle payments".

Answer 2: let the queue own the schedule. BullMQ repeatable jobs store the schedule in Redis. Any number of processes may declare the same repeatable job; Redis holds one entry, and exactly one job instance is produced per tick, then consumed by exactly one worker.

// billing/settlement-schedule.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnApplicationBootstrap } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class SettlementScheduleService implements OnApplicationBootstrap {
  constructor(@InjectQueue('billing') private readonly queue: Queue) {}

  async onApplicationBootstrap() {
    // Declaring the same repeatable job from every replica is safe:
    // the repeat key is derived from name + pattern + tz, so it is upserted, not duplicated.
    await this.queue.add(
      'settlement.nightly',
      { v: 1 },
      {
        repeat: { pattern: '0 2 * * *', tz: 'Asia/Kolkata' },
        // A deterministic id per fire time is added by BullMQ itself; keep attempts low
        // because a settlement retry must be deliberate, not automatic.
        attempts: 1,
        removeOnComplete: { count: 100 },
        removeOnFail: { age: 30 * 24 * 3600 },
      },
    );
  }
}

Newer BullMQ versions expose queue.upsertJobScheduler(id, repeatOpts, template), which makes the upsert explicit and lets you change a schedule without hunting for the old repeat key. Either way, the rule is: changing a cron pattern does not remove the old one. You must call queue.removeRepeatable(...) or queue.removeJobScheduler(id) for the old pattern, or you will silently run both. Teams discover this when a job starts running at both 02:00 and 03:00.

Answer 3: put the schedule in PostgreSQL and claim it with a lock. This is the most durable and the one I reach for when the job is financially significant, because the schedule, the claim and the business writes can all live in one transaction.

35.4.2 A job_schedules table claimed with SKIP LOCKED

CREATE TABLE job_schedules (
  id              text PRIMARY KEY,               -- 'nightly-settlement'
  cron            text        NOT NULL,           -- '0 2 * * *'
  timezone        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',
  enabled         boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  next_run_at     timestamptz NOT NULL,
  last_run_at     timestamptz,
  last_status     text,                           -- 'ok' | 'failed'
  running_until   timestamptz,                    -- lease held by the current runner
  runner_id       text,                           -- pod name, for debugging
  catch_up        boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);

-- The scheduler only ever scans due rows, so index exactly that.
CREATE INDEX idx_job_schedules_due
  ON job_schedules (next_run_at)
  WHERE enabled;

Every replica runs a cheap tick every 10 seconds. The tick tries to claim due rows; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED means the losers do not block, they just find nothing.

-- One tick. Runs inside a transaction, in every replica, every 10 seconds.
WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM job_schedules
  WHERE enabled
    AND next_run_at <= now()
    AND (running_until IS NULL OR running_until < now())
  ORDER BY next_run_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 5
)
UPDATE job_schedules s
SET running_until = now() + interval '10 minutes',
    runner_id     = $1,
    last_run_at   = now()
FROM due
WHERE s.id = due.id
RETURNING s.id, s.cron, s.timezone, s.catch_up, s.next_run_at;

Whoever gets a row runs the job, then sets next_run_at from the cron expression and clears the lease. Whoever gets nothing goes back to sleep. There is no leader election, no ZooKeeper, no distributed lock service — just a row and a transaction.

// scheduler/db-scheduler.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { CronExpressionParser } from 'cron-parser';

@Injectable()
export class DbSchedulerService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DbSchedulerService.name);
  private readonly runnerId = process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local';

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly registry: JobRegistry) {}

  // Safe to run in every replica: the claim is what serializes it.
  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_10_SECONDS, { name: 'schedule-tick' })
  async tick(): Promise<void> {
    const claimed = await this.ds.transaction(async (em) =>
      em.query(CLAIM_DUE_SQL, [this.runnerId]),
    );

    for (const row of claimed) {
      try {
        await this.registry.run(row.id);
        await this.finish(row, 'ok');
      } catch (err) {
        this.log.error({ scheduleId: row.id, err }, 'scheduled job failed');
        await this.finish(row, 'failed');
      }
    }
  }

  private async finish(row: ScheduleRow, status: 'ok' | 'failed') {
    // Compute the next fire time in the schedule's own timezone, from "now",
    // so a slow run does not cause an immediate second run.
    const next = CronExpressionParser.parse(row.cron, { tz: row.timezone }).next().toDate();
    await this.ds.query(
      `UPDATE job_schedules
          SET next_run_at = $2, running_until = NULL, runner_id = NULL, last_status = $3
        WHERE id = $1`,
      [row.id, next, status],
    );
  }
}

Notice running_until. If the pod holding the lease dies, the lease expires after ten minutes and another replica picks the job up. That is a lease, not a lock, and it is why a job can run twice: if the first pod was merely slow (a 12-minute run under a 10-minute lease), two pods run it concurrently. Set the lease longer than the p99 run time, and heartbeat it for long jobs (35.7).

35.4.3 Timezones, DST, and the 2 a.m. problem

Concept

Cron expressions are wall-clock expressions. Wall clocks in most of the world jump twice a year. A job scheduled at 0 2 * * * in America/New_York:

  • On the spring-forward Sunday, 02:00 does not exist. The clock goes 01:59:59 then 03:00:00. The job does not run that day.
  • On the fall-back Sunday, 02:00 happens twice. Naive schedulers run the job twice.

If that job is "settle yesterday's payments", one of those outcomes is a missing day of payouts and the other is double payouts.

How to handle it

  1. Schedule financially significant jobs in UTC. tz: 'UTC' with 0 21 * * * never skips and never repeats. Then convert to local time for the business logic ("yesterday" in Asia/Kolkata), not for the trigger. This is the single best fix and it costs nothing.
  2. If it must be local, avoid 00:00 to 03:00. A job at 0 4 * * * is immune to DST in every timezone that shifts at 02:00 or 03:00.
  3. Make the job idempotent on its business day. A settlement job that takes a business_date and has a unique constraint on (business_date) in a settlement_runs table simply cannot run twice, DST or not. This is the belt to the UTC braces.
  4. Store the timezone with the schedule, never rely on the pod's TZ. Containers default to UTC; developers' laptops do not. A cron that works locally and fires 5.5 hours late in production is a classic.
-- Idempotency for a daily job, enforced by the database, not by the scheduler.
CREATE TABLE settlement_runs (
  business_date date PRIMARY KEY,
  started_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  finished_at   timestamptz,
  status        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'running',
  runner_id     text NOT NULL
);

-- The job's first statement. If it conflicts, another run owns this date: exit quietly.
INSERT INTO settlement_runs (business_date, runner_id)
VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (business_date) DO NOTHING
RETURNING business_date;

If that RETURNING gives you zero rows, someone else has the day. Log and return. Five replicas, a DST double-fire and a manual re-trigger all collapse into exactly one settlement.

35.4.4 Missed runs and the catch-up policy

The scheduler was down from 01:40 to 02:30 (a bad deploy, a node drain, a Redis failover). Three jobs should have fired. What now? There is no universal right answer, so decide per job and write it down.

Policy Behaviour Use for
Skip Ignore missed fires; next run is the next scheduled time Cache warmers, metric rollups that recompute from scratch, health sweeps
Run once Fire immediately, once, regardless of how many were missed Sync jobs whose work is "reconcile current state"
Catch up all Fire once per missed slot, in order Per-period jobs: daily settlement, hourly billing snapshots
Alert only Do not run; page a human Anything where an unsupervised late run is dangerous

With the job_schedules table this is a catch_up boolean column and three lines in finish(): if catch_up is true, advance next_run_at by exactly one cron step from the previous next_run_at rather than from now(), so the scheduler naturally walks forward through the missed slots one tick at a time. If it is false, compute from now() and skip the gap.

Guard the catch-up: if the gap is more than, say, 24 slots, do not run 24 settlements at 09:00 on a Monday. Cap it, log loudly, and page. "The scheduler was down for two days and then fired 48 hourly billing jobs in ninety seconds" is its own incident.

35.5 Delayed jobs

35.5.1 The mechanism

Concept

A delayed job is enqueued now and becomes runnable at a future time. delay: 900_000 means "not before fifteen minutes from now". It is not "exactly in fifteen minutes"; it is "no earlier than".

How it works

BullMQ stores delayed jobs in a Redis sorted set (ZADD) scored by the timestamp at which they become runnable. A worker keeps a timer for the earliest score. When that time arrives, a Lua script atomically moves every job whose score has passed from delayed into wait (or prioritized), and normal workers pick them up.

flowchart LR
    P["Producer: queue.add with delay 900000"] --> Z["ZSET delayed, score = now + 900000"]
    T["Delay timer in a worker"] -->|"score <= now"| MV["Lua: move to wait"]
    Z --> MV
    MV --> WT["LIST wait"]
    WT --> W["Worker picks it up"]

Consequences you must understand:

  • Cost is O(log n) per insert and memory is one sorted-set entry plus one job hash per delayed job. Two million delayed jobs is real memory; measure it.
  • Precision is best-effort. Expect delivery within a second of the deadline on a healthy system, and a burst when the system was unhealthy.
  • If Redis has no persistence, delayed jobs die with it. A 15-minute payment timeout is a business rule; storing it only in a non-persistent Redis is storing a business rule in a cache. See 35.10.

35.5.2 The canonical example: cancel unpaid orders after 15 minutes

Practical example

The requirement: when a customer places an order with "pay later" (UPI intent, bank transfer, cash-on-delivery verification), hold the inventory for 15 minutes. If payment has not arrived, cancel the order and release the stock.

The naive implementation is a cron every minute scanning for status = 'awaiting_payment' AND created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'. That works, and for low volume it is genuinely the right answer — it is simple, it is durable, and it self-heals after downtime. Its cost is a table scan (or an index scan on a partial index) every minute forever, and up to 60 seconds of imprecision.

The delayed-job implementation is precise and costs nothing when idle:

// orders/orders.service.ts (fragment)
await this.expiryQueue.add(
  'order.expire',
  { v: 1, orderId: order.id },
  {
    delay: 15 * 60 * 1000,
    // Deterministic id so a retry of the HTTP request cannot schedule two expiries.
    jobId: `expire:${order.id}`,
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 30_000 },
  },
);
// orders/order-expiry.processor.ts
@Processor('order-expiry', { concurrency: 20 })
export class OrderExpiryProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderExpiryProcessor.name);

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<{ orderId: string }>) {
    const { orderId } = job.data;

    // Re-check state inside a transaction with a row lock. The payload is 15 minutes
    // old and is only a hint that we should LOOK, never a statement of fact.
    return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const order = await em.findOne(Order, {
        where: { id: orderId },
        lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' },   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
      });

      if (!order) return { skipped: 'gone' };
      if (order.status !== 'awaiting_payment') {
        // Paid, cancelled by the user, or already expired. All fine. Do nothing.
        return { skipped: order.status };
      }

      order.status = 'expired';
      order.expiredAt = new Date();
      await em.save(order);
      await this.inventory.releaseReservation(em, order.id); // same transaction
      this.log.log({ orderId }, 'order expired, stock released');
      return { expired: true };
    });
  }
}

35.5.3 Cancellation when payment arrives first

There are two ways to handle "the customer paid at minute 4, so the expiry job must not fire".

Option A: remove the job. Because we used a deterministic jobId, the payment handler can delete it.

// payments/payment-confirmed.handler.ts
const job = await this.expiryQueue.getJob(`expire:${orderId}`);
// remove() throws if the job is currently active; that is fine, the state check saves us.
await job?.remove().catch(() => undefined);

Option B: let it fire and no-op. The handler already checks state, sees status = 'paid', and returns.

Do both, and rely only on B. Removing the job is an optimization that keeps Redis small and keeps the dashboard clean. The state check is the correctness mechanism. This is the most important sentence in this section:

A delayed job's payload describes the world at enqueue time. By the time it runs, that world is minutes or hours old. The job's first act must be to re-read the current state and decide whether the action is still appropriate.

Every delayed-job bug I have debugged in fifteen years is a violation of that rule: the "abandoned cart" email sent to someone who checked out, the "your trial ends tomorrow" email to a paying customer, the subscription cancelled after the user renewed, the order expired after payment landed in a webhook the code raced against.

Failure scenario

A payments team stored the amount in the delayed job payload: { orderId, amountToRefund: 4999 }. Between enqueue and execution the customer removed an item and the order total dropped to 2499. The job refunded 4999. Twelve thousand orders over three weeks, discovered by finance, not by monitoring. Payload said 4999; the database said 2499; nobody asked the database.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A delay longer than your Redis retention or your maxmemory eviction policy will silently drop jobs. Set maxmemory-policy noeviction on a Redis used as a queue. allkeys-lru on a queue Redis is a data-loss bug.
  • Delays of days or weeks belong in PostgreSQL, not a Redis sorted set. Anything beyond about 24 hours: put a row with a due_at column and sweep it.
  • After an outage, thousands of delayed jobs become runnable at the same instant and overwhelm downstream services. Add a queue limiter, and consider jittering delays by a few seconds at enqueue time.
  • Clock skew between the producer and Redis shifts every delay. Redis's own clock decides; producers only supply a duration, which is why delay is a duration and not a timestamp.
  • Cancelling by remove() fails silently if the job is already active. Only the state check protects you.

Interview questions

  1. How would you implement "cancel unpaid orders after 15 minutes" and what are the trade-offs? Expected: delayed job for precision versus a periodic sweep for durability and simplicity; both require a state re-check; ideally run the sweep as a safety net alongside the delayed job.
  2. Your cron job ran five times last night. Why? Expected: @Cron fires per process and the Deployment has five replicas. Follow-up: three fixes, and which one you would pick for a payout job.
  3. What happens to a 0 2 * * * job on the DST fall-back night? Expected: 02:00 occurs twice, so it can run twice; the fixes are UTC scheduling, avoiding 00:00 to 03:00, and a unique constraint on the business date.
  4. Where does BullMQ store delayed jobs and what does that imply? Expected: a Redis sorted set scored by run-at time, moved to wait by a Lua script; implies memory cost, best-effort precision, and total loss if Redis has no persistence.
  5. Why must a delayed job re-read state? Expected: the payload is a stale snapshot; give the refund-amount or cancel-after-payment example.

Practical exercise

Implement order expiry twice: once as a BullMQ delayed job and once as a PostgreSQL sweep over a partial index on (created_at) WHERE status = 'awaiting_payment'.

Acceptance criteria: with 50,000 pending orders, measure the sweep's EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) cost per minute and the Redis memory used by 50,000 delayed jobs; kill Redis without persistence and show the delayed jobs are gone while the sweep still works; pay an order at minute 4 and prove with a test that neither implementation cancels it; restart the app during a delay and prove the job still fires.

35.6 Retries and error classification

35.6.1 Not all errors deserve a retry

Concept

A retry is a bet that the failure was temporary. If the failure is permanent, retrying is pure waste: it burns worker capacity, fills your logs, hammers a dependency that is already unhappy, and delays every other job in the queue. Classifying errors correctly is the difference between a queue that heals itself and a queue that amplifies an outage.

Three classes:

Class Examples What to do
Transient ECONNRESET, ETIMEDOUT, HTTP 502/503/504, HTTP 429, PostgreSQL 40001 serialization failure, 40P01 deadlock, Redis LOADING Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Permanent HTTP 400/404/422, validation failure, "order does not exist", unknown job name, foreign key violation on a row that was deleted Do not retry. Fail immediately to the dead-letter queue
Poison The payload itself crashes the handler: a malformed JSON blob, a 400 MB image, an infinite loop in a template Do not retry. Quarantine and alert. Retrying will take the worker down again

The third class is the one people forget, and it is the one that causes a total queue stall.

Why does it exist?

Because "retry 5 times with backoff" applied uniformly produces two opposite pathologies. Applied to permanent errors, it multiplies your error rate by five and delays the real work. Applied too aggressively to a struggling dependency, it produces a retry storm: the dependency is slow, so requests time out, so every job retries, so load triples, so the dependency dies completely. You did that. Your retry policy did that.

Mental model

Imagine knocking on a door. Nobody answers — maybe they are in the shower, so knocking again in a minute is sensible (transient). The house has been demolished — knocking a hundred times will not rebuild it (permanent). The door is wired to an alarm that shocks you unconscious — knocking again is how you end up in hospital twice (poison).

How it works

BullMQ increments attemptsMade, computes the backoff, and moves the job to delayed until the next attempt. When attemptsMade reaches attempts, the job moves to failed and stays there — that set is your dead-letter queue.

UnrecoverableError short-circuits the whole thing: throwing it moves the job straight to failed regardless of remaining attempts.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> waiting
    waiting --> active
    active --> completed
    active --> delayed : transient error, attempts left
    delayed --> waiting : backoff elapsed
    active --> failed : attempts exhausted
    active --> failed : UnrecoverableError
    active --> stalled : lock expired
    stalled --> waiting : requeued
    stalled --> failed : maxStalledCount exceeded
    completed --> [*]
    failed --> waiting : manual retry

NestJS example

Classification belongs in one place, not scattered through handlers.

// jobs/error-classifier.ts
import { UnrecoverableError } from 'bullmq';
import { AxiosError } from 'axios';

const TRANSIENT_NET = new Set([
  'ECONNRESET', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'EAI_AGAIN', 'EPIPE', 'ENETUNREACH',
]);
const TRANSIENT_PG = new Set([
  '40001', // serialization_failure
  '40P01', // deadlock_detected
  '55P03', // lock_not_available
  '57P01', // admin_shutdown (failover)
  '53300', // too_many_connections
]);

export function isTransient(err: unknown): boolean {
  const e = err as NodeJS.ErrnoException & AxiosError & { code?: string };

  if (e?.code && TRANSIENT_NET.has(e.code)) return true;
  if (e?.code && TRANSIENT_PG.has(e.code)) return true;

  const status = e?.response?.status;
  if (status === 429) return true;              // rate limited: back off, definitely retry
  if (status && status >= 500) return true;     // their problem, probably temporary
  if (status && status >= 400) return false;    // our problem, retrying changes nothing

  return false; // default to NOT retrying: an unknown error retried 5x is 5x the noise
}

/** Convert a classified error into the shape BullMQ understands. */
export function toJobError(err: unknown): Error {
  if (isTransient(err)) return err as Error;    // let BullMQ retry
  const e = err as Error;
  const wrapped = new UnrecoverableError(`${e.name}: ${e.message}`);
  wrapped.cause = e;                            // keep the original stack for the DLQ
  return wrapped;
}

Note the default: unknown errors do not retry. That is a deliberate, slightly controversial choice. The alternative default (retry everything unknown) is friendlier to transient bugs and much less friendly to your log bill and your dependencies. Whichever you pick, pick it consciously and write it in the code as a comment, because the next engineer will wonder.

// integrations/warehouse.processor.ts
@Processor('integrations', { concurrency: 20, limiter: { max: 40, duration: 1_000 } })
export class WarehouseProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  async process(job: Job<{ orderId: string }>) {
    try {
      const order = await this.orders.findOne(job.data.orderId);
      if (!order) throw new UnrecoverableError(`order ${job.data.orderId} not found`);

      return await this.warehouse.pushOrder(order, {
        // The third party's idempotency key. Same key on every retry.
        idempotencyKey: `wh:${order.id}`,
        timeoutMs: 8_000,
      });
    } catch (err) {
      throw toJobError(err);
    }
  }
}

35.6.2 Backoff and jitter

Exponential backoff spreads retries out over time so a struggling dependency gets breathing room. { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 } gives 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s, 32 s.

The problem: if a dependency is down for 30 seconds and 4,000 jobs fail at the same moment, all 4,000 retry at exactly 2 s, then all 4,000 at 4 s. You have built a synchronized hammer. That is the thundering herd, and it is why every backoff needs jitter.

BullMQ lets you register custom backoff strategies on the worker:

// queues/backoff.ts
import { BullRootModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/bullmq';

export const jitteredExponential = (attemptsMade: number): number => {
  const base = 2_000;
  const cap = 5 * 60_000;                       // never wait more than 5 minutes
  const exp = Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** (attemptsMade - 1));
  // Full jitter: uniform in [0, exp). Spreads a synchronized herd across the window.
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * exp);
};
@Processor('integrations', {
  concurrency: 20,
  settings: {
    backoffStrategy: (attemptsMade: number) => jitteredExponential(attemptsMade),
  },
})
export class WarehouseProcessor extends WorkerHost { /* ... */ }

Then use backoff: { type: 'custom' } in the job options.

Two refinements worth knowing:

  • Honour Retry-After. If a 429 or 503 carries Retry-After: 120, waiting 120 seconds is strictly better than guessing. Read the header, and use job.moveToDelayed(Date.now() + seconds * 1000, token) with a DelayedError so the attempt is not consumed.
  • Cap total retry time, not just attempt count. Five attempts with exponential backoff from 30 s is about 15 minutes of trying. For a webhook delivery you may want 24 hours of trying with 12 attempts; for a "your OTP is 4821" SMS you want 2 attempts over 10 seconds, because a late OTP is worse than no OTP.
Job type attempts base delay Total window Why
OTP SMS 2 2 s ~5 s Useless if late
Order confirmation email 5 5 s ~8 min Should arrive fast, tolerates a blip
Partner webhook delivery 12 10 s, capped 1 h ~24 h Partners have long outages
Warehouse sync 8 10 s, capped 15 min ~2 h Their maintenance windows are ~1 h
Nightly settlement 1 n/a n/a A human must decide to re-run

35.6.3 Every retried job must be idempotent

This is not a guideline; it is the entry ticket. The moment you set attempts > 1, you have promised that running the handler twice is safe.

You do not get to choose whether jobs run twice. Even with attempts: 1, a worker can be SIGKILLed after sending the email but before reporting completion, and the stalled-job mechanism will hand the job to another worker. At-least-once delivery is the only delivery guarantee any of these systems actually gives you. Exactly-once is a property of your handler, not of your queue.

Three levels of idempotency, cheapest first:

  1. Naturally idempotent. UPDATE orders SET status='expired' WHERE id=$1 AND status='awaiting_payment' — running it twice changes nothing the second time. Prefer this. Design for it.
  2. Idempotency keys at the boundary. Stripe, most payment gateways and well-built partner APIs accept an Idempotency-Key header and deduplicate server-side. Always send one, always derive it deterministically from the job (refund:${orderId}:${attemptGroup}), never from Date.now() or a fresh UUID.
  3. A local execution ledger. When the side effect is with a partner who has no idempotency support (very common), record locally that you did it, in the same transaction as the business write. That is the job_executions table in 35.8.

35.7 Deduplication and job locking

35.7.1 Deterministic job ids

Concept

BullMQ ignores an add() whose jobId already exists in the queue. So if you can derive an id from the meaning of the work, duplicates collapse for free.

// The same order confirmation can be requested by an HTTP retry, an outbox sweep
// and a manual support action. All three produce the same id, so only one job exists.
await queue.add('order.confirmation', { v: 1, orderId }, { jobId: `confirm:${orderId}` });

The limits you must know

The dedupe is only as durable as the job record. Once the job completes and removeOnComplete deletes it, the id is free again and a new add() creates a new job. That is usually what you want (a job that already ran should be re-runnable), but it means jobId is not a permanent idempotency mechanism. It is a debounce within the queue's retention window.

Concretely:

  • removeOnComplete: true — dedupe window is "while queued or running". Re-enqueueing 1 ms after completion creates a second job.
  • removeOnComplete: { age: 3600 } — dedupe window is roughly one hour.
  • A failed job stays in failed, so its id is still taken. Re-enqueueing the same id after a permanent failure silently does nothing. This surprises everyone once. If you need "retry after fixing the bug", you must remove the failed job first, or use job.retry().

35.7.2 Debouncing repeated work

Practical example

A product's price changes seven times in ninety seconds because a merchant is dragging a slider. Each change fires product.reindex. Seven reindexes of the same product is six wasted Elasticsearch round trips, and the first six results are immediately stale.

The right behaviour is debounce: coalesce them into one job that runs shortly after the last change.

// search/reindex.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class ReindexService {
  constructor(@InjectQueue('search') private readonly queue: Queue) {}

  async scheduleReindex(productId: string): Promise<void> {
    const jobId = `reindex:${productId}`;
    const existing = await this.queue.getJob(jobId);

    // If a job is already waiting or delayed, push its run time out by 5 seconds.
    // If it is already active, leave it alone and add a follow-up.
    if (existing) {
      const state = await existing.getState();
      if (state === 'delayed' || state === 'waiting') {
        await existing.changeDelay(5_000);   // reset the debounce window
        return;
      }
      if (state === 'active') {
        // The running job will index a snapshot older than this change.
        // Queue exactly one follow-up, with a different id.
        await this.queue.add('product.reindex', { v: 1, productId },
          { jobId: `${jobId}:follow`, delay: 5_000 });
        return;
      }
    }

    await this.queue.add('product.reindex', { v: 1, productId },
      { jobId, delay: 5_000, attempts: 5, removeOnComplete: true });
  }
}

Seven slider drags become one reindex five seconds after the last one. Recent BullMQ versions also ship a first-class deduplication: { id, ttl } option that does the window-based part of this in Redis without the read-modify-write; use it if your version has it, but understand the mechanism above, because you will need the active-job case regardless.

The active branch is the subtle part. A job already running holds a snapshot from before your change. Skipping the follow-up means the index silently misses the last edit. This class of bug — "the search index is right 99 percent of the time" — is miserable to debug, so handle it explicitly.

35.7.3 Locks, stalled jobs, and why a job runs twice

Concept

When a BullMQ worker takes a job it sets a lock in Redis with a TTL of lockDuration (default 30 s) and renews it on a timer at roughly half that interval. If the lock expires without renewal, another worker's stalledInterval sweep (default every 30 s) notices an active job with no live lock, declares it stalled, and moves it back to wait.

That is the mechanism, and it is the honest answer to "can a job run twice?" — yes, in four situations:

  1. The pod was SIGKILLed (OOM, node failure, grace period exceeded) mid-job. The lock expires; another worker picks it up; the first worker had already sent the email.
  2. The handler blocked the event loop for longer than lockDuration, so the renewal timer never fired. The worker is alive and still working, and a second worker starts the same job. Now you have two concurrent runs.
  3. A network partition between the worker and Redis prevented renewal.
  4. Redis failed over and lost the lock key (replication is asynchronous).
sequenceDiagram
    participant W1 as Worker1
    participant R as Redis
    participant W2 as Worker2
    W1->>R: take job 42, lock TTL 30s
    W1->>W1: CPU-bound render blocks event loop 45s
    Note over R: lock expires at t+30s
    W2->>R: stalled sweep finds job 42 unlocked
    R-->>W2: job 42 requeued and taken
    W2->>W2: renders the same invoice
    W1->>R: finish job 42, lock lost, move rejected

maxStalledCount (default 1) limits how many times a job may stall before it is failed outright, which stops an infinitely crash-looping job from cycling forever.

How to reduce the odds

  • Set lockDuration above your p99 job duration for that queue. A 90-second PDF job under a 30-second lock stalls constantly.
  • Never block the event loop (35.3.4). This is the single biggest cause.
  • Extend the lock explicitly for long jobs. process(job, token) gives you the token; job.extendLock(token, ms) renews it. Call it from your own progress loop.
async process(job: Job<{ exportId: string }>, token?: string) {
  const rows = await this.repo.streamRows(job.data.exportId);
  let n = 0;
  for await (const row of rows) {
    await this.writer.write(row);
    if (++n % 5_000 === 0) {
      await job.updateProgress(n);              // visible in Bull Board
      if (token) await job.extendLock(token, 60_000); // I am alive, give me 60 more seconds
    }
  }
  return { rows: n };
}
  • Accept that it can still happen and make the handler idempotent. Every mitigation above reduces probability; only idempotency reduces impact to zero.

35.7.4 PostgreSQL leases and heartbeats

The same problem exists in a PostgreSQL queue, and the solution has the same shape but is easier to inspect because it is rows you can SELECT.

CREATE TABLE job_queue (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  queue         text        NOT NULL,
  name          text        NOT NULL,
  payload       jsonb       NOT NULL,
  dedupe_key    text,                              -- deterministic id, optional
  run_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  attempts      int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  max_attempts  int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  status        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ready',  -- ready|running|done|failed
  locked_until  timestamptz,
  locked_by     text,
  heartbeat_at  timestamptz,
  last_error    text,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Only ready-and-due rows are ever scanned. A partial index keeps it tiny
-- even when the table has millions of completed rows.
CREATE INDEX idx_job_queue_ready
  ON job_queue (queue, run_at, id)
  WHERE status = 'ready';

-- Deduplication enforced by the database, not by application logic.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_job_queue_dedupe
  ON job_queue (queue, dedupe_key)
  WHERE dedupe_key IS NOT NULL AND status IN ('ready', 'running');

Claiming a batch:

-- SKIP LOCKED: concurrent workers never block each other; each gets a disjoint batch.
UPDATE job_queue j
SET status = 'running',
    locked_until = now() + interval '2 minutes',
    locked_by = $2,
    heartbeat_at = now(),
    attempts = attempts + 1
FROM (
  SELECT id
  FROM job_queue
  WHERE queue = $1
    AND (
      (status = 'ready'   AND run_at <= now()) OR
      (status = 'running' AND locked_until < now())   -- reclaim a dead worker's lease
    )
  ORDER BY run_at, id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 20
) AS c
WHERE j.id = c.id
RETURNING j.id, j.name, j.payload, j.attempts, j.max_attempts;

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the whole trick. Without it, twenty workers running this statement serialize on the same hot rows and your throughput collapses to one worker's worth. With it, PostgreSQL hands each worker a different set of rows and you scale close to linearly to a few thousand jobs per second — plenty for most systems, and far beyond what people assume a database queue can do.

The heartbeat, for long jobs:

-- Called every 30 seconds from the handler while it works.
UPDATE job_queue
SET heartbeat_at = now(), locked_until = now() + interval '2 minutes'
WHERE id = $1 AND locked_by = $2;

If that UPDATE reports zero rows, someone else has taken your job. The correct response is to stop immediately and not write anything, because a second worker is now doing this work. Checking the row count of your heartbeat is the closest thing to a fencing token you get in a simple queue, and it is worth the four lines.

35.8 Dead-letter queues and idempotent handlers

35.8.1 What a dead-letter queue is for

Concept

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds jobs that failed permanently: attempts exhausted, or an unrecoverable error. In BullMQ the failed set is the DLQ. In SQS and RabbitMQ it is a separate physical queue you configure. In a PostgreSQL queue it is WHERE status = 'failed'.

Its purpose is not storage. Its purpose is that failure becomes visible and replayable instead of silent. A queue without a DLQ discards work, and discarded work is discovered by customers.

Why does it exist?

Because the alternatives are worse. Retrying forever turns one poison job into a permanently blocked worker. Dropping the job loses an order confirmation, a refund, a webhook to a partner who is now out of sync with you. The DLQ is the place where "we could not do this" is written down.

What to do with it

  1. Alert on growth, not on size. A DLQ with 340 old jobs from last month's incident is fine. A DLQ that gained 50 jobs in ten minutes is an incident. Alert on increase(dlq_size[15m]) > 20, and separately on dlq_size > 0 for queues where the correct steady state is genuinely empty (payouts, refunds).
  2. Inspect. Bull Board (@bull-board/nestjs) gives you a web UI over BullMQ: per-queue counts, job payloads, stack traces, and buttons to retry or delete. Put it behind your admin auth, not on the public internet, because job payloads are business data.
  3. Categorize. Nine hundred failures with the same stack trace are one bug. Group by error class before you look at individual jobs.
  4. Replay deliberately. Never a blind "retry all" during an incident: if the dependency is still down, you have just created a second retry storm on top of the first.
// admin/bull-board.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { BullBoardModule } from '@bull-board/nestjs';
import { ExpressAdapter } from '@bull-board/express';
import { BullMQAdapter } from '@bull-board/api/bullMQAdapter';

@Module({
  imports: [
    BullBoardModule.forRoot({
      route: '/admin/queues',
      adapter: ExpressAdapter,
      // Basic auth or your admin guard middleware must be applied to this route.
    }),
    BullBoardModule.forFeature(
      { name: 'notifications', adapter: BullMQAdapter },
      { name: 'documents', adapter: BullMQAdapter },
      { name: 'integrations', adapter: BullMQAdapter },
    ),
  ],
})
export class QueueAdminModule {}

Replay tooling you actually want, as an admin endpoint rather than a developer with a Redis CLI:

// admin/dlq.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class DlqService {
  constructor(@InjectQueue('integrations') private readonly q: Queue) {}

  /** Replay failed jobs matching an error substring, slowly, with a hard cap. */
  async replay(opts: { match?: string; limit: number; spacingMs: number }): Promise<number> {
    const failed = await this.q.getFailed(0, opts.limit - 1);
    let replayed = 0;

    for (const job of failed) {
      if (opts.match && !(job.failedReason ?? '').includes(opts.match)) continue;
      // retry() resets attemptsMade and moves the job back to wait.
      await job.retry();
      replayed++;
      // Spacing prevents replaying 4,000 jobs into a dependency that just came back.
      if (opts.spacingMs) await sleep(opts.spacingMs);
    }
    return replayed;
  }

  async summary(): Promise<Record<string, number>> {
    const failed = await this.q.getFailed(0, 999);
    const byReason: Record<string, number> = {};
    for (const j of failed) {
      const key = (j.failedReason ?? 'unknown').split('\n')[0].slice(0, 120);
      byReason[key] = (byReason[key] ?? 0) + 1;
    }
    return byReason;
  }
}

Failure scenario

A team shipped a change to the invoice template that threw on orders with no billing address (a legacy data case, about 0.3 percent of orders). attempts: 5 with exponential backoff meant each of those jobs occupied a worker slot five times over fifteen minutes. At 400 orders/minute, 0.3 percent is a little over one per minute, which does not sound like much — but the retries stacked, and with concurrency: 3 on the documents queue, within two hours the queue depth was 11,000 and legitimate invoices were four hours late. Nobody was paged, because the alert was on failed count > 100 and the failed count was only rising slowly; the jobs were mostly retrying, not failed.

Two fixes: classify "no billing address" as unrecoverable so it fails immediately (one attempt, not five), and alert on the age of the oldest waiting job, which had been over two hours for most of the incident. That metric is the subject of 35.9 and it is the one I would keep if I could only keep one.

35.8.2 The job_executions table

Concept

A tiny table that records, durably and transactionally, that a specific job did a specific side effect. It converts "at-least-once delivery" into "exactly-once effect", which is the only exactly-once that exists.

CREATE TABLE job_executions (
  execution_key text        PRIMARY KEY,   -- deterministic: 'email:order-confirmation:ord_8812'
  job_id        text        NOT NULL,      -- BullMQ job id, for tracing back
  queue         text        NOT NULL,
  status        text        NOT NULL,      -- 'in_progress' | 'succeeded' | 'failed'
  attempt       int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  result        jsonb,                     -- provider message id, S3 key, whatever proves it
  error         text,
  started_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  finished_at   timestamptz
);

-- Housekeeping: this table grows forever unless you prune it.
CREATE INDEX idx_job_executions_started ON job_executions (started_at);

The execution_key is the heart of it. It must be derived from what the effect is, not from the job id, because a retried or duplicated job gets a new attempt but must map to the same key. email:order-confirmation:ord_8812 is right. job:${job.id} is wrong — a stalled job re-queued as a new id would slip through.

How it works

flowchart TB
    S["Job starts"] --> I["INSERT execution_key ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"]
    I -->|"0 rows: key exists"| C{"status?"}
    C -->|"succeeded"| SK["Return early. Effect already happened"]
    C -->|"in_progress"| ST["Another worker holds it. Throw and let backoff retry"]
    C -->|"failed"| RT["Reset to in_progress and try again"]
    I -->|"1 row inserted"| DO["Perform the side effect"]
    DO --> OK["UPDATE status = succeeded, store result"]
    DO --> ER["UPDATE status = failed, store error, rethrow"]
// jobs/idempotency.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export class AlreadyRunningError extends Error {}

@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /**
   * Runs `fn` at most once per executionKey, ever.
   * Returns the stored result if the effect already happened.
