They always include the tenant filter in the vector query for multi-tenant systems, treating a missing tenant scope as a serious data-leak bug. They keep the embedding dimension matched to the model and re-embed on model change. And they know pgvector's limits (37.1.3) and the conditions under which a dedicated vector database earns its operational cost.

Common mistakes

  • No vector index on a large table, so every search is a full scan.
  • Mismatched dimension between the column and the embedding model.
  • Using the wrong distance operator for the model's metric.
  • Forgetting the tenant filter, leaking cross-tenant documents.
  • Not verifying with EXPLAIN that the index is used; a filter or query shape can defeat it.
  • Expecting exact results from an approximate index without tuning recall.

Interview questions

  1. What does pgvector add to PostgreSQL and why use it over a separate vector database? A vector type and similarity operators/indexes; use it to avoid a new system, keep embeddings joined to relational data and in transactions, and filter by metadata in one SQL query.

  2. HNSW vs IVFFlat — how do you choose? HNSW is the default for best speed at high recall (slower build, more memory); IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory, favored for very large datasets; both are approximate and tunable.

  3. Why is metadata filtering important in a multi-tenant RAG system? Every vector query must scope to the current tenant, or it can retrieve another tenant's documents; pgvector does this with a WHERE clause in the same query.

  4. How do you confirm a vector query uses the index? EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) should show an index scan on the HNSW/IVFFlat index, not a sequential scan.

  5. A tenant-filtered vector query returns 3 rows when you asked for 10. What is happening and how do you fix it? HNSW collects ef_search candidates and filters afterwards, so a selective filter removes most of them. Use iterative index scans (pgvector 0.8+), exact search for small tenants, partitioning or partial indexes for large ones, or a higher ef_search.

  6. How do you know your approximate index is good enough? Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample of real queries, and tune ef_search or probes until recall meets the target at acceptable latency.

  7. Why must CREATE INDEX for HNSW be run carefully on a large table? A plain build blocks writes for its whole duration and is slow if maintenance_work_mem is too small; use CONCURRENTLY, enough memory, parallel workers and off-peak timing.

Practical exercise

Create a product_embeddings table with a vector column and a tenant_id, load a few thousand rows, build an HNSW cosine index, and run a nearest-neighbour query filtered by tenant. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the index is used, then run the same query without the tenant filter and observe the difference. Acceptance criteria: the tenant-scoped query uses the HNSW index and never returns another tenant's rows.

37.1.3 pgvector versus a dedicated vector database

Concept

Dedicated vector databases exist and are sometimes the right choice. The decision is the same build-vs-operate tradeoff as everywhere in this book: pgvector reuses a system you already run; a dedicated vector database is another system with its own scaling, features and operational cost. You choose based on scale, feature needs and how tightly the vectors must join to your relational data.

How it works — the decision table

Factor pgvector Dedicated vector database
Operational cost None extra; it is your PostgreSQL A new system to run, secure, back up, sync
Join to relational data Native (one SQL query, transactions) Separate; you join in application code
Tenant isolation / filtering A WHERE clause More work, varies by product
Scale (vectors) Comfortable to tens of millions; beyond needs care Built for hundreds of millions to billions
Advanced features Core ANN search Richer: sharding, specialized indexes, hybrid built in
Consistency with source data Same database, transactional Must sync (outbox/CDC), eventual
Team familiarity You already know PostgreSQL New tool to learn and operate 
Choose pgvector when:                      Choose a dedicated vector DB when:
- you already run PostgreSQL               - vectors number in the hundreds of millions+
- vectors join tightly to relational data  - you need its specialized scaling/features
- scale is up to ~tens of millions         - vector search is the core product at huge scale
- you want one system to operate           - a dedicated team will own the extra system
- tenant filtering must be easy and exact

Failure scenario

A team chose a hosted vector database "for scale" with 300,000 documents. Products were written to PostgreSQL and then, in the same request handler, upserted to the vector database. When the vector database had a 20-minute incident, the handler's second write failed after the first had committed (a classic dual write, Part 29). About 4,000 product edits never reached the vector store; nobody noticed for a month, until shoppers kept finding discontinued products by semantic search. They added an outbox and a nightly reconciliation job comparing ids and content hashes between the two stores, which is exactly the machinery pgvector would not have needed at that size.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Dual writes to PostgreSQL and a vector store drift on partial failure; use an outbox or CDC (37.3).
  • Deletes are the most forgotten sync event; a deleted or unpublished product still found by search is a common bug.
  • Tenant isolation in a separate store depends on its namespace or filter features and on every caller using them.
  • Two backups, two restore points: after a restore, the stores disagree until re-synced.
  • Vendor limits on metadata size, filter expressiveness or namespace count can force redesigns later.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior starts with pgvector unless a concrete requirement rules it out, because the simplest architecture that meets the need wins (the anti-hype principle from throughout this book) and a second datastore is a real, permanent operational tax — another thing to scale, secure, back up and keep in sync with the source of truth (Part 38). They move to a dedicated vector database only when scale (hundreds of millions of vectors), specialized features, or vector search being the core product at huge scale genuinely demands it, and they account for the sync problem (the vectors must be kept consistent with the relational source via outbox or CDC, which pgvector gets for free by living in the same database). They treat "add a vector database" as an architectural decision requiring an ADR (Part 61), not a default reach.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a dedicated vector database by default when pgvector would do, paying unnecessary operational cost.
  • Ignoring the sync problem a separate vector store creates (keeping it consistent with the source).
  • Underestimating pgvector (it handles far more than people assume).

Interview questions

  1. When is pgvector the right choice and when is a dedicated vector database? pgvector when you already run PostgreSQL, vectors join to relational data, and scale is up to tens of millions; a dedicated database at hundreds of millions of vectors or when specialized features or huge-scale vector-first products demand it.
  2. What hidden cost does a separate vector database add? Keeping it in sync and consistent with the relational source (outbox/CDC), plus operating, scaling, securing and backing up another system.

Practical exercise

Write a one-page decision record (ADR, Part 61) for whether a product-catalog search at your scale should use pgvector or a dedicated vector database, covering scale, join needs, tenant isolation, sync, and operational cost, ending with a recommendation. Acceptance criteria: the recommendation follows from the stated factors, and the sync/consistency cost of the separate-database option is addressed.

37.2 Retrieval-augmented generation

37.2.1 The RAG pipeline

Concept

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the pattern of retrieving relevant data and putting it into the prompt so the LLM answers from your facts instead of its training (which may be stale, generic, or wrong about your domain). The pipeline: chunk your documents, embed and index them, retrieve the most relevant chunks for a query, and generate an answer grounded in those chunks, with citations. RAG is how you build "ask a question about our data" features that are accurate and current.

Why does it exist?

An LLM alone cannot answer questions about your specific, current, private data — your product catalog, your support articles, this customer's orders — because it was never trained on them and cannot see them. Fine-tuning a model on your data is expensive, slow to update, and still hallucinates. RAG is simpler and better for most cases: keep your data in a store, retrieve the relevant pieces at query time, and let the model answer from them. When the data changes, you update the store, not the model. The model supplies language ability; your data supplies the facts.

Mental model

Imagine an open-book exam versus a closed-book one. A closed-book exam (the bare LLM) tests what the student memorized, and they will bluff when they do not know. An open-book exam (RAG) lets the student look up the relevant passage and answer from it, with a page reference. RAG hands the model the right pages for each question and asks it to answer from those pages and cite them. The retrieval step is finding the right pages; the generation step is writing the answer from them.

How it works — the pipeline

flowchart LR
    subgraph Indexing["Indexing (offline / on change)"]
        D["Documents"] --> C["Chunk"]
        C --> E1["Embed each chunk"]
        E1 --> I["Store in pgvector"]
    end
    subgraph Query["Query (per request)"]
        Q["User question"] --> E2["Embed question"]
        E2 --> R["Retrieve top-k chunks"]
        R --> RR["Re-rank (optional)"]
        RR --> P["Build prompt with chunks"]
        P --> G["LLM generates answer + citations"]
    end
    I -.serves.-> R

The two phases:

Indexing (offline, or when data changes):

  1. Chunk: split documents into pieces small enough to be precise and to fit in the prompt (a product description, a paragraph of a support article, a section of a manual). Too large and retrieval is imprecise and the prompt bloats; too small and you lose context. Chunks often overlap slightly so a sentence spanning a boundary is not lost.
  2. Embed: compute an embedding for each chunk.
  3. Index: store the chunk text, its embedding, and metadata (document id, tenant, section) in pgvector.

Query (per request):

  1. Embed the question with the same embedding model.
  2. Retrieve the top-k most similar chunks (a vector search, scoped by tenant/metadata).
  3. Re-rank (optional): a second, more precise step reorders the retrieved chunks by relevance, because the vector search is fast but approximate.
  4. Build the prompt: insert the retrieved chunks into the prompt as context, with instructions to answer only from them and to cite sources.
  5. Generate: the LLM produces the answer, grounded in the chunks, with citations.

How it works — code

// RAG query, continued from Part 36's LlmService and Part 120.1's pgvector.
async function answerWithRag(question: string, tenantId: string): Promise<{ answer: string; sources: string[] }> {
  // 5. Embed the question and retrieve top-k chunks for this tenant.
  const qEmbedding = await embedder.embed(question);
  const chunks = await db.query(
    `SELECT content, document_id, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity
       FROM doc_chunks
      WHERE tenant_id = $2
      ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
      LIMIT 6`,
    [qEmbedding, tenantId],
  );

  // 7. Build a grounded prompt. Number the chunks so the model can cite them.
  const context = chunks
    .map((c, i) => `[${i + 1}] (doc ${c.document_id})\n${c.content}`)
    .join('\n\n');

  const system =
    'Answer the question using ONLY the numbered context below. ' +
    'Cite sources like [1], [2]. If the context does not contain the answer, ' +
    'say you do not have that information. Do not use outside knowledge.';

  // 8. Generate.
  const answer = await llm.complete({
    system,
    user: `Context:\n${context}\n\nQuestion: ${question}`,
    maxTokens: 500,
  });

  return { answer, sources: chunks.map((c) => c.document_id) };
}

The grounding instruction ("answer ONLY from the context, cite sources, say you do not know otherwise") is what keeps RAG honest. Citations let users (and you) verify the answer against the source, which is the main defense against hallucination (Part 36): a cited answer can be checked; an uncited one cannot.

Chunking in practice

Good chunks follow the document's own structure. Split on headings and paragraphs first, then pack neighbouring paragraphs together up to a size budget, carrying a small overlap and the section title into each chunk so it still makes sense on its own.

// rag/chunker.ts -- structure-aware chunking with overlap and a heading prefix
export interface Chunk { chunkNo: number; content: string }

const approxTokens = (s: string) => Math.ceil(s.length / 4); // a budget, not billing: an estimate is fine

export function chunkArticle(title: string, markdown: string, maxTokens = 400, overlapParas = 1): Chunk[] {
  const chunks: Chunk[] = [];
  let section = title;
  let buf: string[] = [];

  const flush = () => {
    if (!buf.length) return;
    chunks.push({ chunkNo: chunks.length, content: `${title} > ${section}\n\n${buf.join('\n\n')}` });
    buf = buf.slice(-overlapParas); // keep the last paragraph as overlap for the next chunk
  };

  for (const block of markdown.split(/\n{2,}/)) {
    const heading = /^#{1,4}\s+(.*)/.exec(block);
    if (heading) { flush(); buf = []; section = heading[1]; continue; } // new section: no overlap across it
    if (approxTokens(buf.join('\n\n') + block) > maxTokens) flush();
    buf.push(block);
  }
  flush();
  return chunks;
}

Typical starting points: 200–500 tokens per chunk for help articles and manuals, one chunk per product for catalog entries (title, key attributes and description together), and 10–15% overlap. Tune with the retrieval evaluation (37.6), not by intuition: measure recall@k for a few chunk sizes and keep the best.

Re-ranking

Vector search is fast but coarse: it compares one query vector with one chunk vector. A re-ranker (a cross-encoder model, or a hosted re-rank API, or a small LLM asked to score relevance) reads the query and each candidate together and scores how well the candidate answers the query. The usual shape is "retrieve wide, re-rank narrow": fetch the top 40–50 by vector (or hybrid) score in a few milliseconds, re-rank them in 50–200 ms, keep the best 5–8 for the prompt. Re-ranking typically lifts answer quality more than any amount of prompt tuning, because the model can only be as good as the context it is given. It costs latency and money per query, so measure whether it pays on your evaluation set.

Citations you can verify

Ask for citations by number, then check them in code before showing anything:

// rag/citations.ts -- keep only citations that point at chunks we actually supplied
export function checkCitations(answer: string, supplied: { documentId: string }[]) {
  const cited = [...answer.matchAll(/\[(\d+)\]/g)].map((m) => Number(m[1]));
  const valid = [...new Set(cited)].filter((n) => n >= 1 && n <= supplied.length);
  return {
    sources: valid.map((n) => supplied[n - 1].documentId), // show only sources really cited
    hasInvalid: cited.some((n) => !valid.includes(n)),     // model cited a chunk that does not exist
    uncited: valid.length === 0,                            // factual answer with no citation: flag it
  };
}

An answer with invalid citations or no citations at all is logged, counted on the dashboard, and either shown with a "could not verify" note or replaced by the top retrieved snippets. Some providers can also return structured citations that point to exact spans of the documents you passed in; where available, those are stronger than parsing [n] markers.

Keeping the index in sync

The indexed chunks must stay consistent with the source data: when a product description or support article changes, its chunks must be re-embedded and updated, or RAG answers from stale data. The reliable pattern is the outbox or CDC (Part 29, Part 38): a change to the source emits an event that a worker consumes to re-chunk, re-embed and update the index. For pgvector this can even be in the same database and transaction as the source change; for a separate vector store it must be an asynchronous sync, which is one of the operational costs of that choice (37.1.3).

Product updated (source of truth)
        |  emits event (outbox / CDC, Part 29, Part 38)
        v
Re-index worker: re-chunk -> re-embed -> upsert into pgvector
        |
        v
RAG retrieval now returns the current content

PostgreSQL example

The chunk table and an outbox written in the same transaction as the source change, so an article can never change without a re-index event (the transactional outbox, Part 29):

CREATE TABLE doc_chunks (
  id              bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  document_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  chunk_no        int  NOT NULL,
  content         text NOT NULL,
  content_hash    text NOT NULL,        -- sha256 of content: unchanged chunks are not re-embedded
  embedding       vector(1536),         -- NULL until embedded
  embedding_model text NOT NULL,
  updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (document_id, chunk_no)
);
CREATE INDEX doc_chunks_hnsw   ON doc_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX doc_chunks_tenant ON doc_chunks (tenant_id);

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id             bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type text NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  event_type     text NOT NULL,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  processed_at   timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_pending ON outbox (id) WHERE processed_at IS NULL;

-- The write path: the article and its re-index event commit together, or not at all.
BEGIN;
UPDATE articles SET body = $2, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $3;
INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type) VALUES ('article', $1, 'article.changed');
COMMIT;

NestJS example

A small worker drains the outbox. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets several worker pods share the work without processing the same event twice (Part 35 — Background Jobs).

// rag/reindex.worker.ts -- outbox-driven re-chunk, re-embed (only what changed), upsert
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { chunkArticle } from './chunker';
import { EmbeddingService } from '../embeddings/embedding.service';

const sha = (s: string) => createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex');

@Injectable()
export class ReindexWorker {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReindexWorker.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly embeddings: EmbeddingService) {}

  @Interval(2_000)
  async drain(): Promise<void> {
    await this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
      const events: { id: string; aggregate_id: string }[] = await m.query(
        `SELECT id, aggregate_id FROM outbox
          WHERE processed_at IS NULL AND aggregate_type = 'article'
          ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`);

      for (const e of events) {
        const [article] = await m.query(
          `SELECT id, tenant_id, title, body, published FROM articles WHERE id = $1`, [e.aggregate_id]);

        if (!article || !article.published) {           // deleted or unpublished: remove from search
          await m.query(`DELETE FROM doc_chunks WHERE document_id = $1`, [e.aggregate_id]);
        } else {
          const chunks = chunkArticle(article.title, article.body);
          const existing: { chunk_no: number; content_hash: string }[] = await m.query(
            `SELECT chunk_no, content_hash FROM doc_chunks WHERE document_id = $1`, [article.id]);
          const known = new Map(existing.map((r) => [r.chunk_no, r.content_hash]));
          const changed = chunks.filter((c) => known.get(c.chunkNo) !== sha(c.content));
          const vectors = await this.embeddings.embedDocuments(changed.map((c) => c.content));

          for (const [i, c] of changed.entries()) {
            await m.query(
              `INSERT INTO doc_chunks (tenant_id, document_id, chunk_no, content, content_hash, embedding, embedding_model)
               VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6::vector, $7)
               ON CONFLICT (document_id, chunk_no) DO UPDATE
                 SET content = EXCLUDED.content, content_hash = EXCLUDED.content_hash,
                     embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding, embedding_model = EXCLUDED.embedding_model,
                     updated_at = now()`,
              [article.tenant_id, article.id, c.chunkNo, c.content, sha(c.content),
               JSON.stringify(vectors[i]), this.embeddings.model]);
          }
          await m.query(`DELETE FROM doc_chunks WHERE document_id = $1 AND chunk_no >= $2`,
            [article.id, chunks.length]);              // the article got shorter: drop the tail
          this.logger.log(`reindexed ${article.id}: ${changed.length}/${chunks.length} chunks embedded`);
        }
        await m.query(`UPDATE outbox SET processed_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, [e.id]);
      }
    });
  }
}

This version holds the outbox row locks while it calls the embedding provider, which is fine at a few events per second. At higher volume, claim events with a lease (claimed_at, claimed_by) in a short transaction, do the embedding outside any transaction, and commit the upsert in a second short transaction. The content-hash comparison matters for cost: editing one paragraph of a 30-chunk article re-embeds one or two chunks, not thirty.

Hybrid search

Pure vector search misses exact matches (a product code, an exact name) that keyword/full-text search (Part 33) handles well, and keyword search misses paraphrases that vector search catches. Hybrid search runs both and combines the results (for example, blend the vector similarity rank and the full-text rank), getting the best of each. In PostgreSQL you can do both in one place: full-text search (Part 33) and pgvector in the same database, combining their scores. For many real search features, hybrid beats either alone. Section 37.5 builds it in full, with the SQL, the score fusion and the EXPLAIN output.

Production scenario

A product-catalog search using RAG retrieves the six most relevant product chunks for a shopper's natural-language query, scoped to the tenant and in-stock products (a metadata filter in the same SQL), and the LLM produces a short grounded summary with the matching products cited. Hybrid search ensures that a query containing an exact SKU still returns that product. The index is kept in sync by an outbox-driven re-index worker, so a price or description change is reflected within seconds. Query embeddings are cached (Part 26) so repeated popular queries skip the embedding call. The result is a search that understands intent, stays current, and does not hallucinate products that do not exist.

Failure scenario

A support RAG system retrieved chunks and generated answers, but when an article was updated, the old chunks stayed in the index because there was no sync mechanism. Customers got confidently wrong answers citing the outdated article for weeks until someone noticed. The fix was an outbox-driven re-index worker (Part 29) that re-embeds and updates chunks whenever an article changes, plus a staleness check on the index. The lesson: RAG is only as good as the freshness of its index, and index sync is a first-class part of the system, not an afterthought.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale index: source data changed but chunks did not; answers from old data. Sync via outbox/CDC.
  • Poor chunking: chunks too large (imprecise, bloated prompt) or too small (lost context); tune size and overlap.
  • Retrieval misses: the relevant chunk is not in the top-k; raise k, improve chunking, add re-ranking or hybrid search.
  • Prompt overflow: too many or too large chunks exceed the context window; bound total retrieved tokens.
  • No grounding instruction: the model answers from training and hallucinates; always instruct "only from the context".
  • Cross-tenant retrieval: missing tenant filter leaks another tenant's chunks (37.3).
  • Ungrounded citations: the model cites a source that does not support its claim; spot-check, and prefer short, verifiable answers.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats RAG as a data pipeline, not a prompt trick: chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, re-ranking and generation are each a tunable stage, and index freshness (sync via outbox/CDC) is as important as the prompt. They ground every answer in retrieved context with explicit "answer only from this, cite sources, say you do not know otherwise" instructions, because grounding plus citations is the main defense against hallucination and the way answers become verifiable. They use hybrid search where exact matches matter, scope every retrieval to the tenant, bound the retrieved token count, and cache query embeddings. They measure retrieval quality (does the right chunk get retrieved?) and answer quality (is the answer correct and grounded?) separately with an evaluation set (37.4), because a RAG system can fail at retrieval or at generation and the fixes differ.

Common mistakes

  • No index sync, so RAG answers from stale data.
  • Bad chunking (too large or too small), hurting retrieval precision.
  • No grounding instruction, so the model hallucinates instead of answering from context.
  • No citations, so answers cannot be verified.
  • Pure vector search where exact matches matter (needs hybrid).
  • Missing tenant filter, leaking other tenants' data.
  • Not measuring retrieval and generation quality separately.

Interview questions

  1. What is RAG and what problem does it solve? Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant data and put it in the prompt so the LLM answers from your current, specific facts instead of its training, avoiding hallucination and staleness without fine-tuning.

  2. Walk through the RAG pipeline. Indexing: chunk, embed, store with metadata. Query: embed the question, retrieve top-k (scoped by tenant), optionally re-rank, build a grounded prompt with citations, generate.

  3. How do you keep the RAG index in sync with source data? Emit an event on source change (outbox/CDC) that a worker consumes to re-chunk, re-embed and upsert the index; staleness otherwise produces confidently wrong answers.

  4. What is hybrid search and why use it? Combining vector (semantic) and keyword/full-text search; vectors catch paraphrases, keywords catch exact matches (codes, names), and together they outperform either alone.

  5. How do you defend a RAG answer against hallucination? Ground it in retrieved context with instructions to answer only from that context and cite sources, and to say it does not know otherwise, so answers are verifiable.

  6. Why use an outbox instead of re-indexing directly in the request that edits the article? The edit and the re-index event must be atomic; a direct call can fail after the commit (dual write) and leave the index stale forever. The outbox commits with the edit, and a worker retries until the index catches up.

  7. What does a re-ranker add, and what does it cost? It scores query and candidate together, which is more precise than comparing two vectors; retrieve 40–50 candidates, re-rank, keep the top 5–8. It adds roughly 50–200 ms and a per-query cost, so justify it with retrieval evaluation.

  8. How do you verify citations in a RAG answer? Number the supplied chunks, parse cited numbers, discard citations to chunks that were not supplied, show only sources actually cited, and flag answers with no valid citations.

Practical exercise

Build a RAG pipeline for support articles: chunk the articles with overlap, embed and store them in pgvector with tenant and document metadata, retrieve the top-k for a question scoped to the tenant, and generate a grounded, cited answer. Add an outbox-driven re-index worker so editing an article updates its chunks. Finally, add a hybrid step so a query containing an exact article title ranks that article highly. Acceptance criteria: answers cite real sources, editing an article changes subsequent answers within seconds, and no cross-tenant chunk is ever retrieved.

37.3 Agents and tool use

37.3.1 Tool loops and giving the model safe tools

Concept

An agent is an LLM that can take actions by calling tools (functions you provide) in a loop: the model decides which tool to call with what arguments, your code runs the tool and returns the result, and the model continues, calling more tools until it has finished the task. Tools let the model do things beyond generating text — look up an order, check inventory, issue a refund — turning it from an answerer into an actor. The engineering challenge is doing this safely.

Why does it exist?

Many tasks require actions, not just answers: "cancel my order and refund me" needs the system to actually cancel and refund. Hard-coding every possible flow is inflexible; letting the model choose tools lets it handle open-ended requests. But an LLM taking actions is dangerous — it can call the wrong tool, with wrong arguments, or be manipulated into a harmful action (prompt injection, Part 36). So agents exist to enable action, and the safety machinery (read-only vs write tools, idempotency, human approval) exists to make that action safe.

Mental model

An agent is a capable but junior employee who can use the company's tools. You would not give a new hire unrestricted access to issue refunds and delete records on day one; you give them read access freely, require a manager's sign-off for anything that moves money or is irreversible, and make every action logged and reversible. An agent gets the same treatment: free read-only tools, approval gates and strict checks on write tools, idempotency so a retry does not double-act, and an audit trail. The model proposes; your guardrails dispose.

How it works — the tool loop

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as Agent (LLM)
    participant S as Your server
    U->>A: "Cancel order 10052 and refund me"
    A->>S: tool_use: getOrder(10052)
    S-->>A: tool_result: {status: paid, total: 4299, owner: usr_7}
    A->>S: tool_use: requestRefund(10052, 4299)
    Note over S: write tool: authz check + human approval gate
    S-->>A: tool_result: {status: pending_approval}
    A-->>U: "I've requested a refund of $42.99, it needs approval."
  1. You declare tools with typed schemas (Part 36 structured output / tool calling).
  2. The model responds with a tool_use (which tool, what arguments) instead of a final answer.
  3. Your code validates the arguments, authorizes the action, runs the tool, and returns the result.
  4. You send the result back; the model continues, possibly calling more tools, until it produces a final answer.
  5. You bound the loop (a maximum number of tool calls) so it cannot run forever.
// A safe tool loop sketch (using the provider's tool-calling, Part 36).
async function runAgent(userMessage: string, ctx: { userId: string; tenantId: string }) {
  const messages = [{ role: 'user', content: userMessage }];
  for (let step = 0; step < 8; step++) {        // bound the loop
    const response = await llm.messagesWithTools({ system: AGENT_SYSTEM, messages, tools });
    if (response.stop_reason !== 'tool_use') return finalText(response);

    const results = [];
    for (const call of toolCalls(response)) {
      const tool = TOOLS[call.name];
      const args = validate(tool.schema, call.input);           // validate arguments (Part 36)
      await authorize(tool, args, ctx);                          // authz: can THIS user do this?
      if (tool.isWrite && tool.needsApproval) {
        results.push(await enqueueForApproval(tool, args, ctx)); // human approval for consequential writes
      } else {
        results.push(await tool.run(args, ctx));                 // read-only or approved write
      }
    }
    messages.push(response.assistantTurn, toolResultsMessage(results));
  }
  throw new Error('agent exceeded step limit');
}

Safe tool design

The principles that keep agents safe:

  • Read-only vs write tools. Prefer read-only tools (look up an order, check inventory); the model can read freely because reading is safe. Write tools (refund, cancel, send email) are few, guarded, and ideally require approval.
  • Authorization on every tool call. A tool call is a request like any other: check that this user (the one the agent is acting for) is allowed to perform this action on this resource (Part 39). The model asking to refund order 10052 does not mean user 7 is allowed to; your code checks.
  • Idempotency for write actions. The loop may retry; a refund tool must be idempotent (an idempotency key, Part 29) so a retry does not refund twice. This is the same discipline as any write API.
  • Human approval for consequential actions. Money movement, data deletion, external communication — route these to a human approval step rather than letting the model execute them directly. The model proposes; a person confirms.
  • Bound the loop and the blast radius. Cap the number of tool calls; limit what tools can touch; log every tool call for audit.
  • Treat tool results as untrusted too. Data a tool returns (especially from external sources) can contain injected instructions; it is data, not commands (Part 36 prompt injection).

NestJS example

The sketch above, with real SDK shapes. Each tool is declared with a JSON schema and strict: true; the model answers with tool_use blocks; you reply with one user message containing a tool_result block per call, matched by tool_use_id, with is_error: true when a tool fails (so the model can recover instead of guessing).

// agent/order-agent.service.ts -- a bounded manual tool loop
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { LLM_CLIENT } from '../llm/llm.module';
import { ToolExecutor, ToolContext } from './tool-executor';

const TOOLS: Anthropic.Tool[] = [
  {
    name: 'get_order',
    description: "Look up one of the current customer's orders by id. Read-only.",
    strict: true,
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: { orderId: { type: 'string', description: 'Numeric order id' } },
      required: ['orderId'],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
  },
  {
    name: 'request_refund',
    description: 'Create a refund REQUEST for a delivered order. A human approves it; nothing is paid now.',
    strict: true,
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        orderId: { type: 'string' },
        reason: { type: 'string', enum: ['damaged', 'wrong_item', 'not_delivered', 'other'] },
      },
      required: ['orderId', 'reason'],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
  },
];

@Injectable()
export class OrderAgentService {
  constructor(@Inject(LLM_CLIENT) private readonly client: Anthropic, private readonly tools: ToolExecutor) {}

  async run(userMessage: string, ctx: ToolContext): Promise<string> {
    const messages: Anthropic.MessageParam[] = [{ role: 'user', content: userMessage }];

    for (let step = 0; step < 6; step++) {                       // bound the loop
      const res = await this.client.messages.create({
        model: 'claude-opus-5-5', max_tokens: 2_048, system: AGENT_SYSTEM, tools: TOOLS, messages,
      });
      if (res.stop_reason !== 'tool_use') {
        return res.content.filter((b): b is Anthropic.TextBlock => b.type === 'text').map((b) => b.text).join('');
      }
      messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: res.content }); // append the full content, not just text

      const results: Anthropic.ToolResultBlockParam[] = [];
      for (const block of res.content) {
        if (block.type !== 'tool_use') continue;
        try {
          // The executor validates input, authorizes against ctx.userId, and enforces idempotency.
          const out = await this.tools.execute(block.name, block.input, ctx);
          results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id, content: JSON.stringify(out) });
        } catch (err) {
          results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id, content: (err as Error).message, is_error: true });
        }
      }
      messages.push({ role: 'user', content: results });          // ALL results in ONE user message
    }
    return 'I could not finish this request. A support agent will follow up.'; // step limit reached
  }
}

The provider SDK also ships a "tool runner" helper that drives this loop for you, with hooks for approval and logging; the manual loop is shown here because every guardrail point is visible.

PostgreSQL example

Write tools do not perform actions; they create action requests. A unique idempotency key makes a repeated tool call (a loop retry, a duplicated request) return the existing request instead of creating a second one.

CREATE TABLE agent_actions (
  id               bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  idempotency_key  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- e.g. sha256(conversation_id | action | canonical args)
  tenant_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  user_id          uuid NOT NULL,          -- the customer the agent acted for
  action           text NOT NULL,          -- 'refund'
  args             jsonb NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending_approval'
                   CHECK (status IN ('pending_approval','approved','rejected','executed','failed')),
  decided_by       uuid,                    -- the human who approved or rejected
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  decided_at       timestamptz
);

-- Tool call: create once, or return the existing request.
INSERT INTO agent_actions (idempotency_key, tenant_id, user_id, action, args)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'refund', $4)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id, status;
-- (no row returned -> SELECT id, status FROM agent_actions WHERE idempotency_key = $1)

-- Human approval: a state transition that can only happen once.
UPDATE agent_actions
   SET status = 'approved', decided_by = $2, decided_at = now()
 WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending_approval'
RETURNING id, args;

The approval endpoint then calls the payments service with the same idempotency key (Part 29), so even an approval clicked twice refunds once. The key is derived from the conversation and the canonical arguments, not from the model's tool_use id, because a retried loop gets new ids for the same intended action.

Production scenario

An order-support agent has read-only tools (get order, get tracking, get return policy) and one write tool (request refund). Read tools run freely and let the agent answer most questions directly. The refund tool validates arguments, checks that the requesting user owns the order, enforces an idempotency key, and — because it moves money — creates a pending refund that a support agent approves rather than executing immediately. Every tool call is logged with the user and arguments. The result is an assistant that handles the common cases autonomously and safely escalates the consequential ones, with a full audit trail.

Failure scenario

An early agent was given a write tool to cancel orders with no authorization check and no approval gate, trusting the model to only cancel the user's own orders. A user sent a message crafted to make the model cancel a different order id (prompt injection, Part 36). The model obediently called the cancel tool with that id, and because there was no authorization check, it worked — one user cancelled another's order through the agent. The fix: authorize every tool call against the acting user's permissions (the agent cannot do anything the user could not do directly), require approval for cancellation, and treat the user message as untrusted. The lesson: an agent's tool call is an action that must pass the same authorization and safety gates as any API call; the model's say-so is never authorization.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unbounded loop: the model calls tools forever; cap the steps.
  • No authorization: the agent performs actions the user is not entitled to (the incident above).
  • Non-idempotent writes retried: double refunds, double cancels; use idempotency keys.
  • Prompt injection via user input or tool results: crafted content makes the model misbehave; treat all as untrusted, restrict tools, require approval.
  • Wrong arguments: the model calls a tool with a hallucinated id; validate arguments and check against reality.
  • No audit trail: you cannot explain or undo what the agent did; log every tool call.
  • Consequential action executed directly: money or deletion without approval; gate these.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior designs agents on the principle that the model's output is untrusted and its tool calls are actions subject to the full security stack: every tool call is authorized against the acting user (the agent can do nothing the user could not do directly), write tools are few, idempotent and approval-gated, consequential actions route to a human, and everything is logged for audit. They prefer read-only tools and let the model read freely, because reads are safe and cover most tasks. They bound the loop and the blast radius, and they treat both user input and tool results as potential prompt-injection vectors. They apply the senior mantra to every tool the agent can call — can it be called with the wrong arguments, by the wrong user, twice, maliciously? — and build the guardrail for each.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting the model's say-so as authorization for an action.
  • Giving the agent powerful write tools with no approval gate.
  • Non-idempotent write tools that double-act on retry.
  • No loop bound, no audit log.
  • Treating user input or tool results as trusted, enabling injection.

Interview questions

  1. What is an agent and how does the tool loop work? An LLM that takes actions via tools in a loop: the model requests a tool call, your code validates/authorizes/runs it and returns the result, the model continues until done; you bound the loop.
  2. How do you make a write tool safe for an agent to call? Validate arguments, authorize against the acting user, enforce idempotency, require human approval for consequential actions, and log the call; the model's request is never authorization.
  3. Why prefer read-only tools? Reading is safe, so the model can use read tools freely to handle most tasks; write tools are the dangerous minority that need guarding.
  4. How does prompt injection threaten an agent, and how do you defend? Crafted user input or tool results can make the model call a harmful tool; defend by authorizing every call against the user, restricting and approval-gating write tools, and treating all input and tool results as untrusted.
  5. Why must agent write tools be idempotent? The tool loop may retry a call; without idempotency a retry double-acts (double refund), so use idempotency keys as with any write API (Part 29).

Practical exercise

Build an order-support agent with read-only tools (get order, get tracking) and one write tool (request refund). Make the refund tool validate its arguments, authorize against the requesting user, enforce an idempotency key, and route to a pending-approval state rather than executing. Bound the tool loop and log every call. Then attempt a prompt-injection message trying to refund another user's order and confirm the authorization check blocks it. Acceptance criteria: the agent answers read questions autonomously, refunds require approval and are idempotent, and no cross-user action succeeds.

37.4 Evaluation and guardrails

37.4.1 Knowing your LLM feature works

Concept

Evaluation is how you measure whether an LLM feature is good and whether a change improved or regressed it. Because LLM output is non-deterministic and prompt/model changes have unpredictable effects, you cannot verify an LLM feature by eyeballing a few examples. You build a golden dataset (representative inputs with known-good expected outputs or grading criteria), run the feature against it, and score the results — automatically where possible — so every change is measured, like a test suite for behavior.

Why does it exist?

Without evaluation, you are flying blind: you tweak a prompt, it looks better on the one example you tried, and you ship a change that silently made the feature worse on the cases you did not check. LLM features regress in ways unit tests do not catch, because the logic is in the prompt and the model, not the code. An evaluation set (built in depth in 37.6) turns "it seems fine" into a measured score, so you can improve the feature deliberately (hill-climbing against the eval) and catch regressions before users do. It is the single most important discipline for operating LLM features responsibly.

Mental model

An evaluation set is a test suite for a component whose behavior you cannot fully specify in code. For ordinary code, a unit test asserts an exact output. For an LLM feature, the "test" is a representative input plus a way to grade the output (exact match where possible, or a rubric, or a judge), run across many cases to produce a score. Just as you would not refactor code without tests, you do not change a prompt or model without an eval, because both are changes to behavior with unpredictable blast radius.

How it works

Golden dataset: representative (input, expected/criteria) pairs
        |
        v
Run the feature on each input  ->  outputs
        |
        v
Grade each output:
  - exact / structured match   (classification, extraction: did it get the label/fields right?)
  - rule-based checks          (is it valid JSON? cites a real source? within length?)
  - LLM-as-judge               (a model scores the answer against a rubric)
  - human review               (a sample, for the subjective parts)
        |
        v
Score  ->  compare to the previous version  ->  ship only if it did not regress

The grading methods, from cheapest to richest:

  • Exact / structured match for deterministic tasks: the classification label or extracted fields are right or wrong. Easy to automate, run in CI.
  • Rule-based checks: is the output valid JSON, does it cite a real document, is it within the length limit, does it avoid forbidden content. Automatable guardrails.
  • LLM-as-judge: a (often larger) model scores an answer against a rubric ("is this answer correct and grounded in the sources?"). Scales better than human review for subjective quality; validate the judge against human labels so you trust it.
  • Human review: a sample, for the genuinely subjective aspects; the ground truth that validates the automated methods.
// A tiny eval harness: run the feature over the golden set and score.
async function runEval(cases: EvalCase[]): Promise<{ score: number; failures: EvalCase[] }> {
  let passed = 0;
  const failures: EvalCase[] = [];
  for (const c of cases) {
    const output = await feature(c.input);
    const ok = grade(output, c);          // exact match, rule check, or judge
    if (ok) passed++;
    else failures.push(c);
  }
  return { score: passed / cases.length, failures };
}

Regression tests in CI and online metrics

A subset of the eval runs in CI (Part 46) so a prompt or model change that regresses quality fails the build, just like a failing unit test. Beyond offline evals, online metrics measure the live feature: thumbs-up/down from users, task completion rates, how often answers are corrected, escalation rates. Offline evals catch regressions before shipping; online metrics catch real-world problems the eval set missed and feed new cases back into the golden dataset.

Guardrails

Guardrails are the runtime checks that keep a live LLM feature safe and on-spec, complementing evaluation (which measures quality offline). They include input filtering (reject or sanitize malicious or out-of-scope input), output filtering (block unsafe or off-policy output before it reaches the user), and — critically for RAG and agents — permission checks on retrieved data: in a multi-tenant system, the retrieval and the tools must be scoped to the current tenant and user, or the model can surface data it should not (37.1, 37.3).

Failure scenario (RAG leaking another tenant's documents)

A RAG system embedded all tenants' documents into one pgvector table and, in a refactor, a query dropped the WHERE tenant_id = $tenant filter. Suddenly, retrieval returned the most semantically similar chunks across all tenants, and the LLM confidently answered one company's question using another company's confidential documents, citing them. The leak went unnoticed until a customer recognized a competitor's product name in an answer. The fixes: make the tenant filter non-optional in the retrieval layer (not something a query can forget), add a guardrail that verifies every retrieved chunk belongs to the requesting tenant before it enters the prompt, and add an eval case that asserts no cross-tenant retrieval. The lesson: tenant isolation in RAG and agents is a guardrail that must be enforced structurally, because a single missing filter is a serious data breach (Part 85). Section 37.9 tells this incident in full, with the timeline and the structural fixes, and 37.7 builds the guardrails.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior will not ship or change an LLM feature without an evaluation set, because a prompt or model change is a behavior change with unpredictable effects that eyeballing cannot catch. They build a golden dataset of representative cases, grade with the cheapest method that fits (exact match, rules, then judge, then human sample), run a subset in CI as a regression gate, and track online metrics to feed new cases back. They enforce guardrails at runtime — input/output filtering and, above all, tenant and user permission checks on retrieved data and tool actions — treating a missing tenant filter in RAG as a data-breach-class bug. They measure retrieval and generation quality separately for RAG, because the two fail differently. In short, they apply the testing and observability discipline of the whole book to the parts of the system whose behavior lives in prompts and models.

Common mistakes

  • Shipping prompt/model changes with no eval, silently regressing quality.
  • Eyeballing a few examples instead of scoring a representative set.
  • No regression gate in CI, so regressions reach production.
  • Trusting an LLM judge without validating it against human labels.
  • No runtime guardrails (input/output filtering, permission checks).
  • Missing tenant/user scope on retrieval or tools, leaking data across tenants.
  • Not feeding real-world failures back into the golden dataset.

Interview questions

  1. Why can't you verify an LLM feature by testing a few examples? Output is non-deterministic and prompt/model changes have unpredictable, non-local effects; you need a representative scored dataset to catch regressions the examples miss.
  2. What grading methods does an eval use and when? Exact/structured match for deterministic tasks, rule-based checks for guardrails, LLM-as-judge for subjective quality (validated against humans), and human review on a sample as ground truth.
  3. How does evaluation fit into CI and production? A subset runs in CI as a regression gate on prompt/model changes; online metrics (feedback, completion, escalation) catch real-world issues and feed new eval cases back.
  4. What are guardrails and why are permission checks on retrieved data critical? Runtime checks (input/output filtering, permission scoping) that keep a live feature safe; without tenant/user scoping on retrieval and tools, a RAG system or agent can surface another tenant's data — a breach.
  5. How do you validate an LLM-as-judge? Compare its scores against human labels on a sample; only trust it where it agrees with humans.

Practical exercise

Build an evaluation set for the order-support RAG assistant: a golden dataset of representative questions with expected answers or grading criteria, automated grading (exact match for extractions, rule checks for citations and length, an LLM-judge for answer quality validated against a handful of human labels), and a CI gate that fails if a prompt change drops the score. Add two guardrail eval cases: one asserting no cross-tenant retrieval, one asserting the assistant says "I do not have that information" when the context lacks the answer. Acceptance criteria: a deliberately worse prompt fails the CI gate, and the cross-tenant case fails if the tenant filter is removed.

37.5 Hybrid search: full-text and vectors in one PostgreSQL query

37.5.1 Combining keyword and semantic retrieval

Concept

Hybrid search runs a keyword search and a vector search for the same query and merges the two ranked lists into one. Keyword search (PostgreSQL full-text search, Part 33 — Search) is precise about words: exact names, SKUs, rare terms. Vector search is good at meaning: paraphrases, synonyms, vague descriptions. Merged, they cover each other's blind spots. The most common merge method is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which combines lists by rank position rather than by raw score.

Why does it exist?

Each method fails in a way the other does not. A shopper typing "4410-B" or "Nitrile Pro XL" wants that exact product; its embedding is nearly meaningless, so vector search returns lookalikes. A shopper typing "gloves that don't rip on sharp tools" uses none of the catalog's words, so full-text search returns nothing. Real traffic mixes both kinds of queries, often in one query ("puncture resistant gloves size XL"). Choosing one method means failing a large share of searches; combining them is cheap because both run inside the same PostgreSQL database.

Mental model

Imagine two librarians. One has memorized the catalog index card by card and finds any title or code instantly, but has no idea what a book is about. The other has read every book and can find "something like this", but is hopeless with call numbers. You ask both, take each one's top picks, and give extra credit to books both of them picked. RRF is that "extra credit for agreement" rule, done with arithmetic.

How it works

  1. Keyword branch: websearch_to_tsquery parses the query; a GIN index on a tsvector column finds matches; ts_rank_cd orders them. Take the top 50.
  2. Semantic branch: embed the query; the HNSW index returns the 50 nearest product vectors.
  3. Exact branch (optional but valuable in e-commerce): a direct lookup on SKU or barcode.
  4. Fuse with RRF: each product's score is the sum over branches of 1 / (k + rank), with k around 60. A product ranked 1st by keywords and 3rd by vectors scores 1/61 + 1/63; a product found by only one branch scores less. An exact SKU hit gets a large fixed boost.
  5. Filter in every branch: tenant, in-stock, visibility. A filter applied in only one branch leaks rows through the other.

Why rank and not score? ts_rank_cd values and cosine similarities live on unrelated scales that change with the query; adding them is meaningless. Ranks are comparable by construction, and RRF needs no tuning beyond k.

PostgreSQL example

-- Keyword side: a generated tsvector with weights (name matters more than description).
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
  setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')), 'A') ||
  setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'B')
) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_tsv_gin ON products USING gin (search_tsv);
CREATE INDEX products_tenant_sku ON products (tenant_id, sku);

-- $1 = query embedding, $2 = tenant id, $3 = raw query text
WITH semantic AS (
  SELECT e.product_id AS id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY e.embedding <=> $1::vector) AS rnk
    FROM product_embeddings e
   WHERE e.tenant_id = $2
   ORDER BY e.embedding <=> $1::vector
   LIMIT 50
),
keyword AS (
  SELECT p.id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(p.search_tsv, q) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM products p, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $3) AS q
   WHERE p.tenant_id = $2 AND p.search_tsv @@ q
   ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(p.search_tsv, q) DESC
   LIMIT 50
),
exact AS (
  SELECT id, 1 AS rnk FROM products WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND sku = upper(trim($3))
)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price_cents,
       coalesce(1.0 / (60 + s.rnk), 0)
     + coalesce(1.0 / (60 + k.rnk), 0)
     + coalesce(0.5 / x.rnk, 0)                AS score   -- an exact SKU hit always wins
  FROM semantic s
  FULL JOIN keyword k USING (id)
  FULL JOIN exact   x USING (id)
  JOIN products p ON p.id = coalesce(s.id, k.id, x.id)
 WHERE p.in_stock AND p.tenant_id = $2                   -- final filters, applied once to the union
 ORDER BY score DESC
 LIMIT 20;

Applying in_stock after fusion keeps the HNSW branch unfiltered except by tenant (avoiding the filtered-search trap from 37.1.2 for a common filter), at the cost of sometimes returning fewer than 20 rows; for very selective filters, push them into the branches and enable iterative scans.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), abbreviated:
Limit  (actual time=11.9..12.0 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=11.9..11.9 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (((COALESCE(...) + COALESCE(...)) + COALESCE(...))) DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 27kB
        ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=4.1..11.6 rows=88 loops=1)
              ->  Hash Full Join  (actual time=4.0..4.3 rows=91 loops=1)
                    ->  Subquery Scan on s  (actual time=0.9..3.0 rows=50 loops=1)
                          ->  Limit -> WindowAgg -> Index Scan using product_embeddings_hnsw
                    ->  Subquery Scan on k  (actual time=2.6..2.8 rows=41 loops=1)
                          ->  Limit -> WindowAgg -> Sort
                                ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (rows=41)
                                      ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_search_tsv_gin
              ->  Index Scan using products_pkey on products p  (actual time=0.07..0.07 rows=1 loops=91)
                    Filter: (in_stock AND (tenant_id = $2))
Execution Time: 12.3 ms

Both indexes are used (product_embeddings_hnsw and products_search_tsv_gin), 91 candidates are fused, and the whole query runs in about 12 ms on a 400,000-product catalog.

NestJS example

// search/hybrid-search.service.ts -- hybrid when possible, keyword-only when the embedder is down
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { EmbeddingService } from '../embeddings/embedding.service';
import { HYBRID_SQL, KEYWORD_ONLY_SQL } from './search.sql';

@Injectable()
export class HybridSearchService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(HybridSearchService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly embeddings: EmbeddingService) {}

  async search(tenantId: string, query: string) {
    const q = query.trim().slice(0, 200);                  // bound input (and cost)
    let vec: number[] | null = null;
    try {
      vec = await Promise.race([
        this.embeddings.embedQuery(q),
        new Promise<never>((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(new Error('embed timeout')), 300)),
      ]);
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn(`semantic branch skipped: ${(err as Error).message}`); // degrade, do not fail
    }
    return vec
      ? this.ds.query(HYBRID_SQL, [JSON.stringify(vec), tenantId, q])
      : this.ds.query(KEYWORD_ONLY_SQL, [tenantId, q]);
  }
}

The 300 ms budget for the query embedding is deliberate: search must stay fast, and keyword-only results are far better than an error page. Count how often the fallback runs; if it is more than a fraction of a percent, the embedding provider (or the cache) needs attention.

Production scenario

A B2B dental-supplies store with 400,000 products measured "search success" (a click in the top 5 within the session) over two weeks per variant: full-text only 61%, vector only 66%, hybrid with an exact-SKU branch 74%. Zero-result searches fell from 9% (full-text) to under 1%. The query costs about 12 ms in PostgreSQL; with the embedding call (cached for 45% of queries) the endpoint's p50 is 55 ms and p99 160 ms. No new infrastructure was added: one generated column, one GIN index and one HNSW index on the existing database.

Failure scenario

The same store first launched vector-only search, because the demo looked impressive. Within a week, sales reps reported that clinics could no longer find products by part number; typing "4410-B" returned five similar-looking but wrong products. B2B buyers search by codes copied from invoices, so conversion for repeat orders dropped 12%. The rollback restored full-text search; the relaunch two weeks later used hybrid search with the exact-SKU branch. The lesson: semantic search is an addition to keyword search, not a replacement, and an evaluation set without SKU queries would never have caught this (37.6).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Text search configuration: 'english' stems words ("gloves" -> "glove") but mangles codes and brand names; consider a second 'simple' tsvector for names and SKUs.
  • Stop-word-only queries ("the", "and") produce an empty tsquery: the keyword branch returns nothing and only vectors answer.
  • Filters in one branch only let excluded rows in through the other branch; apply tenant scope in every branch.
  • Deep pagination over fused results is unstable; cap at a few pages and suggest refining the query.
  • Embedding provider slow or down: time-box the embed call and fall back to keyword-only.
  • Score display: RRF scores are not percentages or "relevance"; never show them to users.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior assumes real query traffic is a mix of exact lookups, keywords and vague descriptions, and does not let a demo of one kind decide the architecture. They keep both retrieval methods in PostgreSQL when the scale allows, fuse by rank because raw scores are not comparable, give exact identifiers a hard boost, apply security filters in every branch, and keep keyword search as the degraded mode when the embedding path fails. They justify each piece with an evaluation set that includes every query type the business sees.

Common mistakes

  • Replacing keyword search with vector search instead of adding to it.
  • Adding raw ts_rank and cosine scores together.
  • Filtering by tenant in one branch only.
  • No fallback when the query embedding cannot be computed.
  • Evaluating only natural-language queries and missing codes and names.

Interview questions

  1. Why combine full-text and vector search? Keyword search is precise for exact terms, codes and names; vector search handles paraphrase and vague intent. Real traffic mixes both, and hybrid search beats either alone.
  2. What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion and why use it instead of adding scores? Score = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank); it combines rankings on a common scale without tuning, whereas raw scores from different methods are not comparable.
  3. How do you keep hybrid search tenant-safe? Apply the tenant filter in every branch and again on the final join; a filter in one branch only leaks through the other.
  4. What happens to your search when the embedding provider is down? With a time-boxed embed call, the service falls back to keyword-only results and records the degradation.

Practical exercise

Add a weighted search_tsv column and GIN index to a products table, build the RRF query with semantic, keyword and exact-SKU branches, and wrap it in a NestJS service with a 300 ms embedding budget and keyword fallback. Build a 60-query evaluation set mixing SKUs, product names and natural-language descriptions. Acceptance criteria: hybrid beats both single methods on recall@5, every SKU query returns its product first, EXPLAIN shows both indexes used, and blocking the embedding provider still returns keyword results.

37.6 Evaluation in depth: golden datasets, judges and CI gates

37.6.1 Building an evaluation you can trust

Concept

Section 37.4 introduced evaluation. This section builds one: a golden dataset stored like test fixtures, retrieval metrics (did we fetch the right chunks?), answer grading with rules and an LLM-as-judge (is the answer correct and grounded?), a CI gate that blocks regressions, and online metrics that keep the dataset honest.

Why does it exist?

Every change to an LLM feature (a prompt edit, a new chunk size, a different model, a re-ranker) changes behavior in ways a reviewer cannot see in a diff. Without measurements, teams ship by vibes: three examples look better, so it merges. An evaluation turns those changes into numbers that can be compared, and the CI gate makes the comparison automatic, exactly as unit tests do for code (Part 40 — Testing).

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that changes its recipes weekly. A trusted panel tastes a fixed menu of 200 dishes after every change and scores each against written criteria: is it the dish that was ordered, is it cooked through, is anything on the plate that should not be there. Some checks are mechanical (temperature, weight); some need a trained taster, and the head chef checks the tasters against her own judgment now and then. The fixed menu is the golden dataset, the mechanical checks are rule-based graders, the tasters are the LLM judge, and the head chef is human review.

How it works

  1. Collect cases from real traffic (with PII removed), support tickets and known failures. Each case has an input, the tenant it runs as, and expectations: the documents that should be retrieved, a reference answer or required facts, and flags such as "should say I don't know".
  2. Cover the categories that matter: common questions, exact identifiers, questions the corpus cannot answer, multi-document questions, injection attempts, and cross-tenant probes. A dataset of 150–400 cases is a useful start.
  3. Score retrieval separately: recall@k (share of expected documents found in the top k) and MRR (how high the first relevant document ranks).
  4. Score answers: rule checks first (valid citations, length, "I don't know" when expected), then an LLM judge for correctness and groundedness.
  5. Compare to a baseline on the same cases, and fail the build on meaningful drops or on any hard-gate failure (a cross-tenant leak).
  6. Feed production back: thumbs-down answers and escalations become new cases weekly.
// eval/metrics.ts -- retrieval metrics are plain code
export function recallAtK(retrieved: string[], expected: string[], k: number): number {
  if (!expected.length) return 1;
  const top = new Set(retrieved.slice(0, k));
  return expected.filter((id) => top.has(id)).length / expected.length;
}

export function reciprocalRank(retrieved: string[], expected: string[]): number {
  const i = retrieved.findIndex((id) => expected.includes(id));
  return i === -1 ? 0 : 1 / (i + 1); // averaged over cases, this is MRR
}

NestJS example

The judge is an LLM call with structured output. Ask it for yes/no judgments on specific criteria rather than a 1–10 score; binary questions are far more consistent between runs and easier to validate against humans.

// eval/judge.ts -- a grounded-correctness judge with a strict verdict shape
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { zodOutputFormat } from '@anthropic-ai/sdk/helpers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';

export const Verdict = z.object({
  correct: z.boolean(),                       // agrees with the reference facts
  grounded: z.boolean(),                      // every claim is supported by the supplied context
  unsupportedClaims: z.array(z.string()).max(5),
  saysUnknownWhenItShould: z.boolean(),
});

const JUDGE_SYSTEM = `You grade answers from a support assistant. Use ONLY the context and the
reference facts given. Judge each criterion independently. Be strict: a claim not supported by the
context is unsupported even if it is true in the real world.`;

export async function judge(client: Anthropic, c: {
  question: string; referenceFacts: string[]; context: string; answer: string; expectUnknown: boolean;
}) {
  const res = await client.messages.parse({
    model: 'claude-opus-5-5', // a capable judge; validate it against human labels before trusting it
    max_tokens: 800,
    system: JUDGE_SYSTEM,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content:
      `<question>${c.question}</question>\n<reference_facts>${c.referenceFacts.join('\n')}</reference_facts>\n` +
      `<context>${c.context}</context>\n<answer>${c.answer}</answer>\n` +
      `<expect_unknown>${c.expectUnknown}</expect_unknown>` }],
    output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(Verdict), effort: 'medium' },
  });
  return Verdict.parse(res.parsed_output);
}

The CI suite is an ordinary Jest test that runs the real pipeline over the cases and compares with a stored baseline:

// eval/rag.eval.spec.ts -- run with: npm run eval (a separate Jest project, not the unit tests)
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { runSuite } from './run-suite';

jest.setTimeout(15 * 60_000);

it('order-support RAG does not regress', async () => {
  const cases = readFileSync('eval/cases/ci.jsonl', 'utf8').trim().split('\n').map((l) => JSON.parse(l));
  const report = await runSuite(cases, { concurrency: 4 });
  writeFileSync('eval/report.json', JSON.stringify(report, null, 2));
  const base = JSON.parse(readFileSync('eval/baseline.json', 'utf8'));

  expect(report.crossTenantLeaks).toBe(0);                                  // hard gate
  expect(report.invalidCitations).toBe(0);                                  // hard gate
  expect(report.recallAt5).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(base.recallAt5 - 0.03);
  expect(report.correctAndGrounded).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(base.correctAndGrounded - 0.05);
});
# .github/workflows/llm-eval.yml -- only when behavior-changing code changes
name: llm-eval
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/prompts/**', 'src/rag/**', 'src/search/**', 'eval/**']
jobs:
  eval:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run eval:seed   # fixed corpus with precomputed embeddings: no embedding cost per run
      - run: npm run eval
        env:
          LLM_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LLM_API_KEY }}
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/postgres
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: eval-report
          path: eval/report.json

PostgreSQL example

Online metrics come from production tables you already have: the call ledger (36.7) and a feedback table.

-- Weekly answer quality by prompt version, from user feedback and escalations.
SELECT c.prompt_version,
       count(*)                                                  AS answers,
       round(100.0 * avg((f.rating = 'down')::int), 2)           AS thumbs_down_pct,
       round(100.0 * avg((f.escalated)::int), 2)                 AS escalated_pct,
       round(100.0 * avg((c.outcome <> 'ok')::int), 2)           AS degraded_pct
  FROM llm_calls c
  LEFT JOIN llm_feedback f ON f.call_id = c.id
 WHERE c.feature = 'order-support' AND c.created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
 GROUP BY c.prompt_version
 ORDER BY c.prompt_version;

Production scenario

The order-support team keeps 380 cases: 120 run in CI on every prompt or retrieval change (about 6 minutes and about $1.50 per run), the full 380 run nightly and before any model switch. They validated the judge on 150 human-labelled answers: it agreed with the humans on 92% of "grounded" judgments, and the disagreements were mostly borderline paraphrases, so they trust it for regression detection but not for absolute quality claims. Each week, 20–30 thumbs-down answers are reviewed and about 10 become new cases.

Failure scenario

The first CI gate compared each run's pass rate with a fixed threshold of 90% on 60 cases. It failed randomly about one run in five with no code change, so engineers learned to click "re-run" until it passed, and the gate became theater. The cause was arithmetic: with 60 cases, one case is 1.7 points, and run-to-run noise from non-deterministic outputs moved the score by 3–5 points. The fix: 120 cases in CI, tolerances based on measured noise, a comparison against the baseline on the same cases, hard gates only for zero-tolerance properties (leaks, invalid citations), and the full set nightly. The lesson: an eval gate must be less noisy than the regressions it is meant to catch, or people will route around it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Small datasets are noisy: with 100 cases, the standard error of a 90% pass rate is about 3 points; gate on larger drops or larger sets.
  • The judge shares the generator's blind spots if it is the same model with a similar prompt; use specific criteria, reference facts, and human validation.
  • Dataset rot: the corpus changes and expected documents no longer exist; version the eval corpus as a fixture.
  • Overfitting to the eval: tuning prompts until 380 cases pass can hurt real traffic; keep a held-out set you do not tune against.
  • Eval cost creep: judge calls on every PR add up; run the full set nightly, a subset per PR.
  • PII in eval cases copied from production; scrub before committing.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the evaluation set as a product asset that grows every week, not a one-off script. They measure retrieval and generation separately so that a failure points at its stage; they prefer cheap deterministic checks and use an LLM judge only for what rules cannot grade, after validating it against humans; and they design the CI gate around measured noise so that it is trusted. Hard gates exist for the properties that must never happen (cross-tenant leaks, fabricated citations), and online metrics close the loop. They explain it to a product manager as "our test suite for the parts of the system written in English".

Common mistakes

  • Only end-to-end answer grading, so retrieval regressions look like prompt problems.
  • Asking a judge for a 1–10 score and treating the decimals as meaningful.
  • Never checking the judge against human labels.
  • A CI gate so noisy that people re-run it until green.
  • Never adding production failures to the dataset.

Interview questions

  1. How do you evaluate a RAG system? Separately: retrieval with recall@k and MRR against expected documents; answers with rule checks and a validated LLM judge for correctness and groundedness; plus hard-gate cases for safety properties and online metrics from feedback.
  2. How do you make an LLM judge trustworthy? Specific binary criteria, reference facts and the context in the prompt, structured verdicts, and measured agreement with human labels on a sample before relying on it.
  3. Your eval gate is flaky. What do you do? Measure run-to-run noise, enlarge the CI set, compare against a baseline on the same cases with tolerances above the noise, keep zero-tolerance hard gates, and run the full suite on a schedule.
  4. Where do new eval cases come from? Production failures (thumbs-down, escalations, incidents), new product features, and adversarial cases such as injection and cross-tenant probes.

Practical exercise

Build the eval harness for your RAG assistant: 120 cases in JSONL with expected document ids, reference facts and an expectUnknown flag; recall@5 and MRR computed in code; a binary-criteria judge with structured output validated against 40 cases you label yourself; a Jest suite with hard gates for cross-tenant leaks and invalid citations; and the GitHub Actions workflow above. Acceptance criteria: removing the tenant filter fails the build; a deliberately worse prompt fails the build; three re-runs of an unchanged branch all pass.

37.7 Guardrails and tenant isolation for RAG and agents

37.7.1 Making isolation structural

Concept

A guardrail is a check that runs on every request, outside the model, and that the model cannot talk its way past. There are four layers: input guardrails (size, scope and injection checks on what the user sends), retrieval guardrails (the database only returns rows this tenant and user may see), output guardrails (the answer is checked for leaked data, fabricated citations and unsafe content before it is shown), and action guardrails (tool calls are authorized and approved, 37.3). The most important is retrieval, because data the model never receives is data it cannot leak.

Why does it exist?

In a multi-tenant system, the prompt is assembled from rows your code selected. If one query forgets WHERE tenant_id = ..., the model receives another tenant's documents and will happily use and cite them; no prompt instruction can undo that. Isolation that depends on every developer remembering a filter in every query will eventually fail (Part 85 — Enterprise and Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture). Guardrails exist to make the safe path the only path: the filter is enforced by the database itself, verified again in code, and tested in CI.

Mental model

Imagine a shared office building. You could ask every visitor to "please only enter your own company's floor" (a prompt instruction), or you could give each badge access to one floor only (row-level security), and also have the receptionist check badges at the lift (post-retrieval verification), and log every door opening (audit). Only the badge system actually prevents the mistake; the other two catch what slips through.

How it works

  1. A request arrives with an authenticated user, which determines the tenant and the user's groups (for document-level permissions inside a tenant, such as "HR documents only for HR").
  2. Retrieval runs inside a transaction that first sets the tenant (and groups) as transaction-local settings.
  3. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) policies on the chunk table add tenant_id = current tenant to every query, including ones a developer writes later and forgets to filter.
  4. The retriever verifies every returned row's tenant again in code; a mismatch is treated as a security incident (throw, alert), not as a warning.
  5. The output guardrail checks the answer: citations must point at supplied chunks, and the text must not contain identifiers (emails, order ids) that were not in the supplied context.

PostgreSQL example

-- Enforce tenant isolation in the database, for every query on the table.
ALTER TABLE doc_chunks ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE doc_chunks FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies even to the table owner

ALTER TABLE doc_chunks ADD COLUMN allowed_groups text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{all}';

CREATE POLICY chunk_tenant_isolation ON doc_chunks
  USING (
