    tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid       -- unset -> NULL -> no rows
    AND allowed_groups && string_to_array(current_setting('app.user_groups', true), ',')
  );

-- The application role must not be a superuser and must not have BYPASSRLS.
-- Per request, inside a transaction (is_local = true: reset at COMMIT, safe with poolers):
BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true), set_config('app.user_groups', $2, true);
SELECT id, document_id, content FROM doc_chunks ORDER BY embedding <=> $3::vector LIMIT 8;
COMMIT;

The true second argument to current_setting means "return NULL if unset", so a code path that forgets to set the tenant gets no rows rather than all rows: the policy fails closed. RLS predicates are applied like a WHERE filter, so the filtered-HNSW behavior from 37.1.2 applies; enable iterative scans for tenant-scoped vector queries.

NestJS example

// rag/tenant-scoped-retriever.ts -- the only way the RAG code can read chunks
import { Injectable, InternalServerErrorException, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export interface RetrievalContext { tenantId: string; groups: string[] }
export interface RetrievedChunk { id: string; tenant_id: string; document_id: string; content: string }

@Injectable()
export class TenantScopedRetriever {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TenantScopedRetriever.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async nearest(ctx: RetrievalContext, queryVec: number[], k = 8): Promise<RetrievedChunk[]> {
    const rows: RetrievedChunk[] = await this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
      await m.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true), set_config('app.user_groups', $2, true)`,
        [ctx.tenantId, ctx.groups.concat('all').join(',')]);
      await m.query(`SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order`);
      return m.query(
        `SELECT id, tenant_id, document_id, content
           FROM doc_chunks
          WHERE tenant_id = $1                       -- explicit filter too: belt and braces with RLS
          ORDER BY embedding <=> $2::vector
          LIMIT $3`,
        [ctx.tenantId, JSON.stringify(queryVec), k]);
    });

    // Post-retrieval verification: never let a foreign row reach a prompt.
    const foreign = rows.filter((r) => r.tenant_id !== ctx.tenantId);
    if (foreign.length) {
      this.logger.error({ event: 'cross_tenant_retrieval', tenant: ctx.tenantId, rows: foreign.map((r) => r.id) });
      throw new InternalServerErrorException('Retrieval failed'); // page someone: this must never happen
    }
    return rows;
  }
}

Make this class the only code with access to the chunk table (a lint rule or module boundary that forbids raw queries on doc_chunks elsewhere), and the structural guarantee becomes real.

Production scenario

On a support platform with 900 tenants and 6 million chunks, RLS plus verification adds about 1–2 ms to a retrieval that takes 8 ms. Input guardrails are cheap rules (length limit, a block-list of known injection phrasings that only flags for review, a language check); an optional small-model classifier for off-topic requests runs in parallel with retrieval so it adds no latency on the happy path. The output guardrail rejects about 0.2% of answers, almost all for citing chunk numbers that were not supplied. The cross_tenant_retrieval alert has fired once in a year, during a staging test that deliberately disabled RLS, which is exactly what the CI eval case (37.6) checks.

Failure scenario

A team set the tenant with a plain session-level SET app.tenant_id = '...' at the start of each request and relied on RLS. It worked in development. In production, the database sat behind a connection pooler in transaction mode, so consecutive transactions from different requests ran on the same server connection, and a session-level setting survived from one request into the next. Under load, a request that took a code path which skipped the SET inherited the previous request's tenant, and RLS faithfully filtered by the wrong tenant. It was caught in a load test, because the post-retrieval check (comparing each row's tenant with the request's tenant) threw. The fix was set_config(..., true) inside an explicit transaction for every retrieval, so the setting is transaction-local and cannot leak. The lesson: RLS is only as good as the way the tenant reaches the database; the code-level verification is what caught it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Session vs transaction settings with connection poolers: always transaction-local.
  • Background workers (re-indexers) need a deliberate, audited way to write across tenants; give them a separate role, never disable RLS for the app role.
  • Caches above the database (query-embedding cache is fine; a cache of retrieved chunks or answers) must include the tenant and groups in the key.
  • Permissions change after indexing: if a document's access groups change, the chunks' allowed_groups must change in the same outbox event.
  • Shared public documents (a global help center) belong in a separate table or tenant id, not in a bypass flag.
  • Logs and traces of prompts contain another layer of tenant data; scope access to them too.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior puts isolation where it cannot be forgotten: in the database with row-level security, in a single retriever class that every RAG path must use, and in a CI test that tries to cross the boundary. They treat code-level verification as a tripwire for bugs in that structure, and they never rely on the model to respect a boundary it can see across. When asked "what stops tenant A from seeing tenant B's documents?", they can answer with three independent mechanisms, none of them a prompt.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on WHERE tenant_id written by hand in every query.
  • Session-level SET behind a transaction-mode pooler.
  • An application role with BYPASSRLS, or RLS enabled without FORCE for the owner role the app uses.
  • Answer caches keyed without tenant and groups.
  • Telling the model "only use documents for tenant X" as if that were a control.

Interview questions

  1. How do you guarantee tenant isolation in a RAG system? Enforce it structurally: RLS on chunk tables with transaction-local tenant settings that fail closed, a single retriever that every path uses, post-retrieval verification that alerts on mismatches, tenant-aware cache keys, and a CI eval case that attempts cross-tenant retrieval.
  2. Why is a prompt instruction not a guardrail? The model can be confused or manipulated; a guardrail is enforced by code or the database regardless of what the model does.
  3. What breaks RLS in practice? Session-level settings with transaction poolers, privileged roles that bypass RLS, missing FORCE, and caches or background jobs that read outside the policy.

Practical exercise

Enable RLS with a fail-closed tenant policy on your chunk table, route all retrieval through a TenantScopedRetriever that sets transaction-local settings and verifies rows, and add document-level groups. Write integration tests that (a) run a query without setting the tenant and expect zero rows, (b) run two tenants' requests interleaved through a pooled connection and expect no crossover, and (c) remove the explicit WHERE and expect RLS alone to keep results correct. Acceptance criteria: all three pass, and a deliberately inserted foreign row triggers the alert.

37.8 Worked example: product-catalog RAG search with pgvector

37.8.1 The requirement

A marketplace platform hosts 120 store tenants and 2.5 million products. Shoppers type queries like "latex-free gloves under $20 for sensitive skin". The search page must return relevant, in-stock products from that store only within 300 ms at p95, at a peak of 150 searches per second. An optional "Ask" button produces a two-sentence grounded summary of the results, citing the products it mentions. Budget: under $3 per 1,000 searches, all-in.

37.8.2 The design

flowchart LR
    Q["Shopper query"] --> P["Parse filters, small model, schema"]
    Q --> E["Embed query, cached"]
    P --> H["Hybrid SQL: vector, full-text, SKU, filters, RLS"]
    E --> H
    H --> RR["Re-rank top 50 to top 12"]
    RR --> RES["Results page"]
    RES --> ASK{"Ask clicked?"}
    ASK -->|"yes"| S["Grounded summary, cites product ids"]
    S --> V["Validate citations against results"]
    V --> OUT["Summary shown"]

The schema reuses the pieces of this Part: a products table with a weighted search_tsv and a GIN index; a product_embeddings table with tenant_id, embedding vector(1024), embedding_model and content_hash, an HNSW index, RLS, and partial HNSW indexes for the five largest tenants (each over 150,000 products); and an outbox from product writes to the re-index worker (37.2). The embedded text is built from the fields a shopper would describe, not the raw description alone: name | brand | category | key attributes (material, size, latex-free) | first 600 characters of description.

37.8.3 The query path in code

Filters are extracted with a small model and a strict schema, then validated, so "under $20" becomes a SQL parameter rather than something the vector search has to "understand".

// catalog/query-parser.ts -- natural language -> validated filters
import { z } from 'zod';

export const ParsedQuery = z.object({
  searchText: z.string().max(200),                       // the query minus the filter phrases
  maxPriceCents: z.number().int().positive().max(10_000_000).nullable(),
  mustHaveAttributes: z.array(z.enum(['latex_free', 'powder_free', 'sterile', 'autoclavable'])).max(4),
  category: z.enum(['gloves', 'instruments', 'consumables', 'equipment', 'other']).nullable(),
});
export type ParsedQuery = z.infer<typeof ParsedQuery>;
// Called with messages.parse({ model: 'claude-haiku-5-5', output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(ParsedQuery), effort: 'low' }, ... })
// and a 250 ms deadline. On timeout or failure: { searchText: raw, maxPriceCents: null, mustHaveAttributes: [], category: null }.
// catalog/catalog-search.service.ts -- orchestration with parallel steps and degradation
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { QueryParser } from './query-parser.service';
import { EmbeddingService } from '../embeddings/embedding.service';
import { CatalogRepository } from './catalog.repository';
import { Reranker } from './reranker';

@Injectable()
export class CatalogSearchService {
  constructor(
    private readonly parser: QueryParser,
    private readonly embeddings: EmbeddingService,
    private readonly repo: CatalogRepository,
    private readonly reranker: Reranker,
  ) {}

  async search(tenantId: string, raw: string) {
    const q = raw.trim().slice(0, 200);
    // Parse and embed in parallel: both are network calls, neither depends on the other.
    const [parsed, vec] = await Promise.all([
      this.parser.parseOrDefault(q),             // 250 ms deadline inside
      this.embeddings.embedQuery(q).catch(() => null), // degrade to keyword-only
    ]);

    const candidates = await this.repo.hybrid(tenantId, {
      vec, text: parsed.searchText, maxPriceCents: parsed.maxPriceCents,
      attributes: parsed.mustHaveAttributes, category: parsed.category, limit: 50,
    });                                           // RLS + tenant filter inside (60.7)

    const top = await this.reranker.rerankOrPassThrough(q, candidates, 12, { deadlineMs: 120 });
    return { products: top, appliedFilters: parsed, mode: vec ? 'hybrid' : 'keyword' };
  }
}

The "Ask" summary uses the numbered results as context and must cite by product id; the server keeps only citations to products that were actually on the page:

// catalog/summary.service.ts (excerpt)
const context = products.map((p, i) => `[${i + 1}] id=${p.id} | ${p.name} | $${(p.priceCents / 100).toFixed(2)} | ${p.attributes.join(', ')}`).join('\n');
const system = 'Summarize which of the numbered products fit the shopper\'s request, in at most two sentences. ' +
  'Mention only numbered products and cite them like [2]. Never mention prices, stock or features not shown.';
// ... call the large model with the cached system prompt, then:
const { sources, hasInvalid } = checkCitations(answer, products.map((p) => ({ documentId: p.id })));
if (hasInvalid || sources.length === 0) return { summary: null };   // show results without a summary
return { summary: answer, citedProductIds: sources };

37.8.4 Numbers

Latency budget (p95 target 300 ms)          measured p50 / p95
  parse filters (small model, parallel)       140 / 230 ms   (deadline 250 ms)
  embed query (parallel, 52% cache hits)        2 / 70 ms
  hybrid SQL (RLS, HNSW iterative + GIN)        9 / 24 ms
  re-rank 50 -> 12                             60 / 110 ms
  total (parse and embed overlap)             215 / 290 ms

Cost per 1,000 searches
  filter parsing    ~300 in / 60 out tokens on a small model   ~$0.06
  query embeddings  48% of queries, ~12 tokens each             <$0.01
  re-ranking        hosted re-rank API, 50 docs per query       ~$1.00
  "Ask" summaries   clicked on 8% of searches, large model,
                    ~2,000 in (1,200 cached) / 120 out          ~$0.47
  total                                                         ~$1.55 (budget $3)

Database sizing: 2.5 million vectors of 1,024 dimensions are about 10 GB plus about 8 GB of HNSW index; the primary has 64 GB of RAM and two read replicas serve search. Re-indexing handles about 400,000 product updates a day; with content hashes, only about 15% of those change the embedded text and trigger an embedding call.

37.8.5 What the evaluation caught before launch

The 300-case evaluation (37.6) included SKU lookups, attribute filters, price filters, typos, other-language queries and cross-tenant probes. It caught two problems before launch: the filter parser sometimes turned "under 20" into 20 cents (fixed by a prompt rule plus a sanity check that rejects prices below the store's cheapest product), and the re-ranker demoted exact SKU matches (fixed by pinning exact-SKU hits to the top before re-ranking). Recall@12 ended at 0.91 against labelled relevant products, up from 0.78 for the original keyword search.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Contradictory filters ("cheap premium gloves"): the parser may produce no price filter; that is acceptable, ranking does the rest.
  • Out-of-stock but perfect matches: show them below in-stock results with a label, a business choice the eval must reflect.
  • New products not yet embedded: the keyword branch finds them meanwhile; monitor the embedding backlog.
  • Huge tenants: partial HNSW indexes keep their filtered queries fast; small tenants are served by exact search over the tenant index.
  • Summary hallucinating a feature: the prompt forbids it, the output check rejects uncited products, and the eval measures groundedness.
  • Re-ranker outage: pass through the hybrid order; the search still works.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior moves in this design are small and boring on purpose: filters become SQL parameters instead of hopes, independent network calls run in parallel, every LLM-dependent step has a deadline and a degraded mode, tenant isolation is enforced by the database, and the expensive large-model call happens only when a shopper asks for it. The result is a search that is mostly PostgreSQL with two small, optional model calls around it, which is why it is fast, cheap and debuggable.

Interview questions

  1. Design semantic product search for a multi-tenant marketplace. Hybrid retrieval in PostgreSQL (pgvector HNSW plus full-text plus exact SKU) with RLS, structured filter extraction into SQL parameters, re-ranking, query-embedding cache, outbox-driven re-indexing with content hashes, optional grounded summaries with validated citations, and an eval set covering all query types.
  2. Where does the latency go, and how do you keep p95 under 300 ms? In network calls to models: run parsing and embedding in parallel with deadlines, cache embeddings, keep the SQL in the low tens of milliseconds with the right indexes, and make re-ranking optional under a deadline.
  3. Why extract filters with a model instead of letting vector search handle "under $20"? Embeddings are poor at numeric constraints; extracting them into validated parameters gives exact filtering, and the vector search handles meaning.

Practical exercise

Implement the catalog search end to end for at least two tenants and 50,000 products: schema with RLS and both indexes, outbox re-indexing with content hashes, the filter parser with a strict schema and fallback, hybrid retrieval, a pass-through-capable re-ranker interface, and the "Ask" summary with citation validation. Acceptance criteria: p95 under 300 ms in a load test at 50 searches per second, no cross-tenant result in a 1,000-query randomized test, keyword-only mode works with the embedding provider blocked, and every summary cites only products on the page.

37.9 Incident story: a RAG system leaking another tenant's documents

37.9.1 The system

A B2B SaaS company sells practice-management software to dental clinics. Each clinic is a tenant. A "Clinic Assistant" answers staff questions ("what is our cancellation policy?", "which supplier do we use for implants?") using RAG over each clinic's own uploaded documents: policies, price lists, supplier contracts. All tenants' chunks live in one doc_chunks table with a tenant_id column and an HNSW index. The table predates the company's adoption of row-level security, so isolation depends on the WHERE tenant_id = $1 in the retrieval query. About 1,400 tenants, 3.2 million chunks, 60,000 assistant questions a day.

37.9.2 Timeline

When What happened
Tue 10:05 Release 2.31 ships a retrieval refactor so a new "public help center" search can reuse the chunk search
Tue 10:05 to Thu 16:42 The assistant answers about 115,000 questions; some answers include other clinics' content
Thu 16:42 A clinic manager reports that the assistant quoted "Brightsmile Dental supplier price list" when asked about their own implant prices
Thu 17:10 Support escalates to the on-call engineer and security; declared SEV-1
Thu 17:25 The assistant is disabled for all tenants with its feature flag (kill switch)
Thu 18:40 Root cause found in the refactored repository method
Thu 20:15 Fix deployed; assistant re-enabled for the internal test tenant only
Fri 11:00 Blast-radius analysis complete from retrieval logs
Fri 15:00 Assistant re-enabled for all tenants after the new CI hard gate passes
Mon Affected tenants notified under their data-processing agreements, with the list of exposed documents

37.9.3 Root cause

The refactor turned the tenant filter into an optional parameter, so that public help-center content (stored with no tenant) could be searched with the same method:

// BEFORE: tenant required by the signature
async searchChunks(tenantId: string, vec: number[], k: number) { /* WHERE tenant_id = $1 ... */ }

// AFTER (the bug): tenant optional, filter added only "if present"
async searchChunks(vec: number[], opts: { tenantId?: string; k?: number }) {
  const where: string[] = [];
  const params: unknown[] = [JSON.stringify(vec)];
  if (opts.tenantId) { params.push(opts.tenantId); where.push(`tenant_id = $${params.length}`); }
  const sql = `SELECT id, tenant_id, document_id, content FROM doc_chunks
               ${where.length ? 'WHERE ' + where.join(' AND ') : ''}
               ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT ${opts.k ?? 8}`;
  return this.ds.query(sql, params);
}

The assistant's call site was updated to pass { k: 8, tenantId: ctx.tenant }. But ctx.tenant was the old property name; the request context had been renamed to tenantId in an unrelated change a month earlier and the field was typed as any in that one place. opts.tenantId was therefore undefined, the if skipped the filter, and every assistant query searched all 1,400 tenants. The nearest chunks were usually still the clinic's own (similar documents are similar), which is why the bug hid for two days: only questions where another clinic had a closer document leaked.

Why nothing caught it, the "five whys" in short: no RLS on the table; the tenant was optional in the method signature; an any hid the wrong property name; unit tests mocked the repository; the evaluation set ran as a single tenant, so there was no other tenant's data to leak.

37.9.4 Blast radius

The team could answer "who saw what" only because they logged retrieved chunk ids for every call (a decision made months earlier for debugging):

-- Every answer that used at least one chunk from a different tenant, since the release.
SELECT r.call_id, c.tenant_id AS asking_tenant, d.tenant_id AS owner_tenant, d.document_id, c.created_at
  FROM llm_retrievals r
  JOIN llm_calls  c ON c.id = r.call_id
  JOIN doc_chunks d ON d.id = r.chunk_id
 WHERE c.feature = 'clinic-assistant'
   AND c.created_at >= '2026-03-10 10:05+00'
   AND d.tenant_id IS DISTINCT FROM c.tenant_id;

Result: 1,912 answers, asked from 37 tenants, included at least one foreign chunk; 214 documents from 61 owner tenants were involved; 403 of those answers quoted or cited foreign content directly. Without the retrieval log, the only honest statement would have been "any document of any tenant may have been exposed", which turns a serious incident into a catastrophic one.

37.9.5 Fixes

Immediate (Thursday night):

  1. The tenant became a required argument again, typed as a branded TenantId that only the authentication layer can construct, so undefined or a raw string does not compile.
  2. Public help-center content moved to its own table, so no code path needs "search without a tenant".
  3. Post-retrieval verification (37.7) throws and pages on any row whose tenant differs from the request's.

Structural (the following two weeks):

  1. Row-level security with FORCE and a fail-closed policy on every table that feeds prompts; tenant set with transaction-local set_config.
  2. A CI hard gate: the evaluation suite now seeds two tenants with deliberately similar documents and asserts zero cross-tenant retrievals (37.6). The gate was run against the buggy commit and failed, as it should.
  3. A lint rule forbidding any in request-context types and raw SQL on chunk tables outside the retriever module.
  4. A per-feature kill switch for every LLM feature, documented in the runbook, plus 90-day retention of retrieval logs.

37.9.6 Lessons

  • Isolation must be structural. A filter that every query must remember will eventually be forgotten; RLS, a required typed tenant and a single retriever make forgetting impossible or loud.
  • "Optional filter" is an anti-pattern for security filters. If some callers need no tenant, they need a different data source, not a missing WHERE.
  • Similarity hides leaks. Because most nearest neighbours are still the tenant's own, cross-tenant RAG bugs produce intermittent, plausible leaks rather than obvious failures.
  • Log retrievals. Retrieved chunk ids per call cost little and are the difference between a bounded and an unbounded disclosure.
  • Evaluate with more than one tenant. A single-tenant eval cannot detect a cross-tenant leak.
  • Have a kill switch for every LLM feature; it took 15 minutes to stop the leak because one existed.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through how you would investigate a report that a RAG assistant showed another customer's document. Disable the feature (kill switch), preserve logs, find the retrieval path and the change that touched it, then compute the blast radius from retrieval logs by joining retrieved chunk owners to asking tenants; notify according to contracts; fix structurally.
  2. Why did this bug take two days to notice? Most nearest chunks still belonged to the asking tenant, so leaks were intermittent and plausible; there was no alerting tripwire and no multi-tenant eval case.
  3. Which single control would have prevented it? Row-level security with a fail-closed policy; the required typed tenant and post-retrieval verification are the other two independent layers.

Practical exercise

Reproduce this incident in a sandbox: two tenants with similar documents, a retriever with an optional tenant filter, and a call site passing the wrong property. Show the leak in a test. Then apply the fixes in order (required branded tenant type, RLS with fail-closed policy, post-retrieval verification, two-tenant eval gate) and show that each one alone blocks the leak. Write the blast-radius query against your retrieval log. Acceptance criteria: the buggy commit fails CI; each layer independently prevents foreign chunks from reaching the prompt.

37.10 Operating retrieval: re-embedding migrations and index health

37.10.1 Changing the embedding model without downtime

Concept

Sooner or later you will change the embedding model: a better or cheaper one appears, or you need a different dimension. Because vectors from different models are not comparable (37.1.1), the change is a data migration of every row, run like any zero-downtime schema change (Part 23): add, backfill, verify, switch, remove.

Why does it exist?

Re-embedding in place mixes models while it runs, which silently degrades search for the duration (the failure scenario in 37.1.1). Stopping search to re-embed millions of rows is not acceptable either. A side-by-side migration keeps the old index serving until the new one is complete and measured.

How it works

  1. Add a new column (embedding_v2 vector(1024), embedding_v2_model text) with no index.
  2. Dual-write: the re-index worker writes both columns for every changed document from now on.
  3. Backfill old rows in batches by primary-key range, using the provider's batch endpoint where available (cheaper), throttled to protect the database and the provider quota.
  4. Index the new column with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY once the backfill is complete.
  5. Verify: run the retrieval evaluation (37.6) against both columns; shadow-query a sample of live traffic against v2 and compare results and latency.
  6. Switch reads to v2 with a feature flag (instant rollback by flipping it back).
  7. Remove the old column and index after a safe period.

PostgreSQL example

ALTER TABLE doc_chunks ADD COLUMN embedding_v2 vector(1024), ADD COLUMN embedding_v2_model text;

-- Backlog and progress, for the dashboard and the go/no-go decision.
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE embedding_v2 IS NULL)                 AS remaining,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE embedding_v2 IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS pct_done
  FROM doc_chunks;

-- Backfill worker: one batch by id range (the worker embeds content, then writes vectors).
SELECT id, content FROM doc_chunks
 WHERE id > $1 AND embedding_v2 IS NULL
 ORDER BY id LIMIT 500;

-- After backfill: build the new index without blocking writes.
SET maintenance_work_mem = '8GB';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY doc_chunks_hnsw_v2 ON doc_chunks USING hnsw (embedding_v2 vector_cosine_ops);

At 3.2 million chunks of about 350 tokens, the backfill is about 1.1 billion tokens (tens to low hundreds of dollars at typical embedding prices); at 2,000 chunks per second of write throughput it takes under an hour of database time, but the provider's rate limit usually makes the real duration hours to a day. The table temporarily holds both vectors, so plan disk and memory for both indexes during the overlap.

Failure scenario

A team skipped step 5 because the new model scored better on a public benchmark. After the switch, searches for their domain jargon (dental procedure codes, brand abbreviations) got noticeably worse; the public benchmark had none of them. Because the old column and index were still present, the rollback was a flag flip. The re-run of their own retrieval eval showed recall@5 dropping from 0.88 to 0.81 on jargon-heavy queries; they kept the old model and revisited later with hybrid weighting. The lesson: benchmarks rank models in general; only your evaluation ranks them for your data.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Index health: monitor index size, VACUUM activity on heavily updated chunk tables, and the share of rows with NULL embeddings (the embedding backlog).
  • Recall drift: as the corpus grows, recall at fixed ef_search can slowly drop; re-measure monthly.
  • Two indexes during migration double memory pressure; schedule the overlap and watch buffer reads.
  • Query cache: query-embedding cache keys include the model name, so the switch does not serve stale vectors.
  • Dimension change breaks any code that hard-codes the size; read it from the provider configuration.

Interview questions

  1. How do you change embedding models for millions of rows without downtime? Add a new column, dual-write, backfill in batches (batch API if available), build the index concurrently, verify with your eval and shadow traffic, switch with a flag, then drop the old column.
  2. What do you monitor for a pgvector-based retrieval system? Query latency percentiles, recall against exact search on a sample, embedding backlog, index size versus RAM, vacuum health, and cross-tenant verification alerts.

Practical exercise

Migrate your chunk table from one embedding model to another using the seven steps above, with a feature flag for reads and a dashboard showing backfill progress and recall@5 for both columns. Acceptance criteria: search keeps working throughout, the flag switches and rolls back instantly, and the old column is dropped only after the new one matches or beats it on the eval.

Senior Checklist — Part 37

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain embeddings, similarity metrics, and that the embedding model is a versioned dependency stored with every row
  • I can size a vector workload: bytes per vector, index memory, embedding cost and latency
  • I can model and index embeddings in pgvector (HNSW/IVFFlat), tune ef_search, and measure recall against exact search
  • I can read pgvector EXPLAIN output and recognize both a missing index and the filtered-HNSW trap
  • I can decide between pgvector and a dedicated vector database, including the sync cost
  • I can build a RAG pipeline with structure-aware chunking, re-ranking, grounding and verified citations
  • I keep the index in sync with a transactional outbox and content hashes, including deletes
  • I can build hybrid search with RRF across vector, full-text and exact-identifier branches
  • I can build an agent with strict tools, authorization, idempotent action requests, approval gates, a bounded loop and an audit log
  • I build evaluation sets with retrieval metrics, a validated judge and a noise-aware CI gate with hard gates
  • I enforce tenant isolation structurally: RLS with transaction-local settings, a single retriever, post-retrieval verification
  • I log retrieved chunk ids per call so I can compute a blast radius
  • I can migrate embedding models with zero downtime

Part 37 — Key Takeaways

  • An embedding represents meaning as a vector; it is only comparable with vectors from the same model, so store the model with every row and re-embed on change.
  • pgvector does vector search inside PostgreSQL, joined to relational data, inside transactions and under RLS; it is the right first choice for most teams.
  • HNSW is the default index; tune ef_search, measure recall against exact search, and build indexes concurrently with enough memory.
  • Filtered HNSW queries can silently return fewer rows than asked; check Rows Removed by Filter and use iterative scans, exact search for small tenants, or partitioning.
  • RAG is a data pipeline: chunk by structure, retrieve wide, re-rank narrow, ground the prompt, and verify citations in code.
  • Keep the index in sync with a transactional outbox and content hashes; a stale index produces confident, wrong answers.
  • Hybrid search (vectors plus full-text plus exact identifiers, fused by rank) beats either method alone in real traffic.
  • An agent's tool call is an action: strict schemas, authorization against the acting user, idempotent action requests, human approval for consequential writes, a bounded loop.
  • Evaluate retrieval and answers separately, validate LLM judges against humans, and design CI gates around measured noise with zero-tolerance hard gates.
  • Tenant isolation in RAG must be structural (RLS, a required tenant type, one retriever, post-retrieval checks); a prompt instruction is not a control.
  • Log retrieved chunk ids for every call; without them a leak's blast radius is "everything".
  • Change embedding models like a schema migration: add, backfill, index, verify, switch, remove.

Part 38 — Data Engineering for Backend Engineers

A backend engineer does not need to become a data engineer, but at any company past a certain size the two worlds meet constantly, and the backend engineer who understands the data side is far more effective. The production database you own is the source of the analytics the business runs on; the events you emit are the raw material of the data warehouse; the schema you change can break a dashboard; the GDPR deletion you implement must reach the warehouse too. This Part teaches the data-engineering concepts a backend engineer needs to work well across that boundary: why analytics and transactional workloads must be separated, how data flows from your database into analytics systems, and how to build analytics features into your own product.

The topics: OLTP versus OLAP (why analytics queries hurt your production database), change data capture (streaming database changes to other systems), ETL versus ELT and batch pipelines, data warehouses and lakes (columnar storage, Parquet), stream processing (windows, watermarks, late events), data contracts between backend and data teams, data quality, privacy in pipelines (PII masking, deletion propagation), and building analytics features in the product (pre-aggregated tables, materialized views, read models). The running example is deriving daily revenue dashboards from the orders database.

This Part builds on the transactional outbox (see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions, 29.10), keeping a search index in sync (see Part 33 — Search, 33.10), Kafka (see Part 27 — Messaging, 27.3), partitioning (see Part 22 — Database Scaling, 22.7) and caching (see Part 26 — Caching and Redis), going wider into the data pipeline those feed. Sections 38.1 to 38.6 introduce each idea; sections 38.7 to 38.11 take the same ideas into production depth (logical replication slots, Debezium configuration, warehouse DDL, Flink SQL windows, contract enforcement); and 38.12 builds the whole pipeline end to end: CDC from the orders database into a warehouse that feeds the daily revenue dashboard.

flowchart LR
    app["NestJS order service"] --> pg["PostgreSQL orders DB"]
    pg -->|"WAL, logical replication"| dbz["Debezium on Kafka Connect"]
    dbz --> kafka["Kafka topics"]
    kafka --> s3["S3 lake, Parquet"]
    kafka --> flink["Stream processor"]
    s3 --> wh["Warehouse"]
    wh --> models["SQL models: staging, facts, marts"]
    models --> dash["Daily revenue dashboard"]
    flink --> live["Live orders per minute"]
    pg -.->|"reconciliation"| models

38.1 OLTP versus OLAP

38.1.1 Why analytics queries hurt the production database

Concept

OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) is what your production database does: many small, fast reads and writes serving the application — fetch an order, insert a payment, update inventory. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) is analytics: a few large queries that scan huge amounts of data to compute aggregates — total revenue by month, top products by region, cohort retention. These two workloads are so different that running OLAP queries on your OLTP database degrades or crashes the application, which is why analytics belongs in a separate system.

Why does it exist?

A transactional database is tuned for OLTP: row-oriented storage, indexes for point lookups, serving thousands of small operations per second with low latency. An analytics query is the opposite: it reads millions of rows, scans whole columns, and runs for seconds or minutes. Run that on the production database and it saturates CPU and I/O, competes with and slows the application's queries, holds locks, blows the cache, and can bring the application down. The separation exists because the two workloads need opposite optimizations and must not fight over the same resources. The distinction drives the entire data pipeline: get analytics off the production database and into a system built for it.

Mental model

Your production database is a busy restaurant kitchen during service — a stream of quick orders, each served fast, everyone moving. An OLAP query is someone walking into that kitchen mid-service to do a full monthly inventory count, blocking the stoves and counters for twenty minutes while service grinds to a halt. You do not do inventory in the kitchen during service; you do it in a back room with a copy of the stock records (the warehouse). OLTP is service; OLAP is inventory; they belong in different rooms.

How it works — the differences

OLTP (production database) OLAP (analytics system)
Workload Many small, fast reads/writes Few large, scanning queries
Query shape Point lookups, small ranges, by key Aggregations over millions of rows
Storage Row-oriented (whole rows together) Column-oriented (whole columns together)
Optimized for Low-latency transactions High-throughput scans and aggregates
Latency Milliseconds Seconds to minutes (acceptable)
Example "Get order 1001" "Total revenue by month for 2 years"
Freshness need Real-time Minutes to hours old is usually fine

The heart of it is row-oriented versus column-oriented storage. OLTP databases store each row's fields together, so fetching one order reads one place — great for point lookups, bad for "sum one column across ten million rows" (which must read every row to get one field). Analytics systems store each column together, so summing a column reads only that column's contiguous data — great for aggregates, and highly compressible (a column of similar values compresses well). That storage difference is why a dedicated analytics system answers "revenue by month" in a fraction of the time and resources, and why forcing it on the row-oriented OLTP database is so costly.

Put numbers on it. An orders row in PostgreSQL is about 200 bytes with headers, so 120 million orders is roughly 24 GB of heap. A query that needs two columns (created_at, total_cents, 16 bytes together) still reads all 24 GB from a row store, because those 16 bytes are scattered inside every 8 KB page. A column store reads only those two columns, which after compression (dates and integers compress 5–10x) is around 200–400 MB. That is a 60–120x difference in bytes read before any other optimization, and bytes read is what costs time and money in analytics.

Practical example

The finance team asks for "revenue by month for the last two years, split by country". The orders service already has orders(id, customer_id, country, status, total_cents, created_at) with 120 million rows and a B-tree index on customer_id and on created_at. The application issues about 3,000 queries per second against this database, each touching a handful of rows through those indexes. The finance query touches 60 million rows (two years) and returns 48 rows (24 months times 2 countries). That ratio, millions in and dozens out, is the signature of OLAP. Whenever you see it, the query belongs somewhere other than the primary.

PostgreSQL example

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, country, sum(total_cents) AS revenue_cents
  FROM orders
 WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '2 years' AND status = 'paid'
 GROUP BY 1, 2
 ORDER BY 1, 2;
Finalize GroupAggregate  (cost=4120334.10..4120402.61 rows=48 width=48) (actual time=41873.2..41890.6 rows=48 loops=1)
  Group Key: (date_trunc('month'::text, created_at)), country
  Buffers: shared hit=212344 read=2861902, temp read=40211 written=40388
  ->  Gather Merge  (cost=4120334.10..4120399.73 rows=144 width=48) (actual time=41870.9..41890.1 rows=144 loops=1)
        Workers Planned: 2
        Workers Launched: 2
        ->  Partial HashAggregate  (actual time=41801.4..41801.6 rows=48 loops=3)
              ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=0.41..36120.7 rows=19870112 loops=3)
                    Filter: ((status = 'paid'::text) AND (created_at >= (now() - '2 years'::interval)))
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 20129880
                    Buffers: shared hit=212344 read=2861902
Planning Time: 0.31 ms
Execution Time: 41893.0 ms

Read it like an incident report. read=2861902 buffers is about 22 GB pulled from disk, which evicts the hot pages the application relies on from shared_buffers (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals, 18.4). Three processes (the leader plus two parallel workers) burn CPU for 42 seconds. The index on created_at is not used, correctly, because the planner knows half the table qualifies and a sequential scan is cheaper than 60 million random index lookups. That is the core reason "just add an index" fails for OLAP: an index helps when you want a few rows, and analytics wants most of them.

Production scenario

An analyst needed a monthly revenue breakdown and ran a large aggregating query directly against the production orders database during business hours. The query scanned two years of orders, saturated the database's I/O for several minutes, and the application's normal queries slowed from 3 ms to 800 ms — checkout latency spiked and customers noticed. The fix was to stop running analytics on the production database and instead replicate the data to an analytics system where such queries run without touching production. The lesson, learned the hard way at many companies, is that OLAP on the OLTP database is a production incident waiting to happen.

Failure scenario

A reporting dashboard was wired directly to the production database, running dozens of aggregating queries every few minutes to refresh its tiles. Under normal load it was tolerable; during a traffic peak, the combination of application load and the dashboard's heavy queries pushed the database past its limits and it fell over, taking the application down with it. The root cause was OLAP and OLTP sharing one database. The fix: move the dashboard's queries to a read replica at minimum (see Part 22 — Database Scaling, 22.3), and properly to an analytics warehouse fed by the pipeline in the rest of this Part. The lesson: never let analytics queries run against the production transactional database.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The read replica is not free either. A 40-second aggregate on a hot standby conflicts with WAL replay. With hot_standby_feedback = off the replica cancels the query (canceling statement due to conflict with recovery); with it on, the primary keeps dead rows for the replica and bloats. Either way, analytics on a replica is a stopgap (see Part 22 — Database Scaling, 22.5).
  • statement_timeout as a seat belt. Give the reporting role ALTER ROLE reporting SET statement_timeout = '30s' so a runaway report dies before it hurts anyone.
  • Long transactions block vacuum. An analyst's open BEGIN in a SQL client holds back the xmin horizon and causes table bloat for hours (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals, 18.8). Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for human roles.
  • Connection exhaustion. BI tools open many connections; one dashboard with 30 tiles can take 30 connections from the pool the API needs.
  • "Small" tables grow. A report that was fine at 2 million rows becomes an incident at 200 million; OLAP-shaped queries have no natural upper bound.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the production transactional database as sacred for OLTP and keeps analytics off it entirely. They recognize an OLAP query — a large scan or aggregation — as something that belongs in a separate analytics system, never on the production primary, and at minimum on a read replica for lighter needs. They understand the row-versus-column storage reason, which is why they do not just "add an index" to make an analytics query fast on the OLTP database (an index helps point lookups, not full-column aggregates). They design the data pipeline (the rest of this Part) to move data from the OLTP source into an OLAP system, so analysts and dashboards get their answers without ever threatening the application. When someone proposes running a report against production, the senior's answer is "not against production — here is the analytics system".

Common mistakes

  • Running analytics queries against the production transactional database, degrading or crashing the application.
  • Wiring a dashboard directly to the production database.
  • Trying to make an analytics query fast with indexes on the OLTP database (wrong tool for full-column aggregates).
  • Not separating OLTP and OLAP until an incident forces it.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP? OLTP is many small fast transactional reads/writes on the production database; OLAP is few large scanning/aggregating analytics queries; they need opposite optimizations and must not share resources.
  2. Why do analytics queries hurt the production database? They scan millions of rows, saturating CPU and I/O, competing with and slowing the application's transactional queries, and can crash the database.
  3. Why does column-oriented storage help analytics? Analytics aggregates read whole columns; storing columns contiguously (and compressing them) makes those scans far faster and cheaper than the row-oriented OLTP layout.
  4. Why not just add an index to make an analytics query fast on the OLTP database? Indexes speed point lookups and small ranges, not full-column aggregates over millions of rows; the fix is a separate analytics system, not an index.

Practical exercise

Take an analytics query (monthly revenue over two years) and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against an orders table to see it scan the whole table, noting the cost. Then describe how the same query would run against a column-oriented analytics system and why it would be dramatically cheaper. Acceptance criteria: you can quantify why the OLTP database struggles with the aggregate and explain the column-store advantage.

38.2 Change data capture and pipelines

38.2.1 Change data capture

Concept

Change Data Capture (CDC) is streaming every change (insert, update, delete) from your production database to other systems in near real time, by reading the database's internal change log rather than querying tables. It is how data flows reliably from your OLTP database into analytics systems, search indexes, caches and other services, keeping them in sync without burdening the production database with repeated queries.

Why does it exist?

Other systems need to know about changes in your database: the analytics warehouse needs new orders, the search index needs updated products (Part 33), a downstream service needs new events. Polling the database ("give me everything changed since last time") is inefficient and can miss changes or burden the database. CDC reads the database's write-ahead log (the log the database already keeps for durability and replication; see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals, 18.5, and Part 20 — Database Transactions, 20.9) and turns each committed change into an event stream, so downstream systems get every change in order, reliably, with minimal load on the source. It exists to propagate changes out of the database the right way.

Mental model

Imagine the production database keeps a perfect running journal of everything that happens — every insert, update and delete, in order (it does; this is the write-ahead log). CDC is a reader who tails that journal and broadcasts each entry to everyone who needs to know. The warehouse, the search index and the downstream services all subscribe to the broadcast and apply the changes, staying in step with the database without ever having to interrogate it. The journal is the WAL; the reader-broadcaster is CDC (a tool like Debezium feeding Kafka).

How it works

PostgreSQL ---(logical replication / WAL)---> Debezium ---> Kafka topic (order changes)
                                                               |
                          +------------------+-----------------+-----------------+
                          v                  v                 v                 v
                   Analytics warehouse   Search index      Cache invalidation   Other service
                   (63.12)               (Part 94.10)       (Part 26)            (Part 11)

The common stack: PostgreSQL's logical replication exposes committed changes from the WAL; Debezium (often via Kafka Connect) reads them and publishes a stream of change events to Kafka (Part 27); downstream consumers apply the changes to their systems. Each change event describes what changed (the table, the operation, the before/after values), in commit order. Because it reads the log the database already maintains, CDC adds little load to the source and does not miss changes.

Handling schema changes is a key CDC concern: when you change the source table's schema (add a column, Part 23), the change stream's shape changes, and downstream consumers must cope. This is a data-contract problem (38.4): schema changes in the source ripple through the pipeline, so they must be made compatibly (additive where possible, Part 24) and coordinated with the data team. Section 38.7 shows the concrete mechanics: publications, replication slots, the Debezium connector configuration and what each schema change does to the stream.

A single change event, as Debezium emits it for an update to an order, looks like this (trimmed):

{
  "before": { "id": "7f3c9a20-1d1e-4c55-9a8e-0b6f2f1a9c11", "status": "pending", "total_cents": 45900 },
  "after":  { "id": "7f3c9a20-1d1e-4c55-9a8e-0b6f2f1a9c11", "status": "paid",    "total_cents": 45900 },
  "source": { "connector": "postgresql", "db": "orders", "schema": "public", "table": "orders",
              "lsn": 2398541736, "txId": 918273, "ts_ms": 1767225600123 },
  "op": "u",
  "ts_ms": 1767225600456
}

op is c (create), u (update), d (delete) or r (read, a row from the initial snapshot). source.lsn is the position in the WAL, which gives you a total order per database and a natural idempotency key. The gap between source.ts_ms (commit time in PostgreSQL) and ts_ms (when Debezium processed it) is your capture lag. The populated before block appears only when the table has REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; with the default setting, before is null on updates.

Practical example

The orders service has three downstream readers of order changes: the warehouse (daily revenue), the search index (order lookup for support agents) and a loyalty service that awards points when an order becomes paid. Before CDC, each had a nightly or every-five-minutes polling job running SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at > $last_seen. Polling missed hard deletes entirely, missed updates where a bug forgot to touch updated_at, and ran three overlapping index scans on the primary every five minutes. Moving to one Debezium connector replaced three polling jobs with one WAL reader, captured deletes, and dropped end-to-end latency from five minutes to about two seconds.

CDC versus the outbox pattern

Part 29 (29.10) taught the outbox pattern: write an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data change, and a worker publishes it. CDC and the outbox solve related problems and are often combined:

  • Outbox: you explicitly write a business event ("order placed") in the same transaction; a relay (often CDC reading the outbox table) publishes it. Precise, semantic events you control.
  • CDC on the tables directly: captures every row change automatically, no code to emit events, but the events are row changes, not business events.

A common robust pattern is CDC reading the outbox table: you get the transaction-safe semantic events of the outbox, delivered by the reliable log-reading mechanism of CDC. Delivery is still at least once, so consumers stay idempotent. The two are complementary, not competing.

Need Raw-table CDC Outbox read by CDC Polling updated_at
Analytics copy of every column Best fit Only what you put in the payload Misses deletes
Business events for other services Leaks table structure Best fit Poor
Captures hard deletes Yes Only if you write a delete event No
Code changes in the service None Insert into outbox in every write path Query per consumer
Coupling to schema High (table is the contract) Low (payload is the contract) High

Production scenario

A marketplace with 400,000 orders per day (peaks of 60 writes per second to orders, about 250 per second across orders, order_items and payments) runs one Debezium PostgreSQL connector on a three-worker Kafka Connect cluster. Capture lag (commit to Kafka) is 300–800 ms at p99. The connector holds one logical replication slot; normal retained WAL behind the slot is under 200 MB. Monitoring alerts when retained WAL exceeds 5 GB, when the connector task state is not RUNNING, or when the last event is older than 2 minutes during business hours. Load on the primary from WAL decoding is about 3–5% of one vCPU.

Failure scenario

At 03:40 the database disk alarm fired at 85% full on a 500 GB volume that normally sat at 40%. The cause was not data growth. A Kafka Connect deploy the previous evening had failed to start the Debezium task (a missing secret), so nothing was reading the replication slot, and PostgreSQL was keeping every WAL segment since then for a consumer that might come back. The slot had retained 210 GB of WAL in nine hours during a promotion. The on-call engineer fixed the secret, the connector caught up in 40 minutes, and the WAL was recycled. The postmortem added three things: an alert on pg_replication_slots retained WAL (38.7 has the query), max_slot_wal_keep_size as a hard cap so a dead consumer can never fill the disk again, and a runbook step for dropping an abandoned slot. The lesson: a replication slot is a promise PostgreSQL keeps even when it hurts, so someone must watch every slot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Inactive slot fills the disk (the story above). Cap with max_slot_wal_keep_size, alert on retained WAL.
  • Duplicate events after a connector restart. Debezium resumes from the last committed offset, so events since then are replayed; consumers dedupe on (source.lsn, table, primary key) or upsert by key.
  • Updates without a before image. With the default REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT, before is null for updates and holds only the primary key for deletes; set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on tables where consumers need old values (at a WAL-size cost, and see 38.7 for how it interacts with publication column lists).
  • Large transactions. A backfill updating 30 million rows in one transaction arrives as 30 million events in a burst, after the commit; consumers and Kafka must absorb it.
  • Failover loses the slot. Before PostgreSQL 17, logical slots lived only on the primary; after a failover the new primary has no slot and Debezium must re-snapshot. PostgreSQL 17 can synchronize failover slots to a physical standby; managed services vary, so test failover with CDC attached.
  • TOAST columns. An update that does not touch a large toasted column sends it as an "unchanged" placeholder rather than the value; consumers must not overwrite the stored value with the placeholder.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses CDC (often with the outbox pattern, Part 19 — 29.10) as the reliable way to get changes out of the database into the rest of the system — warehouse, search, cache, other services — because it reads the WAL the database already keeps, adding minimal load and missing nothing, unlike polling. They treat the change stream as a product with a contract (38.4): downstream systems depend on its shape, so schema changes in the source are made compatibly and coordinated, not sprung on consumers. They design for the stream's realities: it is ordered per source but delivered at least once (so consumers are idempotent; see Part 27 — Messaging, 27.9), and it lags slightly (eventual consistency downstream). They reach for CDC rather than ad-hoc polling or dual writes, because dual writes (write to the database and also to Kafka separately) can diverge if one fails, whereas CDC derives everything from the one committed log.

Common mistakes

  • Polling tables for changes instead of CDC, burdening the database and risking missed changes.
  • Dual writes (to the database and a stream separately) that diverge when one fails; CDC from the single committed log avoids this.
  • Making a source schema change that breaks downstream consumers, with no coordination (38.4).
  • Non-idempotent consumers of the at-least-once change stream, double-applying changes.

Interview questions

  1. What is CDC and why use it over polling? Streaming database changes by reading the write-ahead log (via Debezium/Kafka); it captures every change in order with minimal load on the source, unlike polling which burdens the database and can miss changes.
  2. How do CDC and the outbox pattern relate? The outbox writes semantic events in the same transaction as the change; CDC reliably delivers them (often by reading the outbox table via the WAL); combined, you get transaction-safe semantic events delivered reliably.
  3. Why is CDC better than dual writes? Dual writes (database plus a separate stream) can diverge if one write fails; CDC derives the stream from the single committed log, so it cannot diverge from what was committed.
  4. What must downstream CDC consumers handle? At-least-once delivery (be idempotent, Part 69.9 and Part 71.12), eventual consistency (slight lag), and source schema changes (coordinated, compatible — the data contract).

Practical exercise

Describe (or set up) a CDC pipeline from a PostgreSQL orders table through Debezium and Kafka to a downstream consumer, and make the consumer idempotent so re-delivered change events do not double-apply. Then reason about what happens to the consumer when a new column is added to the orders table and how you would make that change compatibly. Acceptance criteria: the consumer handles at-least-once delivery without double-applying, and you can describe a compatible schema-change process for the source.

38.2.2 ETL, ELT, batch pipelines and orchestration

Concept

Data must be moved from sources into the warehouse and transformed into useful shapes. ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before loading it into the warehouse; ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse. These run as batch pipelines (scheduled jobs processing data in chunks) coordinated by an orchestrator that manages dependencies and schedules as a graph of tasks (a DAG).

Why does it exist?

Raw data from many sources is not in a shape ready for analysis — it needs cleaning, joining, aggregating and reshaping. That transformation has to happen somewhere, on a schedule, with dependencies handled (compute daily revenue only after today's orders have loaded), with retries and monitoring. ETL/ELT pipelines and orchestrators exist to do this reliably and repeatedly, so analysts and dashboards work from clean, current, well-shaped data rather than raw source dumps.

Mental model

Imagine a juice bar. ETL is peeling and pressing the fruit at the farm and shipping only bottled juice: the shop never sees a whole orange, and if a customer wants a smoothie instead, you are out of luck. ELT is shipping whole fruit to the shop's big refrigerated storeroom and pressing whatever each customer orders on the spot: more storage, but you can always make something new from the same fruit. The orchestrator is the shift manager with the morning checklist: do not press anything until the delivery has been checked in, and if the delivery is late, phone the supplier rather than serve yesterday's juice.

How it works — ETL vs ELT

ETL (transform before load):
  Extract from source -> Transform (clean, join, aggregate) -> Load into warehouse
  Transformation happens in a separate processing step.

ELT (load raw, then transform):
  Extract from source -> Load raw into warehouse -> Transform inside the warehouse (SQL)
  Modern cloud warehouses are powerful enough to do the transform themselves.

ELT has become common because cloud warehouses are powerful and cheap enough to transform data in place, and loading raw data first means you keep the original and can re-transform it differently later. ETL is still used when transformation must happen before the data lands (for privacy masking, Part 123.5, or when the warehouse should only ever hold processed data). The choice depends on where the transformation power is and whether raw data should enter the warehouse.

Orchestration

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) of tasks the orchestrator runs on a schedule:

  [extract orders] --+
                     +--> [compute daily revenue] --> [refresh dashboard tables]
  [extract refunds]--+
                     +--> [compute daily refunds] --+

Each box is a task; arrows are dependencies; the orchestrator (Airflow-style) runs
each task when its dependencies succeed, retries failures, and alerts on problems.

An orchestrator (Airflow is the canonical example) defines pipelines as DAGs of tasks with dependencies, runs them on a schedule, retries failed tasks, and alerts on failures. It is the scheduler and dependency manager for the whole data pipeline, ensuring "compute daily revenue" runs only after the day's orders have loaded, and that a failure is retried and surfaced rather than silently producing a wrong dashboard.

Three orchestration ideas matter more than any specific tool:

  1. Each run owns a data interval. The run for 2026-11-04 processes exactly the orders whose business date is 2026-11-04, no matter when it runs. Airflow calls this the run's logical date and data interval. It is what makes reruns and backfills safe.
  2. Tasks are idempotent. Running a task twice for the same interval produces the same result: delete-then-insert the partition, or MERGE by key, never blind INSERT. Section 38.8 shows the SQL.
  3. Backfill is a first-class operation. When the revenue logic changes, you rerun the last 90 intervals. If the pipeline cannot do that without manual surgery, it is not finished.

Production scenario

A mid-sized e-commerce company runs about 140 ELT models in the warehouse, scheduled hourly and nightly. Raw CDC data lands continuously; the nightly DAG starts at 01:30 local time (after the business day closes and late payment captures settle), runs staging models in 6 minutes, fact models in 11 minutes and the finance marts in 4 minutes, and the dashboards are fresh by 02:00 with an SLA of 06:00. Each task retries twice with a 5-minute delay. Warehouse compute for the nightly run costs about $9 per night. The one-off backfill of two years after a revenue-definition change took 3 hours and about $140.

Failure scenario

At 07:10 the head of finance asked why yesterday's revenue was 38% lower than the day before. The nightly DAG had succeeded, every task green. The cause was upstream: the extract task had run at 01:30 as scheduled, but the CDC sink was 90 minutes behind because of a Kafka Connect rebalance, so only part of the day's orders had landed. The DAG had no check that its inputs were complete; it computed correct sums over incomplete data. The fix was a sensor-style gate before the revenue model: wait until the raw table contains events with commit timestamps past the end of the interval plus a margin, and fail loudly (not succeed quietly) if that is not true by 05:00. The lesson: a green pipeline only proves the code ran, not that the data was complete. Freshness and completeness checks belong in the DAG as gates.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Non-idempotent loads. A retried INSERT doubles a day's revenue. Overwrite the partition or MERGE by key.
  • Time zones. "Yesterday" in UTC is not yesterday in Asia/Kolkata (UTC+5:30) or America/New_York; define the business day explicitly and convert once, in staging.
  • Late data. Refunds and chargebacks for an order arrive days or weeks later; models must recompute a trailing window (for example, the last 7 days every night), not just yesterday.
  • Catch-up storms. A scheduler paused for a week that resumes with catch-up enabled launches 7 runs at once and saturates the warehouse; limit concurrent runs.
  • Upstream schema change. A dropped source column fails the staging model; a renamed one silently produces nulls (38.4). Test column presence and null rates.
  • Partial success. Facts updated but marts failed: the dashboard shows a mix. Publish marts atomically (swap a view or table) at the end.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior understands ETL/ELT and orchestration well enough to collaborate with the data team and to see where their own system fits: the backend emits the events and exposes the source data (via CDC) that the pipelines consume, and a change to the source schema or event shape ripples through those pipelines (the data contract, 38.4). They favor ELT with modern warehouses where it fits, keeping raw data for re-transformation, but reach for ETL when transformation must precede loading (privacy masking especially). They know pipelines are batch jobs with dependencies, retries and monitoring, and that a silently failed pipeline produces a wrong dashboard, so freshness and success monitoring matter (38.4). They do not need to own Airflow, but they need to know that their schema change can break a DAG and coordinate accordingly.

Common mistakes

  • Changing a source schema or event shape without considering the downstream pipelines it feeds.
  • No orchestration, so pipeline dependencies, retries and failures are handled ad hoc.
  • Silent pipeline failures producing wrong dashboards with no alert.
  • Transforming away raw data when keeping it (ELT) would allow re-transformation later.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between ETL and ELT? ETL transforms before loading into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data and transforms inside the warehouse. ELT is common with powerful cloud warehouses and keeps raw data for re-transformation; ETL suits cases where transformation must precede loading (e.g. privacy masking).
  2. What does an orchestrator like Airflow do? Defines pipelines as DAGs of dependent tasks, schedules and runs them, retries failures, and alerts — managing dependencies so tasks run in the right order.
  3. Why does a backend engineer care about data pipelines? The backend's source data and events feed them; a source schema or event change ripples through the pipelines, so it must be coordinated (the data contract).

Practical exercise

Sketch a daily revenue pipeline as a DAG: extract orders and refunds, compute daily revenue and refunds, then refresh dashboard tables, with dependencies and a failure alert. Decide whether to use ETL or ELT and justify it. Acceptance criteria: the DAG expresses the dependencies correctly, has retries and a failure alert, and you can justify the ETL/ELT choice.

38.3 Data warehouses, lakes and stream processing

38.3.1 Warehouses, lakes and columnar storage

Concept

A data warehouse is a system built for OLAP: it stores large volumes of structured data in columnar format and answers analytical queries fast (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake are examples). A data lake stores large volumes of raw data (often as files in object storage, in formats like Parquet) cheaply and flexibly, for processing later. Both use columnar storage and partitioning to make scanning huge datasets efficient. They are where analytics data lives, separate from the OLTP database.

Why does it exist?

Analytics needs to store and query far more data than the production database should hold, in a format optimized for scanning and aggregation, cheaply. A warehouse exists to answer analytical queries fast over large structured data. A lake exists to store vast amounts of raw or semi-structured data cheaply (often cheaper than a warehouse) before it is necessarily structured, keeping the option to process it many ways later. Together they hold the organization's analytical data at a scale and cost the OLTP database never could, optimized for the OLAP workload (38.1).

Mental model

Imagine a library. The production database is the circulation desk: fast at "give me this one book". The data lake is the basement archive: everything ever printed, in labelled boxes, cheap to keep, slow to browse unless you know which box to open. The warehouse is the reference room: curated, indexed by subject, built for someone who wants to read across many books at once. Partitioning is writing the year on every box so you never open the 2019 boxes when you want 2026.

How it works — columnar storage and Parquet

The common thread is columnar storage (38.1): data stored by column rather than row, so an aggregate reads only the columns it needs and compresses well (a column of similar values compresses far better than mixed rows). Parquet is the standard columnar file format for data lakes — a compressed, columnar, self-describing file that warehouses and processing engines read efficiently. Partitioning (by date, region, etc.) means a query filtered on the partition key reads only the relevant files, not the whole dataset — the same partition-pruning idea as PostgreSQL partitioning (see Part 22 — Database Scaling, 22.7) and TimescaleDB (see Part 25 — NoSQL Data Modelling, 25.5), applied to warehouse and lake data.

Warehouse / lake efficiency comes from:
  Columnar storage  -> read only the columns the query needs, compress well
  Parquet format     -> compressed, columnar, self-describing files (lakes)
  Partitioning       -> query filtered on partition key reads only relevant files

A "revenue by month, 2 years" query reads just the revenue and date columns,
only the relevant date partitions, compressed -> fast and cheap, unlike the OLTP scan.

Warehouse concepts (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) differ in details (serverless vs cluster, pricing models) but share the columnar, scan-optimized, scalable OLAP design. A backend engineer does not need to run one but should understand that it is where analytics data goes and why it answers big aggregates cheaply. Section 38.9 shows real DDL for each and the pricing that shapes how you write queries.

Production scenario

A company with 5 years of orders (about 700 million order rows and 2.1 billion order-item rows) keeps raw CDC data in S3 as Parquet, roughly 1.4 TB compressed, at about $0.023 per GB-month, so around $32 a month for storage. The warehouse holds modelled tables of about 600 GB. A "revenue by month by country, last two years" query on a table partitioned by order date and clustered by country reads about 6 GB and returns in 3 seconds. The same query without the partition filter (someone wrote WHERE extract(year from created_at) >= 2024, which hides the partition column inside a function on some engines) read 180 GB. Under a per-byte pricing model, that one habit is a 30x cost difference on every run.

Failure scenario

A data engineer added a dashboard tile with an unpartitioned query against a 2 TB events table and set it to refresh every 15 minutes. Under on-demand per-byte pricing, each refresh scanned the whole table, 96 refreshes a day, and the month's bill arrived $36,000 higher than usual. Nothing was broken in the usual sense; the dashboard was correct. The fixes: require a partition filter on the large tables (BigQuery supports require_partition_filter), set a per-query bytes-billed cap for dashboard service accounts, and alert on daily spend. The lesson: in a warehouse, a bad query costs money rather than latency, and nobody gets paged for money unless you build the alert.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Small files. A sink writing one Parquet file per second produces millions of tiny files; every query pays per-file overhead. Compact into files of 128 MB to 1 GB.
  • Partition skew. Partitioning by customer_id puts one enterprise customer in one giant partition; partition by date and cluster by customer instead.
  • Updates and deletes in a lake. Plain Parquet files are immutable; a GDPR deletion means rewriting files. Table formats such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake add row-level deletes and snapshots (38.9).
  • Schema drift in files. Old files lack a new column; readers must treat it as null, not fail.
  • Copy sprawl. The same data copied into five marts by five teams, each slightly different; one revenue number becomes five.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior knows the warehouse/lake is the right home for analytics data — columnar, partitioned, scan-optimized, scalable, and separate from the OLTP database — and that getting data there (via CDC and pipelines, 38.2) is how analytics stays off production. They understand columnar storage and partitioning as the reasons big aggregates are cheap there and expensive on the row-oriented OLTP database. They treat the data they send into the warehouse (through events and CDC) as feeding this system, with a contract (38.4) and privacy obligations (38.5). They do not over-engineer: for a small product, pre-aggregated tables or materialized views in PostgreSQL (38.6) may suffice, and a full warehouse is adopted when analytics scale and needs justify it.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping analytics data in the OLTP database instead of a warehouse/lake, degrading production.
  • Ignoring partitioning, so warehouse queries scan everything.
  • Adopting a full warehouse before the scale justifies it, when materialized views in PostgreSQL would do (38.6).

Interview questions

  1. What is a data warehouse and how does it differ from the OLTP database? A columnar, scan-optimized, scalable system for OLAP analytics queries, separate from the row-oriented OLTP database, so analytics runs fast and off production.
  2. What is a data lake and what is Parquet? A cheap store for large raw/semi-structured data (often files in object storage); Parquet is the standard compressed columnar file format lakes use.
  3. Why does columnar storage plus partitioning make big aggregates cheap? Aggregates read only the needed columns (compressed), and partitioning limits the query to relevant partitions, versus scanning whole rows across the entire dataset.

Practical exercise

Explain how a "revenue by month over two years" query runs against a columnar, partitioned warehouse versus the row-oriented OLTP database, identifying what columns and partitions it reads and why it is cheap. Then decide, for a small product, whether a full warehouse is warranted or whether PostgreSQL materialized views (38.6) would suffice. Acceptance criteria: you can explain the columnar/partitioning advantage and make a right-sized build decision.

38.3.2 Stream processing: windows, watermarks and late events

Concept

Stream processing computes results continuously over an unbounded stream of events as they arrive, rather than in scheduled batches. Its core concepts are windows (grouping events by time — "revenue per 1-minute window"), watermarks (a signal of how far event time has progressed, used to decide when a window is complete), and handling late events (events that arrive after their window was thought complete). Kafka Streams and Flink are the common tools.

Why does it exist?

Some analytics must be real-time or near-real-time: live dashboards, fraud detection, metrics aggregation, alerting. Batch pipelines (38.2) run on a schedule and produce results minutes or hours later, which is too slow for these. Stream processing exists to compute continuously as events flow, so a count or aggregate is up to date within seconds. The challenge is that events arrive out of order and sometimes late (a mobile device was offline and sends its events an hour later), so the processing must decide when a time window is "done" despite stragglers — which is what watermarks and late-event handling address.

Mental model

Imagine counting people entering a venue in 1-minute buckets using a live feed. Events (entries) arrive roughly in order but not perfectly — someone's badge scan is delayed and arrives late. A window is each 1-minute bucket. A watermark is your judgment "it is now 10:05, and I believe all 10:00-10:01 entries have arrived, so I can finalize that bucket." A late event is a 10:00 scan that shows up at 10:07 after you finalized the bucket — you must decide whether to update the finalized count or drop the straggler. Stream processing is doing this bucketing-and-finalizing continuously and correctly despite disorder and lateness.

How it works

Event stream (order events, out of order by a few seconds):
  ... t=10:00:58  t=10:01:02  t=10:00:59 (out of order)  t=10:01:05 ...

Windowing: group events into time windows by EVENT time (when it happened),
           not processing time (when it arrived).
Watermark:  "event time has reached 10:02" -> windows up to ~10:01 can be finalized.
Late event: a 10:00 event arriving after the 10:00-10:01 window closed -> either
            update the result (if allowed lateness covers it) or drop/side-output it.
Stateful:   the processor keeps per-window state (running counts) until finalized.

Key distinctions: event time (when the event actually happened) versus processing time (when it was processed) — correct analytics use event time, because that is the truth. Watermarks let the processor decide a window is complete despite out-of-order arrival. Allowed lateness gives a grace period to incorporate stragglers; events later than that are dropped or side-outputted for separate handling. Stateful processing means the processor holds window state (running aggregates) in memory/state store until the window is finalized, which must survive failures (checkpointing).

Production scenario

A live orders-per-minute dashboard consumes the order event stream with 1-minute tumbling windows by event time. A watermark with a 30-second allowed lateness lets most out-of-order and slightly-late events land in the correct window, and the dashboard updates within seconds of events occurring. A handful of very late events (from devices that were offline) exceed the allowed lateness and are routed to a side output for a separate reconciliation step (38.4), so they are not lost, just not in the live window. The result is a near-real-time dashboard that is correct for the overwhelming majority of events and does not silently drop stragglers.

Failure scenario

On Black Friday at 18:02 the live orders-per-minute chart froze at 17:48 while orders were clearly flowing (the checkout dashboard showed 900 orders a minute). The stream job was healthy and consuming. The cause was the watermark: the input topic had 12 partitions, and after a producer change, all orders were keyed by region, and two regions had almost no traffic in the evening. A watermark in Flink advances only as fast as the slowest input partition, so two idle partitions held event time at 17:48 and no window could close.
