The fix was to declare idleness on the watermark strategy (withIdleness on Flink's WatermarkStrategy, or the table.exec.source.idle-timeout setting in Flink SQL) so idle partitions stop holding back the watermark, plus an alert on "watermark lag" (wall clock minus watermark). The lesson: windows close on event time, not on wall time, and event time is only as fresh as the quietest input.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Idle partitions stall the watermark (the story above).
  • Clock skew on producers. A device with its clock an hour ahead creates events "from the future" that push the watermark forward and make everyone else's events late. Clamp or reject event times far from ingestion time.
  • Replays and reprocessing. Restarting from an old offset replays a day of events in minutes; event-time windows give the same answer, processing-time windows do not.
  • State growth. Session windows or joins without a time bound keep state forever; set state TTL or bound the join interval.
  • Exactly-once boundaries. Kafka transactions give exactly-once inside Kafka; writing results to PostgreSQL or Redis still needs idempotent upserts keyed by window.
  • Rebalancing. When a Kafka Streams instance joins or leaves, its state stores must be restored from changelog topics, which can take minutes for large state; standby replicas shorten that.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for stream processing when analytics genuinely need near-real-time results (live dashboards, fraud, alerting) and accepts the added complexity (state, watermarks, late events, exactly-once semantics) that batch does not have. They process by event time, not processing time, because event time is the truth; they tune allowed lateness to the business's tolerance for stragglers versus freshness; and they never silently drop late events without a reconciliation path, because dropped events mean undercounting. They know stream processing is harder to get exactly right than batch (the exactly-once and late-event problems are genuinely subtle), so they use it only when real-time is required and fall back to batch for everything that can tolerate a schedule. The decision, as always, is driven by the requirement (does this need to be real-time?), not by novelty.

Common mistakes

  • Processing by arrival time instead of event time, producing wrong window results.
  • Dropping late events silently, undercounting without a reconciliation path.
  • No watermark/allowed-lateness tuning, either finalizing windows too early (miss events) or too late (stale results).
  • Using stream processing for analytics that could be batch, taking on needless complexity.
  • Ignoring state recovery, so a processor crash loses in-flight window aggregates.

Interview questions

  1. What are windows, watermarks and late events in stream processing? Windows group events by (event) time; watermarks signal how far event time has progressed so a window can be finalized; late events arrive after their window closed and must be incorporated (within allowed lateness) or handled separately.
  2. Why process by event time rather than processing time? Event time is when things actually happened, which is the correct basis for analytics; processing time depends on arrival order and delays and gives wrong results.
  3. How do you handle late events without losing data? Allow a grace period (allowed lateness) to include them, and route events later than that to a side output for reconciliation rather than silently dropping them.
  4. When do you choose stream processing over batch? When near-real-time results are genuinely required (live dashboards, fraud, alerting); otherwise batch is simpler and sufficient.

Practical exercise

Design a near-real-time orders-per-minute aggregation using tumbling windows by event time, a watermark with an allowed-lateness grace period, and a side output for events too late to include. Explain what happens to an event that is 10 seconds late versus one that is 10 minutes late. Acceptance criteria: windows use event time, in-grace late events land correctly, and very late events are reconciled rather than silently dropped.

38.4 Data contracts and data quality

38.4.1 Contracts between backend and data teams, and data quality

Concept

A data contract is an agreement about the shape, meaning and guarantees of the data one team produces for another — specifically, the events and source data the backend team produces that the data team consumes. Data quality is ensuring that data is correct, complete, fresh and consistent, through validation, reconciliation and freshness checks. Together they keep the pipeline from silently producing wrong analytics.

Why does it exist?

The data team builds dashboards and models on the events and tables the backend team produces. When the backend changes an event's shape, renames a field, changes a field's meaning, or stops emitting an event, the data team's pipelines break or — worse — silently produce wrong numbers. Without a contract, these changes happen unannounced and break analytics. Without data quality checks, bad or missing data flows through and the dashboard is confidently wrong. Data contracts and quality exist because analytics is only as trustworthy as the data feeding it, and that data comes from systems other teams change.

Mental model

The backend team is a supplier and the data team is a customer who builds products (dashboards, models) from the supplier's parts (events). A data contract is the specification sheet for those parts: this event has these fields with these types and this meaning, emitted under these conditions, and we will not change it without notice. Without the spec, the supplier changes a part's dimensions one day and the customer's product breaks on the assembly line, or worse, ships subtly defective. Data quality is the incoming inspection: checking the parts are correct, complete and fresh before building on them.

How it works — data contracts

A data contract treats events and shared data as products with a published, versioned schema and guarantees:

  • Schema and types: the exact fields, types and structure of each event (an order.placed event has these fields).
  • Meaning (semantics): what each field means (total_cents is the amount charged including tax, in cents) — ambiguity here causes wrong analytics even with a correct schema.
  • Guarantees: delivery semantics (at least once), ordering, freshness, and that the producer will not make breaking changes without coordination.
  • Change process: schema changes are additive and backward-compatible where possible (Part 24), breaking changes are versioned and coordinated, and the data team is notified — the same compatibility discipline as any API, because an event stream is an API between teams.

Treating events as data products with contracts is the practice that prevents "the backend renamed a field and the revenue dashboard silently went to zero". The event schema is as much a contract as a REST or gRPC API (Part 24, Part 15), and changing it carelessly breaks consumers.

How it works — data quality

Data quality dimensions and checks:
  Validity      -> does the data match the expected schema and value rules?
  Completeness  -> are all expected records present (no missing days/events)?
  Freshness     -> is the data recent enough? (a freshness SLA: warehouse < 1h behind)
  Consistency   -> does it reconcile with the source? (warehouse revenue == source revenue)

Reconciliation: periodically compare a derived total against the source of truth
  (e.g. daily: does the warehouse's order count match the production database's?)
  -> catches silent data loss or double-counting in the pipeline.

Reconciliation is the most important data-quality practice: periodically compare a derived figure (the warehouse's daily revenue) against the source of truth (the production database's daily revenue) and alert on a mismatch. This catches the silent failures — a pipeline that dropped some events, a double-count from a non-idempotent consumer, a stuck job — that otherwise produce a wrong dashboard nobody questions. Freshness SLAs ("the warehouse is never more than an hour behind") detect a stalled pipeline. Validation at ingestion rejects malformed data before it corrupts the warehouse. Section 38.11 turns this into enforcement: a schema registry compatibility mode, a contract file, contract tests in the producer's CI, and the reconciliation SQL itself.

Production scenario

At a food-delivery company, the orders team publishes order.placed, order.paid, order.delivered and order.refunded, consumed by finance, growth, logistics analytics and the fraud model: four teams, nineteen downstream models. Contracts live as JSON Schema files in the producer's repository; CI fails a pull request that removes a field, changes a type or renames an enum value, and an owner from the data team is an automatic reviewer for changes under contracts/. The warehouse runs freshness checks every 15 minutes (alert if the newest order.paid is older than 20 minutes between 08:00 and 23:00) and a nightly reconciliation of order counts and paid revenue per day against a read replica of the source, with a tolerance of 0.1% for in-flight orders. In a typical quarter, contract CI blocks 6–10 breaking changes before merge, and reconciliation catches one or two pipeline problems that would otherwise have reached finance.

Failure scenario (connecting to a reconciliation catch)

A backend deploy renamed an order event field from amount to total_cents without notifying the data team or versioning the event. The warehouse pipeline, expecting amount, silently recorded null revenue for new orders, and the revenue dashboard quietly flattened. Because there was a reconciliation job comparing warehouse daily revenue against the production database daily revenue, the mismatch alerted within a day, and the cause (the unannounced field rename) was found quickly. Without reconciliation, the wrong dashboard could have driven business decisions for weeks. The fixes: a data contract requiring compatible, coordinated event changes, and reconciliation as a standing safety net. The lesson: event schemas are contracts between teams, and reconciliation is the backstop that catches the contract violations and pipeline failures that slip through.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Semantic change without a schema change. total_cents silently switches from "including tax" to "excluding tax"; the schema check passes and the numbers are wrong. Contracts must document meaning, and meaning changes need a new field name.
  • Enum growth. A new status = 'partially_refunded' falls through a CASE in a model and lands in "other". Treat new enum values as a contract change consumers are told about.
  • Reconciliation against a moving source. Comparing today's partial day always mismatches; reconcile closed intervals only, with a tolerance for in-flight orders.
  • Freshness alerts at 03:00 on a quiet night. A freshness SLA must account for real traffic patterns or it pages for nothing and gets muted.
  • Both sides wrong the same way. A bug that writes the wrong amount to the source passes reconciliation; reconciliation proves the pipeline, not the business logic.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the events and source data their system produces as data products with contracts, knowing the data team builds on them: they version event schemas, make changes compatibly and coordinate breaking ones (Part 24), and document each field's meaning, because an unannounced field rename or a changed meaning silently breaks analytics. They champion reconciliation — comparing derived figures against the source of truth — as the essential backstop that catches silent pipeline failures, because a wrong dashboard that nobody questions is more dangerous than a crashed one. They set freshness SLAs and validate data at ingestion. In short, they extend the API-compatibility and data-integrity discipline they apply to their own system across the team boundary into the data pipeline, because analytics is only as trustworthy as the data and that data is their responsibility too.

Common mistakes

  • Changing event shape or field meaning without a contract or coordination, silently breaking analytics.
  • No reconciliation, so silent data loss or double-counting produces a wrong dashboard unnoticed.
  • No freshness SLA, so a stalled pipeline serves stale data as if current.
  • Ambiguous field semantics, so the same field is interpreted differently by producer and consumer.
  • Treating event streams casually rather than as contracts (they are APIs between teams).

Interview questions

  1. What is a data contract and why does it matter? An agreement on the shape, meaning and guarantees of data one team produces for another; it prevents unannounced changes (renames, meaning changes, dropped events) from silently breaking the consumer's analytics — an event stream is an API between teams.
  2. What is reconciliation and why is it the key data-quality practice? Periodically comparing a derived figure (warehouse revenue) against the source of truth (production revenue) and alerting on mismatch; it catches silent pipeline failures (data loss, double-counting) that produce confidently wrong dashboards.
  3. What are the dimensions of data quality? Validity (matches schema/rules), completeness (no missing records), freshness (recent enough, per an SLA), and consistency (reconciles with the source).
  4. Why treat an event schema like an API contract? Downstream pipelines depend on it; changing it carelessly breaks them, so it needs versioning, compatible changes and coordination (Part 24).

Practical exercise

Write a data contract for an order.placed event (fields, types, meanings, delivery and freshness guarantees, and the change process). Then design a reconciliation job that compares the warehouse's daily revenue against the production database's and alerts on a mismatch beyond a small tolerance. Acceptance criteria: the contract documents field meanings and a compatible-change process, and the reconciliation job would catch a silent field-rename-induced revenue drop.

38.5 Privacy in data pipelines

38.5.1 PII masking and deletion propagation

Concept

Personal data (PII) flows from the production database into the warehouse, lake and analytics systems, so privacy obligations follow it. PII masking removes or obscures personal data in the pipeline so analytics does not hold more than it needs. Deletion propagation ensures that when a user exercises their right to erasure (GDPR; see Part 39 — Security, 39.31, and Part 85 — Enterprise and Multi-Tenant SaaS, 85.7), the deletion reaches every copy of their data — including the warehouse and lake — not just the production database.

Why does it exist?

A user's personal data does not live only in the production database; the pipeline copies it into the warehouse, the lake, backups and analytics tables. Privacy regulations (GDPR, and others) require that you hold personal data only as needed and delete it on request everywhere. If deletion only clears the production database and leaves the data in the warehouse, you are non-compliant and the data persists where you may not even realize. Masking reduces how much PII enters analytics in the first place; deletion propagation ensures erasure is complete. These exist because privacy obligations apply to every copy of the data, and the pipeline makes many copies.

Mental model

Imagine a customer asks a shop to forget them. The shop shreds the paper file in the front office. But copies were faxed to accounting, the marketing team photocopied the mailing list, and the archive in the basement has last year's box. Forgetting the customer means knowing every place a copy went, which is only possible if every copy was made through a door that keeps a log. In a pipeline, CDC and the outbox are that door, and the deletion event follows the same path the data took.

How it works

PII masking in the pipeline (ETL-style transform before loading analytics):
  Source: { user_id, email, name, order_total }
  Masked: { user_id_hash, order_total }   -- drop email/name, hash the id for analytics
  -> analytics gets what it needs (per-user aggregation via the hash) without raw PII.

Deletion propagation on a GDPR erasure request:
  User requests deletion
    -> delete from production database (the source)
    -> emit a deletion event (outbox/CDC) -> pipeline deletes/anonymizes in the warehouse,
       the lake, derived tables, and triggers backup handling per policy
  -> the user's data is gone from EVERY store, not just production.

Masking happens in the pipeline (an ETL transform, 38.2, or at ingestion): drop fields analytics does not need (email, name), and where per-user analysis is needed, use a hashed or pseudonymous id rather than raw identifiers. This minimizes PII in the warehouse, reducing both risk and compliance scope. Deletion propagation means a deletion request must fan out to every store: the deletion event (via outbox/CDC, 38.2) reaches the warehouse, lake and derived tables so the user's data is erased or anonymized everywhere, with a documented process for backups (which cannot always be edited, so policy covers their retention and re-deletion on restore). The key realization is that deleting from production is necessary but not sufficient — the pipeline's copies must be handled too. One caution on hashing: an unsalted SHA-256 of an email is not anonymous, because anyone with a list of emails can hash them and match. Use a keyed hash (HMAC with a secret kept outside the warehouse; see Part 39 — Security, 39.13) or a random surrogate id from a mapping table, so that deleting the mapping row breaks the link. Section 38.11 shows the erasure SQL for a warehouse and for an Iceberg table in the lake.

Failure scenario

A regulator's audit sampled twenty erasure requests completed in the previous year and asked the company to prove each person was gone. Production: gone. Warehouse: gone, because a nightly job applied deletion events. But the lake still held the raw CDC Parquet files from before the erasure, untouched, because "raw is immutable", and an analyst's ad-hoc export in a shared S3 bucket held 14 of the 20 emails. The remediation took two months: a lake table format that supports row-level deletes, a retention policy of 35 days on raw CDC files with a modelled (masked) copy kept long-term, and a ban on unmanaged exports of PII. The lesson: "immutable raw data" and "right to erasure" conflict, and you must design the conflict away before an auditor finds it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deletion arrives before the data. A late CDC event for a user arrives after the erasure was applied and resurrects the row; keep a tombstone list of erased ids and filter on load.
  • Free text. Delivery notes and support messages contain phone numbers and addresses; column-level masking misses them.
  • Derived aggregates. Daily totals do not identify a person and can stay; a "top customers" table with names cannot.
  • Backups. Restoring a 30-day-old backup restores erased users; re-apply the erasure log after every restore (see Part 49 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery).
  • Kafka retention. Topics with long or infinite retention hold PII too; compacted topics keyed by user id can be tombstoned, plain topics must expire.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats PII as flowing through the whole pipeline, not sitting only in production, so privacy obligations follow it everywhere. They mask or drop PII as early in the pipeline as possible (data minimization), sending analytics only the pseudonymous ids and fields it actually needs, which shrinks both risk and the compliance scope of the warehouse. They design deletion propagation so a GDPR erasure fans out via the pipeline to every store (warehouse, lake, derived tables, with a backup policy), because deleting only from production leaves personal data lingering where regulators and users expect it gone. They coordinate this with the data team as part of the data contract (38.4), since privacy is a shared responsibility across the pipeline. This is the Part 39 and Part 85 privacy discipline extended into the data-engineering world.

Common mistakes

  • Deleting PII only from the production database, leaving it in the warehouse, lake and derived tables (non-compliant).
  • Sending raw PII into analytics that only needs aggregates, inflating risk and compliance scope.
  • No deletion-propagation mechanism, so erasure requests cannot be fully honored.
  • Ignoring backups in the deletion policy.
  • Treating privacy as production-only rather than pipeline-wide.

Interview questions

  1. Why must a GDPR deletion reach the data warehouse, not just the production database? The pipeline copies personal data into the warehouse, lake and derived tables; erasure must remove it everywhere, or you are non-compliant and the data persists.
  2. What is PII masking in a pipeline and why do it? Dropping or obscuring personal fields (use a hashed/pseudonymous id, drop email/name) as early as possible, so analytics gets what it needs without raw PII — data minimization that reduces risk and compliance scope.
  3. How do you propagate a deletion across the pipeline? Emit a deletion event (outbox/CDC) that fans out to the warehouse, lake and derived tables to delete or anonymize the data, with a documented policy for backups.

Practical exercise

Design the PII handling for an analytics pipeline: specify which fields of an order/user are masked or dropped before loading into the warehouse (using a pseudonymous id for per-user analysis), and design a deletion-propagation flow so a user's erasure request removes their data from production, the warehouse and derived tables. Acceptance criteria: analytics receives no raw PII it does not need, and a deletion request provably reaches every store, with a stated backup policy.

38.6 Building analytics features in the product

38.6.1 Pre-aggregated tables, materialized views and read models

Concept

Not all analytics needs a warehouse; often the product itself must show aggregated data — a seller's dashboard, a user's spending summary, counts and trends in the app. For these, you build analytics features inside your own system using pre-aggregated tables (summary tables updated incrementally), materialized views (stored query results PostgreSQL maintains), and read models (purpose-built denormalized tables optimized for a specific read). These give fast in-product analytics without hammering the OLTP tables or needing a full warehouse.

Why does it exist?

Computing a dashboard figure on the fly from raw OLTP tables (sum all of a seller's orders every time they open their dashboard) is slow and loads the production database (38.1). But the data team's warehouse is for internal analytics, not low-latency in-product features, and may be hours stale. So for product-facing analytics you precompute and store the aggregates close to the application, updating them incrementally, so the dashboard reads a small summary table instantly. This bridges the gap between "recompute from raw data every time" (too slow) and "use the warehouse" (not for in-product, low-latency reads).

Mental model

Imagine a cricket scoreboard. Nobody recounts every ball of the match when someone asks the score; the scorer adds runs as each ball is bowled and the board shows the running total. A pre-aggregated table is that scorer. A materialized view is a photographer who takes a picture of the full scorecard every ten minutes: cheap to look at, slightly out of date. A read model is a dedicated board for one audience, such as the batting averages screen, kept updated from the same scorer's notes.

How it works

-- Pre-aggregated summary table, updated incrementally (e.g. by the order-placed handler
-- or a CDC consumer), so the dashboard reads one small row instead of aggregating.
CREATE TABLE seller_daily_stats (
  seller_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  day         date NOT NULL,
  order_count bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  revenue_cents bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (seller_id, day)
);

-- On each order, upsert the aggregate (incremental maintenance):
INSERT INTO seller_daily_stats (seller_id, day, order_count, revenue_cents)
VALUES ($1, current_date, 1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (seller_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET order_count = seller_daily_stats.order_count + 1,
              revenue_cents = seller_daily_stats.revenue_cents + EXCLUDED.revenue_cents;

-- The dashboard query reads the small summary table by key -> instant, no scan.
SELECT day, order_count, revenue_cents FROM seller_daily_stats
 WHERE seller_id = $1 AND day > current_date - 30 ORDER BY day;
-- Materialized view: PostgreSQL stores the result of a query and you refresh it.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW product_sales_30d AS
SELECT product_id, count(*) AS sales, sum(total_cents) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
 WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days'
 GROUP BY product_id;
-- Refresh periodically (CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking reads):
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY product_sales_30d;

The techniques:

  • Pre-aggregated tables maintained incrementally (on each relevant write, or by a CDC consumer, 38.2): the dashboard reads a tiny summary instead of aggregating raw rows. This is the pattern used in the URL shortener's link_daily_stats (see Part 52 — System Design Case Studies, 52.1) and anywhere a count/sum is shown frequently.
  • Materialized views: PostgreSQL stores a query's result and you REFRESH it on a schedule; good for aggregates that can be a bit stale and are expensive to compute. REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking reads during refresh, but it requires a unique index on the view (here CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON product_sales_30d (product_id)), and it still recomputes the whole query every time; PostgreSQL has no built-in incremental refresh.
  • Read models (the CQRS idea; see Part 59 — Real-World Architecture Patterns, 59.19 and 59.21): a denormalized table shaped exactly for a specific read, kept in sync from the write side, so the read is a simple fast lookup.

The common thread is precomputing and storing the answer so the read is cheap, trading some staleness and some write-time or refresh work for fast reads — the same read-optimization and caching philosophy as Part 26, applied with database structures.

NestJS example

The upsert in the SQL above double-counts if the same order event is processed twice, and CDC and Kafka both deliver at least once. The fix is to record which orders have been counted, in the same transaction as the increment.

// seller-stats.service.ts -- idempotent incremental aggregation from an order.paid event
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export interface OrderPaidEvent {
  orderId: string;
  sellerId: string;
  totalCents: number;
  paidAt: string; // ISO timestamp from the source, not "now"
}

@Injectable()
export class SellerStatsService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async applyOrderPaid(evt: OrderPaidEvent): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      // 1. Claim the order. If it was already counted, the insert does nothing.
      const claimed: unknown[] = await manager.query(
        `INSERT INTO seller_stats_applied (order_id) VALUES ($1)
         ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING order_id`,
        [evt.orderId],
      );
      if (claimed.length === 0) return; // duplicate delivery: skip

      // 2. Increment the bucket for the business day the order was PAID (event time).
      await manager.query(
        `INSERT INTO seller_daily_stats (seller_id, day, order_count, revenue_cents)
         VALUES ($1, ($2::timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date, 1, $3)
         ON CONFLICT (seller_id, day) DO UPDATE
           SET order_count   = seller_daily_stats.order_count + 1,
               revenue_cents = seller_daily_stats.revenue_cents + EXCLUDED.revenue_cents`,
        [evt.sellerId, evt.paidAt, evt.totalCents],
      );
    });
  }
}

Two decisions in that code matter more than the syntax: the dedupe row and the increment commit together (so a crash between them cannot count twice or lose a count), and the day is computed from the event's paidAt in the business time zone, not from current_date when the consumer happens to run, so a consumer that falls an hour behind at midnight still puts orders on the right day.

Failure scenario

A seller dashboard showed revenue 3–4% higher than the payout report every month, and sellers noticed before engineers did. The incremental aggregate was updated by a Kafka consumer that used the SQL upsert without a dedupe table. Every consumer-group rebalance (deploys, autoscaling) re-delivered a few hundred uncommitted messages, and each was counted again. Reconciliation would have caught it on day one; there was none. The fix was the idempotent version above, a nightly job that recomputed the last 35 days of seller_daily_stats from orders and overwrote them, and a reconciliation alert comparing the two. The lesson: an incremental counter fed by an at-least-once stream drifts upward unless it is idempotent, and recomputing a trailing window from the source is the cheap way to heal any drift you missed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Refunds and cancellations. An increment-only table never goes down; apply negative deltas for refunds, keyed by refund id for idempotency.
  • Hot rows. A seller with 50 orders per second turns (seller_id, day) into a hot row with lock contention; buffer increments in Redis or batch them per second (see Part 59 — Real-World Architecture Patterns, 59.23).
  • Materialized view refresh cost. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY on a 30-day join over 40 million rows can take minutes and heavy I/O; schedule it, and do not refresh more often than it takes to run.
  • Dedupe table growth. seller_stats_applied grows forever; partition it by month and drop partitions older than the replay window.
  • Time-zone boundaries. Sellers in different time zones see different "days"; store UTC buckets at hour grain if you must serve several zones.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior builds in-product analytics with precomputed structures — incrementally maintained summary tables, materialized views, read models — so dashboards read small, fast aggregates instead of scanning OLTP tables on every view, keeping product analytics fast without touching production's transactional performance or needing the warehouse. They choose the technique by freshness need and cost: incremental summary tables for real-time counts that must be current, materialized views for expensive aggregates that tolerate periodic refresh, read models for a specific hot read. They right-size: for in-product features these structures beat both naive on-the-fly aggregation (too slow, loads production) and a full warehouse (not for low-latency in-product reads, and operationally heavy). They keep the aggregates correct via idempotent incremental updates or scheduled refreshes, and reconcile them against the source (38.4) so a summary table cannot silently drift from reality.

Common mistakes

  • Computing dashboard aggregates on the fly from raw OLTP tables every view, loading production and being slow.
  • Using the warehouse for low-latency in-product analytics (wrong tool, too stale, heavy).
  • Non-idempotent incremental aggregation that double-counts.
  • Never refreshing or reconciling precomputed structures, letting them drift from the source.
  • Adding a full warehouse when materialized views in PostgreSQL would serve the product feature.

Interview questions

  1. How do you build a fast in-product analytics feature without hammering the OLTP tables? Precompute aggregates into summary tables (maintained incrementally), materialized views, or read models, so the dashboard reads a small precomputed result instead of scanning raw rows.
  2. When do you use a materialized view versus an incrementally maintained summary table? A materialized view for expensive aggregates that tolerate periodic refresh staleness; an incremental summary table for figures that must be current and are updated on each relevant write.
  3. Why not use the data warehouse for in-product analytics? It is built for internal analytics, not low-latency product reads, and is often hours stale; in-product features need fast, fresh reads from structures close to the application.
  4. How do you keep precomputed aggregates correct? Use idempotent incremental updates (or scheduled refreshes) and reconcile against the source so the summary cannot silently drift.

Practical exercise

Build a seller dashboard analytics feature: an incrementally maintained seller_daily_stats table updated on each order (idempotently), a materialized view for a 30-day top-products aggregate refreshed on a schedule, and a dashboard query that reads these instead of scanning the orders tables. Add a reconciliation check comparing the summary table's revenue against the raw orders for a day. Acceptance criteria: the dashboard reads precomputed structures (no raw-table scans), the incremental update does not double-count on retries, and reconciliation would catch drift.

38.7 Change data capture in practice: logical replication, Debezium and Kafka Connect

Concept

Section 38.2.1 explained what CDC is. This section is the operator's view: the PostgreSQL settings and objects CDC depends on (logical decoding, publications, replication slots), how Debezium runs as a Kafka Connect connector, how the initial copy of existing data (the snapshot) works, how source schema changes flow through, and what you must monitor so CDC never becomes the thing that takes the production database down.

Why does it exist?

CDC looks like "install Debezium, get events". In production it is a long-lived consumer attached to your primary database, with the power to fill its disk (an unread slot keeps WAL forever), bloat its tables (a long snapshot transaction blocks vacuum), and silently stop (a failed task produces no errors in the application). The mechanics in this section exist so a backend engineer can set it up safely, review the connector config like any other production change, and recognize the three or four failure modes that cause nearly every CDC incident.

Mental model

Imagine the WAL as a conveyor belt of every change, running past the database's back door. A publication is a list on the door saying which tables' boxes may leave. A replication slot is a named bookmark that tells PostgreSQL "this reader has taken everything up to here; keep everything after it". PostgreSQL never throws away belt contents past the oldest bookmark. Debezium is the courier who reads from its bookmark, carries each box to Kafka, and then moves the bookmark forward. If the courier goes home without telling anyone, the belt piles up behind the bookmark until the room is full.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as OrderService
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant Slot as ReplicationSlot
    participant DBZ as Debezium
    participant K as Kafka
    App->>PG: COMMIT update orders
    PG->>PG: write WAL record
    DBZ->>Slot: stream changes since confirmed LSN
    Slot-->>DBZ: decoded change via pgoutput
    DBZ->>K: produce event to orders.public.orders
    K-->>DBZ: ack
    DBZ->>K: commit offset with LSN to offsets topic
    DBZ->>Slot: confirm flush LSN
    PG->>PG: recycle WAL older than restart LSN
  1. wal_level = logical makes PostgreSQL write enough information in the WAL to reconstruct row changes, not just physical page changes.
  2. A publication (CREATE PUBLICATION) names the tables whose changes are exposed. Since PostgreSQL 15 it can also restrict columns and filter rows.
  3. A logical replication slot using the built-in pgoutput plugin decodes the WAL for that publication and remembers how far the consumer has confirmed (confirmed_flush_lsn). WAL older than the slot's restart_lsn can be recycled; WAL newer must be kept.
  4. Debezium, running as a source connector inside a Kafka Connect cluster (a separate JVM service that runs connectors, stores their offsets in Kafka topics and restarts failed tasks), first takes a snapshot of existing rows, then streams changes from the slot.
  5. Each change becomes a Kafka record on a topic named <topic.prefix>.<schema>.<table>, keyed by the row's primary key, so all changes to one order land in one partition in commit order.
  6. After Kafka acknowledges the records, Connect commits the source offset (which contains the LSN) and Debezium confirms that LSN to the slot, letting PostgreSQL recycle WAL.

PostgreSQL example

-- Server settings (self-managed). On Amazon RDS set the parameter rds.logical_replication = 1
-- in the DB parameter group instead; both require a restart.
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = 'logical';
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_replication_slots = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_senders = 10;
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_slot_wal_keep_size = '100GB';  -- PG13+: a dead consumer cannot fill the disk

-- A dedicated, least-privilege role. On RDS use: GRANT rds_replication TO debezium;
CREATE ROLE debezium WITH LOGIN REPLICATION;     -- set the password with \password, from the secret manager
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO debezium;
GRANT SELECT ON orders, order_items, payments, refunds TO debezium;  -- needed for snapshots

-- Helper tables Debezium writes to (heartbeats) and reads from (signals)
CREATE TABLE debezium_heartbeat (id int PRIMARY KEY, ts timestamptz NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE debezium_signal (id varchar(64) PRIMARY KEY, type varchar(32) NOT NULL, data text);
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE ON debezium_heartbeat TO debezium;
GRANT SELECT ON debezium_signal TO debezium;

-- Create the publication yourself so the connector does not need table-owner rights.
-- PG15+ column list: keep raw PII columns out of the stream entirely.
CREATE PUBLICATION dbz_orders FOR TABLE
  orders (id, customer_id, seller_id, status, currency, total_cents, created_at, updated_at, paid_at),
  order_items, payments, refunds, debezium_heartbeat, debezium_signal;

-- Optional: full before-images for updates and deletes (larger WAL, roughly 1.3-2x for these tables).
-- Only on tables WITHOUT a column list: with a column list, REPLICA IDENTITY FULL would require every
-- column to be listed, and UPDATEs on orders would fail with "column list ... does not cover the replica identity".
ALTER TABLE payments REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;

Monitor every slot. This one query is worth an alert:

SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn))        AS retained_wal,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS unconfirmed,
       pg_size_pretty(safe_wal_size)                                             AS safe_before_loss
  FROM pg_replication_slots
 WHERE slot_type = 'logical';
 slot_name  | active | wal_status | retained_wal | unconfirmed | safe_before_loss
------------+--------+------------+--------------+-------------+------------------
 dbz_orders | t      | reserved   | 142 MB       | 3104 kB     | 99 GB
 old_search | f      | extended   | 61 GB        | 61 GB       | 38 GB

The second row is the incident waiting to happen: an abandoned slot (active = f) from a search-sync experiment holding 61 GB. wal_status moves from reserved to extended to unreserved and finally lost, at which point the slot is useless and the consumer must re-snapshot. If nobody owns it, SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('old_search'); and move on.

Practical example: the Debezium connector

Kafka Connect is configured over REST. This is the full config for the orders connector (Debezium 2.x/3.x property names), applied with PUT /connectors/orders-cdc/config:

{
  "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
  "tasks.max": "1",
  "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
  "database.hostname": "orders-db.internal.example.com",
  "database.port": "5432",
  "database.user": "debezium",
  "database.password": "${file:/opt/connect/secrets/orders-db.properties:password}",
  "database.dbname": "orders",
  "topic.prefix": "orders",
  "slot.name": "dbz_orders",
  "publication.name": "dbz_orders",
  "publication.autocreate.mode": "disabled",
  "table.include.list": "public.orders,public.order_items,public.payments,public.refunds,public.debezium_heartbeat,public.debezium_signal",
  "column.exclude.list": "public.orders.customer_email,public.orders.shipping_phone,public.orders.shipping_address",
  "snapshot.mode": "initial",
  "signal.data.collection": "public.debezium_signal",
  "incremental.snapshot.chunk.size": "5000",
  "heartbeat.interval.ms": "10000",
  "heartbeat.action.query": "INSERT INTO debezium_heartbeat (id, ts) VALUES (1, now()) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ts = EXCLUDED.ts",
  "decimal.handling.mode": "precise",
  "tombstones.on.delete": "true",
  "key.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
  "key.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry.internal:8081",
  "value.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
  "value.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry.internal:8081"
}

The lines that matter in review:

  • database.password uses Kafka's built-in FileConfigProvider (enabled in the worker with config.providers=file), so the secret is a mounted file from the secret manager, not text in the REST call or in Connect's config topic.
  • publication.autocreate.mode: disabled means the connector uses the publication you created, with its column list, rather than creating one for all tables. column.exclude.list repeats the PII exclusion on the Debezium side, so the event schema agrees with what the publication sends and a later publication change cannot leak those columns by accident.
  • heartbeat.* keeps the slot advancing even when the captured tables are quiet but other databases on the same server are busy; without it, the slot's restart_lsn can fall far behind on a low-traffic database and retain WAL.
  • signal.data.collection enables incremental snapshots on demand, which matter more than the initial snapshot (failure scenario below).
  • Avro with a schema registry gives every event a registered schema, so downstream sinks (Parquet files, 38.12) and the compatibility checks in 38.11 work.

NestJS example

A NestJS service that maintains a support-agent read model from the order change stream. The guard on source_lsn makes it idempotent and safe against reordering after a replay.

// order-changes.consumer.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Consumer, Kafka } from 'kafkajs';
import { SchemaRegistry } from '@kafkajs/confluent-schema-registry';

interface OrderRow { id: string; customer_id: string; status: string; total_cents: number; updated_at: string }
interface ChangeEvent { op: 'c' | 'u' | 'd' | 'r'; before: OrderRow | null; after: OrderRow | null; source: { lsn: number } }

@Injectable()
export class OrderChangesConsumer implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderChangesConsumer.name);
  private consumer!: Consumer;
  private registry!: SchemaRegistry;

  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService, private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'support-read-model', brokers: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('KAFKA_BROKERS').split(',') });
    this.registry = new SchemaRegistry({ host: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL') });
    this.consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: 'support-read-model' });
    await this.consumer.connect();
    await this.consumer.subscribe({ topic: 'orders.public.orders', fromBeginning: true });
    await this.consumer.run({
      eachMessage: async ({ message }) => {
        if (!message.value) return;                        // tombstone after a delete: nothing to do
        const evt = (await this.registry.decode(message.value)) as ChangeEvent;
        await this.apply(evt);                             // throw -> kafkajs retries, offset not committed
      },
    });
  }

  private async apply(evt: ChangeEvent): Promise<void> {
    if (evt.op === 'd' && evt.before) {
      await this.dataSource.query(
        `DELETE FROM support_order_view WHERE order_id = $1 AND source_lsn < $2`, [evt.before.id, evt.source.lsn]);
      return;
    }
    const row = evt.after!;
    // Upsert only if this event is newer than what we stored: replays and duplicates become no-ops.
    await this.dataSource.query(
      `INSERT INTO support_order_view (order_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, updated_at, source_lsn)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6)
       ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE
         SET customer_id = EXCLUDED.customer_id, status = EXCLUDED.status, total_cents = EXCLUDED.total_cents,
             updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at, source_lsn = EXCLUDED.source_lsn
       WHERE support_order_view.source_lsn < EXCLUDED.source_lsn`,
      [row.id, row.customer_id, row.status, row.total_cents, row.updated_at, evt.source.lsn]);
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> {
    await this.consumer?.disconnect();                   // commit offsets and leave the group cleanly
  }
}

One subtlety: all changes from one transaction share the commit's ordering but each row change has its own LSN, and rows of the same order always share a partition because the record key is the primary key. The LSN guard therefore works per row. If you need "the whole transaction or nothing" downstream, read the outbox instead (38.2.1), where one event carries the business fact.

How schema changes flow through

pgoutput does not stream DDL statements. When a table's structure changes, the next row change is preceded by a relation message describing the new columns, and Debezium registers a new schema version for the topic. What that does downstream depends on the change:

Source change What the stream does Safe? What to do
Add nullable column New optional field appears from the next change Yes (backward compatible) Announce it; consumers ignore unknown fields
Add NOT NULL DEFAULT x column New field, existing rows only show it when next updated Mostly Backfill reads need the default; document it
Drop column Field disappears Breaks consumers that read it Expand/contract (see Part 23 — Database Migrations, 23.5); deprecate first
Rename column Looks like drop plus add Breaking Add new, dual-write, migrate consumers, drop old
integer to bigint Avro int to long Yes (type promotion) None
text to integer Incompatible type Breaking; registry rejects it New column instead
New table Nothing, until added to the publication n/a ALTER PUBLICATION ... ADD TABLE, add to include list, incremental snapshot

An incremental snapshot is started by inserting a signal row; Debezium reads the table in primary-key chunks while streaming continues, without a long-running transaction:

INSERT INTO debezium_signal (id, type, data)
VALUES ('snap-refunds-2026-11-05', 'execute-snapshot',
        '{"data-collections": ["public.refunds"], "type": "incremental"}');

Production scenario

Orders database: PostgreSQL 17 on a db.r6g.2xlarge, 700 million orders rows, 2.1 billion order_items. The connector runs on a three-worker Kafka Connect cluster (2 vCPU, 4 GB each) on ECS, producing to a 3-broker Kafka cluster. Steady state: about 250 change events per second, 1,800 per second during sales, p99 capture lag under 1 second, retained WAL under 300 MB. A full incremental snapshot of orders at 5,000-row chunks runs at about 25,000 rows per second, so roughly 8 hours, while normal streaming continues. Alerts: retained WAL over 5 GB, slot inactive for more than 5 minutes, connector or task not RUNNING, heartbeat older than 1 minute in Kafka, schema-registry compatibility failure.

Failure scenario

The first CDC rollout used snapshot.mode: initial on the 700-million-row orders table. A blocking initial snapshot reads all rows inside one long REPEATABLE READ transaction so it sees a consistent picture. It ran for 14 hours. For those 14 hours the xmin horizon was pinned, autovacuum could not remove any dead tuples created after the snapshot began, and the busiest tables bloated: orders grew 35%, index scans slowed, p99 checkout latency rose from 120 ms to 260 ms by the afternoon. The team cancelled the snapshot at hour 14, ran VACUUM to recover, and restarted with snapshot.mode: no_data (named never in older Debezium releases) plus an incremental snapshot via the signal table, which reads in small chunks with short transactions. The lesson: a snapshot is a long-running reader on your primary, and long-running transactions are one of PostgreSQL's oldest foot-guns (see Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals, 18.8). Prefer incremental snapshots on large tables, and snapshot at night.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Abandoned or inactive slot fills the disk. Cap with max_slot_wal_keep_size; alert on retained WAL; drop slots nobody owns.
  • Slot lost after failover. Before PostgreSQL 17 logical slots are not on standbys; after failover, re-create the slot and incremental-snapshot. On 17, create the slot with failover enabled and set sync_replication_slots on the standby, then test it.
  • Wrong user privileges on managed databases. RDS has no superuser; the REPLICATION attribute is replaced by the rds_replication role.
  • Connector restarts replay events. Up to the last committed offset; at-least-once by design. Consumers dedupe by LSN or upsert by key.
  • Huge transaction. A one-statement backfill of 30 million rows arrives as 30 million events after the commit; batch backfills into small transactions (see Part 23 — Database Migrations, 23.7).
  • TRUNCATE. Captured as a truncate event only if the publication publishes truncates; many sinks ignore it. Forbid TRUNCATE on CDC tables.
  • Unchanged TOAST values. Updates that do not touch a large column send a placeholder (__debezium_unavailable_value); never write it over the stored value.
  • Time and money types. numeric without decimal.handling.mode: precise (or string) can lose precision as a double; store money as integer cents anyway.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the CDC connector as part of the database's production surface, reviewed and monitored like the database itself. Before enabling it they ask: who owns this slot, what is the WAL cap, what alerts fire if it stops, how will we snapshot 700 million rows without a 14-hour transaction, which columns are we deliberately not publishing, and what happens on failover? They create the publication by hand with a column list rather than letting a tool capture every table. They keep consumers idempotent with an LSN guard or a key upsert, and they route breaking schema changes through expand/contract and the data contract, because CDC turns the table schema into a public API. They also know when not to use it: for business events that other services act on, the outbox (read by the same CDC machinery) is the better contract.

Common mistakes

  • No max_slot_wal_keep_size and no slot alert; one dead connector fills the primary's disk.
  • Blocking initial snapshot of a huge table during business hours.
  • Letting the connector auto-create a publication for all tables, streaming PII and internal tables no one asked for.
  • Putting the database password in the connector JSON sent over REST.
  • Renaming a column on a CDC'd table without telling the data team.
  • Assuming exactly-once; writing consumers that blindly insert.

Interview questions

  1. What is a logical replication slot and why can it take down a database? It is a server-side bookmark for a logical decoding consumer; PostgreSQL retains all WAL after the slot's restart LSN, so an inactive consumer causes unbounded WAL retention until the disk fills. Mitigate with max_slot_wal_keep_size and alerts on pg_replication_slots. Follow-up: what happens when the cap is hit? The slot becomes lost and the consumer must re-snapshot.
  2. How does Debezium take the initial copy of a large table, and what is the risk? A blocking snapshot reads all rows in one long repeatable-read transaction, pinning the xmin horizon and blocking vacuum; incremental snapshots read in primary-key chunks while streaming continues.
  3. What is a publication and why create it yourself? The set of tables (and since PostgreSQL 15, columns and row filters) exposed to logical decoding; creating it by hand limits what leaves the database and avoids granting the connector ownership rights.
  4. How do you make a CDC consumer idempotent and order-safe? Upsert by primary key with a guard that only applies an event whose LSN is newer than the stored one; deletes check the LSN too.
  5. Which source schema changes are breaking for CDC consumers? Drops, renames and incompatible type changes; adding nullable columns and widening integer types are safe. Breaking changes go through expand/contract and the data contract.
  6. What does the heartbeat setting do? Periodically produces an event (optionally by writing to a heartbeat table) so the slot's confirmed position keeps moving even when captured tables are idle, preventing WAL retention on low-traffic databases.

Practical exercise

With Docker Compose, run PostgreSQL 17, Kafka, a schema registry and Kafka Connect with the Debezium PostgreSQL connector. Create the publication with a column list, deploy the connector config above, and build the NestJS read-model consumer. Then: stop Connect for 10 minutes while a script writes 100,000 updates and watch retained_wal grow; restart and watch it fall; add a nullable column and observe the new schema version; trigger an incremental snapshot of refunds with a signal row. Acceptance criteria: the slot query shows retention rising and recovering; the read model ends identical to the source table after replaying the topic twice from the beginning; no PII column appears in any topic.

38.8 Batch pipelines in practice: ELT models, idempotent loads and backfills

Concept

Once raw change events land in the warehouse (38.12 shows how), batch ELT turns them into tables people can trust. The common shape is three layers of SQL models: staging (clean and deduplicate raw data, one row per source row's latest version), facts and dimensions (business entities such as fct_orders and dim_customers), and marts (aggregates for a specific use, such as mart_daily_revenue). Tools like dbt let you write each model as a SELECT with dependencies declared through ref(), and the tool builds them in order; plain SQL run by a scheduler works on the same principles.

Why does it exist?

Raw CDC data has every version of every row, deletes as flags, events in technical units (cents, UTC, LSNs) and duplicates from at-least-once delivery. Analysts should not repeat that cleanup in every query, each slightly differently, producing five versions of revenue. Layered models put each rule (dedupe, time zone, what counts as revenue) in exactly one place, under version control and code review, with tests, and with an orchestrator that knows the dependency order.

How it works

flowchart LR
    rawo["raw.orders_cdc"] --> stgo["stg_orders"]
    rawi["raw.order_items_cdc"] --> stgi["stg_order_items"]
    rawr["raw.refunds_cdc"] --> stgr["stg_refunds"]
    stgo --> fo["fct_orders"]
    stgi --> fo
    stgr --> fr["fct_refunds"]
    fo --> mdr["mart_daily_revenue"]
    fr --> mdr
    mdr --> dash["Finance dashboard"]
  1. Staging picks the latest version of each row by LSN and drops deleted rows.
  2. Facts apply business rules: which statuses count, which time zone defines the business day, how refunds net out.
  3. Marts aggregate to the grain the dashboard needs and are rebuilt for a trailing window so late refunds land on the right day.
  4. Tests run after each model: uniqueness of keys, not-null, accepted status values, referential integrity, and freshness of sources.
  5. The orchestrator runs the graph on a schedule, one run per data interval, with retries, a concurrency limit of one run at a time, and gates for input completeness (38.2.2).

PostgreSQL example (warehouse SQL, dbt-style)

-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql : latest version of each order from raw CDC rows
with ranked as (
  select
    id                                  as order_id,
    customer_id, seller_id, status, currency, total_cents,
    cast(created_at as timestamp)       as created_at_utc,
    cast(paid_at as timestamp)          as paid_at_utc,
    __deleted                           as is_deleted,
    __source_lsn                        as source_lsn,
    row_number() over (partition by id order by __source_lsn desc) as rn
  from {{ source('raw', 'orders_cdc') }}
)
select * from ranked
where rn = 1 and not coalesce(is_deleted, false)
-- models/marts/mart_daily_revenue.sql : one row per business day and currency
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key=['business_date', 'currency'],
          incremental_strategy='merge') }}
with paid as (
  select date(convert_timezone('UTC', 'Asia/Kolkata', paid_at_utc)) as business_date,
         currency, total_cents
  from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
  where status in ('paid', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'refunded', 'partially_refunded')
), refunds as (
  select date(convert_timezone('UTC', 'Asia/Kolkata', refunded_at_utc)) as business_date,
         currency, amount_cents
  from {{ ref('fct_refunds') }}
)
select d.business_date, d.currency,
       count(*)                                         as orders,
       sum(d.total_cents)                               as gross_cents,
       coalesce(max(r.refund_cents), 0)                 as refund_cents,
       sum(d.total_cents) - coalesce(max(r.refund_cents), 0) as net_cents
from paid d
left join (select business_date, currency, sum(amount_cents) as refund_cents
             from refunds group by 1, 2) r
       on r.business_date = d.business_date and r.currency = d.currency
{% if is_incremental() %}
where d.business_date >= dateadd(day, -7, current_date)  -- recompute a trailing week for late refunds
{% endif %}
group by d.business_date, d.currency

convert_timezone and dateadd are Snowflake/Redshift functions; in BigQuery you would write DATE(paid_at_utc, 'Asia/Kolkata') and DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY). dbt adapters hide some of those differences through macros, but the business rules (statuses, time zone, refund netting, seven-day lookback) are the part that matters.

Tests and source freshness are declared next to the models:

# models/schema.yml
version: 2
sources:
  - name: raw
    loaded_at_field: _loaded_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: { count: 30, period: minute }
      error_after: { count: 2, period: hour }
    tables:
      - name: orders_cdc
      - name: refunds_cdc
models:
  - name: stg_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled', 'refunded', 'partially_refunded']
  - name: mart_daily_revenue
    columns:
      - name: net_cents
        tests: [not_null]

Without dbt, the same idempotent load is a transaction that replaces one interval:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM mart_daily_revenue WHERE business_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-10-29' AND DATE '2026-11-04';
INSERT INTO mart_daily_revenue (business_date, currency, orders, gross_cents, refund_cents, net_cents)
SELECT ... FROM fct_orders ... WHERE business_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-10-29' AND DATE '2026-11-04' GROUP BY 1, 2;
COMMIT;

Rerun it any number of times and the result is the same, which is the only property that makes retries and backfills safe.

Choosing how to orchestrate

Option Good for Weak at
Warehouse scheduled queries 5–20 simple models, one team Dependencies, tests, backfills
cron or Kubernetes CronJob running SQL Small teams that already run Kubernetes Dependency graph, retries per step, visibility
dbt plus a scheduler (dbt Cloud, or a CronJob) Most analytics teams: SQL models, tests, lineage Non-SQL steps (API extracts, ML)
Airflow or Dagster Many pipelines mixing extracts, SQL, ML, file drops Operating another platform
Stream processor (38.10) Seconds-fresh results Complex joins over history, cheap backfills

Production scenario

The finance marts above run hourly (for an intraday view) and nightly at 01:30 local time with a seven-day lookback. A full rebuild of mart_daily_revenue over five years, needed when the definition of "revenue" changed to exclude gift cards, scanned about 90 GB and took 7 minutes on a medium warehouse. Tests run on every build; a failing accepted_values test on status (a new on_hold status appeared) stopped the nightly run at 01:42, the on-call data engineer added the value with a mapping, and the marts were published at 02:30, well inside the 06:00 SLA.

Failure scenario

A product engineer added status = 'payment_review' for orders held by the fraud model. The fact model's where status in (...) list did not include it, so those orders vanished from revenue until they cleared, and on a heavy fraud-review day the dashboard dropped 6%. There was no accepted_values test, so nothing failed. The fix was the test above (new statuses now fail the build loudly instead of silently disappearing) and a line in the orders team's contract: "new status values are announced one release ahead". The lesson: business rules expressed as allow-lists need a test that fails when the world grows a new value.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deduplication by the wrong column. Ordering by updated_at instead of LSN picks the wrong row when two updates share a timestamp.
  • Merge without a unique key. An incremental model with no unique_key appends duplicates on every run.
  • Full refresh of a huge table by accident. dbt run --full-refresh on a 2 TB fact table costs real money; restrict it in production.
  • Lookback too short. Chargebacks arrive up to 120 days later; decide which numbers are final and when.
  • Mixed currencies. Summing INR and USD cents is meaningless; aggregate per currency or convert with a dated rate table.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees the staging model as the place where the backend's technical reality (LSNs, delete flags, UTC, cents) is translated once, and they help write it, because they know what the source columns mean. They insist on idempotent loads by interval, a trailing recompute window sized to how late facts really arrive, and tests that fail loudly when the source grows a new enum value. They right-size the orchestration: dbt plus a scheduler for SQL, a full workflow engine only when there are genuinely many non-SQL steps.

Common mistakes

  • INSERT-only loads that double on retry.
  • Business rules copied into dashboard queries instead of a model.
  • No tests on status values or keys.
  • Computing "yesterday" in UTC for a business that runs in another time zone.
  • Backfills done by hand-editing tables rather than rerunning models.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make a daily batch load idempotent? Each run owns an interval and replaces it (delete-then-insert in a transaction, or MERGE by a unique key), so reruns produce the same result.
  2. Why recompute a trailing window instead of only yesterday? Late facts (refunds, chargebacks, late CDC delivery) change past days; a trailing recompute puts them on the right day.
  3. What tests would you put on an orders staging model? Unique and not-null primary key, accepted status values, relationships to customers, freshness of the raw source, and a reconciliation against the source.
  4. When is Airflow worth it over dbt plus cron? When pipelines mix many non-SQL steps (API extracts, file transfers, ML training) with dependencies and backfills across them.

Practical exercise

Write stg_orders, fct_orders, fct_refunds and mart_daily_revenue against a raw CDC table with duplicates, deletes and out-of-order versions. Add the tests and freshness checks above. Acceptance criteria: running the build twice yields identical marts; inserting a new status value fails the build; a refund inserted for a date six days ago changes that day's net_cents on the next run.

38.9 Warehouses and lakes in practice: Parquet, table formats and the big three

Concept

Section 38.3.1 explained why columnar, partitioned storage makes aggregates cheap. This section shows what that looks like in real systems: how a Parquet file is laid out, what a table format (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake) adds on top of plain files, the DDL for partitioning and clustering in BigQuery, Redshift and Snowflake, and how each one charges you, because the pricing model decides how you should write queries.

How it works — inside a Parquet file

orders-2026-11-04-0001.parquet  (about 256 MB)
  Row group 1 (about 128 MB, roughly 4 million rows)
    Column chunk: order_id     -> pages, dictionary encoded
    Column chunk: status       -> pages, dictionary + run-length encoded (7 distinct values)
    Column chunk: total_cents  -> pages, plain/delta encoded; min=100, max=9,850,000
    Column chunk: paid_at      -> pages; min=2026-11-04T00:00:02, max=2026-11-04T09:12:40
  Row group 2 ...
  Footer: schema + per-row-group, per-column statistics (min, max, null count)

A reader opens the footer first. For WHERE paid_at >= '2026-11-04T10:00' it can skip row group 1 entirely because its paid_at maximum is 09:12. For SELECT sum(total_cents) it reads only the total_cents chunks. Low-cardinality columns like status shrink to almost nothing with dictionary plus run-length encoding. That is why the same orders data is about 24 GB as PostgreSQL heap and around 3–5 GB as Parquet.

Plain Parquet files in S3 have no transactions: a reader can see half-written data, there is no DELETE, and "the table" is whatever files happen to be in a prefix. Table formats add a metadata layer that tracks which files make up each version (snapshot) of the table. Iceberg and Delta give you atomic commits, schema evolution, row-level DELETE and MERGE (needed for CDC upserts and GDPR erasure), time travel, and, in Iceberg's case, hidden partitioning (you partition by day(commit_ts) and readers filter on commit_ts without knowing the layout).

PostgreSQL example (warehouse DDL)

The same fct_orders table in the three common warehouses and in an Iceberg lake table:

-- BigQuery: partition by day, cluster by common filters, refuse unpartitioned scans
CREATE TABLE analytics.fct_orders (
  order_id STRING NOT NULL, customer_key STRING, seller_id STRING, status STRING,
  currency STRING, total_cents INT64, paid_at TIMESTAMP, business_date DATE
)
PARTITION BY business_date
CLUSTER BY seller_id, status
OPTIONS (require_partition_filter = TRUE);

-- Amazon Redshift: distribute rows to co-locate joins, sort for range filters
CREATE TABLE analytics.fct_orders (
  order_id VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL, customer_key VARCHAR(64), seller_id VARCHAR(36), status VARCHAR(24),
  currency CHAR(3), total_cents BIGINT, paid_at TIMESTAMP, business_date DATE
)
DISTSTYLE KEY DISTKEY (customer_key)
SORTKEY (business_date);

-- Snowflake: micro-partitions are automatic; a clustering key helps very large tables
CREATE TABLE analytics.fct_orders (
  order_id VARCHAR NOT NULL, customer_key VARCHAR, seller_id VARCHAR, status VARCHAR,
  currency VARCHAR(3), total_cents NUMBER(18,0), paid_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ, business_date DATE
)
CLUSTER BY (business_date, seller_id);

-- Iceberg table in S3, created through Amazon Athena (supports DELETE, MERGE, time travel)
CREATE TABLE lake.orders_cdc (
  order_id string, customer_key string, status string, currency string,
  total_cents bigint, source_lsn bigint, is_deleted boolean, commit_ts timestamp
)
PARTITIONED BY (day(commit_ts))
LOCATION 's3://acme-lake/orders_cdc/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('table_type' = 'ICEBERG');

Choosing and paying

BigQuery Snowflake Redshift Athena or Trino on an S3 lake PostgreSQL plus read replica
Model Serverless Virtual warehouses you size and suspend Provisioned cluster or Serverless Serverless query over files Your existing database
Main cost driver Bytes scanned (on-demand about $6.25 per TiB) or reserved slots Credits per second while a warehouse runs (XS = 1 credit/hour) Node-hours, or RPU-hours on Serverless Bytes scanned (about $5 per TB) Instance hours
Write queries to Prune partitions, select few columns Suspend idle warehouses, size per workload Pick DISTKEY/SORTKEY well Partition and compact files Keep aggregates small
Sweet spot Spiky analytics, little ops Many teams, mixed workloads AWS shops with steady load Huge raw history, cheap storage Under ~100 GB analytics, one team

A pragmatic path for a growing product: start with materialized views and summary tables in PostgreSQL (38.6); add a read replica for analysts; move to a warehouse fed by CDC when analytics data passes roughly 100–200 GB, when queries need history the primary should not keep, or when more than one team builds on the data. Keep raw CDC in an Iceberg lake when you need cheap long-term history and replay.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Iceberg delete is not physical erasure yet. DELETE writes a new snapshot; old snapshots still reference files that contain the row until snapshots are expired and orphan files removed (Athena: VACUUM; Spark: the expire_snapshots procedure).
  • Function on the partition column. WHERE DATE(paid_at) = ... when the table is partitioned by business_date prunes nothing.
  • Redshift skew. A DISTKEY on a column where one value is 30% of rows puts 30% of the work on one slice.
  • Suspended warehouse latency. A Snowflake warehouse auto-resumes in seconds, but a dashboard that wakes it every minute keeps it billing all day.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads the pricing page before the architecture diagram, because in a warehouse the bill is the performance metric. They ask what the dominant query shape is (filters by date, by seller), and they design partitioning and clustering for it, then enforce partition filters for anyone who forgets. They prefer the smallest system that fits: PostgreSQL first, a managed warehouse when the data or the number of teams outgrows it, a lake with a table format when history and replay matter.

Interview questions

  1. Why can a query engine skip most of a Parquet file? Row-group statistics in the footer let it skip row groups whose min/max cannot match the filter, and columnar layout lets it read only the needed columns.
  2. What does a table format like Iceberg add over plain Parquet? Atomic snapshots, schema evolution, row-level deletes and merges, time travel and hidden partitioning.
  3. How does pricing change how you write warehouse queries? Per-byte pricing rewards pruning partitions and selecting few columns; per-compute-time pricing rewards suspending idle compute and sizing warehouses per workload.

Practical exercise

Load one month of synthetic orders (10 million rows) into Parquet with daily partitions and query it with DuckDB or Athena. Compare bytes scanned for SELECT * against one day versus SELECT sum(total_cents) against the same day. Acceptance criteria: you report bytes scanned for both and explain the difference using row groups and column chunks.

38.10 Stream processing in practice: Kafka Streams and Flink

Concept

Section 38.3.2 introduced windows, watermarks and late events. This section maps them onto the two common engines. Kafka Streams is a Java library you embed in your own service: it reads from Kafka, keeps state in local RocksDB stores backed by Kafka changelog topics, and writes back to Kafka. Apache Flink is a separate cluster that runs jobs written in Java, Python or SQL, with its own checkpointed state and connectors to many systems. Both give exactly-once processing for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines; neither makes an external side effect exactly-once for you.

How it works — window types

Window Definition Example Kafka Streams Flink
Tumbling Fixed size, no overlap Orders per minute TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(...) TUMBLE in SQL
Hopping Fixed size, overlapping, advances by a step 5-minute revenue every minute TimeWindows...advanceBy(...) HOP in SQL ("sliding" in the DataStream API)
Sliding (Kafka Streams) Defined by maximum time difference between events Two payment attempts within 30 seconds SlidingWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(...) Interval joins or custom logic
Session Closes after a gap of inactivity A user's browsing session SessionWindows.ofInactivityGapAndGrace(...) Session windows
Cumulative Growing window inside a fixed period Revenue so far today, every minute Not built in CUMULATE in SQL

Note the naming trap: Flink's DataStream "sliding window" is what Kafka Streams calls a hopping window.

How it works — state, checkpoints and exactly-once

Kafka Streams                                   Flink
  state: RocksDB on the instance's disk           state: heap or RocksDB state backend
  durability: every update also written to       durability: periodic checkpoints (barriers flow
    a compacted changelog topic in Kafka            through the job; state snapshot to S3)
  failure: another instance restores the store   failure: job restarts from the last checkpoint
    from the changelog (standby replicas speed      and rewinds Kafka offsets to match
    this up: num.standby.replicas)                 upgrade: take a savepoint, deploy, restore
  exactly-once: processing.guarantee=            exactly-once: checkpoints + transactional
    exactly_once_v2 (Kafka transactions)           Kafka sink (two-phase commit on checkpoint)
  late events: grace period; suppress()          late events: watermark; SQL drops rows behind
    emits only final results per window            the watermark; DataStream API has
                                                   allowedLateness() and sideOutputLateData()

The exactly-once guarantee covers "read from Kafka, update state, write to Kafka" as one atomic step. If the job writes to PostgreSQL, Redis or an HTTP API, that write is at least once, so make it an idempotent upsert keyed by the window.

PostgreSQL example (Flink SQL, with a PostgreSQL sink)

A live revenue-per-minute job in Flink SQL that reads order.paid events from the outbox topic and upserts one row per minute and currency into PostgreSQL:

CREATE TABLE order_paid (
  order_id    STRING,
  seller_id   STRING,
  currency    STRING,
  total_cents BIGINT,
  paid_at     TIMESTAMP(3),
  WATERMARK FOR paid_at AS paid_at - INTERVAL '30' SECOND    -- tolerate 30 s of disorder
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'kafka',
  'topic' = 'orders.events.order-paid',
  'properties.bootstrap.servers' = 'kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092',
  'properties.group.id' = 'live-revenue',
  'scan.startup.mode' = 'group-offsets',
  'properties.auto.offset.reset' = 'earliest',
  'format' = 'json',
  'json.timestamp-format.standard' = 'ISO-8601'
);

CREATE TABLE live_revenue_per_minute (
  window_start  TIMESTAMP(3),
  currency      STRING,
  orders        BIGINT,
  revenue_cents BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (window_start, currency) NOT ENFORCED          -- upsert: replays overwrite, never add
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'jdbc',
  'url' = 'jdbc:postgresql://live-analytics-db:5432/live',
  'table-name' = 'live_revenue_per_minute'
);

INSERT INTO live_revenue_per_minute
SELECT window_start, currency, COUNT(*), SUM(total_cents)
  FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE order_paid, DESCRIPTOR(paid_at), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))
 GROUP BY window_start, window_end, currency;

Set table.exec.source.idle-timeout (for example '30 s') so quiet partitions do not hold back the watermark (the Black Friday story in 38.3.2), and enable checkpointing (execution.checkpointing.interval: 30 s). Each minute's row appears about 30 seconds after the minute ends, once the watermark passes. Events more than 30 seconds late are dropped by this SQL aggregation; the nightly batch mart (38.8) is the reconciled, final number, and the live chart is labelled as provisional.

The same idea in Kafka Streams, as the Java DSL calls (shown as text because application code in this book is TypeScript):

builder.stream("orders.events.order-paid")
  .groupBy((key, evt) -> evt.currency)                    // repartition topic keyed by currency
  .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
  .aggregate(Revenue::zero, (cur, evt, agg) -> agg.add(evt.totalCents), Materialized.as("rev-per-min"))
  .suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(BufferConfig.unbounded()))   // emit once, when final
  .toStream()
  .to("analytics.revenue-per-minute");

Choosing an engine

Option Use when Avoid when
NestJS consumer with PostgreSQL upserts into minute buckets Under a few thousand events per second, simple counts and sums Joins between streams, large state
Kafka Streams JVM team, logic lives with one service, Kafka in and out Non-JVM team; sources other than Kafka
Flink (SQL or DataStream) Many jobs, joins, large state, SQL for analysts, many connectors One simple counter
Micro-batch every 1–5 minutes in the warehouse "Near real time" means 5 minutes Seconds matter (fraud, live ops)

The first row deserves respect. A consumer that does INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (minute, currency) DO UPDATE with a dedupe table (the pattern from 38.6.1) gives you event-time buckets with unlimited lateness for free, because a late event simply updates an older row. Many teams never need more.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Repartition topics. groupBy on a new key writes through an internal topic; it doubles Kafka traffic for that stream and must be sized.
  • Checkpoint timeouts. Large RocksDB state plus slow S3 makes checkpoints exceed their timeout; the job then fails repeatedly. Use incremental checkpoints and monitor checkpoint duration.
  • Changing a job's state schema. Restoring a savepoint into a job whose state layout changed can fail; plan state migrations like database migrations.
  • Co-partitioning for joins. Kafka Streams joins require both topics to have the same partition count and key.
  • Restore time. A Kafka Streams instance with 40 GB of state can take many minutes to restore after a crash; standby replicas avoid that wait.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior asks "how fresh, and how correct?" before choosing an engine. If a five-minute delay is fine, micro-batch wins. If seconds matter and the logic is a counter, a plain consumer with idempotent upserts wins. Flink or Kafka Streams earn their operational cost when there are joins, large state or many jobs. Whatever runs, the live number is labelled provisional, and the reconciled batch number is the one finance uses.

Interview questions

  1. What does exactly-once mean in Kafka Streams or Flink, and where does it stop? Reading, updating state and writing to Kafka commit atomically; writes to external systems are at least once and need idempotency.
  2. How does Flink recover a stateful job after a crash? It restarts from the last completed checkpoint, restoring state and rewinding source offsets to the positions recorded in that checkpoint.
  3. What is suppress(untilWindowCloses) for? To emit one final result per window after the grace period instead of an update for every event, so downstream systems do not see intermediate counts.
